Being an avid fan of Sherlock Holmes games, I have to say this had the most compelling story so far. Although its predecessors were also very intriguing, their plots twists and endings were somewhat obvious, because most gamers were very familiar with stories of Arsene Lupin, Jack the Ripper and Lovecraft. This one kept me interested and guessing throughout the game and I was pleasantly surprised with the ending. Some small details may put you off in the beginning but rest assured that all will be very neatly explained towards the end a la Sherlock Holmes fashion. It is very nicely paced also and character driven instead of the usual murder mystery thriller style, which works very well with the theme and feels fresh.
Apart from the story, the gameplay is easy to get used to but you can still see the console port forced in there when you look at the user interfaces.  A point&click camera angle can be used to bypass this effect but the menus remain the same of course.
Looking at the mechanics involved (besides the puzzles), one thing that really fascinates me is that almost every Sherlock Holmes game tries to invent some new gameplay element. Don't get me wrong I don't mind designers experimenting with the gameplay but I expect the see the good ones becoming permanent mechanics in the series. For example, the Ripper murder scene investigation method is gone now, which is a pity. There seems to be a dialogue wheel present in the game which serves no purpose whatsoever. Deduction board is still fun and there is a very good puzzle element involved with it. But sadly the game does not use it very often, for reasons unknown to this reviewer. Inventory puzzles are not annoying contrary to the rest of the genre. But pixel hunting nightmares strike once or twice during the game (I encourage gamers to consult a walkthough at these points because they're not worth wasting time over, you should just get on with the story instead). The game would have been a better one without them sure but none of these gets in our way of enjoying the story and marveling at Sherlock’s wit and prowess.
Putting aside all these bumps, the game plays well and is long enough to satisfy the average user (15 hours).  Board puzzles are nicely done and interact with the world in a sensible way (as far as these sort of games go).  Watson and Sherlock’s dialogues are smart and funny as always and the delivery is very good, though the pace is a bit off; you get too long pauses between some lines that were obviously meant to be interrupting each other. You are still being provided with lots of documents and papers throughout the game (which is nice), some of which you need to read and understand in order to solve puzzles. Locations look very nice but they aren’t many but the Baker St. flat is there as always. Familiar faces pop up once in a while if you know who’s who. The murders are very gruesome and creative. The game is not very difficult also so in a way it feels like a smooth ride if you can overlook stuff mentioned above.
So all in all, Testament of S. Holmes is good follow up to his predecessors and if you’re a fan of the previous games, you should definitely get it. If you like point&click adventures, the story is enough reason to pick this one up. But if you’re new to the genre, don’t start here.
Pros: very good story, well designed puzzles, true to its source material, familiar voice acting, long gameplay,
Cons: UI looks very old, locations are sparse, some near misses with gameplay mechanics
Verdict: 4/5

A good game that is part of an absolutely excellent series.
The action of the game is very well paced and easy to enjoy. If you play on easy or medium you'll be able to play a cool and fun game. The hard game mode is for minimaxers and requires you to avoid wasting resources and carefully choose your plasmids and tonics.
The story is adequate. The story pushes the action into two sharply divided sections which is somewhat dissonate from an immersion standpoint. There are also several plotholes and oddities about the motivation in the plot that became irritatingly apparent to me on my second playthrough. All that said, if you're not terribly worried about the artistic quality of the plot, it isn't so bad that it will distract from the other elements of the game.
The environment is the true high point of the game. Each part of Rapture is fascinating to explore. The world feels like a real world that people inhabited. If you're into lore and immersion, the recordings you can find reveal side plots and background information that is not available through the main plot. The main characters (Fontaine, Andrew Ryan, Atlas, and Tenn♥♥♥♥♥) are nicely fleshed out in recordings.
All of my time on steam was spent on a single playthrough on the hardest difficulty combing through every room for loot and recordings. The difficulty scales reasonably well but if you have the right tonics and plasmids then the final level is unfortunately easy.
For those interested in the series, Bioshock 2 is a fitting sequel that expands on the story and lore of this game; in my opinion, it is a better game. Bioshock Infinite does not tie directly to 1 and 2 (excluding the rapture-related DLC) but is a similar game in both how the action plays out and how detailed the lore is.
I usually wait for sales but I'd say this game is good enough to get at full price.

Words really can't describe how I feel about this game. It came out some time when I was in 7th grade and (thankfully) it wasn't as popular as it should've been where I lived. Its been 7 years since this game came out. I finished high school, got a job, and was finally able to afford a laptop and play this game. I've heard stories of how this game redefined visuals, and honestly, you can tell. The graphics and animation of this game are up to snuff with some of the best indie games available on Steam. From a 7 year old game, thats saying things. But what really drew me in and made me not wanna stop playing was the story. SEVEN YEARS OF MY LIFE spent dodging any kind of spoilers about bioshock. I never read or watched a single review about the first or even its predecessors, 2 and infinite, in hopes of savoring the storyline all that much more when I actually played it. And ♥♥♥♥ was I not dissapointed. Dark, abbysmal atmosphere coupled with some real spooks, and the ever inspiring respect demanded by each and every big daddy. That intense buildup leading to the massive reveal was some of the best story direction I've ever experienced. From this ♥♥♥♥ing seven year old game. If you haven't experienced bioshock, the oldest of the series, buy it. Play it. I don't care if you're all about next gen graphics and streamlined gameplay, Bioshock told one of the best stories in this decade of gaming, and its absolutely paramount that you experience it for yourself.

The different endings for the game (i.e. how you eventually die) are varied, some are brilliant. All of them feel like they fit the narrative, I don't think I've ever felt cheaped out by one.
My one... I suppose it's not really a complaint; It's as big a part of the game as anything else: It is really, REALLY hard to see a well-explored, master of the Unterzee go, and start a new game. I'll probably play it again, eventually, but I feel the need to grieve for my last captain (if he's even really dead).
Heartily recommended, over and over again. The content is all absolutely brilliant.

This game is the Oregon Trail of first person shooters.
There's really no other way of describing it.  Though it's not really about getting from one specific place to another, it's about exploring and surviving when the odds are entirely against you.  Hours in you realize so many small choices are life and death: using that cloth to repair your clothing, keeping you warm, or tearing them up for bandages, in case you are attacked.
Or staying where you are, which is safe, but your food sources are running out, or hiking through the blizzard down an unknown path hoping to find game, something to eat, or an abandoned house to raid.
Even the miniscule amounts of ammunition you can scavenge adds to this:  do you use your last three bullets hoping to take down the wolf at a distance? Or do you get closer, improving your chance to hit, but giving it a chance to charge you?
It ook a few hours to fully get the experience, but once I got it, I was hooked.

It wouldn't be right to give this game a rating out of ten, it's not that kind of product, it's too much of a personal endeavour on the developer's part. Like 'The Stanley Parable' this is quite conceptual - it's a game about making games, and about the creative process in general. However, strictly speaking, it's more of a journey than an out-and-out 'game' in the strictest sense of the word. It's a journey through someone's mind, a view behind the curtain, a glimpse at the cogs and gears working their way through different avenues and different possibilities. Ultimately though, this game is - for me- about the idea of meaning: what we mean to others(and vice versa), why we seek to apply a meaning to things, and how much that meaning matters to us. This game probably won't be for everyone (what game is?), but if you play it and come with an open mind, you won't be disappointed.

The Long Dark is quite simply, the best survival game I have experienced so far, throughout all of early access I enjoyed myself immensely while playing, and Hinterland's continued dedication to the game has only brought in more good things since release. Unlike many other games, The Long Dark doesn't stop being challenging after you get the best gear, or best clothes, in fact the devs are working hard to ensure that the game remains challenging all the way through (the game is constantly being balanced in various ways to help acheive this). Hinterland updates fairly frequently, each update bringing decent, new content. The devs have good communication with their playerbase, and can often be seen replying in the forums, you can tell they really care about the game and their players, the roadmap they released shows they're thinking about working on the game for a looooooong time, and all the updates presenting new challenges and aspects of the game to keep you from getting bored.
As for the game itself, it's brutal and harsh, and is an incredible blend of realism and game logic, realistic enough to provide a challenge that will make you think and consider every action, while bending the rules just enough to provide a fun and engaging experience. The graphics of the game are stylized, but this doesn't take away from the harshness of trying to scrape out an existence, and provides brilliant scenery and views. Many a player has died from trying to take a screencapture. The sound design is extremely well done, the mixing of envionmental ambience, audio cues and brief snippets of music really make the whole experience spectacular. There are several different maps, all unique and presenting their own benefits and difficulties, four different game modes for difficulty (one being almost impossible to survive long term) and the devs are rolling out challenge modes for some added play prospects. I will also add that while in many other games you choose one map to play on and thats it, in TLD you can travel between the maps regardless of what you picked.
Full release also brought with it the long-awaited story mode, Wintermute, to TLD. Despite a few glitches early on the dev team VERY quickly released many, many fixes to solve,although I personally prefer Survival Mode (I just tend to prefer that in my survival games than story) I love both Survival Mode and the first two episodes of Wintermute that have been released. The story is intruiging and introduces some minor differences in gameplay, some different maps, and is a different experience without losing the traditional Long Dark feeling we know and love.
This game will make you cherish warmth and good food, highly reccomend unless you're allergic to wolves. Absolutely incredible.

I bought this game during the 2017 Summer Sale for $3, but in retrospect it would have easily been worth the fair market value of $15.  This sums up my first hour of gameplay:
While circling the island in a stolen speedboat with the intent of identifying as many points of interest as possible, I noticed what appeared to be a major airport on my map.  But when I scanned the area with my Mark-I eyeballs all I could see was green forest and mountains.  So I ran my speedboat aground to investigate.  Referencing the map again while standing on the beach, the airport was dead ahead but all I could see was some trees at the base of a cliff.  So I used the grappling hook to climb the cliff face and...TA-DA, imagine my surprise to be standing at the the end of a runway on a military airport.  I didn't know it was military at first, until a shadow went over me and I looked up just in time to see a C-17 military transport complete final and touch down maybe 100 feet in front of me.  Good pilot.  And then I heard a few bullets hiss and snap past my head.  No clue where they came from since enemies don't show up on the map, but my back was to the ocean and planes were landing directly in front of me, so it had to be coming from my right.  I sprinted in that general direction and headed for the nearest building to take cover.  When I got there I decided to keep sprinting since the shots sounded like they came from pretty far off, so imagine my surprise when I came around the corner of the building and saw about 5 commando-looking guys running right at me; great minds think alike.  So I stop, take real good aim at the first guy's head, and hold down the trigger to headshot him and spray everybody near him.  And instead of bullets coming out, my f*****g grappling hook comes out- I forgot to switch back to a weapon after climbing that cliff, I was so dumbfounded by being on an active military runway and then taking fire.  It hooks this "bad guy" and he comes flinging at me, all the while I"m furiously spinning my mouse wheel to change weps.  So while the guy is in mid-air my grappling hook disconnects, I switch to weapons, and I'm shooting this guy in mid-air as he's flying towards me.  His body goes spinning off to the side as the bullets slam into him.  Wasn't expecting that.  So I switch to the hook again while the other 4 guys are still trying to figure out what to do.  I mash the button to snag this other guy, but in all the excitement I don't let go (guess I thought I still had a full auto gun out).  The hook snags onto him, but it's still connected to my arm and not pulling him.  What gives???  Well the last enemy I panicked, changed guns, and started shooting.  So I let go of the trigger to switch guns, and the guy comes flying at me.  Ahhh.... so if I click and hold, it won't retract!  Got it.  So then I snag a 3rd guy, but while experimenting I take fire and try to look around to see where it's coming from.  As I scanned for the shooter I accidentally let go of the trigger, and the grappling hook shot out of my arm again.  What the f**k???  The other end of the grappling hook shot out and attached to what appeared to be an O2 tank, or a tank of some sort of pressurized gas.  Just to make sure I'm actually seeing this I look at the bad guy again, I see the grappling hook attached to him and he's as stunned as I am, so I backpedal as fast an possible and decide to shoot at the tank of pressurized gas.  I figure it'll explode.  It doesn't.  It squeels for a second, I see vapor shooting out of it, and this tank shoots off the rack it was on and drags the bad guy along with it.  So as I'm watching this 02 tank corckscrewing through the air while dragging a screaming guy behind it, I couldn't help but giggle.  And then it exploded.
That's when I knew that this was money well spent.
If you ever have had a bad day and think to yourself "Well, might as well ruin my evening, too" play this game. This would give Tracer from Overwatch depression.

This is probably the most challenging game I've ever played. I managed to defeat the likes of You Have to Win the Game, but this is a whole different arena of hard. By no means is this a negative aspect for me - as an avid achievement hunter, I live for the challenge - but it may scare away many less dedicated players.
Jigoku Kisetsukan: Sense of the Seasons is an anime-style F2P bullet hell that will put your wits, reactions, and timing to the ultimate test. The game has multiple unlockable characters, each with their own footnote of back story and unique traits.  The plot takes an obvious back seat here, but there are dialogue points before and after bosses to give you a justifiable reason for fighting / defeating them.
The game has a Galaga-inspired formula in terms of movement and attacks. Fighting waves of enemies is technically optional, albeit painfully difficult - dodging / evading is just as effective. I found this mechanic to be outstanding and a breath of fresh air from other games in the bullet hell genre. Score bonuses will also be awarded based on your speed of depleting each tier of HP from noteworthy enemies and bosses, adding a unique sense of urgency to every battle.
The game offers a catchy soundtrack of chiptunes that will be stuck in your head for ages. Even after countless deaths and retries, every track seems welcoming and fun to listen to. The musical atmosphere during boss sequences is quite exceptional.
If you're looking for the ultimate challenge from a game with no price tag, then let it be this one. On a gaming platform over-saturated with trivial games, let Jigoku Kisetsukan: Sense of the Seasons rekindle your burning passion to beat something actually difficult.

All QTE. 98% of the title is QTE. That does not make it a bad game but as a mechanic it is used so much it should be noted. Though if you like Telltale games, that comes as no surprise and certainly no disappointment. I enjoyed the way the story weaved multiple villains together into a quasi-hierarchy, forcing you to consider villains as multi-layered. The way this story was woven should be mirrored in all games.
A single villain wasn't the threat, but villainy itself.
I found myself wishing the game were more open world so I could explore the story in a larger environment with less linear progression but I understand that would sacrifice the integrity of the story by diluting it with superfluous content.
I found some of the scenes choppy and there were some bugs with playback showing scenes that I hadn't actually chosen, such as Lucius showing up at the Bat computer in one scene he wasn't even in during the choice phase.
With this game, if you can lock down the full series for under $20 is a good deal.
I'm not a fan of Telltale generally due to the QTE element of their games, but I love batman so when this title came on sale -  It was a no-brainer.
Pro: Story development is engaging, graphics are solid, batman, integrity of story overall
Con: Some minor glitches with loading choppy periodically, story recaps inconsistent with choices made, some scenes where your combat prowess (QTE execution) is throttled forcibly by the story even if your QTE execution is perfect.

Have you ever played monster hunter series with friends? Have you played Left for Dead with friends? I have to say that Evolve is like a mixture of those games.
It has a unique concept of 4v1 pvp.
4 Hunters VS 1 Badass Monster.
4 First Person View VS  1 Third Person View
THE HUNTERS
As the hunter, well obviously you hunt! You hunt down this 1 specific brain powered clever monster.
Each hunter has a specific role that is vital in order to take down this one beast. Medic, support, assault and trapper.
Track the monster down as fast as you can, and never ever give him a chance to get fat (and by fat i mean evolve to stage 3), cause he'll bring hell down on you.
THE MONSTER
There are two ways to win as the monster. Kill all the hunter using your monstrosity, or destroy the generator that the hunters protecting with your monstrosity as well.
Early in the game you must get as far away from the hunter and devour the many wildlife that you can get your hands on in order to evolve and get strong enough so you can face your opponent and take down that generator.
*It has a quite nice graphics. (it might still be tough for a wooden pc)
*Decent map size: Not to big not to small, evens the odds. It gives chance for the hunter to catch up with the monster and for the monster to run around. To scale lets just say it's like playing chase in the school.
*Hostile Environment: Man eating plant, giant crocodile creature in a puddle of mud, scared birds, scavengers. This things actually provides variation of situation depending on how the match is played.
*Balance & Competitive: The game is well balanced, The monster is defeatable even at their final stage, just need a good coordinated teamwork. A clever monster vs a well coordinated team is the key to a fierce yet awesome match.
*You obtain upgrades/improvement (such as more damage, more jetpack fuel, etc.) after each match. Personally i think this could ruin the balance in the future. bigger lvl player will surely dominate. But on the other hand, without this the game might just be too dull and repetitive, this gives a meaning to level up. well people have their preferences
*Price? Personally i think its too costly. But is it worth it? Keep in mind that this is a multiplayer based game, you need other player to play as well. usually less people are willing to pay for an expensive game, but looking at how the game is developed so far, i will have to recommend you to try it..

Started playing on Monday night and I've just finished it. I'm a very slow player and I needed a lot of time to solve a few of the puzzles: that being said, all in all, I've needed about six hours to complete the game.
They were six truly fabulous hours.
First of all, I think I've been a bit misleaded by the tagline and by a few of my friends' suggestions: I don't know why, I was expecting sort of a soft game? With a bit of retro atmosphere, black-and-white pleasant backgrounds and, I don't know, a playful kid lovingly prancing around in a fond search for his sister?
Yeah, well, no. Limbo is macabre, is dark, is scary and truly isn't the right game for someone as jumpy and nervy as me. I had to stop a few times to calm down and I closed my eyes during at least half of the deaths. Of COURSE it's black and white, you really don't want to see SO MUCH RED on your screen.
You won't be able to play this game if you're arachnophobic; you won't be able to play this game if you're scared by deep waters and, likely, if you often suffer from vertigo. I think you'll better be careful if you're against gore and if seeing a child - yeah, I know it's a smallish cartoonish cutout, still a child - being hurt is going to unsettle you. By the way, the last warning goes for me, too.
Even so, this game is one of the things nearest to perfection I've ever played with. The graphic! Graphics are wonderful, from the wonderful font choosen for the title, from the menu and the first background up to each one of those black silhouettes of monsters and enemies and traps, each one perfectly in tone and easy recognizable despite the surrounding misty darkness. The soundtrack, soft and barely there, carrying you on through the scariest moments and keeping you on your toes! Each one of those marvellous, problematic, complex, truly original puzzles: you won't be able to get bored, there're no dead times, there's no pause, no slowing down up to the very end.
I've a lot of PROs and just a few CONs, so, let's go on.
PROs:
- Detailed, interesting, original graphics. Wonderful. No colours at all to distract you from beautiful lines and marvellously designed backgrounds.
- Themed atmosphere. All the atmosphere you'll ever want in a game and more. You really need to play Limbo in a dark room, I've jumped so many times I think I've drilled an hole in the chair.
- Useful and pleasant sounds/soundtrack. There isn't a clear music going on, more a kind of soft, vibrating sound sometimes taking consistency and sometimes leaving everything in the deepest silence. Sounds are a completing and essential part of the whole experience and you'll need them to solve more easily a few puzzles.
- Complex obstacles. Like I said, each one of them is original and interesting; they're disposed by growing difficulty and  different sceneries will have different themes going on. Loved it.
- Well-built animations. They're sometimes lovely and more often unsettling and always wonderfully rendered. You can interact with lots of things in your playground and your character will react to each one of them in a different way. Truly not a sloppy work. Really, it's the care poured in each detail which made me fall in love.
CONs:
- Total lack of explanations. Like, I've got it, really, you want me to explore and discover, but I'm not asking for much - thirty seconds of an introductive sequence to try and get me understanding your choice of controls? I come from a time when double clicking the Up Arrow got you jumping higher and clicking it for a longer time got you... nothing. If it's a deliberate way to skim out less expert and/or older players, I can understand it, but low blow, guys, low blow.
- No warnings. Like, at all. And I think that's a game which would need them deeply. I usually buy new games without reading any review, to preserve the full surprise effect, and this time the tagline was a bit misleading. Please, warn me about the HUGE SPIDERS - I like spiders, but I don't like them when they're trying to skewering me - and the fact that I'll be DISEMBOWELED at least a few times during the game, and all of this while I'm a child.
- No introduction. You know that you're searching for your sister because you've read the tagline. And what if you got this game as a gift? Or if you're playing it at a friends' place? I think a game has to start with the first scene and end with the last one; here, if you haven't read the tagline, you won't be able to truly understand the last scene.
Which is, by the way, ambiguous and wonderful.
This is the kind of game you play and play and play again trying to beat your own best time - and your own death count. I'm surely restarting it right now.
9/10.

I love this game because it helps me relax after work.
It's pretty casual compared to some builders. The graphics are so-so, but they work well for the scope of the game. If you're just looking to sit back and watch your town run while making little tweaks here and there (with the occasional crisis popping up), this would be a good choice for you.
I think the most satisfying thing is building a huge town out of nothing and admiring it. Even with the graphics being what they are, it's fulfilling to zoom out and take a look at how much you've grown. I don't know, maybe its a zen thing. The soundtrack is pretty decent as well.
The only downside is that once you've built a huge town, there's not much else to do other than expand it. There aren't any high tier buildings to unlock. I would appreciate more of an end game, but for the price, it's definitely worth it.
If you're only into city-building when defending and conquering are part of the mix, you probably wouldn't enjoy this game. There are no bandits, warbands, or enemy settlements: no militaries of any kind.

This is a game I have been very excited for and it didn't dissapoint. Every boss was unique and memorable, having various attacks, patterns and transformattions that they utilize. Not only that, but there were no clones of previous boss fights in this game, in addition to this I was genuniely suprised and delighted on many occasions by the absurd and over the top nature of how many of the fights played out. And the icing on the cake is that overall this game is very fair. It was a rare occurence that I actually thougt something was kind of cheap (this was usually because there are a couple of bosses where the foreground would occasionally obstruct my view to a small degree, but it was nothing game breaking, more just somewhat annoying). Combine this with smooth controls and (if you couldn't already tell) some of the best visuals I have ever seen in a game and "Cuphead" stands out as one the best games I have played this year.
My only major complaint is that the "Run and Gun" stages felt lack luster compared to the incredible bosses. While many of them would have at least one section of interesting platforming a lot of them felt like basic jumps with a bunch of enemies spawning on screen, which wasn't really all that fun or interesting. These stages weren't necessarily bad, just kind of bland. Thankfully these make up a very small portion of the game.
I give a strong recommendation to anyone who has the stomach for a difficult game.

Limbo, the game, is special in that while it does not wholly depict that mysterious dimension as my mind did, it captures its essence. You are a boy who wakes up in a lonely world made up only of black, white, and shades of gray. Video game logic demands you walk from left to right, jumping over obstacles as they appear, a simple task that needs little attention in the initial moments. This is your chance to absorb your surroundings. The background provides an illusion of depth, but its branches and bridges are out of focus, as if you are dreaming them into existence. The pint-sized hero, his bright blinking eyes shining from his blackened silhouette, trots ahead with the charming gangliness of a six-year-old.
You can check out any time you like, but you can never leave.
Then comes death. Limbo is a hostile place, home to giant spiders that would feast upon you, and traps apparently scattered by the world's other denizens. You step onto a claw trap, and it closes on your neck. Your head falls to the ground and wobbles just for a moment before lying still. No tears are shed, no music plays--the game provides no grand gesture to honor your demise. It simply happens, and you revive at the most recent checkpoint to try the puzzle again. Some of these deaths aren't outright fair; stepping on a pressure plate could mean certain death, but so could jumping over it. Such inconsistencies aren't common, but your first time in Limbo requires some trial-and-error experimentation. Loading times are short, and checkpoints are frequent, however, so death is rarely a frustration, though often a horror.
What does it all mean? People pondered that question when Limbo was first released on the Xbox 360 in 2010, and the PC version adds nothing new that would illuminate the mystery of this world, so there's little reason to splurge on another version if you've already played. Nevertheless, the ending offers important clues to the greater plot, if not to the details of the game's events and objects--the imposing neon hotel sign that you must cross, for instance, or the murderous children, seemingly escaped from Lord of the Flies, that aim their blowguns at you. Limbo means for its atmosphere to consume you in the moment, and in that sense, it succeeds. You drag a dead child's corpse to solve a puzzle, and perhaps wonder if anyone grieves this lost soul given the apathy of the realm. You glimpse a figure and regard her with tenderness, but the brief glimmer of hope is snuffed out in an instant.
After life, before death.
It isn't until the final third of its two- to three-hour runtime that Limbo's puzzles become challenging. The first half of the game is more concerned with building dread and ambiguity. Even after being vanquished, a colossal spider's remaining leg thrusts at you from its thorax, one final act of defiance that could leave two corpses for the crows to pick. When you pull the leg from the spider, the audible cracks and visible white splatters emphasize just how recently its life force was crushed. Elsewhere, you push boxes and pull levers, rushing to finish the puzzle before the rising water fills the room. Failure means watching the dear boy go as limp as a ragdoll as liquid fills his lungs.
The second half leaves behind the horrors in favor of puzzles involving gravity and complex machinery. As memorable as it is to navigate tilting rooms with only a few hanging lamps to light the way, it is that spider that most embodies Limbo's somber spirit. The later puzzles are complex and clever, but they don't haunt the heart. The finale feels abrupt because it returns to the first hour's imagery, having abandoned it for long enough to have altered your personal connection with the game from an emotional one to an intellectual one. And yet the end offers insight into a backstory left otherwise untouched--enough of it to inspire another playthrough, this time ever so much wiser than you were before.
THE GOOD
Striking atmosphere that chills the heart
Excellent, poignant moments that stay with you
Cold, gruesome deaths are presented with memorable and horrific apathy
Introduces more involved puzzles at a satisfying pace
THE BAD
The most haunting imagery is limited to the first half
Ending doesn't emerge organically from the hour leading to it
8/10

Five Nights at Freddy's is an indie horror game made by Scott Cawthon. You have to survive 5 nights at a Chuck E. Cheese-esque place called 'Freddy Fazbear's Pizza'. What do you have to survive? Animatronics, yes, animatronics. The four main animatronics are Freddy, Bonnie, Chica and Foxy who all have different attack patterns; different ways to get to YOU. Here are some things that Five Nights at Freddy's does well: Making the player feel challenged: Five Nights at Freddy's starts out very easy but then ramps up the difficulty, especially in the later nights. Making the player feel helpless: Now, it goes without saying that if you were stuck in a place with 4 killer robot furries, you'd feel pretty helpless. And sense you're in a tiny office just waiting for you to get stuffed into a suit, it amplifies it. Fear: Five Nights at Freddy's will obviously be scary, right? Yes, it is scary. If you fail to stay alive through a night, you will be killed by one of the robots in a... jumpscare... "A cheap jumpscare? Really?" you might ask. Yeah, the deaths are jumpscares, but it isn't the jumpscare that scares you, it's not knowing when it will happen. If the death is predictable, then it isn't as scary.
As a final review for Five Nights at Freddy's, I give it a 9.9/10.

Sunless Sea is a complicated mix of genres, and while I had some good times with the game, there were a lot of frustrations and flat out boredom in my 70 hours of playtime. Make sure you fully understand the kind of game Sunless Sea is before you decide it's right for you.
The game has sailing, combat, and resource management, but mostly, Sunless Sea is Interactive Fiction. You travel from island to island on your ship, perhaps running into monsters along the way. Once you reach land, your exploration takes place by reading fairly large blocks of text. The story has a lot to recommend it. You can also play the developer's other game, Fallen London for free if you want a taste of the world of the Unterzee. But be prepared to have most of your rewards come in the form of the story. Sometimes unraveling a mystery that has perplexed the residents of an island for centuries will disgorge the exact same loot as fighting a monster in the overworld. A lot of the game plays more like a Choose Your Own Adventure than a CRPG.
The game has a few other design quirks. It has a few roguelike and survival elements. If you lose (and there are some colorful ways to die or go mad) and restart, certain islands move around a bit, and you can carry over certain bonuses from your previous playthroughs. The game also defaults to a single save file, like most roguelites. This is easily changed in the menu, and I strongly suggest you do it. The game doesn't actually benefit from such trappings. Unlike something like FTL, where you might have a completely different playthrough each time, if you die and restart in SS, your first couple hours on the new run are going to be EXACTLY the same as you grind the first few profitable trade routes. And each island's story, which is where the heart of this game is, unfolds the same way each time. Once you have figured out the mystery of Visage once, all you can do on the next playthrough is do it the exact same way for the exact same material rewards. And some fairly big events come down to simple chance. You can spend a couple hours to do the quest for one of your crew members to fulfill his destiny, and also net you the best engine in the game, then at the end of the quest the game flips a coin to determine if you get the engine or not. Chance like that in a game that can be beat in a couple hours is one thing. But half my runtime on Sunless Sea is a single plythrough. In a game that long, I want my successes and filures to be based on my own choices and skills. There's even an interview floating out there where the lead developer said the roguelike elements were a mistake.
Sunless Sea isn't a roguelite. It's not a CRPG. It's interactive fiction with some RPG elements. There's still a lot to recommend, but if you do buy the game,
1) be prepared to do a lot of reading,
2) make some save backups to cut down on the grinding,
3) maybe install the "easy mod" to make the sailing faster, and
4) don't be afraid to use a guide to figure certain things out.

For a big fan of Sherlock Holmes, especially if you read the books or watched the TV show with Jeremy Brett as Sherlock Holmes, this game can be really good. But take note: this is not a big production so don't expect the game to be perfect or to blow your mind. Just have fun solving the puzzles and enjoy the story :)
Story: In The Testament of Sherlock Holmes you see the crazily good detective investigating the dead of a prominent figure of 1898 London. And that has a lot more to it that first meets the eye. After a mini-case, that serves as a tuturial, which is about a necklace that disappeared from a closed room, the rest of the story revolves about the same case, even if more people die and more strange things happen for you to investigate. Overall I liked the story. The beginning and also the very end can be a bit sketchy but the rest is a solid good with a lot of references that the fans will catch with a smile on theirs faces.
Gameplay: It is diverse, sometimes difficult, others rather simple, and when you finally figure it out it's just as Sherlock Holmes says: "It is simplicity itself". I got stuck two or three times without knowing what I should do next and I found that two puzzles were very difficult, but nothing that will spoil the game for you. You can control Dr. John Watson and Sherlock Holmes, and some areas are solved with both characters doing different actions. Most of the game consists in looking for clues in the environment and solving puzzles, which can be simply to connect the clues you found or to open something (some box, door, secret compartment, etc). There is not much action, so don't go for this with the latest Sherlock film in mind.
Technical aspects: The graphics are good, the voicing is good for the main characters but could be a lot better for others, the animations could be a lot better also, and the soundtrack it's not bad but goes unnoticed most of time.

I'll preface this by saying that
with currently only 4 hours of sandbox gametime under my belt. I am a fan of the survival genre, and have really enjoyed games like 7DTD, but my exposure to survival games has been very limited to the ones featuring zombies as a central game aspect.
The Long Dark is much different, and it's the sort of different that I find refreshing. I like the fact that it's just you, all alone in the frozen wilderness with the beautiful (deadly) nature. It's very realistic: you start with a few basic items and from there have to scavenge, hunt, forage, and craft your way to survival. If you're too hasty or careless, you can easily get sick or injured (or die), and you'll have to recover from the consequences.
In spite of the complete lack of zombies or even other humans (note: talking about sandbox mode), there are still
ways to die. I'll summarize a few of the main ones briefly.
I have found this game to be a fun, realistic challenge. I am slowly learning things that work and things that don't, and I'm dying a lot, but that's part of the experience. I look forward to getting better at this game and developing strategies in it. I highly recommend to anyone who is a survivalist or appreciates the survival genre.

I don't know what gripped me to get this game early access, maybe because I'm a fan of survival games in general and had heard good things, but I am glad I didn't follow my "No early access" policy when this game came around on sale.
The Long Dark as of now has only the sandbox mode but, to be honest, that mode alone carries the survival gameplay incredibly well.  The sheer isolation of never seeing another living soul while you simply try to survive in a harsh, unforgiving and breathtakingly beautiful landscape adds an eeriness to the gameplay that adds to the survival gameplay instead of leaving it feeling empty.
I'm happy to say I've never had a bug occur to me in this game, one of my early access fears.  The sandbox state is very stable.
Furthermore, the game developers have been adding things into the game on the sly, and while they are clear about some updates, they make others and let the community discover them on their own.  This leaves your playthrough to remain a mystery and even with the best maps you'll find in the community, they won't all be 100% right, which really adds a sense of discovery and wonder to your survival experience.  It's an interesting feeling when you play through it.
Make no mistake though.  This game is all about survival at this point and nothing more.  You aren't going to have any "missions" or goals aside from the ones you set for yourself, and most of the time that is going to be "Organize my pack to make the journey to the place I haven't visited yet for supplies" or "Successfully hunt an elk without getting mauled to death by wolves or lost in the process."
This game doesn't forgive mistakes, but it can't if it is going to be a good survival game.  Along with permadeath, you'll really feel the pain when you shoot one of your four bullets and miss, or, god forbid, lose an arrow.  Heck you'll be swearing more that the wolf that mauled you ripped up your deerskin pants than you would if it gave you an infection.
I love every minute of surviving in this game.  I most likely will still stick to my "no early access" rule, but I'm entirely happy that The Long Dark is my one exception.

Really funny city simulator.
The campaign is solid and its objectives are really nice.
There are several different (and all valid) options to get fast cash, from farms to factories, from tourism to offices.
In this game you are the people manager, for real - not only the buildings positioner -, you need to understand how many educated citizen you have (high school and university), how many not educated, and how your economic development choices will impact on the high school / not educated ratio - for example a farm based economy just needs not educated ppl / a offices based economy needs all ppl from university.
Besides the education the population is sorted by age, wealth and preferences, since the population is divided in factions, often asking the opposites, like nationalists vs globalists.
During my almost 40 hours play-through I experimented several different economies and I had fun with them all, which is the most important thing to me.
To succeed you have to find the right balances between multiple contemporary conditions, all spiced up by random disasters and the various rebellions / invasions.
Suggesting the game, my personal score is 8/10

I don't often review games. I play a lot, and I have a lot, but not many of them feel special enough to warrant me saying something, nor bad enough that I feel I should warn anyone.
This is not really a game. It's more of a journey for the narrator through his friend's old games he made.  His friend stopped, and the narrator wants to understand why and talks through what he thinks his friend was thinking at each point in his life when he made games.
This is short. I got it on sale. But it leaves an impact. I feel sorrow, maybe some guilt for playing it, but I also feel hope for the Narrator and his friend to both find what they need in life. There are no answers to find by playing this. No real answers anyway. It kind of leaves a lot up to your own interpretation.
Buy this game if: You value people and are fascinated by psychology, sociology, and possibly game development.  Consider the experience like a book that leaves you wondering at the end. You may not be satisfied with the ending, I wasn't, but I do not regret the experience or the purchase.
Don't buy this game if: You need interaction or feedback from a game. This will not give you any satisfaction, but it may make you think about your life a bit. The Beginner's Guide poses a question to the player and never answers it, and you may never be able to answer it. You are only learning about the Narrator and his friend, who designed the games.

I was expecting a light-hearted city-building sim, and I got that for the most part.  But the game isn't at all pleasing to play in the long term due to issues with the UI and hidden mechanics which aren't easily understood except by lengthy trial and error.
[PRO] * Light-hearted military dictatorship game, with really cheesy and surprisingly dated humor.  (How long was this game in development?  Simpsons quotes from twenty years ago!)
[PRO] * Fairly simple building UI.  Drawing roads is annoyingly finicky, though.
[PRO] * Initially looks like it is really simple game but does have some depth when you scratch the surface.
[PRO] * Production values are quite good for this style of game.  Graphics are fine, voice-overs are fine, sound and effects are fine.  It's no Sim City 5 but I would say it's on par with an older Maxis game, like SC4.
----
[CON] * HEY.  HEY.  HEY, LISTEN.  Your advisors will be popping up constantly, interrupting you.  New build requests, new edict requests, new declarations, etc.  I can't count the number of times I was about to change some micro-managed setting only to have everything backed out when the dialog opens.
[CON] * Combat is lame and poorly executed.  You either typically pwn the enemy or get rolled over, and it's never entirely clear why.  I've also seen a tank squad try to drive to the other side of the map by its lonesome self, because an intended target was some far-off mine, but the enemy was halted by guard towers along the way.  (Meanwhile, said tower gets destroyed because my tanks are out sight-seeing.)
[CON] * Poorly thought out era system.  Some buildings are era specific, in particular military buildings.  There's no way to upgrade or change them so they are useful for newer eras.  Eras also feel like artifical limitations on what the player can build or do, in order to lengthen the game.  (It's frustating to have severe crime problems in colonial era that you can't do anything about until the World Wars, when you are allowed to build a police station.)
[CON] * A lot of the game mechanics are hidden from you and not exposed in the UI.  There are stats that I wish I could see in the Almanac or graph that are not visible -- Which is frustrating when you see the data (and graphs) exposed for other things.  The devs already had code for making pretty drill-down nested lists and graphs, why couldn't they use it everywhere?  Another example:  Buildings give certain bonuses and modify other sim values (such as a water treatment plant reducing pollution), but the game doesn't give you visual feedback for how far these bonuses/modifications reach, leading to expensive trial and error city layouts.
[CON] * Obtuse gameplay elements.  For example: Factions become very important in later eras, but it requires that you click an unmarked, hidden label on your Politics screen of the almanac to get information about factions.  Even so, the information is obtuse.  You know a faction hates you but the game does not make it clear how to please said faction.  Generally you can use common sense (ie: communists want more free social services, militarists want more guns to play with, etc) but when it comes to constitutions and edicts, this isn't always clear.  Lots of trial and error are required, and the game doesn't let you experiment easily.  For example, you can only change your constitution infrequently, so you are stuck with a bad decision for several in-game years.
[CON] * Disasters are random.  I wouldn't mind a tornado or volanco eruption to spice up the game where there has been a lengthy period of inactivity, but when I am under attack from a foreign power, my treasury is bankrupt and civil rest is high -- And then the game tosses in a natura disaster?  At the same time?  I just feel like I am being kicked in the teeth by a random number generator.
[CON] * Dynasty system is initially neat, but then you realize you utilize your family members for simple building managers (or, later, building new empires).  I find myself just skipping past all the customization stuff since I'll never see these people outside of a random event face icon or a generic indicator in a building info panel.
[CON] * Single player campaign is a mess.  What the game does not explain early on is that you have two islands, and the campaign missions take place over either of the two islands.  (Sometimes you can choose what island, otherwise the island choice is fixed.)  You retain your buildings and your empire setup between missions.  It is INCREDIBLY easy to screw yourself over in later campaign missions by having a "thrown together" or imbalanced empire.  ie: You build just what you need to complete a mission scenerio.  On the next mission, your prior choices might be detrimental and you might find yourself in sudden and unexpected debt, as task bonuses (which were given in prior missions) are removed.  Playing the campaign requires foresight and understanding of late-game mechanics, which is a bit too much to ask of new players.
In conclusion:  I would pass.  I hear Tropico 4 is a better game, but I suppose that will have to wait for my Tropico 4 review...

Evolve, the waiting game.
And by waiting game, I don't mean laying a trap for a monster and ambushing it as it searches for food.
No, I'm talking about the matchmaking system for this game. The fun multiplayer game that is played the best with friends, actually requires you to play with 4/5 friends at maximum. You are unable to invite a monster to your party. Why? Nobody knows. It -has- to be a random player.
Not only does it force you to play with randoms, it also has a terrible waiting time due to an insane amount of demand for monster players, because most people queue up together, which means you can't play monster.
And that's just one aspect of this game, but there's more (yup!).
The game also immediately turns on voice chat for you, even if you prefer not to.
Then again, even if you're a shy person and prefer chatting over voice chat, there's a positive aspect about it. Namely that an experienced player can tell you what to do... which is really needed in this game.
As a new player, you have no tutorials, nothing. There's not even a random map where you can test out your abilities. You queue up, you get thrown into open waters... "Good luck, man! Hunt some monsters ^^"
They do however, show a quick tutorial on how to use your chosen class... but that doesn't mean you know what all your buttons do.
Anyhow, let's move onto other aspects of the game, like graphics and actual gameplay.
The game looks really great in terms of graphics, but we all know that graphics don't make the game.
The gameplay however does, which is actually surprisingly fun, even for players who aren't as experienced in the shooting genre. That is, however, if you actually know what buttons to press.
Ofcourse, this is an Alpha test so they have room for improvement, but for now... I'd advise against buying this game.
Maybe, just maybe, if they fix the matchmaking system in this game, add a tutorial and some quality of life improvements, it might just be worth the money.

I've been a huge fan or Telltale since the first Walking Dead series. If you are a first-timer then be aware that you are not going to be playing a 'game' in the way that you might play, say, CoD or Half-Life; it's far mor akin to one of those old choose your own adventure books (but with less ability to turn to the page and change your mind after you make a decision).
For those who are familiar to the other titles, you'll be in for a bit of a treat. It maintains the intensity of making snap choices in high pressure situations, but this time it's with an established and familiar character. It also introduces some elements similar to the Arkham games, specifically the crime scene investigations. Whilst these new features feel connected to the aforementioned titles (bear in mind they have more than a few voice actors in common, and for good reason), the actual mechanics are very unique.
The comic book fan in me loves the plethora of references; some blatently obvious and some so small you'll need a batcomputer to find them. Theres enough subtlety to keep you wondering who the main villain is (especially if you have read the New 52 Batman), and while you see many familiar faces, it's feet are on solid ground. Granted, within 5 minutes into the first episode you meet Catwoman and Harvey Dent (not Two-Face at this point), it seems to foucus more on his gangbusting days against the crime lords (for now...)
As I said in the beggining, I've loved everything that Telltale have done (really want to see them do Battlestar Gallactica), however I do feel that they are needlessly overstretching thier tech requirements. I purchased this as soon as it was released and it was buggy a nest of antlions, but I was running it on a low spec laptop and in 2 months have patched it to make it not only playable, but also enjoyable, on my♥♥♥♥♥♥poor excuse for a PC. Still some lagging issues but they are forgivable for such an intense story.
Quick comment on the action and variable storytelling: There is far more action in this game than in previous titles, and it certainly seems to havew more of an eff3ect on the overall choices available. A lot of my firends have criticised TTG in the past for not making the choices you make more pivotal, but I am of the opinion that they are playing the long game and putting the transferrable save games into sequels into thier basket.
In summary: Great storytelling with some great voice acting. A good 6 hours per playthrough with a feeling you want more.

Morphopolis is a puzzle game mixed with a point and click hidden object genre. It's casual and slow paced, yet redeems itself with the artistic choices and atmosphere it has. The scenery on every screen is packed with details and every environment is unique, same goes for the puzzles - every puzzle is based on it's own theme, and plays completely different from each other.
The only dealbreaking issue is how the game controls and how cheaply it's ported to the PC. First of all, there are no settings for the game whatsoever - no resolution or windowed mode, sound, or control adjustments. Second of all, since the game is intended to run on a tablet, everything is done through on-screen UI, the keyboard is completely useless and the controls are limited to mouse movement and left click, even the pause menu isn't mapped to the ESC key as a common courtesy.  As a result, character movement is nearly broken, the puzzle controls are heavy and deliberate, as one would use the tablet.
Additionally the game does deal with a lot of death, including, but not limited, to collecting, reanimating and essentially playing a puzzle game with a multitude of corpses. Collecting dismembered or torn limbs from fallen insects is also a reoccuring theme, which isn't necessarily an issue, but can be seen as more brutal than expected.
The game lasted me only 3 hours, but it's worth for the experience.

Limbo, the game, is special in that while it does not wholly depict that mysterious dimension as my mind did, it captures its essence. You are a boy who wakes up in a lonely world made up only of black, white, and shades of gray. Video game logic demands you walk from left to right, jumping over obstacles as they appear, a simple task that needs little attention in the initial moments. This is your chance to absorb your surroundings. The background provides an illusion of depth, but its branches and bridges are out of focus, as if you are dreaming them into existence. The pint-sized hero, his bright blinking eyes shining from his blackened silhouette, trots ahead with the charming gangliness of a six-year-old.
You can check out any time you like, but you can never leave.
Then comes death. Limbo is a hostile place, home to giant spiders that would feast upon you, and traps apparently scattered by the world's other denizens. You step onto a claw trap, and it closes on your neck. Your head falls to the ground and wobbles just for a moment before lying still. No tears are shed, no music plays--the game provides no grand gesture to honor your demise. It simply happens, and you revive at the most recent checkpoint to try the puzzle again. Some of these deaths aren't outright fair; stepping on a pressure plate could mean certain death, but so could jumping over it. Such inconsistencies aren't common, but your first time in Limbo requires some trial-and-error experimentation. Loading times are short, and checkpoints are frequent, however, so death is rarely a frustration, though often a horror.
What does it all mean? People pondered that question when Limbo was first released on the Xbox 360 in 2010, and the PC version adds nothing new that would illuminate the mystery of this world, so there's little reason to splurge on another version if you've already played. Nevertheless, the ending offers important clues to the greater plot, if not to the details of the game's events and objects--the imposing neon hotel sign that you must cross, for instance, or the murderous children, seemingly escaped from Lord of the Flies, that aim their blowguns at you. Limbo means for its atmosphere to consume you in the moment, and in that sense, it succeeds. You drag a dead child's corpse to solve a puzzle, and perhaps wonder if anyone grieves this lost soul given the apathy of the realm. You glimpse a figure and regard her with tenderness, but the brief glimmer of hope is snuffed out in an instant.
After life, before death.
It isn't until the final third of its two- to three-hour runtime that Limbo's puzzles become challenging. The first half of the game is more concerned with building dread and ambiguity. Even after being vanquished, a colossal spider's remaining leg thrusts at you from its thorax, one final act of defiance that could leave two corpses for the crows to pick. When you pull the leg from the spider, the audible cracks and visible white splatters emphasize just how recently its life force was crushed. Elsewhere, you push boxes and pull levers, rushing to finish the puzzle before the rising water fills the room. Failure means watching the dear boy go as limp as a ragdoll as liquid fills his lungs.
The second half leaves behind the horrors in favor of puzzles involving gravity and complex machinery. As memorable as it is to navigate tilting rooms with only a few hanging lamps to light the way, it is that spider that most embodies Limbo's somber spirit. The later puzzles are complex and clever, but they don't haunt the heart. The finale feels abrupt because it returns to the first hour's imagery, having abandoned it for long enough to have altered your personal connection with the game from an emotional one to an intellectual one. And yet the end offers insight into a backstory left otherwise untouched--enough of it to inspire another playthrough, this time ever so much wiser than you were before.
THE GOOD
Striking atmosphere that chills the heart
Excellent, poignant moments that stay with you
Cold, gruesome deaths are presented with memorable and horrific apathy
Introduces more involved puzzles at a satisfying pace
THE BAD
The most haunting imagery is limited to the first half
Ending doesn't emerge organically from the hour leading to it

I'll start off by saying the visuals are amazing. The survival mechanics are very in depth and well-integrated into the environment you play in. Things such as wind chill, the amount of calories it takes to chop up a table for firewood, the fact that you cant just start a fire with one match and a log (you need a starter, tinder, and kindling, and even then sometimes you get unlucky and it wont't start), all make it apparent that there are some great minds behind this project.
However, it is brutal. If you don't get some sort of purchase and I mean fast, the game will destroy you. In some ways this is good, seeing as they are going for realism, but in other ways its a bit too fast. The hunger and thirst guages, for example, get to critical levels after pretty much every time you sleep, which you have to do or else your exhaustion guage goes up. I get the idea that they want you to constantly be absorbed by a feeling of desperation, but when my character is on the brink of death from starvation after one day without food (people can go up to three weeks without food), it actually pulls me out of my immersion by drawing my attention to something not very realistic, reminding me that I'm only playing a game. Of course, once you start starving and can't sleep enough to restore your exhaustion guage, your survivor is basically moving at a crawl, which makes it almost impossible to find anything that will keep you alive, especially since your vision becomes so blurry you can't even see where your cursor is to pick up anything. At this point, I'm already out of my immersion state, so I usually just quit the game before I die, and that's the biggest problem. The whole point of the game is to stick it out as long as you can before the long dark, but there's such a tiny chance of you making a comback once you're at this point that you don't want to bother crawling around for five minutes, unable to see and waiting for your health to disappear.
The reason I do reccommend this game is for everything else that there is, and for the awesomeness that I believe is yet to come. In the meantime, I sincerely hope some of these problems are patched, because it kills me to see a game so nearly perfect but not quite there.

Great game but only for a niche audience.
The stories, the lores, the themes and the characters are awesome. There are few games that reach this level of good story telling. The only stuff missing there is voice acting. The game would have been almost perfect in terms of story telling with good voice acting.
The gameplay is average. It's not bad, but it's not great either. You have a few base stats that are used during the various stories and to a lesser degree during combat. One of the implicit goal is to increase those stats by completing stories. You are tasked to choose the proper choices for dealing with each stories by guessing or having encountered it before. This hidden knowledge concept is a big part of the game. The open nature of the game can be daunting for some with few details to guide them. Combat is somewhat dull. For the most part, you will just avoid enemies until you reach mid to late game. There is a tedious grind to keep up with your constantly depleting vital resources but it can be relieved by completing big stories or using some trade routes.
This game is unforgiving. You will die easily and often until you get a good comprehension of all the game concepts. You will have to start over from nothing or using a few perks if you managed to get some legacies for your next captain. That last aspect can be depressing for many.
The soundtrack is great although you will not hear it often during the game. The few sound effects are alright. The animations are well done and on par with the great visual graphics. They help create a good underground and creepy theme.
If you like exploration, rich stories and the survival genre, this game is for you. If you are not a fan any of these, you should probably pass on this game.

After 6 hours of playing this game, I just can't play anymore. I want to get into it, I *really* do; but there are just so many glaring issues that make this game more frustrating than interesting, and ultimately, not fun. Some pros and cons that I've witnessed while playing this game so far:
PROS
+ Wonderfully eerie and spooky art design.
+ Fascinating and bizarre (albiet non-coherent) story set in a post-apocalyptic, Gothic Victorian-era universe with a Lovecraftian edge.
+ Soundtrack is pretty good and captures the feel of being a lonely Zee Captain and their crew sailing the dark Unterzee.
+ The game is actually challenging and flat-out tells you your first captain will most likely die.
CONS
- While the story is interesting, the game does a terrible job of doing any worldbuilding. You're just dropped into the game with zero context and no idea what anything is or whats going on. Apparently you need to have played Fallen London, the browser game this game is based on, to get a lot of the lore, but that's like needing to watch an entire season of Agents of Shield to be able to understand whats going on in an Avengers movie. It's really hard to stay invested when you don't know what the hell is going on.
- The tutorials are barely helpful and don't tell you a lot of what you need to get started. It tells you how the controls, stats, resource management system, and the barebones of how combat generally works but that's basically it.
- The speed of your starting ship is god-awful slow and upgrades to your ship's engines are not only prohibitively expensive, but the actual increase in speed is insignificant and it actually makes your ship consume fuel faster, making it even more expensive to maintain. The only reason for this that I can tell is that the map simply isn't that big and thus the developers decided to slow travel speed down to try to make everything feel bigger, but in the end it still only feels like you're sailing a medium-sized lake rather than a vast, expansive underground sea.
- Combat is uninspired. It basically boils down to pointing your ship in the vague direction of whatever's trying to kill you, waiting around 4 seconds for your weapon to get a firing solution, and then press the appropriate number key to fire. Rinse and repeat several times, depending on your weapon's damage and your Irons statistic, which can increase the damage you do in combat. Shining your ships' lights on the target or firing a flare and having a higher Mirrors stat will speed up how quickly you obtain a firing solution. You can get out of the firing arc of enemy ships, which delays their next firing solution on you, but monster's attacks are almost always unavoidable. Evasive manuevers with your ship basically boil down to getting behind an enemy ship so they cant target you or running away from a monster, desperately hoping they don't catch you.
- The same resource you use to feed your crew is also the same one you use to repair your ship when you're not in port, meaning if you take a lot of damage from a fight (you will) and aren't able to get back to a port safely (an almost certain possibility), you have to use up your supplies to repair your ship at an inefficient rate (1 unit of supplies per 5 HP, your starting ship has 75 HP max), but then your crew will probably starve before you get there.
- There is no reliable way to make money in this game, so unless you're very lucky and find some good treasure or trigger a fortuitous random event, you will constantly be coming up short on cash. Also, not every port even has a shop or a way to repair your ship, so even if you have the money, if you're low on fuel/supplies/HP and not near a port that can help you, you're screwed.
- Probably the biggest issue I've had with the game is the♥♥♥♥♥♥poor UI design when it comes to the in-game Journal, where quests, objectives, and character qualities are located. I hope you have Notepad open in another window or a pen and paper, because most of the time this game doesn't record a damn thing when it comes to missions or objectives. Need to remember which port that thug in Fallen London asked you to deliver his illegal Crate of Human Souls to? You'll have to keep track of all of that yourself, because this game isn't gonna remind you, oh no, that would make it far too convenient. Everything about the Journal is confusing and lacks almost any useful information. All it does is have little cards with the name of the quest or quality, a portrait and some flavor text. The same is true for the majority of in-game items, besides the weapons and engine upgrades, which give you some stats, but again, it doesn't explain to you what those stats mean.

I shimmy up a rope, wind beating me into the rock face. A blizzard of huge proportions surrounds me. As I walk away from the recently-climbed rope, I gather sticks and things to burn. I find the tail section of a cargo plane, or an airliner, and I start a meager fire. I know this fire will only last for a pitiful 30 minutes before the blizzard's harsh cold consumes it. I boil a cup of coffee, leaving the fire with 7 minutes.
As it crackles away, I drink the coffee, and await death, but then... The storm clears, and I'm on a panoramic summit of a large mountain, I can see the wings and engines of the same plane scattered across the land, a wolf chases a deer in the distance. I see a case with a flare gun in it, I take the flare gun, load a flare into it, and fire it, hoping for a rescue.
This was only my most recent experience in The Long Dark. It's a very cozy, very immersive game, and survival only adds to the feeling of 'being there.' Buy this game as soon as you can, it will change you.

Gun metal is a fun, but flawed, third person shooter. In it you pilot a "Havoc suit" that is a humanoid mecha that can transform into a fighter jet and blow stuff up.
There is a skeleton of a story somewhere, something about the enemy attacking your people and somesuch, so you hop in your prototype super suit and go kick some butt. Because... reasons.
The missions are relatively straightforward and short: destroy X location, defend a convoy, defend Y location, destroy X,Y and Z locations and then a huge battle ship, etc. They last no more than 15 minutes each (some going for 4 ~ 5 minutes) and I have to say they're fun and challenging. The difficulty level is significant, but it never gets unfair. Each level is some sort of puzzle that you need to figure out in order to succeed and as you progress you will unlock more guns, armor types and fun bits to add to your arsenal to blow stuff up.
The game however is a bit dated on the graphics. The only problem I had is mapping the controls to my XBox controller, and even when fully mapped by pressing certain combinations other buttons would simply not work. My current set up where I'm most confortable makes me unable to roll away to avoid enemy fire; even though I have the correct setup it works when it wants to.
Recommended purchase in a sale if you want some old school shooting action and want to turn off your brain for a bit.

Alright, here we go. This game.
STORY
The story was very.. different, at least in terms of the Batman universe. I can understand how some people may not particularily care for this story, I personally enjoyed it. It's fresh to the Batman universe (
) which was cool. There didn't seem to be a hell of a lot "REMEBER THIS CHARACTER???" cameos in this, which is nice. It took a couple villians and ran with it for the duration.
I don't feel like going into more detail. To sum it up, interesting take on Batman, one that you'll either love or hate.
GAMEPLAY
It's a Telltale game, so gameplay is expectantly lacking. If you're complaining about gameplay in a Telltale game, then you must be new. Anyway, what like gameplay there is is a series of quick time events. However, there is also the detetcive events where you solve murders, kidnappings, heists, etc. I really like that this in here, as I feel like recent Batman movies and even games forget that Batman is the world's greatest detective. It's mostly just action, Batman beating the♥♥♥♥♥♥out baddies (which isn't necessarily a bad thing, just more detective stuff would be cool).
Now, the biggest detriment to this game, as everyone else has been ♥♥♥♥♥ing about (and rightfully so), is...
PERFORMANCE
Holy ♥♥♥♥. What a ♥♥♥♥♥how. I want to clarify that I never experienced a crash, and I know that a lot of other people have. I also want to make a note that I play on the Win 7 version of the game. But goddamn. People talk but their mouths aren't moving; lag during QTE's; whenever Bruce watches the telly its just a blank screen, which is just confusing cause people are reacting to what they're watching but you have no ♥♥♥♥ing idea what the hell they're talking about; a lot of FPS fluctuations at random times; sometimes the game takes forever to load specifically during the "Previously on..." scenes (weird how its only at these sections, but alright, could be worse); and some other things I can't think of off the top of my head.
VERDICT
Is this game worth buying? Well, performance isn't a deal breaker for this game seeing how 80% of the game is just sitting back and listening to the story progress and occasionally walking 20 feet to get to the next cutscenes. Not to give Telltale a pass though, or to excuse them for their faults, because the performance is unexceptable when their earlier games seem to run better than Batman currently runs (especially since with the success Telltale has been seeing lately they SHOULD be able to hire on some extra programmers or testers or whoever the ♥♥♥♥ they need to AVOID this problem).
Luckily, they gave us the first episode to demo so we can decide. I'm recommending cause I enjoyed the experience, but it is not without its faults, so I'd say to buy this game on sale, like I did. It really isn't worth the full price tag.

Morphopolis is a beautiful, but ultimately unpolished little gem of a game. I got it on sale for about $1. For that price, it is definitely worth it. For anything more, I might not have considered it had I known what I know about it now.
First impressions were good; the hand-drawn art is gorgeous and scrolls seamlessly, and the music is okay enough, albeit a little repetitive.
My frustration began in the tutorial chapter. Morphopolis, true to its nature as a game about insects, has no written language components anywhere. Everything is indicated through a series of visual pop-ups and hand icons, which unfortunately extends to the interface of the game. Just trying to move my insect at the beginning devolved into the hand icon relentlessly mocking me as I tried various clicking, dragging, and clicking-and-dragging motions until I randomly stumbled upon something that worked. It turns out that in order to move the insect, you have to click and hold down on the spot where you want it to move, making the tutorial's hand motion completely misleading.
Despite this, once I got used to the demands of having to figure out not only the solution to each puzzle, but what I was trying to accomplish in the first place, I started to get into the rhythm of clicking on bugs, gathering objects, and opening up new pathways to other bugs so I could backtrack and get more objects. The hint feature was helpful; however, one thing that was not helpful was having no hint feature nor exit button on the mini-puzzle segments. The languid pace of the game encouraged me to take my time, however on more than one occasion I had to tab out of the game to look up a guide because literally none of the mouse movements I tried were showing any sign of progress.
Each level ends with having to collect the body parts and eggs of a giant insect, after which the grub burrows into its flesh(?), metamorphoses, and gains a new appearance and powers (which are activated by clicking the left mouse button once -- another thing I had to figure out through laborious trial and error). Once I figured out that mechanic, it was fun to use environmental cues to determine what the likely outcomes of using the bug's power would be. The bug got stuck on the environment sometimes, including on the exit of the final level, though the jerky flipping motion at least indicated to me that something unintended was going on.
For all the frustration the game gave me, I did finish it, in under two hours. Overall I give it a 6/10, which is a recommendation, but just barely. I enjoyed the core gameplay and setting, immersing myself in the world and the journey of the aphid, but there are way too many omissions of features that would have reduced the amount of times I was simply jarred out of the game by frustration at its minimal interface and sometimes buggy mechanics.
