This is where I wish Steam's review system offered more than a recommended yes/no option, because saying that this game is recommended implies that the game is more than it is and ignores a couple of frustrations, but saying the game is not recommended does the game an undeserved disservice.  So bear in mind this recommendation is actually a MAYBE, and read on to know whether this is the game for you...
Morphopolis is a casual and short puzzle/hidden-object game crafted over 5 beautiful levels.  You start life as a small insect and, using point-and-click, must find your way through each level where you will metamorphose into a bigger insect.  If you've played the excellent Machinarium, the gameplay style is very similar (point and click, and find hidden objects) but there is where the similarity ends.  Morphopolis is nowhere near as long as Machinarium, the puzzles are not as challenging nor as varied, and overall the game is very simple to complete, with only the final puzzle offering any greater degree of difficulty.
The unique artwork and ambient music are a joy to experience (the visuals are gorgeous), and the lack of hand-holding will be a blessing for gamers who like to work out what they must do.  Every insect and every flower might offer some interaction (or might not) and it's left to you to discover.  Once you uncover an insect or flower that you can interact with, it will have some basic needs to be fulfilled (ie hidden objects - like finding 10 pollen seeds and feeding them to the flower) before it will enable a new pathway for your insect to use (either by unfolding a new branch to climb or unblocking the way to a new area).  Each level will have a final puzzle to solve, which are mostly of average difficulty and very enjoyable (if brief).
The lack of hand-holding would be most welcome if only elements that were meant to be interacted with would be a little more responsive.  As it stands, many interactive things need several experimental clicks before they yield (or not), and because there is no clue offered by the interface as to whether an element is interactive or not, you'll be clicking a lot of things to progress.  Navigation was a particular issue, with the player's insect dawdling at an annoyingly slow pace and frequently becoming stuck in areas that weren't actually blocked - especially frustrating given there was a fair bit of back-tracking to do.  There was a lack of variety in solving each stage (outside of the end puzzles) and it became too easy to solve as a result.  Finally, the last level had a disappointing ending: given that my insect successfully metamorphosed through each of the previous 4 stages, I truly expected to metamorphose into some big and beautiful butterfly at the end of the game.  Instead, the game simply faded to black, leaving me wondering whether the game had ended or not.  Because of the game's simplicity, there is no real replay value.
Morphopolis is a pleasant diversion from bigger and more challenging games, and it's a piece of art in many ways.  However, it's somewhat let down by its short length without any real ending, frustrating interface and the lack of variety needed to complete each stage and reach the end-of-level puzzle.  I would recommend it in a heartbeat at a sale price, and would also recommend it at its full £3.99 price if you are looking for something pretty and lightweight to play for a short while (especially if you do enjoy games like Machinarium).  Otherwise, there are longer and more challenging games with a little less frustration that might be more worthwhile for you.

On the other hand, if the hunters aren't very good at being a team, they are going to lose. Again I played another match as Val the medic, and I was pretty much the only one hunting the monster with my tranq gun, we lost two teammates to npc monsters.
I love the concept and the gameplay, being the monster on level 1 where you're weak and have to run and hide, while trying to feed on other animals to get stronger, knowingly that the hunters are getting closer every second, it's nervewracking good! At the same time, once you've evovled to rank 3, you'll feel like one hell of a god. Well not much to say here, considering I haven't played too much.

The music is fantastic.
Again, the game is alpha so there are times where one side is more overpowered than the other because of different factors. Don't whine 'bout that, ay? It's A-L-P-H-A, they'll fix it over time. I tried, i really tried to like this game. To win the battle against the horrible UI, annoying crafting system, constant dying, dull surroundings, dull music, dull combat, dull mining, dull building, dull everything. And to find the "potential" that people seem to be talking about. But it was a failure.
I mean, what were the devs thinking? You know, "BETA" stage of development starts when you have an almost ready-to-go product, so you just need to eliminate bugs and test some features. Not when you have a game that's almost unplayable, AS WELL as buggy and unstable.
Where do i start? The world is pretty tight, so you can only explore downwards, but since you have no way to tell what's below you, 90% of the time you'll end up falling from great height, crashing and dying on impact. Not to mention that you can't go too deep since the exposure and/or mobs will kill you there. In my book that's not "exploring", just pointless trial and error.
You can build a base, but what's the point if you can't even respawn there? And it's not like in Terraria, where you always build a base near the surface - here you won't be able to get back up there unless you die again. And if you build it deeper, then every time you die, you'll have to go and find it again in the midst of a thousand identical floating islands. Oh yeah, and who would've guessed that these super-advanced spacefaring guys won't have a device to make a MAP of the area.
So here's how your first couple of hours in EoS will look like: you'll be jumping around, searching for at least something different from the dirt\mud\clay surrounding you, trying to get deeper, but mostly falling and dying constantly. Even if you succeed, you'll see that nothing really changes down there, except for tougher and more aggressive mobs, and the exposure timer won't let you go deeper until you get better equipment. And unless you think that painfully slow mining and crafting some aluminium pants or whatever is fun, then that's it, that's your only option here - you won't have anything else to do.
To make things worse the game gives you no clue on how things work and why would you need them. So i can build a GENERATOR and a COMMAND CENTER, cowabunga, now what? It won't even explain the basics. Like if you played Terraria, you know there's a difference between a block and a wall. But here, there are only "walls", by default functioning as blocks. You actually need to hit "TAB" button to be able to place your "wall" in the background where it belongs. Only you'll never guess it unless you stumble on it in some random guide, like i did.
Yeah, whoever in the devs team is responsible for the UI deserves a bullet to the face. Why can't i place items just by dragging them from my inventory? Why do i always need to bind a hotkey to do this basic thing? Why the crafting window is so bizarre and complex? Did you see how crafting looks in Terraria? Well, look again.
Probably there is some difference in the later stages of the game, but i gave up here. It's not like "playing a game" to me, more like trying to fix a car without any idea of what you're supposed to do. And with the wrench constantly slipping out of your hands and falling so you need to go pick it up again and again.
Overall, this is my most frustrating early access experience since Project Zomboid, but at least i didn't spend my money there.

The Red Orchestra series is one of my favorites ever made. I have been playing Red Orchestra since it was first released as a mod for Unreal Tournament 2004. Red Orchestra 2 delivers a realistic WW2 experience on the Eastern Front mainly focused on the Stalingrad campaign.
Let me say first off this is not a game where you can run and gun your way to victory. Many maps have average encounters of over 150 yards and at times much larger. When moving you have to take your time and make sure no one has a clear shot at you. This is a game for people who want a gritty WW2 experience where strategy, teamwork, and thinking your next move is essential.
Red Orchestra 2 contains maps that are based entirely or inspired by real locations from battles during the Stalingrad campaign. Take a look at the inspiration for the level Grain Elevator
. As you can tell Tripwire Studies is interested in making Red Orchestra as historically accurate as possible.
Gameplay mechanics are very immersive and impressive. You have stamina used for running, the amount of stamina you have also effects the sway of your weapon due to you being winded. When sniping and zoomed in you can wait till your character exhauls his breath to fire allowing your gun to be more stable for a few seconds (actual sniping technique). When firing your weapon you have to take bullet drop into account and weapon recoil is realistic. Hip firing is inaccurate with most guns and bolt action rifles take practice at range. You can also make your gun more stable by aiming your gun when standing in front of a solid object.
Red Orchestra 2 is also one of the most intense games you will ever play. The game contains a supression meter which goes down when you are being fired at. This causes your character to become scared, start breathing heavily, and sway his weapon. When you are fired upon you will hear the bullet wiz by and your stamina meter will go down as you are being fired upon.
The only problem with Red Orchestra 2 is it is not as popular as it should be. Though you will never have a problem finding a server to join, I wish more servers existed. Please get your friends to play it, they commonly run sales on the game and it comes with Rising Storm, the Japanese theatre.
If you get the game based off my review feel free to add me. I will play with you and help you learn if you have a mic :).

Updated: Having now played the other Frogwares games in this series, I can honestly say this is the best of the bunch of their works.  The original review stands, but be aware that the other games are AWFUL
The Testament Of Shrlock Homes is a hybrid point and click 3d exploration game.  Theres a lot of work that has gone into this, with numerous backgrounds and environments, costumes, 3d level constructions, some nice facial animations (that are occasionally totally out of sync with the speech), some questionable voice acting and some mind testing puzzles.
From a story perspective, this game is rather faithful to the Sherlock Holmes books, and theres been some obvious research done into the character, his relationships and the world he inhabits.  Theres also some obvious  problems with the game that mar an otherwise enjoyable 3D explorer.
The story is fairly good.  It does take some liberties with the historic Holmes and brings back the baddest bad guy ever, but overall, it stays faithful to the period.  That said, there are some points when it breaks down and you have to take a leap of faith with the character to continue playing.  I didnt like that sometimes, plot devices were revealed bythe narration and cut scenes before they had happened in the game, but its not a terribly unforgivable problem.
The puzzle solving is where this game excels.  some of the quests require lateral thinking and some interesting approaches to solve.  some however require you to go through a monotonous sqeuence of events.  They are less enjoyable, but thankfully are few and far between.
Ive seen elsewhere comments about "ugliest children ever!" and that aspect of the game could have been much better.  Some of the events you have to follow make no sense at all.  theres a massive twist in the game that you expect from Sherlock Holmes, but it makes no attempt to explain why, how or what its playing at.
The multi character system is a great idea, allowing you to be in two places at once, and its a good way to link up character arcs in game, but sometimes its overused.
The entire last act of the game is, frankly, boring.  the first 2 thirds of the game work rather well and were far more enjoyable.  Some puzzles require you to find a specirfic item, and those are REALLY annyoing particularly because the location of some of the items make no sense.  in the same breath however, some of the interactions with third person characters  is innovative, although some of them are so diaposable, you forget about them.  I consider that a problem of the character developlment, and some interesting characters never re-occur, leaving you let down a their underuse.
All in all, this is a solid adventure, but it wont win any awards, which is unfortunate.  Id like to see one of these tackled with a proper development budget, better voice acting and some streamlined quests, but if youre a fan of the genre or sherlock holmes, you'll probably find something in this game to satisfy you.  give it a go!  its mega cheap in the Steam Sale!

I shimmy up a rope, wind beating me into the rock face. A blizzard of huge proportions surrounds me. As I walk away from the recently-climbed rope, I gather sticks and things to burn. I boil a cup of coffee, leaving the fire with 7 minutes.

The storm clears, and I'm on a panoramic summit of a large mountain, I can see the wings and engines of the same plane scattered across the land, a wolf chases a deer in the distance. I see a case with a flare gun in it, I take the flare gun, load a flare into it, and fire it, hoping for a rescue.

Sunless Sea is a choose your own adventure, exploration game. At the beginning of the game you choose the victory condition, and then start exploring. You sail around the map to find islands, complete quest and unlock story. The nature of story is very different than normal development. There is no linear story. When you go to an island the game turns to text-based decision making as the vehicle for the story. Through interactions on the island and choices you make, stories are found. Each “Island story” can be described as modular event, but are all weaved into the story and can influence and trigger other events. More and more is revealed as you visit islands and work towards your chosen victory condition. WHY DOES THIS GAME SOUND SO AWESOME?!
There is one problem with Sunless Sea, and this the necessary farming. This disgusting element in the game is the result of resource management. Farming money for food and fuel takes away from the fun of the game, exploration and story. If you are fortunate to start the game well and find some money through various quests you will continue playing the game in fear, remembering those 5 other deaths before this prosperous life.
This could be part of the fun of the game, raising money and supplies for an exploration into the unknown to find riches. But for whatever reason, the farming does not appeal to me. However it is not game breaking and sometimes farming expand your understanding of the world. This is important to know as farming might harm your enjoyment of the game as it is a barrier to exploring.
Tl;dr: Choose your own adventure by exploring islands in a text-based format, farming can hinder enjoyment of the game because it is a barrier to exploring. Although it is manageable barrier!

I have logged about 20 hours of gameplay so far and upgraded my rating from 3 to 4 stars. I got this on steam so I was able to download it on May 23. This is very different from the previous Tropicos. The difference between tropic 3 and tropic 4 was a few more buildings, but overall was the same game. Tropico 5 looks and feels completely different. You will find this game much harder and challenging on campaign mode but now has difficulty settings. There are many new building and upgrades as well. Multiplayer is still not up but I will update this review when this mode is working as it seems like it will be fun. I have played many hours of tropico 3 and tropico 4 so I am very familiar with the series. They released patch 1.02 on June 9th, which fixed numerous issues with both multiplayer and single player.
Pros
-Graphics are updated and is much smoother than previous tropicos.
-The trading system has been overhauled and you now have a guaranteed trade ship every six months. You now also have an additional ship that you can use to trade a certain commodity at above default rate of the computer generated trade ship. Also the ships will change every so many years and look like a ship of that time period.
-You no longer have to build a separate tourist dock. All tourist ships use the same dock as what is given to you at the start of the game.
-You can now hire a manager for each building. Each manager with have certain bonuses they bring such as better efficiency or better job quality.
-Each place where tropicans work will display what income level they will be at. For example a dock worker or a farmer will be a poor tropican, but you can increase their pay to make them well-off. The housing will tell you how it corresponds to their income level. A tenement will suit a poor worker but a house requires their income to be well-off. This also applies to the restaurants and pubs, which serve the poor tropicans whereas opera houses and casinos appeal more to the rich tropicans/tourists. This is much more detailed than previous tropicos.
-There is now a constitution that will have selections such as for the labor market-all citizens 16 and older must work, child labor, or work if you want; each with its own pros and cons.
-Many new buildings including cotton and cocoa plantations. You can now build a textile mill and use the cotton you grow to make tshirts. You can now mine uranium and coal and either sell it or use it for power plants. There is now a library which is used to research buildings and upgrades per era.
-The construction priorities feel like they work much better than previous tropicos.
-The dock now shows exactly what you are exporting and the money you will generate with each item. For example: Corn-$3000
-You can now have a population well over the 650 person cap in the previous tropicos. (I currently have a population of 800 on one island and it is not even that built up, there is even one mission where I have to have over 900 people.) The low population cap in tropic 3 and 4 really limited how much you could expand and grow your island because you would not have enough workers to fill positions for every building later in the game, especially when you threw tourists in the mix.
-Plantations now have plots of dedicated land that crops will be planted on. This is much better than previous tropicos where farmers would just plant crops in random places around the farm.
-I like that in the campaign, as you move to the next mission, you continue on the same island with everything you already built and expand upon it.
Cons
-The overlays no longer include a map of minerals, instead you have to explore the undiscovered portions of the island to find mines. You now have to pay an expedition $1000 to explore differnt parts of the island and can get expensive. Also mines are only located by hills or cliffs now. You start out only seeing about 1/10 of the island and the rest is fog. I find it kind of annoying that as you build you city and reach the edge of what you can see of the island, the fog doesn't clear. You still have to send an expedition, even its across a busy street.
-You can no longer build factories until you hit a certain era.
-When trying to place a farm, the crop condition map is not as easy to read as it the square tiles are now outlined in a green, yellow, or red border, not a full green or red square. I personally found it harder to distiguish the yellow and green conditions of the map.
-In the campaign you only have a certain number of years to rule, known as mandates, and if you cant complete the level in time you lose. More challenging though.
-You have to wait to get most of the upgrades for factories till certain eras.
-You cant set wages for all farms or mines anymore (Fixed in patch 1.02). You can only set the sames wages for specific farms or mines such as all gold mines or all corn farms.
-The game will pause and go to a loading screen when it autosaves for about 5 seconds. This is just kind of annoying when playing, I hope they can patch this issue.
Overall, this game is more fun and challenging than tropico 3 or 4 in my opinion. I bet with a few updates some of the cons I listed will make this game much more fun and enjoyable. I was use to just building up my island at my leisure and building up money to purchase better buildings but tropico 5 is not like that anymore. This version requires patience and a see what this does approach in the campaign. I really like that aspect as it has created a much higher replay value. And this is like most game downloads from amazon, it will be on steam. This has been the case for many years now so don't be shocked. (And it says DRM-steam). I will update after more gameplay.

A decade after it's initial release, and Gun Metal is still awesome.  For me, this game is a masterclass in focussed design.  It doesn't try to be clever, with lots of gimmicks that are only there for their own sake.  It just gives you good, solid, arcade-style action, and it does it extremely well.  Your mech isn't loaded with three dozen special features that you completely forget about in the heat of the action.  It does a limited number of things, but those are the only things you need it to do, and they all feel relevant.  Running, strafing, transforming, boosting, barrel-rolling to dodge fire, and all the while firing, firing, firing on the enemy.
Yes, it does betray it's Xbox origins in the slightly awkward mouse control and limited graphics options, but honestly, once you dive in and get blasting, it all feels very natural.  The barrel-rolling to dodge in jet mode feels particularly intuitive, as it's on the keys you use for strafing in mech mode (A and D by defaut as you'd expect).  And you can always plug a control pad in if you find the mouse control a bit too hazy.
As far as I'm aware there's only one voice in the game, the guy who gives you orders, and he puts in a good performance.  Maybe not award-winning, but solid, with simple dialogue, no ridiculous cringe-inducing histrionics, and status updates and encouragements as you progress through each mission.  It's nice to actually be told you're doing well instead of being berated for something or other all the time! =P
In closing, if you want some simple, straightforward action with just enough depth to be engaging without being overwhelming, Gun Metal is for you.

This game is stupid, and by far (!) the weakest of the Telltale Series games I've played.
I think there's not much to be said about the usual Telltale "interactive movie" format... it's an open secret that few of the "choices" actually matter, and either you're fine with being railroaded through a story that unfolds with or without your compliance or these games just aren't for you. That said, since these games are games only insofar as the player is occasionally required to push a button to move the narrative forward, the whole experience depends on the quality of the narrative... and HOLY SHENANIGANS BATMAN, this title is one convoluted mess of a brainfart.
***CONTAINS SPOILERS***
I suppose there's something complimentary to be said when developers decide for a new take on the whole Batman thing instead of trying to deliver the tried-and-true stuff we've all seen a dozen times in other games, in comics, or in the cinema. However, the way Telltale messes up the canon without rhyme or reason is just mind-boggling.
For the most aggravating plot point, the Wayne family itself now belongs to the mob. Actually, they're probably the worst of the whole bunch, and the supposedly senseless robbery-turned-murder of Bruce's parents now is the assassination of one mob boss by another's goon. Well, good thing that's only dissipating the entire reason why there's a Batman in the first place...
The characters are all over the place. Basically, everybody does stupid♥♥♥♥♥♥all the time, and afterwards you have a chat about earlier mistakes where you can tell them that it wasn't that bad. In combination with the aforementioned twist, this makes particularly the recurring exchanges between Bruce Wayne and his butler Alfred hard to swallow. Two accessories to organized crime (one willingly, the other as profiteer by negligence) constantly - and I mean: constantly - jerk each other off while bragging about their selflessness and what good, virtous persons they are. (By the way: you can decide yourself if they're jerking tears or something entirely different in these scenes... I'm just putting this out there, this is NOT how you depict a healthy relationship between a father-figure and his adoptive son.) Also, Vicky Vale is now a criminal mastermind... for some reason.
Just to illustrate how monumentally asinine the characterizations are: The most loyal and trustworthy character you meet in the game - in fact, the only one who doesn't screw you over at any point during this mess of a story - is the Joker. That's right, not a typo, it's the Joker. The one dude in this Series who tells the truth and actually helps you as promised. Of course, only those of us with encyclopedic knowledge of the comics will be able to identify this Arkham inmate who calls himself "John Doe" and who looks like the Joker, talks like the Joker, and has this big red fluorescent warning sign over his head that says: "Hey, guys, do you remember the Joker?" as the Joker. As you see, there's lots of twists and secrets in this game, so don't let your basic reading comprehension come in the way of a surprising reveal.
Last but not least, what's really astonishing - besides the sheer stupidity of the plot, the characters, and the pointlessly shoehorned "surprises" that make no sense whatsoever - is that the player's dialogue options often don't match the dialogue. So, you click "Let's talk later", and then your character proceeds to go on a maniacal rant telling everybody within earshot how much he hates them. This is of course, well, somewhat irritating in a game that is 80% multiple choice dialogues, but at least it makes your own behavior in the game just as schizophrenic as the behavior of all NPCs.
So, for a final recommendation:
If you're not a hardcore Batman fan, go play Wolf Among Us instead, that's a neat little game.
If you're a hardcore Batman fan, go play Arkham Asylum.
If you've played both of those, this game is currently on sale, you're bored out of your mind, you like the Telltale games, and you don't have any strong feelings about Batman one way or the other... just watch a movie instead.

Simple, fluid fun action, and a lot of it. That's the game's winning formula. You go to one of the hundreds of settlements, military bases, airports, oil platforms, etc on the map, and fight pitched battles against the local police and army to take it over by blowing up key installations, such as fuel tanks, power transformers, cranes, etc, and collecting all upgrade crates in the area. You could go in guns blazing right away, or you can try to sneak first to collect the crates with less fighting, and then steal an attack helicopter or a plane and strafe the settlement with rockets to blow up what's left. You can hook up a statue to a truck and yank it down by driving, then use the granite head of the two-bit dictator roped to your truck like a flail to smash stuff with it.
The whole thing is quick, high-octane fun, though it is very repetitive. You tire of it after about 2 hours. But here's the beauty of it: next day it will again be fun for 2 more hours. I've had this game for years and I still come back to it all the time, steadily making progress towards taking over the whole country, one day at a time.
This game has a storyline and missions too, and they are quite good. But the real story here is the fantastic sandbox experience.

If you're looking for a game review you've come to the wrong place. But if youre looking for a fantastic ravioli recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients
- To Make the Dough
375 grams (3 cups) plain flour
1/2 teaspoon salt
2 eggs
1/4 cup (50 ml / 3½ tablespoons) olive oil
1/2 cup (120 ml / 8 tablespoons) water
Extra flour for dusting
- To Make Cheese Filling
15 ounces (425 grams) container Ricotta cheese
5 ounces (142 g/about 1/2 cup plus 2 tablespoons) "3 Cheese Italian Blend" (Parmesan, Romano & Asiago)
Note: grate these cheeses yourself and create your own custom blend.
1/2 cup cheddar cheese
2 eggs, lightly beaten
1/2 teaspoon salt
1/2 teaspoon pepper
- Extras
Your favorite sauce for the ravioli (i.e. marinara/ marijuana)
Parmesan cheese
Basil
Fried vegetables
Shrimp
Fish slices
Chicken pieces
Make the Ravioli filling.
- In a small mixing bowl, add the ricotta and mash with a fork.
- Add in the 3-cheese blend, Cheddar cheese, eggs, salt, and pepper.
- Mix all ingredients thoroughly until you have a smooth, paste-like consistency.
- Cover the bowl with plastic wrap and place it in the refrigerator for about 30 minutes.
Make the Ravioli dough.
- Crack eggs into a large mixing bowl and beat them with a fork. Add water, oil, and salt. Mix.
- Add 1 cup flour to the bowl. Use a fork to mix the flour with the eggs, water, oil, and salt. Repeat with the rest of the flour. Mix until a smooth dough is formed.
- Clear and clean off a large work surface and dust it with flour. This is where you are going to roll out your dough.
- Take the dough out of the mixing bowl, shape it into a ball, and place it on your work surface. Knead for at least 10 minutes or until it becomes elastic.
- Dust a rolling pin with flour to prevent the dough from sticking. Roll out the dough until it is about 1/8 inch (1/3 cm) thick, or about the thickness of 2 stacked quarters.
- With a cookie cutter or upside-down water glass, cut out circles in the dough (will make about 15-20 dough circles).
- Ball up the unused dough and either roll it out and make a couple more raviolis, or wrap it and put in the freezer for another time. Dough can keep for weeks when frozen. Just make sure to wrap well so that it doesn’t suffer from freezer burn or absorb freezer odor.
Fill the Ravioli shells.
- Take the ravioli filling out of the refrigerator and place a tablespoon of it in middle of a dough.
- Fill a small bowl with water, dip your fingers in, and moisten around the outer edge of the dough circle.
- Fold the dough in half over the filling, making a half-moon shape. Be sure all the filling stays inside. Pinch the edges together and then seal the edges of the ravioli with a fork. Make sure to press firmly and go all the way around. This will add a “homemade” touch as well.
- Repeat this process for all your dough circles.
- Dust the finished ravioli with flour to keep them from sticking together.
Form the Shells and Fill Using a Ravioli maker.
- Roll the dough into two sheets
- Place one sheet on the ravioli maker, and form the filling cups.
- Fill with the ravioli mixture.
- Lay the second sheet of dough on top, and roll it out. This will seal in the filling.
- Remove and separate the finished raviolis.
Cook the Ravioli.
- Fill a large pot with water and bring to a boil.
- Place the ravioli in boiling water for 5-6 minutes, or until they float. You can also test for doneness by nibbling on the edges to test.
- If you don't want to make all the ravioli at one time, you can freeze the rest
- Take ravioli out of boiling water with large slotted spoon and place on warmed plates
Serve it up.
Top with your favorite sauce, grate some fresh cheese over it, and enjoy!

As of summer 2017, I still haven't gotten around to trying 3, but JC2 holds up beautifully.
The graphics (on highest settings) were ahead of their time, the world is absolutely GINORMOUS and absolutely lovely to explore. There's a really magnificent sense of scale, and grappling/chuting through the myriad mountains and rivers and towns never entirely gets old, The weapons and combat are fun, albeit not very deep. I don't care about story in games like this, but I'd say all the cinematics and character interactions are above average and keep things reasonably interesting, without impeding on your fundamental freedom to roam and do as you will.
Not a lot of mods available, but there are a few cheats that are definitely worth checking into if you just want to tear sh*t up.
All in all, one of the best open-world action RPGs around -- a bit shallow next to something like GTA, and almost no true RPG elements sadly. If I were to nitpick, I'd say I'd like to see more RPG and stealth-friendly elements in future installments (doesn't sound like JC3 delivered much new in those departments) -- but for what this is, it's one of the best.
Stability-wise, I'm on an nVidia SLI setup -- I've had a few, occasional crashes, but they're pretty rare, nothing like what I often see reported with 3, and nothing too frustrating. Just save often to be safe.
If you see this one on sale, I say grab it, you're unlikely to be disappointed, there's a lot of great content here.

Game is unfinished and abandoned by developers. I don't recommend purchasing this as all the problems from when I initially played this game years ago are still present.
Please remember that Edge of Space is not completed, and more features will be added as the game develops. As such, in the future this article may not be a fair representation of the game.
Edge of Space, developed by Handyman Studios and published by Reverb Publishing, is a 2D dynamically generated space adventure. Much to the likes of ever popular Terraria and recent debut of Starbound, Edge of Space allows you go venture through alien planets, build a home base, fend off the local wildlife, and most importantly, survive. It may seem like these survival games are a dime-a-dozen, but the fine folks at Handyman Studios have put their own spin on the whole “survivalcraft” genre.
I am going to preface this by saying that Edge of Space is in a very early stage of development. It was recently updated and gained some traction through Steam’s Early Access, but the fact of the matter Edge of Space is a bit rough around the edges as of right now. It can be quite a turn off to play a game so early in development, especially if it gives you the wrong impressions due to bugs and other strange anomalies. I will say, though, that in the two weeks that I’ve been playing the game, there has been a staggering amount of bug fixes and patches that have really improved the experience. I wholeheartedly believe that Edge of Space will improve in this respect as the developers iron out bugs, UI issues, and add in more content.
In Edge of Space, you play as a lonely operative representing the Ark Corporation. After catching some beauty sleep in a cryo-chamber, you wake up and realize that you’re basically lost. Your only chance of survival is to depend on the amazing technologies that brought you to the, ahem, edge of space. The only problem here is that you’ll have to find the materials you will need to survive amidst a hostile and dangerous planet. Actually, planet right not even be the right word for Edge of Space. It’s more like an asteroid field where you bounce to and from different small land masses.
One facet of Edge of Space that’s particularly interesting is how the environment is constantly working to kill you. Make no doubt about it, you’ve arrived in a hell-hole that is out for your blood. There are plenty of enemies wandering around trying to eat you, but more than that, the entire gameworld wants your flesh. As you descend lower and lower in space, you’ll take exposure damage if you’re not fully equipped. This can really be a range of things, including radiation or lack of oxygen. In order to prevent this, you’ll want to fully make sure you’ll have the supplies on you to oxygenate the area, or get rid of the radiation. As an ArkCo Operative, you can also defend your new territory with a series of droids or turrets.
As of March 2014, combat in Edge of Space is completely centered around guns. There aren’t any melee weapons as of now. However, there are some interesting ideas with the guns. My favorite example is the Arklight, a gun that shoots out a sticky, glowing canister. This is extremely useful when spelunking through the various caverns you’ll find scattered throughout space, and it sure beats placing a torch down every 10 feet. In fact, torches have such a low-light radius that I tended to stick with the narrow glow of my laser pick and the Arklight.
As someone who has never played Edge of Space before, first impressions can kill the experience. I’m not going to lie, Edge of Space is pretty rough around the edges, especially in the first hour or so. Although it has improved dramatically since I’ve recieved the game, the biggest problem is still the UI. There are some peculiarities that really need adjusting to, especially if you compare them to the flexibility of similar games. One such example would be the hotbar, which is a bit complicated because it can take multiple clicks to slot in different items. The crafting menu is categorized into different sections, but you’ll have to individually click each item you want to use in a recipe. I see what it’s trying to do, and I really like the fact that in some recipes you can substitute many different items, but it’s clunky.There are other little things like this that really drag down the experience despite the survival aspects of the game working as intended.
Edge of Space has a nonlinear sense of progression, but sometimes it is more complicated than it’s own good. There are plenty of machines that you can use to craft items, but when it comes to weapons and armor, you’ll have to go to an armory. This is really more tedious than it needs to be because you’ll have to drop down various unmarked chutes, and you’ll be given whatever weapon lies at the bottom as well as the recipe for said weapon. The first time I went into the armory, I fell down the chute and got a shotgun. Don’t get me wrong, shotguns are awesome, but I didn’t get to look at the other weapons I could have made.
In one of the recent patches, one of the developers of Terraria actually added a few things into Edge of Space. It’s great to see that Edge of Space has the support of a well-known and beloved developer, and it’s even better to see Skeletron inside of Edge of Space. Omegatron, as it’s called in-game, adds some much needed flavor to the typical crabs and floating snails you’ll find outside your base, not to mention he’s very difficult.
In the end, Edge of Space is still very much a work in progress. If you go in expecting a full-fledged game with lots of content and polish, you’ll be sorely disappointed. What Edge of Space excels at is creating a unique environment with interesting gunplay and addictive gameplay. It’s tough to quit playing when you’re in the middle of setting up a fortress, or going on an expedition to dangerous zones. Given a few extra months in the oven and I have no doubt that Edge of Space will easily turn into something that will be worth your money.

Old Review:
Easily the most dull game of the year.
I've been playing Edge of Space the past eight hours; with the single thought in my mind of: "This game must get better eventually, right?"  well; I've been essentially in the same spot with the same equipment for the past five hours.  Killing crabs n' jelly fish, and mining titanium, aluminum, stone, mud, clay, and dirt does get old after a while.  I found a strange white box with a blue arrow on it in a cave and tried to us eit, but that just flashed some screen for half a second and went away; and I was unable to interact with it again.  But let's put things into points for the sake of organization:
Good things:
*Good movement system.
*Good art & music.
*Online co-op.
*Interesting concept.
Bad Things:
*Very unpolished.
*Bad interface & not very user-friendly.
*No explanation for the purpose of alot of things, for example the matter recombiner; the game does not tell you what it does, and the description is simply: "You can't even wager a guess as to how this crazy machine works.", normally checking a wiki would help an issue like this, but their wiki is ancient and not updated.  And then there are things like the random events that go on in the world like the crab nests, and random things such as the weird white box with blue arrow-  no idea what purpose the box served, didn't realize the crab nest was an event.
*Lack of things to do; the only goal you might have in the game is simply go lower.. And there is no reason to go lower as you have all the resources you need in the top areas.
*Lack of resources; it may seem like a good thing that alluminum is basically the most awesome freakin' resource in existence, but it really makes the game boring when you're not bothering to actually look for things.
*Uninteresting enemies.
*Uninteresting areas; why would the devs think it was a good idea to make the entire game take place on some floating rocks ?
*The relaxing music and police sirens(?) doesn't lower the boring factor of this game.
*Terrible enemy AI.
*Poorly made tutorial levels, tutorial more interesting than the actual game.
*Extremely useless chests; for this let me explain how chests work, you craft one then place it in the world; then you right click it to open it, you then have to manually drag and drop each item you wish to place in it, into it; and the chest only has three slots.
*Lack of creativity; how many times has the space shark and space animals concept been done now?
*Very unprofessional dev team.
*Just a shoddy game in general; people like to consider it as a terraria and starbound ripoff- but in all honesty that's an insult to both Terraria and Starbound.
*I'm fairly certain the preview images which show awesome things happening are all fake.
*Dropped items from full inventory disappear within seconds, made 7 chests to put my items somewhere- didn't realize my inventory was full,  chests vanish.  Make a full suit of aluminum armor, don't realize inventory is full,  poof.
*Glitchy items:  Made two chests, had two slots free- placed a chest, the other chest vanished into nowhere.  Used an emergency recall, had two in my inventory; the other vanished.
If I had any suggestions for this game; I recommend they take a page from Windforge and add player made spaceships to fly around the edge of space.
ps:  Don't use the Omega research unless you have good equipment, it just brings you to a boss whom will murder you if you still are using low level stuff.
Well,  all in all I recommend the game; but make sure you don't play it at night or else you're liable to fall asleep from the sheer boredom it causes; and if you're planning on buying the game because of the awesome screenshots you saw of like a desert and mechs and whatnot- those are definitely faked, there are four biomes; you can go to about two of them, a grassy biome and a cold biome.  There's also about 8 or so enemies currently and about six(?) different resources.
Edit August 2016:
So, it is now the distant future since I last reviewed the game; and honestly it's worse than before.  The game opens to a beautiful 404 page error after the Unity Logo and Splash screen.  And the game starts with you in the middle of nowhere with a shark with lasers and crap attached to it with a high pitch voice that asks you to do pointless tasks such as gathering dirt and clay for it.   Simple actions in the inventory system such as dragging an item to the trash drops the FPS immensely, nests are incredibly annoying to destroy as they infinitely respawn the enemy guards every time you shoot it; and you need to shoot one quite a lot to destroy it.
AI is terrible, they wander back and forth not really trying to get to you, in part because their AI is considering the bullets you shoot as ground, so if they're jumping into the air and you shoot them, they will continue to jump as high as they want, or they'll just plain turn around when shot at with a little ? symbol.    The animations and art is weird, the physics is bad, the overall game is mayhaps more boring than it used to be.
But all in all, better than No Man's Sky.  So at least there is that.

This is a darkly beautiful game. You should play it in a dark room. The animation and visuals in Limbo are perfect: simplistic, and somehow all the more beautiful for it. The sounds are mostly soft and subtle, with only limited ambient music. It's actually rather peaceful gaming until the last few chapters.
Limbo's controls are simple. Just five buttons: walk left/right, jump/climb up/down, and an action button.
Limbo's difficulty was just right for me. i like a mild challenge, but i have a low threshold for frustration, especially with too much timed stuff. i'm not a hard core gamer. i would rate Limbo as easier than later levels of World Of Goo (the rotating chamber stopped me playing that one). i became frustrated near the end, but that part didn't last too long. It was the last couple chapters. i didn't realize how close i was to finishing, so the increased difficulty made sense once i reached the end. The checkpoints were almost perfect for me (frequent). Only once did i get frustrated with the granularity of the automatic restart points.
The play length is maybe short (i played through it in 4.3 hours, including many fails on later chapters), but i don't mind. i got it on sale, and it's very beautifully made, so i am content with the experience.
The only complaint i have is that the ending didn't quite deliver in the final seconds. It's cinematic, pretty, and artful, but i wanted them to go all the way with the resolution (after all the work to get there).
i'd happily recommend the game and will probably play it again some day.

I'll start off by saying the visuals are amazing. The survival mechanics are very in depth and well-integrated into the environment you play in. Things such as wind chill, the amount of calories it takes to chop up a table for firewood, the fact that you cant just start a fire with one match and a log (you need a starter, tinder, and kindling, and even then sometimes you get unlucky and it wont't start), all make it apparent that there are some great minds behind this project.
However, it is brutal. If you don't get some sort of purchase and I mean fast, the game will destroy you. In some ways this is good, seeing as they are going for realism, but in other ways its a bit too fast. The hunger and thirst guages, for example, get to critical levels after pretty much every time you sleep, which you have to do or else your exhaustion guage goes up. I get the idea that they want you to constantly be absorbed by a feeling of desperation, but when my character is on the brink of death from starvation after one day without food (people can go up to three weeks without food), it actually pulls me out of my immersion by drawing my attention to something not very realistic, reminding me that I'm only playing a game. Of course, once you start starving and can't sleep enough to restore your exhaustion guage, your survivor is basically moving at a crawl, which makes it almost impossible to find anything that will keep you alive, especially since your vision becomes so blurry you can't even see where your cursor is to pick up anything. At this point, I'm already out of my immersion state, so I usually just quit the game before I die, and that's the biggest problem. The whole point of the game is to stick it out as long as you can before the long dark, but there's such a tiny chance of you making a comback once you're at this point that you don't want to bother crawling around for five minutes, unable to see and waiting for your health to disappear.
The reason I do reccommend this game is for everything else that there is, and for the awesomeness that I believe is yet to come. In the meantime, I sincerely hope some of these problems are patched, because it kills me to see a game so nearly perfect but not quite there.

I shimmy up a rope, wind beating me into the rock face. A blizzard of huge proportions surrounds me. As I walk away from the recently-climbed rope, I gather sticks and things to burn. I find the tail section of a cargo plane, or an airliner, and I start a meager fire. I know this fire will only last for a pitiful 30 minutes before the blizzard's harsh cold consumes it. The storm clears, and I'm on a panoramic summit of a large mountain, I can see the wings and engines of the same plane scattered across the land, a wolf chases a deer in the distance. I see a case with a flare gun in it, I take the flare gun, load a flare into it, and fire it, hoping for a rescue.
This was only my most recent experience in The Long Dark. It's a very cozy, very immersive game, and survival only adds to the feeling of 'being there.' Buy this game as soon as you can, it will change you.

This is a really good danmaku game. It's obviously inspired by Touhou Project; and if you like those games, you will absolutely enjoy this one.
The art and music are top notch. The story is about what you'd expect (hint: there's not much to it.) The stages are well designed, with a good balance of difficult sections and breathing breaks. Overall, I'd say the difficulty is pretty high. It's about on par with most Touhou Project games, actually. There's not too much random twitch dodging in Jigoku Kisetsukan - most everything is pattern based. If you're used to playing Touhou, you'll recognize the setup of the stages. Random enemies, miniboss, random enemies, boss. Bosses follow the same sort of "spell card" system as they do in Touhou. (I.E. Normal attack, special pattern with a point bonus if you clear it within a time limit and without dying, normal attack, repeat until somebody dies.)
I love the art in this game. The character portraits are gorgeous, and the sprites are so charming. They've got a sort of pixilated look about them which serves to distinguish them from Touhou, and is super adorable. Unlike some danmaku games, it's almost always clear what's happening on the screen. The backdrops don't intrude, and the only time you might lose track of your character is when a boss is preparing a special attack, at which point their portrait will scoot across the screen. You're safe during these intervals, though, so it's not a problem.
A very nice thing is the ability to practice all the stages on all the difficulty levels right from the get go. The only thing you'll have to unlock is characters.
There's also a section with information about the characters and their backstories, which I quite like.
All in all, this could pretty much be considered a Touhou Project clone. But it's a really well done one, and it's obvious that a lot of love went into this thing. I can't recommend it highly enough.

This game is really really fun but I do think its almost mandatory for you to use a mod to speed up the boat speed and everything because a few minutes in between every island is a bit much. -certain amount of replayability

-fairly challenging riddles/puzzles

what people may find frustrating because its a roguelike game, roguelike fans like this though

People may think that those above are cons but it is a roguelike game and to play the game with any other expectations is kinda silly. Only true con is the vanilla speed and pace of the game which is easily changed at your own discretion. I <3 this game though, the story is beautiful and the story is great, the game is surprisingly indepth, and there is no way you can find everything through one playthrough, don't be afraid to google when you are stuck though, no point in beating up something you dont understand XD.

This game is currently in Alpha, everything I say will be subject to change on full release.
That being said, for an Alpha I would say the game is very well developed. Moving on;
I would give the gameplay to start off with a solid 8/10.
As the Evolved, you have 3 charges of an ability that allow you to traverse terrain quickly and efficiently, as well as the ability to climb the terrain. The key as the Evolved is leaving no evidence of where you have been - Sneaking is key. This aspect allows you to bait the hunters into traps and allow for some pretty exciting battles.
As the Hunters, you have a jetpack that allows you to traverse similarly to the Evolved, however due to being about 1/10th of the size at an obviously limited rate - a key tip as a Hunter though is the neat feature they've included which allows you to dash covering more ground than you should be able to; Meaning the Hunters aren't so slow after all!!
I would say the graphics are about 6/10.
Currently the graphics aren't the best, however appears to tax pretty hard on the ol' GPU, running a GTX 780Ti on High pushes my graphics card to temperatures I've never seen it go to before (72+ degrees Celsius) however this could be down to low optimisation due to being in Alpha.
The method of unlocking new weapons/perks/characters in the game is a strange one.
For example playing as the goliath to unlock The Kraken requires you to deal a certain amount of damage with each ability on the Goliath, and it will not allow you to proceed with the next ranks of these abilities until you have completed ALL the abilities, this makes for some pretty stale unlocking when you want to unlock a new character.
Currently in Alpha there is one game mode - the hunt, this basically consists of the 4 hunters trying to find the monster and the monster hiding until it reaches its max stage and can take them all on (stage 3). This can get a little repetitive if you play the same class over and over, so the fact you have 5 different classes (monster + 4 hunters) can help spice things up a bit.
The Matchmaking system tries to get you your preferred role as often as possible, after reaching level 13 I have played the majority of my games as the role that I have selected as my first preferred role.
Meaning that this system works, however it can make for some long queue times meaning that this isnt exactly perfect.

Tropico 5 is a good game that has the potential to be great.  In this iteration, the developers seemed to have maintained the core mechanics that makes the game work and took several tentative half-steps in a new and mostly good direction.  This cautious innovation has produced mixed results.  Few of the new changes or features are bad, they’re just unfinished or poorly implemented and it becomes painfully obvious when one plays the game that they were not carried out to their logical ends.  And even though, on the whole, it is still a fun experience the game suffers because of these half-steps.
The Good:
-Ambiance and artwork.  Tropico is more scenic and beautiful than ever and the soundtrack is the best yet.  While I don’t find the humor in Tropico 5 to be nearly as amusing as Tropcio 4, it still maintains that sardonic sense of humor that is part of the Tropican experience.  I was also underwhelmed by the voice acting and characters.  While not bad, they lack the personality of the characters in 4.
-The Eras.  This is actually one of my favorite parts of the game.  I like the progression from era to era and the way national and international politics is different depending on which era you are in.  I like the continuity as well.  I like the aesthetic of having colonial buildings existing alongside modern ones.  I thought that the addition of tourist buildings that derive extra benefits from nearby colonial buildings was a nice touch.
The Bad:
-The almanac.  In Tropico 3 and 4, all the information that a diligent dictator needed to run a country was easily accessible and clearly presented.  In 5, the almanac, while still containing most (but not all) of the same information, has made it much less accessible and readable.
-Rebels, coups and civil unrest.  It is not uncommon, for me at least, during the cold war era to have an approval rating above 75% and yet still have a major problem with rebels which often number in the dozens and seem to spawn out of nowhere.  This relates to the almanac in the sense that it can be difficult to discern what exactly the problem is based on the information provided.  Sometimes when I examine individual rebels it is not uncommon for me to find that they are often gainfully employed, generously compensated, comfortably housed and give my regime high approval ratings.  This makes no sense to me.  In addition, the rebels seem overpowered.  I actually like the idea of not having exact numbers and perfect intel on rebel forces, it adds a level or realism to the game.  However the mechanics that govern their behavior and combat abilities seems broken to me.
-Missing Features and buildings.  This is, hands down, the biggest complaint that I have.  To give one example of this: the police now serve as law enforcement and fire protection.  The latter they do well enough.  The former I’m pretty sure they don’t do at all.  It’s maddening to see people identified as crime lords and rebels by the police, walking around without the slightest fear of being arrested or shot.  And in any case, there’s no jail, dungeon or labor camp to lock them up in.  That’s just one example.  There are several buildings, edicts, and activities (e.g. campaign speeches, official workplace visits from El Presidente, the secret police with their extremely useful and covert skillset.) that are missing from Tropico 5 that really need to be there.  In this respect Tropico 4 is actually, at this point, still far superior to Tropico 5.
The Half-Steps (i.e. good and bad):
-The Dynasty.  The most underwhelming of the new features, the dynasty function feels like it was tacked on at the last minute and is not fully integrated into the game mechanics which is too bad because I think there are some interesting possibilities.
-Research Tree.  While not especially deep or complex, this feature does add a nice progression mechanism to the game.  I like it much better than buildings simply becoming available after a certain year.
-The Tropican Army.  It’s nice to see that the Tropican armed forces have finally learned how to fight as units as opposed to individual soldiers.  It’s also nice that they’ve learned how to drive tanks and fly jet fighters as opposed to displaying them as useless set pieces like in Tropico 4.  That being said, it is very unfortunate that, for all their improvements, they basically still suck at what they do.  As far as I can tell, when the palace is threatened, all units (that haven’t already been routed by the super-rebels) will converge on it to defend it.  Other than that, there seems to be no centralized command and control mechanic that governs how your soldiers and their support vehicles behave.
-Multiplayer.  I have not tried the multiplayer mechanic and have no interest in it.  While I’m sure that there are those who enjoy it, I thought from its announcement that it was unnecessary and out of place in a game like Tropico and I wish that the resources dedicated to its development had been tasked to other aspects of the game that are lacking.

8 hours in and I still have absolutely no idea what people are complaining about. I've been an avid Tropico player since the very first game. I sank and hours and hours into Tropico 3 (on the Xbox360) and have a ton of time racked up on 4 as well. So when 5 was released and everyone started complaining I was kind of confused. I held off on buying the game until it went on Sale and let me just say that I think it is more than worth the full price.
So far it has absolutely everything I love about Tropico and more. No longer is it game over when the US or USSR decide to invade. You can defend yourself!
Your presidente gets a single trait, and all of the members of your dynasty get one as well, every time there's an election you can decide which dynasty member you're going to have run for office. You can appoint managers to your buildings which offers a bunch of different ways in which to modify the behavior of the game.
No longer are protests are just the populace voicing their displeasure. You can choose to negotiate with them and trigger an event that increases that faction's opinion of you if you complete it.
The import/export system has been overhauled to great effect and the trade system is absolutely a pleasure to work with. Same with the reasearch section which adds a new element to the game and removes the feeling that all problems in El Presidente's life can be solved by throwing money at them.
I have a mid-low end computer and even on somewhat low settings the game looks gorgeous. It runs smoothly and feels well optimized.
There's so much more I could probably go on and on about it. I honestly don't have any complaints. As someone who has played these games from the start I've had so much fun watching it grow and change over the years. This newest iteration doesn't disappoint and promises many hours of play in the future.

I loved Dungeon Defenders 1, DD2 is terrible. The connection problems alone make the game miserable. It generally takes about 15 minutes just to get our 3-person group into the same game, and then at the end of the map, two of the players can't get out of the map and have to force quit the game, then we get to try to get into a group again. On the plus side, they seem to have stopped the majority of the hacking problems DD1 had. Unfortunately they also lost the vast majority of the players so there's no real reason to hack anyway. This game was supremely disappointing.

If you and your friends are looking for a Hack & Slash/Tower Defense game that's fun, full of content, diverse, the ability to host your own server, local multiplayer, doesn't have towers that feel like♥♥♥♥♥ good graphics, loads of large maps, DLC that doesn't cost $20+ for a single hero, decent end-game, awesome boss fights, barely any bugs, doesn't feel like a mobile game, and isn't a cash grab... I highly recommend you to ignore this game, and go for Dungeon Defenders 1.
Dungeon Defenders 2 is the worst sequal to a game I have ever played.
It's literally a downgrade riddled with microtransactions and bugs the developers wont bother fixing. Boring end-game,♥♥♥♥♥♥poor servers, can't unlock DLC heroes on the get-go without gaving to grind for the medallions to unlock them, but they also give you the option to spend money to unlock these DLC heroes. How much? Too much. I've been playing this game on and off since 2014, and there's not a whole lot that's been changed or updated since. It honestly still feels like an early access game.
Enemies defy the rules of Tower Defense.
I can't tell you how many times I lost a game because a Lady Orc decides to walk around or OVER my defenses. You will always get ♥♥♥♥ed in the♥♥♥♥♥by these lesbian♥♥♥♥♥♥♥wielding Orcs if you don't place your towers in very specific ways. You also can't place towers directly behind a crystal because a jevelin thrower can penetrate every tower, which will allow them to damage your crystal.
Towers suck♥♥♥♥♥
They begin incredibly slow and rangeless. Your towers feel like they're struggling to take stuff out, and it will continue to be this way until you start your Chaos Trials, which is a huge grind. During Chaos Trials, you are awarded shards for every map completion, and shards power up your heroes and towers. Every 10 games, you'll find MAYBE 2 shards out of 20 that are actually useful. The other 18 shards will remain in your inventory taking up space. Each game can take around 15 - 20 minutes to complete. Your average hero will have the ability to build 4 towers. Yeah, 4. As opposed to Dungeon Defender 1's 5.
The engine is inferior to its predecessor.
In Dungeon Defenders 1, there's a tower the Squire can build called the Cannonball Tower. This tower was amazing because it fired cannonballs that bounced and rolled off every surface. When it makes contact with an enemy, it will knock them back and bounce away in a random direction. Very cool interaction. In Dungeon Defenders 2, the squire has a Cannonball Tower that doesn't shoot actual rolling cannonballs. Instead, it fires a "cannonball" that deals physical damage to one enemy. But, there's a shard you can equip that allows your Cannonball Tower to sometimes fire a real cannonball. You'd think it will act exactly like the Cannonball Tower from Dungeon Defenders 1. Nope. This little ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥cannonball rolls straight. Straight through enemies. Straight up hills. Straight up inclines. Straight. Up. Walls. There's no physics applied to the cannonball. Then you realize there's pretty much no physical interactions in this game.
Everything about this game is disappointing. And yet somehow, these guys crafted Dungeon Defenders 1. It's really baffling.
TL;DR: Do not waste your time playing Dungeon Defenders 2. Instead, play Dungeon Defenders 1.

With Terraria you get alota building functionality but... only one world, on the upside in Terraria you also get to transfer items on your character with you to other servers.
With this game Edge of Space you... get working building mechanics (barely anything to craft though), good music (when its not tearing horribly or desyncing), horribly slow mining, extremely aggressive enemy npcs that fight you based on how far down you go, and how pre-occupied you are not paying attention to your surroundings, and limited idea of how to really play altogether with out continued communication through the steam forums with other players, and the developer(s)/staff of Edge of Space.

*Note*
Still consider this game and check back on it though! It does show promise assuming alot of the negatives i've listed, not including thousands of other negatives listed in the forums are taken care of.

If you like platformers that require a little bit of thought and not so much of the rapidly quick precisely timed reflexes then this game is worth checking out.

If there's one thing to congratulate Five Nights at Freddy's for it's that it succeeds at being intense and oppressive even without the horror elements. The game could easily be about combatting viruses as opposed to the game's animatronics and it would still be as intimidating to play thanks to the management of power.
Much as the game loves to tell you otherwise, it's actually not a jump scare showcase. In reality, FNaF is about preventing the most sharp and uneasing jump scares through your effective management of power through the use of doors, your camera and the lights which reveals nearby animatronics. The other jump scares barely warrant as "scares" as they're basically just warnings to make you do the equivalent of a quick time event but in a very organic way that requires you to actually think. I welcomed it greatly, as the actual jump scares are not worth the build up the game gives you (though thus far, I've only died once by animatronic, all the rest have been power outtages). The game relies on you to be able to track the activity of the animatronics which greatly contributes to the fear factor.
However, tracking the activity of the animatronics essentially makes the game very much based on trial and error and the animitronics lose much of their creepiness factor once you learn how they operate. The sole animatronic to induce fear to me was Bonnie the Bunny, and it wasn't on account of his appearence (he comes off as silly in many of the camera shots), it's because he quite literally teleports to whatever room his can move into. It makes it near impossible to guess when he will show up outside the Office. Chica and Freddy have specific routes, and you manage how Foxy and Golden Freddy operate. Incidentally, Golden Freddy is a pathetic jump scare which is just unfair to new players. Lift your camera up when he shows up and you'll be fine.
Leaving that aside, though, the game does a spectacular job at creating an atmosphere as well as providing gameplay that encourages constant retries. Each night only lasts between ten to fifteen minutes in real time (assuming you don't die), which speaks very well for the game given that it can very quickly establish itself. Even if marred by Bonnie the Bunny and Golden Freddy, the animatronics all have personality and do well to work with the already intense power saving gameplay. It's worth playing simply to say that you've spent a night at Freddy Fazbear's Pizza.

A fantastically well executed player versus environment survival game.
The Long Dark strikes the right balance with struggeling to survive against a cold and sometimes brutal environment.
Expect to have many close shaves with death. Whether its getting stuck in a blizzard and finding yourself on 15% health and hypothermia, to contracting an illness after being mauled by wolves, to desperatly exploring new lands for medicine.
The number of life and death situations you encounter make sure you don't get too comfortable in the early game.
Despite the ever present risks of death, the player is given many ways to fight and scrap so you can survive a few more hours.
As the game processes, your survivability gradually increases as you discover renewable food sources and forage and hunt for the materials to craft cold resistant clothing and weapons.
The game so polished and well executed I didn't notice it was still in Alpha.

TL;DR: Cuphead is a great game with amazing visuals and a stellar soundtrack. However, in order to best some bosses, the game will require near perfection. This can be really frustrating, but the game never seems unfair. I would give it about an 8/10 taking into account price, visuals, soundtrack, length of game, and amount of "fun".
Pros:
-Nobody will disagree with the fact that the old cartoon style visuals and music are fantastic
-The boss designs are unique with each requiring a different strategy to defeat
-The game is hard, but never seems unfair
-Boss fights are not very lengthy (once you understand their patterns) so it is easy to pick up and play in your free time
-Beating a boss feels incredible and gives you an incredible feelings of accomplishment
-Replayability is unique because understanding a bosses phases from the start changes the fight
Cons:
-The Run & Gun levels don't feel as good as the boss levels
-Game is rather short, unless you feel like trying to S rank all of the bosses
-There are multiple weapons, charms, and supers, but I always found myself using a combo of 3 weapons, 2 charms, and one super
-The plane levels are nice, but I feel there could have been more levels or choosing of powers like normal levels
-That Dragon boss (probably the most annoying one in the game)
Review:
Cuphead is a very good game. Amazing to look at and listen too and interesting to play. The game is very difficult and most bosses will not be bestest on the first try. Or even the tenth try. Cuphead is all about understading boss patterns. Once you have died enough to understand how the boss acts and when they do what move you can choose a weapon kit, charm, and super in order to turn the tide and gain the advantage. Once you "download" a boss and are able to beat them, the rush and feeling of accomplishment is fantastic. That is why people are comparing this game to Dark Souls. The feeling of beating a tough-as-nails boss that killed you tens (or hundreds) of times is where the enjoyment of this type of game comes from. So if you like the masochistic feeling of getting beat up for 10-30 minutes and then finally doing some beating up of your own you will enjoy this game.
I did have some things I didn't like however. The Run & Gun levels are nice. In fact, I wish the game was based more around the run and gun levels and each level would end in a boss fight. However, these experiences are completely seperate. There are maybe 6 R&G level compared to the 18 boss fights. At that point they serve as an interesting distraction, but don't feel quite fleshed out. They do serve as an ability to get coins so you can buy weapons and charms, but I found that only 3 weapons and 3 charms were ever useful.
The game is also rather short. As someone who played solo and no co-op (so far), it took me about 7 hours. The replayability comes from trying to get better ranks as the boss fights. Playing them again feels good because you understand how the fight is going to work, but constantly banging your head against a wall trying to get that perfect S rank isn't my style though I won't begrudge those that like to. Going back and trying everything in co-op might prove more fun.
Overall, Cuphead was a good game and I feel like it was well worth $20. The going certaintly does get rough and some bosses feel invincible when you first start fighting them (GODDAMN THAT DRAGON BOSS), but overcoming the challenge feels great and keeps you coming back for more.

Short: Recommended. The Walking Undead Sims - just the bleak desperate end, no magic chainsaws or exploding zombies.
Who will enjoy this? Anyone who is a true fan of the zombie genre and lover of games that cover apocalyptic worlds (e.g. Fallout).
What not to expect: Left 4 Dead, Day Z, etc. This is not a game where you just run from point A to B on a small map shooting zombies all over the place. There are no "special undead". (I blame Romero for that stupid "smart zombie" part where they walk across the bottom of the river.) It's also not an MMO where the zombies are just the backdrop for mass PVP killing.
So what to expect: Imagine playing the Sims. Exit the game. For real, girls play that stuff. Start Project Zomboid. Okay, granted it looks a little like the Sims. But with zombies. And the rest is up to you. The most important thing is that you finally get to test the ideas you've talked about with friends/brothers ever since you watched your first zombie movie. "I would just lock myself in the attic and survive!" No, you won't. You will starve. And that is just one of the many mistakes you will make. Better make them in Project Zomboid rather than when the♥♥♥♥♥♥hits the fan.
Is it a 10/10? It isn't. Fair enough with the Early Access (writing this as of 2/17/2014) but any game that is asking more than $10 should bring something to the table. One of the things that will most likely bug you at first are the graphics. Now, they have improved since the game first appeared and will probably continue to do so. Another thing that might bother you is the somewhat clunky interface at times. This is mostly a matter of taste though. If you see Project Zomboid as a fast action game like 3D zombie shooters then it is clunky. However in my opinion PZ is more of a simulation and inventory management is an essential part of survival. You can't carry everything so you will have to be smart about it. "Did I just leave my antibiotics in the other safehouse?" Mistakes like that will kill you in a real life zombie outbreak, and so will they in PZ.
Worth it? I think it is. In comparison to the many other zombie games on Steam it does something very different. There are no special things going on, it's just bleak and desperate. In fact, it is one of the few zombie games where I felt anxiety. On my first playthroughs I basically was a total coward staying in a few houses in one neighborhood hoping for the zombies not to show up. And even when they don't show up there is this feeling that they might be around the corner. It's a game where, if you set off a burglary alarm you will actually do a facepalm and pull out of there as quickly as possible.
The future? Apparently multiplayer is in the works. While I would personally not join big/public servers because of the potential for it to spiral down into anarchy, I think it's great for coop with friends. Watch an "of the Dead" and then play a bit of PZ. Excellent. As for the rest, in my experience the devs are quite involved which is a good sign. Personally I'm hoping for a more gritty feel to the game. (More trash, crashed cars, random rubble, houses on fire, etc.)
