Do not purchase this game.
Now that you've got a conclusion, let's cover the reasoning.  This game is, at best, a pre-beta.  It's not stable enough to be a beta, the mechanics are either half broken or entirely unbalanced, and the game lacks enough content to be playable.
This game is unstable, and runs poorly even on a beast of a machine (3930k and 7970 GPU).  I've had numerous crashes, and the game occasionally just hangs for a minute.  During that time I've been destroyed by numerous enemies, lost progress, and lost items.
The crafting system is entirely broken.  Enemies level up several orders of magnitude faster than your equipment can.  There's no invincibility mechanics, so a swarm of enemies can strip even a well equipped character in seconds.  You bounce when an enemy hits under you, so you can be air juggled to death.  Numbers mean nothing.  You start with a paltry heath and shield, but coming back with 10 times bettter stats doesn't make you live longer, because the game occasionally just spawns a dozen enemies around you.  All of this is predicated upon oyu exploring, but that's realy a joke because any upgrade past to most basic will require hours of random tunneling to get anything.  The real kicker is the crap weapons.  You have to craft ammo, but even worse the weapons requiring ammo aren't great.
Content has recently been dramatically expanded.  The waiting for resources to process has been removed, and there's more to make.  Unfortunately again, this is useless.  You spend huge amounts of time now searching for resources, to synthesize into other resources, to synthesize into useable goods.  After all of that grind, you're left with gear which still allows the enemies to absolutely curb stomp you constantly.  If the point of this game is crafting, then they really need to go back and rebalance enemy strength, progression rates, and the insane cost of items.  There's no reason that you shouldn't have all research completed prior to finishing the second area, and even if you do some of the end game items require an amount of resources which literally exceeds those present on a single biome.
In a single sentence: this game is fundamentally broken and the rate of progression indicates that we'll see completed project in a few years at best.
Negative comments generally warrant some thought.  In the case of a review, you should provide the people who made the prokect a way to fix it.  Let's start there.
1) Stop trying to be Terraria.  You've got guns with and without ammo, crafting, and resource gathering.  That doesn't mean you are as good as Terraria, and you shouldn't invite the comparison.
2) Ditch your current crafting system.  It requires too many diverse resources, it's convoluted, and there's no 1:1 comparison for item utility.  Combining that with the random nature of weapons means I can get a weapon worse than my current one, while spending much rarer resources.  That's frustrating, but what's even worse is having dozens of different armors that show no clear progression.  You've got a needlessly complex system, too many resources, and none of it is balanced.  Stop adding more, and just get the bare bones in place.
3) Rebalance enemies.  They're cheap, their spawns are a giant middle finger to the player, and more often than not they have too much health.  Spending 45 minutes fending off the Head Hunter boss isn't a challenge, it's a gruelling grind.  This particular point is arguably compounded by the crap weapons choice.
4) Develop the game.  I'm going to be blunt here, you aren't putting any appreciable effort in here.  It may actually be huge from your side, but I can't see it as the consumer.  In almost a year I'm still dealing with poor balance, no content, and unfulfilled promises.  Either discontinue the game, or finish it.  Right now this is looking to be an alpha we have to bay for, that will never be up to beta standards.  I can tell you that I'll never be giving another cent to anyone involved with this project unless they've got a completed game.  This extended beta is absolutely worthless, because its triumphs are drowned in a sea of failure and unfinished code.
After 3 separate returns to this game, I'm done.  You don't deserve anyone's patronage, unless you can tell us when we're going to get something worth the money.  This garbage surely isn't.

Excellent town builder where survival of the population is the goal. Challenging, satisfying, unique.
You don't directly control your people, but you do assign jobs, building placement, resources, what they grow, what they make, etc. You are like a town planner who guides your population, and if they have the food and resources to do so, they will do exactly what you've planned. This presents a unique challenge, different from most games, and is very enjoyable once you get the hang of it. It's satisfying to see your town grow.
+ Visually looks good
+ Very few bugs
+ Full Steam Workshop support for endless modding
+ Challenging (Winter? Sickness? Food or tool shortage? You will learn the hard way several times)
+ Full freedom to plan and build the town over time
+ Simple, good UI
+ Well balanced gameplay
- Vanilla game can get stale (Workshop mods solve this big time)
- No vanilla way to make even simple terrain alterations (Mods solve this easily)
- Not enough starting conditions / map types (Mods solve this too)
Fully recommend this game to anyone who wants a unique take on the town building genre. This game knows what it is and does it well. It looks good, it's easy to get into, and has a very approachable learning curve that can be enjoyed by both casual and hardcore gamers. This game is worth the $20, you don't need to wait for a sale.

A wonder and frustrating puzzle - The Testament of Sherlock Holmes provides hours of gameplay that ease you into the role of consulting detective. Set as a rememberance by three small children, you go about London, solving crimes that, at first, seem non-related. With point and click clues, deduction boards and the creating of new items from what you've found, there's always something to discover! That is, if you don't quit after getting caught in the cutscenes. Often long and unneeded, they cut into an otherwise seemless gameplay. Perhaps replace them with requiring more action from the player would work. Need a place to hide? Don't cutscene, go find one!
Perhaps the greatest challenge personally, were some of the "boss" puzzles. Often, they come with little or vague instruction and no hint to guide you in the right path. Some are easier than others but if you're not Holmes yourself, perhaps have a hint page pulled up online. (That way, you still get the satisfaction of 'having done it mostly myself'.)
All in all, a pleasing game with graphics you grow fond of and an ending that tugs at the heart. The credits are displayed in a style that would suit better at the beginning of the game for they were quite well done. Instead of so many cutscenes, use this work as chapters? Either way, if you're a Holmes fan or love mind aching puzzles, here's a good game to spend some time with.

Short version:
Bioshock is a great game, still looks dashing, is set in a disturbing dystopian place and plays really really well.
Long version:
Bioshock is part of our modern video game history and as such should be played by those who can afford it and spend the time. Visually, this game is nice. Control and documentation/instructions, this game is not so good.
I picked this up on sale for $0.19 USD during Steam Summer Sale 2015. The value of the entertainment provided is at least worth a dollar, so this was in my opinion a good value.
This is basically a hidden object/click and find game with a few puzzles thrown in. There are 5 levels. A short game, but fun enough. The puzzles are a nice easy casual level. The hidden object portion is clunky. You usually have at least two different screens to look for your objects. Your insect starts in one corner of a screen, you click and hold to tell it where to go. You have a hint box in the upper right corner. You can use it if you get a bit lost. It takes time to replenish. The insect moves slow and the paths are not always clear/easy to navigate. You spend a lot of time going back and forth.
Some of the puzzles are not so evident as far as what you're supposed to do. For example, there is a puzzle that is basically a peg game. You have a grid of objects with the center unoccupied. You need to jump one object over another to remove it from the grid. Repeat until you only have one object remaining. Pretty simple. The problem was that there were no instructions telling you how to do this. You need to click and hold then drag. Artifact of being a mobile app/game for a touch screen?
The background music, is just that, background music. It's not an epic fighting game, it's a puzzle game, so the music is repetitive new age sounding instrumentals. Easy to ignore, but really, nothing bad.
Overall, get it on sale and it's worth a few minutes of distraction.

*So for the spoiler free part.* More or less the game is pretty solid it takes a unique take on an already crowded field of Batman mythos. Did I enjoy my experience? Yes? Was I at some points frustrated? Yes. If you're expecting a typical generic Batman game, or story you'd be wrong. There are a lot of things that you won't expect, and will catch you off guard. I don't know how to really feel about finishing it. It wasn't short, but it wasn't long. The story was interesting, but it wasn't groundbreaking. The game I guess was an average experience for me?
*Spoiler part* So some of the things that bothered me were the liberties they took with traditional characters. Arkham Lady I suppose would be the obvious character to point out. I mean I guess Vicki Vales character was alright in the role, but for the roel Arkham Lady was supposed to play, why didn't they just use Scarecrow? I feel that's what she was supposed to supplment, and I guess the character did alright in the role they did a better job concealing her identity than Arkham Knight did. I guess my next complaint would be with the Joker? I mean he plays such a minor role in the overall narrative I guess I was disatisfied at the backseat role he played here. Cobblepot? I mean he was alright. He was a supplement for the Joker (who was playing a backseat role), and for Anarky who didn't show up in this game either. I guess my biggest problem was the Thomas Wayne being a Villian arc. It was uneeded? It was there purely to stir up drama, and while the game was rather frustrating and you feel frustrated. The rumors are substainated and it kind of delegitmized Batman's backstory? You find out Thomas Wayne was a villian and his family was knocked off because Martha was going to rat out Thomas,... I don't know. It's not terrible? I just wish they would've just kept with the original narrative.

Ummm.  I guess I'll start with the positives for "Morphopolis."  It's graphically well done and pretty.  It's short (2.3 hours).  I bought it dirt cheap ($0.19 instead of its list price of $4.99).  And, that's about it.
Now for the negative.  For the most part, while playing it, you usually have no idea what you're supposed to be doing or how to do it.  It's one of those artsy-craftsy games that's exploring the boundaries of gaming.  Hand-in-hand with that, there is no win state.  You get to the end and say:  "Is that it?" (I actually had to check that I'd got 100% Achievements to figure out that it was over).  And, it's SLOW.  You move an insect from screen to screen, and the game cleverly animates that movement.  At a crawl.  It's and exercise in frustration because you have to crawl from screen to screen over and over again looking for little sprites buried in the scenery.  And, along with all of that, during the game, you don't even know if you can quit and save your state.  After an hour of this frustration, I really wanted to put it aside and recover.  But, I was afraid to quit because I was worried I'd have to repeat everything up to that point again.
So, if you want an "interesting" game with "interesting" art and "interesting" mechanics and can find this at practically nothing, go ahead and buy it.  Otherwise, just pass on by.

I've liked every tropico game to date (except for the pirate cove) and this one is no different. Of course, if you want to try out the game, you could just as well spend a little less money on Tropico 4 (or even 3); there are differences, but each of those games is pretty cool in itself. However, if you've played those games and are looking for more of the same yet a little different, this game will not disappoint you. The humor is still 'bad in a good way', there's a lot of nice surprises in it, and the mechanics (factions, world powers, economy, etc) are better than ever. Some functions seem to have disappeared (for example, I really liked making a tavern the secret police headquarters and than having secret agents dressed as barmaids) and others (like the 'managers') have not yet proven very useful. On the other hand, the sort of sexist job regulations (only women in taverns, only men in mines, only male policemen or soldiers etc) or gone. This was not a huge issue in the playability of earlier installments, but it kind of bothered me anyhow so I'm glad you can have GI Janes now. The fact that the timeline is longer (colonial era up to modern times) and the dynasty mode are nice additions as well. All in all, still one of the best and funniest games around, both for casual gaming and for longer marathons (it really is addictive).

I've just played the big alpha of this game and here are my impressions. Xbox one players will get an exclusive beta that will be available in January. For those of you who has never heard of this game; This is a co-op game where 4 players as hunters has to find and kill one monster that is also controlled by one player. The big alpha limits the monsters to kraken and goliath and there are only 3 maps. The game runs on Cryengine from crytek if your pc could handle crysis 3 it can handle this game. If the players play their assigned roles as assualt, medic, support and trapper, they can bring the monster down. This game is at its peak when the player who plays the monster can hide and evolve into a bigger monster.
Here is the problem, the maps are usually too small for the monster to get away from the hunters and they can track him via his footprints or the sounds he makes. So it wont take long before you find him and get into the deathmatch. Even if the monster manages to runaway there is a time limit for the monster to destroy a power relay in one of the maps.
This game is made by the same team that brough us left 4 dead 1 and 2. So i see great potential into this game it just needs more content in term of game modes. I hope we can see reduced loading times and maybe being able to practice with bots at launch in February next year.
Anyway, i think its a great game and everyone should try it if they get their hands on the invite codes but Evolve is not the E3 game of the show i was expecting.

The game has basis to be great.
But. From what I have played so far, it lacks a certain...dynamic to it. For example I find most maps too small for the monster to get away from the hunters, Too soon am I caught between the outer walls of the map, trying to escape them and feed and evolve, but They just track me waaaay too fast.
Also I feel almost bound by what the game sets you up to do, run, feed, evolve, run, feed, evolve, kill.
In between that I would like to be able to set up traps for the hunters and ambushes, mislead them by making false tracks, I would like to be able to do more, to have more choice of what to do then simply run and eat.
and IF I get caught by the hunters, It seems in the interest of the mosnter to stay and fight to the end in the dome, because the health you lost is gone... You might aswell fight through it, so far I've seen mosnters do this and mosto f the time they win I did it myself and I won too. Running once captured jsut doesn't feel like a good option. IT's too hard to get away from the hunters and you have to start from scratch feeding again... Imo there's just not enough dynamic to it. there needs to be more freedom and chances to make other choices. I find this lacking.
Hunter wise, I like the characters, I like how they talk in the game about each other, what's going on. It gives a sense of immersion you do'nt get in a lot of games like you get that here. And I think that's pretty cool.
the classes themselves are fine, their abilities are fine, some are cool. It's sometimes hard to move around with them, their jetpack full goes empty really fast at times, but That's more of a feeling and my lack of experience maybe, so I'm making note of it but it could jsut by due to inexperience.
The biggest problem I have with the hunters, is that I do'nt feel the need for teamwork.
Maybe it's too easy to work alone ? or a lack of fear sensation when going off alone. I don't know how but if there was some way to make you feel the absolute need to work together, communicate, stay in a group, make a plan. it would make it much more enjoyable in the long run.
Kind of like Left for dead, it's so important to work as a team and plan and communicate, it's almsot essential , because if one person fails, the whole team starts to get affected by it. I don't feel that in this game.
I fear that this game will spike at realese but will drop rapidly in the months after that in the state it is in now, it simply doesn't feel like a game I would play with my friends months or even years after a row, like I do now with l4d2.
A few ideas you might want to consider.
- Make the local wildlife more dangerous to the hunters, let them be a real obstacle between them and the monster.
- put in less birds to show the location of the monster, you move 20 feet and you got birds, another 20 feet, birds again.... too much birds.
- let the monster set traps for the hunters, let him lure them into ambushes by local wildlife and so on.
- increase the speed by which the hunters can move across the terrain, IF they get past all the barriers put up, let them move agile and consitantly across the terain towards their prey.
well that's my opinion of the game so far. I hope it get's better I Love the concept of it I like what I see there's a LOT of potential to it, it really is fun, but if you want it to be Epic, there needs to be some more work put into it.

Excellent town builder where survival of the population is the goal. Challenging, satisfying, unique.
You don't directly control your people, but you do assign jobs, building placement, resources, what they grow, what they make, etc. You are like a town planner who guides your population, and if they have the food and resources to do so, they will do exactly what you've planned. This presents a unique challenge, different from most games, and is very enjoyable once you get the hang of it. It's satisfying to see your town grow.
+ Visually looks good
+ Very few bugs
+ Full Steam Workshop support for endless modding
+ Challenging (Winter? Sickness? Food or tool shortage? You will learn the hard way several times)
+ Full freedom to plan and build the town over time
+ Simple, good UI
+ Well balanced gameplay
- Vanilla game can get stale (Workshop mods solve this big time)
- No vanilla way to make even simple terrain alterations (Mods solve this easily)
- Not enough starting conditions / map types (Mods solve this too)
Fully recommend this game to anyone who wants a unique take on the town building genre. This game knows what it is and does it well. It looks good, it's easy to get into, and has a very approachable learning curve that can be enjoyed by both casual and hardcore gamers. This game is worth the $20, you don't need to wait for a sale.

As an initial impression, close to the end of the 2nd Island, the game is fun but not nearly as punishing as the fanbase makes it out to be. Perhaps a lot of this is thanks to that one Journalist being horrible at the tutorial but the game is far from that punishing. Most fights barely last over 2 minutes. If you get a par time kill, you're probably under 2 minutes. For a "punishing" game that isn't a lot of time lost.
Most of the time spent on it being "hard" is spent on being risky with your tactics, or going for A+ ranks. The par times for stages aren't listed, so the goal is to just push the boss down as fast as possible. This also reduces how much you have to dodge but what you dodge will be far more dangerous since you'll be swapping to the shotgun for high damage. Most bosses reward distance and don't punish taking your time. So for a casual run through, you'll have very few issues.
You can argue that getting a high rank is the entire point, but there are plenty of people just going through for completion. There's yet still a section of these people saying the game is "so hard." Maybe they're more casual gamers (hence them not going for A+) and probably on the lower difficulty too. Would explain why the game is "so hard." Graphics & sound are good, especially for an adventure game where you usually don't expect much. "Hunt the pixel" is mostly avoided, though you may have to seek around a bit sometimes. There's brilliant moments where you actually feel like Sherlock Holmes when you're deducting the true circumstances of a crime, but those are outnumbered by dodgy moments where you're confronted with unconnected puzzles that really have no reason to be there. Fortunately all such puzzles are skippable, so you won't get frustrated. The story is interesting enough to motivate and feels like classic Holmes, with a twist at the end that may not be everyone's cup of tea but is certainly original.
Snap this up when it's on sale, especially if you're a Holmes fan. It feels slightly overpriced at full ($20 at the time of writing).
is the latest installment (as of writing) in a series that I haven't played. No knowledge of events in the previous games is required, fortunately; there's some allusions but you don't need to know anything about them to play this one. Your very first investigation serves as a tutorial on the controls, and you can simply go from there. This game does not rely on you carefully scanning every inch of the screen with your mouse until you've found the hotspot; you don't have to do more than get close enough and you will get clear indications of what can be investigated. At the same time, this is not so obvious that it takes all the fun out of exploring, and sometimes you do have to backtrack carefully to see what you've missed.
For an adventure game in particular, the graphics are good. You won't fall out of your chair in amazement, but character models and environments are all well done and fit the atmosphere of the story. The soundtrack does its job, in that you hardly notice it's there, except for one notably bad case of it playing with an intensity that the situation doesn't warrant -- things only start to happen in that location later, yet the soundtrack is ominous and frantic right from the start. The voice acting for both Holmes and Watson is excellent and the characters come across just right. The other characters are mostly believable, with two notable exceptions: one character who is required to pass for another with a British accent has a painfully obvious faux German accent that shouldn't have fooled anyone, and the actor voicing the main villain sounds like he's taking his cues from cartoons, with the only thing missing being an evil laugh. Both of these break immersion quite badly and mess up what is otherwise fine voice acting.
Enough about the window dressing, let's get to the gameplay. Here we get to both the game's best and worst parts. As in all adventure games, you walk around, gathering information and objects, and occasionally apply one object to another. Especially commendable in this regard is that when you do have to combine objects, this makes sense and is easy to do (like combining pieces of rope to make a longer piece of rope) -- sounds obvious, but there are many adventure games where you have to combine unlikely objects in bizarre ways to solve puzzles in the most roundabout way possible. You won't find such puzzles here -- whenever you need to overcome obstacles by combining objects it feels perfectly natural.
Unfortunately, what you will find are puzzles that are generic brain teasers (like matching colored balls in some interesting sense or rotating tiles) that have no believable connection to the story and are just there to make you stop and solve them. To the game's great credit, all of these puzzles are skippable after some time has passed, because it would feel really frustrating to *have* to solve them if you didn't want to, or couldn't. Some can be solved by trial and error, some are impossible to do that way, but almost all of them feel like they don't belong in the game and they don't fit in with the narrative. Apparently everybody in Victorian England used intricate locks that can nevertheless be opened without outside help to safeguard their valuables, instead of, you know, keys. The lowest point for me was a series of puzzles in an elementary school that really break immersion by their sheer contrivedness and lack of justification for solving them at all (rather than simply forcing the issue). Elementary, dear player? Hardly.
If those were the only puzzles, I couldn't really recommend this game, but it redeems itself with the deduction puzzles. The game's best moments come when you actually get to feel like you're solving crime like the great detective himself, carefully observing for clues and piecing them together in a logical whole using "deduction boards", where you choose from several logical (and less logical) alternatives until both the clues and your deductions line up. Solving these puzzles with a minimum of guessing rewards you with the feeling that you're Holmes himself, coming to seemingly impossible conclusions by eliminating the actually impossible. Even the "chemical analysis" puzzles, which are not really about deduction but about memorizing colored blobs, tie in with the overall atmosphere of crime-solving. The game could have elevated itself considerably if it had more of this and less of the arbitrary puzzles -- in fact, if they ever make another installment, I'd strongly recommend that they only do these deduction puzzles and no more of the mechanical ones. As it is, there are only three or four in the game, with the regular puzzles padding out most of the playtime.
The story is the other selling point of the game. The flavor is excellent, and when it works, it's worthy of anything Sir Arthur Conan Doyle has written, with both the mundane and slightly fantastical/unbelievable elements mixed together in a familiar way. The characterization is fine -- Holmes has his dry quips and stoic determination, while Watson is there to reign in his friend's unique brand of callousness where it's warranted, without coming off as a dunce (a common sin in other adaptations). There's nothing original here (except for the end, which we'll get to in a bit) and you've seen most of these elements before in other Holmes stories, but it's all well put together, with the exposition scene where Holmes recaps what's really happened for Watson before the final showdown being especially memorable. It doesn't quite exceed its source material, but it's a valiant effort nonetheless.
There's a twist at the end that might leave opinions divided on whether it's of benefit to the story (or whether it should be there at all), but I liked it. After all, this is only one of many stories told of Holmes, and if you don't like what this one's selling, you can always ignore it, but I thought it was a charming idea that I hadn't seen before. Not everything is wrapped up in a neat little bow and there are one or two spots that I'd consider plot holes, but I found myself intrigued and entertained. Overall the level is more "penny dreadful" than Shakespeare, but then, that fits the Victorian era nicely.
Bottom line: this is a strong recommendation if you're a fan of Sherlock Holmes as he appears in the Doyle stories. If you're just an adventure game aficionado in general, be warned that this contains some pure puzzles which have little or nothing to do with adventuring, and the remainder is probably not going to challenge you a lot. In either case, at the $20 that is its current asking price it's probably slightly disappointing, but this would be a good one to pick up on a sale.

An hybrid of IF and privateer genres.
You sail to various ports trying not to die, in top down, reminiscent slightly of my beloved Vangers. There you can interact with the text stories (quests), the larger of which spanning multiple locations. The stories are tied to the zeefaring side of the game by somewhat convoluted system of resources represented by little cards. UI was influenced by Fallen London (the previous, browser, game by the devs) as much as IF part of the game; you might want to try it also, to get the taste of the IF stories style, as it's free.
What makes this game stand out is the setting, of course. And the style of all the text quests. It's really very well done. The whole plot, as disjointed as it might appear to me after playing through maybe a half of a single complete run, is like a weird dream. The dreams do seem to be a frequent theme in the game as well. It's all one big weird tale. The setting's as dark as underground victorian London on the shore of a giant cave ocean full of demons, madmen, and other extraordinary stuff, can be.
Again, look at Fallen London to see if you like the writing style. The whole dark art also adds to the feeling of despair of the inhabitants of this strange underworld (some in-game illustrations for stories could use a bit of work though).
The most dangerous things for a captain in this world are not the beasts of the zee or dreaded pirates (there really aren't any as in, say, Pirates!), but resources, or rather the scarcity of them. There is fuel, food and also sanity, which just diminishes while you swim. Running out of any of them may mean death, but there are quite a few safety nets to prevent you from perishing too early. So if you play it smart and cautious, it's rather OK, but that means you sometimes have to return home before even getting where you wanted to go. The resource system makes you plan, which is also a part of your role as a captain of the vessel, right?
It's not all that obvious how to make money as well. There are very grindy ways to get income, but I haven't resorted to them yet (and the developers even outright tell you not to grind by trading the common resources). So all of that really does make you feel on the edge of that nasty permadeath. And you can even die from choices in the text quests!  You can continue your legacy if you work on it, with a new character getting some stuff from the recently deceased, but all the stories will be reset.
Monsters and other ships are very rare, and don't seem like much of a threat. They either get helplessly rekted by your guns or you run away.
The map is not too small, but not too big either. As fuel and supplies become less of a concern and you get new engines with more speed, the map size starts to seem smaller and smaller.
The NPC population density is relatively low. You can sometimes swim for a few minutes, and there would be nothing but the dark waters and the dim lights of your ship. It's quite atmospheric, when it's not boring. Also music is silent most of the time for some reason. Maybe the developers tried to make it more atmospheric that way - lonely dark zee, little ship in the middle of vast void. But that music would really sooth my zailors on their long boring trips with nothing to shoot at (or flee from, if you started the game less than two hours ago).
But when music does sound it's quite good and adds to the sombre surroundings. I liked it, but I can't say I was impressed.
While I already played for more than 20 hours on two separate runs (my first save got corrupted after BSOD, so I had to start a new game without any "previous character legacy" options), I don't think replayability is strong with this one. Early game seems tedious, and you just really have to force yourself to restart. But maybe I'm wrong. I still haven't finished a single run after all.
The developers seem to update the game regularly with fixes and new text quests and other things and there is also a fresh DLC. Looks like they really want to support the game.

Real fans of classic point and click adventure games will be ashamed to have played this. The core mechanics of finding and analyzing clues are grossly linear. And as far as I can tell, much of the story is filled out by Holmes' sporadic arbitrary narratives, which relate only vaguely to the clues you've gathered. It makes you feel like you just have to go pick up a prescribed number of rocks before Holmes divulges impossibly-omniscient information on the case. While this may or may not be in the style of traditional Sherlock Holmes, it is not in any way satisfying as a plot progression mechanic in a game.
Also the few puzzle-based asides are entirely self-contained and have little or nothing to do with the story or any details you may have observed. On top of that the movement, much like the GUI, is clunky and annoying, in all 3 of the view modes, and makes you feel like you have nubs for hands.
The "deduction board" is a fairly smart mechanic, but is ruined by the fact that it's closely tied to whether or not you simply clicked on certain pre-determined clue hotspots. It would be infinitely more challenging if you were allowed to simply examine the various scenes and fill out the deduction board yourself, instead of it breaking everything down to meaningless and often absurd multiple choice statements.
TL:DR; Far too linear and simplistic for a veteran adventure gamer, but much too tedious and clunky for casual gaming.

The first time I encountered this I thought "oh this is interesting" now I look at the analog gauge that shows the difficulty and if it's a hard one I think "this one's going to be literally impossible or at least really obnoxious". It gives you a shock and you have to try again. Again and again and again. Then you are successful and guess what... you go around the corner and there's another thing to hack.
Now back to Big Daddy. This big guy has a few different attacks, once you figure out the pattern, it's pretty boring and repeatitive. Even if you don't even really care to try you can just keep running into him guns blazing and just die and keep respawning and do it again and again until he dies. There isn't really any punishment to dying, You don't have to reload your game, just pop out of some respawn machine.
The story seems pretty interesting though, so I'll play through it and see how it ends, then I'll uninstall it and never look at it again.

The best zombie game ever created, and guess what. It now has MULTIPLAYER!!!! :DDDD
Basically, this game is "the story of how you died". I like to call it a simulator even though it has RPG elements like levels but levels feel pretty realistic, like if you're level 1 farming then the info on crops won't tell you when they're done etc so it's basically like real life. You can read books to level stuff up faster, and there's 5 levels in each category (there's lots of categories, like blunt, blade, carpentry, cooking, sprinting, sneaking and stuff liket that.) The electricity and water supply gets shut off after a few weeks in-game time, which means you'll have to prepare a big farm and water collecting barrels for when that time comes. Fighting zombies is pretty dangerous. Even a single zombie gives your character panic and that means reduced speed and accuracy, but the actual fighting is usually pretty easy, even tho it can be dangerous since a single bite can penetrate your skin and infect you, and then you're a gonner.
You can become sick from things like being out in the rain for too long or eating bad food and then you have to stay at home and eat lots of healthy food, preferrably equip a tissue so your character doesn't sneeze and alert zombies outside.
There's also the crafting aspect that everyone loves. There's so much crafting opportunities in this game, like you can craft a rope that you can hang from a window as an emergency escape route, you can get plaster powder, a bucket and some water, then paint and a paint brush to paint both normal walls and walls you've built yourself, you can barricade doors or chop them down completely, you can destroy walls and furniture with sledgehammers, you can build entire houses yourself (even though that's pretty hard and time-consuming), there's so much to do.
Please, if you're a zombie survival fan, download the demo. You won't be dissapointed in the slightest.

This is, as of right now, the review for Evolve Alpha.
Pros:
- Gameplay feels fun and fastpaced
- Level progression and badge system helps add variety to unlocking stuff
- Fun teamwork building
- Each character offers a slightly different way of playing
Cons:
- All the levels feel pretty similar, and they're honestly pretty boring
- The monster is incredibly unbalanced. It's way too easy at all levels to cheese the hunters, and, by extension, survive long enough to become Level 3, which is crazy OP and can easily steamroll teams.
- Stemming off from that, it doesn't really feel like the hunters have any early game advantage. The monster is weak, yes, but again there's the point that it's too easy for the monster to flee and escape attempted forcefield snares.
- If the monster corners a player on their own and brings them to near death, it's essentially impossible for the player to escape, as the monster's leap spam far outmanuevers the player's jetpack.
Suggestions:
- More diversity to levels. All the areas have pretty drab color schemes. Trying to add some crazy flora with bright colors, or bring some more sun into the level would definitely help.
- As the monster levels, it becomes harder for it to escape a confrontation, I.E it's slower, can't leap as far, etc.
My overall opinion right now is that it isn't really worth it in it's current state. We'll see if it's improved once it moves out of alpha.

Okay so I payed for me and my friends so I made a rather large investment, only after I had played the game on my own of course and found that this game given its current flaws is excellent.
1. balance- many I have seen are complaining that the monster always seems to lose, or that they are forced to play the monster, or that it is really hard to be the monster. well having played the monster for about 10 games I noticed that I won 7/10 of those games as the monster the only losses were the first 3 as I was learning how to be the monster. A lot of the "difficulty" In being the monster stemms from not understanding how to be the monster. You are NOT an unstoppable killing machine when you first start out, and arguably so even at level 3. What you are is a very dangerous predetor, so... You really need to act like one!. don't go rushing into fair fights, hide sneak, be cheap. focus the medic and trappers, be sneaky and mess with their minds, try to split up the group, because 1v1, 1v2 and even 1v3 IS VERY difficult for the humans to take you down, given you are aware of your limits and health and armor pools etc. The humans require ALL of their teamates to take down the monster at level 3, highly reccomended at evolve 2, and good for safety at level 1.
2. gameplay- the mechanics appear to be solid, the controls feel responsive, never once did I have the "Goddamnit why did you shoot when I clicked" moments, the monsters attacks feel VERY viceral, and feel fantastic when they connect with the hunters. The abilities are very powerful, and if the hunters aren't careful then they will easily die, even at evolve 1.  again however this game requires you to think and plan as both sides, for example in one of my games as a hunter we won in 1:45 why? because the monster thought he could fight us at level 1 with no armor. The weapons of each of the classes are unique and feel very nice, even the subclasses are very different and fun in their own ways.
3. bugs and general negatives- right now I haven't experianced any real gamebreaking bugs. I have however experianced a few annoying bugs. The class preference idea seams a wee bit broken, I had medic as number one, but when my friend joined it would place him as medic even thought his was at number five, well we learned that the icons bugged out, and switched representaions. my "medic" was assault and his "assault was medic. the net coding in this game is OK, not great but not terrible, the ques for games very a lot, sometimes people never load in etc. However this could easily be contributed to alpha
Final notes-REMEMBER THIS GAME IS IN ALPHA, alpha is not beta, they haven't done any optimizing, they haven't worked out what they want in the game, they haven't fully tested each character, they haven't fully tested the progression system, they haven't fully tested every monster. SO remember ALPHA is ALPHA and let's watch this game evolve..... get it?

Actually managed to get into the alpha, and all I can say is I'm blown away.
As the creature, you start off weak and hunted, but play your cards right... and by right I mean be sneaky, and soon you will evolve enough to turn tables and become the hunter. Sounds generic I know but this game does it so well in a smooth seasaw motion.
At first being the 4 hunters (Humans) Is kinda easy mode, and yes sometimes games can end fast due to an unskilled monster player or just dumb luck.
To give a rough idea, the humans have to find this one monster and shoot it to bits all while navagating through a harsh eco system filled with other annoying monsters. And the main monster itself must avoid contact long enough to feed and evolve (Get more skills, hit harder and become larger... up to the point where you're practically godzilla) All classes have their abilities. As predicted human abilities can combo together to create a trap of a sorts.
What is great about this game?
- Looks pretty
- Plays well
- Lots of room for customisation (Play styles through chosing different abilities and perks)
- Lots of potential for improvement
- Addictive and satisfying
- Cool little map thingy at the end of the game where you can watch everyone run around in circles
What is bad about this game?
- Can be fustrating at times if you're unlucky
- I guess some may call the gameplay repetative... I can understand this, but we shall see what things they add upon release.
Concerns for the game?
- The pontential to be destroyed by hacks, unfortunately such is the risk, but definately a game you want to pull out at a lan party.
Oh and on a final note, you can get some pretty funny moments. One game I got tracked early on as a monster, and they trapped me in a forcefield bubble, running around in circles I was using hit and run tactics up untill the point where I figured I was about to die. Running away I accidently wedged myself between two rocks, obviously my even my unevolved rear end was too big to fit through, oddly enough I stopped getting shot at, curiously I peaked around only to watch all four hunters run right around the rocks and myself, two to each side and continue off in the direction I was heading... thats when I realised that my back actually looked kinda rocky (Minus all the blood and wounds that had been inflicted... but they didn't notice that.)
Here is a tip, the monster can actually hide rather well, sometimes it might be best not to move at all, even when you are spotted, seems people are too much on the look out for movement rather than a big angry looking pile of meat.

This game has become (rightfully so) a major benchmark for citybuilders. Absolutely phenomenal premise and execution. Mod community is 11/10. Some of the mods, especially the Community Charter series, are basically free DLC that should really have at least a $10-15 price tag on it.
One of the greatest aspects of the game is that it plays so differently at a micro and macro level. The strategic differences between running a village of 10 as opposed to a city of >1,000 are challenging and rewarding as you learn them. You are continually faced with problems that evolve and become more complex as the game continues.
In the early game you will ask yourself "how many people can I spare to gather that iron to make tools?" In the late game you'll ask "how many dozens of people need to be in my iron mines to mainatin the supply chain? Are blacksmiths adequatly distributed so that every sector has enough access to tools? Will I have food/fuel shortages two years from now if I don't act immediatly?"
The game is really just a masterpiece. All the more impressive that it was created by one person initially. Buy it already.

Can't say I have ever played a better FPS shooter, or, at least, a shooter that has given me this much appreciation towards it. RO2 is by no means a normal FPS, it is hard, it is intense, and it is realistic. You'll find yourself mercilessly get killed if you are only just jumping in, and it doesn't take too long to realize the game requires you to play smart, calculatively, and, most of all, as a team, to do well. There is no room for those who play twitch "I shot you first I win" or lonewofl FPS players in RO2.
It's hard for me to actually write a review for RO2 now what I got this far, simply because the game is just simply matching my taste in FPS, and that should actually be what it comes down to if you're trying you decide if you want to buy this game. If you think you'd enjoy a realistic, difficult, and challenging, but a rewarding, fun, and intense game with emphasis on teamplay and strategy, I want to say that you will almost certainly enjoy this game. If none of those sound like the type of game you'd enjoy, and you prefer games like BF3, COD, or CS, this game either isn't for you or will be a rough transition.

This is my dream strategy citybuilder, with the mods. Alone, it is pretty great still, but there is a huge community that adds so much more to the game, and is encouraged by the creators of the game! The developers of the game even give example mods for you to download, use and examine so that you can make your own mods for the game! On it's own, howerver, the game is still great. I recommend learning to play it first without the mods so you can see what sort of mods would suit you best. Personally, I have found the aging mods the most useful, and the "pick me up" mods for the fields, so that when the farmers work the fields, they make a quick first pass to put the produce into containers, then a slower second pass to put the foodstock into storage. It has saved whole fields from suddenly harsh winters!
Pointers for starting out: First build a gathering hut, then within circle distance, place a forester shack. Then place one more gathering hut on the opposite side of the forester's shack, as far from the original gathering hut as you can, but within the circle of the forester's shack. Two workers per hut, and one forester. This will take care of food, and firewood/building supplies. (the forester will cut down and replant trees that shelter the food that gatherers pick up) Then build the woodcutter and put in one worker. This should keep you in good with food and firewood for a bit, but be sure to build them a place to live in, either a Boarding House or no more than two to three houses. Once you feel a bit more stable again with food, build a school, because the more educated your workers are, the more they can gather and produce. Also DON'T go too long without a blacksmith and tailor, so that your people can continue to work and be protected from the elements. A herbalist should also come early, so that the herbs can keep your people healthy.
Fields for crops should only come after you are short on land and space for gatherers and fishers, since they need to be a distance away from each other. Farming should not be bothered with early in the game; it consumes a great number of workers, and it can all be for naught if your field suddenly dies in an early winter or from a sudden disease that ruins your crop.
As for iron, coal, and stone; gather all you can around your little village. Once your people have to travel too far to gather more however, it is time to build mines and stone pits. If your people have "Warm Coats" and are plentiful on food, they can travel a larger distance with little risk to their health.
In any case, this is the Strategy Citybuilding game I have always dreamed of. Get it and enjoy!

TL;DR, co-op is neither co nor op.
I bought the 2 pack looking forward to a co-op city building campaign that my buddy and I oculd play together, maybe this was expecting too much. Load up the game (after stealing an old graphics card of his, because my dumbass cant read the stickies, or the game requirements), start the campaign, no multiplayer/co-op option.
Fair enough, maybe we expected too much hoping to play through the campaign together, maybe we can just jointly build a city, and go freeform/sandbox on it. the first time we get into game together (why cant we make private lobbies?) we start across map from each other, with "victory objectives", well wait a second, there was an option for co-op or versus, I must've selected the wrong one, because we are on opposing sides from each other, with no clear way to interact.
Restart the game, make sure we are on co-op instead of versus, pick a new island just because. Once we get into the game (not a knock at the loading times, it runs quite smoothly) it's apparent that no part of the "co-operative" gameplay will involve interaction between the two of us, he is on his side of the island, I am on my side, and we still have "team 1 victory points" Ummm, there is only one team.
His fright ships come in on their own schedule, mine come in on their own schedule. He accepts certain missions (such as sell us 3000 lbs of coco), I accept certain missions, on the ocassions that those missions DO overlap, our counters each fill up independently!!
Add to that the unchanging, bullet-fast gameplay (in which we don't have time to properly read the rewards/punishments, a slower option would be nice, if it could pause when dialog is happening would be friggin wonderful), and the complete lack of notification when one of us gets knocked out of the game.. oh and why do all of their buildings and civilians cursedly die upon their leaders flight? ITS A CO-OP GAME, Why dont you let the remaining/surviving partner take over the buildings?
this game has a LONG way to go, I am incredibly disappointed.
Avoid until, forever?

Although I've just started this game, I have put a lot of hours into it and I am enjoying immensely and heres why.
Each start of a new game feels fresh, a bit desperate (especially if you're not familiar with the map) and intuitively you give yourself a set of goals for what you need to find first. If the map is unfamiliar you first go wandering to find a suitable homebase or shelter at least but after a few attempts at the same map I find that it switches to trying to find the necessary tools of survival such as a rifle (which has random spawn locations) that you can lug back with you to the homebase and safety you know is there.
The next few days can be bothersome because you eventually run into wolves and they can be a chore to deal with but fortunatly there is Pilgrim mode for when I just feel like exploring the world. This has to be on a different character as you can't switch between modes in the same playthrough. It's actually a very relaxing game to just enjoy the environments and the layout of the maps while exploring and watching the changes of the day as time rolls by. There is no fear of danger or even of dying in the cold weather as it is mostly milder and soon you'll be wearing the top tier homemade gear from a crafting table. After exploring in pilgrim mode you can than return to voyager or stalker mode to give yourself a survival challenge where dangerous animals lurk and hunt you, especially if you don't feel like staying indoors for days on end sleeping and starving or dehydrating yourself to get to the next day on the bare minimum and want to push yourself to the next map.
There are currently five maps in sandbox mode. Each with a transition zone in between to explore and challenge. Soon there will be a story mode, and the devs continually add to the game mechanics I hear. From screenshots I've seen the menus have changed which inform your stats. Before it would show the meters filling to indicate the bad things happening to your character; like cold, or hunger. Now they drain which is more intuitive, I think. when fully  drained and things start to go from bad to worse there will be an indicator on screen telling which bar has been drained or is near empty. Icicles for cold, a stomach for hunger, an eye for sleep, and a droplet for thirst. Cold is worst but your condition can drop to 65% before suffering the consequences like getting hypothermia.
I think the fun of this game comes from trying to push your character to the brink and desperatly fighting to come back from it. Living through animal encounters where all your clothes have been torn to tatters and having to go out and hunt anyways because you need those skins for the repairs. Gambling on foraging for even more supplies like meds and bandages or plants when you only have a few more bullets in your rifle or a handful of flares to fend off wolves or bears. And finally when you are on the brink after a bear attack and you hear the sound of your own heartbeat as it slows and your character cant even walk straight as you bleed out. You at least have a chance to use bandages and run for safety but if you don't it can be an epic end to your run.
In short, I really like this game as it is right now but look forward to what else the devs will add. I hope they put in beavers. I want a homemade hat.

This is one of the best adventures games I've ever played.  The story was deep and immersive with unpredictable twists and turns.  Too many games lead down the same take it or leave it, predictable path but this game grips you and doesn't let go until the very last, moving cut scene.  This is the first Sherlock Holmes game I've played and I'm so pleased I chose this one as I can't see any others matching or surpassing this one.
One of the highlights for me was the way the games AI populated the Victorian world with an array of believable and authentic looking people, whether they be poverty stricken waifs and strays or high society.  I love just looking out the windows of their Baker Street room and watching the world pass by!
There's just one niggle that spoiled the gameplay at times and that was the AI controlling Watson.  When you're controlling Holmes, and Watson isn't off completing his own mission, Watson has this urge to get right up close to Holmes which often impedes Holmes' movement.  After a while you start to anticipate this behaviour and you go round him before he corners you.  It's an annoyance but overall didn't spoil the game and there are plenty of locations where they explore separately and hence this isn't an issue.
Pros:
*Character Driven Storyline
*Rich, Detailed Locations
*Excellent Voice Acting
*Cinematic Cut Scenes
*Perfect Soundtrack
*Thought Provoking Puzzles
*20+ Hours Gameplay
Cons:
*AI - Character Movement

Overall, I enjoyed the game.  It has a really interesting world, great atmosphere, good style, and for a game about the sea really captures that exploratory nature.  A neat twist to the rogue-like nature is that you can leave something(s) for your future games.  That said, this may be the longest perma-death game I've ever played.  You pick your victory condition at the beginning, and at least for mine it took about 45hours to achieve.  Thankfully, the counterbalance is that once you get the hang of it, its not a very difficult game.
So yes, I like the game, but there is room for improvement.  First problem...  the sea is vast and your journal sucks.  The number of times you are asked to do something and it's not recorded anywhere is infuriating.  I didn't start enjoying the game until I started keeping a log on another computer.  It would be a nice improvement to be able to keep your own notes in game (I ended with about 5-6 pages of notes).   Also, nothing takes you out of a game more than seeing a developer reference a requred DLC to complete a quest in-game.  Worse?   Developers who do this and only provide the DLC to kickstarter backers.  Yup, that's right, you can't even buy the Pirate Poet DLC, but you find out you need it halfway through one of your crew's storylines.
Lastly, I don't get the FTL comparisons that are scattered though the reviews.  Other than being from indie developers they don't have much in common.  FTL acceled at great and varied strategic combat while the combat in this is simple and takes no strategy.  On the plus side the story interaction here is varied with a rich world while FTL had a very bland story.

I guess a lot of people must be masochists because I found this game to be an absolute pain. Sunless Sea feels like an attempt to combine an FTL style rogue-like with an interactive novel by taking all of the worst parts of each genre and abandoning their qualities. It wants to absorb you in a supposedly rich and deep setting dripping with a sense of place but then has gameplay mechanics that seem expressly designed to prevent you from doing that.
Death lurks constantly as you have to try to maintain fuel, food and crew while fighting or avoiding the pirates and monsters that get in your way of exploring the pretentiously named 'zea'. Which sounds fun until you realise you spent the last ten minutes doing nothing but crawling across the mostly empty map with all the vigour of a sickly snail. Chasing after fragmentary sentances of bizarre nonsense and enough resources to just about break even. If you are unlucky and die then you get to repeat everything you've just been through all over again, the same tedious slog, the same boring fights and the same exasperating overwrought wiritng. There are ways to keep some of your progress between deaths but the prospect of spending long frustrating hours eeking out enough resources to acquire them drained any desire to bother.

I can't stand to play this game more then about 30 minutes to an hour. 90% of this game is hacking things: safes, robots, vending machines, etc. Everytime you hack something it's the same mini game - moving pipes around to get the fluid from one side to another, usually with obstacles. The first time I encountered this I thought "oh this is interesting" now I look at the analog gauge that shows the difficulty and if it's a hard one I think "this one's going to be literally impossible or at least really obnoxious". It gives you a shock and you have to try again. Again and again and again. Then you are successful and guess what... you go around the corner and there's another thing to hack.
Now back to Big Daddy. This big guy has a few different attacks, once you figure out the pattern, it's pretty boring and repeatitive. Even if you don't even really care to try you can just keep running into him guns blazing and just die and keep respawning and do it again and again until he dies. There isn't really any punishment to dying, You don't have to reload your game, just pop out of some respawn machine.
The story seems pretty interesting though, so I'll play through it and see how it ends, then I'll uninstall it and never look at it again.

I've never played a game that makes the player feel like they're truly exploring, taking risks, and constantly scrounging for money and items as well as Sunless Sea does.
Every expedition into unknown seas has to be planned for the worst case scenario, and every bit of loot you find is exciting, especially when you don't know what it is. I like to hoard everything I can in case it's useful somewhere, but usually end up selling it all because I need the money...
The game isn't nearly as hard as they portray it to be. I've explored about half the world (which is satisfyingly large) and have yet to die. As long as you keep an eye on your fuel and food and run away from (nearly) every early fight, you'll have no trouble.

It's...well, it's not dull, that's for sure.

This is the zombie survival experience I've been waiting for for a long time. While it consists of typical zombie survival fare such as looting houses and shops for weapons and supplies, fighting off hordes of zombies and barricading windows and doors, it offers many more unique facets of gameplay that set it apart from other games of the genre.
There truly is so much packed into this game, such as the "moodlets" which indicate current emotional, mental and physical state, not unalike the something from the Sims, or details as simple yet intuitive as hanging up bedsheets above uncurtained windows so as to break the line of sight of zombies, who would otherwise attempt (and succeed) in breaking in and murdering you. Foods rot without refridgeration, but then utilities such as water and electricity will cut off eventually, forcing you to stock up on non-perishables like canned soup or farming your own, and rain collecting barrels must be built. You can add an additional level to your house for a greater field of view and to reinforce your defenses. If you find even these features lacking, there is already a vibrant selection of mods to add even more to already rich game.
The best part is that this is only just the beginning for this game. There are so many features to come, such as local and online multiplayer, NPC's and animals (and therefore hunting as well) and I can only see a bright future for it. Yet despite it's the fact that it is still in an early stage of development, it is already enormously playable.
I strongly urge you to buy this game if you have an interest in the zombie survival genre, and I would like to remind you that every dollar aids the developers in it's creation.

Honestly, this game just doesn't do it for me. I wanted to like the game, I really did. Despite the game having some strong points (which I won't delve into, to avoid spoilers), while playing it, I tried to come up with a compelling reason not to refund it, and I couldn't. I loved The Stanley Parable, but this is completely different. There is no replayability, no secret endings, no special rooms, no real puzzles, it's just a story.
That's not a bad thing either, as my collection of TellTale games attests to, I love a good interactive story. But that's the thing, this is just a story. It's not interactive. It's hand fed to you directly from the narrator. Sure, you're pressing buttons to do things, but none of it really matters. It doens't help that, in the end, I just really didn't like the story.
As UnseenGalaxy noted in the comments section, the game wasn't meant for my entertainment. It was made to reach out to the developers friend. But since I'm not that developers friend, I don't really feel a compelling reason to pay for the privalege of being a voyeur to their relational delemma.
I hate to click the "no" button under recommendation, because obviously a ton of people love it, but I have to. My justification is this; If I could talk to my former self an hour ago, I'd tell myself not to bother, the game isn't for me.
In my situation, most of the negative reviews list the very reasons I don't like the game. I only gave it a chance because of the "Very Positive" user reviews (and I loved Stanley Parable). So, my recommendation to you? If the positive reviews really strike a chorde in your heart, and you just know you have to try the game out, then please do, I'm "Very Positive" that you will like it.
If you, like me, reading the other negative reviews feel that the game probably just isn't for you, then trust me, it's not.

I grew up as a Sherlock Fan, so I try to get my hand on anything Holmesian.  All the other games in this series came out before 2008, so the old graphic prevented me from playing the game through.  That is why I was delighted when I saw the trailer for this game on TV.  Wow, an adventure game making a TV spot!  It must be good!  I guess the fact the BBC mini-series was so popular helped.
I bought this game on Steam when it was on sale through Humble Bundle in Oct 2013, and it took me about 3 month on and off to finish it.  I guess my mind has been too used to fast paced shooters and could never play for more than 30-60 minutes at a time.  Nevertheless, I enjoyed the time.  It took me about 17 hours to finish and that is with the help of looking up answer online.
There are a lot of puzzles, but I suppose that is what you want in a thinking game.  Sherlock has to unlock a lot of… well locks.  The puzzle basically all makes sense, but a LOT of them does not give instruction on how to solve it.  I guess that is real life, there is no instructional manual.
If you stare at a puzzle for about 5 minutes, then the game give you a chance to just skip the puzzle and get on with story.
This game does feature a nice story.  As I play through it I do enjoy the twist and turn.  You get to play Sherlock, Watson, and even their dog Toby.  You cannot die in the game, nor is there any timed puzzle.  Despite the trailer showing a lot of brandishing of guns, and a lot of graphic depiction of dead bodies, most of the game involves non-violent solution where you have to trap someone or create distraction to sneak past an obstacle.
There are some confusing story plot points.  One is the chase of the suspect Henry to Wharf 321, for me it did not make sense how it fit into the main plot.  Another one is when Sherlock brought cake to Judge Beckett’s house, it is the only times in the game where you see him carry something, but why would he carry cake?   I know about the plot twist in the end but it was never explained well.
It is fun to see Sherlock and all the gothic element of the Victorian era.  Watson came off as a well-rounded character; he did serve in the Afghan War and definitely uses his medical skill in the game.  Sherlock is cool as always.  The graphic is pretty good.  So play it if you are an adventure fan, and play it if you like a good mystery, just know there is no arcade action at all in here.

Quick pros and cons of Tropico 5
Pros:
-Grander scope
-You can research techs (as opposed to Modern Times where you had to wait for buildings to unlock)
-Constitution is a fun dynamic
-Trade routes are a great addition and extra docks are more than just another pick up point for exports
-New edicts and edict system ("freebies" to the people aren't a sure fire way to please the people I've actually had to repeal free food in some cases)
-More unique raw resources and industry options
-More robust politics and diplomacy
-No more "one economy fits all" economic strategies
-Less "build building x to make people y happy" missions
-Campaign is greatly improved, you play on two islands that remain unchanged mission to mission
-Building upgrades no longer exclusive to industrial and residential buildings
-"Repair All" button after a disaster is a welcomed addition
Cons:
-Learning curve might be a little steep for newcomers compared to older Tropico games
-Politics can be muddled at times
-Spending money to explore the island is dumb
-Invasion combat seems one sided as my defenders have only won twice despite being fairly robust
-Building aesthetics through the eras are unchanged
Other Thoughts:
-Managers system is a little useless in the early game
-Dynasty system is interesting but there's no real introduction to it
-It's slightly more difficult to gauge what your citizens want so popping up a few churches, clinics, and markets is not a sure way to make your early game citizens happy
-I saw a lot of reviews saying most of the humor was taken out of the game which may be true when it comes to building descriptions and the radio broadcasts but the dialogue of your advisers and foreign powers is still pretty funny
If you're a fan of the Tropico franchise or city builders this game is easy to recommend. However, if you were expecting the same old Tropico you may be little disappointed at first.

Let me share a story with you before my review. It's quite long, but it really was one heck of a ride and I hope you enjoy it as much as I did.
>Crash plane in probably Canada. Cold as hell
>Run down a hill trying to find shelter, fall and sprain various limbs. Limp towards a cabin. Find some stuff.
>Keep walking forever until I see a logging camp. Find more stuff, keep walking.
>Find a ranger outpost, find a few bits and bobs but not much.
>Make a fire for the night and try to sleep under a train bridge. Wake up cold after my fire goes out during the night and I'm getting cold.
>Wander until I find the enterance to a dam facility. Dark as all night inside. Remember I have flares, use one.
>Find more flares and a lamp with fuel. Spend my night scouring the facility for supplies, find some useful stuff.
>I need to find supplies so I don't sleep. Wander until I eventually find my way outside to a balcony of sorts on the other side of the dam.
>Walk down the snowy path to a frozen river. Figure something must be nearby so I walk along it and eventually find a cave with some wood. Getting really, really tired but it's daytime and I don't want to waste daylight, but I sleep anyways. Wake up with a few hours of light left.
>Keep walking until I find a cave system. Figure it leads somewhere, it doesn't. It gets dark so I spend the night there with a fire made of wood I found and chopped in the cave. I toil the hours away sewing my clothes, cooking meat I found on dead animals, melting snow.
>Come daylight I'm ready to roll. Wander until I reach the end of the river. I can't find anywhere it leads to. Nothing.
>Keep searching for some buildings or something, but can't find anything. Getting cold so I decide to backtrack to the dam and try my luck on the side I came from.
>As I ascend the slope to the balcony it gets dark and I get sleepy. A blizzard starts to set in, but I don't think it will be an issue.
>I see another balcony across the dam, so I cross the small ledge of the dams' wall to it. Find some palettes for firewood. >I start freezing to death. I make a fire, add the wood I found and figure it will last 5 hours like it says it will.
>Tired, so I try to place my bed roll down. Not enough room on the ledge so I move it a few feet away into an alcove in the wall.
>Think I'm close enough to the fire so I sleep for a few hours.
>Wake up suddenly. I'm freezing to death. My vison is blurry and my movement is lurching. Frantically make a fire. It fails so I try again. It works. Maybe I won't die after all...
>I heat some soup and make some snow water. Unbeknownst to me, my fire is dying and I'm still barely not dead from the cold. Fire dies. I walk over (Trying my best not to fall to my death) and chop a palette into wood. Takes 45 mins and now my vison is getting blurrier.
>Run to the fire and add the wood. Watch it all get eaten up in a matter of seconds due to the cold. Panic and run towards the door to go inside the dam.
>For some reason it won't let me open it when clicking. I think maybe somehow it's too dark for me to find the door and open it? I don't know what's going on. I frantically chop some wood and try to make a fire. It fails. Too windy. Light my lantern, but it doesn't help. Poof lantern dies. I click on the door like a madman, but to no avail.
>I try to make another fire, it fails. I decide there's only one thing to do. I make my peace. The door has bested me.
>Fling myself off of the dam and fall to my death. RIP.
In conclusion, those 3 and a half hours were the most frighteningly intense and immersive I've ever experienced in any game. I felt the emotions as if they were real. Fear, desperation, hopelessness. I heard this game was good and it was on sale so I bought it. Nothing could have possibly prepared me for how great this game is. It is an absolute masterpiece. The art is beautiful, and the world feels believable. The gameplay is nearly seamless, and it's insanely fun. If you're considering this game, but it right now. I promise you'll love it. It's worth every penny.

If the map is unfamiliar you first go wandering to find a suitable homebase or shelter at least but after a few attempts at the same map I find that it switches to trying to find the necessary tools of survival such as a rifle (which has random spawn locations) that you can lug back with you to the homebase and safety you know is there.
The next few days can be bothersome because you eventually run into wolves and they can be a chore to deal with but fortunatly there is Pilgrim mode for when I just feel like exploring the world. This has to be on a different character as you can't switch between modes in the same playthrough. It's actually a very relaxing game to just enjoy the environments and the layout of the maps while exploring and watching the changes of the day as time rolls by. There is no fear of danger or even of dying in the cold weather as it is mostly milder and soon you'll be wearing the top tier homemade gear from a crafting table. After exploring in pilgrim mode you can than return to voyager or stalker mode to give yourself a survival challenge where dangerous animals lurk and hunt you, especially if you don't feel like staying indoors for days on end sleeping and starving or dehydrating yourself to get to the next day on the bare minimum and want to push yourself to the next map.
There are currently five maps in sandbox mode. Each with a transition zone in between to explore and challenge. Soon there will be a story mode, and the devs continually add to the game mechanics I hear. From screenshots I've seen the menus have changed which inform your stats. Before it would show the meters filling to indicate the bad things happening to your character; like cold, or hunger. Now they drain which is more intuitive, I think. when fully  drained and things start to go from bad to worse there will be an indicator on screen telling which bar has been drained or is near empty. Icicles for cold, a stomach for hunger, an eye for sleep, and a droplet for thirst. Cold is worst but your condition can drop to 65% before suffering the consequences like getting hypothermia.
I think the fun of this game comes from trying to push your character to the brink and desperatly fighting to come back from it. Living through animal encounters where all your clothes have been torn to tatters and having to go out and hunt anyways because you need those skins for the repairs. Gambling on foraging for even more supplies like meds and bandages or plants when you only have a few more bullets in your rifle or a handful of flares to fend off wolves or bears. And finally when you are on the brink after a bear attack and you hear the sound of your own heartbeat as it slows and your character cant even walk straight as you bleed out. You at least have a chance to use bandages and run for safety but if you don't it can be an epic end to your run.
In short, I really like this game as it is right now but look forward to what else the devs will add. I hope they put in beavers. I want a homemade hat.

Actually managed to get into the alpha, and all I can say is I'm blown away.
As the creature, you start off weak and hunted, but play your cards right... and by right I mean be sneaky, and soon you will evolve enough to turn tables and become the hunter. Sounds generic I know but this game does it so well in a smooth seasaw motion.
At first being the 4 hunters (Humans) Is kinda easy mode, and yes sometimes games can end fast due to an unskilled monster player or just dumb luck.
To give a rough idea, the humans have to find this one monster and shoot it to bits all while navagating through a harsh eco system filled with other annoying monsters. And the main monster itself must avoid contact long enough to feed and evolve (Get more skills, hit harder and become larger... up to the point where you're practically godzilla) All classes have their abilities. As predicted human abilities can combo together to create a trap of a sorts.
What is great about this game?
- Looks pretty
- Plays well
- Lots of room for customisation (Play styles through chosing different abilities and perks)
- Lots of potential for improvement
- Addictive and satisfying
- Cool little map thingy at the end of the game where you can watch everyone run around in circles
What is bad about this game?
- Can be fustrating at times if you're unlucky
- I guess some may call the gameplay repetative... I can understand this, but we shall see what things they add upon release.
Concerns for the game?
- The pontential to be destroyed by hacks, unfortunately such is the risk, but definately a game you want to pull out at a lan party.
Oh and on a final note, you can get some pretty funny moments. One game I got tracked early on as a monster, and they trapped me in a forcefield bubble, running around in circles I was using hit and run tactics up untill the point where I figured I was about to die. Running away I accidently wedged myself between two rocks, obviously my even my unevolved rear end was too big to fit through, oddly enough I stopped getting shot at, curiously I peaked around only to watch all four hunters run right around the rocks and myself, two to each side and continue off in the direction I was heading... thats when I realised that my back actually looked kinda rocky (Minus all the blood and wounds that had been inflicted... but they didn't notice that.)
Here is a tip, the monster can actually hide rather well, sometimes it might be best not to move at all, even when you are spotted, seems people are too much on the look out for movement rather than a big angry looking pile of meat.
