So far this game is coming along quite nicely. I think I will discuss some suggestions that could increase the end product of the game and leave the superllatives for another review.
First; I think this game has some unfair aspects. It seems like everytime you gather all the food you end up using it up too quickly. An attack is almost gaurenteed to have you use some of your health recoveries even with a good set of equipment. Out exploring and come across a larger enemy you are most likely to use half of your resources. Depending on how muchh you actually hoard, but you always encounter something during gatherings and that eats it away. Especially against a bear or a bison. If you go mining you will come across quite a bit of enemies and if you arent at capped health you could die. For some reason the mines tic away your health... If you come across a troll, you better be very well prepared for you are going to use up all of your food and potions. I also think its unfair that said trolls gaurd treasures that actually help you craft the better equipment needed to help take out these enemies. So with all of that said I thhink you should be able to recover your HP while inside your base...Have it tic up just as the mines tic down. It takes time running from point A to point B shuffling through your chests and crafting your goods, so I think having a small regenerating health while inside your base would be more fair.
Second I think that there should be a way to craft extra inventory space. There are so many different resources that you need to survive and progress that all too many times I am having to return to the base to empty the inventory...Maybe a craft for extra backpacks. Its not very fair when you have to carry around a good number of food on top of what you collect.
Third, it seems like the defensive percentages dont really add up. Skeletons seem to drain almost just as much with a nice set of armor compared to low quality. When you get some of these rare armors the trolls still kick your♥♥♥♥♥quite frivolously.
Fourth I think there should be a potion or a charm that makes you run and fight faster. If there is already in the game and I havent found it yet I apologize but I played about 12 hours now. I know its still in early access.
Lastly I think there should be more information on the UI on controls. Been many times where I accidently ate something when trying to move a stack or divide items. Thats just me though.
I hope the devs read this and takes some of these suggestions to heart. I know its in early access and I hope its stuff they are already working on. With all thats said this game is excellent and I recommend it. It's addicting and unique. Its still clunky and unbalanced but fun. Good price.
Keep up the good work guys. Love it.

I'm going to give this game a thumbs up with a bit of a caveat...
First of all, the game is exactly as advertised: Early access alpha, period! If you are interested in this game you had best fully understand what that means. That being said, this game is awfully addicting. It does take a while to get used to... infact when I played the Demo I was not all that impressed, however, after getting used to the combat system and rough UI the game truly turned out to be a gem. Now this is comming from someone who plays Rust, Dayz, Minecraft & other open world games with a survival twist. I'm not going to go into features cause many other reviewers have done that already and being an alpha release means that features are subject to change. What I will say is that you are getting exactly what they advertise.
The caveat is this: This game is being developed at a snails pace. Keep in mind that this game was first released in early 2011. It's not to say that I'm particularly turned off by this as I know that this small dev team, and the community, is pouring thier heart and souls into this project; however, I do know that most people's expectations on speedy updates will not be satisfied. Just take a look at "7 days to die" reviews to see what I mean. That being said, also take into consideration the price difference of the two games.
IMHO, Project Zomboid is fairly priced for what you will get. A fun game that will (slowly) get more fun at a great price.
BOTTOM LINE:
1. If you are looking for a game that is near its end product, look elsewhere.
2. If you have no imagination or crativity, look elsewhere.
3. If 15$ is not that big of a deal to you, BUY THIS GAME NOW!
4. And for god's sake, if you buy this without first playing the demo ... shame on you!

This is a really good strategy game. It is NOT a city-building game, and not really a puzzle game, though it looks like both. It involves placing city elements (houses, parks, warehouses, shopping centers) onto an isometric grid via cards in your deck. The grid regularly scrolls forward, opening up new squares to fill and "scoring" the elements you've already placed (and consigning them to some eternal limbo as they are left behind).
Many elements are worth points (+1, +2, etc.).  Other elements affect the board (and surrounding squares) by adding, subtracting, multiplying, and nullifying scores in specific ways. Although Concrete Jungle is way too complex for my little mind, I recognize it as a very good game. This game is for you if:
* You like "deck-building" games that require you to adapt to random draws
* You can think several moves ahead... no really, several moves ahead. Not just two.
* You want games with solid, colorful graphics.
* You are not easily frustrated by strategy games (like me).
* You don't mind reading (and skipping over) the same dialogue OVER and OVER. And OVER.
Me? I keep playing the first few levels. I can win those. It's really fun!

"a zombie game thats main focus was the elements of survival not the zombies themselves"
I followed this game about a year before it popped on steam, unfortunately, I lost my previous copy due to tranferring computers. But I bought a second copy and noticed the improvement. This is a game where you die. No avoiding it. You just die eventually, which i've seen a few people question what the point was. Theres your answer. But its dependant on how soon you die, how your fate is sealed, is what makes this game enjoyable.
Graphics are simple, but improved before early access. It does use a console though, which says something. Options isn't high quality, but its acceptable.
The game is quite impressive of making you learn from your mistakes. You get to create a character and apply him with perks and also change how the world works. The perk system is a counter-weighing system, allowing you to have positive perks, as long as you weigh it with negatives. The game itself is quite difficult at first, any encounter with a zombie can have you infected and dead, but if you really want to, you can live with the infection, it'll just be harder. Zombies themselves are quite brutal, but easy when alone. they have senses, so guns shouldn't be your first option and you should allways make sure your not being stalked. Random events occur aswell, such as burgular alarms, gunshots and helicopter flybys. Don't expect to be saved though, these just rile up the zeds.
Personally I've been looking for a zombie game thats main focus was the elements of survival not the zombies themselves, and this is what the developers seemed to be achieving, however it just needs more mechanics and complications. Being in early access does mean it'll be improved and I can't wait to see the final product.

The Asymmetric gameplay is very fun. Nothing like playing as a Goliath and hunting down Prey, and then humans.
Besides the Goliath I also played the Medic for a good amount, and it was very fun.
The game uses the CryEngine, and not only looks good but plays extremely well when on High, with Tessellation on and FXAA. The game does use a lot of VRAM at the moment, easily using 4+GB of graphics memory during heavy combat with lots of effects.
Effects which are fantastic looking.
Each class plays a vital role, and team play is extremely important. I would heartily recommend you play with friends as a team over voice comms. You're sure to have fun, especially if you liked games like Left 4 Dead, which was also created by the same developer.
Alpha Game Footage at 60 FPS
Don't be too concerned with performance either. I managed to play and record the game at 55-60 FPS without issue on a single AMD FirePro D700, which is the equivalent to an R9 280X in gaming.
Sadly there is no AMD Crossfire support yet, and if you have it enabled you will see horrible negative scaling. I actually ran at about 15-40fps with Crossfire on. With dips as low at 5fps.
I'm still extremely surprised how well the Alpha plays, and the performance offered so far on a single graphics card.

When you finally clear a level in SUPERHOT, you feel like you've stepped out of an action movie and, well, into another action movie. This feeling is tempered by the existential pain of taking a bullet to the back... for the hundredth time... on the same level. Even though one of the major attractions of SUPERHOT is getting to be Neo for a day (so to speak), it doesn't give you that feeling easily, and for most of my time playing it, I felt more like a Stormtrooper with no armor. If I'm going to spend my time playing a game (instead of writing a largely irrelevant review that isn't even funny), I'd like to be enjoying that time, and I can't say that's the case with SUPERHOT.
In addition to the frustrating gameplay, SUPERHOT contains a confusing conundrum of a story, which is, moreso than the combat, the main attraction of the title. However, I'd have to say the game's plot isn't worth your time either. It raises some interesting questions about simulated reality, free will, and violence, but it never really delivers a satisfying answer to any of them. If you want to ponder such things, there's no need to spend your money or your time on a game that isn't fun most of the time you play it.

As a kid, the majority of my gaming in this area was with Sim City and other tycoon games. Generally faster paced management on a large scale. Sim City especially is an example where if you try to limit yourself to a small scale you will flounder and fail. Banished is a wonderful, relaxing alternative.... Relatively... It induces stress but the good kind.
First off, banished takes place on a much, much smaller, slower schedule. A small population that you must carefully grow but also choose where to quickly expand. Focus too much on farming and while you may be fed, you'll find your little colony freezing from a lack of firewood and inefficient homes. Try to focus on educating your students and you may have to take them out of the school to meet the demand for food. You don't just sit back and watch your little group on fast forward. You have to keep an eye on it at all times. You find yourself drawn in. Caring about the people, they all have names and finite lives. I actually feel the weight of losing them. You don't just lose a person, especially when its in this game. If you don't plan and prepare for the loss of people you may find yourself without a critical supply of tools which can spell doom for your little settlement.
I can easily give this game a 5/5 or 10/10. It is well build, runs exceptionally well, and as an added bonus actually makes you learn. This isn't a game that you just play. You have to actively grow with it. With steam doing awards. I've decided to create my own for the sake of rewards.

Usually it takes me maybe 6 hours of game time to post a review because by then I can sort of gauge wether I recommend a game or not, but Cuphead made me do this differently.
After 11 hours of gameplay in order to play the game to completion, I can assure everyone that Cuphead is absolutely worth your attention.
---------------------------------------------------
REVIEW STARTS HERE
---------------------------------------------------
Story:
As per its cheeky pre Hays Code Cartoon aesthetic, the story of Cuphead is actually pretty dark.
Two anthropomorphic cups named Cuphead and Mugman wander too far from home and end up in a casino. Cuphead, blinded by a large winning streak at the craps table, decides to make a bet with the devil, and obviously he loses. As a result, Cuphead and Mugman are forced to hunt down and collect the souls of the Devil's other debtors, whom will serve as your bosses. A simple story that the developers make sure isn't sidelined during the course of the game, which is nice.
Graphics and Audio:
This game's graphics and audio is a shining example of the passion that Studio MDHR had for this project. Each character, animation, background, and so on is hand drawn in that sort of iconic 1930's cartoon style and not once is the illusion that you're playing a cartoon ever lost or even skewed. The game is absolutely gorgeous to look at and the sound design is even better. With the 1930's and the sort of limitation of technology of the time, sound quality in media was often grainy and sort of muted. This fact remains with Cuphead, but the beauty of this sort of sub par and scratchy sound is that it in fact even improves the immersiveness of the game. The music is exceptional and sounds like it's ripped straight from a record of the era, from the somber barbershop quartet singing about cuphead's woes on the game's title screen, to frantic and upbeat big band tracks that seem almost neverending as you run jump and shoot your way through a wild boss battle.
Gameplay
I'm not going to do the usual "this game is like dark souls" thing. This game is DIFFICULT. Sometimes infuriatingly so, but the beauty of the game's inherent "just one more try" design is that Studio MDHR knows exactly how to keep you glued to it, and in this case it's as simple as showing you how close you are to the end of a fight if you die at any point. It's a tease, it's engrossing, and it works. As far as the controls go I'd recommend playing the game with a controller as the game was clearly developed with this type of scheme in mind. The controls are super tight and you'll never die from your character floating into some projectile that you mean to avoid after you stop moving. There was only one instance where I felt like I was damaged by nothing at all and this wasn't until the very end of the game, and although admitedly I was very angry, I told myself "It's Cuphead" and moved on to finish the game.
Boss variety is where the creativity of the development team really shines. Not a single boss mechanic is redone or rehashed in some way and every single boss is a unique fight. And what's even more impressive is that the entire game is made up of just boss fights and the game never ever gets old. There are a few run and gun levels but these just seem to be added as a way for the player to obtain currency to buy powerups from the shop, which is fine.
Final Verdict:
Cuphead is a masterpiece in every regard. With exceptional game design, graphical fidelity, and audio quality, Cuphead will be able to remain as immortal as the cartoons it's inspired by, making it the first of its kind. This game is an absolute must have for anyone and everyone with access to a console or PC.

Bottom line: Expect a surprising story, challenging, yet fun puzzle games, and wrap your head around the case to fill in the deduction board.

This game is a demonstration of where review aggregation fails. It is not an 80% game, it's closer to 95%. Unfortunately, it's extremely difficult with no hand holding and large amounts of (spectacular) writing, which polarises the traditional gaming audience.
Make no mistake; this game is absolutely fantastic. The world it creates gives me the same sort of giddy excitement that I used to get reading the Edge Chronicles as child, that I haven't felt since playing The Witcher 3. There is a perfect splash of dark humour in this dystopian and sideways world, with obvious Lovecraft influence and a 'horror from below' theme. Characters and plots are amazing, one of the games where I can wholely recommend you to read as little as possible before playing.
It is also frustrating, and at the beginning may seem impossibly slow. However, keep exploring and experimenting, do not be dissuaded by a death or two, you may not retain many tangible upgrades with the next captain, but you do retain something more important: knowledge (knawwledge). The combat is probably the weakest link and essentially involves trying to stay behind the enemy, but moreso involves fleeing from them desperately for the first 5 hours or so.
Basically, if you're a fan of exploration, stories, Lovecraft or world-building, you probably know who you are. This game is absolutely worth it. 9.5/10.

I am a big fan of the Sherlock Holmes games. I love the character, I love the mysteries, I love the atmosphere, and I love the pixel-hunting. There, I said it! Now that I've gotten that back, let me tell you what I think of the Testement of Sherlock Holmes.
First, the good things. 1. As usual, the atmosphere is spot on. And I could swear that the dialogue is written by Conan Doyle himself. It genuinely feels like a Sherlock Holmes adventure. 2. The investigation is really well done. Whenever you need to search a body for marks or a room for clues, it feels like L. A. Noire. 3. The tension in the first half of the game is really thrilling. The sense that Sherlock Holmes may be insane, or not who he says he is is gripping and kept me playing to try and decipher why exactly Sherlock Holmes was being so edgy and confrontation. There is no greater conflict in a Sherlock Holmes adventure than questioning the legitimacy of your hero.
Now, let's talk about what' bad. 1. Puzzles. Puzzles, Puzzles, Puzzles, Puzzles, Puzzles! Way too many puzzles, and most of them are stupid, complicated, and have no explanation of mechanics, objective, or context. I am grateful that the game includes a "skip puzzle" button, but it's a bad sign when it needs to be included. 2. Adventure-game inventory management. In the early game, the investigation of murders was so strong in gameplay, that it was a shock when I started to have to search for random objects with no idea why I needed them or how they were supposed to be used. Most of the rest of the game is classic combine this with that and use it on that. This wouldn't be a problem, if it was simply transitions between one mystery to another. But instead it makes up the majority of gameplay, and doesn't do it particularly well. 3. The ending is completely non-sequitor and the prologue with awkwardly animated and voice-acted children is really poorly handled, it almost felt like a completely different story spliced into one about Sherlock Holmes struggling with an insidious threat to his integrity. 4. I hesitate to mention this, because I am a strong believer that poor graphics, animation, voice acting, etc. can be compensated for by compelling gamplay. And Bullfrog has come a long way since Sherlock Holmes: the Awakened in terms of animation and cinematics, but it still looks pretty amateur, and it would go a long way for their franchise if they worked on animation and cinematic timing.
So ultimately, I recommend this game for its strong beginning and great tension. But regret that it missed its mark in a lot of technical respects.

This game has a punishing learning curve, miles of text, and a (at times) frustratingly deliberate pace.  But if you have the patience, Sunless Sea is a thing of wonder.  Yes, your captains will die; this is a rougelike after all.  Hang in there; each captain will outlive the last, enabling you to explore Sunless Sea's hidden depths.
This may be the most literate game I've ever played.  Lovecraftian, yes, but it's more “Dreamquest of Unknown Kadath” than “Call of Cthulhu.”  Samuel Taylor Coleridge's “Rime of the Ancient Mariner” and “Kubla Kahn” are also clear influences, as is Edgar Allen Poe's “The Narrative of Arthur Gordon Pym of Nantucket.”
Playing Sunless Sea evokes a weird combination of relaxation and creeping tension. A cult game in the truest sense, players seeking visceral thrills will leave disappointed.  For those willing to make the trip, though, this little opium den of a game is well worth the price of admission.

I played version 0.9.8 which should be close to a release version. I played Salt and Sanctuary which is a 2D game like this mixed in with Dark Souls. I decided to give this a try because I liked the 2D art style and the Viking theme in the presentation on the store page.
+ Opening cutscene is really amazing
+ Devs seem very interactive in the community, a lot of languages supported
+ Great idea for the game
+ Steam achievements
+ Steam trading cards
- Opening cut-scene was kind of false advertising. The graphics in the cut-scene are amazing, but the graphics in game look terrible. Some of the art is beautiful, but the animations ruin that.
- There was a lot of potential in the idea of the game, kind of an Era of Majesty/Kingdom feel but more in-depth. They failed to effectively pull it off though.
- Terrible controls, I rebound the controls and the display still shows the default, this should be an easy fix. Mix in terrible movement as well.
- The combat is bad. There's no jumping or dodging, you will just switch weapons with a button and and hold down the attack button until its dead. Throwing in a block every now and then. The lack of change in combat makes for a dull repetitive grind-fest.
- Most of the game is just clicking a button on a resource to gather an item. There's no decision making at all. This leads to a very boring experience.
- Not user friendly at all, this seems to be a common complaint among negative reviews and in the forums. Developers response is they will post guides when it's released, so it's not built into the game. This seems lazy and doesn't account for my next complaint about the price.
- Story is lackluster for being so close to a release version. I think at this point in the version you should be baiting people with some story that hooks them and makes them want more. This game does not do that.
- For the multiplayer players out there, there is technically a multiplayer option, but you won't find any games. Steam charts
puts the game as having 15 players on at a time as a record.
- Price, the game is not worth $19.99, nor the $15.99 I paid during the Steam Winter Sale. I have over 900 games in my steam library so I think I have a pretty good gauge of where prices should be for each game. I think it's worth $7.99 with some of the problems fixed.

The best survival experience I have found in a game yet.
It is challenging without feeling entirely unfair.  When you fail, you can generally look back at a moment of poor decsion making.  The game play is fairly simple with a basic gathering / crafting mechanic.  The hunting is one of the best I have played with wounded prey collapsing from their injuries at the end of long trackable trails of blood droplets.  The combat system is more of a struggle system and does a fair job of capturing the desperate feeling of being mauled by a wild animal.
I wish I knew who to thank for this quote, "It is like living in a painting that wants to kill you."  And it is like that.  The game is gorgeous.  Every sunset and daybreak warrants a screen capture.  The sound effects are splendidly encompassing.  The music is subtle and lovely.  This is one of the rare games that I feel like I am in another world.
A great game and must buy for any survival game or immersion gaming focused player.

This game is brillliant. Absolutely brilliant. From the way you see things, to the way you cook things, to the way you scavenge. It's almost perfect. It's realistic, and allows you to go through as if you were living in an actual zombie apocalypse: mortally. Just the opening to when you load up a save file:
"There was no hope for survival. This is how you died."
Is so powerful, and realisitic. No one survives the zombie apocalypse, unless of course, you have millions (billions if you want to take back the entirety of Earth) of bullets.
Every aspect is perfect. You need to pay attention to what you're cooking, or your entire safehouse burns down. You need to fortify your base, of zombies can crawl in through the windows. You need to cover the windows, so zombies don't see you. You need to increase your skills, so the game becomes easier. You need to stock up on food and water, so that when the electricity and water go out, you can survive. You need to create a farm, so you can make your own food when it runs out. You need to get weapons, sheets, nails, seeds, food, water carriers, a few bandages.
And this is only before NPCs are added in. I can't even imagine how useful lipstick, combs, shavers will be so you can stay civilised in front of other people.
Of course, this is all temporary. You won't win. No one does. Instead, you'll die. Whether it's bleach, the 25% chance from a scratch, the 96% chance from a bite, starvation, being beaten to death by zombies, jumping from the second story, dehydration, hypothermia, the other polar end of hypothermia, eventually NPCs, or even eventually the friends you're playing with, you won't survive.
After 22 Days, and 5 hours, you may rush into a warehouse, only to hear the sound of several zombies clawing at the door. Then, the alarm goes off. Every zombie in the vicinity rushes towards you. You quickly race out of the building, and narrowly escape the many zombies chasing you. You jump into some bushes, only to find yourself bitten by a crawler. It's all downhill from here. Spend your last few days well. Or, drink some bleach and quench your thirst. These are the end times, after all.

I wanted to let this one sit for a bit before I discussed what I thought about the game, since this was probably the Telltale Game with the biggest split in responses. It felt to me that about as many people disliked this game as liked it, for various reasons, and I can see why. This particular game gave me so many conflicting feelings that either a recommendation to play or skip this game is likely to be half-hearted, since for every reason I can think of to play this game, I can think of one to not play it, and vice-versa.
It's hard to comment on the story without spoiling things, so the bottom line is: the story is interesting, with its share of cool moments and moments that wouldn't feel out of place in a bad Batman fanfic. I think the best part of the story is the fact that it is as much a Bruce Wayne story as it is a Batman story, complete with a few scenes where the player gets to choose which persona to use.
This DOES come at the cost of making a lot of your choices not really matter, though. The story is basically the same front to back with the difference in the details.....sometimes, which isn't really anything new for Telltale, and since this same problem existed even back when The Walking Dead came out, I won't bother holding it against this game. Though I do feel like they could have masked it a little better.
In terms of gameplay, I think the only real gripe about it is the fact that it's REALLY easy. And by that, I mean I only saw one game over, and that was because my controller wasn't working, rather than actually failing a QTE. Additionally, though this is also nothing new for the series, the puzzles really shouldn't take the player long to solve. Not that this is a bad thing, but if you're looking for challenging gameplay, you probably won't find it here.
Mixed feelings aside, there is one thing I can praise without much reservation: the voice acting. Even though these are all voice actors you've heard before, they make use of their experience to make each scene better for them being there.
At the end of the day, this is definitely not the WORST Telltale game that's been released, but it certainly pales in comparison to Walking Dead Season 1 or Tales From the Borderlands. If you're really unsure, wait for a sale or play the demo, since it includes the entire first episode.

*Alpha Review- 11/1/14*
It's...well, it's not dull, that's for sure.
A lot of comparisons are going to be made with Left 4 Dead- an apt comparison, if you ask me. They both rely heavily on teamwork in order to reach the goal, and if you try going off and doing your own thing you're going to get your face pummeled in.
At first I was more than a little bit lost as to who I was and what I was doing, which isn't helped by the fact that the screen has a lot of information firing off constantly. After about an hour of play (~10 matches or so) I kind of got into the groove of the game and really started to enjoy it.
The levels are big, and the jetpack gives you the sense of free movement in a big way. However, there are a lot of smaller mobs running around that you need to be wary of, and in chaotic moments the fighting can best be described as a clusterf*ck.
Performance was okay. Some lag earlier on, nothing too much to complain about. Never really had to wait to get into a lobby.
EDIT 1
Just unlocked Griffin, and I'm glad to see that there's more variety within the classes. Progression does seem to be slowing down, however. Game is performing much better than it was this morning.

I thoroughly admire the nordic charm layed thick by this game, its atmosphere resounds with that certain rustic beauty that can put you at ease for hours. The art style is easy on the eyes allowing you to play for hours on end in this painting of an experience and the sounds of the environment constantly remind you that though lonely you are not alone. All this being said I have some serious issues with the game on a mechanical level. It feels like its trying desperately to hit on the "darksouls notoriety" being unfair in aspects of combat and general difficulty. Resources are sparse and often guarded by fierce combatants that regardless of your level can break your life down. Armor seems only marginally helpful regardless of tier and bosses seem like dieties when you waggle your toothpick of a blade or weapon at them. Overall, this game is charming but intensely frustrating. It will improve with age, and experience, but overall its still going to kick you in the throat like a bad bottle of 200 proof. I give a marginal recommendation only because it CAN be fun if your willing to invest the necessary time to "git gud".

One or two zombies might be easy enough to knock down and head stomp, but get surrounded by three or four in a tight corner and you are in serious trouble.  And looting those big downtown centers?  At NIGHT?  Good luck.  You better bring a shotgun, a pistol, an axe, and lots of ammo.  And maybe some beta blockers, painkillers, and bandages.  And a journal to read, in case you get lonely and depressed.
The potential in this game is self-evident.  I can't wait to see the finished product.  Crafting, building, farming, cooking, looting, zombie-stomping, door-bashing - it's all here.  I just wish they'd give me a way to use the Bleach to clean up all the braaaaaains...my hideout's a mess!

The concept of this game is pretty good: you have to survive for as long as you can by finding resources, build forts, fight off the horde, etc... I personally like this game because there's no main objectives other than to live. It's pretty much do whatever your little heart desires. There are some people who rip these kind of games (i.e. Minecraft) because they say there is no point. The point is that there is no point. It's up to the player on how the character interacts without an higher power (I'm refering to objectives, waypoints, stuff like that) controlling your interactions.
However, there are a couple problems that I've experienced while playing this game. First off, the zombies would sometimes vanish from sight, but then reappear. I don't know if anyone else is experiencing this problem, but I hope it's something that is fixed in the near future. Next problem I have is that the character window in the character customization tab is too small. It's hard to see the difference between body types when trying to make a selection. Another problem in the customization tab is that when I tried to make another character (Mostly because I accidentally closed the loot menu and didn't know how to open it back up), some of the buttons weren't responding. I would try to get different hairstyles, but nothing would happen when I clicked on the arrow. I hope that bug is also fixed too. One more thing. It isn't a major issue or anything, but it would be nice to have more clothing options. I mean, a shirt, pants, shoes, and sweater is pretty generic. It'd be nice to have other options like leather jackets, steel toed boots, shorts, hell even sandals. This would make the characters more unique because there would be more clothing options and that they wouldn't all look the same.
Overall, this game is still fun to play. Sure, there are some bugs to the game, but it's still in alpha, so it isn't something that should come as a shock to people. If you're into this kind of gaming, then I'd definitely recommend checking it out like watching gameplays of the game.
Also, thanks for the time to read my review. If there's anything that you want me to go into further detail, please leave so in the comments.

TL;DR: Cuphead is a great game with amazing visuals and a stellar soundtrack. However, in order to best some bosses, the game will require near perfection. This can be really frustrating, but the game never seems unfair. I would give it about an 8/10 taking into account price, visuals, soundtrack, length of game, and amount of "fun".
Pros:
-Nobody will disagree with the fact that the old cartoon style visuals and music are fantastic
-The boss designs are unique with each requiring a different strategy to defeat
-The game is hard, but never seems unfair
-Boss fights are not very lengthy (once you understand their patterns) so it is easy to pick up and play in your free time
-Beating a boss feels incredible and gives you an incredible feelings of accomplishment
-Replayability is unique because understanding a bosses phases from the start changes the fight
Cons:
-The Run & Gun levels don't feel as good as the boss levels
-Game is rather short, unless you feel like trying to S rank all of the bosses
-There are multiple weapons, charms, and supers, but I always found myself using a combo of 3 weapons, 2 charms, and one super
-The plane levels are nice, but I feel there could have been more levels or choosing of powers like normal levels
-That Dragon boss (probably the most annoying one in the game)
Review:
Cuphead is a very good game. Amazing to look at and listen too and interesting to play. The game is very difficult and most bosses will not be bestest on the first try. Or even the tenth try. Cuphead is all about understading boss patterns. Once you have died enough to understand how the boss acts and when they do what move you can choose a weapon kit, charm, and super in order to turn the tide and gain the advantage. Once you "download" a boss and are able to beat them, the rush and feeling of accomplishment is fantastic. That is why people are comparing this game to Dark Souls. The feeling of beating a tough-as-nails boss that killed you tens (or hundreds) of times is where the enjoyment of this type of game comes from. So if you like the masochistic feeling of getting beat up for 10-30 minutes and then finally doing some beating up of your own you will enjoy this game.
I did have some things I didn't like however. The Run & Gun levels are nice. In fact, I wish the game was based more around the run and gun levels and each level would end in a boss fight. However, these experiences are completely seperate. There are maybe 6 R&G level compared to the 18 boss fights. At that point they serve as an interesting distraction, but don't feel quite fleshed out. They do serve as an ability to get coins so you can buy weapons and charms, but I found that only 3 weapons and 3 charms were ever useful.
The game is also rather short. As someone who played solo and no co-op (so far), it took me about 7 hours. The replayability comes from trying to get better ranks as the boss fights. Playing them again feels good because you understand how the fight is going to work, but constantly banging your head against a wall trying to get that perfect S rank isn't my style though I won't begrudge those that like to. Going back and trying everything in co-op might prove more fun.
Overall, Cuphead was a good game and I feel like it was well worth $20. The going certaintly does get rough and some bosses feel invincible when you first start fighting them (GODDAMN THAT DRAGON BOSS), but overcoming the challenge feels great and keeps you coming back for more.

To be fair, you have to have a very high IQ to understand the Cuphead tutorial. The instructions are extremely subtle, and without a solid grasp of the whole situation most of the tips will go over a typical players head. There's also Cuphead's imprecise movements, which is deftly woven into his characterisation- his wavering self draws heavily from Narodnaya Volya literature, for instance. The fans understand this stuff; they have the intellectual capacity to truly appreciate the depths of the animations, to realise that they're not just cartoon-y - they say something deep about LIFE. As a consequence people who say they cleared the Cuphead tutorial in minutes truly ARE lying- of course they would have looked up, for instance, the solution to this obstacle "Y DASH QUICK EVADE ON GROUND OR AIR," which itself is a cryptic reference to the control manual. I'm smirking right now just imagining one of those addlepated simpletons scratching their heads in confusion as Jared Moldenhauer's genius wit unfolds itself on their game screens. What fools.. how I pity them.

Wow. This game. I recommend it in some ways, but really don't in other ways, if you know what I mean.
I'll start off by saying Scott Cawthorn is a genius. Never did I expect a game like this to have so many little details that have a massive effect. This could be some creepy picture that randomly spawns from time to time, and which you either miss or see and get surprised by. Or, it could be Freddy randomly staring at you from the show stage when you least expect it. Everything in this game seems to have a purpose, from an endoskeleton on a table to Freddy's nose. I find it amazing that there's so many different rare screens that could occur and take you by surprise at any moment. This is what makes this game special.
The idea of it is also unique. Most horror games (and by this I mean almost every other horror game in existence) require YOU to do something that usually ends up in your surprising death. However, Five Night's At Freddy's has an entirely different concept. All you do is sit in a chair and look at cameras. This sounds like the easiest thing in the world, but once you play it, you realise how paranoid this makes you feel. You're basically waiting for them to decide when they want to come and attack you. This is an incredibly scary experience, and the game barely ever gets boring (unless you're Markiplier and have spent the past 7 hours trying to avoid an endless cycle of death).
So yes, I do recommend this game, and for many good reasons. If you have a heart condition, then this game is a suicide mission. If you do not, then it is still a suicide mission, but a bit less dangerous. Have a good stay at Freddy Fazbear's Pizza!

Intriguing game, but not without flaws.
I just love investigation games where you have to find clues and then deduce to figure out what really happened, and you definitely expect that from a Sherlock Holmes game. In that department it doesn't fail to deliver, except that I wish there was more of it. The story of the game is fairly interesting too, quite dark and a bit out there. Actually I feel it is a bit too far out there at times.
You can choose to play from a 3rd person perspective or 1st person. Because of the somewhat clunky controls and movement I ended up playing it in 1st person to not become too frustrated. You alternate between controlling Sherlock Holmes and Dr. Watson through the story and even Toby the dog. Especially Toby here felt out of place and especially clunky and odd. Not only did that part feel unrealistic to the point of ridiculousness, but for he most part it did not even make any sense. I do not want to spoil too many details, but let's just say don't get caught up in where the tracks lead you. Half the time they didn't even show up. At least not until you'd been going back and forth several times. It is good to see that a developer is trying something new and original, but this was not a success in my eyes.
What really stands out in this game, in my opinion, is the voice acting. They were just really really good. I don't know if it is because the British language just seems more dramatic and sincere or what it is, but everyone felt very believable.
There's a good mix of search and find, puzzles, mini-games and exploration. I found the deduction boards to be creative and fun and the puzzle boxes to be less so. Either way I enjoyed the game as a whole and would easily recommend it to anyone enjoying these types of games.

Actually very well done, though sometimes a little buggy and jumpy. The puzzles were pretty clever, as to be expected of a Sherlock Holmes game. The story was a bit lackluster and underdramatic, and the voice acting was a little shoddy, with actors putting a little bit too much overemphasis on some of their characters lines. One of the "great reveals" at the end was pretty predictable, at least to anyone has has any two-sense of Sherlock Holmes fiction, and a lot of the story scenes used in the game were mashups of different Holmes stories.  It fits the theme of the older Sherlock Holmes stories however, something people forget about due to the two shows that place Sherlock's tales in a more modern setting. The game contains many references to Sherlock's more famous previous adventures as well, which served as a plus and a great homage to the character's legacy.
The game allowed a great choice of being played in third-person, first-person or even point and click, which is what most games of this genre usually end up being. It was a delight to play in first-person view and search the areas for clues, as if you were the great Holmes himself. Also, playing that random scene as the dog in first person view was a good chuckle.
The game adds the use of a "Deduction Board" where you use clues found in the area to piece together the facts of the case. It was a marvelous idea, definitely one of the better features of the game, though I wish it could have been used more than the three times it is in the game.
Overall I think the game is a worthy buy, especially to fans of the mystery/adventure genre. Pick it up, I had good fun with it.
Additionally, the visuals and music during the ending credits sequence were and absolute marvel to watch, if only they had put something similar in the beginning of the game, allowing it to open with such an impact.

So, Tropico 5. We meet at last. Do you know why you were brought here, Tropico #5? Because El Presidente believes with the right sort of, let's say, motivation, you could become so much more useful as a citizen of our great virtual island. But as it is right now? I don't know, Tropico 5. I don't know. Considering the work of the four previous Tropicos who have come through town, who have very rarely made any significant changes to the status quo, which I have to admit, around here we can appreciate that sort of slow gradual change considering how everything has been working just fine, you decided you wanted to make a few more, shall we say, radical changes. This has El Presidente very concerned. Let's go over the dossier, shall we?
Let's start with what you've been doing around town that's got so many fellow citizens vocally supporting you. One of the biggest changes you've made is to the infrastructure. It's nice to see that you've scaled down the size of the parking garages to something manageable, and look, in the Modern area you've introduced the Metro to our tiny island! Letting citizens get from one point of the island to the other nearly instantaneously is quite the feet. Something that El Presidente truly appreciates when he wants to get out to the llama farms for some quiet and relaxation without having to drive through all of that horrible traffic. Which is another issue we see significantly less of. It is good to see more people walking instead of filling the streets with cars! I applaud you, Tropico 5, for finally resolving that issue.
That reminds me, the whole Era thing. It is, if of a somewhat debatable quality, nice to have Eras from which to transition. Going from the Colonial Era to the World War Era is probably the largest change of the four. The other two are the Cold War and the Modern Era. Having the ability to upgrade certain residential units to other certain residential units is nice as the era transitions, and new constructions become available.Having Edicts become available as the Era progresses is another thing to look forward to, until finally you have access to all of them. And the Constitution! Who would have expected something like that to be introduced into our tiny island? The discovery of science, which is used to enhance the Constitution and advance the Eras, was nice as we can finally figure out that whole sliced bread thing.
The price of docks is considerable cheaper than they were previously, which allows El Presidente to build many, many docks to help speed up the export of his new delicious cheese. And speaking of money, it's nice to finally be able to have a use for El Presidente's, shall we say 'private' income. Being able to use the Swiss Bank account balance level up El Presidente and his family members abilities is quite good at encouraging you to play multiple maps with the same family so you realize their full power! Oh yes, and El Presidente would like me to pass along his thanks in allowing multiple members of the family to share power on our island.
For the workforce, being able to hire managers with minor Presidente-like powers to manage buildings is a nice touch indeed. The people of our island enjoy being empowered in such a way that makes them more useful to El Presidente.
But now onto some concerning trends that I am seeing here. The buildings snap to a rather large grid system that while nice when fitting buildings together sometimes, is terrible unimaginative and can leave a lot of extra space between buildings where they meet at odd angles. It doesn't help any that you have taken away El Presidente's favorite toys. No longer can we build statues to honor El Presidente's might. No, now parks and decorations only come in two units, small and large. The small is one grid or two, while the large fluctuates slightly more, starting at a 4x4, and going to such sizes as 4x6, to the mighty 5x5 and 5x6. But what happened to the gardeners, Tropico 5? Did you murder them in the study with a lead pipe? Because we can no longer plant individual trees, or benches, or any of the small single items. This is a great disappointment to El Presidente, for he had quite the green-thumb.
Housing has now turned into something of a mess, since, as we said, Tropicans walk far more than they did last time. Now if a Tropican can not find a house near where they live, they will opt to just build a shack near their work-site, even if there is ample housing on the island. I have been told by many who do this, Tropico #5, that they were encouraged to ignore El Presidente's benevolence and build these eyesores around the city by you.
And another thing. Why have you taken away the ability of El Presidente to personally manage the wages of our citizens? Not only that, but he can no longer set prices for buildings or services. Everything has instead been rolled up into one "budget" function. Tropico 5, I'm concerned about this power grab. These are function that should be left up to El Presidente himself to manage, not some overly simplified "budget bar" that controls everything. This has actually made it HARDER to manage the economy, since if we want to pay people less, we now have to also decrease the efficiency of a building by lowering the budget. This is a big problem, and I suspect it may be sabotage!
I was also shocked to discover that we need to discover our own island now! When we start administering our great government in the Colonial Era, our island is shrouded in mist, and must be explored by our soldiers during "expeditions" that cost a thousand dollars an event! And you can't even control them, you just click on a way point and hope they go the right route in getting there to discover it. Though the discovery of the Compass does negate this, it is none-the-less irksome.
And speaking of discovery, why are our people no longer able to improve their skills concerning their profession? Why have you taken this source of pride from our people, Tropico #5? The people are also kept more out of sight as well, as no longer is El Presidente able to see them when they utilize a building. Gone are the queues that show up when you click on a service building. Instead, they are reduced to mere numbers.
Having to mine minerals out of very specific "mines" instead of just having to dig it out of the ground did not actually turn out to be helpful. These "mines" take up permanent space on the map, even after they are used up and collapse. Which is another issue! When a resource node, with the exception of the fishing wharf, is used up, it is automatically destroyed, regardless of whether or not the output storage is full! This destruction of El Presidente's property at the hands of no other than you, Tropico 5, is a great crime! It is most irritating and wasteful. If a facility no longer has resources to mine, El Presidente will choose when and how it is removed, not you!
And with the Edicts, while we do have some nice new interesting ones, I see the Pope is no longer able to visit our island, Tropic 5. That is a little disappointing.
Elections are now quite a bit more boring. Why do you not allow El Presidente to do speeches anymore, Tropico #5? In fact, why is it that El Presidente, and the family, are not able to directly control their actions on the map? Gone are the day when El Presidente could walk up to a construction site and encourage the workers to construct faster, or walk into a service building an inspire greater service. This is very disappointing that you have talked otherwise upright citizens into ignoring El Presidente in such a way.
In the end, I find my appreciation for you mixed, Tropico 5. I can stay with Tropico 4 and not really miss much, I think, but I do still enjoy your presence, even if I think you're a half step back in progress.

Would I recommend this game? Whenever the price drops for a while again, then yes, especially if you feel charmed by the look of the game. However everything above 2 Euro would seem too much pricy n my opinion... Here's why:
Pro:
* the artful drawings and likable meditation-inducing piano-sound give off a very nice and enjoyable atmosphere
* this game is in reality a Hidden Object Game - search for half-hidden stuff in 2D-sceneries filled to the rim with details and in between play a number of different minigames. Which is great in my opinion because I love HOGs. Well, if you don't, that might not be a Plus for you then...
* if you have ever played a bunch of HOGs, you will immediately recognize the minigames and will know what you have to do, as they are all very typical and not too hard to solve
* Morphopolis also has elements of an adventure as you have to "control" an insect and make it crawl around a bit plus you'll have to click on some cratures or plants to "hand in" stuff you've found/collected. But this is very little adventure-like gameplay all in all, much less than most modern HOGs feature actually. Not even as much "adventure" as in Botanicula or Samorost, although Morphopolis might make you think of games like that instinctively
Contra:
* the game is extremely short. E.x.t.r.e.m.e.l.y. I finished it within 2 hours, which included a coffee-break. To be more precisely: Morphopolis only has 5 "chapters", consisting of 17 screens/scenes and 7 minigames in total (if I did not miscalculate).
I really wonder why it has to be so short? It couldn't have been so hard to add many more sceneries, more stuff to collect, and perhaps also more of the re-usable types of minigames - especially the beautiful butterfly jigsaw or the "plant repair"-game. Did the developers just lose interest all of a sudden whilst making the game, or did they have a fight and decided to stop working together instantly?
* if Morphopolis was just a point-and-click-game I would have finished it within 1 hour. But the developers had this "brilliant" *coughs* idea to make the game "last longer" by letting your insectoid avatar crawl only very, very slowly. Painfully slowly :(
* the controls add to your discomfort - the way how to move and where to move your insect are horribly rigid. It does not help much that by clicking and holding your left mouse button on the insect it will emit dark greenish ... uh... I really think it looks like dung ... to give a hint about possible paths it can take next within a close radius
* it takes a lot of patience to make your insect go where you want it to, but then you make one wrong click and your insect will quickly switch to the next/former screen even if you didn't want that -_-
* in chapter two your insect has to eat/suck three egglike things, which you can only find out by sheer luck like by clicking around wildly and hitting one of the eggs per chance. And there's this one minigame in chapter 5 where you have to "swipe" with the cursor to let a small heap of seeds "jump" over others. It took me quite a while and luck to find out how to move these piles of seed :( No explanations for the controls to be found for minigames anywhere. Is this supposed to be "part of the fun"? Well, not for me, sorry.
* you also cannot skip any minigames, which can be really frustrating for some people. Well, but if you could, then the game would be over in the blink of an eye; so I guess that's why you can't... Pity.
* for an Hidden Object Game the stuff you have to find is not "hidden" well nor cleverly. Sometimes it is nearly invisible, which will make you click wildly all over your screen after a while - that will do the trick, but will leave you unsatisfied. With this kind of interesting, detailled and colorful background, blending stuff in could have been done 100 times better
* the "story" about transformation lacks a bit too in my opinion, as in three levels the "goal" of your insect is to meet with a much larger insect and seemingly to dig into it's head, which does not make much sense...
Conclusion: there are many beautiful hand-drawn artistic games with relaxing music and interesting ideas out there. Morphopolis definitely has the potential to be a real gem of this genre. But it turned out to be a mere sherd. Makes me want to replay Botanicula and sing along with the frogs ;)

Brilliant(ly flawed). I have such mixed feelings about this game. It's an amazing game in concept, it provides an entirely unique gameplay experience, the humor is childish but spot-on, and it feels like it should be fun. I want to like this game SO BAD! That said, I've only played three or four hours and have already found myself repeatedly asking "what were the devs thinking?".
For example, this game, which involves permantently placing objects on a board in a way that one misplaced item can lose you the game no matter how early you make said mistake, gives you a hand size of TWO. This results in extremely luck-based gameplay, even for a deck-building CCG.
Another example: if you tie with an AI opponent, instead of adding another column as a tie-breaker, you straight up lose.
Add this to the fact that there are numerous UI issues (reseting takes a solid 10-15 seconds on many maps, sometimes clicking menu objects will instead place objects underneath the menus (remember my first point), no way to disable tutorial popups, etc.) and I am reluctant to recommend this otherwise awesome game.
HOWEVER, Steam's bad design has forced my hand. Like so many other games which fall into this category, I can't give a review of "neither amazing nor terrible". I have to say either it's awesome or it's awful. Devs, I'm giving you a thumbs up because I want this game to succeed. Valve, this isn't a children's lemonade stand. Adapt or GOG will replace you. Well, replace you faster.
Edit: I changed my mind after another half hour of play. Thumbs down. One more clarification: I said it was building things behind the UI. I was wrong. Clicking on the bar on the left side of the screen will often build things in the center or right of the screen. There is a "solution" for this in the menu ("Are you sure?" messages for each building placement), but that doesn't fix the problem; throwing up pestering messages every five seconds will just train the user to say "yes" to any such messages.
By buying this game, you are basically buying a really, REALLY bad slot machine. Will it give you an unwinnable situation which you can't forsee or predict? It's all the luck of the draw!
Well, lesson learned: set a timer for 1 hour 55 minutes ANY TIME you buy a Steam game.
Seriously, how in the world do you screw up mouse controls that badly?

Aside from being one of the most open-ended zombie apocalypse simulators in gaming, this masterpiece is nothing short of amazing.
Right off the bat - is the game challenging? You are encouraged to use the game's tools to tailor-make your own version of the apocalypse, editing zed rules, environment weather and loot rates. Does everyone reanimate with the zed disease? Do the zombies in your apocalypse break whatever is in their way, or will they only attempt to infiltrate if they are chasing a noise? Are the zombies never ending, or is there a set population spread out across Kentucky?
Once you have set your parameters you are dropped in as the stock character you have set up, choosing from a wide variety of previous jobs and traits, each with their own effect and skill boosts (this gets even juicier with multiplayer as you will be playing with people with different abilities and central skills).Your build can range from a burger flipper with an iron-gut and thick skin to a brave firefighter with additional first-aid skills to a desensitized war veteran with an eagle eye.
Once you spawn in, you will be in what was presumably your home with randomly generated loot. You have the keys to the place, but are not forced to live there. What will you do? Will you take what's in the kitchen and live off of whatever meal you can throw together until you need to leave? Will you take everything you can with you as you search for a better place to live? Will you leave the stove on and burn your house down with you in it? This is Project Zomboid, and this is the story of how you died.
Aside from being a fun and challenging game to play on your own or with friends, Project Zomboid is pretty good for seeing how well you could potentially take care of yourself in a situation where society's rules are out of the window. Compare your current life to how your story began in Project Zomboid. Did you always have somebody who could cook for you? Did you not bother to learn anything about basic carpentry? What skills do you have? You are only yourself, and you can't do everything great (or even good enough) off the bat. So what will you do? Either way, you will have to learn new things. But what skills do you plan on using? Do you have a friend you can work with who can help take a load off? Are you going to be on the run solo until you can predict the dangers you may run into?
If you can micromanage your character to ensure that you can maintain a healthy diet with no health complications or depression months past the power dies, odds are you are doing something right in your plan. And if you are at that point and are surviving off of worms and anti-depressants, you must really hate yourself.
From camping under the stars to camping on the roof, the options for staying alive are endless. Do what suits you best. You may not be a carpentry/electrical based character. Maybe you are a park ranger? Use your herbology knowledge to forage for medical herbs, and set up camp somewhere deep in the woods. Not so good with the outdoors, but are even better than most with a baseball bat and are in the shape of your life? Maybe living on the move or in a safer suburban area could do you good. Great with a hammer, but not so great at fighting zombies? Construct a perimeter and use your skills to maintain it.
And again, I can not stress how much better this game gets on multiplayer. Having a group of friends with different central skills and profession benefits will create it's own dynamic and let you fully experience everything the game has to offer.
If you are a creator of any type, play this game.

This is a review for anyone who enjoys perfecting a simple game like this. Concrete Jungle is a game that is learned quickly, but takes some careful planning to master. And part of the fun of these games is learning all the patterns, unlocking all the top-tier cards, and then creating an unstoppable deck. The problem is this game doesn't allow you to become an end-game god.
It's not because the game is difficult. I could respect a game that ramps up in difficulty to the point where it is unbeatable. Concrete Jungle certainly has those types of elements. However, the game stopper for a skilled player is something insidious: hidden caps. For instance, one card allows you to increase your building allowences (think of it as a budget), but eventually you hit a limit and the game stops counthing them. So effectively this normally great card becomes useless. Actually, worse, it's a penalty because the card is forever in deck wasting space. And the limit isn't because you reach some obsene number that could cause an integer overflow. No it's because you reach 200-- a value easily reached in custom game play.
Also, the block sizes are capped. Normally blocks are limited to 4 tiles. Some cards allow you to increase the block size which can be helpful for cases where where you have a ton of +1 bonuses attached to that block. You can rack up a lot of points this way. But then, at around 15 tiles in the block, you can't increase the size of the block anymore. This hidden cap snuck up on me at the worst moment. I spent 30 turns carefully planning how to make a maximal efficiency block only to find when I needed to reap the rewards, I no longer could because my carefully crafted block maxed out in size. There's no logical reason for this limitation and it feels like a punishement for playing the game too well.
tl;dr If you're a perfectionist who enjoys mastering games, CJ isn't worth your time. It'll punish you for playing too well.

My first experience in The Long Dark:
I landed on a road next to a car and found some basic supplies. I followed the road and soon found a small farm: I stayed in the barn and made a fire while I snacked on candy bars I found on a dead guy. I got pretty tired and napped next to the fire for an hour or two, when I woke up the fire had gone out. I journeyed outside just to find out there was a blizzard. I grabbed some wood and headed back inside. I started up the fire and slept almost the rest of the night. When I awoke I was somehow dying of dehydration even though it had only been 8 hours since my bar was full. I decided to head out into the snow in search of water (ironic, right?). The game had become a walking simulator for about 25 minutes real time before I started freezing to death. I made a fire and took a quick nap, then continued my (what seemed to be) endless journey down a snowy road. I began to feel extremely tired even though I had just slept 8 hours 2 hours ago, so I set up my sleeping bag. I died in my sleep.
8/8 would die again.

The game starts off interesting enough, but rapidly goes downhill.  It's a deck-building board game at heart that has absolutely nothing to do with city management and very little flexibility in the deck building.
You have a set of cards that correspond to various types of developments and must place them into a grid of city spaces in such a way as to earn points.  The game is purely a puzzle game with randomized pieces. (Think Tetris, but with a bit of theme.)
The campaign starts you off slowly.  Houses are the point earning buildings.  Schools, shops, and entertainment make houses worth more points.  Factories, power plants, and warehouses remove points.  Your deck starts off with basic cards that you generally don't ever to use once more cards are unlocked, but you're always stuck with the junk in your deck and no good way to get rid of it for most characters.  Pretty soon more cards are thrown into the mix but no strategic advice is provided to determine how the cards can work well together.  There are a plethora of cards to unlock, but doing so requires an incredibly difficult and lengthy grind of replaying the same game over and over to level up each character.  Each character also has a complicated tech-tree full of abilities for you to figure out how to use (with very ambiguous descriptions provided).
Levels very quickly ramp up in difficulty and even stack the board against you.  The solo campaign ends before you even have a full understanding of how the game works.  After that you're forced into multiplayer battles against AI who always have better decks than you.  The game doesn't really provide any feedback to how you are doing until it's too late.  You can start a match thinking you're doing well only to later realize that you don't have enough of the good cards in your deck to score any points in the end game, whereas your opponent is perfectly poised to score over and over again.
I think the game has an interesting premise, but the execution and delivery are just downright terrible.  The tutorial needs to be completely revamped so that it actually teaches players how to fully play the game.  It may be more enjoyable if you didn't have to struggle for hours on end trying to understand how each mechanic works and how to actually play strategically.  The game also needs a playable campaign for each character that focuses on the strengths and weaknesses specific to each character's deck instead of what it currently does, which is to just throws you into a new character role with no explanation on the particularities of the character.  These poor design choices force you to repeat the same handful of levels over and over again, which grow boring very quickly.

"SUPERHOT" demonstrates that Steam needs more than just a "Yes" and "No" to the question, "Do I recommend this game?" Somewhere inbetween the absolutes of "Yes" and "No" there is a third option, "Meh."
SUPERHOT is amazingly cool for about 3-4 hours. Then you're kind of done. The endless challenge modes you can unlock aren't really all that satisfying.
The developers shot themselves in the foot, and then in the leg several times and probably another few places as well by deciding during development to use a proprietary lighting engine which requires each level to be baked in a secret process which the community won't be able to duplicate, which means no user generated content.
That was the dumbest decision I've ever heard of a game developer making since John Romero's Daikatana / Ion Storm debacle. Skyrim should have taught us that MODS SELL GAMES! SUPERHOT was absolutely the game which could have benefited most from user generated content ... and didn't.
This lighting was completely frivolous and unnecessary. The prototype they released for their crowdfunding campaign didn't have this lighting and it looked fine! The gaming press praised it for it's simplistic visuals. There was no need to sacrifice such a fundamentally important feature for a minor aesthetic tweak that hardly anyone will notice.
Overall, that prototype was better in many ways than the final product. It's limitation of only pistols and melee as combat options actually made the gameplay feel strategic, while the shotgun you can't dodge and the necessity of using whatever weapon happens to be in front of you at the moment makes the full game of SUPERHOT feel more arcadey.
Still, it's a pretty fun game for that initial 3-4 hours despite these problems, and I hear the developers are working on some DLC to add procedurally generated levels. That should be cool. So I can still recommend, but in a more laid back "Meh" kind of way rather than with the full enthusiasm I felt when I backed SUPERHOT on kickstarter.

Artsy hidden object points&click game. The puzzles are decent and the objects are hard enough to find. There is a hint button with a fairly low cooldown that points to a missed object if there is one in the area of use, or plays a sound meaning there is no hidden object here. There is no introduction or hints to the puzzles; you'll have to figure it all out yourself.
Very clunky movement/pathing. Have to hold down the mouse button to move. A lot of backtracking and the bug is really slow.
The art and music are fantastically atmospheric though. Play for a meditation type entertainment rather than mentally challenging, though some of the puzzles do take some brain work.
All achievements are earned on first run. The ingame menu consists of 'to title menu' and 'return to game' and the title menu of chapter select and exit game. So options are extremely limited. There is no save button, and the puzzles have no exit button, so you'll have to restart level if you have to quit.
The game is short; only five small levels with 2-6 areas in each.
Recommended for the artsy, atmospheric, meditational feeling it has. All the small nuisances makes it not worth its price unless on sale though.

I don't know what is it about this VN that it
managed captured my full attention from the get-go. Usually when I read VN in general, I easily got distracted by literally just anything and I found myself either alt-tabbing a lot or put it on windowed mode and check Reddit or something real quick before got back to it. Maybe because it's quite different than the stuff I've usually read, and looking back at it, the last time I read something similar to this was only with Kara no Shoujo and Sound of Drop -fall into poison-. There's the most recent case with The Letter but I really have no idea what it's all about (it's still on my wishlist) and I want to keep it that way so that I won't spoil myself. Excluding Higurashi since I've already seen the anime and not planning to read it until they release all the part here on Steam, there's Umineko on my library which holds some potential, that and The House in Fata Morgana too (again, I didn't read the synopsis or anything. Going blind is always the best).
Anyway enough about that, let's talk about the game itself. Just a fair warning that there is some incest in this game so if that is not your cup of tea, well, might want to just skip this game. With that said, I really appreciated the fact that the developer kept adding new content with each update, and with the most recent update they added one last route to the game. As the other reviewer said, there's obviously some inspiration taken from Dexter (leading double life, sister plays important role in the story, story hinting toward his own "dark passenger" or sickness as the MC called it) and since Dexter is one of my favorite show, I just smiled when I noticed it the first time around during my read.

Now despite being called Sickness, the VN itself isn't about explaining the sickness itself, but rather how the MC deal with it and how it affect his judgement and the people around him. And I keep expecting his sickness to take over (kinda like a momentary lapse or blackout, losing track of time etc) but thankfully that never happen. Another thing I almost forgot to mention is that you get to play a certain's character route after beating the story and boy this was my favorite part right here. It's just so... different that I was like "what, really? That's what she thought at that time?"
And now onto the bad part. I feel like the second half of the VN is a bit... rushed out? As there's quite a bit of inconsistency with some characters and there's a lot of time skip too. And this resulted in the conclusion that may be a bit underwhelming at times. Kinda hard to explain it without spoiling the story, really. But even with all of that I can safely say that I enjoyed it and I ended up buying some trading cards just to get it to lvl 4 hehe.
Funny story, I got so heavily invested on one route (you can check the Steam discussion for this) that I was shocked to find a bug at the ending of that route. It spoils another character that I have never seen nor mentioned up until that point. And I believed I spent quite some time on google on how to fix this bug and all that search led me to just rollback to the previous version of the game. So I did all that and voila! I can get pass the bug and finally see the ending. Being the nice guy that I am, I thought it would be a good idea to share the temporary fix to this problem so that people won't get stuck at the same place, and I did just that and post my the fix on the discussion. The next morning, I woke up and to my amazement I saw some people reply back! Only to find out that the dev posted the fix to this bug just a couple hours after my attempt at fixing it. I'd be lying if I say I didn't cry a little there.

Niffelheim:
~~~~~~~~

You were a brave, strong soldier and your funeral was the pinnacle of your existence. You are farewelled in the traditional Nordic fashion which is to be sent into the sea on a burning ship for your last voyage. The demon of death had something else planned for you; they stole your ship and welcomed you to the world of darkness. Fallen soldier, welcome to Niffelheim!!
Niffelheim is a 2D/ Adventure/Action game were you take control of a fallen warrior in the world of Darkness called Niffelheim. At the start of the game, you will have to choose which faction (four in total) you want to play. You will start the game in front of a mine, which, by the way, is yours. On the screen, you will notice four icons, two on the right hand side and two on the left hand side of your screen. On the right, you will have the character icon which will include your character health with ten levelling abilities (Miner, Blacksmith, Carpenter and more) and a chest where you can store items. On the left hand side, you will have the map of the world as well as the mail icon where you can activate quests!
In this game, you have to gather wood, food and minerals so you can not only build useful structures within your own castle (base) or on its perimeters, but also craft useful items.  In your castle, you will be able to build a sawmill, a forge, a kitchen, an alchemy and an additional chest to store more items. In addition, you will be able to venture deeper within your castle through the mines where you will find useful minerals.
Niffelheim is really an exploring side scrolling game. You will be able to visit the temple city or conquer the other three provinces on the main map.
For the combat phase, you will come across several wild animals and undead enemies. In basic terms, you will just use your mouse to hit your foe. Just keep pressing the mouse button and you will constantly hit your enemies. If your enemy is too strong, you are probably going to die. If you do, you’ll become a ghost (well, it is the best term I can come up with) and you will have to find your fallen body to resurrect.
I really like the artwork and the crafting aspect in this game but I do feel that the fighting phase is a little bit of a letdown. However, this game is currently on early access and therefore there may be some improvements to come.
Positives:
~~~~~~~
-	Great artwork
-	Interesting theme based on the Viking mythology
-	Good exploring and crafting elements
-	Achievements and trading cards
Negatives:
~~~~~~~~
-	Fighting phase could be better
-	This is a slow pace game
Niffelheim is currently on early access and has great aspect about it. I personally feel that the game need to be refined in regards to the fighting phase but apart from that it is a very interesting game.
