Thesis: A Dissappointing sequel, suffering from all the problems of the current generation.
The graphics are very nice. I'd go so far as to say they're gorgeous. And Tropico 5 now has a clear reason to build multiple docks: the trade route system. Now, if you want to, you can find a trade route to export or import certain materials for better prices than base. However, there is still a base cost. This system hits that ideal balance: for players that want that extra granularity, it's there. But if you don't want it, don't bother.
Those are all the nice things I can say about this game. Tropico 5 has less than half the content of Tropico 4, in terms of options, buildings, and characters. I'm not including any of the DLC in that statement. I mean, base game to base game, half the content. Further, most of the content is Unlockable. That would be fine, except their decisions are baffling and frustrating.
I personally enjoy building Tourist economies. Tropico 5 doesn't unlock any tourism until the Third phase of the game, Cold War. This doesn't make sense. There was plenty of Tourism in the Colonial age, and Nazis and Allies had down-time in between all the fighting. We had the potentail to make Casablanca, and Kalypso denied us! By the time the Cold War comes along, it no longer makes sense to build Tourism, because your Industry will be well established.
The touted Eras mechanic is choppy and shallow. There's no fluidity, like in Modern Times. It's an abrupt Scene-change that CANCELS ALL YOUR ACTIVE TRADE ROUTES. And there's not much to it except the names of the people you trade with and who might invade you change. Seriously. Even in the Story Mode, the different Eras mean almost nothing.
And the Dynasty system might as well not be there. Instead of choosing a variety of skills for your Presidente, you pick one. And then you randomly get heirs who RANDOMLY get one skill. You can then choose which member of the Dynasty to run in an Election. That's it. Hooray. But your main Presidente is apparently Ra's a Ghul, because they don't die of old age, so you can have the same Presidente for close to 100 years.
The biggest issue is the lack of character. None of the missions have the same feel as in Tropico 4. I just didn't get invested in it. None of the different characters show up, except Penultimo, but he's got a giant moustache and a new voice actor. No naive Sunny Flowes, no sultry Miss Pineapple, no greedy Antonio Lopez, no drunken Father Esteban. There's some new characters, but Kalypso cut down on those as well, so you have characters pulling double- or triple-duty on representing the different factions of Tropico.  We don't even get special, Era-specific characters. The Foreign representative is the same dude from Colonial Times. No Nazi weasel or Imperial Japanese bureaucrat contact you with enticing demands. Just Lord British of Englandshire, who then relays the message to you of Axis offers.
To summarize, Tropico 5 offers insultingly little content for a brand new game. If you're coming into the Tropico Franchise brand-new, buy Tropico 4 with all the DLC and expansions. If you already own Tropico 4 with all the DLC and expansions and have played them to death, keep playing them.
As a final note: There is the possibility that Kalypso will release an expansion that makes me change my mind. I only played Tropico 4 once all the way through before Modern Times addicted me. It so thouroughly changed the game in my mind that I have replayed the entire game, even the base, multiple times.
So if they release an expansion pack that adds depth to the Eras or characters or maybe even a Tourist Heaven, with eight new missions and twelve new buildings that allows Tourism throughout the whole game, I promise to change this review.
That said, their first DLC out of the gate is a building for cheese making.

Tropico 5 is not a disappointment, but it isn't a smash hit either.
There are some notable improvements. I love the building grid, it allows me to quickly and accurately place everything without obsessing about being off by a few inches. I love the new graphic elements (the ones that weren't recycled from previous iterations). I enjoy the "modernize" feature - no need to bulldoze your tenements if you want to move on to apartments, and to modern apartments later.
Then there are things that I hate. Castrated Presidente customization screen. The fact that the Presidente and his family are uncontrollable drones just like the rest of the public - I can't go visit my favorite factory or my favorite base or whatnot when I want to, or go resolve a protest by visiting it. Army bases and barracks don't provide living space for the soldiers anymore. Budget system is stupid as hell and can cause you to accidentally crash a thriving economy in the matter of minutes. Teamsters are dumber than ever, and traffic problems are the worst I've seen yet - once you get to World Wars era and beyond, you are presented with a choice of not having enough teamsters to move things around and having your roads gridlocked because cars refuse to take alternate routes.
Be prepared to run out of resources and never get them back. That coal mine? It's going to be emptied out by the time you hit Cold War. That oil well? It might last you a bit into modern times, then it's gone baby gone. Want to build a nuclear power station? Be prepared to see it gobble up uranium like it was coal. Once you hit Modern Times,  your long-term income options are: farming, cigars, wood, furniture, chocolate, rum, textiles and clothes, and pharmaceuticals which the pharma company produces from thin air. Imports are broken, so it's almost impossible to produce cars, electronics or jewelry long-term. You could also buy low/sell high, but that puts you at the mercy of random number generator. This seems like a lot of things, but once you get big and need a lot of power stations and apartments to house people, your economy gets positively voracious. I've seen my balance go from positive six digits to negative six digits in matter of minutes.
And to top it off, we have the good old issues such as: road placement, non-square corners that you can't fill with anything, tropicans that refuse to take public transportation to drive to work and for some reason build shacks in front of unoccupied buildings... not game breaking, but annoying as all get out.
A lot of these issues are solved with mods somewhat, so I recommend you give those a long hard look.
Overall I recommend the game - I had a great time playing it - but be prepared to be a little or a lot frustrated with simple stuff that should have been solved in previous iterations of the game. Oh, and all this extra content you are used to from Tropico 4 (statues, gardens, ploppable trees) - gone baby gone. Get ready to pay for more DLC.

I've seen the term alternate used to describe this title but what I discovered was... well... absurd. Assuming that alternate is a reasonable adjective for longer term players and absurd was my first, then we could say I stumbled upon an "alterurd" or an "absurdnate" title.
For the sake of some (any?) kind of adjective to describe... this... let's go with absurdnate. And why the hell not? Absurdnate? It's fitting. Perfectly fitting. If only I could explain how.
It's called Sunless Sea. That means it's probably Dark. Check. There's Boats. Check. A "base" (London). Check. Map. Check. Sea creatures. Check. Characters. Check. Story. Check. Exploration. Check. Bats. Check. Wait, what? Bats?? Ermmm... OK... let's just go with that.
So I find myself with a small vessel equipped with a tiny deck gun, a strange crew - who are always hungry - and always scared. I have a ship cat. I have rats. The cat eats rats. Everything is normal right?
Yes, yes indeed... Right up until bats something something London, something something water and the map fills with something something glowing, fighting, weird sea creatures that want to eat my boat. I was once an urchin and I'm now a captain. Some guy wants to give me things, someone wants a ride on my boat and someone wants me to take something somewhere. The island I just visited had some weird priest (among other things), the next island had some dark mystery (I have yet to discover what it is and when I do, it won't be - there's always that).
The harbour master wants my port reports, the university wants specimens of the sea creatures I encounter. And of course, I need fuel, supplies and a way and a place to repair my boat. Presumably, doing all these things will give me that thing that I need the most - an income.. income.. income. (is there an echo in here?)
(There's also something about keeping the lights on, which uses up fuel of course, because my crew suffers "Terror".  How... normal can it get?)
Of several quests, I selected what seems the most, I don't know.. appropriate? I have to find my fathers bones (since I'm an urchin my history is probably important to me right?). To find out where they are all I have to do is stumble unknowingly around dark unexplored seas with my aforementioned boat, my dysfunctional crew. And my cat.
Did I mention that everything starts with Z? No? And this is all done with absurdnate storytelling in text based format - with entirely fitting and immersive music... replete with rippling water ambience as you might expect when you have "zee".
This totally makes sense. Totally. What more do you need? A swimthrough?
Absurdnate?  Just buy it already.

What I love about the game is the out of the box thinking in terms of story development, concept in general (!). It makes you feel as if you're Neo in the Matrix.
Some criticisms:

Brought to us by Davey Wreden, the creator of the much acclaimed The Stanley Parable, The Beginner’s Guide is a narrative video game that (as Wreden puts it) “tells the story of a person struggling to deal with something they do not understand”. Lasting only 90 minutes and lacking any real goal or objectives, The Beginner’s Guide shares a story that is both deep and thrilling.
The game begins with Davey Wreden narrating; he tells us about his friend Coda, a game developer who created a compilation of video games. Wreden guides us as we experience and explore this series of games. He talks about the connection between a game and the creator and how the player can get to understand the creator as they play the game.
The individual games are truly fascinating. In one game, you can only walk backwards while in another, you’re shown a series of prisons that Coda has designed As we progress through each game, Wreden tells us about Coda and presents his interpretation of each game and why Coda made it. Some of the games were made to play unplayable; in one game, the player is placed in a prison cell and has to wait an hour, while in another, the player climbs a set of stairs only to find their movement slowed to a stop. Wreden changes these features in the games in an attempt to make the game “playable”.
Wreden guides us through what seems to be a horribly personal journey as he addresses very heavy topics such as self-doubt and depression.
This is one of the few games that made me wish I could forget everything and play it again. Having played and thoroughly enjoyed The Stanley Parable, I was extremely hyped for this and I can say, without hesitation, that it exceeded my expectations. The Beginner’s Guide is a short interactive story with a very deep message.

In BioShock you are a survivor of a plane crash in the middle of the Atlantic Ocean. You are able to make your way to an island where a submarine is waiting to take you to into the great depths below where the mysterious underwater city of Rapture awaits. The city is trashed and genetic freaks called splicers roam around, attacking anything that gets in front of them. In order to survive you will have fight through these Splicers and other oddities keeping your eyes and ears open for clues into what has gone wrong, how you may be able to help or how you can escape.
One aspect that makes the storyline work so well is the way it is told. BioShock uses a real time method of telling the story through random radio reports, overheard conversations and audio recordings.
You can choose from a variety of different weapons, anywhere from pistols and shotguns to chemical throwers and grenade launchers. Each gun has different ammo that you can use. There are also many plasmids that you can use. You can electrify the water to kill everyone in it, set people on fire, freeze them and then smash them with a wrench, among other things.
The graphics in this game are good, out of date, but still good.
The sound of BioShock really puts you into the game. From the creepy things the splicers say to the background music, everything fits perfect.
BioShock builds a great atmosphere by using terrific graphics and sound to set a creepy mood. BioShock is truly a stunning game and worth to buy.

Studio MDHR
Run and Gun, Platform and Boss Rush
September 29 2017
"It's time for a world class bout, now GO!" - The Devil speaks itself after the countdown
Cuphead is a run and gun game, created by small indie company Studio MDHR. The game was originally announced back in E3 2014 but it was delayed because they needed more time to polish the game. It is safe to say that this game delivered way beyond expectation, like seriously, give these guys a round of applause for their greatest work and deserve a recognition. I will address some negative reviews later because it is irritating me. So let's talk about Cuphead in depth.
It is a tale of Cuphead and Mughead. Two boys are having fun and wondering around the map until they discover The Devil's Casino. Cuphead and Mughead decide to gamble and they are on a winning streak. Until the Devil himself appeared, he makes a proposition; if the Cuphead and Mughead wins the gamble, they are going to take the casino and everything, if they lose; their souls will be consumed by the Devil. Cuphead decides to be greedy and they lose the bet, meaning that their souls will be taken but they want to live instead. So they make another proposition from them. The Devil wants the Soul Contracts and they are in deep trouble once they got kicked out. Luckily, the Elder Kettle will help you out and do what the Devil says.
The gameplay of Cuphead is very simple yet effective. It really reminds me of run and gun games like Contra series or should I say Contra-esque gameplay. The game provides an open world exploration but it is linear, that doesn't mean it's not a bad thing since it's supposed to capture the aesthetics of the game or more like what if there's a video game in 1930s. They added an upgrade system and you spend coins to buy shot types (spreads, charged shots, etc.) and charms (extra lives, supers regeneration, etc.) There is a parry system and it is intuitive to use. It is not a traditional parry like Dark Souls (lmfao), it is a visual cue (any pink projectiles or enemies). The controls are tight and customisable which is a great additional in case of everyone wants to have their own controls. It's easy to pick up the controller and master the mechanics. Every boss fights are unique and I love each bosses (even though it made me cry internally when I almost kill every bosses in the game). Cuphead implemented Co-Op during the playthrough, but unfortunately the game does not support online and I am not against it.
The setting sets in 1930s like I mention on Gameplay paragraph. They absolutely capture the jazz musical scores, the animation of every single characters (I can't believe it's a frame by frame animation), the lively background during boss fights. The musical score and graphics, they are a 10 out of 10 rating. I was actually humming some boss fight's theme and they are catchy as. I love the references they add, like Acme from Looney Tunes or other things that is related to 1930s cartoon shows.
I am going to address the negative reviews, so bear with me. Cuphead is challenging and fair, not impossible and difficult. This is what the game is meant to be played. The game throws back to the 90s platform run and gun shooter and boss rushes game. It helps you to be a perfectionist or getting better at it. Sickness is a really unique game. I don't want to say much, as going in pretty much blind is best. From the very first scene you really have no idea where the plot is going. I'd say every hour or so something new is introduced, so it always keeps you guessing and has some brutal surprises.
It is a very dark game about embracing your dark side, so it is not for everyone. But it does balance it all well, as there are many funny moments of dialogue during the lighter scenes. And that is what works so well overall. It is how it balances more day to day activities with the dark side of life. It manages to keep things more grounded in reality even as things just keep getting more violent and dark.
The characters ended up being much more well developed than expected. Two really stood out to me in particular. One of them seemed very grounded, but was so full of contradictions and busy lying to themselves that they came off as very human to me. Overall the dialogue is very precise. It is well written and to the point, which really helped keep the pacing tight. No one goes off on long, unrealstic speeches to drive the plot forward or anything like that. It just flows naturally.
The pacing at times may be a little too fast, though. There were a couple of times that the plot continued on after what I considered an important event and I was thinking "Wait, we're not exploring what just happened any further?". But overall, the pacing is a good thing.
The thing I was most hoping for were a lot of choices. There were a few at the start, but as the game progressed  you began having a ton of choices. You have dialogue options, choices of where to go and of how to physically handle situations. So I was very happy it delivered in that area.
The game took me a few nights to play, so it's actually pretty long. I left steam running, but I'd guess it was probably at least 8 hours long for just one playthrough. And there are many paths I didn't take yet(judging by the photo gallery).
All around a really dark, but fun title. This is the first game I purchased on Steam due to the plot sounding interesting, and I'm very glad I did.

Sickness is definitely one of the best visual novels that I had the luck to play. The art is not bad but it is not any master piece. However, the story of this game is a really good one. It’s unique, realistic and quite relatable. It shows how things on the world aren’t black and white and explore a quite interesting theme such as what a common person may be capable to do to protect and guarantee the survival of those close to them. It’s interesting that despite the clearly “evil” and ♥♥♥♥ed up actions that the main character do during the game you also feel that it would be hypocritical to label him as evil, and you cannot change your view regarding that because even when the main character eventually becomes completely amoral, he still human and quite relatable, and it makes you ask yourself even if you would do any different of what he did .The story in itself is also always interesting, I won’t lie that every time that I had to turn of the computer to do something else I wanted to stay a little longer playing the visual novel. And although sickness is a really dark, demented and well … sick it is also a truly deep story that make us question ourselves and challenge some of our views of the world. Oh and if you came here expecting fanservice I suggest you to turn back and go after something like sakura beach because although there is a few fanservice moments they are truly rare during the game, also if you cannot handle heavy violence this is not also a good game for you since there is a lot of it in this game (although it is not overly exaggerated like psp version of corpse party) . I hope to have helped to you at least give a glimpse of what great game this is.

One of, if not the, most competent lesser known vns on Steam. Has a story thats been steadily given free updates that has improved the flow and length, long enough you dont feel cheated and short enough it doesn't make you feel like you have to fast forward to get to a part worth anything. Has a unique feature thats rarely seen, if at all, that can really screw with your head and immerse you into the character. Multiple routes with fleshed out characters and heroines, brutal scenes not only used once or twice for shock value like some others, several bad ends that are really *bad* and not just "ggnore you lose lol", cgs with a unique art style that really gives some of the close up bloody scenes much more impact, while not being too questionable like some other novels. Doesn't have voice work and instead put the time and effort into making an actual plot which really pays off. Doesn't rely on softcore fan service to draw people in, and doesn't have to. Even if you've touched, completed or heard of the big dogs of vns like Clannad, Little Busters, Muv Luv, Rewrite, Aselia etc. Sickness holds it's own. If you can handle adult content, are alright with/ actually enjoy reading (gasp), or have a passing/serious interest of visual novels in general, this definitely belongs with the top tier and has a much, much more approachable price point with equal story as others.

I love this game!!!  I have played it extensively over the last couple of weeks.  There is so much potential here and the possibilities are endless.  This is a fantastic work in progress!!  Mostly I have been playing Single Player Mode.
Multiplayer is fun as well and you can all work together on the same Castle/Homestead or you can each start at separate Castle/Homesteads and eventually meet up once you can get past that bear/buffalo/boar.
The only difference is that if you start at the same Castle/Homestead you are friendly to each other and all have access to the same Castle/Homestead.  If you begin at different Castle/Homesteads, then you can still trade by just dropping stuff, but you can attack each other, plus you cannot gain access to each others Castle/Homestead.
SPOILER ALERT!!!
At the beginning you have to stay pretty close (very close) to base and farm and mine but then once you have a constant food supply you can then begin to move farther out and eventually get to the city and beyond.  So farm some trees and mine some ore below the base and begin by building the Cooking Workstation, Sawmill, and Forge.  Also, start constructing your home on top and setup at least one if not two Farming Workstations, try to acquire some seeds from scavenging up top especially Honey Pumpkin seeds, if possible, (Bean seeds are not too bad either), place them in your farm, and then you should be set from a food standpoint.  You still need to upgrade your Farming Workstation on top to collect 15 produce at a time but both Honey Pumpkins and Bean can be cooked in the Cooking Workstation and will yield 100HP each.  This is the easiest and simplest food to cook and it is available in the 1st level Cooking Workstation.
Money can be earned easily once you have the ability to get past the Buffalo or Bear and get to the city.  There is a 1st Level Wolf Headpiece that can be made at the Sawmill that yields 94G each.  Takes just (2) Wolf Skin per Wolf Headpiece.
You can also get by those buffalo's or bears (if you don't want to fight one) and get to the city, if you are willing to spend 50G, by accessing the Map in the upper left hand corner, then you just select the city in the middle and you just beam there.
I do believe this only works AFTER you actually visit the city once so you still have to fight your way past that bear or buffalo the 1st time.
Also, build those inventory chests because you will probably need every one!  I do because I am such a hoarder!  Actually it would be nice for way to add more slots to your inventory chests.  I did discover in that if you are able to eventually purchase another Castle/Homestead (takes 12K Gold) then you have access to a new Castle/Homestead that needs to be leveled up, plus a brand new mine to get your ores, etc., but you can begin the inventory chest creation process all over again and you can transfer some of that extra inventory to that new Castle/Homestead.  Upgrading your castle goes a lot faster if you move excess materials to the new location.
I was also able, at the new location, to build (2) extra farming workstations on top, throw sheep or the chicken in and start producing eggs or wool.  I still have the (2) Honey Pumpkin farming workstations at my original Homestead/Castle producing (15) each Honey Pumpkins which can be taken downstairs to the Cooking Station to produce the 100 HP food.
One of the things I love about this game is that when crafting, all items required for crafting may take a little bit of work but still they are attainable with just a little bit of effort.  I have constructed all of the highest levels items so far with the exception of the sword that requires that Demon Skull, which I still haven't found.  Today, I found the Dragon Forebearer charm in my mine, trapped the required (20) sheep, earned the 10K Gold required, acquired the Dragon, and fought the (3) huge demons that come and attack your castle.  That was a blast!
This game is a lot of fun if you like mining, crafting, gathering, and fighting.  Hopefully this game will see its true potential.  There are still (3) other lands for the developers to finish (currently they are just duplicates of the 1st land) plus Ancient Portals plus the Witch, etc.  I can even see a day, developers willing, to be able to build boats (Viking Ship) and be able to travel to other continents with further adventures.

TL;DR Sickness is an experience well worth every penny it costs!
Now to the longer reason why it's worth to have in your library. The game is very different from one playthrough to another (given you don't make the same choices of course), every storyline is deep in its own way and sometimes events turn 180° from one scene to the other. Sickness is gripping, and soon after you start playing you will find yoursef going fast throught the scenes not because you want to finish one more game from your library and move to the next, or just get all the achievements, but because you can't wait to see how things will unravel. Without spoiling, I'll admit there were quite a few times I was caught off guard by the events in the story. So much infact that I'm not so comfortable to admit it was a game that moved me.
The bottom line.
Sickness is dark, sad, disgusting, intricate, disturbing, happy and memorable. It makes you think and feel as the characters do, and as of my two cents.... It's hands down a game I would recommend to visual novel lovers in a heart beat  :)

This game appears to be a roguelike, until after the first couple restarts.
When I began playing, I was excited to explore the world, taking risks, exploring the seas, stretching my resources thin in hopes of finding some hidden treasure trove, or unknown shore, or new quest. Naturally, I soon died, and you know what? I was OK with that; it's to be expected in what I believed to be a roguelike, and so I happily restarted, hoping to have a luckier run next time around.
Rinse and repeat a couple times, and I came to the realization that this game isn't so much a roguelike, as it is an absurd combination of a roguelike and an RPG, combining the aspects of both which are least able to function together.
Where a roguelike may be impossible to predict, with vastly different loot distributions, enemy difficulty, and level layout per restart, Sunless Sea offers a disappointingly static world, with no geographical changes I can perceive between games other than the slight reshuffling of islands. How is it in any way fulfilling to perform the same quests, trade the same goods, and and re-discover the same islands over and over again, with no variation but the reshuffling of otherwise unchanging locations? Admittedly, most minor story events occur randomly, and some quests may vary depending on decisions made in the playthrough, but these variables are few and far between, and do little to alleivate the woeful repetition that begins to set in after the 3rd or 4th death.
Ultimately, there's no sense of adventure, no hope of some amazing discovery, no possibility of finding anything "new". The game becomes an excercise in tedium, an endless repetition of a couple tactics, at which one must become as efficient as possible in order to beat the punishing gameplay, which would have been an enjoyable challenge in a truly random environment, but which is reduced to a chore when implemented in a world with no meaningful variation whatsoever.
The woefully static nature of the game is best summed up by the gameplay guide to be found on the Sunless Sea subreddit: In later sections, the author describes what are essentially the few narrow ways of power-gaming the economy, by means of tediously ferrying a few different types of goods between specific islands.
In short? I can not recommend this game as either a roguelike or an RPG; as the former, it lacks any meaningful randomization of its environment, and as the latter, it absurdly supposes that repetition of the same tasks over and over again for sparse reward is in any way fulfilling. Certainly, playing on merciful is an option, but in so doing the game becomes simply a punishing and relatively short RPG.

Sunless Sea is the hardcore version of Faster Than Light. And it's a lot more in-depth in every way possible than FTL.
You are a captain of a sea vessel and you basically carve out a legacy for yourself and pass it on to your children or die at the bottom of the sea with noname etched in the history books. While the story for FTL is almost like the plot of Star Wars IV: A New Hope (well a much more basic version if it)...you have to reach the federation with 'data' you stole from the rebels.
You have to take great care of not only yourself, but your vessel and your crew. Choices you make in the game will have a big impact as the game progesses. While as FTL you make your choices....and your done right then and there, no real "side of caution" just pick choice A or choice B.
Before I continue. The reason why I am comparing FTL to this game is that a lot of people have made the same comparisons or contrasts. Depending upon your point of view. FTL is basically the kiddy version while Sunless Sea is the hardcore version, like I mentioned at the start of this review. Yes, it's two different games but the mechanics are almost simliar.
Moving on....
Sunless Sea you actually care about the people you meet and the people you take along with you on your ship. While FTL it's just sprite characters with no real connection. Sure you can roleplay and try to make it look like you care. But in the end it's just shrugs and "mehs". Sunless Sea characters are fleshed out with their own background and set of perks. Which by the way can be said the same of the races in FTL but that only applies to the races and not the invdiual characters.
Economy in Sunless Sea is obviously different from FTL but it is handled a bit differently. Economy in Sunless Sea (like all other RPG games) is handled by doing quests, trading, and other things. While FTL it's just handled through combat situations and doing quests....if your lucky to get such things that is. For those who are saying earning "echoes" (which is the economy in Sunless Sea) is hard, it's because you have to go outside your comfort zone and explore far more reaching dangerous areas and do more and more quests that take you to said locations.
Combat is pretty straight forward. Sunless Sea you can buy upgrades for your ship to survive longer and heck, even buy ships themselves. (and I know this sounds a silly thing to compare) but unlike FTL where you have to earn it. Sunless Sea simply says "If you got the echoes and the confidence. Then buy the ship" each ship has it's own layout, weapons are easy to come by rather than scared like what you see in FTL.
Lastly the DLC you can take control of a submarine which explores the depths of the sea. Which sounds pretty cool and also terrifying.
If you want a hardcore version of FTL. I suggest getting Sunless Sea it's a very fun game to play.

Visually fascinating, with some brilliant sound design, this is an immersive lush world to get lost into for an hour or two, surreal and unsettling yet soothing at the same time. It's a game allright, but it's really not about the gameplay, that's just a superficial excuse to spend some time in this eery atmosphere.
Stripped of its artstyle this would be a mediocre HOG, with some of the most unimaginative puzzles ever. Worse even, the controls are really bad - though it gets less noticeable after the first level (stick it out). Basically, translating the (clearly originally for touchscreens) tap / drag into click / click&drag means the game can't really tell what your input is half the time, which will be quite frustrating for some people.
Personally, I wanted to be annoyed by another half baked mobile port and couldn't, and I don't even like insects and flowers that much. It looks stunning on a big screen, the images here hardly do it justice. The music and sound design have the same eerie, mildly unsettling quality as the visuals. The loving attention to detail in both the art and the sound design is really impressive, as is the way they blend and flow together, completely overshadowing everything the gameplay is lacking. I also found the slow pace and even the length (it's short) fitting and appropriate.
I enjoyed my time with it, and for anyone after the experience rather than the game, it's definitely worth checking out.

Project Zomboid is one of the most unique zombie games ever made. It asks the question "In the zombie apocalypse, How will you survive, and what will be the cause of your demise?" This is a game that, if all its planned features are added, will rival other zombie survival horror games such as DayZ or 7 Days to Die. In the event you do not know the full extent of what they are looking to add, this includes an in depth survivor system that will allow you to join or start your own enclave of survivors, then supply them with the means to protect your new home. They also plan to add hostile NPC's because everyone knows in the event of the zombie apocalypse, their is nothing to stop a group of people from coming to your home and robbing everything you used to own, then shooting you and putting an end to your shortlived life in the Project Zomboid world. Did I mention that one day these muggers may not be NPC's, but entire bands of other players? No? Thats one of this games planned features as well.
With all this being said, and there are still hundreds of more things to come, Project Zomboid is a game worth getting now, and a game worth the wait for later. I will recollect some of my expereinces to all who read this so you may furthur understand how this game is the zombie game we have all been waiting for.
This story begins as it is my first time playing, my charactar is wearing a sweater and a little moodlet pops up on the side showing that it makes him a little warm, and so I swap the sweater with a vest and start to loot the rest of the house I had spawned in. After a long day of looting my charactar becomes hungry, thirsty and tired. After taking care of his Food and Water needs, I put him to bed. However in the middle of the night, two gunshots ring off close to the house, and while there are no NPC's yet, it still put me under the impression that someone was outside my house. The gunshots almost immediatly woke me up, and after waking up I heard a very distinct set of moans, and it is obvious to anyone that the gunshot drew a couple of the undead. However I did not grasp the danger of this situation until I stepped outside to a full on Horde. Only one of them noticed me as I bolted back inside and I hatched a plan. I would draw the horde in, then attempt to burn down the house. After coming up with this Idea I kept in mind this house had 6 exits, 4 including the windows around the house, and the 2 doors on opposite ends. I shoved a bunch of food and maybe some things not meant for the oven- into the oven, and turned it on. Over time electricity and plumbing turn off in this game but for now I was fortunate that it had not. After this I drew a large chunk of the horde into my home once the kitchen set ablaze. I didn't stop to see if it worked, I just simply ran on and on, putting as much distance between me and that horde as possible.
I beleive that story to be best to show off how diverse the system of Project Zomboid is, with the appropriatly named "Sinister Ai" the game will generate random events such as house alarms for when you break into the window in an attempt to loot the place, or as you saw, random enviromental sounds such as jets, helicopters, gunshots and alarms that will draw or lead away hordes. Overall the pros of this game leave your screen and roll outside your house, yet the cons do as well. While this game is a great colaboration of everything any zombie fan has ever wanted in a zombie game, it still doesnt have ALL the features and it still is in Early Access, which means there will be a LOT of bugs, but if you can get past this you will get a game that will truly give you a fresh expereince every time.

Concrete Jungle is a wild mix of deckbuilding, city management and Tetris.
The main game mode has you either on your own or against an opponent building row upon row of buildings. The goal is to gather more points than the enemy. Your "deck" consists of various kinds of cards you select before a game. These cards represent "point cards" (housing), "buff cards" (anything that increases the value of your point cards) and "debuff cards" (decreasing the value of preferably your opponent's cards). You basically just select 1 of 2 available cards per turn and place the represented building on a free tile. These tiles are either blank or have numbers associated to them. The higher the number, the more points you get for placing a point card on top. This number can be increased or decreased by the buff and debuff cards respectively and can also turn negative, meaning you can actually lose points. Once a "row" is completed by achieving the appropriate number of points, these points are added to or subtracted from your balance. This continues until the final row, after which the game ends. In solo mode you are also awarded bonus multipliers for completing several rows at once. This is used to unlock new cards and regenerate your health (you can use a life to delete the row at the bottom). Rows are always deleted from bottom to top.
However, that would be an oversimplification. The game is MUCH more detailed than that. The campaign leads you through a series of quite difficult missions alone and against NPC characters. Every new mission adds a new gameplay element and new cards that can completely change the way you play. You can also unlock these characters for different play styles, as each has their own theme and "skill tree". For starters cards have 2 values assigned to them that are represented by 2 bars. Filling the top bar grants you either a new card to include into your deck or a skill, with the best skills only available very late in a given game. These skills can be unique cards to that character or other bonuses. Filling the lower bar means you have to achieve more points per row to complete them.
The rest of the game is hardcore planning as build space gets ever tighter and your opponent may still foil your grand plans of victory. Cards are sorted into different categories which can be combined to form blocks of several adjacent cards. Blocks can be further enhanced to grant a massive influx of points for example. Basically every card interacts with the board in a different way and there are a lot of cards. It's easy to lose track of everything.
Unfortunately the game does not offer online multiplayer, which may be a reason not to purchase it for some people, since the SP value is limited. After almost 5 hours I only have the extreme missions in the campaign left, but many many more cards to unlock. However, the campaign gets tedious because of the randomness and how some missions are structured. Especially the VS modes take a terribly long time and can end in defeat after you're almost certain of victory. Personally I see no reason to continue playing. In a world of endless brown shooters (2010 AAA Releases), comes a little indie title released on the Xbox at the end of the summer. What attracted me to LIMBO (and I would posit major review sites as well) was the tone and art style in context of the greater gaming market at the time. 2010 was indeed a great year for gaming in terms of variety and overall quality. The big sequels were (arguably) not too contrived, pre-ordering still a reason to exist (albeit a pretty thin reason), and AAA releases actually worked when you bought them. What does this have to do with LIMBO? Take a look at the top rated games of 2010:
One of these is not like the others. LIMBO is like James Cameron's Titanic: released at the perfect time with basically no competition in it's market and just interesting and different enough to gain critical and financial success. What makes LIMBO stand out is it's presentation. The gloomy atmosphere and dark tone were things not being explored by any other game on the market. It manages to satisfy the puzzle/platformer and survival/horror genres that the AAA publishers had all but written off as "unsellable." I refer to the quote, "there is no perfect pasta sauce, only perfect pasta sauces."
Now for the game itself...
LIMBO is a game best played a few times through.
The first playthrough is marred with frustration with the trial-and-error gameplay and disapointment with the abrupt and ambiguous ending. Still, something compelled me to play it again. I was reminded of the fantastic opening in which the boy rides a boat from one side of a lake to another. The camera slowly pulls back revealing a fog-shrouded background and while a frog croaks in the distance. I immediately remember why I love this game. Not for the puzzles or gameplay, but for the quiet moments. The moments when the view pushes back and allows you to reflect on the world the game has created and the implications thereof. As such the game is much better when it is not constantly being interrutped by player death. It flows as an art piece with the boy narrowly escaping death at every turn as the challenge ramps up more and more.
That is what LIMBO is really: an art piece. It's meant to be experienced in one sitting with little to no interuptions (deaths). At least, that's the feeling I get from a few replays. That being said, it's confusing as to why the game is so opaque in its puzzle design for first-time players. I personally don't remember getting very frustrated except for one specific puzzle involving saw blades, a box, and precise timing but from reading some of the other reviews on here I seem to be in the minority.
Criticisms often leveled at the game usually are "there's not really a story", "the ending is anticlimatic", and the aforementioned "the puzzles get way too hard, way too fast, near the end." I can't say I disagree with any of these. I'm fine with there not being a plot other than "boy needs to survive death traps", but the ending is quite sudden and very ambiguous with the smash cut to black. Say what you will, but it's the most "arthouse" moment of the whole game and doesn't say anything about the boy, the sister, Limbo or really anything at all. I would have preferred a reveal that he was dead the whole time or
other than the ending that's there. After such a violent, gruesome game it seems odd that the developers would pull punches right at the end.
With all of that said, I do recommend this game highly. It rises above its flaws and creates a truely unique world. I would also recommend picking it up onsale as $10 for a 2-3 hour game is asking a bit much.
Aside: I experimented with this game
style and found that Radiohead's
syncs up pretty well with the areas in this game. Give it a try if you're so inclined.

The Testament of Sherlock Holmes, a game I'd never heard of before. The fact that is was 75% off and was recommended by some steam users made me buy it. I never would have expected that it would be one of the best games I've played i the past few months.
The story is pretty obviuos and sometimes predictable, and the ending was, in my opinion, a bit ridiculous. the graphics are pretty okay, considering this is not a triple A title. The animations are sometimes a bit dodgy and funny looking, and the lack of lip sync is also pretty funny if you start to notice it. But these are not the points that make or break a game for me. No, for me it's all about gameplay, and boy did this game do that right.
The searching for clues is sometimes really straight forward, but many times you will be really surprised by where you'll have to look or what you'll have to do to find that one little clue or object you desperately need. And when you do find it, you WILL feel satisfied.
The only little downside to this is a little lack of freedom. For example when you already know what needs do be done next, the game forces you to find that one last clue before you can go any further in the story, even of you already know the solution.
The puzzles are awesome and sometimes you really have to think about them (hardest one took me half an hour of scribbling possible solutions on pieces of paper at my desk).
The dialogue is brilliant, and despite the above named lack of lip sync, the facial expressions are rather good. You can really tell how someone feels by looking at them. The witty remarks of Sherlock Holmes are really entertaining and overall the crime solving duo has been really well represented in the game.
Conclusion: I can't wait untill the next game from this company and give it a solid 8.5/10

This game covers the Eastern Front during WWII: Russians vs. Germans. The core of the game is TEAMWORK. So, every time you join a match you pray you’ll find a cooperative team. There are various roles that each player must cover: Rifleman (basic class), Elite Rifleman (has a semi-auto rifle at his disposal), Assault (has one or more SMGs), Elite Assault (it has an additional weapon akin to an assault rifle), Engineer (the guy with satchels and throwable AT mines), Sniper (a.k.a. Marksman), Machine-gunner (the “suppressor”), Squad Leader (basically a mobile spawn point), Commander (usually referred as TL, his job is gather information on the enemy with Recon and call Artillery on various marks deployed either by him or the SLs) and, in some specific maps, even tank crewman and their infantry counterpart: the AT gunner.
.By gaining experience your character levels up till max level 99 and every gun you use levels up too up until level 50. By gaining experience your character becomes more proficient at running and shooting. Each gun has various mods (e.g. bayonet, modified iron sights etc.) and you can choose which one to use once you unlock them.
“Be an example to your men, in your duty and in private life. Never spare yourself and let your troops see that you don’t in your endurance of fatigue and privation. Always be tactful and well-mannered. Avoid excessive sharpness or harshness of voice, which usually indicates the man who has shortcomings of his own to hide.” (Field Marshal Erwin Rommel).
I think that this game ought to be played on “hardcore” servers (e.g. [40-1] UK Servers). The reason behind this is because this game itself was designed to be as realistic as possible (e.g. accurate ballistics, “one-shot one-kill” wounding system (if you aim well of course), fatigue (i.e. stamina) etc.). So, do not expect to rush like a fool toward enemy guns (unless told so by your Commander, but that is a specific case called Mass Charge). What gives a team a competitive advantage is having good SLs that follow orders. As said before they are mobile spawn points and, to allow their squad mates to effectively capture an enemy held position, must get near to it (by deploying smoke and using the flanks).
There are various game modes but I will cover the most popular one: territories. One team is defending and the other is attacking. There are several cap zones that might favour the attackers instead of the defenders and vice versa. This game mode is usually played in a campaign where the two opposing factions have manpower as their unique resource (if one faction is low on manpower it is forced to defend).  Prior to an attack, the attacking team must choose which map to select. Each one might favour one side more than the other so it is best to choose carefully. So, as you can clearly understand this game is all about strategy and tactics.
The guns have a realistic feel about it: you can’t effectively use a Ppsh or an MP40 against a distant target because the rounds will disperse. So, you better choose your class with care: for instance, if you are more adept rushing up close to the enemy, then go for the Assault role (SMG gunner), if you like to pick up targets from a distance pick up the Sniper/Marksman class and so on.
This game focuses on the Pacific Front where the USMC Corps faces the Imperial Japanese Army on various islands (e.g. Guadalcanal, Iwo Jima, Betio etc.). I can’t stress this enough: TEAMWORK is important. The set changes but the core does not. The key difference in this game is the unorthodox strategies that the Japanese team has at its disposal: booby traps, banzai charges, hiding in bushes with camouflaged uniforms etc. The same levelling up system applies here. Classes change a bit: flamethrower and the Automatic Rifleman for the Americans and Light Mortar unit for the Japanese.
“In my dreams, I hear again the crash of guns, the rattle of musketry, the strange, mournful mutter of the battlefield.” (D. MacArthur)
The gameplay in the Pacific is slightly more dynamic than in the European Front. And that's because of banzai charges. Plus the Pacific have a totally different terrain morphology (i.e. jungles, beaches etc.).
I think that this game ought to be played on “hardcore” servers (e.g. [40-1] UK Servers) (again). For the same reasons above I recommend playing it hardcore.
Same as RO2.
The guns are realistic and are different from the ones found in the Russian Theatre. The Americans have the best weaponry compared to the Japanese, let me give you some examples:
Take the Rifleman Class:
The American M1 Garand is a semi-automatic rifle that gives the shooter the ability to take follow-up shots that come in handy while up close or mid-range (Note: in Guadalcanal the Garand is not available so the only rifle the US has is the is the M1903 Springfield that, while being a bit more accurate, is a bolt-action and it’s practically useless at close range).
The Japanese Arisaka comes in two types: 38 and 99. The 38 is old but more accurate and less powerful while the 99 is modern, more powerful but less accurate. BUT: they are both bolt-action. So, they may come in handy while in long and mid-range but they become useless once the enemy is near.
So from an accuracy standpoint the Japanese 38 is similar to the M1903 but since battles are usually dynamic the Garand can be regarded as superior since it is more versatile.
Take the two faction-related classes US Flamethrower and Japanese Knee-Mortar:
While the American flamethrower does a grand job up close clearing bunkers, buildings and jungle environment the knee-mortar is excellent up close, mid-range and long-range. So where there is an advantage for one side there is a disadvantage for the other but this trade-off balances the fact that the US have generally better weaponry than the Japanese as a whole.
There are other examples but to me these give more the idea of how different the two factions are and consequently how much tough is to play as a Japanese (even though a well-trained and well-coordinated Jap team can be even more dangerous than the American team because of banzai and traps, mostly).
Thanks for reading and I hope I've helped you gain some useful information about this masterpiece.

A decent enough adventure game and a treat for fans of Sherlock Holmes.
I won't say this is the best adventure game I've ever played, but I enjoyed it for what it was worth.  The fact that I'm a big fan of Sherlock Holmes did help me look past some of the game's rougher spots, but I'm not sure someone else would be so forgiving.  The overall narrative, suffice it to say, is no match for the Sir Arthur Conan Doyle originals, but it's enough to hold the game together, which is really the most you can expect from a video game story.
I called this an adventure game, but I think "puzzle game" might be a more fitting description.  Who knew the denizens of Victorian London were so fond of locking their secrets behind intricate logic puzzles?  You will encounter around two-dozen puzzles throughout the course of completing the game, and while I didn't find the puzzles particularly difficult once I understood them, the rules and operations of the puzzles were sometimes vague, so it wasn't always obvious to me what I was supposed to do, or if it was obvious, it wasn't obvious exactly how I was supposed to go about doing it.  I suppose that's part of the gameplay experience, figuring out exactly what the puzzle is and how to solve it, but there were times I honestly wasn't sure if this was intentional or simply poor game design.  No matter, walk throughs are easy enough to find on the internet these days if you need a prod in the right direction; alternatively, the game does present the option to simply skip a puzzle if you're well and truly stumped, but what self-respecting gamer would choose that route?
There are also the more traditional adventure game puzzles that have you exploring your environment for clues, picking up everything you possibly can, and occasionally combining various objects in your inventory so you can proceed.  Thankfully, the game has a "Sixth Sense" feature where you press the spacebar to momentarily have points of interest highlighted for you which eliminates the frustrating pixel hunt.
The presentation is a somewhat mixed bag.  The environments and character models are generally oustanding with great attention to detail and lots of atmospheric touches that really make Victorian London come to life.  The overall character animations are good for the most part, but the lipsynching is atrocious with the characters frequently flapping their lips for a few seconds after delivering their lines, which I found distracting, and the voice acting is average at best.  I never really took to Watson's melodramatic delivery where every line is spoken with an awkward urgency, and Holmes speaks in a drone, sounding almost bored at times, as if the whole business of crime solving no longer interested him.  Curiously, the bit players you encounter throughout the game are often better acted and sound more convincing then the stars of the show.
The game controls well enough with a mouse and keyboard, although the mouse movements felt somewhat sluggish even with the sensitivity turned up to maximum in the settings. I played mostly from the third-person perspective which gives you a good view of your surroundings, and while a traditional adventure game perspective is offered, I found the controls too awkward (although people with a gamepad seem to have good success playing from this perspective).  I'd like to pass on a couple of tips on controlling the game since I'm not sure if it's mentioned in the manual: 1) you can use the mouse wheel to quickly scroll through individual items in your inventory; this is a lot faster and more convenient than opening your inventory screen, although you still have to open it if you want to combine one object with another; 2) if you have a bunch of hotspots clustered together, you can click the left-mouse button to highlight one and then use the WASD keys to cycle through them until you've highlighted the one you want; click the left-mouse button a second time to activate it; otherwise it's just way too fiddly to try and maneuver your character into the right position.
I realize this review might seem overly critical, but none of the criticisms I've noted are fatal, and I did spend an enjoyable 14-hours completing this game.  With the noted exceptions, the puzzles are clever and fun to solve, and I have to say again that I found the art design to be terrific making each area a joy to explore, particularly when I came across obscure references to the original Conan Doyle stories.  If you're a fan of adventrue games, and especially Sherlock Holmes, and you think you could look past the weaknesses I've noted, then I would recommend this game.

Niffelheim
2D Action Exploration
Ellada Games
Ellada Games
is a 2D action exploration game developed and published by Ellada Games, and it is currently in Early Access.
The game is set in a Nordic fantasy setting. You play as a dead viking who is stopped by some demons from entering Valhalla, and instead they bring him to Niffelheim, which is a sort of limbo. Here, you will fight monsters, skeletons and other creatures of Norse mythology.
There is no story in the rest of the game, but I do appreciate the setting, which isn't used often in gaming, and it was a breath of fresh air from all the Greek mythology games.
The hand-drawn graphics are a beauty to look at: the backgrounds are full of detail and the character models are excellent. The only nitpick I have are the animations, which are a little bit too stiff and static.
This is going to make or break the game for you. If you are into Minecraft or any other game in which you collect resources to build houses and such, you are going to love this game. If you prefer a focus on action, you will be hugely disappointed.
The controls are very awkward, both with k/m and a controller. Chopping down trees and mining mines are really tedious, and the combat is very unresponsive: you keep mashing the attack button hoping that your opponent dies first, since trying to use the shield doesn't stop the attacks. Exploring the environments isn't even all that fun because your viking moves at a snail's pace.
These are all issues that those who enjoy this genre will look past, but other players will be hugely disappointed. Since it's in Early Access, I hope it gets fixed in the future to make the overall experience more enjoyable.
As stated before, the combat is very hard to grasp, and most encounters turn into a constant "attack-drink potion-attack" loop. Finding resources, while not necessarily hard, is very boring and long.
The voice acting is decent, and the soundtrack and ambient noises are very good.
There is definitely a lot of content in the game, and with more features being added over time, this has the potential of becoming one of the best games in the genre.
Overall, this is a great game for fans of this genre and one of the better Early Access releases in the last few months. But, if you are like me and prefer a more action-oriented game, I think you should give this a pass.

I wish I could recomend this game. There is a lot of interesting potential that is wasted here. Unfortunately that's what it does: waste your time and it's own potential.
The "city planning" aspect of the game is purely cosmetic. There is nothing about this that relates to city building aside from  the cosmetics. You could pallet swap this with any theme and it would still be a puzzle game. I feel thoroughly mislead that this has anything to do with city planning.
It's also almost entirely multiplayer focused. The single player campaign is over before you even learn all of the mechanics. Any length you get from it is purely from replaying the same levels in an effort to get a better score.
The core of the game is deck building, followed by placing your cards as tiles. You will grind endlessly to unlock new cards and there are a couple of hundred cards to unlock. I was bored about 10% of the way through. The new cards you unlock feel shallow and are often just the same thing you could already do but now unlocked for a different character...
And the game doesn't even bother to give you any clue how to build decks or strategy. Difficulty ramps up pretty quick and while I was able to adapt it felt more like memorizing the board for an advantage than actually using real skill. Any skill you attempt to use is simply thwarted by the random nature of the card draws.
Your only advantages are in the deck building itself and than leaning towards one side of the map or the other depending on terrain (restart until you memorize location).
Overall there's some potential here but it's squandered by the tiny map, the grind to unlock mostly useless cards, the short campaign, the shortsighted tutorial that can't be bothered to teach you anything (good luck figuring out the scoring system without looking it up on the forums), and so on. Even the balance between characters is shady. Some of them just stomp all over the others which means you are pretty limited in your choices unless you want to play with a penalty.
I can't even bring myself to write about it further, part of me is OCD and wants to keep playing the game to unlock things purely out of compulsion but I'm really just bored and not having much fun with it. Once past the campaign (which didn't take long) it becomes a boring grind fest to unlock stuff, and the more you unlock the more you realize how shallow the game is.
If you are still curious, wait for a sale. I picked this up in a humble bundle (where I was already buying the bundle for something else I wanted), so I'm not really out any money over it. I'd be kind of annoyed if I'd paid full price.
EDIT: And I feel like there is something shady going on with all the positive reviews this has. Way too many of them have very few hours into the game. If they have 20+ hours and really love the game, that's awesome for them. But the 5 hour and under crowd, may not have played enough to realize how short the game is. But whatever, I'm done caring.

Horror movies don't scare me. So, I can say I am less scared of the usual horror stuff than an average man.
PREVIOUS HORROR GAMES
Well, there are a few games, though that cause that chilling sensations in my spines. Silent Hill games do that very well. Homecoming proved so spooky that I read the walkthrough and checked only those hotel rooms that were needed, apparently to avoid unwanted confrontation.
Silent Hill Shattered Memories was great for me. It was scary but had a nice storyline that kept you stuck till the end.
Obscure II was a pretty good co-op experience.
Alan Wake was okay... not very scary.
OUTLAST
Needless to say, this game does it pretty well. I started playing it around the time it was released and left it after an hour (horrified) and thought I would not touch it again. But here I am playing it again. I don't think I have completed much of the game, but I have played it for a while now. I am playing it on HARD (second difficulty level).
If I compare the gameplay, Outlast is more like Silent Hill Shattered Memories than the other games I have mentioned above. Let alone any sort of gun or melee weapon, you can not even push the enemies while escaping. The only you can do to survive is move stealthily, run if detected and hide. If you are playing the game, make sure you are well acquainted with all the hiding places around.
The locations, the music and the sound effects in the game are done very well. Enemies are repeatitive, but I feel there would be no value addition to add variety in them.
Other than 'run and hide', there are occassional simple missions that elevate the tension sky-high.
I never played any silent hill game twice, although I loved each one of them. So, I am pretty sure I won't come back to OUTLAST once I beat it. This game is a star on the shoulders of a gamer. Beating these games feels like an achievement, not because they are hard, but because you need real guts to walk through their sinister worlds.
If horror games are your cup of coffee, THIS GAME IS A MUST PLAY. For a non-AAA game, this game is unbelievably well-done.
Happy Gaming!

Usually it takes me maybe 6 hours of game time to post a review because by then I can sort of gauge wether I recommend a game or not, but Cuphead made me do this differently.
After 11 hours of gameplay in order to play the game to completion, I can assure everyone that Cuphead is absolutely worth your attention.
---------------------------------------------------
REVIEW STARTS HERE
---------------------------------------------------
Story:
As per its cheeky pre Hays Code Cartoon aesthetic, the story of Cuphead is actually pretty dark.
Two anthropomorphic cups named Cuphead and Mugman wander too far from home and end up in a casino. Cuphead, blinded by a large winning streak at the craps table, decides to make a bet with the devil, and obviously he loses. As a result, Cuphead and Mugman are forced to hunt down and collect the souls of the Devil's other debtors, whom will serve as your bosses. A simple story that the developers make sure isn't sidelined during the course of the game, which is nice.
Graphics and Audio:
This game's graphics and audio is a shining example of the passion that Studio MDHR had for this project. Each character, animation, background, and so on is hand drawn in that sort of iconic 1930's cartoon style and not once is the illusion that you're playing a cartoon ever lost or even skewed. The game is absolutely gorgeous to look at and the sound design is even better. With the 1930's and the sort of limitation of technology of the time, sound quality in media was often grainy and sort of muted. This fact remains with Cuphead, but the beauty of this sort of sub par and scratchy sound is that it in fact even improves the immersiveness of the game. The music is exceptional and sounds like it's ripped straight from a record of the era, from the somber barbershop quartet singing about cuphead's woes on the game's title screen, to frantic and upbeat big band tracks that seem almost neverending as you run jump and shoot your way through a wild boss battle.
Gameplay
I'm not going to do the usual "this game is like dark souls" thing. This game is DIFFICULT. Sometimes infuriatingly so, but the beauty of the game's inherent "just one more try" design is that Studio MDHR knows exactly how to keep you glued to it, and in this case it's as simple as showing you how close you are to the end of a fight if you die at any point. It's a tease, it's engrossing, and it works. As far as the controls go I'd recommend playing the game with a controller as the game was clearly developed with this type of scheme in mind. The controls are super tight and you'll never die from your character floating into some projectile that you mean to avoid after you stop moving. There was only one instance where I felt like I was damaged by nothing at all and this wasn't until the very end of the game, and although admitedly I was very angry, I told myself "It's Cuphead" and moved on to finish the game.
Boss variety is where the creativity of the development team really shines. Not a single boss mechanic is redone or rehashed in some way and every single boss is a unique fight. And what's even more impressive is that the entire game is made up of just boss fights and the game never ever gets old. There are a few run and gun levels but these just seem to be added as a way for the player to obtain currency to buy powerups from the shop, which is fine.
Final Verdict:
Cuphead is a masterpiece in every regard. With exceptional game design, graphical fidelity, and audio quality, Cuphead will be able to remain as immortal as the cartoons it's inspired by, making it the first of its kind. This game is an absolute must have for anyone and everyone with access to a console or PC.

The basic setup of Jigoku Kisetsukan will be familiar to most bullet hell players. You have a shoot button, a smart bomb with limited uses, and a "focus" button that shows your character's actual hitbox -- far smaller than the character's size onscreen -- and slows down your movements. While there is some element of aiming and shooting at opponents, for the most part you're intent on dodging intricate mathematical patterns of enemy fire.
Jigoku Kisetsukan is very, very Touhou. The main character bears a strong physical resemblance to Reimu, the most common enemies are Christmas-tree-angel fairies, even the danmaku patterns make me think of the middle Touhou games. The major distinction is that Jigoku Kisetsukan is almost a demake; the synthesized orchestral music is replaced by chiptunes, and the game artwork is downgraded and pixelized.
There's also just overall a lot less ... character. While the designs aren't bad (better, in fact, than some of the early Touhou characters) the characters just don't have as much personality. Their before-battle conversations are utterly humorless, to the point that I wondered why the author bothered. Perhaps there's better dialogue when playing with other characters, but Tenshi just seems generically "good" and not much else.
On the other hand, the ability to unlock other characters' stories is interesting, and you do get more playable characters than average for the genre. That's a lot of replayability.
Which, of course, brings us to the price. I'd have been happy with anything up to about $6.99, but the game is being provided free and legally. It also has a slightly easier difficulty curve than most bullet hell games, so it is a good introduction to the genre.

This game is super freaking good, and it grew on me very quickly. I was initially attracted to the SimCity 2000 inspired graphics, and the ads/trailers for the game were pretty enjoyable. What I did NOT expect was just how well put together this game would be.
The gameplay and core concepts for this game are fantastic. Basically it works like this: you build a deck and modify it through the level (easy enough), each card builds a building that does something (collects points, adds points, buys stuff, etc.), and the board has limited space to build said buildings. It sounds easy enough, but the mechanics all come together in a way that makes you think in order to solve some pretty complex goals.
The art assets in the game, particularly the music, stand out as well. I have found myself humming the main theme while showering in the morning and would honestly listen to this music independently of the game. That said, it still melds really well with the city theme; the creators of the game got the feel of that style down perfectly. Speaking of audio, can someone please give Laney's voice actor a medal or ribbon or something?
Really, the devs did good work all around, and it's really hard to nitpick the few rough edges the game has since the indie charm more than makes up for it. If any of the tags for this game catch your eye -- at the time of writing this, strategy, indie, card game, puzzle, or isometric -- then you will almost certainly enjoy this game. And since it's so easy to pick up and play, say, after work, don't be surprised if you find that you have "accidentally" spent 20+ hours in it playing "just a few rounds."

This is fast becoming one of my all time favorites in the genre,
You start off making your charater in the character creation screen that has all the normal options like being male or female as well as the style of hair etc. You also have to choose your occupation from the few ingame already (such as firefighter or construction worker each giving their own bonuses), as well as traits that give certain bonus to skills such as being able to carry more items or moving more silently.
After all that you start off in a random location on a pre generated map, of which there is two to pick from, each being rather large in size with places such as, mini malls, police station and farms etc.
From the start your time is up, you will struggle to get to the safety of the nearest house while behind you the whole time are of course, ZOMBIES, lots and lots of zombies :)
After you get your bearings you go out into the danger filled zombie towns in search of food water weapons and anything you can find to help in anyway possible to your survival, including a good safe house to hide out in during the cold nights. You can also build things like fences, furniture etc as well as boarding up your safehouse to keep those darn zombies from breaking your windows. :)
The game has a few bugs here and there sure but considering it's still in alpha it's very playable and to date i've been lucky and not had many bugs at all affect my overall experience (only one that crashed my game and that is about the only major bug i've ran into).
Probably the best alpha of a game ive played to date and in my honest opinion this is the basic quality all early access should aim for when putting out an alpha (of course that is my own opinion only).
The developers still have a lot of stuff to add/fix but i have full faith in IndieStone to make this game even more special than it already is :)

My immediate response on finally completing the game is negative. Perhaps, with some time and some retrospection, my opinion will change for the better. Now, however?
My first complain about this game is that falls into the usual comic book adaptation pitfall of assigning names from the comics to characters that might as well be totally new, because they definitely don't resemble their namesakes. For example, why is there a Prometheus/Scarecrow/Strange hybrid with the name and civilian identity of Vicki Vale? And why is a character more like Hush than anyone else parading around calling himself Penguin? (Don't get me wrong, Penguin was a great character. Just not very...
).
The story is yet another retelling of Batman's earlier days as a crimefighter, because we needed another of those, obviously. The only way it could get more boring and overdone is if Telltale filled it with references to Frank Miller's work. To Telltale's credit, they do try to spice it up and set it apart from the rest, but they don't do a very good job. The plot is hackneyed and swerves between overly predictable and clearly puling stuff from nowhere in poor attempts at plot twists, and most of the attempts to make things more interesting, like making Thomas Wayne a mobster, are boring and/or just plain dumb. Compounding this is the constant failure to utilize promising pieces of plot - Bruce is out of Arkham in barely any time at all, we barely see anything of Wesker, and so on.
Furthermore, few if any of the choices you make actually feel like they affect anything. This is most glaring with the choice between saving Harvey and Selina, because even if Penguin doesn't scar Harvey up, he still goes Two-Face in short order, and the excuse they give for it (feeling betrayed by Bruce and still feeling the after-effects of the toxin) honestly ends up feeling contrived and weak, at least in execution.
This one is more of a personal complaint, but with all the focus the writers put on the concept of family, I'm deeply disappointed that a grand total of
of Bruce's many, many children - adopted or otherwise - make an appearance. No Grayson (freakin' censors not letting me call him♥♥♥♥♥♥, no Jason, no Cass, no Damian, no - well, you get the idea. Actually, very few members of the Batfamily appear or are even alluded to. The only ones I can remember (aside of Lucius and Alfred) is a mention of Lucius' son, Luke (later to become Batwing), and the presence of Ryder and Montoya (later to become the Creeper and the second Question, respectively), but even then, there's not so much as the slightest reference to their future superhero identities. You'd think that at least Jim's daughter (Barbara Gordon/Batgirl/Oracle) or Bruce's cousin (Kate Kane/Batwoman) would get mentioned.
The gameplay is good and the fights are usually thrilling - beating Cobblepot into the ground in the secret lab felt especially cathartic - but in a game as story-based as this one, that's no saving grace. Art style and animation are nice too, but, again, not much of a saving grace. The plot has some good moments, especially the part with the Vales' foster son, but not enough to save it.
Telltale had everything they needed to make perhaps the best Batman game ever, and I really, genuinely, thought that they would do it.
They failed.

I like how the way they re-tell this batman origin, it's difficult considering it's a story that has been told so many times and in different ways, but yet, they are still able to do a pretty decent job on this part.
Now, with that good foundation, how good is the whole Experience actually is? Well, not that good.
It's the same formula that Telltales has been using for a while, there's nothing new really. And if you have played a lot of their games like me, I guess you will started to get tired of it. The choices are mostly obvious, and how they make us learn about the characters? Trust me, they have done a better job.
I'm just not invested enough into the characters, the dialogues doesn't work for me. Unless the parts where you learn about the relationship between Bruce-Harvey, Bruce-Selina and

. How they interact to each other is the moments I grew to love/hate the character based on a believeable reasons, interactions that relateable to our daily life. But unfortunately, aside from that small portion of those three characters interactions and situations, the rest of the story fell flat.

I don't know if I can say this is a bad game, but it is certainly not for me and there are plenty of other 2D Flash/HTML5 games I'd rather play than this. That said, at the time of me playing this, there are plenty of people playing this because many people (notably teenagers and the like) saw a free game that apes Counter-Strike in a top down 2D fashion for free.
I was hoping for something similar to Stick Arena and while this game is familar to play control wise, the mechanics don't feel great to me. Seems like it is EXTREMELY easy to die and probably just as easy to kill, though I'm not remotely good at this game (I only had one kill the entire time I played). One the one hand, you appear to have a "limited vision" so you wouldn't be able to see people through walls, but on the other hand, it seems like you can see anybody who is on your screen, so the blocky "cone of vision" effect seems useless and just annoyance than a mechanic to overcome.
I'm sure there are strategies to "gittin gud" so you will be more effective - there were players that had many kills and kill streaks. The game kept playing soundstreaks of DOUBLE KILL stolen from Unreal Tournament 99. This game borrows alot of sound assets from Counter-Strike and Unreal Tournament. That said, the game never felt great to play. Player can purchase machine guns and then get their gun to "stick out side of walls" so they can shoot enemies through walls - which felt like an unintended mechanic.
This game is ugly to look at and has little professional polish at all, but there seems to be a decent amount of players and the game is free for you to try for yourself instead of hearing me ramble. But what I played was pretty bad and should be left as some game for kids and teens with no money to play.
