I was not ready for Freddy. Or Bonnie. Or Chica. Or Foxy. Or this game. Or having a mental breakdown. Or buying a new laptop after I threw it out the third floor window (or at least wanting to).
10/10, would be unprepared again.
**EDIT**
Okay, so you saw my rather silly review of the game above, quite resembling many reviews for this game. Now, having beaten nights 1-6 without cheats, I have a more experienced and balanced view of the quality of Five Nights at Freddy's (I had only beaten Night 1 when I wrote the original review).
So: Five Nights At Freddy's. We've all heard the phrase 'Easy to learn, difficult to master', and I don't know if that suits anything more than this game. The gameplay and controls are very, very simple, requiring only the pointing and clicking of the mouse. Using lights, doors and cameras to hinder the villainous animatronics, you must survive five (actually seven including the Custom Night) nights at Freddy's.
The biggest two questions that need to be answered about this game are as follows: is it difficult, and is it scary. Yes, and yes. However, even more important are these questions: is it as difficult, and as scary, as everyone makes it out to be? No, and no. Let me elaborate on my  statements.
When I originally purchased Five Nights At Freddy's, less than a week ago, I expected to experience one of the scariest and most difficult games ever. A few days later, I beat Night 4 on my first try, and Night 5 on my second. I'm not claiming that it wasn't hard, but I certainly expected a larger challenge. If you have a good strategy and you're quick at executing it, you should get by, though luck can always go away from your favor. It must be noted, though, that the pressure that you have as a result of the impending atmosphere most certainly makes it more difficult to effeciently carry out your strategy. It is a very difficult game, but not as difficult as people make it out to be sometimes (like saying Night 4 is impossible).
Now: is it as scary as people say? Also no. The atmosphere is terrifying, the creatures are freaky and the jump scares are truly startling, but I'm afraid that this game could never be as scary as people say, because so many say it's the scariest game of all time. If you watched PewDiePie's reaction to Bonnie peering into his office, you'd think it was absolutely horrifying. In all honesty, it's just makes me give a little shudder, and get back to the game. Plenty of things in this game fall into that same category. Again, please do not get me wrong, this game is very scary. I just doubt it's the scariest game of all time. Actually, the lore and theories behind the game are probably the scariest part (watch the Game Theorist's video about it).
Overall, this is a very difficult, very frustrating (in a good way), very tense and suprisingly well designed game, which I highly recommend for horror fanatics or someone looking for a challenge. 9/10, well done Scott, can't wait to play the second.

This review is coming from someone who is interested in RTS style games, yet has never played any of the Tropico series.
Overall, I find this game quite enjoyable - there is a wide variety of ways that the player is able to go about making money / advancing throughout the game.  The buildings are tiered at a good pace in that you won't feel as though things are moving too quick or too slow as you go through each era, however they somehow feel a little limited.  Factions / Politics is an interesting facet of the game, often you'll find yourself beating down a rebellion in the later stages or trying to appease each of the complaints that various citizens have.
Possibly the only complaint about the game I have is that combat seems a little iffy to me (you can't really control what your armies are attacking, only what they defend).  Otherwise, the game is very solid and I'm sure it builds off of all the previous versions.  It took me a couple plays to really figure out the mechanics and flow of the game, but once you do it becomes very enjoyable / relaxing.

I played Edge of Space since the early days of its EA release, and while I enjoyed it a lot, I have to admit it doesn’t quite measure up to two more prominent games of its genre: Terraria and Starbound.
The majority of exploration and progress is top-bottom, as is fairly common for sandbox exploration/building games, but where other games take place at a single land mass, EoS’ world is composed of numerous floating islands, some tiny, some very large. If you don’t feel like digging down, walking to an island’s edge and jumping to the one bellow is always an option. (And having a jetpack from the start helps you not to fall to death this way. Usually.)
When it comes to combat, Edge of Space gives highest “Player vs Environment” feeling than other games of its genre. Instead of challenging powerful bosses like in Terraria, EoS’ focus in on fighting ever present and deadly “common” enemies, who present constant and serious threat.
However, ever-present enemy threat has side effect of limiting player’s ability to build in lower areas of the world. Aside from danger to player, many mid-late game enemies has structure-damaging attacks, and will easily wreck both your base and landscape you were trying to preserve.
Also on the negative side, Edge of Space is rather lacking in variety: there are only 3 main biomes in the game, and they don’t feel as unique as Terraria or Starbound’s biomes. Visually the game isn’t very pleasing to an eye either, and everything is mostly brown or metallic-gray (possibly done on purpose for “realism” – we all know that Real Is Brown).
Overall, Edge of Space is quite good, and I can fully recommend it to fans of sandbox exploration/building, who already had their fill with Terraria and Starbound. And those who are more interesting in action than building will probably find that aspect of EoS even more appealing than that of other games of its genre.

Verdict: Take a peek at the posted screenshots to enjoy the hand drawn art if that is what drew you to this, no need to buy and play the game for that. The 'game', as implemented, is an exercise in frustration.
- Cute hand drawn graphics.
- It's different, stands out in used art and 'delivery' of the puzzles.
- At 95% off, really cheap.
- Total lack of graphics/sound/control settings (why do people keep doing this for PC games?)
- Zero instructions, tutorial or guidance, so just click around and watch what happens and see if you can figure out what the devs were thinking at the time.
- 5 levels total, with 1-4 hidden object puzzles each, some of which have additional puzzles after. Again, zero instructions so just click stuff and maybe you'll see something happen that will give you a clue about what's expected of you.
- Level puzzles are spread out over several screens, so you have to make your bug crawl around, with regular backtracking required. Excruciatingly slow method of scrolling between level screens, and no way to speed it up.
- There is not even a hint at what paths your bug can even take. No arrows, no clearly different coloured or constructed pathways, nothing. Just click the screen edges at different spots and wait to see how far the bug will crawl and maybe by the time it gets there it'll scroll the screen and hey, now you know. Or click a different spot and wait some more.
- No save/load options. It will remember a level as fully finished, but leaving a level unfinished forces you to restart all the puzzles you already solved on that level.
- Even with all that, it's an extremely short game. I fully finished it in under 3 hours, of which almost half was spent just clicking randomly and most of the other half waiting for the bugs to crawl to scroll the screen, and only a fraction actually doing any puzzle solving.
I can understand trying to do things different from all the others. I can understand trying to be artsy. I can understand trying to minimize user interface and controls.
But for the love of all that is good and right in PC gaming, please never let any of that prevent you from implementing the required basics:
- PC's are not a standard environment, and PC users are used to having pretty detailed control. A settings dialog allowing to change graphics/sound/controls is a
on the PC platform.
- Some basic instructions about controls, method and goal of the game. Random clicking to see what happens is not 'learning to play', it's just plain annoying.
- Save/load/checkpoint mechanics, especially in a game that makes one waste a lot of time just getting around on a level.
Sorry, but even at pennies, I can't recommend this as a game. Cute art style though, so check out the screenshots.

General summary: Sunless Sea is a phenomenal game with some of the best writing I've ever seen. It's really up there with titles like Planescape Torment, Pillars of Eternity, 80 Days, etc.. The atmosphere is very distinctive, and the world is baffling, hilarious, and terrifying.
However, it's not an easy game to get into - the learning curve is exceptionally steep, and not just in an FTL die-twenty-times-before-you-win way - it can be initially hard to figure out what you're even supposed to be doing or what half the 'items' in the game are. This can be tough because at the heart of SS is a cold unforgiving economy that can be very rewarding if you know how to hustle and painfully frustrating for a beginner. However, if you can stick with it for a few few playthroughs, you'll find massive satisfaction in becoming a wealthy, lethal, well connected master of the Unterzee.
PROS
- Phenomenal writing.
- Fascinating world.
- Varied locations.
- Interesting characters.
- Brutal but rewarding difficulty curve.
- Superb DLC in the form of the new Zubmariner Expansion
CONS
- Confusing to begin with.
- Steep difficulty curve.
- Combat is simplistic.

Having read a few positive reviews I decided to delve into Niffelheim myself.  I've not played Kingdoms, but I have put in my fair share of hours into Terraria.  As one who has played many Early Access titles, I find this one to be more than satisfactory in terms of stability, bugs, and progress.  I'm 2 or 3 hours into gameplay at the time of this First Impression.
In short: I'm having fun.  The movement is slow, but the longer I've played the more I've come to accept it.  This is not a fast-paced, adrenaline filled action packed ride.  This is a plodding, lonely story of a Viking alone in the winter, building himself up as time allows.  Once I accepted this and sat back to enjoy the ride, the pace became both bearable and understandable.  I've not yet played co-op/multiplayer, but it intrigues me - the pace may well bother me more with others involved, we shall see.
What I have done is die.  I've died to boars, I've died to bears.  I've died to rock giants.  And I've enjoyed it.  In addition to that however, I've built a place for sheep I have yet to figure out how to catch, collected a stack of wolf pelts and a handful of bear and boar skins, crafted some better armor, built up a woodworking area and a small, level one smeltery.  I've mine down a few levels below my hovel, slaying skeletons along the way and avoiding the rock giants as best I can.  In doing this, I'm aware I'm only scratching the surface.
I see the direction this is headed, and the potential it holds.  It is a solid Early Access entry, and I look forward to watching it evolve.  Currently:  It is slow.  Combat is very basic.  Chopping trees takes a long time compared to similar games.  Food is odd, as I can apparently eat 7 or 8 entire bears before I'm fully healed.  However, the game is unfinished - there is a lot of ground yet to cover, and despite the previous drawbacks, everything else provides for a very solid framework moving forward, and is already currently an enjoyable experience.

The main reason I purchased this game was due to the local multiplayer function.
In the two player multi-player game (but you can play up to 4 people) you have 6 lanes of building squares.  2 lanes on each side are exclusive to one player, and the middle two are open for anyone to build.
Building houses gets you points, while other buildings boost the points houses get, or take points away.  So if you build a nasty polluting factory next to the other player's houses they lose points.
As you progress you can purchase new cards and abilities, so the buildings in each player's deck will diverge.  There are a good variety of cards, and it's a nice strategic turn-based strategy game to play against others.
Conclusion:  If you like to play board games, then I think you will enjoy this game a lot.  You have a fun single-player puzzle game and fun local multiplayer city-tile battle game.

I'm here to review this game a second time. The first time I was completely unable to play the game as a result to a very poorly done port, however after Steam refused to refund the game, I forced myself to get my monies worth from it by playing through the lag regardless.
The story itself isn't awful, but it's definitely not up to Telltales standard of games. There are so many things wrong with the coding and animations... I'll just list a few.
While this first one is nit-picky, it's annoying. The subtitles are sometimes cut off and they don't match what is actually being said in the audio. Secondly, there are times where character models lips don't match the dialogue, or they do something that doesn't seem right. At one point there's a camera angle to push a reactive key, but the icon is turned 90 degrees away from the screen so you can't see it. Televisions that were supposed to display viewings wouldn't work in any scene they were supposed to, instead just showing a grey screen with audio playing in the background.  Also, at one point a character walked away from a conversation and left her eye lashes behind.
The biggest fault, in my eye at least, lies in the fact that Telltale games are great because of their immersion. To that fact, these games pride themselves on being a "Choose your own adventure" type of game that remembers your choices.. and has consequences for them. This game, on three seperate counts no less, had continuity errors with choices I have made in the past. That's unforgivable in this type of game.
I really hope that in the second season, if there is one, some of these issues are addressed.
TL;DR: Buy it on sale if you aren't using an AMD computer, but you may be disappointed if you've gotten used to the normally high standard of Telltalegames anyways.

This was exactly what I expected from the newer Telltale games. It is heavily focused on the story, has a lot of dialogue choices and simple interactive cutscenes, and has very little regular gameplay in between. The gameplay that's there is decent and the story is interesting, so it works well for what it's trying to do. Like the other Telltale games, the choices affect what other characters say to you, but most of the choices get canceled out by the end. I really enjoyed this game.  I love the Batman universe in general, and Telltale created an interesting take on it.  Most of the general ideas in the story were familiar, but they took some liberties with the characters, changing some key things which led to some surprises for me.  Meanwhile, some other characters progressed exactly as I expected they would based on knowing who they are in the comics, so it felt "right" to see things unfold that way.  Overall it was an interesting blend of familiar faces and new ideas.
In general I usually hate interactive cutscenes, but the quick-time-events in this game were actually pretty fun.  I started the game playing with keyboard/mouse and a few of the button combos were a little awkward (I had a lot of trouble pressing Shift and Q at the same time) so I switched to my gamepad and then it was cool doing all of the fight sequences.  It usually gave me enough time to realize which buttons I had to press, so I didn't have to redo them, and with that in mind it was pretty awesome to watch the fighting moves and feel so badass :-D
Also, I really liked some of the new gadgets they gave Batman, like camera drones, and they came up with some good ideas to vary the gameplay a bit, like scouting the area with the drone and planning out Batman's attack sequence in advance prior to executing it via interactive cutscene.  There wasn't that much regular gameplay overall, but what was there was good and it felt appropriately paced for the story.

Telltale has a reputation for putting out great narratives. This entry doesn't disappoint. The story is compelling and captivating.
Most Batman games allow the player to play as Batman, with all the fun that brings. The Arkham series does a great job of allowing the player to control the Dark Knight on his quest to save Gotham City. This game does a great job giving the player the thrill taking on foes as the gadget-wielding Batman while trying to keep up appearances and play the political game as Bruce Wayne.
While I do understand most people and their gripes against how Telltale games don't offer real choices (you're speeding toward an outcome no matter what) this game does improve upon the formula. You're given options at times to either handle a situation as Bruce Wayne or as Batman, and that's refreshing because it's never been done in a Batman game before.
What's more, while you're speeding toward a conclusion, the decisions you make effect
. The decisions in the end don't matter because, of course, the hero is going to prevail. But at least you can experience the game differently depending on the route you choose. Though it would be nice to see a story where your decisions can actually cause you to fail in some way, I highly doubt you should look for that in a Batman game.
Without delving into spoilers, never has a Batman game (or movie!) delved so deeply into the Wayne family history as this game, and fans of the comic will not be disappointed with this.
My biggest drawback for this game is that you're spoonfed everything. Once, I'd like to play a game as Batman and feel the part of a genuine detective. You're dropped into areas with clues and you have to link them together to get a picture of what happened, but it feels too easy. This goes with this, that with that, and now I'm fighting again. This game gave it the old college try, but it'd be nice to go into an area and have to find the clues (with the potential to miss something crucial). That would make the experience richer.
As far as how this stacks up with other Telltale games, I'd say this is pretty high on the list. I loved Wolf Among Us, but this is better. Walking Dead started it all, and I have to play more Tales from the Borderlands in order to truly get a feel for that (I honestly think that might be the best Telltale has done having only played Episode 1 of that series).
All in all, this game provides an enjoyable experience. As a fan of the comic/lore, I highly recommend it to people in a similar position, but some out there who aren't as keen on the superhero would do well to wait for a big sale. I give it a 7 of 10: A great entry in the Telltale Series, but not for everybody.  I loved it, for what it's worth.

Niffelheim is one of those rare creatures which seems to have turned up at just the right time, ever since the advent of Kingdom there's been a calling for a game which does Kingdom, but in a more meaningful and interesting way. One where you have a much more personal connection with the world you're involved with, and one where the lore is much more tightly woven with your character and their goals. Enter Niffelheim, one part Kingdom, one part Tormentum, one part Banner Saga. A world which judging by the areas you wander through, have had the kind of detail lavished upon them that you rarely see outside of games -like- Tormentum, which is high praise, this is genuinely good stuff here.
You play a recently deceased Viking on their way to Asgard, as you sail in your funeral boat, burning brightly in the pyre, your soul is captured and you are taken to Niffelheim, where you must fight your way to Asgard by showing that yes, you are indeed worthy of your rest in the halls of the hereafter. However, to begin with you start in a place which can be best summed up as bleak, yet beautiful. Wind and snow swept vistas combine with gorgeous hand painted scenery and a steady trudging viking complete with historically -accurate- (no horns!) armour, who must turn the little pittance of land he has found himself on into a defensible position, and then fight his way outwards, earning glory and fame before taking the fight to those that brought him to this forsaken land.
The current state of Niffelheim is best described as rough. There's very little guidance for the player, and you're more or less left to your own devices to figure out exactly what is going on. There's a few quests to kindof guide you, but at least at this point, you're entirely on your own. Understanding how to navigate the world can prove a bit of a challenge in itself, combat is most definitely not a finished article and feels clunky and unrefined, the control mappings are unreliable and feel like they could do with some visual UI and UX elements to help ensure the player knows what's going on on-screen when they press various buttons.
Even understanding how the character gains experience is going to be a real challenge to begin with, not to mention what items go in which slots, this is all stuff that will get fixed as time goes on, but make no mistake, on the Early Access scale, right now? This one is *Early*. Really Early. Having said that? I like it. I genuinely like it. There's a charm here that just grows on you, from the almost Tormentum like puzzle in the Workshop to open the safe to the various graphical indications to show how wounded the wildlife is, there's a lot of incidental detail that helps make the world feel *alive*. There's clearly a lot of will to make this game -great-, and if the execution can be brought up to the level of ambition, Niffelheim has the potential to be a genuine classic.
Niffelheim is a very specific recommendation. If you're not afraid of dealing with bugs, control mappings suddenly not working, more bugs, strange obscurities like "WHAT ON EARTH DOES WARRIOR LVL 2 MEAN?", yet more bugs. Under that very unfinished surface is the raw metal of an excellent game. Once it's been put through the fires and the forge, once it's been finished and polished, this could be an essential game. I truly hope the devs make it the game it deserves to be, because this is one I've got my eye on, and dearly hope it will come through on what it promises.

TL;DR: Cuphead is a great game with amazing visuals and a stellar soundtrack. However, in order to best some bosses, the game will require near perfection. This can be really frustrating, but the game never seems unfair. I would give it about an 8/10 taking into account price, visuals, soundtrack, length of game, and amount of "fun".
Pros:
-Nobody will disagree with the fact that the old cartoon style visuals and music are fantastic
-The boss designs are unique with each requiring a different strategy to defeat
-The game is hard, but never seems unfair
-Boss fights are not very lengthy (once you understand their patterns) so it is easy to pick up and play in your free time
-Beating a boss feels incredible and gives you an incredible feelings of accomplishment
-Replayability is unique because understanding a bosses phases from the start changes the fight
Cons:
-The Run & Gun levels don't feel as good as the boss levels
-Game is rather short, unless you feel like trying to S rank all of the bosses
-There are multiple weapons, charms, and supers, but I always found myself using a combo of 3 weapons, 2 charms, and one super
-The plane levels are nice, but I feel there could have been more levels or choosing of powers like normal levels
-That Dragon boss (probably the most annoying one in the game)
Review:
Cuphead is a very good game. Amazing to look at and listen too and interesting to play. The game is very difficult and most bosses will not be bestest on the first try. Or even the tenth try. Cuphead is all about understading boss patterns. Once you have died enough to understand how the boss acts and when they do what move you can choose a weapon kit, charm, and super in order to turn the tide and gain the advantage. Once you "download" a boss and are able to beat them, the rush and feeling of accomplishment is fantastic. That is why people are comparing this game to Dark Souls. The feeling of beating a tough-as-nails boss that killed you tens (or hundreds) of times is where the enjoyment of this type of game comes from. So if you like the masochistic feeling of getting beat up for 10-30 minutes and then finally doing some beating up of your own you will enjoy this game.
I did have some things I didn't like however. The Run & Gun levels are nice. In fact, I wish the game was based more around the run and gun levels and each level would end in a boss fight. However, these experiences are completely seperate. There are maybe 6 R&G level compared to the 18 boss fights. At that point they serve as an interesting distraction, but don't feel quite fleshed out. They do serve as an ability to get coins so you can buy weapons and charms, but I found that only 3 weapons and 3 charms were ever useful.
The game is also rather short. As someone who played solo and no co-op (so far), it took me about 7 hours. The replayability comes from trying to get better ranks as the boss fights. Playing them again feels good because you understand how the fight is going to work, but constantly banging your head against a wall trying to get that perfect S rank isn't my style though I won't begrudge those that like to. Going back and trying everything in co-op might prove more fun.
Overall, Cuphead was a good game and I feel like it was well worth $20. The going certaintly does get rough and some bosses feel invincible when you first start fighting them (GODDAMN THAT DRAGON BOSS), but overcoming the challenge feels great and keeps you coming back for more.

To be fair, you have to have a very high IQ to understand the Cuphead tutorial. The instructions are extremely subtle, and without a solid grasp of the whole situation most of the tips will go over a typical players head. There's also Cuphead's imprecise movements, which is deftly woven into his characterisation- his wavering self draws heavily from Narodnaya Volya literature, for instance. The fans understand this stuff; they have the intellectual capacity to truly appreciate the depths of the animations, to realise that they're not just cartoon-y - they say something deep about LIFE. As a consequence people who say they cleared the Cuphead tutorial in minutes truly ARE lying- of course they would have looked up, for instance, the solution to this obstacle "Y DASH QUICK EVADE ON GROUND OR AIR," which itself is a cryptic reference to the control manual. I'm smirking right now just imagining one of those addlepated simpletons scratching their heads in confusion as Jared Moldenhauer's genius wit unfolds itself on their game screens. What fools.. how I pity them.

I am very picky with my visual novel (VN) games, but was interested in playing Sickness because of the premise of being a “sick” murderer. I noticed a review on Steam comparing this title to Song of Saya (Saya no Uta) and felt it was important to comment that this game is far tamer – I actually enjoyed the ride in Sickness and did not have a constant feeling of dread and disgust that lingered during my Saya playthrough. There are many “nice/calm” moments in Sickness, while none really exist in Saya.
If you like well-written visual novels with a good storyline and being an assassin, then you will enjoy Sickness. An important note – this game has a lot of writing and requires a great amount of reading, so if you like simple, short VNs this may not be for you.
The aesthetics are very good – the amount of detail in each scene is high and the artstyle is clean. Be advised, this is not an eroge game, so there are no hentai scenes. There are, however, a few gory instances (but nowhere as bad as Saya). The music and sounds are decent and add to the atmosphere of the story – there is no voice acting, unfortunately. The story is interesting and well-written with quite a bit of content – ~5 hours at least if you are reading every dialogue piece. You have a “sickness” that gives you psychotic, serial killer urges, and you must support your sister because the two of you have been orphaned.
Controls are typical of a visual novel game – you will mainly be clicking with your mouse, but you can use the keyboard if you wish. There are fast forward and skip options if you do not want to (or already have) read the dialogue. There isn’t really a difficulty or learning curve because the game plays more as a novel, however, you can die. Save often, as is the golden rule of any visual novel.
Gameplay involves you reading a lot of text for most of the game, with decisions during different points – fortunately, in Sickness your choices actually affect the gameplay to a noticeable degree. Again, save often if you like checking what the alternative options will result in. You can rewind through scenes with the mouse wheel, however, it will only go back so far, and you won’t always be able to use this feature to revert your decisions (save/load your game instead). There are plenty of save slots, so take advantage of this.
Compared to many high-quality VNs (both with and without eroge elements), there are a lot of decisions to make in this game, and the choice rubric for determining which ending you get is fairly complex. I really appreciated and enjoyed the quality of the story, choices, and endings – one actually made me very emotional. A very interesting theme surrounding incest can be explored, and the way it is approached in this game does not feel too ridiculous or forced – it may even make you think about the concept differently. Questioning reality and the morality (or immorality) of being an assassin is also a hot topic in Sickness. The character progression is fleshed out well, with the main character’s slow transformation from  someone caught in a bad spot to one who can kill without remorse.
Overall, I would definitely suggest Sickness as a top-quality VN, and to check it out if you want something lighter than Song of Saya (you should probably stay away from Saya unless you have a high tolerance for depravity like me). If you like good stories with compelling themes surrounding the ambiguity of violence, then you will really like the ride found in Sickness.
Recommend!

Tropico 5 was a game I picked up after watching a few YouTubers mess around with it, and so I investigated the steam page and from there things went swish!
It has a nice quirky story, while might slightly infuriate you, is quite rewarding in the end but sadly not made out to be that much of an achievement.  The characters you'll come to either love or dislike.  I, however, never got tired of Penulitimo's comments or Lord Oaksworth's trails.
For the most part this game made me feel like I could actually achieve something by building a settlement and attempting to set it up right and in the most efficient way possible, something that Simcity 5 couldnt really achieve, or at least not very well.  While Simcity didnt do a terrible job at creating your own settlement, there were no actual problems or issues with money or power politically at all after completing your city, effectively making your only problem at that point the efficiency and placement of buildings, or the bugs inscripted in the game itself which rendered a problem unsolveable.
Tropico 5 puts you in control of everything as the ''President For Life'', as a Roman ruler once said, for production of all goods and foods, public buildings, the army, and social and constitutional matters.  Stuff up and fail to get the support of your people, and your time as El Presidente could well be up with military coups, rebel attackers, major powers invading your island (if you get them really peeved), or an annoying combination of two of these issues, OR the simple fact the you should have cheated or cheated harder in the elections.
Simcity was lacking this redeeming feature of actually trying to hold onto power, and after a decade you were basically done in that city alone (even though the game controls said otherwise).
I am a bit disappointed with the emptyness of multiplayer rooms and hearing that it had problems early on also didnt help its reputation either. I really enjoyed this game. It can be really disturbing and creepy at times, but that is the best thing about the game. There is none of that 'sunshine and flowers' stuff, the unrealistic optimism and unbelievable sense of jubilance; this is created to show more of the real world, showing how a family can be so easily shattered in a short amount of time, and showing the horrific reality that exists underneath the wealth and privilege of Western society. If you like a dark story, and you are not afraid of knowing the ills of the world, then this game is for you.
This story is not all darkness, though. There are some scenes that are quite funny, and there are others that are rather touching; but the dark story takes prominence. The exchanges between Suoh and his twin sister were my favourite.
The only thing I didn't like it was the strange 'warning' before playing the game. In all honesty, if you bought the game rather reading the summary and some of the reviews, then you pretty much know exactly what you're getting yourself into by playing this visual novel. It ruined the surprise of some of the future scenes, and my gaming experience suffered for it, albeit mildly.
There is so much more about the game I would wish I could talk about, especially in terms of orginal thoughts of the game in contrast to those after it, but to do that would spoil a lot of the story for future players. I wish there where private suggestion boxes or something on here, but little can be done to help with that.

TL;DR Kingdom and Terraria had a baby and it was a slow viking.
The game gets you going: you want to unlock new facilities, see more of crafting and explore the world. There's no freedom of digging like in Terraria, but there are tunnels 2 floors down of your starting location. Clearing tunnels is linear but quite satisfying. There's defense element about once an hour - you have skeleton waves which threaten destroying your home, that way you lose the whole game.
What I also like:
- every single icon of loot is well drawn, you want to have everything
- gold gets you home quickly! and buys you nice stuff from the shop (city)
- quests guide and teach you
My personal concerns, it may feel different for you:
- walking is slow, comparing to Terraria
- going back to your body after death is odd, although that way you will never lose your loot
- melee combat is sloppy, but it must be a subject of easy improvement
- I see no reasons to buy more lands, probably it's just backup bases
- skill system is disabled and looks shallow at the moment
What's making it Early Access:
- UI needs improvement
- balance issues
- some annoying bugs but nothing critical
- some content is locked
Feels like a few months away from full release.

UPDATE: I have updated my review because Telltale has patched the game a few times to improve performance. When I first received the game, I was playing on a GTX 760, and the game ran but only barely. Now, after upgrading my GPU, I am running the game on a GTX 1070. The framerate is acceptable now, but it should have ran fine from the beginning per the game's recommended system requirements.
For one, the game doesn't run that well, and there's no excuse for that in a simple game like this. It's an interactive movie, basically, it shouldn't struggle when I'm running it on one of the best GPUs available. The frame rate
had constant issues prior to its many patches and then some afterwards, the game crashes randomly, the audio cuts out at times, the controls sometimes don't work -- the game
was a mess, technically, and it's very disappointing.
For two, the story is so...bizarre. Forget everything you know about Batman, because this game goes out of its way to subvert your expectations. I'm not saying this is a bad thing, but the issue lies in the fact that the way it's written, the game feels like it's punishing you for doing what seems "right" or natural. But instead of the twists being clever and thoughtful, it's more like choosing to let your character kick a can on the ground and then the can explodes and you lose a foot. Not to mention some of the dialogue choices do NOT reflect what Bruce Wayne actually says, leading to some "restart to main menu" moments. Lots of them. Just keep in mind that if you intend on having what may seem like a good ending to you, this game is going to fight you tooth and nail to wrestle it away from you. This is not good writing, it's annoying and stressful. Maybe a little ironically so, the action is really cool in this game and does feel very Batman-esque, albeit like I mentioned before the frame rate issues and unreliable controls will frustrate you so. There's also the small matter that some of Batman's "detective moments" are absurdly dumb, to the point where I was both laughing and shouting at my monitor because they make Batman look like he misses the most obvious of the obvious; thankfully, not all of the "detective moments" were dumb, but some of them were, and that was enough.
All of that being said, I did enjoy myself. Obviously, because I finished it. If you love Batman, you will find a lot to like about this game. When all was said and done, I can't say it wasn't worth playing, but my feelings were very mixed. I am looking forward to the next Batman story, but hopefully the writers will step up their game, because the choices and end results in this particular story left me feeling unsatisfied. But, maybe that's the point. You decide.

Another solid title from Telltale, this time focusing on Batman. This isn't exactly an origin story, in that Batman has obviously been operating for at least a while, but it's still early days. Harvey Dent is still DA, his relationship with Gordon is still a bit rocky...things like that. This is definitely a non canon story though and I really don't mind that, some of the better Batman stories I've read have been alternate takes on the Dark Knight, and while some things are going to annoy people (Perhaps one twist especially) I found them intruiging and fascinating.
If you have ever played a Telltale game before, you know what to expect gameplay wise, conversation choices mixed in with quick time event action. Cinematically and narratively, this is good work from Telltale. The narrative is consistently engaging and the action scenes are tense and well choreographed. An interesting twist is that on a few occasions, you will have the choice to go to a certain scene either as Bruce Wayne or as Batman, basically a choice between diplomacy or intimidation and violence. I actually quite enjoyed the focus a little more on Bruce as mostly he is kind of in the background, his relationship with Harvey was quite well developed and you get a feeling for their friendship. Other characters are well realised too, Alfred and Gordon are excellent as always and there is a really frefreshing take on the Penguin. Also worth mentioning is the new villian, who I also found quite compelling. Anyway, to say more about the plot would spoil the fun.
The cartoon graphics are excellent and really capture the grimyness of Gotham. That said, this is the Telltale engine, so their are occasion framerate hickups and a few animationg glitches. It's nothing deal breaking, but god I hope these guys make a full blown new engine soon. Sound and music are excellent, as is the voice acting.
In conclusion, I really enjoyed Telltale's Batman. It is not their greatest game (In my bias opinion that's Tales from the Borderlands) but its still a solid ride and I really can't wait to see where they go with season 2)

Review contains slight spoilers, so avoid if you have yet to play
There have been countless games and an indefinite amount of Batman stories since his inception but its nice to see Telltale put their own unique spin on the Caped Crusader. After all he is one of the most well known superheroes of all time, up there with the likes of Superman and Spider-man. His presence on both the big and small screens is a big one and in recent years, even video games have been dominated by him, specifically the Arkham series, which proved that the Caped Crusader’s fighting style can be accurately replicated in a game.
As is Telltale’s standard, the game is split into 5 episodes, each one taking roughly 60-90 minutes to beat, both serving as a continuation of the previous episodes as well as building upon them. In their take on Batman, we’re placed into a universe in which he has only been Batman for some time and thus has met only a few of his rogues. And the way some of the rogues become the people they are is a unique take rarely seen in the comics. And yes, Joker does indeed show up but it’s more of a cameo.
Realm of Shadows
(Note: the following are short summaries of each episode, as light on spoilers as possible) Bruce is already friends with Harvey Dent, who is currently running for mayor and whose campaign Bruce is funding. However, Carmine Falcone wishes for his friend, the incumbent and corrupt mayor to remain as the mayor so he continue his crimes. After meeting with Bruce, the Wayne family’s name is suddenly bought under attack and Bruce’s parents are accused of not being who they really were. We’re also introduced to staple Batman characters such as Jim Gordon, Catwoman, and Penguin.
Children of Arkham
In this we’re introduced to the Children of Arkham, a new terrorist group aiming to expose the Wayne family’s true actions to the people of Gotham, which they eventually do at the end.
New World Order
The previous mayor is dead, Dent is slowly transforming into Two-Face, Penguin ousts Bruce as head of Wayne Enterprises, and we get ever closer to the identity of this “Lady Arkham”
Guardian of Gotham
After being drugged by Lady Arkham, Bruce is thrown into Arkham, the very place where his rogues are contained, with the addition of some “new” ones. This is also where we meet this universe’s version of the Joker, known as John Doe at this point. Bruce of course escapes and manages to track down and identify Lady Arkham and why she’s doing what she is. Dent has completed his descent into Two-Face and attacks Wayne manor before being taken down and further disfigured, finishing his iconic look.
City of Light
In the penultimate episode, Bruce begins to work towards bringing the Wayne family back into the good side of the public opinion, says goodbye to Catwoman, and rescues Alfred from Lady Arkham before defeating her.
Conclusion
Telltale’s Batman really is an amazing game with a captivating story, albeit one that is riddled with frame rate issues, which is something of a Telltale staple at this point. When you’re thrown into combat and die because the frame rate plummets, it’s far from fun. There’s also character models glitching out and the occasional audio desync.
Gives off strong vibes of the classic Year One arc.
The real villain is a genuinely surprising twist as well as their backstory and reasoning for their being there and overall motives. It’s just a shame that they were killed off so…casually.
Batmobile design is fantastic, doubles as both Bruce’s main car and the Batmobile via a neat transformation mechanic.
If Telltale ever fix their damn frame rate issues for future games, that would be neat. And between that and the wait between episodes, this is why I always wait until the full season is out, as well as why I’m only just publishing this review.

Russians...Russians are everywhere. They took objective A, B, and C so quickly that our fellow soliders began to panic. My Honor Rank is 73 and a squad leader for Squad Two. I ordered my men to fall back to Objective G, the outskirts of Druzhina, and command them to fortify the position. Squad One fought valiantly against the Russians on Objective D, but most of them were wiped out. The dense forest that cover Objective D and E favor the Russians than our German forces. The Bolsheviks were clever to use smoke grenades to advance their position while our men fired wildly into the thick, white smoke. What are they shooting at? Who knows.
As Objective E was spammed with Russians, the commander order the squad leaders, including me, to send in artillery coordinates. Unfortunately, there were too many artillery requests sent to the commander. The first coordinate is at the Russians on Objective E, the second coordinate is pointed directly at the Russian T-34, and the third coordinate was sent in close to Objective G. I was the one who sent in the third coordinate. I debated with my commander that the third coordinate is the best because the Russians would most likely be sending 2/3 of their forces to take G. The commander didn't listen and called the artillery at the first coordinate. As the artillery roars the sky and slams into the ground, the Russians were clever to run away from Objective E. Some of them died while the rest who were at Objective E rush to Objective G in a frontal assault. The machine gunner in my squad, whose Honor Rank is 58, fired his MG-34 in a control burst, but was killed by a sniper from 148 meters. I watch the machine gunner got shot and his body slump into the fragile, wooden floor. I was traumatized by this and order my men to not be exposed by the window. The rest of my squad consist of newer members, ranging the Honor Rank from 12 - 36 didn't listen to my command. The second squad member (Honor Rank - 26) was killed by the same sniper.
Two squad members killed and the Russians are swarming in front of the sandbags near Objective G...and I have to make a choice. I ordered my squad to suppress fire at the Russians while waiting for additional reinforcements to come and defend Objective G. Unfortunately, the Bolsheviks pulled a hard, right flank at Objective F, wiping out Squad Three in under 20 seconds. Even though my squad was able to pluck a few kills around Objective G, the Russians purposely made this frontal assault as a distraction so that their comrades can take Objective F. Knowing that Objective G would be overrun from the right side, I ordered my lower ranking members to retreat back to the apartments in Objective I. Strangely, there were signs of courage and fury in my men's eyes. One of the squad members (Honor Rank - 21, Anti-Tank class) demanded me to let him risk his own life as the T-34 rushes to the main road that leads to Druzhina. I refused in his request and ordered him to tactically withdraw, but he didn't listen. Before I was about to demand an order to him, he pulls out the Hafthohlladung anti-tank grenade and runs directly in front of the T-34. He starts to scream and was about to swing the grenade, but was mowed down in a hail of machine gun fire from the Russians. However, I heard an explosion and I took a slight peak in the window. The T-34's main gun was pointing in front of me and the last I said to my men is: Run! This is Red Orchestra 2.

Red Orchestra 2 is the ultimate first-person tactical shooter that advocate very strong team coodination and communication, complex cover system, and each life (or ticket) is precious. When playing as the Russian, German, American, or Japanese, each solider fight just to survive. There will be instances in the game that discourage reckless assaults or exposure to the enemy. You will learn the game by experience and not repeating the same mistakes twice. There are weapons, class, and character rankings that encourages replay value. The best experience you will get in Red Orchestra 2 is playing on a full server. You will hear the best team coordination, the best varieties of newer and veteran players, and the greatest responsibility for your own life and theirs. Red Orchestra 2 does not shy away from the actuality of war as you will hear meeps, horrific groans, and the development of post-traumatic stress disorder. There is no "I" in war; there is brother and comrade. Red Orchestra 2 is simply, the best tactical first-person shooter to ever develop.

This game has quite a few performance issues, I've noted heavy stuttering when the camera pans or cuts to a different position, and I've got a pretty hefty machine.
Batman is pretty boring to play as, action sequences are mostly just QTEs, though for a game like this that's not totally unexpected.
Bruce Wayne is more interesting, you get to decide what Bruce will say and have some neat choices. Unfortunately your choices only sort of affect the game. Troy Baker is a pretty good Bruce Wayne/Batman, even if he's not Kevin Conroy.
Story-wise, I liked some of the direction they went in, Catwoman and Harvey Dent were certainly interesting to see as friends. I was a bit surprised Bruce Wayne isn't the Chairman of his own company with his majority stake, as he usually is. I wasn't a big fan of what they did with Penguin, basically merging him with Hush and dropping his usual short ugly old man look in favor of some kind of hipster.
Lady Arkham was kind of a disappointing reveal, like Arkham Knight was, but they did give her an interesting backstory. However, I did like the exploration of Bruce and Alfred's relationship.
What disappointed me most was the Wayne family scandal. Making it up was fine, but it's left as the truth for the whole game, rather than being a debunked lie. This totally ruins the Wayne family backstory, making Bruce's ultimate motivation for becoming Batman a total lie. The murder of Bruce's parents is supposed to have an effect on him because he loved them and was close to them, but also because as an adult he looks at them as the only good people in a city mired in corruption. Unfortunately this game took that part away, making them the same as all the others.
While the story has some intriguing twists and a few interesting takes on the characters, ultimately the plot was disappointing and took too many liberties with the Wayne family. Ultimately this game's plot was nothing more than a poorly attempted rehash of the much better Long Halloween comic. For this reason, along with the performance issues, I can't really recommend the game.

With story mode soon to be released, I thought I might actually sit down and write a review for this game.
The Long Dark is the best survival game I've played in years. There's a certain sense of desperation that you sometimes feel when you're playing this game - you might be out in the cold, with your character's condition steadily decreasing, and you hear a howl. So you look around, and on the crest of a nearby ridge is a dark silhouette. It's a wolf, and suddenly the situation becomes more dire. Your character moves slowly when their stamina is drained, or if they are injured. Sometimes escaping from predators is not as easy as it sounds or seems. The elements are deadly too - navigating through fog or a snowstorm can be a challenge, if you aren't prepared.
The world of the Long Dark is a lonely world indeed. Searching through abandoned houses is always interesting - while searching for clothing you might stumble across the empty bedroom of a child, toys still scattered across the floor. You'll walk along lonely coastlines and across frozen lakes, through deserted settlements and climb up windswept mountains. When exploring new areas, you never really know what you might discover. The frozen bodies of those who could not survive serve as a warning and reminder of the post-disaster world the Long Dark takes place in.
Every major update adds something new and interesting to find. I look forward to the upcoming story mode. Thank you for this game, Hinterland. Thank you.

(TL:DR at the bottom if you're looking for that) Cuphead is a masterwork of what gaming could and should be. It has a phenominal and wildly unique art style, excellent gameplay loop, very responsive controls, interesting story, great comedy, and all around exceptional experience. But of course, like everything, it has it's flaws, and they're very prominent.
Pros
- Excellent gameplay loop. Boss fights are fun and diverse
- Excellent control response. The game handles like a dream
- Excellent soundtrack. I don't buy many game soundtracks, but I bought this one
- Excellent art style. I think you already know this
- It's a hard game, and I love that
Cons
- No online multiplayer. We'll talk more about this in a bit
- No scaling for 2 or 1 player fights. This is a balancing issue
- It's a hard game, and I hate that
"No online multiplayer"
-This one is a huge issue. I don't know what StudioMDHR were thinking when they decided to do this, but it's an awful idea. Cuphead is a game that almost requires two players for most fights (unless you're very very very good at this game). I can not even begin to think of a possible reason why there would be no online coop. Hey devs, if you're reading this, FIX YOUR ♥♥♥♥ING GAME! Why would you make such a masterpiece and then ruin it by leaving out such a vital feature! What an awful decision!
"No scaling for 1 or 2 players"
-Another big issue that I don't really understand. Cuphead is actually an easier game with 2 people. This doesn't make any sense, scaling should be a part of every game that offers multiplayer, yet in Cuphead playing alone means playing at a massive disadvantage. The game is still a wallop to play by yourself, but it is a lot harder and some bosses might take you a solid few days to beat. I see no good reason not halve the health of all bosses or something if playing the stage alone. Needless to say this is one of the games stupidest mistakes.
And one final word before closing out on the difficulty of Cuphead. Cuphead is ♥♥♥♥ing hard. If you're a casual gamer, or you just don't enjoy constantly failing, DO NOT buy this game. Cuphead will own you, thousands of times. We fought that damned clown boss maybe 100 times before we got him dead. This game is punishing, this game is unforgiving, this game is cruel. But the feeling of beating a boss makes it all worth it. Again, if you're a casual gamer, DO NOT BUY THIS GAME.
In conclusion, Cuphead is a masterpiece. If you like the art style and you like boss rush games then this is the perfect thing for you. It checks off almost every box on the perfect game list, making just a few pretty key mistakes that you can fortunately overlook in most cases. Cuphead is a game you should buy, at full price, no need to wait for a sale.
(TL:DR - The game is a ♥♥♥♥ing work of art, you should absolutely buy it, it's phenominal. But, it has no online multiplayer, and the fights don't scale for 1 or 2 players, which means it's a LOT easier with a friend. That being said, even if you're playing alone, it's still definitely worth getting at full price.)

Alright, so, I was urged to play the game again, in which I agreed to. Before writing this, I was reading other reviews, and I completely disagree with one of them, which said something about the game being a little hard or it being objectiveless, and even it being difficult to progress, and even when you did, you would not feel like there was even any progression at all(Review posted June 11). All of it is sorta BS because how is it hard if you literally have 3-4 minutes of night, when things start spawning?(In the caves) How can you feel objectiveless if you have a kick♥♥♥♥♥NPC right from the beginning, asking you to help it, and even making cute little sounds when you agree to help it or not be mean to it? How can there not be any progression at all if when you even mine a single block, you get 5 exp, but it then adds up? There really can't be any objective if you set one yourself, or you ask the NPC right from the beginning, yet, I believe i remember the game even saying that you can talk to said NPC.
Anyways, although I did end up finding fun in the game again, like riding snails, or making pits of hell for passive crabs to jump down, it did a few things that irked me, even though it's in early access. Well, for one, the tutorial. When you spawn in, you get pretty nice videos, dont get me wrong, they were nice, but they took up the entire right bottom corner of your screen. I don't want to go and say that they're bad, but it would probably be better if a message popped up asking if you wanted to watch the videos during the tutorial. Another thing was that when it was 12:00 at night, and you were in a cave,(Especially early game) 1: The monsters that spawn hurt. 2: Why spawn in the middle of the night, only to stay during the day?
Personally, I'm very mixed on this game. It really varies from person to person. If I were able to buy it again, but with the current amount of knowledge I have on the game, I would wait until it comes out  with reviews. But you know what? I enjoyed the 34 hours on this game. No regrets. Not that I'm not going to ever play the game again, since i did buy the special edition. However, there are a few aspects that can be so easily exploited, like if you're going to die, you can just exit the game, only to appear at your cryopod, aka spawn point. Even at the tutorial, there's mounds of resources you can get, with no threats, giving a very significant edge in the early game.
TL:DR; The game is amazing, even though there are a few parts to it that can be questionable, but the exception is that it's early access, and it is already a game that has so much potential of being an even better game. Best to wait until it is released out of early access, but it can be even better if you choose to buy it during early access. It's always nice to see games grow.

Concrete Jungle is a city builder themed deck building card placement game. What the heck does that even mean? Don't think SimCity, Anno or The Settlers. Buildings are placed on a board to collect points. No mining gold or production chains.
Basically, the game goes like this. The board is arranged into columns. Buildings (cards) are placed onto the board for a variety of effects. Tiles can have a point value associated with it, either due to starting conditions or from the effect of played cards. Some cards can claim points, adding them to your score. Others have different effects - such as raise or lower the point value of tiles, moving the points from one tile and putting them on another, negating the value, and more. Most cards differentiate themselves by the pattern of tiles that they affect, but some of the special ones are a bit more interesting.
Overall, I've had a good time with it. Since it is a deck building game, there is luck involved but I feel the player has enough agency to have enough of an effect on the outcome. The campaign wasn't too challenging until the final 4 scenarios or so. Two were particularly tough.
Some players may be turned off by having to unlock characters by playing the campaign, and needing to play to unlock some cards, but I like having the carrots dangled in front of me.
While I think competitive mode offers that most interesting decisions, and I enjoyed the competitive missions in the campaign, I don't think I'll revisit them in custom games. I'm kind of a score chaser by heart and there aren't any leaderboards for competitive mode. The AI did smartly place their buildings. I was glad the AI didn't blunder its way through the game.
Frankly, I may try a handful of endless mode solo games with the different characters, but I feel that I've seen what the game has to offer. I enjoyed my time with Concrete Jungle and have played for 30 hours or so. To me, that's plenty for a $13 game. While I don't think it is probably on many people's' "Must Play" lists, Concrete Jungle is a solid game. Short review:
+Decent story
+Creative use of Batman lore - Telltale takes enough liberties to keep you interested, yet not too much to detract from the base IP
+Use of both Bruce and Batman is refreshing, as few games explore Gotham politics as Bruce
-Lack of rewind feature that is normally available in Telltale games, making replaying it a bit of a pain
-In classic Telltale style, your decisions don't actually have a huge impact on the end results
-Some technical issues I encountered (most prominent: frame rate drops in certain scenes)
-It's a good game, but the Walking Dead, Wolf Among Us, and Tales from the Borderlands are better Telltale games
Telltale once again strikes out with yet another licenesed IP, this time Batman. The story takes place early in Bruce's career, where the basics have already been laid out but there is tons of room for character development.
What makes this interesting is that Telltale was ballsy enough to take some liberties with the Batman lore. Many of the basics are still there, like Batman beating up bad guys and Alfred still being his faithful butller. However, several characters have altered origins or developments that are quite different from the comics, leading to surprising and entertaining twists to keep you hooked. Case in point, not everyone is exactly the same as the comics, and this gives Telltale the room to basically make their own alternative Batman universe that still feels like it's "Batman", but is still novel enough to keep you interested.
Another nice thing is this is probably the only Batman game so far that lets you play as Bruce Wayne - as in, the other side of the coin. Bruce obviously interacts with characters differently and you'll soon find yourselve embroiled in Gotham politics and scandals. Your use of Bruce's reputation and resources is just as important as prowling around as Batman, and it is really refreshing to realize both sides of the Bruce/Batman character. Who is the true person? Who is a mask for the other?
This game marks their first debut of an upgrade to their aging engine used in all their previous games, but unfortunately it looks like they need more practice. The main problem for me was simply frame rate drops in certain scenes as well as some minor humorous bugs that distracted from the story. The rewind feature, a staple in previous Telltale games, is mysteriously missing in this, which kills replayability as you'll always have to start from the beginning rather than being able to choose chapters.
And of course, in classic Telltale fashion, your decisions don't actually have a huge impact on the end results. A lot of times you'll find your decisions create a 'fork' in the journey, but then it ends up melding with the other possibilities so the end results are pretty similar no matter how you play. Still, the journey is still entertaining, as with previous Telltale games.
Overall, the game is pretty decent and I can recommend it to anyone interested in a story. However, at the same time, their Walking Dead, Wolf Among Us, and Tales from the Borderland series are way better games than this. Play those first if you're looking to get into Telltale games.

This game is a lot of fun.
You build a deck of cards, beforehand, which you use to "build" out a city (this is not a "city building" game, like Sim City, however). As you place these cards, you get points in the rows that they are placed in, based off of certain point collecting buildings and other buildings that increase and reduce points in different ways. When a row reaches a certain number of points, it becomes "ripe" and those points are ready to be collected, but only if all the rows before it have been completed (you basically have to "fill out" all the rows in order from first to last). Multiplayer is a little more complicated, where a row can be collected if it is full and the other player or CPU can sabotage you.
Those are just some of the details, however. It's obvious that a lot of thought was put into this and the end result is a game that is a joy to learn.
The game does a good job of easing you in, too, by giving you single player games first, in the campaign.
Get it.

For the Batman fan, some incredibly stupid liberties are taken with the lore that dont serve the mythos at all, in fact they act to weaken it making for a Batman that often feels more... doofy and illogical. Dont even get me started on Harvey Dent adn the highs chool ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t that's supposed to be his big undoing.
TL DR, I stongly, emphatically and utterly recommend avoiding this game.

My introduction to Telltale Games was long ago at the times of The Walking Dead (as I suppose everyone else), but I was never able to finish it (too dark of a setting, too clunky of gameplay for someone as bad at games as me). And since then I haven't played anything from them.
So the first thing I should say - gameplay really did EVOLVE during this time. Batman - The Telltale Series is where Telltale games come to shine. Finally I really felt like I am a part of comics, the media that I really love. It was great to have choices that didn't force me to choose who dies or lives, but that mean something more. Quicktime events may be overwhelming for a newbie (like me), but eventually you learn to love them and you wait for them with excitement. Honestly, sometimes it feels like you are the one doing all the punches - my brain would convince me the next button is E, but it was Q and the dance my inexperienced fingers had to do... xD
But of course the main thing was the story. Being not very familiar with DС comics, I still felt joy each time I recognised a character. And the turns were pretty unexpected anyways. I loved how the plot wrapped up... and the promise of more left me very excited. Thanks for the opportunity to built a hopeful, compassionate Batman!
All in all - great game! Worth a buy.

I'm not kidding when I say that this game is frustrating. But it is so frustrating that it is good. It's like one of those puzzles that you just have to keep working on, not because it's a particularly interesting puzzle but because... Actually I have no idea.
Let me illustrate for you how a typical game goes (for me). You start, somewhere where you have no idea. Yes you can google for maps, but you still have no idea where you are. OK, so you try to find some landmark that you can remember from the last however many times you've died. Great! A shack with a door! It's got a stove inside! Yes!
Everything goes swell for a couple of days. You scout out the local area, discover some fishing huts and loot a whole bunch of cabins. Then you start running out of supplies (food, wood, whatever), so you decide to venture out a bit further.
Then a blizzard hits and you're lost in 360° of white. Or you're heading out to fish, and you get attacked by a wolf or a bear or whatever. You might be able to stagger back, frostbitten or actually bitten, to shelter and live out a couple more days, but you know it's game over.
And then you try again. Because the game is that good. The concept is brilliant and the execution great. The game is early access, and the promised Story Mode looks like it could be good, but it is ready to play and enjoy now.
I also just wanted to comment on the visuals. It seems to me that, a lot of the time, you look at the screenshots for a game and they're all cinematic. Not so with this game. The visuals are entrancingly beautiful. Day time, night time, if it weren't for the fact that the outside is genuinely going to kill you, I would be perfectly happy to explore around just to immerse myself in the environment.
All told, The Long Dark is a great game and I highly recommend it.
Please note that this review is based on the Early Access version of the game, specifically the Timber Wolf Mountain update. Things may change before the game is complete. I'll update this review when the game is complete.

WOW!!! I wasn't expecting that. I've only recently got into indie games and enjoyed party hard + undertale, so thought I'd see what looked good on some top 10 indie games of all time list. Limbo cropped up a lot and the graphics really caught my eye. That's the first thing about this game, the way it looks, the smoothness of the animations. It's a work of art. I found myself stopping play to take in the aesthetics on quite a few times.
On top of that it is a fantastic game to play. The puzzles are challenging and thought provoking, I'd call this game a trial and die experience, because you will die, a lot. Not to worry though, you respawn just after the last puzzle you completed.
The controls are simple, with movement, including UP for jump and 1 action button. While this sounds a bit bare bones, it doesn't feel this way and it's perfectly executed. Any other controls would have spoilt the experience and what you get is a smooth and satisfying playing experience due to such tight and perfectly programmed control movements. As for the programming, the game never glitched once and I never found any mistakes, with anything.
If there is a flaw, I'd say the way the game evolved into the sci fi sections with the anti grav didn't seem to fit the theme up to that point and made the first half of the game more enjoyable, but it did have the effect of making the puzzles more challenging.
Another triumph is the sound. It's exceptional, total perfection and really adds to the experience.
There's some gruesome death scenes, even with the balck and white graphics, so this is definitely aimed towards a maturer audience.
It's a masterpiece and is one of the best games I've ever played, even when put up against AAA titles. I'm not one for replaying games, but I will definitely be completing Limbo again in the future.

After 33 brilliant hours, I have 100%, completely completed SUPERHOT, which is now easily my favourite game of 2016. It's the most innovative shooter I've played in years.
SUPERHOT is a mostly HUD-less minimalistic shooter with one great gimmick:
(or, well, moves very slowly when you don't). The core gameplay loop is extremely satisfying and gives it a feel that no other shooter can replicate. It is an action game at heart, but has an almost turn-based pace. The core of high level play can be summed up as 'stealing' turns and killing multiple red guys without giving them recourse, all while surviving. Everything dies in a single shot and the game even has a joke about it if you try to score headshots.
The minimalism of the game carries over into the simple Bauhaus-inspired aesthetic, though it has a strong touch of bizarre Dadaism to it, particularly if you go after the secrets. This much should be apparent from your first death, whereupon you glitch through the world as your body is blown apart. In any other game, this would be classified as a bug, but in SUPERHOT, it totally fits with the theme and never fails to look cool.
You will get to the end of the story in under 2 hours. It is quite self-aware, in a way that I think will leave a smile on your face by the end of it (mega bonus points for ggroups.exe, which can be launched in-game).
One word of warning: a lot of reviews will tell you that the game is 'short'. This is true for the 'story mode' (though I wouldn't play this for the story), which should take under 2 hours to complete. But much like Bayonetta, if you beat it once and never play it again -- you have
played SUPERHOT. Playing it at high level, on the challenge and endless modes feels like a wholly different game.
By the end of the 20+ hours (depends on your skill) of content, I started treating it like I used to treat Dynasty Warriors growing up; something I can pop in at anytime and enjoy without thinking too hard. It filled the same niche but gave me ten times the satisfaction and fun. I recommend SUPERHOT without reserve.

This is probably the most enjoyable Early Access Beta I've participated in.
The Dev support for this game has been stellar, with all my submitted bug reports and support tickets being responded to within a day at most, and the bugs themselves fixed within a few days. As of the Thanksgiving Patch, I have had no crashes or freezes, but there is also an in-game save option for those of us who get paranoid about beta crashes.
There's a lot of systems testing and bug-hunting going on at the present stage of development, but there is enough content to really have a blast.
The mobs at present are not pushovers, and can really tear you apart if you aren't careful. Personally, I like that the mob danger factor is so high, as it adds a real tension to the exploration aspect of the game. There is a mechanism in place for craftable respawns, which takes out some of the sting from dying.
I've gone on some intense-to-the-point-of-adrenaline-rush missions descending down through the biomes to find and unlock tech upgrades, while mobs and missiles chased my tail. I love the descent into danger mechanism of this game, where there is always an element of risk involved, and skill with manoeuvring and shooting is rewarded.
The gameplay is a combination of resource gathering, mob killing, building, crafting, and exploration.
There are quest/mission equivalents, in the form of finding Tech Waypoints, where the reward for success is unlocking boosted statistics and/or new craftables, such as better weapons and armour.
There are also wormhole events - at present these are time-constrained events where you have a specific timeframe to explore and loot what you can before your time runs out and the wormhole collapses. (Word from the Devs is that there will be a number of different kinds of wormhole events, including boss battles, which I am looking forward to)
At present time, there are only two complete Biomes in the Beta, and a limited number of tech upgrades and crafting options. That being said, I haven't exhausted that limited content in the 30 hours I've played thus far, which isn't bad at all for a beta. Furthermore, from the official forums and chats with the devs, it looks like what is presently in game is but a small fraction of the content planned for launch and post-launch.
I've found myself losing hours to this game, and do not regret spending money on it at all. As of 30/11, Multiplayer is still disabled, but word from the Devs indicates that this is only temporary while they finetune the coding. So at present, and likely for a few more weeks to come given the time of year, the game does only have single player mode.
That hasn't stopped me from having a damn good time with the game though. I definitely recommend it if Terraria or Metroidvania-styled gameplay tickles your fancy.

It will be fun and worth its price ONLY if you're one of the minority of gamers: a really, I mean really hardcore player, both a completionist by nature, and a lover of hardest difficulty by nature, because then you'll have a ton of replayability after finishing the story — you can complete challenges, which perfectly justify their name and are not simply called "challenges" to create an illusion of achievement, and also you can just relax by playing the endless mode, but other than that, there's literally nothing else to this game. Okay, there are easter eggs both in the game and in the menu, but easter eggs are part of every game — there's no credit due here. My main complaint is the story, and although it is pretty good, it is too short for my liking — I'm a fan of immersion and video game storytelling, especially from a first-person view, it is my most favorite thing in the world. I would not have been so disappointed if the story was just arbitrary, if it was there just for the sake of it being there, but as I said — it is pretty good, or at least decent if you have extremely high standards, so it's twice as shameful that it's short. Also, I'd just like to warn people who have at least some understanding of how physics work — don't expect realistic physics. And I'm not talking about the whole time-stop mechanic, I'm talking about weapons flying who knows where for no reason, weapons going through a red dude or being stuck between his arms although you certainly threw them right at his face from a distance of an extended hand and couldn't have missed if you were blind, weapons or enemies moving out of your reticule at the exact moment you pressed the left mouse button, somehow, which most of the time will result in you hitting a red dude instead of picking a weapon (despite the fact that reticule clearly showed an icon of picking up a weapon) — it's all out just an awful mess. It tries to come off as realistic despite the visuals and the story, but it fails miserably. Physics of this game have been a reason for many hits of my hand upon a table. I fear that I may have broken a bone in this rage.

Love dark stories?
Love death in general?
Love humour in general?
Love murder and violence?
Then this is the VN for you.
The MC of this VN is Suoh. He used to be normal, but all that changed after his parents were killed in a freak accident and he was hospitalized - losing memories whilst at it. His insanity (hearing voices to be more precise) is what he calls his Sickness. Because his parents' accounts were frozen, he needed money to support both him and his sister. What better way for a teenager to get cash then to work in the underground? Especially if said teenager has no guilty conciousness to speak off one bit.

Is it a Touhou ripoff? Yes. It's not as good as any Touhou? Absolutely.
Is it completely bad? No. Actually, it's very good for it's "price tag".
It has quite a few shortcomings gameplay-wise, such as your characters having a gargantuan hitbox, common enemies being annoying, nimble bullet sponges; you getting absolutely roflpwned if you die even once in more intense portions of the game because you don't regenerate bombs (or Aura, in this case, whatever) and you hardly get any considerable amount of power items in boss fights.
Story-wise... Well, let's be honest. Touhou has a♥♥♥♥♥♥story that is all about an infinite loop of "poorly drawn girl meets another poorly drawn girl > they throw some obscure references to JoJo, Agatha Christie and eventually japanese folklore and pop culture or say some nonsense > they try to kill each other with some bullet hells > you win > your poorly drawn girl meets another one > rinse and repeat". This game does pretty much the same, just with some less JoJo and Agatha Christie and some more anime clichés... A LOT MORE of anime clichés, if I may say. And the dialogues are not as skippable as Touhou's, which can get on your nerves eventually.
The chiptunes get quite zany at times, but are okay-ish for the most part.
As for the graphics, the pixel art is very cute and pleasant. The drawn sprites are not perfect but at least the designs aren't as much of unholy abominations as Touhou's. At least this artist can drawn legs and hands, and facial features in their proper places.
And I might have got too accostumed to LoLK and some other bullet hell games like Hitogata Happa, but this game is easy (judging by bullet hell standards). Almost 1cc'ed my first run and I was being extremely reckless on item collection.
