Concrete Jungle is not a building game, but a card-playing/Tetris style game that uses a much simplified residential/commercial/industrial Simcity layout where you need to avoid negative points (or at least 'repair' them with a few parks and other buffs).  If you've played card games like Hearthstone or Castle Wars, you'll be familiar with the style already (cards that either buff or nerf the already-played cards on the table), however, instead of placing your cards on the table, you have a grid of city squares that you fill with each property card in the hope of adding a required number of points to each row.  When the left-most row reaches the required points, it vanishes (Tetris-style) and a new empty row is added on the right which you can then use to buff preceding rows that might not have reached sufficient points.  You collect points from every row you clear, and you earn points from partiular cards played that can be saved to buy rarer and more powerful cards, or alternatively upgrade your skills via a simple RPG-style skills tree.  The game ends either when you've earnt the prerequisite points to beat the town level, or conversely when the left-most row can no longer be cleared (at which point it's game over if you've run out of lives!
The just-one-more-go addictiveness of it!  It's maddening really.  All those posh, expensive games you have, but instead this one will usurp your time!  It has a good tutorial to start you off, and the characters add some humour to the game.  It's such a clever blend of ideas that sound bizarre on a storyboard: what if Simcity was played like Hearthstone, and rows must be cleared like Tetris?  The developers have quite the imagination to make this combination work, but it does!  Indie games just go from strength to strength when it comes to originality, and this game does not disappoint (hence the overwhelmingly positive review score).  The price at first gives the impression of being a little steep for a casual game, but that's the thing: it's NOT as much of a casual game as it first appears.  It has more depth and stretegy to it than Hearthstone, and an infuriating yet funny AI to confound your attempts to breeze through the game.
Only the most minor of things.  Like many more casual games, there are spoken bits (speech bubbles to read) at the beginning of the tutorial levels.  There is an awful lot to click through and, while you CAN skip them, buried within are some necessary tips and guidance that you won't want to skip at first (so bear with it).  Because there is a lot more to the game than first appears, it can feel like the game is throwing a lot at you all at once, but after a few replays you will start to understand how the different component parts of the game (deck balancing, upgrades, avoiding blocked rows and using nerfs in a constructive way) come together, and it feels simple yet challenging to play.
Concrete Jungle is  deceptively light-hearted and simple whilst offering a Hearthstone-style level of depth and strategy beneath its cartoony surface.  It's also surprisingly addictive (you have been warned)!  Highly recommended!

I know nobody gives a rats♥♥♥♥♥ but this game gets my vote for best indie game of the year. The art, voiceovers, feel, and most of all glorious unique gameplay are all absolutely top shelf. I could write pages and pages, and I would still feel that there wasn't enough evidence of the quality of this amazing game.
First, the wrapping paper. Concrete Jungle looks and sounds amazing. From the routine act of navigating the intricately illustrated menus to the explosive crackle of celebratory fireworks that follow a large swing in points, the look and feel of this game wraps the user in. The intricate and cozy detail on every one of the hundreds of unque buildings, the chest vibrating thump when a building is placed, the thumbnail art for each of the characters' skills all ooze charm. The game makes the player feel like a welcome guest.
The campaign perpetuates this welcoming atmosphere with well written and surprisingly well voiced cast of characters who, like good sitcom personalities, begin to feel like friends of the player. The banter between characters feels natural and spirited, and the comfortable progression of the missions introduces the player to a series of complex gameplay elements with casual charm.
The gameplay itself is extremely nuanced, especially because the same set of cards are used in a few very different gameplay modes. Concrete Jungle lives up to its promise of a city-building deck builder, challenging the player to plan their city by collecting points and thinking many moves ahead in solo mode, or by uplifting their own residents and punishing their enemys' in verses mode. The design of the game does strain a bit to balance the cards between these two very different modes, but both prove very entertaining, and both provide very different challenges. In both modes, however, planning ahead is a necessity, and tactics must be layered into strategies that stretch multiple turns into the future. The many different characters and huge variety of buildings available allow for a high level of replayability of a hugely entertaining game.
Concrete Jungle is a modern classic. It bucks every current trend in indie game development and delivers an beautiful experience that will certainly inspire future efforts. Pass it by at your peril!

This game is an advancement to the medium. It is not coincidental that the game designer behind it was also one of the people responsible for The Stanley Parable, which is another notable contribution. I do believe, though, that while
was more accessible, The Beginner's Guide is original to the point of being ahead of its time - to avoid spoilers I will keep the explanation to this statement short, but let's just say that there have been some pretty unrealistic, detrimental assumptions about the game. You should not be thrown off by the fact that this game is, from a very strict, mechanical standpoint, a walking simulator (although if you play games for their complexity in interaction or systems alone and are not looking for a different kind of experience, this is most likely still not for you.)
Most games in this genre do not explore their medium or the genre itself correctly - they rely so much on their story that the fact that you're experiencing them is actually a setback to your enjoyment -, but in The Beginner's Guide your experience aside from the narration is also essential to the narrative. One could not have been achieved without the other, much like in The Stanley Parable, which is a game that, as does this one, makes you think about yourself. The main difference between the two is in intent: while in
you were in for a witty, funny, weird, in-your-face commentary on your expectations as a player,
allows you to explore more meaningful, serious, broad, and unconfortable aspects of your psyche, along with expectations. A truly awesome and important achievement.

I bought this game on the strength of the words "There are no zombies". I am a huge fan of the survival genre, own many games with strong survival elements and have installed survival oriented mods for many others. For many years I have longed for a serious. challenging wilderness survival game. When I read the words "There are no zombies" I thought I had finally found it. Sadly, I was wrong. I have waited a long time before writing this review, hoping that the game would improve. Unfortunately, it has become clear that the core focus of the game is unlikely to change.
"Wolf - The Wolf-Long Wolf: Darkwolf" is a game about wolves. It features compelling and challenging wolf-avoiding, wolf-hunting, wolf-fighting and wolf-escaping mechanics. To be fair to the developers, individual wolves are well balanced - formidable initially, but increasingly manageable with practice. As a wolf apocalypse survival game, this game could be quite enjoyable - and no doubt a great many people do enjoy it. Unfortunately, the threat posed by the wolves utterly overshadows the threats of hunger, thirst and exposure that would be the focus of a serious wilderness survival game.
In choosing to focus on monsters, the devs have trivialized aspects of survival that *should* be challenging. On standard difficulty, food is too plentiful; deer let you get too close, requiring no effort to track or hunt; buildings are never cold enough for the player to need a fire; there is no requirement for any kind of food variety and no hint of effects such as "rabbit starvation"; water can be boiled without a cooking vessel and stored without containers. If it seems that these features are too fiddly and would break playability, I have played other games and mods that have successfully handled all of these issues, while enriching rather than breaking their gameplay.
Where other survival games might have a goal of becoming self-sufficient, in The Long Dark, the closest you can hope for is to make your non-renewable items last beyond the point at which you become bored with the game and give up. Unfortunately, this effectively disincentivizes many parts of the game that would otherwise be enjoyable. By "intentional design choice", even arrows are non-renewable. Every deer you hunt now is an arrowshaft lost forever, a wolf you won't be able to defend yourself against later. After 41 hours in-game, I've abandoned 3 successful games in the face of mind-numbing repetition, knowing that engaging in any of the more interesting parts of the game would shorten my survival time. No doubt, the finite resources are intended to create tension, and in a setting with finite goals (such as the forth-coming story mode) they might. In an open ended sandbox, finite resources simply close off portions of the game.
Had the same game been pitched instead as a down-tempo, horror survival game of finite length - a wolf-infested Resident Evil perhaps - I'd have nothing but praise. The Long Dark is absolutely stunning and, at times, thoroughly engaging. Having set up expectations of playing out a frontiersman fantasy of living off the land, The Long Dark bitterly disappoints.

As with all these Choice-of-Games games, whether you'll like it or not depends mostly upon interest in the premise and the writing talent of the author.  As usual, there's a demo that can give you enough of both to let you see whether you'll be interested in shelling out for more.
As far as the premise goes... I'm just left wondering why on earth nobody did this sooner?!  There's a glut of superhero and D&D-type Choice-of-Games, but while there's a few (quite good, as well) Jules Verne/steampunk-flavored games out there, just straight-up going for the foppery of the old British upper class is virgin territory.  Playing as an impossibly talented and dedicated butler or maid trying to save an utter wastrel from themselves wasn't something I'd thought I'd needed until I knew it existed, but now I can't live without it.
So far as the writing goes, it clearly takes its digs at the era, but without getting into overtly acerbic territory.  It's lighthearted comedic fair, and while it has some moments of it (character speech is era-appropriate, but the narration is more modern casual), the text lacks consistent flourishes of supersilious wit more of the purple prose of the era might have.  Whether that's good or bad is up to you, since intentional loquciousness would undoubtably unnerve some readers, but it feels to me like a missed opportunity to spice up the more obviously comedic passages with some of the language of the penny dreadfuls that would help set the mood of the entire genre this game plays up as its setting.
As a butler or maid, you are a member of the most-definitely-not-invisible servantry.  To attain that prestigious post, you naturally have a background in some presumably vastly more lucrative field that logic would imply requires more skilled training than mopping the floors, such as art gallery curator, professional boxer, lion tamer, or international jewel thief. This informal training is just barely enough to qualify you for your baseline duties as a member of the servantry, such as cooking, cleaning, tutoring your master and their family's young ones, backtalking your master and his/her guests, fisticuffs with ruffians, sabotaging police investigations, jailbreaking, assuming control over police investigations in spite of being a vigilante, participating in espionage on behalf of an international housekeeping syndicate, directly controlling the fate of your employer's dynasty, and participating in contests in quaint county fairs.
Please be advised that it is frowned upon in upright, dignified upperclass families of the era for a a gentleman's gentleman or lady's lady to seduce their same-sex employer, or to steal their fiance out from under their noses, but for gentlemen and ladies of extraordinary talent and poise (you get a 'score' stat for succeeding at skill checks that are required for some endings), some eyes may wind up turned.

This game is excellent, especially considering where it is in its development.
While wolves pose a serious threat to you, they are not that difficult to fight off once the struggle occurs, at least if you have a knife or hatchet. It takes some time to figure out, but mashing the LMB and RMB in quick succession will generally save you. - I do wish that there was a way to use a weapon to fight off a wolf BEFORE the struggle occurs, such as a wooden spear or even a club. If i'm going to be fighting a wolf im not going to want to wait until its on top of me to fight back.
The weather system is fantastic, with the game actively forcing you to make decisions. Do I wait out the blizzard in my cave or go try to find food? Do I stay here and try to keep the fire going all night or do I leave and try to find an indoor shelter to sleep in.
The game mechanics of starvation, dehydration and exhaustion are also intricate, and provide a game where you are challenged, but not in an unreasonable way.
Visually the game is also fantastic. I play on medium graphics, as my computer is not as great as I wish it was, and everything is still expertly done. From artwork, to the way the world reacts to wind (visually and auditory).
Obviously it would be nice if I did not need to travel to the forge to make arrow heads, or if I could create makeshift weapons to equip besides the rifle and the bow (such as spears, axes, clubs, etc), and I do get bothered by how fast I get dehydrated. But nothing melting a little snow won't fix.
I look forward to the game's progress.

This game is surprisingly very addicting.
I bought it two weeks ago on the search of something different.
So it kinda plays like Tropico, but with immigration set to off. Building a small community that relies only on its own people is very challenging. If you want positions to be filled quickly, you need to have an active population, otherwise you need immigration. With immigration not an option, your growth is much much slower and you have to plan your moves carefully if you don't want to waste labor. It can really be the choice between life and death.
Some tips, you have to attend to the basic needs of your people very quickly. At the start, you have the basic needs: food, clothing, tools, building materials. When all that is expended, that's when the game becomes increasingly challenging. If you don't satisfy at least one of them, you're going to have a problem that leads to another until you have a problem. An example would be having a shortage of tools would lead to a slowdown of production, slowing down production of food, firewood, tools, construction, etc. You're citizens will die from starvation or freeze in their homes as a result. So you need to keep supplies healthy.
Another challenge is trade. For starters, the game doesn't start with the most interesting of crops. I mean chestnuts, wheat and pepper doesn't sound exciting and you obviously want variety. You also don't have livestock to begin with. That's were the trading dock becomes handy. You exchange goods to buy seeds or livestock. The thing is, they're very pricey at 2500 units for 1 seed variety or 600-800 units for one live stock.
Technical-wise, the game is graphically above average. Nothing fancy here. What's impressive though is the file size. The game is only under 300MB. It's also one of those rare games where the game actually runs better in V-sync. But if you must know, my GTX 660Ti can run it above 240FPS and the screen-tearing is strong here. It's not something you see for a game released in 2014.
The game also comes DRM free from that other place ;).

You can loose speed unpredictably with small hit at some obstacle, colliding with oponents is more or less predictable but the model in general is poor. Opponents drive unpredictable, sometimes making stupid mistakes, sometimes the leading rival is just unstoppable. And the worst thing is that this game runs only when you are looged in at Steam! Disclosure: I marathoned the full season over the course of a few days, rather than playing (and replaying) the installments as they came out, so I haven't experienced some of the game-breaking performance issues that seemed to have been plagued this game earlier on.
Anyway...
Despite some rough edges, I had a blast. The TT engine still needs some serious love, and I did experience periodic stuttering issues on a pretty capable gaming PC – and particularly during the earlier episodes – but I still really dig the art style of these games. However, I sincerely hope that TT debuts a legitimately new engine soon, because this game does not look as good as it should OR run as well as it ought to considering the quality of its visuals.
I enjoyed the voice-acting, story, and the narrative's major plot twists, although I can understand why it has been a turn-off for some. TT has definitely given their own spin to some pretty notable baddies and their origin stories, and sometimes quite extensively. We also get a new villain, which I found compelling. I’m fine with that, since I thought they generally did a good job, although I wished some of the Wayne family revelations had been handled with a bit more… subtlety.
It feels like we lost some interactivity this time, at least compared to the likes of The Walking Dead S1. I still enjoyed the event/crime scene reconstruction sequences, although I admittedly don’t really have any serious desire to play through them again now that the magic of discovery is gone. They were still fun for me initially – albeit a bit simplistic. I have mixed feelings about the best balance of interactivity in what are essentially modern point-and-click adventure games, but its reduction here did not harm my enjoyment. However, players that are looking for more dynamic environments or deeper player reactivity should know that it’s just not there.
This was a fun, new Batman adventure that tipped some genre tropes on its head, had a few nice surprises, and actually makes it fun and engaging to play as Bruce Wayne – perhaps even more so than his alter ego. I eagerly await the next season.

If you are looking for a true city builder, this game is certainly not it. But for fans of puzzle and strategy games, Concrete Jungle hits the right spot. It's hard to describe this game accurately so I will state that it lives up to what it says on the box: city building meets deck building meets puzzle game (I think that about covers it!)
Gameplay: You build a city with cards that represent various buildings. Each building has its own expense and economy costs (city building mechanics). The cards are shuffled randomly but you can make purchases to customie your deck and there is also a 'tech tree' of skills, unique to each character in the game (deck building/card game). The puzzle aspect comes in because you need to score a given number of points per column (each column has just 6 tiles in which you can place buildings, essentially how much you can score is limited by available land/tiles) to clear it and move forward.
This game is very well thought out and has immense depth. The campaign mode is exhaustive and helps with the sort of steep learning curve. In vs mode, it can get quite challenging and tense but in solo, this can be a very relaxing game! it's great for playing with friends, family on local co-op and since it works with controller you can play it on your TV (which is what I do, it's awesome).
Well worth the asking price and the dev has already promised a free update with nigth mode and more pretty buildings! Concrete Jungle easily has hours of gameplay and it can be difficult to master but it's also very fun.

To play optimally, you have to stop and move very small distances all the time, it is not easy to describe for me, but it feels like playing a racing simulator with the keyboard.
It doesn't help that the animations look and feel clonky too and are of bad quality.
That is even more apparent when the game shows you your completed mission at normal speed, where you can clearly see the poor animation quality, which results in poor player feedback and controls that feel unresponsive. The game has a cool artstyle and there are moments which are spectacular, but even the death animation of the enemies gets old really fast, partly because I think they aren't actually physics based, but pre-made animations, so they look the same all the time, but maybe that's just me.
It is not that fun to shoot the weapons, it is definitly not fun to use melee weapons or throwables. Another factor for that is the TERRIBLE sound design. Weapons and melee weapons sound terrible, especially the sound when you punch an enemy is just weird. All these factors hurt the flow and rythm of the game, which makes it not very enjoyable for me. Yes, I could play in a way where I have more "flow", but then I'm intentionally playing worse to make the game more fun to play, which is stupid.
I don't know what the developers could do to improve the problems I have, except having more budget and time, and higher production value, but after completing the game I lost all motivation to do anything further. The story was interesting, but doesn't gave me anything, it was just an excuse for playing random levels. And again, that would be okay, if the gameplay wasn't so dull and unresponsive.

Let's get one thing straight: Concrete Jungle is
a city management simulation. That much should be apparent from the trailer but I think I failed to fully grasp it before I made my purchase. Youtubing some Let's Play videos would have probably been useful in this regard. Anyway, don't let that scare you away. Yes, even you, guy who has 2000+ hours in City: Skylines, along with faithful recreations of every major city in the world. You frighten me, but I admire your passion for building stuff.
Concrete Jungle
a game that skillfully combines the heart of a city management simulation and the brain of a hardcore puzzler, gushing with style and substance. That was a mouthful so let me try that again:
Concrete Jungle is a damn good game.
When you start a game, you're given a handful of cards and a plot of land tiles arranged in a grid. The cards represent the various buildings you can construct and contain statistics and rules about their impact on your city. As you add new buildings to the plot, they'll often change the value of tiles around them. Shops and restaurants will add value whereas factories and landfills will cause nearby values to plummet. When all the cards are played, the deck is shuffled and you continue to draw from the fresh pile. What you want to do is play houses, which collect points, in high value areas to maximize your score. Scoring happens when you fill a row (the game refers to them as columns but I insist they are rows) with buildings and the value of those buildings hits your current target number. Like Tetris, the filled row is cleared and more space is created for buildings. How well you score is determined by how you min/max your placement of buildings. The round starts with a deck of a few basic buildings but more powerful buildings can be purchased from a semi-random pool with economy points. There's also a roster of eight different characters to play as with unique skill trees that are gradually unlocked as the round progresses.
The proceeding was an, admittedly, clinical explanation of what amounts to an utterly engrossing experience. The visuals are bright and charming and the music is a soothing backdrop for thoughtful play. Each of the campaign levels includes voice-acted scenes that may not be perfect but were still enjoyable. However, it was a relief to discover they could be skipped after failed attemps. There's also a strong flavor of city building which is well reinforced by it's 200+ buildings with well thought-out, thematic powers. Car dealerships target rich neighborhoods to give you economy points. Train stations add more points based on how many connections they create. Recycling centers can delete underpowered cards from your hand. Youth centers look to the future, allowing you to draw more cards and plan ahead etc. It was a ton of fun just figuring out why each building does what it does and this kind of mechanical immersion is exactly what makes Concrete Jungle such a brilliant game.
The game can be played solo but also includes a versus variant. Having not learned my lesson about preconceived notions, I imagined that this would be a tacked-on, horribly underdeveloped and unnecessary alternative to the "core" gameplay. Nothing could be further from the truth. Versus mode has both 1v1 and 2v2 variants (for the love of God, please add online multiplayer!) and changes the rules in a few key aspects. The most compelling difference is the scoring: the player with the most points in each row gets both theirs
their opponents points for that row, which is genius. What ensues is a sharp and tactical battle of risk and reward. It has some small elements of luck, sure, but ultimately, it favors players with a knack for planning and inventiveness. Many of the cards also have to be reevaluated in this environment and open the door for some very cool advanced strategies. That factory you don't want stinking up your valuable real estate? Perhaps your opponent will enjoy having it dropped right in the middle of their housing project. Because local multiplayer is currently the only option, I'm in the process of contriving a friends-on-the-couch situation solely so I can confound everyone with my competitive city engineering skills.
Concrete Jungle has completely defied my expectations and I'm so glad that it did. It's a fantastic specimen in the genre of puzzle games. There's still a ton of content left for me to unlock and I expect to be playing this one for many, many hours to come.

A brief puzzle game for the patient.
If you've played and enjoyed Tiny Bang Story, you will most likely enjoy Morphopolis. While controlling an insect, you retrieve a certain number of certain objects for certain taskgivers whether they be other insects or plants. The game in all takes maybe around 30-40 minutes. This 30-40 minutes can easily be filled with relaxation for this breed of game has its calming effects with its soothing music and simple find-the-things gameplay. However, if you are not the most patient person, you may not enjoy this game due to the slow movement speed of the insect that you control to move through different parts of a level. When you know what you are to do, you complete the task in a matter of seconds. It takes just as long, if not longer, to move between the different sections to progress.
Overall, if you are patient and want a low-stress game to occupy yourself for under an hour, I would reccomend Tiny Bang Story, but this would come soon after.

The biggest challenge in this game would be timing, given the simple functions, you are tested mentally as well as *kinda* physically. It raises your heart beat every time you to try to time your character movements, I got jolted out a little when I miss a little here and there and it's really nerve-wreaking but at the same time enjoyable.
Though there werent any story telling as you journey your way out but if you notice each obstacles or puzzles you went through would provide some sort of insights of how you perceive the world to be. The struggles, dazing music, chilling sounds, and the strenght needed to go on about exploring the unknowns, all this elements are in the game. To me, this is more that just a platform puzzle game, it's a thought provoking game. Definitely would recommend this game to those who appreciates the eccentric nature of dwelling in Limbo.

I REALLY REALLY want to like this game, but frankly, it's boring. There is a fine line between "challenging" and unnessesarilly difficult. Unfortunately, Sunless Sea is the latter. I don't mind a hard game, however, in Sunless Sea there doesnt seem to be any point - or realism - to its difficulty. It seems like the developers wanted to create a Rogue-like permadeath game and in order to do that they gave you next to nothing in resources - so few resources, in fact, that you are often punished for exploring too far from the start location. You can find trade routes near by that net you a profit, but running the same routes over and over is not what I'd call a fun game.
If you're interested wait for it to go on sale. Game is worth $5 - $10.

This game is functionally excellent, but has unfortunately undergone a number of negative changes as a result of the slow whittling down of the playerbase.
Many of the players now remaining online are in high bot-count servers and are simply camping a location with a machinegun in order to rack up high kill-counts. The players who are in populated servers are largely also camping, leading to the rank absurdity of objective games where the only "players" contributing to a push are the bots.
With a game this established the glitch points on the various maps have been well established and are constantly in use by the playerbase, to the point where every game will contain players glitching into inaccessible locations on the map or shooting from physically absurd positions, sometimes for the entire length of the match as they cannot be hit or approached from in-bounds areas.
I would recommend this game in a heartbeat if the playerbase was comprised less of individuals intent on glitching and/or camping, and more of players who intended to play the objectives.
Sadly this is not the case, and I cannot recommend this as the days when this game was enjoyable are well and truly over.

The Man warned him not to return without completing the job, but couldn't actually mark Laka's map to show him where he was supposed to go.  Laka could not find the island, desperately returned to London to resupply, and was murdered by his employer.
So, actually, this is the story of Ashta Ruual.  A war veteran who set out north, Ruual decided to go past the world's end, and lost all his supplies.  Desperate for food, he engaged a pirate vessel many times his strength and was sunk.
So, actually, this is the story of Tilly DuPont.  An urchin, she was way more successful than her rivals before her.  The first to visit the world above, and raise a foundling as a Scion.  Her affairs with her engineer, however, earned the ire of her lover in London, who left with the child.  Driven to madness, she attempted to sail past the Dawn Machine, which only drove her deeper into insanity.  Invariably, her crew turned on her, and she was killed.
So, actually, this is the story of the Shadowed Stranger, who's owner gave up and started reading the Wiki.  The Stranger was able to get several important tomes necessary to raise the stats of his predecessor.  He was the first to actually be able to upgrade his ship, and ventured beyond the High Gate with the Merchant.
So, actually, this is the story of Mara Sei.  A disgraced priest, Mara Sei...
Et cetera.
The most frustrating part of this game is its lack of direction.  You'll get vague instructions like "in the southern corner of the map" which is a vast expanse that will sap all of your fuel to reach, let alone explore, and then you'll struggle and die.  On the other hand, if you explore too slowly, the Admiralty doesn't pay well enough to keep food in your hold.
This is a game that simultaneously rewards and punishes caution.  They want you to play on their hardcore mode (autosaves only), but it's pretty brutal.  Especially since the map changes on each playthrough.
On the other hand, this is a fascinating world and story, but I have no sense of what the history of the world is.

I put more time into this game than I should've. I only went back recently to record and document how well I could finish the game. Obviously when it's been a couple of months I got out of practice and had to play a little bit more.
There is a training room in this bullet hell, some others in the genre have it as well. It's very good for learning where enemies spawn into the screen, their patterns, and the bullets. Like many other in the genre, memorization will help. To be honest however, if you're trying to get into this game don't be put off by that. Memory will help, but it's not needed. You can play this game on reaction alone, although some practice will be needed as well.
One thing that I notice some newer players struggling with, in part because it's never said in the game dialogue wise, but it might be in the game somewhere (options menu perhaps?). The use of holding down SHIFT creates a dot on your character that you are playing. Your character also moves slower that normal with a tighter shot spread depending on your character. Since there are 6 characters, with a secret character they all have different uses of holding down shift. I've called it "Focus Mode" because I remember another bullet hell game that used the name/function, and it really does make you focus in on your character. Most of the time you will be looking at your own character and not what you're shooting at.
The game has a level progression during your run, that can go up to 5 (That's the power meter). I've made a small basics video that went over some of the game, but there are some other details that I left out. Bosses have a number of phases and it's even possible to get pass them by waiting out their timer, in the top right. Because of that its entirely possible to do a run without killing anything (Pacifist achievement).
I'm not exactly sure why I enjoy this game as much as I did. The difficulty was hard at first, I was getting frustrated with some of the levels. In time however I realized that I wasn't upset with the game, but with myself - how could I get hit right there? I didn't save my lives by expending an aura blast or bomb, etc. Getting better at the game was its own little achievement for me, even if it took a few restarts. I started demanding better runs from myself until I got the no-hit run and I'm guessing Pacifist is out of reach for me. I'm still not that great at the game, I'm only decent enough to beat Normal/Easy and I'm not as interested in practicing some more for Hard and onwards. Players that enjoy a decent challenge, I'd recommend this game - it's free for one thing, so just trying it won't hurt that much. I'm not sure how it stands up to other bullet hells, I'm fairly new to the genre but it isn't very difficult. Pass some time with Jigoku it's free.

First of all, this game is not suitable for children in any way, form nor shape. Secondly, if you get angry because character is different from your favorite storyline, you don't know anything about storytelling and you should go away. Forever. That, of course, is in regard to other characters than Batman, since you decide how he behaves. Thirdly, I can't be objective when it comes to Batman and this is no exception. I absolutely love this game. It is an interactive Batman movie, what would you want more?
Story is immersive and amazing -  villains are great, you get their motivation, and, like everybody, they react to what you're saying and doing. Some motives are so cool you have a giant grin on your face. Choices are either heartbreaking or intriguing, which makes you want to replay the game. To be honest I usually can't bring myself to strafe away from my responses since I want to be the best Batman I can be. Music is alright, two or three memorable tracks, and I don't think there should be more - you're more focused on dialogs. Gameplay is alright as well - game isn't hard, detective work neither(it mostly consists of checking all 'clickables' and connecting the right ones), and I don't think it should be. After all, this isn't that kind of game.
To be fair, there are some glitches, but they are random, so you can walkthrough the entire game without every encoutering one. Once I had Bruce looking in other direction than he should while talking - it was hilarious, but it took me out of the game for a moment.
Overall, if you are a Batman fan, you should get this. you should get this NOW. If not, I have no idea - I own three telltales titles, and despite loving this one and liking very much the other two I don't have any desire to check out others.

Allrighty, folks, we are looking at a gem that doesn't even know what KIND of gem it is. Is it a strategy? Yes. Is it an Indie? Yes. Is it a Tetris-like game? Yes. Is it procedurally generated? Yes. Is it a Rogue-lite? Yes. Is it Ironman? Yes. Does it involve competition? Yes. Can you play it for hours and hours on end? YES!!!
I was absolutely surprised just how much the game did right. So, in true fashion, let's take at the good and the Bad.
The Good:
1. Awesome AI. I love AI that can make my life a living hell. The AI will exploit your mistakes, take advantage of them, and crush you, rather than just hang back and let you feel all good for beating it.
2. An ever changing world - be it on Campaign, or on custom, you need to plan for the future and play accordingly. I love this about a game, as it doesn't force you to take a level after another like a zombie.
3. Pleasant graphics and relaxing music.
4. Learning as you go - some people have complained that the game is hard - it is not. You just need to let it teach you, and then crush your opponents with a huge point lead.
5. A card collection game - lots and lots of cards to collect, and that in itself, makes you play it over and over again till you find the bestcards that would suit your deck, principles, philosophy, and pattern of playstyle.
6. Buildable decks - if you're into card games, this will reel you in big time. Based on your deck, you can do various builds and play or throw your opponent off big time.
7. Thinking a number of moves ahead - as you have a complete visibility of the ever-changing field, your hand and the cards that come, you can plan a good number of turns ahead, just like in chess.
8. Good replayability - as no two games are the same, you can have heaps of fun with this game, as the map layouts and the AI will challenge you big time.
9. Good value for the money - right now the game costs twice the hours I played (7.2), and I easily see myself doing more and more of it. I expect to get my money's worth twice over.
10. Even if I don't really care about settings menues and such, this game does provide a good amount of them.
11. A nice amount of jokes that will put a smile on your face.
12. The AI opponent diversity is great - from ones that will contest your city-beatutifying skills to those that will outright nuke your stuff, you will contantly be forced to adapt, and that is a huge bonus in my book.
And now let's take a look at the BAD:
1. Steep learning curve. You will need to do the walkthrough, get used to every character and play to their strengths on the fly. This is not as easy to do as it might sound. And don't get me started on card variety...
2. You can lose games through no fault of your own. This for me is a huge gripe. I hate playing my best cards, or to the perfect strengths of my build and still lose because the opponent got lucky.
3. No online MP. I hope the devs will add it, because local co-op without a coop partner is an SP game. While they did make the AI great, you will eventually get bored of it.
Conclusion:
As you see, getting used to the game and the multiplayer are its only huge setbacks. It is absolutely no wonder why it's so well accepted on steam. It does so much right - replyability, varying challenges, versus AI mode, procedural generation, cards, buildable decks, varying builds, puzzle-like mechanics, and whatnot.  If you're of fan of any of those genres, you will absolutely adore it. However, if you get easily irritated by loss, dislike games with huge learning curves, procedural generation or luck, I would easily say that this game is not for you.

At the time of writing [1/18/2014] Project Zomboid is an early-access game by Indie Stone Studios. For the price of 14.99 and the current state that the game is in, this is worth a buy for those who are willing to wait yet still want a taste of what the finished product will be. Currently the game is a bit buggy and slow, and playing the demo is not only recommended, but NECESSARY in my opinion. Some machines may not be able to run the game, and it might be a while for the developers to rectify that in a future update. Remember, this is indeed an early-access game, so bugs and glitches are to be expected.
You'll make the choice between the towns of Muldragh or West Point, both situated in Kentucky. Muldragh is a small town with outlying farms and trailer parks with some commercial centers, while West Point is a more urbanized city. Zombies tend to congregate in urban areas rather than rural, where some of the better loot is acquired.
Once you choose your town, you will create your character. You'll have a variety of jobs to choose from, such as a Construction Worker that gains better carpentry skills and has thicker skin, to a Security Guard that requires less sleep and is more attentive to his surroundings during rest. You'll also be able to pick traits, but you'll need to balance the good with the bad. You're character may be Brave, but you'll need to give him/her a few negative traits to gain points to use - Such as Near-Sighted and Light Drinker.
After creating your character, you'll randomly spawn in a house somwhere in your chosen town. It's up to you now to scavenge food to stave of starvation, battle the ever-growing hordes, and build up a safe-haven - Your future tomb. This isn't the story of how you survived, this is how you died.

But the game is beautifully done, with lovely graphics, animations and a super nice interface, so if you like puzzle solving, card collecting, deck building, Tetris and the city building theme, I say go for it!

It's definitely more of a book than a game. The choices offered still make it feel narrow and you know there is little you can do to change the the majority of the story, but the the surprises in the story and the character elements really help to make you be a part of the story. There's room for emotions and actions to be personalized and you handle the situations in your own approach, which is reward enough. It will be nice to see something like this go on...

Following the standard formula for hidden object / adventure game motifs, 'Voodoo Chronicles' stumbles a lot with player accessibility.  Room transitions are not well indicated, puzzle connections require leaps of faith instead of logic, and the reuse of identical hidden object screens makes the game feel rushed.
I definitely love this game
Such a fun and exciting, yet scary, game!

Gameplay
=======
A puzzle game with building elements, it seems deceptively simple at a glance but is actually quite deep.  The combinations of cards and randomness can make for agonizing decisions.
You start with a set of basic cards (which you can change).  Cards largely represent buildings of various types.  Your goal is to use these cards to earn points for each "row" of land.  You can earn more cards/skills during a scenario, but cards that give you currency typically have drawbacks, so you will need to balance your economy and point getting at the same time.
The campaign is engaging, with a decently entertaining backstory that pushes it along.  The campaign introduces new elements and features gradually, but quickly enough that you shouldn't get bored.  Each scenario gives you have limited space and resources to achieve your goal, sometimes throwing you a curveball (for example, Coalfields has the AI place a random building down every 4 turns, disrupting your carefully laid plans).
Characters each have their own set of "Skills" that you unlock during a given play, lending to varied playstyles and replayability.
Audio
====
Decent ambient sound, but the highlight is the soundtrack.  Not obstrusive but easy to listen to.  You might even find yourself humming along after awhile!
Voice Acting was a surprise - a pleasant one, I quite enjoy the narration/dialog, as tropey as they are sometimes.
Graphics
======
Surprisingly good graphics for what, at first glance, appears to be a low-budget title.  Detailed, varied tilesets and even weather effects are present!
That said, quality is mixed, some areas are well polished, and others less so, but you don't buy a puzzle game for graphics, right?

The player takes the role of James, a successful detective searching for clues regarding several mysterious deaths occurring. Offering his services to the police and adventuring in a world where simple weapons won't work, James must fight a curse to save his own life.
, is an adventure game with a fantastic steampunk influence involved in a noir atmosphere, involving crime, mystery, greed and some deep dark secrets, that remote to the beginning of civilization. Travel from America to remote places such as a spooky village or an isolated island that works as a secret military operation base. Unveil what lurks behind the empire of the most ambitious and rich man of Ritchcity.
As the story goes, this one nails the player to the screen as we enjoy the mix between classic noir and a world of magic unveiling in front of our eyes. This has a major impact for those looking for intense adventures, and rather not predictable, boring concepts that have been squeezed dozens of times before.
James is rather suspicious of such thing as the black arts, but eventually finds himself in a very strange mission, where everything awkward seems to happen. With this, comes NPC's that are also interesting, mysterious, and they are all interactive.
The amazing plot follows the fantastic design, with different areas being available, all in 2D and sometimes a few extras so we can feel a 3D around the corner. It's great to change places and keep the same visual quality, and smartness relating to objects, directions and overall presentation.
The Puzzles are somehow easy, but fun, doesn't feel repetitive at all, and can be enjoyed without much thought into them. The HO's scenes however, can be slightly confusing because the
is far from accurate or polished. Sometimes you really have to click around the object to pick it.
Although Steam has the HD - Director’s Cut Edition, the HO's scenes are still in 4:3 and using old resolution, while everything else looks beautifully in 16:9, and feels HD, probably at 1280x720.
The problems don't stop here, unfortunately for me and everyone else, the first (and possibly the last) adventure of James in Voodoo Chronicles franchise is impossible to complete due to a glitch in the game, very near to the end. This presents the player with no option but to quit the game and content himself with just a half finish adventure, or trying to get the original non HD version at the
Store. (I can't guarantee it will work either!)
Because this game is unplayable, I could never give a positive feedback, and that's really a shame because
looks and feels a terrific game from
, I would go even further and say this is their best work in terms of plot, storyline and visuals. Too bad the game suffers from a Glitch that it's impossible to finish such amazing adventure.
Why is this game on sale? Will a patch become available at anytime in the future? Who knows. Until then, do not buy this game under no circumstance.

You constantly have to buy vehicles from the black market or steal them.  You have the ability to upgrade the blackmarket vehicles, but why.  Threre is no permanemce to them. The Long Dark is a *fantastic* survival game and it's only getting better, if you're a fan of hardcore (permadeath) survival games then TLD will likely rate in your top 5, although it's more likely to be the top 3 (maybe even number 1).
It differs from other hardcore survival games in the sense that it's grounded in reality, there are no zombies, monsters, demons or other players, it's just you VS nature. There are no threats to you in the game that wouldn't be a threat to you in the real world (wolves, bears, thin ice, the cold, etc).
I could rant for ages about it, but I'll just go with the tried and true pros and cons.
Pros:
+ For the most part, it's realistic. You're not going to find a jetpack, you don't have a mega buster or anything like that, you're just a normal man / women who got dealt a bad hand (crash landing in the "Canadian outback"). If you hear ice cracking, MOVE (quickly), if you hear growling, get the hell out of there (quickly) or if you hear a blizzard outside and you have little clothing, DON'T go outside. 95% of the decisions you make require only common sense, you won't need a walkthrough or a deep understanding of the games mechanics to survive (thriving is a different matter though).
+ There's a variety of survival methods. You can stay in a forest cabin and hunt the wildlife (or scavenge what they leave behind), you can stay by the lake / coast and survive by fishing, you can stay in urban areas and survive off of the food left behind by other people, you can go out gathering mushrooms, stalks, lichen and other natural things to eat (or turn into medicine) or you can leave traps out overnight and go back the next day to see if you caught anything.
+ Each method of survival works differently, hunting requires you to go out and find prey (or predators) but don't think because you're hunting that you are not being hunted, you could have a stag in your sights and be being stalked by a wolf or charged from behind by a bear (watch your back). Traps are "auto-gathering", once you place them you can leave them and (hopefully) when you return you'll have a rabbit or two (but if you leave them too long a predator will take them, likely destroying your trap in the process). Fishing requires you to stay in the fishing hut with the rig that speeds up time when fishing until you catch something or the pre-alloted time you spend fishing runs out. Gathering is the less effective at keeping hunger at bay, but requires no tools, is safer than hunting and fishing and has a wider array of uses. Some can be made into drinks that hydrate (and even warm) you, some can be eaten, some can be made into medicines for a variety of conditions and will (eventually) regrow in the wild. Scavanging from abandoned houses, towns or structures of any kind is the best thing to do, but it won't take long until you deplete them and when they are gone, they are gone forever.
You balance these out as you see fit for your current circumstances and location, ensuring there will be some variety in your days activitys and that eventually your surroundings and circumstances change dramatically. e.g; When you've used all the resorces from one area and making fire becomes a problem, there's no sense in surviveing by the skin of your teeth without fire when you can pack your bags and move to the coast where there will be matches, (maybe) rifles, ammo', food, clothes, etc.
+ The game has a logical dynamic. You can get all the water you want, you just melt snow, but melted snow can make you sick, you need to boil it first. To do so you need fire, so you need a source of fire (matches, magnifiying glass, etc), tinder (newspapers, books, tinder plugs, etc), and fuel (reclamined wood, hard wood, soft wood) with the option of an accelerant (lighter fuel or gasoline). You can make a fire in a stove (inside) or build your own firepit (outside), the firepit must have wind cover (in a cave, behind a rock, by a cliff, etc) and can ofc burn you (don't walk on the fire.....), but once you have fire you can melt all the snow and boil the unclean water all you want. It also opens up the oppertunity to cook food (to remove the chance of food poisoning), warm you up (staying warm will be your number 1 priority) and even deter predators.
I could go on for days, but the point is it's a survival game set in extreme circumstances that pulls off realism and enjoyment almost entirely, but I think I've gobbled it off enough, so now for the cons.
Cons:
- As it is still in development the game is likely to change, for better or worse I don't know, but if there's a chance it could get worse then it's a con.
- The way the game updates doesn't fit with the games intention at all. If you're surviving well then there will have likely be a couple of updates since you started playing, chances are not all of thier contents will be available to you meaning you either carry on without the content that can't be updated or intentionally die so you can start again with all the content you can't have on your old file. **This is not this games fault, most -if not ALL- games update this way. Surviving as long as you can doesn't work at all if the game either changes between playthroughs (a good playthrough will last weeks, maybe months) or doesn't give you everything that should be available. It's not the games fault, it's just a nessecery evil of early access.**
- There's no jumping OR scailing. Jumping is no big deal, you're in 2 feet of snow in -20C (or lower) with -20C windchill (or lower) with a shedload of gear on you, jumping just wouldn't work. But SCAILING? We need that, it doesn't have to be  cliff scailing or anything like that, but from time to time you'll find yourself stuck, unable to move forward because of a branch on the floor that's 2 - 3 inchs tall. If you're being chased by a wolf or bear and die (permadeath remember) because something smaller than your shoe was in the way..... you'd be pretty ****** off. Trust me, I've been there, done that and lost the T-shirt becasue a bloody bear killed me because I couldn't scail a 3 INCH TALL BRANCH! Some fashion of scailing small obsticales is VITAL. It might not get you for a while, but eventually, it will, and when it does I will consume your salty to make mine stronger, for there can be ONLY ONE!
Conclusion
It basically breaks down to the pros being around 8/10 and the cons being about 2/10. The only bad things I can say about this game is that it's in early access. I'm sure they will add scailing at some point, it'd be insane not to. The way the game updates won't be an issue forever and neither will the ambiguety towards it being early access, so when the game's finished I won't have a bad word to say about it.
If you like realistic hardcore survival, then this game is simply a must have, when it's finished I'd be dissapionted it if got any lower than a 9/10. For the moment it's a 8/10 simply because of the cons (and they won't be an issue forever).

MORPHOPOLIS is a gorgeous-looking, casual slow-burn puzzler fueled by hidden object elements; one that I recommend with the caveat that it will certainly not be for everyone.  While not brutally difficult, it is a sometimes frustrating experience that it is well-suited for the casual puzzle and artistic game fan.   There is little direction; and the lack of the ability to save while in the middle of one of MORPHOPOLIS' five beautiful segments is rough, as the inherent beauty of this game is it's calm, wickedly slow movement and it's mesmerizing artwork.  So failing to finish a segment during a sitting results in the dreaded do-over, with your ever-morphing insect ponderously revisiting the beautiful yet limited screens.
That said, the episodes are fairly short, and the game can be finished in a short span (as short as 90 minutes), with all achievements.  But there is the rub; this is not a game you speed through; it is one you savor.  And for someone like myself who's immersion is often limited to nights and weekends by work exhaustion or time constraints, I thoroughly enjoyed playing through the various trials of our weary bug, as a calming cool down for the brain if you will... Though the puzzles vary from fairly difficult to rather simple, puzzle veterans may have a leg up on recognizing what it is you are supposed to actually do.  There is zero direction... but hit the discussion board for the concept, and off you go.  Only other minor fret was that in some cases, the hidden object items you are required to collect are quite difficult to discern and at times don't really resemble what you need to find; and I am not hot on clicking randomly as a strategy.
Still, for what it is, MORPHOPOLIS succeeds in being an engrossing, beautiful, casual, albeit short experience that is worth a go if you want to step away from the bullet hell for a moment.  If you enjoy it for what it is, you are bound to be rewarded with a fun little puzzler that is certainly like no other...

RO has a a very "indie" vibe to it and is not at all a AAA game.

After surviving a terrible plane crash in the middle of the ocean, the hero swims to what seems to be a structure in the middle of nothingness leading to an alien world -- not on a different planet... but to the city of Rapture in the gloomy depths.
The game grows on you as you progress in strength and unravel a story of twists and deception worth witnessing through to the end.
A pivotal choice is given: gather the much needed ADAM to expand your power, or spare the innocent children whom harbor it inside themselves.
The iconic and imposing Big Daddy fits so well like a piece of a collage for the scenery, but once threatened becomes a challenging force.
Each Plasmid power is valuable in combat, each gun has varied purpose, and each enemy type has a defining feature.
For a game with few bosses, the pacing is perfect with regular and unexpected combat at any moment.
Crafting and choosing which skills to advance give the game its needed RPG element to keep it from drowning as a mundane shooter.
Just enough fear to not feel like a horror game, but all the while being a fun addition.
Sounds and music are immersive, for example, ocean sounds are heard in the underwater tube pathways.
Recordings have been dispersed across Rapture to develop a backstory if the player is interested.
The hacking minigame is repetitive not even considering it is done over a hundred times.
Excitement does not pick up until somewhere after you have gained stronger upgrades, or the mid-arc revelation.

As a batman fan, I was dismayed when I discovered the creative adjustments to the batman mythology. In an effort to shake things up in storytelling, tell-tale neglected to recognize the core fanbase: Fans of DC comics. Granted, I persevered and played the game all the way through, but had to ignore a plethora of the game's key flaws in order to do so.
These errors within the game consist of bugs in the cinematic framework, as well as slightly stilted character animations and overall performance issues I experienced halfway through which caused the game to crash constantly. Much patchwork was needed for this game (but that is pointing out the obvious. graphics appear to be passable... for XBOX 360. Also, Tell-tale's formula seems as if it is getting a tad bit stale and repetative.
Putting the elements I found inconvenient aside, I actually found myself enjoying different features about the game. The dialogue flowed well, and the character development was top notch. It has been a while since a video game made me care so much whether or not the characters lived or died. Above all else, it made me forget that I despised the direction they went with the story. That deserves applause in my book.
WIth all that has been said, it saddens me that I cannot recommend this game. I want to, but while I thoroughly enjoy their games, Tell-tale needs to expand their horizons. I personally say make a solid Action/RPG with the staple interactive, choices-matter content we have experienced through and through. But with the game as is, I cannot promote to everyone in good conscience, unless they are an avid Tell-Tale and DC fan.

is a card-based puzzle game where the goal is to have the most amount of points after completing a determined number of city blocks, or "columns".  Don't let the game's graphics or screenshots fool you, though - there is a lot of depth behind this game which will keep you busy for hours on end.  After logging over 40 hours (only 11 post-release, a little over a day's worth of time during the game's beta), I can definitely recommend this incredibly fun game.   Why?  Read on...
Every building in the game has a lot of detail that could be easy to miss at first glance.  The art style is consistant throughout the game, from the urban metropolis to the rolling farmlands.  When cards with the same color group are placed side-by-side, they create larger city blocks that, depending on the angle placed, will have different visuals - this is really apparent with parks and smaller houses.  Little vehicles whiz by on the streets surrounding buildings while elevated trains can be seen rolling by in the mid-late game (when placing Train Stations).  It even rains on occasion, with condensation forming at the top and bottom of the screen as rain begins to fall and everything darkens slightly - a feature that oddly feels right.  Various world landmarks are represented in-game as well, from the Empire State Building to the Sydney Opera House.
I lot of care and love went into the graphics, and it shows.
All the music in the game is very relaxing - quite fitting for a game like this where you aren't forced to rush through turns.  Sound effects that you hear while playing are determined by the types of cards you have on the board - you'll hear animals and children playing when you have lots of farm and early-game residential cards in play, whereas the sounds of a bustling city (sirens, construction, honking horns, cash registers) are heard when many industrial and commerical cards are out.
There are many audio cues throughout the game as well, based on the actions of yourself and others while playing.  For example, if you clear a row and earn more than 20 points as a result, fireworks pop in the sky over the cleared buildings.  And, of course, the sound of reshuffling cards when you've exhausted your deck is one sound you'll hear often!
Lastly, the voice-acting is surprisingly good!  The campaign dialogue that you hear between characters can be amusing at times, and cheesy during others, but at no point did I feel the dialogue was forced by anyone.  Love every bit of it!
Functionally, the card graphics themselves are to-the-point and leave little guesswork as to what the cards do - once you learn what the different colors and icons mean.  You know, at a glance, when something is bad or good for you on the board based on colors used and shading applied to the spaces.  That said, the in-game tutorial, which spans the first few campaign levels, covers all core aspects of the game, so by the time you have your first versus campaign level you're given all the details and tools needed to succeed.
That said... the campaign really ramps up the difficulty curve pretty fast, which can catch most players off-guard, giving the impression that the game can be unforgiving.  Honestly... the challenge really comes from the somewhat scripted Campaign levels (some levels have pre-placed buildings, making things quite hard at times), but mostly from Versus games, where you face off against another character (or against two, in 2v2 mode).  Every selectable character in the game - there are eight in all - have a specific focus in terms of how they're meant to be played, and have several special abilities to synergize with said gameplay.  Where things get interesting is how these characters match up in Versus mode; though each character has been play-tested scores (probably hundreds) of times over, there are some situations where one character gameplay preference can absolutely dominate another.  Like any card game, this is because of good old RNG, which combined with your character's abilities, can result in either really easy wins, or incredibly harsh losses.
Of course, the more cards you unlock, the greater the chances of your winning more often than not - and there are a lot of cards to unlock as you progress through the game.  Every match played, whether Solo or Versus, win or lose, will net you experience points.  When you gain a level, you unlock a new card for your starter deck.  In addition, you unlock a small number of cards for each character unlocked, though these cards are only accessible as you play a game (they cannot be added to your starting deck).
When you take all of this into account, there is a fair amount of replayability in the game.  The number of cards available make for interesting and complex strategies, which are only reinforced by the character abilities. Between unlocking cards and characters, versus mode, and simply aiming to see each card in play at least once (some of them look amazing), you'll be coming back for more!

This is one miracle of a videogame by just animation alone. After years in development, Cuphead is a beautiful game by style alone from beginning to end, The effort put in it clearly shows in every fight and stage you enter.
But while graphics is clearly the main selling point, gameplay is far from being bad. Based in games like Contra and Gunstar Heroes (With a few references), Cuphead is all about fighting bosses. This might not be a game for everyone due how hard some fights can become, but due how short are (1-3 minutes) and being mostly learning patterns is not that big of a hassle to keep retrying and studying the fight. Combined with upgrades you can unlock, soon enough you'll have a set perfect for your style and even counterpick for certain fights.
The game can be said is perfect and one of the best games in the recent years, but I have some nitpicks with it. The parry system while simple to learn it doesn't provide reliable invincibility frames, so you might end parrying between obstacles and still take a hit. The RNG of some bosses might put you in a rough position to avoid damage, but as said due their short duration retrying is far from a problem. What i really have problems with is the Run n Gun stages, obviously longer than the boss fights and can become a real hassle to retry over and over.
But as said, those are just nitpicks and some players might find them not big of a deal. And it shouldn't be, as Cuphead is a gem anyone should try out even if they aren't the demographic due its difficulty spikes. There's a easy mode but some of the latter stages forces you to play the default difficulty, so is recommended to enjoy the game both graphically and its learning curve.

Sorry; not my cup of tea. It's not actually got anything to do with city building, and the difficulty ramp is simply brutal - which is generally fine so long as people are aware, but games take a REALLY long time and you don't get any warning if the later terrain is stacked against your character or not.
As a card game, I'd class it as a deck builder (like Marvel's Legendary) played on a board; you start each game with a shallow pool of tier 1 cards (which you do get to customize with a limited range you unlock while slowly leveling), and you gain more - or replace them - by spending economy points from placing particular structures. You don't keep cards between games, beyond unlocking them for your starting slection/randomized pool.
There are 5/6 card colours, but most are only useful/viable to a single character so helpful unlocks are pretty far apart (they don't generally clog you up too bad though, as you get a random selection of 4 to choose from when purchasing in-game). I did not find the characters to be remotely balanced; there's a woeful techie guy who posed no resistance at all (no point scoring abilities in a point scoring game), then at the opposite end of the spectrum there's a military lady who scores points in an inverted fashion - which gives her free reign to 'poison' the entire board, which is an incredible hinderance to others and gains her massive economic advantage.
Positives
+ Unique (on PC - not sure about table-top)
+ Good game if you're looking for a challenge & can play for long sessions
+ Charming
Negatives
- Brutal diffculty
- Games are very long & not very dynamic
- Questionable balance
- Not actually anything to do with city building

Despite the look of the game, people should be aware that it is NOT a city builder in any significant way. It’s a score-based puzzler, and a fairly unforgiving one at that.
For people who like the relaxed tempo and forgiving tone of the city building genre, this is almost certainly not going to be your game.
Which should not be read as implying that Concrete Jungle is not a good game, it’s extremely well done and recommended.
Game play progresses broadly as follows.
Each block (buildings, fields, etc.) is a "card". Cards are generally divided into two types, scoring blocks (houses) and everything else (parks, industry, fields, etc.) which either buff or nerf the scoring blocks (or both buff and nerf blocks).
Cards are fed randomly forward from your deck with only the top two available to play immediately, with some extra cards visible so that you know what's coming up in advance. (Although in the early campaign levels cards and layout are fully scripted - this can be brutal when you're still not 100% confident of how the mechanics work.)
To progress forward you have to score 3 points in each row before that row is removed and a new row created at the end (later on, the points required per row increase). If you can't get 3 points in a row you lose a life in order to delete that row and let the game progress. After you've lost a certain number of lives the game ends.
The game includes a solo mode where you have to complete a certain number of rows before running out of lives. There is also a verses mode (hotseat or against the AI) where each player takes turns playing three cards each on a partially shared game board.
There are a number of additional complicating factors like buying cards and abilities, and experience, which add complexity but don't substantially change the core gameplay.
Strategy is basically about ensuring an even placement of buff and nerf cards while ensuring that the minimum score is achieved in each row so that you can continue to progress.

Morphopolis looks like a weird game. And an unique one. I can definitely tell you that it’s weird, especially in its art design and storytelling (if you can even call it that), but it’s not as unique as you would think. The game will feel very familiar to those who’ve played hidden object games before and have taken on a couple of simple puzzles in the past. And once you start playing it’s really not even that weird. You’ll see.
But Morphopolis isn’t for just anyone in my opinion. It’s short with only 5 levels, but it’s also very slow. The creature you control moves at the slowest pace possible and you unfortunately need him to navigate through the levels.
Not much is explained when you start; a simple gesture to move your mouse from one point to the other is pretty much all it will tell you to do. The rest is up to you.
I like the fact that it doesn’t hold your hand all the way through, but some of the level designs aren’t easily navigated and that results in your character getting stuck in parts of the environment or your character not knowing which way to go when you’re clearly moving your mouse to the right direction.
If we ignore these flaws the gameplay basically comes down to you clicking anywhere on the screen, hoping to unlock new objectives. New objectives can usually be found by clicking on other creatures and it then comes down to finding the requested items. Some of these items are expertly hidden and some of them are way too obvious. If you really can’t find a certain item you can always ask for a hint; a meter in the upper right corner will refill after you click on it once. After that you can request another hint if you wish. Anyway, it also requires a fair amount of backtracking, but the slow pace keeps it from being (and becoming) any fun.
Sometimes a better, deeper puzzle unlocks after finishing a certain objective. These range from a solitaire-like puzzle to solving a jigsaw puzzle. Around level 4 the difficulty picks up and I must admit I had a hard time solving the puzzles found in level 4 and 5.
A story can be interpreted but isn’t necessarily there I would say. It’s about your character growing up I think but please keep in mind that that’s my very basic interpretation of it all. The game doesn’t end with credits rolling; it just brings you back to the ‘level select’ menu. So I’m not sure if it’s even trying to tell a story.
The art direction is phenomenal. I don’t know what I would call it exactly, but it’s colorful and full of detail. It’s definitely worth a look. Sounds are pretty much non-existent and the music on the other hand is pretty good. The game runs in a window that can be resized as you see fit but I’m not sure if I would recommend it as I had issues solving the music/memory puzzle because of it (or else it’s just a bug). In any case, the graphics remain sharp, even when the window is maxed out.
Morphopolis is certainly a pretty game. But it’s not a really fun game. Even though the game isn’t terribly long I wish it ended sooner. It might be because of the (semi-)casual gameplay, it might be because of the slow pacing, I’m not really sure. One thing I am sure of however is that I would suggest people to wait for a price drop. The current price is just a tad too high for now.
