The Long Dark is a video game published and developed by Northern Vancouver Island video game company Hinterland Games Inc.  The Long Dark is a first person survival simulator. This game has a unique graphic style, while the graphics are cartoony the developers have still managed to still keep that cold dark feeling of a desolate wintry environment, the whole place feels like an abandoned fishing village in Alaska or Canada where the game takes place.  In this article we’ll be discussing the different elements, which make up The Long Dark a pretty cool (see what I did there? Laugh please.) Game.
Because the game is still in Early Access not all the game modes are open, you have the Story mode (which isn’t available till release) but is launching later in 2015 (Hinterland Games Inc.). You do have Sandbox which is open, and being updated often for more content.  The sandbox mode is basically that, you work to survive for as long as you can.  The game has achievements for surviving for up to consecutive 200 days.  As you play through the game, you’ll be working to survive constantly against the harsh environment by yourself.  You have 4 main resources you have to manage, rest, nutrition, body temp, and hydration.  While none of the individual resources are difficult to manage, trying to keep all 4 up can be, on top of that if you’re injured, find yourself trying to get to shelter before it gets too dark, or you’re being chased by a predator like a wolf or bear.
Rest:
From what I can tell the amount you run, walk and how much you carry are affected, as well as the how much you can do of all those activities.  As you grow weary you’ll see your max weight values go down.  You’ll fatigue faster, and eventually you may just pass out.
Food:
You also have to worry about your nutrition.  The more you do the more you’re going to be hungry, and you can actually starve, eventually you’ll run out of food in the houses near-by, then you’ll be struggling to find a carcass or trying to get some fishing tackle for a nearby lake.  You can cook meat if you find it, usually there will be a dead deer or wolf somewhere, and you can harvest the body for food, intestines and a carcass.  You can also do the same with fish, throughout your environment the lakes are frozen and have fishing huts, make sure when you go to a fishing hut you take some supplies for starting a fire.  Traveling on the lake is also dangerous as it’s usually patrolled by wolves.
Body Temp:
Body Temp isn’t too hard to maintain as long as you’re able to find Tinder, Fuel (IE Wood, and sticks), and a light such as a match, there is a fourth item accelerant you’ll find it in random places, usually you can find a small bottle in cupboards if you’re lucky or a gas can somewhere.  Fire is probably your best friend you’ll always need it. So make sure when you start the game you start picking up sticks, and get some newspaper.  Eventually when you find a hammer you can break down larger pieces of wood for the Reclaimed Wood items, which you’ll find to be more useful to keep the fire than the regular tree branch.
Hydration:
We all know hydration is an integral part of our lives, we need water to live, well in The Long Dark you need it to.  You’ll find yourself being parched just about everywhere you go.  Initially you can get clean water from toilets inside buildings, eventually though that water will run out.  You can melt the snow in the Winter wasteland using fire but be careful because it’ll make your fire timer run out quicker.  Then melting snow only lets you produce non-potable water which you’ll either have to burn or find some purification tablets.
Other Mechanics:
You also have other mechanics throughout The Long Dark.  You still have to maintain your physical status, and you have to careful about your time of day and how you’re spending your time.  If you’re out fishing with 4 hours of sunlight, it would be useful if you saved at least one hour to travel.  Although the graphics to the game are beautiful it still feels very dark.  You can’t see anything if you don’t have a torch or a flare, but the lit up night sky.
While the graphics are cartoony they still manage to capture a wild wintery wasteland that feels like it’s been abandoned. A lot of the area feels like people just up and left, as you seek shelter in the houses you’ll see pictures of families, you’ll see old books, and even at times you’ll find a body nestled up where the poor soul ended up succumbing to his exhaustion, while you feel bad you’re more than grateful to take the granola bar and that nice jacket he had in backpack.  The ambience will also make you curl up and remind you how lucky you are to have heating and shelter during the winter months. The sandbox is a huge sandbox map that will keep you searching around if you like to explore, plot, plan. According to the site the map spans almost “20 square km” (Hinterland Games Inc.)
You start the game off as if you’re in the middle of a silent listening halt you can see a light dusting of snow, you can feel the cold start nipping at your nose and through your clothes, and you can hear a faint howling of a wolf calling out to its pack in the distance.  The clouds are heavy, the houses around you are worn, and some have burned down since the tragic apocalyptic event.  It’s strange how just a few years ago this was a quiet little fishing village, neighbors would wave as they went to work, and hikers would come down off the trail, and now nature has shown its resiliency and taken back what was once its own.  Some of the houses are burnt down, the floor is riddled with sticks, and the cars are parked in a hurried disarray which are also covered in snow.   You move to a nearby building and enter it, it’s quiet, dark and lonely.  You can see the dust floating through the air, you can hear the wind whistling against the walls that surround you.  You start looking around for what resources you can find, you find some cokes, a couple bags of jerky, in the kitchen and maybe start a fire in the fireplace in the living room.  You decide to check up stairs and notice an odd figure curled up against the wall, it’s a body, you loo t it and find some new boots and some condensed milk.
You still have some time till sunset and you may still need some more firewood took what perishables you have and make some tea to warm up.  Stepping outside you notice some stick, and while they don’t last very long it still makes good for emergency fuel and good for starting you initial fire.  You’re starting to get cold, and notice something moving along.  It’s a wolf and it’s charging at you.  Turning and running back to the house you just left you make it to the door when the wolf gets you, you’re able to fight it off and you do but not without getting bitten.  You make your way inside and up to the bedroom into a bathroom, looking around you get lucky and find a bandage, and some painkillers.  Applying the bandage you’re still susceptible to infection but you don’t have any antibiotics to heal, you go back down stairs eat some of what you won and cook some spare rabbit’s meat you found.  Finding that you’re parched and freezing you make some tea and drink some water, eat your dinner and sleep for 12 hours while you let yourself heal and do it all over again the next day.
So far the time I’ve spent playing it I’ve had fun, it’s a challenge to maintain yourself and a cold reminder of how lonely things can feel in a tragic event, but also a reminder of how strong some people's drive will take them.  I don’t see myself completing and exploring the content anytime soon, not out of boredom but simply because it feels like there’s so much to see, and those damn wolves keep chasing me.  Thank you for reading and I hope I gave you a little taste how the game looks feels, and plays.

Do you like murdering lots of things? Do you like beautiful dark fantasy settings? Are you a fan of simple yet skillful melee combat with a variety of weapons with some guns/bows/magic thrown in to top it all off? Need a 4 player co-op game to play with your mates? Then this game may well be for you.
Pros
Visceral melee and ranged combat, every hit feels satisfying.
A wide variety of weapons, melee and ranged, that keeps slaughtering ratmen fresh.
I'll be honest, before this game I'd never even heard of Warhammer Fantasy, but this game is a gorgeous realization of it. The art style and levels are a delight to behold and there's a good amount of variety between levels.
There's a respectable amount of levels in the base game and the DLC maps keep things fresh if you are craving more.
On the subject of DLC, the game has received a number of significant free updates as well as paid map packs that are well worth the value in my opinion. You can't queue for the DLC maps if you don't own them, but if you have a friend that has them you can play on them and receive the map-specific weapon drops for free.
The combat is skillful and has a good range of difficulties to challenge experienced players.
A robust crafting system to help you improve your arsenal and a set of special hats/weapons for experienced players to show off with.
Knowledge of a level pays off with items that can improve your loot and or even increase the difficulty of the map if you want a proper challenge.
Charming characters and amusing party banter. Miss a bomb throw? Your companions aren't likely to let you live it down.
Cons
With the game being melee-focused, a bad internet connection can lead to a bad experience, i.e. rats hitting you from far away, blocks not registering etc.
Item drops at the end of missions are semi-random, so it's possible to go on dry streaks of the stuff you want. This is mitigated with the crafting system, however.
The game has a somewhat small player base, so doing specific non-contract missions if you don't have a 3 or 4 man group can occasionally be difficult. This is more true on the highest difficulties. Overall though the playerbase is more than large enough to enjoy the whole game solo.
The game is a very fun and satisfying experience and I highly recommend it.

Sunless Sea is a roguelike spinoff of Fallen London, a choose-your-own-adventure browser game. In the world of Sunless Sea, London has been dragged down a mile into the earth in a rather vague event. Rather than being destroyed, it was deposited into a vast underground sea, the Unterzee. You are the captain of one of the many steamers that brave the Zee's dark reaches, searching for success.
LIKES:
VERY unique world that's a joy to explore and experience.
Very atmospheric. From dark waters to the steady dripping of liquid from the cavern roof, much effort is put into making the experience authentic.
Excellent writing.
GRIPES:
Very grind heavy. To get anywhere in the game one would need to be lucky at the random events or grind milk runs to get enough money to do anything. Things cost a lot in the Unterzee and few ports have shops. Fewer still offer fuel and food.
Rather slow paced. The starter ship is very slow and fuel inefficient and it can take a long time to gather up enough resources to afford a better engine.
VERDICT:
If you're a fan of roguelikes, enjoy exploring unique worlds, and don't mind grinding Sunless Sea is a pretty safe buy.

BioShock 1 was an entertaining game.  There were plenty of startling scares and funny tidbits, but most importantly, there was a great storyline.  There's also more to do than just run from point A to B all the time - security cameras and turrets can be "hacked" with a pipe-flow tile mini-game, you can collect parts to craft items such as bullets and auto-hack tools, take photos of the bad guys to perform 'research', unlocking damage bonuses and abilities (plasmids).  It's almost open world, but not quite since the 'world' is a series of buildings and tubes connecting them. You can explore a lot of non-important areas for bonus loot and cassette players, which reveal more of the storyline.  I must have re-started this game from scratch a dozen times since it came out, but I finally finished it up recently, and even the ending (there are multiple, I believe) was worth seeing.  Now I can finally play BioShock 2 without feeling like I skipped something crucial!

When you want to build an ideallic city that is unreachable and truly isolated from corruption, you don't have a lot of choices. Andrew Ryan chose to build his on the bottom of the ocean. However his perfect city has fallen to decay. You, the silent and nameless protagonist, venture into the forgotten city of Rapture to find out its mysteries and why it's come to be like this.
Right off the start you're not given a lot of information. Is this bad? Not really. I felt myself sucked into the story rather quickly. There's a simple goal you're given and you have to go do it. You are armed with various weapons that you acquire in a nice curve and 'plasmids', injections of a material that rewrites your genetic coding. These plasmids act like magic powers, like for example, shooting lightning from your fingers or incinerating stuff on your command.
Exploration of the lost city of Rapture is always rewarded and very necessary. There's a harsh cap on every ammo, first aid kit, even money so you are never truly comfortable and overstacked. This seems unfair but it serves to keep you desperate which is, in fact, what horror games should do. Unlike, for example, Fallout (where you eventually give up scavenging because the weight of all that ammo is just too much.) Fans of horror will probably not be disappointed as the atmosphere of Rapture is fantastically creepy and unsettling.
Now off to the bad parts. First off, the audio cut the second I started the game and had to exit to Google it, eventually having it to run on Vista compatibility mode and even then I had occasional audio stutters. Second, and BY FAR THE MOST ANNOYING; whenever anyone talks, the subtitles fade prematurely. Each. And. Every. Time. And you do need those subtitles, the voices tend to be drowned under gunfire. It became so annoying everytime I got a message from someone, I would pause the game and instead read it from the menu log. This is a big flaw because Rapture's past is told via audiologs which you find scattered through the place. If you can't hear these, you are missing out on 50% of the game. Third of all, combat is fast and very panicy. Enemies immediately attack upon seeing you, not giving you even 0,5 seconds of reaction time.
Then there's the controls sometimes just bugging up, wanting to hit X to hack something and instead it doesn't target right and spills one of your precious EVE hypo's. Very annoying as you are so undersupplied anyway. And even though I thought I was a great scavenger, I apparently missed like half of the plasmids available. Last but certainly not least: the amount of frustration I got from hacking. Hacking is done by laying a kind of pipeline-tilepuzzle and it is -very- common for you to need to change the very first tile, or else being boxed in by exploding tiles that hurt you in game. You'll see what I mean.
So in conclusion, I tend to a slightly more negative judgment of the whole game. By far I don't regret playing it, it still holds up very well even today. Rapture is still a very intriguing story, brilliantly done and really creepy... but also carries with it a lot of frustration over controls and unfair hacking and buggyness. It was worth the effort, in the end it was truly a classic, but it definitely could've been better.
The Good: Horror from atmosphere, not just creepy monsters and jumpscares. Rapture a very unique and greatly thought out place for a horror game. The whole concept just rocks.
The Bad: Subtitles. Audio. Combat could've been a little slower in my opinion (but maybe that's a taste thing). Went on a bit too long. Excluding the additional content, the game lasts for about 8 and 1/2 hours. The game itself I really enjoyed, the story line was good and the voice acting was on point. The controversial nature of the story I enjoyed and the art work lived up to Telltales reputable standards.
There were a few factors that detracted from the good work put into it. Formally, that it didn't flow like a finished game. It would jitter in parts, noticable enough to take away from being immersed in the game and the cut-scenes between episodes were somewhat disjointed from one shot to the next, it even included parts, that due to my choices, shouldn't have been in there. Occasionally, although admittedly not often, the voices and the lip movement didn't match up but for the most part the two married up pretty well.
All in all, I think TT games should give it a few patches, to sort out some of the bugs/kinks but it's a good game, IMO of course. All you have to decide now is does the game duration (8.5 hours) and the bugs warrant the price tag. For me, it was a yes.

I wanted very badly to love this game. The art and music are pitch perfect. Controls are responsive. Visually and aurally, this game exceeds the hype.
Gameplay on the other hand...  A challenging game was promised. What we got was packed with artificial difficulty far greater than anything the 80s or 90s threw at gamers. There's a lot going on onscreen most of the time. There's so much coming toward you that it's just arbitrary that the greatest danger in many fights is stuff coming from offscreen behind you completely out of nowhere. And you will lose quite enough of your meager hit points from screwing up without the game deciding it has to steal them for no reason too. If old-school hard simply means cheap, then a return to it is nothing to celebrate.
When you are lucky and manage to avoid the cheap shots, the boss fights are over usually in under 2 minutes. Once you account for all the time wasted repeating the same level 27 times, there's actually just not that much content. Certainly not enough for finally completing a level to feel like an accomplishment.

It's hard to describe Concrete Jungle. This game is a truly beautiful card game with a dash of city builder that makes gameplay both simple and complicated at the same time.
The gameplay is simple enough. Your goal is to get the total value in each column to tally up to the required target until you've eliminated all columns on the board by setting down different types of cards (buildings) that can either raise or lower your total for a column. What ends up making the game so complicated (and so fun) is that it forces you to strategize how each card you place now might affect your chances of clearing a column in the next turn or many turns into the future. And so, this simple game becomes really complicated really quickly.
The art and the music are perfect and the gameplay is very solidly built. You can clearly see the developer has spent a lot of time balancing out the cards and creating a tutorial that goes a long way to make sure you have every advantage without completely holding your hand. This is one of those games that you sit down to play for a few minutes only to continually find yourself playing "just one more!"

Cole Jeffries, a.k.a, Cole Powered should be held up as the model of "Kickstarters done right." He asked for the most modest of sums. A trifling £3,000 to cover art, asset, voice and pre-production costs for the spiritual successor to the fairly successful mobile game Megacity. He had a prototype ready to release to backers, so anyone who pitched in would get to tinker with the core gameplay loop and see what was on offer, and as far as tiers go, this was impulse backing territory. In the end he got over £13,000 from a core of dedicated fans of all shapes and sizes, enough to substantially expand the game, furnish it with various flourishes, but at the same time he stuck rigidly to his project goal. To make Concrete Jungle happen.
What came out of that £13,000 was glory. A simple, yet absolutely devious and devillish game that epitomises the concept of "Simple to grasp, hard to master", there's an awful lot of high level play, especially when you get into the versus mode (oh the shennanigans you can pull there). But more on that below. Over the course of the kickstarter, Cole communicated clearly, posted progress reports in a timely manner, ensured that fresh betas were made available, so backers could provide feedback, and a lot of suggestions were folded into the final product.
Megacity was a really, really good mobile game. It could easily swallow hours of your life, and there's an awful lot of love for it, but there was a sense that some strategies could eventually allow you to keep ahead (at least to some extent) for quite a period of time. With Concrete Jungle, Cole Powered has had the opportunity to revisit the core formula of megacity, and then take it apart, looking at the concept of deck building and turn it into a fully fledged card game a-la Ascension, Chronicle of the Godslayer, where you start with a set of starter cards, and as your city evolves, you purchase progressively higher level cards which permit more advanced strategies and combos.
In addition to this deckbuilding concept, Cole also introduces the concept of "One shot" cards, disposable cards which when used, are destroyed and no longer recycled within your deck, forcing you to make hard decisions with each of your card purchases, because powerful cards are often "one shots", you're forced to decide between building an expanded pool of weaker, but more stable cards, or buying those powerful one shots, and then falling back on your base cards when they're spent.
As an alteration to the core game mechanic, it's genius, it instantly turns the deckbuilding into something that fosters a level of strategy and planning, and your purchases become the material of much headscratching as a purchase early on may have repercussions some fifty or even eighty turns down the line. You're no longer reliant on the old mobile strategies that pervaded megacity because
.
On top of this is the cast of characters, all voice acted and in the campaign, brilliantly narrated, with dry british humour interspersed with some PG-13 rated jokes that even in the early stage got a wide grin from this tiger. Cole has managed to create a story that whilst it's no Lord of the Rings, it'll keep you amused as you work your way through, unlocking the various characters and winding your way through a set of maps that have their own unique challenges and trials. Puzzles that will test your brain to breaking point.
Even when you've finished those, custom games await, and versus mode, where you can play the AI or even other real people in a battle to see who really is the king of the jungle. The gameplay in the Versus may prove yet to be Concrete Jungles' finest moments, the level of potential chicanery and backstabbing that you can achieve by clever use of buildings that have negative effects is -beautiful-, provoking strategies that normally would otherwise not even be considered.
It's been a long time since I've used this word on the end of a review. But for Concrete Jungle, I have no other word I can use for it. I absolutely insist people try it out, and I entirely recommend to any puzzle gamer, or strategy buff, that they immediately make space in their gaming budget, and make a few good evenings with a hot drink ready. This game deserves your time, your attention, and your brain.

This is probably one of the most unique games I've ever played. The first half or so feels almost like a kind of interactive documentary, enjoyable and interesting if not challenging in the traditional kind of way for games. The second half is where most of the emotional gut punches come through, and they left me feeling incredibly uncomfortable. Like when you're stuck in a room with people having a very personal argument. But in a good way since it was pulled off so well! It all comes across as uncomfortably personal.
This is the kind of game that I think you'll be able to tell right off the bat if you'll enjoy it. Yes, it is a walking simulator, and yes you are technically just listening to a guy talk over things for an hour and half. The writing, the narration, and the environment are what really brings lets this story shine. The reason you play this is for the story.
As a small sidenote, I don't feel any trouble in calling this a game though, because it really only works as well as it does because it IS a game. The narrative uses it's medium very well

First game I'm reviewing, so here goes.
I really want to like this game. I played a decent number of hours, did several restarts, and basically won the game, but I just can't bring myself to actually finish it.
The problem? There's not actually that much *game* in this game.
The visuals are fantasitc, the sound and music are perfect, the story is top-notch. But in terms of actual gameplay, you eventually realise that it's sorely lacking.
Sunless Sea basically has you going around a fictional world, completing various quests, in order to ultimately accomplish your life goal, one of several choices you make at the start of the game. The concept is great, and it definitely works as far as the story and pitch are concerned.
Where the game falls flat is when you make it through the rather tough early and mid game.
In the game, there are basically three things you can do - you can fight other ships and sea monsters, you can trade goods at different ports, and you can visit ports and accomplish story objectives through a "choose your own adventure" type interface.
The fighting is done through a real-time broadside combat, where you're sailing around trying to take potshots at the other ships or monsters. The problem with the combat though, is that for the easier ships, it's dead easy - you just circle around behind them and then keep either circling with them, or reversing to stay behind them while they try to turn. On the other hand, against the monsters, it's almost impossible, since they move way faster than you, and can circle and hit you before *you* can turn. If you do take damage, the game is very punishing - ships hit hard, and you lose crew members and eventually ship speed, which is devastating considering how hard money is to get. Overall, the combat implementation is quite weak.
On the trading front, you realise that it is absolutely not profitable at all. Most ports barely offer decent deals - do a bit of google searching to see "profitable" trade routes, and you realise that most of them yield 3-5 credits per shipment of the goods, which is absolutely nothing. This is especially compounded when you realise that you can basically get unlimited money once you make it to the surface, by just clicking a few buttons over and over.
What that reduces the game to, is essentially a slow grind through the early quests until you get enough for the big merchant ship, and then some repetitive clicking until you get as much money as you want. Then once that's done, you're off sailing between ports and just clicking reading options.
Overall I can't recommend this game. I really want to, but it's just not got enough actual gameplay to be worth it. I just wish I had realised that before putting so much time into the game.

I've been a founder of this game since the very beginning of DD2.
I really loved the first Dungeon Defender and Dungeon Defender II has addressed the biggest issue – anti-cheat, by making it server side only.
I've never regretted getting the founders' pack and big packs of gems (in game premium currency) as a support to make this game better.
And now it's free to play I see no reason for any hero/tower defence lovers out there to give this a try!
Alright I will get to the point of my positive opinions about this game:
•	NOT pay to win, you use premium currencies on costumes, sure you can pay to skip by unlocking heroes early and buy some skill gem shard packs to try your random luck on getting some powerful skill modifications early, but why would you want to do that? It’s super expansive and the fun of the game is the progression of getting the best things yourself!
•	Game is pretty and smooth with a cartoony look
•	You can switch to any classes out of combat and each different class offers you a unique experience.
•	They’ve now added stories and cinematics for the campaign!
•	This game is a hero and tower defence game, trying to beat the game with just your hero or tower alone will be very difficult to impossible, you need the best of both worlds!
•	There is a good amount of challenging game play ahead, took me about 3-4 weeks to get to end game gear. Hey it’s free to play what are you complaining 😊
Now the not so good part, or what I wish to see in the future:
•	Where is the real end game?
There is no real challenge after you get a full set of chaos 7 legendary gear for all your characters, and it really doesn’t take long once you deck your best tower defence hero with it.  I just recently logged back on after few months of out of content and see a big update with the incursion chaos. But after unlocking the special weapons they didn’t give me the real “WOW”, instead I feel my old gear is still better for the only option offered for the class. Incursion chaos need to offer more weapons maybe even set gear for the specific class at different chaos levels. Make it harder, make it that you need friends or some pubs to help you defeat it, add a gear score requirement to enter higher tiers so you don’t get under geared leechers. I admit that beating chaos 7 incursions is hard solo as there are just too many things to juggle, but I think it will be a free farm as soon as I invite my other chaos 7 friend. Even if I beat the hardest incursion, what “Wow” rewards do I get? what do I do next? Grind character levels so I have more points to spend on making myself even more powerful? Why would I do that I got nothing that I can’t really beat if I really try.
I’m really hoping to see something I can work towards to at end game. Here are some ideas:
	Endless waves that offers special reward such as a new currency to be used to purchase set bonus gear or really powerful weapons to help reaching higher tier Endless waves, maybe at certain waves like 50, 100 we get titles, special skins, more goodies!
	Where are the damage combos from DD1? The current combo are just too weak to be bothered, I will just use flame aura it beats everything it’s cheap , huge range, hits both air and land why combo?
	Skill Shard just simply take too much space , not stackable and hard to differentiate, I have almost 4 bags of shards, there is no proper sort function that can put a class specific gem, type of skill shards into the right place. And I have duplicates that I can’t easily identify. I get it that once you upgrade the skill shards it become a different item, then give us an unlimited skill shard bag or have a new grouping function built in , so once you click on a stacked skill shard it will pop up a menu ask you which one you’d like to choose from (almost like a sub inventory for each shard). As time goes you add more classes and shards I don’t think there will be enough inventory space to store them and sorting them out and find duplicates ,,, don’t even go there..
	Pets, not strong enough, not worth working towards to, not something that you ever rely on other than have an extra stun, pets do too little damage to be useful in general, any big aoe burse comes with a cost of long as cooldown. The most useful I find is a cat that can stun, so you don’t get disabled by the assassins. I’d like to see them being more useful, at the moment rarity also means nothing for pets, doesn’t matter if it’s green or legendary, only the looks can be different.
	I want to also say something about the 2 new classes that were added, I’m sorry but, out of ideas? Half the abilities or towers or more are the same as existing class, it’s just a female version of the existing, skill shard modification are just too minimal to make them worthwhile, maybe once I max out the medals I will buy them but I don’t see the point. I own every other class that just don’t see any uniqueness for these 2 new classes for me to be interested.
•	Where is the promotion to multiplayer?
Most of the game is heavily Solo based, because multiplayer just don’t give us the incentives to do so. Mobs have more health, hard to kill and beat the mission with the existing towers, we don’t get more loot nor xp because there are more players. And there is no level/gear restriction for those to join the chaos trials, so why would I want to hasten the other players just for them to suffer the same “no end game” feeling I have. Which is why I always play private games. Look at the public games available, there is barely any chaos games going that I want to be part of.
Conclusion: I still love this game, I come back and play DD2 and always hope for a bit of surprise with the new contents / changes they’ve added. I’ve seen how much it has changed since the beginning of time and I can see the DD2 team haven’t given up on making it better. And I recommend everyone to give it a try.

Not inculding the massive ammounts of secrets and extra stuff to look at in the menus (including "the game of life" and other retro computer things), the game basically focuses on the player who is trying to eliminate all of the "red dudes" in each level using a variety of melee and ranged weapons. The main gimmick is that the level (including enemies and flying objects) only move at the same speed the player is moving at. The game is actually extremely fast-paced, which can be seen in the replays after a level, but what would be extreme difficulty and a need for inhuman reflexes is solved by the slowing mechanic, making you seem like a ♥♥♥♥ing ninja at the normal speed (so much so that they have a website just for uploading replays).

I highly, highly recommend this game to anyone. It's so close to being the most perfect game I have ever played. The gameplay, which is the most important aspect, is wonderful. The story is wonderful and well written, I couldn't find any plotholes either, and the characters are typically quite likable, or hateable depending on who it is. Andrew Ryan is probably one of my favourite antagonists in any video game. He's clever, he's witty, he's smart. Great character, he. And the atmosphere of Rapture is just so perfect. An underwater city in 1960 and this game captures that perfectly. The combination of the surroundings and what you see out the window and the audio and the insane ramblings of splicers just make the atmosphere immersive and creepy and great.
However, every game has its flaws and this has a few that really stand out to me. Hacking is far too easy and way too boring. It can be panicky at times, but otherwise it's just dull. Take pipes and make the water go here. Whoop-dee-doo. *yawn* Another thing I noticed about this game is how unoriginal it is. Yeah, it is unoriginal. You see, there was this game a long time ago that is a lot like BioShock. It was released in 1999 and it's even on Steam. It's called System Shock 2 and it is exactly the same as BioShock in almost every single way. However, System Shock 2 is more complex than BioShock so you can actually argue that BioShock is actually a dumbed down version of System Shock 2. Also I thought the ending was pretty disappointing and the boss fight was way too easy. And the Vita Chambers are a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥and feel like your mother holding yor hand through the whole game and saying "i told you to be more careful"
Despite all that, BioShock is a great game and is definitely something different compared to modern shooters. If you have a PC, Ps3, or Xbox 360, this is a definite must buy. It is worth the $20, and I would have paid it if I had the money, but fortunately I have a wonderful girlfriend who bought this for me during the Steam Summer sale with BioShock 2 and Infinite when it was only $10.29 for all three. Concrete Jungle is the type of game that you would get if you combined a city builder game like Sim City with a deck building card game.
In Concrete Jungle you play as a city planner that has to build up the city of Caribou City. You get a deck of cards which you use to place buildings and other structures in the city. You place point collecting buildings and use other buildings' special abilities to build up the points that the building ends up scoring. Your objective is to score as many points as possible in each row since you need to score a certain number of points in each row in order to clear that row and open up a new row which you can place building on.
The deck building comes into play since you will earn economic points which can be used to purchase special abilities and cards that you can add to your deck.
What I liked most about Concrete Jungle is that the game is easy to play but also allows for a lot of strategy. The game takes a while to adjust to but once you get a hang of it, you shouldn't have too much trouble with it anymore. You really need to plan out your moves though since a lot of the cards can be used to build combos that score a lot of points which help you clear levels.
The game has two main modes. I personally preferred the "solo" mode where you build the city by yourself. The game also includes a "competitive" mode where two players build on the same plot of land which requires an additional level of strategy as you try to build up your points while hindering your opponent.
At this time I have played the game for over seven hours and have not yet completed the campaign. I would guess that the campaign is at least ten hours. The story is pretty interesting and the graphics in the game are fantastic.
Concrete Jungle will not be for everyone. If the game's concept doesn't seem interesting to you, you probably won't like the game. If you have any interest in the game though I think you will really enjoy the game. I never thought I would have so much fun with city planning.
Note: I received a free review copy from the developer.

A good story makes or breaks any game. The Blackwell games are a perfect example. There is no need for fancy graphics or building-sized guns. As a player I only need a desire to support the main character(s), save the world, solve a mystery, 'read' the story till the end.
The Blackwell games tell a great story, which is basically about a young woman and a ghost, who help people realize they have died and have to move on. The playable pre-title sequence makes the games resemble a movie series, but there is no time for the player to sit back and relax. This involves a lot of clicking and pointing. The main characters have to find the cause of death. For clues they have to track people online (in game) and visit dorm rooms and churches, homes and offices, derelict buildings and construction sites. They have to connect the right items and names to get the right answers to their questions.
I played and loved the first four games when they were only available through Adventure Game Studio, the engine used for these games. When they became available through Steam, I bought the whole series, including the fifth game, replayed them all and loved them even more. They are not perfect. It's annoying to hear the characters say there is no connection between two items, when there obviously is. But overall, the Blackwell series are a must-play for anybody who enjoys a good story in an old-school game.
And just to make this clear, the graphics might not be smooth or fancy, but still are a job well done, while the voice-acting is just great.

The Beginners Guide is unique, not only as a concept but through the commentary it offers on many elements within the videogame industry. If you’re looking for a powerful narrative experience with a lot to say, The Beginners Guide is a must, but to many others this will be a pretentious, difficult experience.
The Beginners Guide is the latest creation of Davey Wreden, the man behind The Stanley Parable. The Beginners Guide draws a lot from The Stanley Parable, including the meta interpretation of games, a first person experience through an enclosed environment, and an omniscient narrator. Unlike Stanley however, Guide is a very linear experience which directly funnels the player through a series of random and abstract environments. All the while, Wreden’s assured voice permeates through the experience, explaining what you are ‘playing’ and where it derives from. Ultimately the story told is about a man simply called Coda, and how making short games was an outlet for him to escape from his anxiety and depression.
Its a fascinating way to tell a story, and touches on many powerful emotional beats and twists. Not only that, but the story comments on recurring ideas about videogames themselves – the relationship between player and designer, the interpretation of games and the experience of the player itself. Its very thoughtful and well-told, although I would criticise the end by being a bit too clear-cut. Personally I think having a more ambiguous ending would have been better for the experience of the player, simply as it would force them to piece it all together. Simply put, Guide does sometimes rely too heavily on showing rather than telling, which is not a particularly stellar storytelling technique.
The entire game also drips with gorgeous design and music. The little creations you go through are varied and vast, but still tightly constructed and the music along with Wreden’s voice leads to a palpable atmosphere of discovery and emotion. However, your enjoyment of the game doesn't rely on the story or the atmosphere. Its dependant on your expectations – what you expect the game to be, and what you hope to take away from that experience. Experience is probably a better word for The Beginners Guide than game. At only 90 minutes long, this is more of a lightly interactive movie, and if you’re hoping for anything less you’re going to be disappointed - but if you are looking for a purely well-told story, powerful emotional resonance and commentary on interesting issues I cannot recommend this game highly enough.
Narrative-Driven: Must-play
Indie Gamers: Must-play
Casual Gamers: Meh
Harcore Gamers: Recommended

If you like to city builders, strategy and card games, this is, unquestionably, the game for you. Even if you don’t like them, you’ll find something to love in this game, whether you’re a hardcore gamer, a regular gamer, or even just a casual gamer.
Without any further delay, I present to you my review of Concrete Jungle.
Starting with an interesting concept, Concrete Jungle (CJ) starts captivating its players with its pleasing looks. Those (small) few that didn’t find CJ’s looks to be enough, will, undoubtedly find its gameplay incredibly entertaining. Those brave enough to start with the tutorial/campaign might feel some extra difficulty, but fret not, as the game is quite intuitive. The more points, the better!
The objective is pretty simple (for the vs mode): whoever has the most points at the end of the game wins. Those points are obtained by placing point-holding cards and providing them with points, whether by using plus-points buildings, or by increasing the block size therefor gaining bonus points. Points are calculated after the first column is either full or one of the players has reached the goal for that column.
Obviously, not every player is the same, so the strategy is up to them. From an aggressive stance, to a more defensive one, or even a strategy to disrupt your opponent, there’s a number of ways to defeat your opponents, whether by crushing them, or by simply slightly outscoring them. There’s also the possibility of the strategy backfiring, due to a bad deck choice, or even because the opponent’s deck/strategy was a good counter to yours.
There’s also the solo mode, which consists of reaching the column goals until the map finishes.
Aside from the cards, there’s also a Card Shop and a Skills tab, where you can use your purchase points, as well as an expenditure bar, which will make the column goals go up once you fill the bar.
The campaign is filled with a entertainment, from both the dialogue and the characters. It’s also quite challenging, so you must bring your A game, or gain some more experience. If those aren’t enough, don’t worry, the more you play, the more cards will be made available.
Truthfully, I could only find one real “Con”.
. I found myself speechless when I started writing this review, as I didn’t know how to start it. Hopefully I’ve done justice to it. It’s indeed a fantastic game, my favorite card game without a question. It’s as addictive as it is entertaining.

Dear Coda,
I'm terrified that I've misjudged your work, seeing it through this compilation. So here goes:
I'm terrified how I view this work has been clouded by its presentation. People are always trying to rationalize, to understand, what they cannot understand.
What they cannot feel.
I'll be open-I've done that plenty myself, but I always find myself hating myself for it. And hated people even more when I was the receiving end.
So I'm not going to try. For once in my life, I promise I'll force myself to not ask that always-asked question: Why? How? What is wrong, do they even know? No. I won't ask that. Not of you. Not after I've seen this. Because I know the answer isn't for me to know.
It's more important to me to not ask, "Why?" It matters more that I say that you're not alone. You're not the only one.
You're not the only one who was content as they were, only to be poisoned by those who thought they were right. Thought you could benefit.
Poisoned by those who fail to see that people can be happy living differently.
I don't know how to keep going on with what I'm trying to say here. It's one of those things of mine that people refuse to accept. They want to see what's churning in my brain when I can't share it. Sometimes won't share it. So I'll end here. Based on what I've seen, that's what you want isn't it? But that's what I'm terrified I've misjudged. Is that what you want? No way out? It's okay, I won't judge, 'cause I've been there. Still am.
I have no idea if you'll ever see this, or if you'll read it if you do. After all, I am just some guy writing a review of a set of works you never wanted shared. But if you do, just know that if you ever need someone who might look at your work without criticizing the mind behind it, there's someone in the next prison over.
I mangled that ending didn't I? You get the general idea, though, right?
Sincerely,
T

As an avid enthusiast of wilderness travel and survival skills, I have been daydreaming of a PC game like The Long Dark for quite a while.
For me the two aspects of a solo wilderness experience that this game nails are:
-Long periods of serenity interrupted by moments of great intensity
-Important decisions disguised as mundane events
For example, you are three days in to your survival situation and you have been lucky enough to find a beat-up old rifle and three rounds with which to load it. You are still avoiding wolves when you see them, because who knows if you will find more ammo?  You crest a blind hill to hear growling and then barking as a wolf is staring you in the face. It can sense that you are tired and limping due a sprained ankle. It charges. You aim your rifle and wait until the last moment, knowing that you only have one shot before it is on you. You fire and the echo of the shot rings out across the valley...You may not fire the rifle again for a week, but those moments of intensity are unreal.
Another example; It is late in the day and you are returning to your home base after checking your snares for rabbits and picking up a bit of firewood.  The wind is picking up and you are chilly.  You come across the corpse of a recently downed deer. You know you have seen a bear around here before but the hide from that deer -not to mention the meat- could be a huge boon later on. There will be no dialogue box promting you, it is up to you to recognize the importance of the decision you are making and evaluate the risks and rewards for yourself.
The game is still in early access at the moment, but is very stable and has lots of content.
The art style is gorgeous and the ambient sounds of the wilderness are incredibly immersive.
If you have been thinking about it, get it!

I'm just going to start out by saying this, I bloody love this game.
Sunless Sea is a beautiful roguelike set in the world of Fallen London (which is actually a free, browser based story game with not to dissimiliar mechanics to mafia wars on facebook but with incredible stories and tales to follow) where an entity merely known as the bazaar exchanged london with old queen Vic, circa 1861, in return for her husbands mortal soul. This results in london being dragged down to the Unterzee, a world where the rules are only known by those in power and those in power really like keeping it that way.
Enough background, on to the game (i just think the backstory is one the most facinating and unique parts of the game).
Gameplay wise you are in control of a vessel (which at later stages you can trade in for a better one) with which you must explore the Unterzee. The ship requires fuel for the engine and lamp (as without a sun the Unterzee is pitch black) and supplies for your crew. You also need to manage your crews terror as it can negatively effect several aspects and also result in your crew either commiting suicide, going mad and killing other crew members or worse yet killing you for being such a bad captain. Run out of fuel you can wait for rescue until your supplies run out but as the game so aptly says without fuel your ship is just a mishapen house on water. Run out of supplies and, well, cannabilism is always a better choice than starvation for most. If you do die (and trust me you will as you learn the ropes and do's and don't's) there is this really unique system where you can decide what you inherit form the previous captain picking from rival, correspondant, pupil, shipmate or salvager each offering you particular bonuses. You can also choose a past or choose not to have one and reveal it later (again each decision really ripples outward as you can simultaneously limit and expand what you can do just by devoting yourself on a particular path).
There are many, many beautiful and unique places to visit but the ones really worth seeing are the ones beyond the local cluster of islands that surround london as these are technically protectorates of london and so they don't have much of the weird and whacky variety. In these places are equally cool story lines that just really grip the imagination with beautiful written passages and stories. As for the Zee itself, well, beautiful and terrifying really come to mind and so much fun to explore.

Not inculding the massive ammounts of secrets and extra stuff to look at in the menus (including "the game of life" and other retro computer things), the game basically focuses on the player who is trying to eliminate all of the "red dudes" in each level using a variety of melee and ranged weapons. The main gimmick is that the level (including enemies and flying objects) only move at the same speed the player is moving at. The game is actually extremely fast-paced, which can be seen in the replays after a level, but what would be extreme difficulty and a need for inhuman reflexes is solved by the slowing mechanic, making you seem like a ♥♥♥♥ing ninja at the normal speed (so much so that they have a website just for uploading replays).

A fun little vertical shooter/danmaku, which tries a bit too hard to be Touhou. I've experienced some framerate issues a few times, but a quick restart of the game solves it. Anyway, on to the review!
The pixel art graphics are nice and colorful, the patterns look nice and the character sprites, while nothing extraordinary, are nice as well. The menu is quite bland and generic and could've done better with some better fonts and a menu system that looks, well, like anything more than some text on an animated background.
On the audio front, the chiptune music fits the game very well. I especially loved the tracks on levels 3 and 5 along with a lot of boss/character themes. Ingame audio effects are simple, unobrtusive and don't get in the way much. Could be better, but could be worse.
The story... Eh, let's just skip this one, as there is something resembling a story in there, but let's not kid ourselves, these kinds of games are rarely played for the story.
Finally, the characters. Nothing all that special here either, to be honest. The characters are generally flat-ish and are in there to fill the minimal role of level intro, pre-bossfight and level outro dialog participants. The dialogs are quirky at best and cringeworthy at worst. I'm looking at you, end bosses and "Dev." On the matter of Dev, that character is a brilliant trainwreck. Brilliant, as his mode of attacking is rather fresh, and a trainwreck because of his dialogue and because how annoying it is in practice to play as him. The secret character is nice and for the hardcore players, a nice challenge, I think. Would've loved more, if we got the first one of the bosses instead.
Overall, this game is rough at some points, but then again, some like it rough. It is also FREE, by the way, and that is a fact I had to remind myself while writing this review. This game would certainly deserve a solid $10 price tag or similar. If you're a fan of the genre, you're gonna enjoy it a bunch, and if you haven't played a danmaku game before, give it a go, you won't regret it.

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

Telltales take on Batman has been refreshing for me personally, more than anything. Especially after dedicatedly playing all the Arkham games by Rocksteady, being Batman for all that time beating up thugs and hiding around in vents it feels good to finally get to be the man behind the cowl that is Bruce Wayne. Yes, this series is more about Bruce Wayne than Batman and don't let the title tell you otherwise. Some might go "Oh! but Bruce Wayne's boring we want Bats" but trust me you will enjoy projecting your image of Bruce onto the game Bruce and that makes you feel more Batman like than any other game ever has.
I say 'project your version of Bruce' because you don't completely replace Bruce's inherent characteristics because of the way game let's you make decisions for him, but he still does them in his own flare and that's just the right amount, I think.
The reason why I feel it makes you feel more like Batman is because you make the mistakes and correct decisions for Bruce Wayne you are essentially facing the consequences of those choices as someone who leads a double life as a Vigilante.
I've not played other popular Telltale games yet (Just baught The Walking Dead though, it's next up in my playthrough list). But I definitely like the formula of the characters dealing with the consequences of your decisions and since the creators have most of the control on the camera angles and the cinematics the big moments in the story really stand out.

I bought this game thinking it was a light version of a city builder like for example Children of the Nile. Unfortunately, it seems to be VERY light, with hardly any features at all. You'll see everything the game has to offer in one hour or so. And what there is isn't very interesting.
The basics of the game is that you construct buildings, assign a number of workers to those buildings, and they will produce resources for you. Everything is more or less automated and once you assign workers and hire some carriers/porters you can leave the building alone. There are 5 main resources (food, water, gold, wood and stone), along with ostrich feathers which as far as I can tell doesn't seem to do anything. You pretty much only need one building for each resource, which you can setup in a few minutes. There's also a market you can build which sells all resources for extremely low prices, making most production buildings obsolete once you have one up and running.
There are some support buildings and units, but they are fairly costly and generally doesn't seem to do anything except boost resource production which you probably won't need more of at that point in the game. It's easier just to hire more workers or use the market for everything. The support buildings seems to mainly be there as requirements for the various campaign stages. Unfortunately the campaign very frequently asks you to start over from scratch, making you construct the same very small settlement over and over.
The game graphics, sound and interface seems designed for mobile phones, making the game very easy to control. You do everything with the mouse cursor. The game is also fairly slow paced making it easy to learn. No experience from city builders is needed and the game is usually very user friendly. There is one big exeption to this, which is that the translation to English is very poor and inconsistent, sometimes using the wrong word for key gameplay terms. For example, when starting an endless mode game the text asks you to pick between Normal and Casual, but the buttons are labeled Normal and Relaxed. You can usually figure out what to do by just looking at the pictures, though.
I have unfortunately had the game crash on me during the campaign, forcing me to replay a part of the game. Combined with the very short length and overall very shallow gameplay this means the game definitely isn't worth the price. It's much cheaper on Android phones and the gold version only seem to offer higher graphics resolution and not much more.

I'm just going to start out by saying this, I bloody love this game.
Sunless Sea is a beautiful roguelike set in the world of Fallen London (which is actually a free, browser based story game with not to dissimiliar mechanics to mafia wars on facebook but with incredible stories and tales to follow) where an entity merely known as the bazaar exchanged london with old queen Vic, circa 1861, in return for her husbands mortal soul. This results in london being dragged down to the Unterzee, a world where the rules are only known by those in power and those in power really like keeping it that way.
Enough background, on to the game (i just think the backstory is one the most facinating and unique parts of the game).
Gameplay wise you are in control of a vessel (which at later stages you can trade in for a better one) with which you must explore the Unterzee. The ship requires fuel for the engine and lamp (as without a sun the Unterzee is pitch black) and supplies for your crew. You also need to manage your crews terror as it can negatively effect several aspects and also result in your crew either commiting suicide, going mad and killing other crew members or worse yet killing you for being such a bad captain. Run out of fuel you can wait for rescue until your supplies run out but as the game so aptly says without fuel your ship is just a mishapen house on water. Run out of supplies and, well, cannabilism is always a better choice than starvation for most. If you do die (and trust me you will as you learn the ropes and do's and don't's) there is this really unique system where you can decide what you inherit form the previous captain picking from rival, correspondant, pupil, shipmate or salvager each offering you particular bonuses. You can also choose a past or choose not to have one and reveal it later (again each decision really ripples outward as you can simultaneously limit and expand what you can do just by devoting yourself on a particular path).
There are many, many beautiful and unique places to visit but the ones really worth seeing are the ones beyond the local cluster of islands that surround london as these are technically protectorates of london and so they don't have much of the weird and whacky variety. In these places are equally cool story lines that just really grip the imagination with beautiful written passages and stories. As for the Zee itself, well, beautiful and terrifying really come to mind and so much fun to explore.

My review is about the entire Blackwell series, not about a specific episode.
TL;DR - highly recommended if you're looking for good quest games.
Although being quest series, the Blackwell series isn't difficult comparing to other games in that genre as there aren't logic puzzles to solve. However, the games don't suffer from one flaw that exists in many quests, and that is excessive use of items. In some quest games you usually stack up a lot of items and end up trying every combination of item and something clickable on the screen until you find that absurd combination that makes you progress. The Blackwell series doesn't have that flaw as items aren't the main part of the game. Also, when places become irrelevant you can't access them anymore, which also prevents having to go back and try to find something useful in every place that you've been through at the endgame.
The progression in the game is made by combining the abilities of Rosa (or Lauren in Blackwell Unbound) and Joey, which complete each other. Joey can enter locked rooms but cannot interact with anything, and Rosa can do the opposite. Only by combining their abilities you will make progress. There's also a built in search engine inside a game in which you have to use in order to progress, which makes you feel that you're doing detective work and not just trying to figure out how to use your inventory.
The plot becomes "bigger" in each episode and ends with a grand finale in Blackwell Epiphany, so you don't feel like you're doing that same thing in each game.
I really enjoyed the series and I highly recommend it.

As an avid enthusiast of wilderness travel and survival skills, I have been daydreaming of a PC game like The Long Dark for quite a while.
For me the two aspects of a solo wilderness experience that this game nails are:
-Long periods of serenity interrupted by moments of great intensity
-Important decisions disguised as mundane events
For example, you are three days in to your survival situation and you have been lucky enough to find a beat-up old rifle and three rounds with which to load it. You are still avoiding wolves when you see them, because who knows if you will find more ammo?  You crest a blind hill to hear growling and then barking as a wolf is staring you in the face. It can sense that you are tired and limping due a sprained ankle. It charges. You aim your rifle and wait until the last moment, knowing that you only have one shot before it is on you. You fire and the echo of the shot rings out across the valley...You may not fire the rifle again for a week, but those moments of intensity are unreal.
Another example; It is late in the day and you are returning to your home base after checking your snares for rabbits and picking up a bit of firewood.  The wind is picking up and you are chilly.  You come across the corpse of a recently downed deer. You know you have seen a bear around here before but the hide from that deer -not to mention the meat- could be a huge boon later on. There will be no dialogue box promting you, it is up to you to recognize the importance of the decision you are making and evaluate the risks and rewards for yourself.
The game is still in early access at the moment, but is very stable and has lots of content.
The art style is gorgeous and the ambient sounds of the wilderness are incredibly immersive.
If you have been thinking about it, get it!

TL;DR - 7/10. Lots of jump scares, but as a person prone to them, I was scared. However, it doesn't rely on them only.
So I guess I should start off by saying that I am very prone to jump scares. Even though they might not necessarily actually scare me, I will jump in my chair and think about punching the thing that popped out. Luckily I didn't punch my monitor.
The game has lots of jump scares. There were times when they were obvious (yeah, dude on the wheelchair, I know you'll stand up to grab me in 0,2s), sometimes a bit less. Sometimes you knew something is going to happen, but not sure exactly what. And I liked that. I know a lot of people think jump scares are the cheapest, least scary things, but they do work on me. So if they work on you too, you might like it as well. On the other hand, thankfully, jump scares were not the only scary thing. The mood was there. Perhaps it's one of the most cliche settings - an asylum overrun by it's patients after a failed experiment - but it was presented very well. The models (as long as you didn't look at them for too long), the environment, the music and the green-ish nightvision postprocess made the (almost) whole experience very heavy and creepy. Overall, the horror part was very good on many levels. One exception is described below, but IT MIGHT BE CONSIDERED A SPOILER.
Sadly, aside from being just a horror, it's a horror game. Sadly, that was it's weakest point, that also made the horror part worse, sometimes. Lets start with the least important stuff - there were bugs. Mostly graphical issues of assets popping in on low distance or visibly switching between differing LODs. Sometimes it's also possible to spot how sloppy the artist were, placing buckets that were supposed to be on a table, slightly too low which caused them to clip through it, or by putting some kind of document slightly too low, which caused it to constantly flicker. Another rather technical issue, that made things less scary, were poorly done animations. Multiple times opponents were walkin in a silly way, hovering over terrain etc. The multitude of those issues is a problem, but rather small compared to the others.
The biggest faults of this game, gameplay-wise, were it's globally used schemes and mechanics. Almost every level was a sequence of objectives - follow the blood (with jump scares and creepy stuff happening, but nothing lethatl) > figure out that to progress further you need to find/turn on/switch X > get chased by an opponent while doing so > activate the thing that you were supposed to initially, that was inactive > cutscene. Sometimes there was also a "final chase" that led usually to climbing a vent. It was extremely repetitive on that side.
Opponent's AI is another issue. Their behavior is as predictable as it goes. They move along a very simple, hand-drawn path unless they spot you. Then they chase you, without the ability to catch you as long as you're running, until you get away. Being clumsy dummas they are, they get slowed down a lot by closed doors or obstacles that you jump over, which means you need a couple of those, then some shadow and you're safe. Then they go back to their predefined path. Additionally, some of the obstacles are a safe haven for you - enemies cannot pass narrow passages, climb vents or tall furniture, so you can use them as the area reset if necessary.
Last two things that annoyed me were - lack of ability to fight back. I understand that I cannot harm the 2m high, 120kg monster, but why can't I at least try to fight back normal sized, crazy people that were experimented on and are most likely weakened by it, when I am a perfectly healthy male? Why can't I grab anything and make it a weapon? Sadly, that is the concept of horror walkers. Other thing is - if I can parkour so well, climbe ledges etc. why, in order to escape the asylum, won't I just break the window (that has no bars!), climb down and the hell out of there? That was the kind of logical issues that annoyed me.
SLIGHT SPOILERS AHEAD, I WILL TRY NOT TO ACTUALLY SPOIL ANYTHING, BUT SOME MIGHT NOT LIKE IT ANYWAY.
Final issues. Typically to almost all of the horrors, The Big Evil is no longer scare once you show it. Sadly that was the case in this game as well. Fortunately, despite being present since more or less half of the game, it was only the most important thing in the last chapter. Unfortunately, the last chapter gets in my opinion the worse the further we progress, making the very last couple of seconds of the game not logical, considering what we found out previously. I'm not going to spoil anything more, I just think it contradicts the notes, journals and emails that we have found.
END OF SPOILERS.
Despite those issues I enjoyed this game, got scared ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ multiple times and I think it's worth the money. If it would be more polished and if the logical issues would be removed, it would be one hell of a game. Sadly it was "only" good.

Dear Coda,
I'm terrified that I've misjudged your work, seeing it through this compilation. So here goes:
I'm terrified how I view this work has been clouded by its presentation. People are always trying to rationalize, to understand, what they cannot understand.
What they cannot feel.
I'll be open-I've done that plenty myself, but I always find myself hating myself for it. And hated people even more when I was the receiving end.
So I'm not going to try. For once in my life, I promise I'll force myself to not ask that always-asked question: Why? How? What is wrong, do they even know? No. I won't ask that. Not of you. Not after I've seen this. Because I know the answer isn't for me to know.
It's more important to me to not ask, "Why?" It matters more that I say that you're not alone. You're not the only one.
You're not the only one who was content as they were, only to be poisoned by those who thought they were right. Thought you could benefit.

I have stood in dirt turned to mud by the spilled blood of the fallen and have watched my brothers in arms torn to shreds by machinegun fire. I have seen mangled corpses tossed high into the air by artillery fire.
I have driven the Russians out of bombed-out husks of buildings and into the streets where they were ripped to pieces by the crossfire of two different squads. I have shot German fascists in the lungs with my Tokarev and heard them use their last precious breaths gurgling for their mothers. I have participated in a thirty-man banzai charge and skewered the American swine with my bayonet as they fire feebly into the midst of the oncoming storm of blades. I have roasted Japanese soldiers alive with a flamethrower in the dark jungles of Guadalcanal, and when I close my eyes I can still see them burning and hear them screaming.
I have killed. I have been killed. I fight and I die. And for what?
For the Motherland.
For the Fatherland.
For the Emperor.
For mom and apple pie.
Even after I uninstall this game, even after I leave these horrors behind me, I will carry the things I have seen and the things I have done with me to my grave. I will look at myself in the mirror and know that even though I still breathe and though my heart still beats, some part of me died on those digital battlefields. And I will close my eyes.
And I will see those men burning alive in the dark jungles of Guadalcanal.

A great First Person Survival Horror.
Mount Massive Asylum hides a terrible and a bloody secret. You play an investigative journalist Miles, given a tip off that horrible and unnatural experiments are being conducted on the inmates at the Asylum. You set off into the Colorado Mountains with your camera to uncover the truth.
Outlast is very tense and very satisfying experience mostly due to the outstandingly well designed environment of the Mount Massive Asylum. The asylum layout and near pitch black enviroments create a powerful tension where you feel like, and infact are, constantly hunted. The experience is added to by the outstanding musical score that keeps you on edge and very nervous at all times, enhancing the whole experience and making your dark journey into the heart of the Asylum all the more unnerving.
You are immersed. You can smell the mold and taste the cold air. The rotting tiles and dank enviroments are fantastic and all consuming. Even the charcters heavy breathing keeps you on edge during the various frightining cat and mouse chases.
Outlast is very scary and not because of cheap jumps scares, there are a few jump moments, but they never feel cheap or tacky for me, the majority of the terror comes from the outstanding enviroment and the helplessness you feel as the player sourrounded by the grotesque unhindged inhabitents that may, or may not attack you at any random moment.
Well written notes located around the map help to explore and expand the story of the asylums past and present for players who wish to delve into the story.
Outlast is one of thoes brilliant games with Achievements that change the way you play and experience the game a 2nd or 3rd time.
-'Lunatic mode' is a play through on the hardest setting without dying or saving once. Beyond punishing.
-'Claustrophobe' is a play through completed without hiding in a locker or under a bed. Quite tricky.
-'Energiser' is plaing on Insane without using any batteries for your night vision. Very difficult!
This is probably my favorite survival horror game of all time. I highly recommend it to anyone wanting to test their nerve and survival abilities.

As a Batman fan, this game was worth it at the sale price of just under $17.
Pro:
-most of the bugs and technical issues appear to have been resolved. I did experience some crazy slow downs during times when Batman was in the Batmobile (what is it with PC games and frame rate issues with the Batmobile)? But fortunately, this affected only a very tiny portion of the overall game.
-with one exception, the story was engaging and interesting. It was on par with watching some of the direct to video DC animated films of the past several years (and better than some of those).
-the game did a pretty good job mechanically with making sure there was actually detective work for The World's Greatest Detective. The nature of the engine here limits how far they could push this, but it was nice to see.
-Batman gets down with Catwoman. Would give Selena the special Batarang again.
Cons:
-The Telltale game format is really starting to get stale. Over time you start to realize just how little player agency there really is in these games and you begin to see the sleight of hand they're using to give players the illusion that their choices matter. That makes these games a PITA to play anytime the story lags at all.
-One of the annoying things about superheroes is how every writer feels the need to revisit the origin stories. In this case a *significant* part of Batman's origin story was revisited and recast in a way that I absolutely detested. This is a major plot point and seemed to be part of the writers' efforts to reframe the origin and, thus, Batman/Bruce Wayne. Writers: please cut this s*** out.

Aces of the Galaxy is a competent game that gets on my nerves. Aces reveals console-port-itus by making it impossible to change the controls ingame, and if you have a 360 controller hooked up expect to get lots of rumble you can't do anything about.
I was attracted to Aces because it looks and plays a bit like Rez HD. You can move side to side and dodge, but you have no ability to change your path. When executed well, this can be alot of fun. However, shooting in Aces is accomplished by clicking the mouse button instead of holding it. Within the first few minutes of play, I encountered swarms of enemies, and I do mean swarms. You can fire missiles by holding the right mouse button and dragging it over your enemies, but the recharge for this ability encourages you to click away with your guns, and this quickly becomes a pain.
Outside of gameplay, two more issues quickly made the experience intolerable. Firstly, the majority of the enemies arn't well-differentiated from the background, the shots they fire back at you, or thier own vapor trails. The result is an incredibly busy, confusing, and deadly mess, and that's before you start adding your own shots to the mix. Secondly, I quickly encontered a piece of music that was ear-splittingly painful, and while I could certainly turn off all the music, I really don't see the point of playing a game like this without decent beats.
This is obviously a subjective review, so I encourage you to examine other sources.
