Pros:
* It's Telltale Batman. It's everything you expect it to be. It's great. You won't regret playing it.
* Performance issues are now also fixed. No reason not to play it.
* Playing Bruce Wayne often feels like playing Commander Shepard.
Cons:
* Keep in mind it's possibly the shortest Telltale game and it feels rushed often. Each episode takes 90-120 minutes.
The upside is that the pacing is good and fast you won't ever be bored with long sequences of inaction,
* Frankly the plot feels weak often if you stop and think about it. The "main twist" in particular really feels pulled out of some dark hole and makes next to no story sense - if anything it's laughable. Logic often suffers for the sake of heroic drama.
* It has an unusual take on Batman lore. It takes the original characters and twists them into something you don't expect... for better or for worse. Just don't expect everything to be canon, or you might be (un)pleasantly surprised.
* You get to play the nice guy and the bad guy. But as usual with Telltale, don't expect your choices mattering much on the overall story.
* There are some NASTY issues with your saves deleting. I suggest disabling cloud save and backing your local saves up after each episode so you won't waste your precious hours.

Okay, as a start, I don't hate this game, on the contrary. I'm doing a search for the worst rated games on steam, and I came acrossed this game, because of the user rating. I don't see why this game was as bad as stated. In fact, I liked it! Please keep working on this premise, and fix some of these faults. Heres a quick run through of some problems I saw, you can correct me if I just missed something:
-A drawer that I found at the start said that it was locked, I found a key. So I made a rightful assumption saying the key was for the drawer. Well, I spent a total of 5 minutes trying to find out how to use the key. 'I' was for inventory, I knew, but when I was trying to use the key for the locked drawer, I didn't know that the key for the door was for the door, not the drawer.
-(dumb nitpick) the walls sometimes clip through other walls, the walls are paper thin, and the flashlight doesn't shine on some things, and the text on the notes don't fit. But none the less this is a simple thing that I don't really care about. I'm just mentioning so it's known.
-Some people are pointing out grammatical errors, but I still know what's supposed to be said so I don't mind it. (I'm a fluent English speaker and my grammar can be just as bad so I don't see what the big deal is)
-Sometimes random sound effects would play.
-Apparently there was some intro? I'm not too sure but I thought someone said there was an intro explaining why you were in the hospital.
That's really all I saw that I didn't like, moving on to what I liked:
-All the mechanics included (though kinda pointless objectively) to duck left or duck right.
-I like the options to alternate between the flashlight and the nightvision, giving more options to survive.
-One thing that I wish was still in the game: the bugged AI. While watching the trailer, I laughed so hard when I saw the jumpscare at the end! It's something that I wish could be added back into the game just to take us out of the game for a minute. Without the funny jumps, the game just takes itself too seriously.
-I got the game for only 89 cents, that's pretty neat.
-It's a standard horror game, but it does create a creepy atmosphere, and has a nice premise.
-This game isn't like other washed down games that wouldn't even give the player a flashlight/night vision, this relies on actual horror not just a lack-of-sight type game.
In conclusion, if the description I gave of this game convinces you of this game, then get the game while it's on sale. I hope the developer might see this post and improve the features mentioned in my complaints.

I've waited a long time before writing this review, and maybe in a way I still need to process it. I still can't go back to this game without feeling that bit of emptiness, that void that's filling my mind. I think it's the fact that for a while I've been looking forward to a new entry in the Blackwell series that I've come to love all these characters. To think that I started to play this series because it starred a glasses wearing redhead.
The game can be pretty challenging, and in that regard seems to be an improvement over the previous Blackwell games. At times though it does seem unclear what to do, and you keep on trying many things before you get just one step further. Sure, with some logical thinking you could get there, but at times it doesn't even seem all that logical. You do need to think like a ghost at times.
But I do think the game shines the most when it comes to the story itself. It all sets itself up for the final moments of the game, and it does take a lot of elements from previous games as well, integrates them to make it seem like it was planned all along. I mean, it might have been, I don't know. It does feel like one big world, and honestly, I can't wait to jump into this world again in a future game (though not necessarily a Blackwell game).

This game takes clear cues from the

feel that it has already established. The tech tree is a clear example of this. There are eras within which you must research most of the technologies before you are capable of advancing to the next era. However, again, these have the Tropico flair to them.
Another improvement or expansion that I have particularly found enjoyable is the Dynasty feature. This allows you to maintain a set of rulers each which can provide specific boosts to your island. Likewise, each of these can be upgraded through an expanded Swiss Bank system. Ultimately, you can retire Dynasty members which you dislike, and all can be customized in their
. Yes, just their style as, after your first ruler which permits full customization, all subsequent members are "born" and you can only make changes that would be realistic in this regard (their hair and clothes basically). While I appreciate that some will certainly dislike this anti-feature, I actually like it.
While I have enjoyed these and other aspects of the game, I am also unfortunately already getting a bit bored with it. A slight cure to this has been going back and forth between the Story and the Sandbox modes. The story allows me to play with very specific goals in mind, boost my Swiss Bank, upgrade my Dynasty, and ultimately to learn how to better optimize my islands. In contrast, the sandbox allows me to go nuts with attempting my idealized configuration of island. Similarly, I have started to use the achievements to a similar end. I will also begin to utilize the new co-op feature in this regard as well.
Generally speaking this has been my main problem with Tropico 5 (as well as 3 and 4), as for whatever reason, I just do not find the game to be highly replayable and indeed find it fairly repetitive after I get the basic setups figured out. In essentially every other way I find the game to be fun and well done. It just fails to hook me for extended periods of time (though I have the same problem with

This is not an inherently negative aspect to this game, but as I indicated above in my quest for extensive customization in these types of games, this is something that stands out to me.

Hello Random Person On The Internet I Shall Call Friend. You should check this game out, it is the most innovative shooter I have played in years.
...Okay, now that I got that out of the way, let's get real here.
Getting the elephant in the room out of the way here: Yes, SUPERHOT is a short game. I completed the campaign mode in about 2 hours. For a game that is regularly $25 (I picked it up when it was on sale for $20), I can see that being a hard sale. If you are the type who wants to get some playtime out of their buck, then your enjoyment of this game will heavily rely some post-game stuff, namely Endless mode and Challenges. If neither of those sound like your cup of tea, then you may want to wait for SUPERHOT to drop in price a bit more.
That out of the way, I had a lot of fun with SUPERHOT. The "time moves when you do" mechanic works great. With that giving you the time you need to plan moves, this game does a great job of making you feel like a complete badass. Shooting one guy, throwing your gun into another dude so he drops his gun, grabbing that gun out of mid-air and blasting him with it never gets old. I enjoyed the graphics, and the enemy models shatter in an extremely satisfying fashion. Around the game-play is an weird little story layer. Dare I say it...it feels somewhat "artsy". But unlike most games that fall into that category, SUPERHOT gets that the weird story stuff is there to spice up solid game-play.
All told, I give a thumbs up to SUPERHOT. I can see myself coming back to it every now and then to screw around in the Endless modes and whatnot, so I figure sooner or later I'll get my money's worth out of it.

There was once when I overcame all odds, but set up a campfire carelessly close to myself, and died a fiery death. (I assume that's what happened. I stared at my computer screen that was steadily updating me about the state of my boots and jeans and then - death. Boy, was that quick.)
Another time, I wandered through the night, hopelessly lost and supremely screwed, only to have my boots fall into a state of total disrepair. Completely ruined. I watched as my warmth stats plummeted laughingly quick despite the warmth from the campfire. It had been a really long night, and I badly wanted to give up and go out in a dangerously dumb style since I was due to die anyway.
I wanted to use up everything I had, then commit suicide so that I didn't have to wait for the cold to kill me. So I ate and drank whatever I could, threw everything I had into the fire and watched in amazement as my warmth stats stopped plummeting. Shrugging, I took off my jeans for 3 seconds. Put them back on. Decided not to commit suicide after all.
Ran off after the campfire died. Found the farmstead minutes after I left. Laughed, cursed, and entered the house. Found a pair of boots, what the actual F, stopped caring about everything else, went straight to sleep.
I'm still on that game. I monitor the condition of my boots and clothes obsessively. I can't put this goddamn thing down. 10/10 screwed and grudgingly loving it.

Ever wondered what happened to Liam Neeson after his intense 1 on 1 with the alpha at the end of his 2011 film, 'The Grey'?? Well worry no more. This game explains everything.
Set in a post-apocolyptic event (not yet explained) which causes your plane to crash, your character finds him/herself in the middle of a lifeless world on the brink of winter surrounded by snow, wolves and death. For a game in alpha 'the long dark' is a pretty intense first person experience testing your limit as a true survivalist from the very start. Your objective is to survive for as long as you can in this barren world. With limited resources and relentless wildlife..it's certainly easier said than done.
Providing numerous threats such as bears and wolves, a big factor which seperates this game from any other is the weather. The environment itself can switch from the gentle image of narnia to the horiffic set of the day after tomorrow in a heartbeat, this games holds no boundries as it attempts to murder you in any way possible. Visibilty, hunger, thirst, hyperthimia, sleep deprivation...you're no longer the top of the food chain. And it only gets harder as resources deplete.
For early access, the game itself holds a decent sized map which is still in develpoment for expansion. Resources within the game can be scarce however there are various ways of obtaining food and water without scavenging. Melting snow for example, and or hunting. Snares and bows are additionally available for crafting, however other than that there is not much else to build. This is clearly and area for improvement, in additon to this there is not much variety in objectives.
Once the map is explored and you've obtained the one and only gun in the game, there is not much to do. Although story mode is an upcoming update so I could be wrong. It also offers various game modes, such as hardcore and peaceful if you can't be bothered fighting off wildlife 24/7. Cleary as it is still in alpha I expect no more. Yet it's an intriguing game non the less. Decent graphics. Good game play. Sh*t scary wolves. A great game if you can snag it on offer, I mean.. It's only going to improve.

Right now this game is a technical mess, disconnects abound, chat broken, bad UI, PS4 commands on PC.
However, unfortunately, technical issues aside, despite its huge depth and being fairly unique in the market, this game is ultimately not good. I really wish it were, but its not. Its too complicated and matches are too long. If I had to put my finger on the key design flaws, it would have to be the units and the action points system.
Units have way too many abilities and traits, the're impossible to keep track of, specially because the're also too varied. "Too varied" sounds like a weird problem, but there's a reason why other CGs rely heavily on keyword abilities with standardized effects: Learn it once, know it always. In this game there are many similar units that do similar things, yet to these things using different abilities, making them needlessly hard to learn and remember.
The devs should have built units around a few key abilities instead of a slew of smaller ones, and should have made more general-purpose abilities that could be applied to many units, instead of the highly specialized abilities the game is full of. There are some ten abilities just related to being a frost creature, for example. Is that really necessary?
The second major design flaw is the action points system. I guess it seems like a good idea in theory, but in practice it just adds a layer of number crunching to the game without adding much to the actual tactics of it. It slows down the game dramatically and multiplies the abilities problem, because off course every ability has its own considerations regarding range of effect and its own AP costs. One extra step can make a huge difference due to no longer being able to trigger some ability or make an extra attack, which is not something fun to have to calculate. They should just have stuck to a classic move and act system.

This game started out really well - with quirky humor, loveable characters and occasional fourth-wall-breaking and held that level for quite a while.
I underestimated just how many puzzles there were, and I got to the point where I couldn't solve them anymore - a great part of those aren't mandatory for the plot, but there's still no way around them. You might also get trapped in puzzle blocks or the game changes the rules, like resetting the puzzle suddenly becomes necessary.
But that wasn't what actually disappointed me - after the hours of occasional chit-chat between the characters, additional banter and Sasha's state worsening, the script suddenly went quite bleak. The sisters no longer where the focus, Viper became the protagonist, but even that didn't last. The City of the Vanquished (Viper's personal quest, in a way) made no sense because nobody reacted to what it unveiled.
It was pretty much the same with Griffin and Enoch. Since this is the first game out of three so far, there might be more about it, but I'm not optimistic.
All in all, it was still good. If you enjoy puzzle games, you will have fun with this one, and the humor is sometimes subtle and sometimes witty.
Note, however, that if this game encounters a topic it can't treat with humor, it will ignore it completely.
I will probably leave it at that, despite the cliffhanger.

Want a game that is so realistic that you have an encounter with a German soldier in a building on your own that is exactly like the knife scene in 'Saving Private Ryan'? Well, this game is what you need. There have been many times that I will always remember in this game. Like this time when me and my squad were running through smoke after being pinned down my an MG42 for about 10 minutes. Someone said that it was "all clear". We began to advance down a slope with smoke surrounding us. There was silence, the only noises were our feet hitting the floor. But then, I heard someone next to me say "Wait! The MG is still.....". Then a hail of MG fire ripped through the smoke. I dived to the floor. As I looked up, three of my squad members were cut down and one of their helmets rolled towards me. I cowered in a fox hole and began to throw grenades over. It all went slient. I was then that I realised that I was the sole survivor of the suprise attack. I was too scared to stand up. Then I heard footsteps coming my way. Then there he was.  A German infantry soldier sprinting towards me with his bayonet at the ready. I managed to shoot him in the leg, but by then it was too late. He embeded the bayonet deep into my chest. As I fell to the floor, I saw the rest of my team, all laying there motionless with their weapons laying by their side. My squad's death was the start of a 1 hour and 30 minute intense, amazing and emotional battle.

With this review, I'd like to answer one question for you: "Is The Long Dark (TLD) for me?"
If you like BBQ's, and don't mind eating meat 3 times a day, you will love TLD.
If you think sewing in the dark with a fish-hook is a great way to spend the evening, you will love TLD.
If you enjoy picking up sticks, at night, in a raging blizzard, you will love TLD.
If fishing in the cold through a hole that is freezing up again sounds like fun, you will love TLD.
If the smell of curing deer hides, wolf pelts and drying gut doesn't put you off from a good night's rest, you will love TLD.
If you find it rewarding to spend 3 days in your shelter preparing to travel half a mile on day 4, you will love TLD.
If you are fascinated by wildlife observation, reading their behaviour for your own benefit, you will love TLD.
If you don't mind waiting 6 days for a branch to dry out, so you can make a bow from it, you will love TLD.
If you like running as a form of exercise, say from wolves, you will love TLD.
If you are into traditional herbal remedies, not neccesarily by choice, you will love TLD.
If you can endure carrying 40kg (80 pounds) for hours on end, in the snow, you will love TLD.
If beautifully rendered, artistic, yet realistic landscapes is something you appreciate, you will love TLD.
If you find pleasure in harvesting useful things like lichen of trees and granola bars of frozen corpses, you will love TLD.
If the thought of spending a mind numbing 24 hours to make a coat out of wolf pelt excites you, you will love TLD.
If you prefer watching fire instead of watching TV, you will love TLD.
If terms like "windbreak", "windchill factor" and "calory burn" is not just acedemic to you, you will love TLD.
If you ever wondered if you could live of just candy, peanut butter and soda for 4 days, TLD will show you how.
If you'd like to hack open a can of sliced peaches with an axe, and still eat what's left, TLD will let you do that.
If you are afraid of the dark, TLD is just an extension of your real life.
If you have fond memories of sneaking back into your own house, to avoid your parents or perhaps wolves, TLD will let you relive those fond memories again.
If you think Canada is cool, TLD will teach you it's not just cool, it's %!&$@-ing freezing.
If you believe patience is a virtue, TLD will develop your virtue to a whole new level.
If you think paper cuts hurt, TLD will introduce you to sprains, infections, blood loss and hypothermia.
If you thought "hypothermia" is just fancy talk for "a bit cold", TLD will fix that for you.
If you think Bear Grylls knows something about survival, TLD will surely bring him to his knees.
If you think you can draw a bow and aim straight while tired, TLD will force you to rethink that.
But above all, just as you think you got this survival thing sorted, TLD will take your cocky, over-confident attitude, and throw it down the cold dark abyss as a stark reminder that your greatest enemy in the end, is yourself.
An almost personal, but certainly immersive and gripping challenge. Hugely rewarding to play. And not even complete/fully released yet. The Long Dark is great and I cannot over recommend it.

This fifth and final installment, Epiphany, is the culmination of all that the Blackwell series has been building up to. The art has really come into its own after a poor showing in the last game, and a focus on exterior locations has resulted in some truly beautiful backgrounds. Puzzles feel completely natural which could be an effect of the game design changing so little between Epiphany and Deception or simply from the fine tuning done over the past four games.
This is also by far the longest of the Blackwell games. The story focuses on the job ahead of our heroes this time rather than mystery of the duty itself, but still manages to be epic. As a spirit medium, Rosangela is involved in the most important moment of each of these peoples' lives (existences), which is brought home by another string of excellent voice performances. Those individual stories are then woven together to create something that not only hits harder than it ever could have alone but also provides answers to what has become the Blackwell legacy.
By the time the credits role, every loose end has been tied up as well as if could have ever been - save for one. Sadly, the society the pair vowed to hunt down at the end of Deception has been largely forgotten in order to focus on the finale of the series. As important as it was for the last game, it just didn't fit in this game. The writer includes a deleted scene in the commentary to point out exactly why that line of investigation would have overcomplicated an already complex story. The commentary track as a whole is more robust in this game than in the last. It now features explanations from the artist alongside Gilbert's traditional commentary and the occasional blooper from the voice recording sessions.
This game has so much offer, but going any further in depth would run the risk of spoiling its stirring conclusion. So without giving too much away: this was a satisfying and moving end to a fantastic series.

Overall the game feels somewhat amateurish and made by a very small (one person?) team. With basic mistakes/low quality on gameplay, artwork quality, fighting system balance, storyline, side-quest system, music, etc. Which is common for most RPGMaker titles. Comparatively speaking it's a pretty acceptable game, atleast i've seen and played much worse. But when you compare it to the JRPG classics of the SNES era it falls short on several points. It does however have good depth in the map world and storyline.
My main grief with this game is with a lack of auto-fight, making the repetitive fights more tedious then they already are in a typical JRPG game. Then there is the clunky gameplay that won't let you move around fast and easy with arrow keys, i can only assume the developer focused on mouse driven gameplay, not being able to navigate around properly can be quite nerve wrecking. When you add to that the bad info menu skipping mechanics that forces you to wait for menu animations on repeated events, it practically doubles the playing time of the game, with plenty of moments idling in wait for the game to proceed to a skippable part.
There are some puzzle elements in the game, which is good, but they are so simple that you just get bored from wasting your time having to deal with yet another one of the same type.
All these small things combined make this game quite boring to explore and finish. It's quite a shame because it has lots of attention to detail, especially the world map. The characters and the storyline are also quite acceptable, albeit perhaps a bit cliché for the genre, but they do feel like they have their own personality.
The artwork of the characters feels too bland and the world could also use a little more interactivity, random treasure to find searching in bushes and pots and such. There are some things you can pick from the world map, but they are far too few to be worth exploring every corner.
There are other small positive points. The auto-equipment assignment was nice considering how simple the inventory is. The pet system was also nice. The menus looked pretty clean and functional.
I'm quite divided if i would overall recommend this game or not. It's not an overwhelming game experience which i can recommend to any random person, i feel they would get bored and get a bad image of the genre. I guess a regular RPG player might find it more interesting, i got a little fix from playing it atleast, but then again, they would also expect more from it, unless they are used to the typical low quality of what people put out using RPGMaker.
You have to play this game. It's the most innovative game i've played in years!

I really liked this game. This is part one of 3, as of this review I haven't played the other parts yet. I just beat this game today. It's a fun and a lot of times funny game. The humor hits most of the time, I think it's probably hard to nail timing with unexpresive graphics and text. So for as funny as it is, it's well written.
You are pretty much playing this for the story and a little fun with the puzzles. The RPG elements are bare bones. Like I never used the special abilities other than to see what they did, they just aren't effective. It's a better strategy to save your stamina for your secondary move. That's basically combat. You use your strong attack until you are low on stamina, then use your normal attack till you regain it. So if you are looking for an indepth RPG experience, then it's not here.

I think the longest I spent on a puzzle was like 5-10 minutes or so. Not challenging, more "Oh duh" kind of puzzles. Which I enjoy.
It goes on sale a lot, so check it out when it's a dollar. I recommend it for full price though. It's worth it.

Batman - The Telltale Series is the next major game from Telltale, the creators behind the award winning Walking Dead franchise. This game follows the same structure of many of Telltale's other games - an episodic story which is altered by the decisions you make. A major obstacle for this game is the fact that it's riding off the heels of the critically acclaimed Arkham Franchise (With Asylum and City in particular, as they are known to be the best of the series), so it had a lot to live up to. Lets see if it delivered:

. Engaging story, brilliantly told through solid voice acting and intersting and compelling choices, as well as very good dialogue.
. Troy Baker is amazing as Bruce Wayne/Batman and in my opinion should be the successor to Kevin Conroy as the voice of Batman.
. A unique look on some characters, especially Oswald Cobblepott and Harvey Dent. Cobblepott in this game is completely different to any other depiction of him and Dent's personality is different to other depictions. These are both for the best as they breath new lives into the characters and make them more dynamic and unique to this universe.
. Interactivity is very well implimented into this game: Allowing to plan tactics, reconstruct a crime scene (probably better than the Arkham Series handled it), and deciding how to deal with an enemy are the highlights of what this episode does well.
. Literally no performance issues. Game ran very smoothly.
. Pacing can be a bit slow, which could bore the action-driven players.
. Game is not very well made in terms of presentation. Evidence is:
- Lip syncing is off - quite heavily in some bits.
- Textures on far away objects are not rendered very well (What? Did Telltale think we wouldn't Notice?)
- One scene where the door is opened and the outside is literally a pasted image. No, literally, they pasted a very pixelated image of a forest in their game, in 2016. A very lazy move by Telltale.
- Very bad animation, with the eyes and lips of Catwoman going very crooked in one scene, along with constant juttering in head and body movements by people, causing heads to suddenly snap into looking a different direction or for them to turn away from who they are talking to completely. This is very noticeable towards the end of the episode.
- There were one or two instances where people would interupt themselves and start their next sentence before finishing the one they were saying.

The first episode is a sound start to the game with a compelling story, likeable characters, good interaction and very good voice acting. However, the score has to be decducted by a few due to the sloppiness from the developers in some areas of presentation and the very obvious bugs in the game's animation.

. The story in this episode improves from the first episode. It's excellently told through a unique viewpoint that gives a different spin on the Batman mythos that we all know. Followed on by a few surprises that you won't see coming.
. The game's interpretation of the Penquin continues to grow on me and is at the moment my favourite villain in this game.
. Troy Baker did an okay job as Batman/Bruce Wayne, but episode 1 did it better in my opinion.
. Animation issues are mostly cleared up in this episode, apart from one or two small instances that are barely noticeable.
. Some characters are very well done in this episode, which helps influence decision making in this game more, making you genuinely feel whether or not you made the right decisions for the characters.
. Voice acting isn't very good with some characters (Renee Montoya comes to mind).
. Multiple texture and shading issues throughout the episode that was very noticeable and very off-putting.
. This episode was a lot shorter than the previous episode and I feel as if a bit more could've been done with it (This is only a small gripe as the story was really good).
. The new enemy faction introduced just sort of came out of nowhere and maybe a bit more could've been done to make me care a bit more about this new enemy force in Gotham.
. Again with the unrendered textures and pasted AND pixelated backgrounds! (Come on guys, really?)
. Lip syncing is off again.
In terms of storytelling, characters, and interactivity, the second episode is better than the first. However visual presentation is on the sloppy side again with texture and shading issues which can easily be fixed and many visual decisions made by them which really shouldn't have been made in this day and age.

The game offers deep tactical depth and the number of strategies you can viably use is quite high. There are 8 factions and you can use either 30 cards from the same faction to get a strong bonus, or a 15/15 split between any of the factions to get a lesser bonus but more flexibility. It will take you some time to learn whats played most often, and how to play what  you have to your best advantage. The system is quite deep even from the deck building phase....you only get so much Resourse per turn to use your cards, and the pro players pay strict attention to the resource cost of EVERY card in there deck....its every bit as deep if not deeper then MTG.
Learning curve is STEEP and there are relatively few players on even during peak times.  Drafting and tournaments are GONE..like completely gone.  Big cons.
the revamp most likely changed the game for the better, opinion is still out on that. Power creep was decidedly reigned in though.  Game is still pay to win, but not nearly as bad as it was before Desert Owl took it back.  If you play the daily skirmishes you can win Exotic cards, ive won two in the last week or so. Also you can "shard" extra cards and use the shards to buy Rares, Exos and Legendary cards....which is much friendlier to the F2P community.
Supposedly the game is getting a UI facelift and will be released for the Ps 4...hopefully there is  a large flux of new players to go with that.
There are STILL some cards that are bugged in the game, and some interactions that are really, really sketchy, but overall everything works kinda how you expect it too.....More work needs to be done in this area however.(Pilfered Armory etc)
Overall as it stands now, i would rate the game 6 out of 10.  Once it has a better UI and more players, that will likely go to an 8 out of 10.

A cinematic, episodic, interactive viewing experience with classic "point and click" elements based on Batman's early years in a new, modern day universe not tied to any existing DC universes. Filled with dark plots, multiple choices to make, rendering important story details to your consiquences and actions, and simple gameplay. Basic Telltale gameplay with a strong story.
Featuring a mildly complex plot with each characters leading to the pleasure, or downcoming of another in a deeply dark and modern representation of Gotham City. Powerful crime leaders of different factions portray power and control scarily realistically as Bruce has to work alongside the threats made to Gotham and his family's past involvements with the building of the golden age of Gotham. (Crime boss) Falconey, (childhood friend) Oswald Cobblepot and (Mayoral candidate) Harvey Dent are the 3 main characters who make a substancial deliverance to plot in the first half of the 5 episode game. Each building the world Bruce lives in, teaching us of the wrongs of Thomas Wayne, building over Cobblepot's family's land for Wayne Enterprises funded by Falconey and other forms of dirty money, while Harvey plans to help clear up Gotham's wretched past of crime with future foundations. Unfortinately, Bruce is new to the fact Thomas Wayne dealed with dirty money, as well as secretly performing hideous actions towards the Cobblepot family. What makes this plot stand out is the demons Bruce faces; the unfortinate truth of the Wayne family, his own public image and the secret of being the Batman twisting his personality. This is the way a fresh Batman story should be told as more complex relationships and situations occur as the story progress, making each choice count somewhat fundamentally towards Bruce as a human being, as well as the Dark Knight. As other iconic, and lesser known, characters are intrduced, the plot only gets more complex and interesting.
Visually, this game looks close to being a comic book brought to life. Vibrant colours, inked characters and an animated look makes this game look as visually pleasing as a work of art. Mostly unnoticed, the music holds some credibility to the Batman franchise in terms of what has been previously heard in Batman films, shows and games. The orchestial delivering mimics the likes of the 70's Batman films (which also play a role in some Lego Batman games.
Of course, the game plays like any other Telltale game. This is welcomed nicely, since I'd rather focus on the interesting story to be told, rather than learning how to play. The game is slowly paced, focussing more on dialogue than action. There's still plenty of action, played as varied, easy quick time events with some brilliant new additions, compared to other Telltale games. In some cases, you can plan your next few moves then watch as your own way of dealing with goons actually happens. Not to mention, seeing Bruce Wayne pull some punches himself is a treat, truly showing how vulnerable he is as a human physically and mentally.
Annoyingly, this game has performance problems. My computer can run many games, especially all Telltale games perfectly. However, Batman seems to have given my computer some grief. Frame rate drops, poor lip syncing, graphical glitches, character's animations bugging out, one instance of blue screen of death and various crashes have made this playing experience rather frustrating. If the story wasn't engaging, then I'd have left the game alone or got a refund.
I should also mention; the quick time events and some dialogue choices are rather pointless. Some actions lead to no consiquences if missed or show no change in plot whatsoever. I insulted Harvey at one point, clearly trying to get on his nerves, then a minute olater he quickly forgot how I just told him to randomly kill someone for me. Not to mention, the story reaaaally wanted me to like Catwoman, expecting me to be like the majority of (stereotypical) Catwoman fans and wanting to start a false relationship with her or Vicki Vale, when both were predictabley evil in their own way I didn't fancy getting involved with. Yes, Bruce is a playboy millionaire, but Harvey, Gordon and Alfred are my bros. That's not to say I didn't like either Selina or Vicki. They're interesting in this plot, but their forced romance was unwanted by me and I refused every romantic chance I had with them. Yes, Selina's character is based on loneliness and unpracticed nature of friendliness and trustworthiness, while Vicki is a rporter getting a scoop in any way she finds works, but they both just seemed annoying and made for some awkward and stupid circumstances, messing with other character's thoughts on Bruce, despite my aim to be truthful and innocent in the matter.
This game really makes you think more of Bruce Wayne than Batman. Your choices made have weight on either Bruce as a person, or Batman as a hero. Choosing to be more of a hero as either person is what drives the events forward. That is genius, since I found myself playing more as Bruce, exploring his inner weaknesses and attempts at keeping a positive public figure in respect of dramatic events towards himself and Gotham. The city is basically Clementine from The Walking Dead Season 1, as you are it's protector, or it's undoing. Not only that, but learning of the corrupt past of the Wayne family, and how they effected the state of Gotham today is more than interesting. While the bugs made the game nearly unplayable at random segmants, I'd still recommend this game, purely for it's fantastic narrative and likable characters.

A freeware bullet hell game that borrows heavily from the Touhou series, Jigoku Kisetsukan is a surpringly delightful little game that perhaps relies a bit too much on its influences. For those unfamiliar with the Touhou games, they are a self published series of vertical shooting games made by one man, ZUN. In them, a group of colorful anime girls do battle with the player, filling the screen with hundreds of projectiles to be dodged and weaved through as you attempt to grasp victory. Against these overwhelming odds, you are given a few advantages; a tiny hitbox that is much smaller than your character sprite, the ability to slow your character and focus fire for pinpoint maneuvering, and liberal lives and bombs to clear the screen and take pressure off.
It is from this blueprint that Jigoku Kisetsukan takes its design from. A cast of anime inspired characters must blast through 5 stages of increasingly difficult bullet patterns and boss fights, culminating in a final battle that pushes the players skills to the limits. It's in these gameplay setups that the game does particularly well, providing what feels like a solid and fun take on the Touhou games. The game features various characters to unlock, and they all have unique shot types which switch up the feel of the game quite a bit -- one character has a powerful close range attack while another relies on a particularly unconventional homing shot. The mechanics also lean towards punishing the player for deaths, with bombs that rely on killing enemies to be replenished instead of being given with a new life, and a shot power down that has to be earned back. It leads to a focus on proper execution in the face of harder patterns, rather than the war of attrition with lots of bombs that harder shooting game bosses can turn into.
While the core gameplay itself is good, the game does falter in its attempt to tell the story. Parts of it are revealed through the game as you play via each of the characters, but it remains confusing and obliquely told, only really making sense with the supplimental material in the game. As you work through the game, the consequences of whats happening remain vague, and the final arc of the game lacks narrative context and feels arbitrary. A person might say "why care about story in a shooting game?", but the developer put quite a bit of time and effort into the one this game has, and it doesn't quite stand on its own legs.
Perhaps the games greatest flaw though, is that it doesn't pull far enough away from the Touhou games to feel like much more than a fangame. One of the things that could have benefitted Jigoku Kisetsukan the most would be a proper scoring system; the game feels painfully basic in that regard, giving a player little to do but dodge and shoot, and the addition of even something as simple as Battle Garegga style medal chaining or Ketsui style point blanking could add a lot of life to the levels, giving more incentives for players to take risks through the game. Without more advanced scoring mechanics, the game feels like it's missing the biggest draw these types of games have. For the rest of the game, it enthusiastically copies the Touhou games in many aspects, and while this is a successful set of ideas to copy from, it makes the game feel like it lacks its own identity.
Still, despite its flaws, it is a great little game. It's completely free. I would go so far as to say that Jigoku Kisetsukan is better than quite a number of paid shooting games on Steam. Having learned that the developer released it as their first game, I am extremely impressed. It is a very promising indie release, and a western game that actually gets bullet hell right. The unlockables are fun to get, the game gives a fair amount of challenge with its patterns, and is completely worth a look at for both newcomers to the genre and fans of the Touhou games.

What is "Jigoku Kisetsukan: Sense of the Seasons"?
Sense of the Seasons is a glorious bullet hell provided by an interesting dev. I say "interesting dev" because of the ending to each character. (Play and beat for yourself, because I'm spoiling naught.) It's certainly not something I expected from such a colorful game, and I'm not disappointed in the outcomes in the least. Emad certainly put some thought into it, which is something I can appreciate in and of itself.
Jigoku Kisetsukan: Sense of the Seasons is fun, addicting, and will leave you in a state of "how am I supposed to dodge that?!" if you were new to this genre like I was.
Do I recommend?  Yes. Definitely. It's a fantastic gateway to newbies and what appears to be a very nice love letter to fans of the Touhou series.
To the dev: Twelve hours of gameplay in a week, and considering it has to be truly enthralling (or hooked-on mindlessness, which this game isn't) to some degree for me to play into it to this extent, that alone is a compliment. But if that isn't enough to-- Y'know what, no. Let me put it this way. I [currently] have 79 cents in my Steam wallet. Despite it not being much, I'd happily give every penny in my...hm...my STEAM pocket to you if I knew of such a way for opening a door to a brutal, exciting, and glorious new world of gaming. Because of this, my enjoyment for gaming has been reignited and I've begun playing the Touhou series starting from the sixth installment. I sincerely thank you for putting such hard work into this game and making it free for those of us who are a bit tight on cash.
Do I have any suggestions or requests for the future? Yes, and only one. Keep going. Build on top of what you have created. Extra levels, characters, soundtracks, whatever. All I ask is that you keep the fire going, because this one will have a special spot in my gaming library for many years to come.

So let me get this out of the way first. I'm going much easier on this game than say, Final Fantasy. There are multiple reasons for this such as the game having a lower budget, being made by not as experienced developers, and the game is only $0.99 at the most. So yeah if you guys think I'm going too easy on it then I'd say get over it.
Pros - The graphics and music are nice. The worlds aren't grey and lifeless, they have color and make me feel like I'm in an actual world rather than a dull boring game. The world is expansive with numerous places to go and different paths you could take. It's not linear, but not too non linear at the same time. I also love the fact that you can choose the main characters class at the beginning, it really makes me feel more involved in the gameplay factor rather than forcing me to be some generic warrior class in the entire game. Boss battles are also pretty fun since it cna sometimes get intense when one of your guys are about to be knocked out and you need to keep them alive since they might have a spell that's the enemies weakness.
Cons - While boss battles are fun, normal battles are a bit boring. They also happen way too much when it comes to random encounters. While the world is fine, the dungeons are not, since they are these way too large mazes that make you want to tear your hair out due to all the random encounters. The story is also pretty bad wiht a generic chosen one plot that makes no sense, but I can look past that. There are also some typo's in the game but they're not too bad.
Overall the game is a mixed bag for me. On the one hand I think the fact that this game is only $0.99 excuses it from some of its flaws like the plot and typo's, but flaws like random encounter rates and boring battles really drag this game down to painfully average. After I finish this game I will move on to Final Quest II and see if that game is any better. Trust me I hope it is.

As with most things that receive so much hype that they're made out to be the holy grail, you may be asking whether Five Nights at Freddy's lives up to that hype. Now I want to make it clear, I do think it's a pretty good game but I don't think it's the masterpiece people make it out to be. People are of course welcome to think it is and it's understandable why, as the game certainly has its fair share of great merits. I will address both the good points and bad points of this game. Keep in mind while reading that I do have an overall positive opinion on FNAF.
One of the most important factors of a horror game is obviously whether it's scary. FNAF is scary... to an extent. The atmosphere is most definitely there. The player fills the role of a security guard working the nightshift at a family pizzeria inhabited by animatronic characters. The sounds are largely what make the atmosphere so amazing. From faint tunes apparently coming from attractions within the building, to ambient spooky noises, to even the whirs of the security cameras, the sound design is absolutely excellent in building suspense. The animatronics look terrifying simply standing there on the stage, in the dark, looking a far cry from the delightful entertainers they're supposed to be. One can't help but feel the fear build as they become aware of these characters beginning to skulk the halls, simply roaming, with no programmed objective, thus making them unpredictable.
So where does the horror fail? In what it all ultimately builds up to. It's actually something the game points out when it starts up. To me, it's like the game's announcing a major flaw that it doesn't actually see as a flaw. I am of course referring to jumpscares. They're not inherently bad but by god can a work of horror fall back on them too much and FNAF certainly does... not just a little bit, quite a lot. Fortunately I do personally think two of the common jumpscare game overs aren't badly done - these being Foxy's and one of Freddy's (if he catches you before the power goes out.) This is because the animatronics in question look horrifying while doing the attacking. They look nothing like cuddly mascots, only wretched husks of metal and plastic, horribly failed attempts at endearing characters... just as the creator of the game no doubt intended.
The other common jumpscare game overs unfortunately don't pull this off in my opinion. The animatronics attacking in those game overs... really do just look like cuddly mascots. It's a delicate art making colourful cartoon animatronics look and seem scary. The game succeeds most of the time but it almost looks like the creator didn't try during those jumpscare screens. Of course jump scaring is a lazy tactic that doesn't require any effort in the first place, so it needs some kind of scary imagery to go along with it. But there is nothing really off about the animatronics during these screens. Arguably Chica looks a little off but I don't feel it.
That is the horror of FNAF at its core. Absolutely brilliant build-up, so-so execution due to the far, far too common practice of all horror works - jumpscares. It's just fortunate the game wasn't spoiled altogether by the jumpscares. It's also worth noting, there is a story to the game, both immediately obvious and not so obvious. Those who like to theorise and investigate should like it. That is, if the godawful community doesn't spoil the story for you. I'm also fond of how the game gives you the very brief "pauses" between the horror. The only thing that could possibly be considered something of a break in the horror is the guy who leaves a phone message for you every night. They're short, and in parts creepy in themselves, though usually there's still some lightheartedness to the creepiness. I don't know whether the creator intended for these phone calls to be something for the player to latch to due to there being nothing else to distract from the horror but it certainly works well. Unfortunately if one tries the same night more than once during one game session, the phone call no longer activates, so they have to restart. This is something I'd personally like to see patched.
I have a few other issues with the game. First of all, its ending... if it can be considered that. FNAF is in a lot of ways a fairly simple game that one can get a lot out of, so a simple ending works in theory. But for all the effort that one has to put into this frankly very challenging game, the ending kind of feels like a slap in the face. I'd have preferred a bit more, even if it was short. As for the difficulty, I do feel it's somewhat too difficult for a horror game. It ends up making retrying the night feel like routine and the horror starts to fade as a result. Kind of like Slender: The Eight Pages but NOWHERE near as bad. Again, only SOMEWHAT too difficult. Finally, the lack of an option to adjust the screen resolution or any other option for that matter. This is probably why I had to restart my computer to start the game the first time. Why exclude such basic features?
So those are my thoughts on FNAF. A pretty good horror experience that could serve to be amazing with a few tweaks here and there. Certainly a thrill to play, however and I would recommend it. It's also quite cheap. If you like horror and generally like what you've heard about this game, there's no reason not to get it.

Banished is probably the closest I'll come to owning an ant farm.
Let me explain:
You start off a game with a small group of families, often totaling no more than a dozen people.  With meager supplies and only a few months until winter, you must guide them to establish food stores and shelter, and prepare the stockpile of firewood. You will find that over time, your population naturally grows, providing you with a larger generation of workers, but requiring an increased infrastructure to support everything.
Between generations, while waiting for the kids to grow to adulthood, you plan out the next expansion of your village. Ok, you are probably planning out the next five generations, and a city that will span a third of the map. Don't think that it is all waiting and a few clicks here and there. Disasters, accidents, and the ever changing weather will inturupt your plans and test your flexibility. However, don't let me overcomplicate things.
It is about slow progression, and most issues you will face will grow slowly as well, giving you the time to correct it if you recognize the warning signs. This is a game you play for a few hours at the end of a long day; when you don't want to think too hard. As you can see, I have had many of those days.

Are you kidding me? Easy Red for $3.99? After playing this game, I'd happily pay $19.99! Can't believe I hesitated....wow! All the makings of Saving Private Ryan...explosions that rattle your brain...troops screaming out orders in both English and German...pitifully calling for a medic when wounded...bullets wizzing by your ears...realistic gun effects...dropping by parachute into France at zero dark thirty and barely able to see anything...and more! Single player for now (multi in the future) the AI is crafty and will move tactically to outflank your squad. AND, you can play either American or German or British or Italian to get a feel of what it is like to be on the "other side". There's a crap load of scenarios covering D-Day onward and, according to the Devs, more historical action on the way! All this for less than a cheeseburger, fries and a coke? I recommend this game for anyone interested in historical battle simulation. I was seriously impressed after the Point du Hoc scenario playing as a German defender...although it was distressing to mow down those Rangers as they crested the cliffside, only to fall back down to the beach like a sack of potatoes. NOTE: The game has beautiful graphics, but I had to set them up to "high" in each different scenario...make sure you do this to get great graphics. I suppose the Devs will take care of this issue as updates come in.   I give Easy Red a 9/10 ...easy.

Awesome game! Really had fun with the storyline and the horror of the utopia that envelopes this game. Only advice to future players, save frequently, especially towards the end of the game. You never know when you're going to need to re-do something in order to gain more money, ammo, ADAM, etc.

Gameplay: The city builder machanics at the games core are coupled with very well designed survival mechanics that involve balancing food, firewood, tools, clothing and natural resources. The most important thing to keep in mind is don't bite off more than you can chew. If you try to grow too quickly, you can quickly outstrip your resources and start loosing settlers as a result.  I would have liked to see maybe one more layer of tech before your max out your settlement,
Level design: Each play through is assigned a random number seed that determines how resources will be populated throughtout the level. Each new game feels like a unique map full of mountains, hills, rivers, forest and lakes ripe for exploration and expansion.
Interface: The gameplay interface always felt a little to me like Windows 98, not that that's a bad thing. It primarily involves clicking on buttons to designate what subset of your population should be doing what. Balncing how many people should be working at what task and how many of a certain resource they should gather.
Sound: Soundtrack is basic, but suits the environment well. Mostly accostic guitar. No voice acting.
Graphics: The view is primarily isometric. The graphics are extremely well textured and animated considering the price of the game. I've seen the framerate dip a bit when on max zoom out, but never falling below 50 fps. Otherwise, the framerate remains solid.
Overall: I've never been a large fan of city builder/management/planner games. For the most part I find the mechanics tedious and not rewarding enough to delve into for long periods of time. This game has proved a tremendous exception. The primary reason being the survival aspects that it incorporates. Don't have enough housing to keep your population warm? They die. Don't have enough food for your population? They die. Don't have enough doctors to treat your citizens? They die. Fun, challeging but fair, coupled with a great astetic make this game an easy recommendation. Worth every cent of the $20 asking price.

I started playing Sunless Sea after playing a fair bit of Fallen London(a browser based game set in the same world), so many of the oddities of Sunless Sea were familiar to me(the heavy emphasis on story, the need to gather items for certain plot gates, etc). If you like the story or setting in one, I highly recommend playing the other for new insights into the lore.
With that out of the way: The writing in this game is stellar. It trends towards weirdness, sly comedy, and horror, but you usually don't feel like you're being beaten over the head with it.
The non-story gameplay feels tacked on, to put it nicely. Exploring the map and discovering new ports is fun, but your ship is slow(even after some improvements). Once you're at the point where you're mainly going through known waters, you'll be dying for a fast forward button. Managing fuel and supplies vs the rest of your cargo is okay at first, but gets tiresome as you venture further and further out to zee. Combat is awkward, and tends to be more trouble than it's worth unless you're after something specific.
There's no system to bookmark story options you're working towards(like Fallen London's Plan system), and the objectives section of your gazeteer often lacks helpful information(like directions) given at the time a quest was. I recommend making a text file for notes about what you're doing, where to go, and what you need.
The music is very atmospheric, and I love the art style. No complaints on either front.
The game does have some bugs in it - for instance, I had an event that was clearly intended to damage my hull, but completely restored my hull instead. I haven't seen any gamebreaking bugs, though.
tl;dr: If you love story-heavy games, try Sunless Sea. If you just want non-story gameplay, give this a pass. Think of it as a great CYOA game with a mediocre sailing/sea combat simulator stapled to it.

Telltale's Batman is pretty much what you would expect if you've played any of Telltale's previous games, so I'm not going to spend a lot of time explaining the gameplay mechanics.
The story is pretty good, and it has a main villain that I'd not seen before in other Batman games or films, who is linked to Bruce Wayne's past in an interesting way. I liked having the opportunity to play more as Bruce and explore his relationships with important characters such as Selina Kyle, Harvey Dent, Jim Gordon and Alfred Pennyworth while not wearing the Bat suit. Voice acting is top quality, headlined by Troy Baker (Bioshock Infinite, Tales from the Borderlands) as Bruce and Laura Bailey (who is awesome in far too many things to list) as Selina.
However I'm not sure if the Batman universe is a particularly good fit for a Telltale game. Although there a few story choices to make, I never felt like any of them were critically important, especially if you compare it to the likes of The Walking Dead or Game of Thrones where you always feel like any character could die at any time if you make the wrong choice. And because the player is controlling a famous character whose personality is already quite well established, any potential moral choice is heavily restricted. You can't let the player do anything too drastic (for example, kill someone) that Batman would never do. It also doesn't have the sense of humour that made Tales from the Borderlands so good.
The QTE based combat sequences are visually exciting, but they have almost zero challenge. In fact I'm sure there were a few times that I actually missed the button press without suffering any consequences. It might be an unfair comparison, but when you've already played the Arkham games which have excellent combat, these scenes can feel a bit weak.
However, there is a stronger puzzle element than any of the Telltale games that I've played. There are 3 or 4 occasions where Batman has to investigate a crime scene, search for clues, and then link pieces of evidence together to figure out what happened. I've often heard Batman referred to as the "World's Greatest Detective", and Telltale managed to display those skills better than any of the Arkham games, and any of the films.
The game's length is a little disappointing though, at 8 hours in total across the 5 episodes. This is significantly shorter than Walking Dead season 1, Tales from the Borderlands and Game of Thrones, although its a little longer than Walking Dead season 2 and around the same as Wolf Among Us. Other developer's episodic story games such as Life Is Strange and Dreamfall Chapters are also much longer.
I think this is a good, but not great, game that is worth playing if you're a fan of Batman, although it might be best to wait for a minor sale. I bought at 33% off which seems like a fair price. Telltale continue to be one of the best storytellers in the games industry, but I still would like to see them try to change up their formula and improve the gameplay - or implement some truly branching narratives (I'm thinking like how Witcher 2 has two completely different versions of chapter 2) - to help their games become even better.

Here is a "big picture" review: not about the game's specifics, but rather about the overall experience of playing it. Despite what Steam's hours display, I've been playing this game off and on since 2008 or 2009; I've sunk at least hundreds of hours into it, and hundreds of dollars. I had never played any collectible trading card games before Pox Nora, but I've always liked turn-based strategy games, everything from Chess to Warhammer to Civilization.
So, I'll be writing this review from that sort of perspective ... as well as from the perspective of one of the game's players who's put as much of his playing time into its single-player campaigns (which are numerous by now, to say the least, after many years worth of clockwork expansions) as multiplayer matches.
Pox Nora is Chess on steroids.
If you've ever played one of the earlier Master of Orion games (I or II), and then played Space Empires IV or V, it's that level of "next level" that I'm speaking of. Forget steroids, actually. More like PCP, no, screw it, bath salts, face-eating, madness inducing, streaking down the highway naked, bath salts.
Chess is an unforgiving game of skill that involves some luck; while card games can often be unforgivingly about luck, despite all the skill involved.
When I was younger, I took a regular 52-card deck of poker cards, and four sets of Chess pieces (16 per player), and helped my nephew construct a Chess variant with fantasy-themed factions and different kinds of ameliorating strategies for each.
Hearts were courageous and noble and were aligned with "good" magic-using Diamonds; Clubs were cunning and nefarious and were aligned with "evil" necromancy-using Spades. Cards drawn and used went on a cool-down pile.
All of these cards represented magical abilities or special moves but, in a sense, can all be boiled down to difficulty
; they added variety and complexity to Chess, which is fun ... but probably stripped away much of its difficulty, having given each faction 13 ameliorating "get out of jail" cards if played halfway decently (52 cards divided by four "factions" equals 13 cards per faction). Still, somebody's got to win and somebody's got to lose; it's still a game of strategy.
Well imagine my delight at discovering Pox Nora, a game that features
factions ("good and evil" alignments intact, allowing two versus two multiplayer),
of playing pieces and
of cards representing spells, abilities, artifacts, even structures (30 of which can be fielded per faction, per game, including faction-split 15/15 decks) ... as well as playing-boards that turn Chess's flat, 64-square environment on its ear, with elements of terrain, cover, strategic points, magic zones, and so on.
Pox Nora's campaigns, many of them free to play, go even further with imaginative scenarios and storylines that will take your playing pieces and decks across scrolling, irregular playing-boards reminiscent of table-top wargaming.
In other words, Pox Nora took the 52-card deck, 64-piece bag of steroids I dreamed up, and poured bath salts all over it.
If you can't see how flipping cool that is, get out of here, you're fired.

Oh, where do I start with this game? I love it, and you should too. If you have ever wanted a more tactical experience from your shooters, this is it. None of that common run and gun ideals that modern shooters like to use, and being able to respawn after doing really well and starting again gives it an edge over Counter-Strike. If you prefer Red Orchestra or Rising Storm is up to you, but I will speak of both. In Red Orchestra you play as either the German Wermacht or the Russian Red Army. Both have weapons that feel equal to each other, and you never feel that one weapon or two is overpowered. Most of the time, when shot you have no idea where it is coming from and you begin to run into a state of blind panic, which most games try to achieve, and fail at. This shooter is able to stir feelings inside of me that other games that were mostly story based couldn't. Now, Rising Storm is the western counterpart to Red Orchestra. Set in the Pacific Theater, you and the enemy will fight to the death in much more close quartered maps then in Red Orchestra. Just as what actually happened in history, the American Army has better weapons. Most if not all rifles are semi-automatic and those that aren't are either machine guns or the deadly flamethrower. However, the Japanese are able to counter this by having crafty ways to balance out the fight. Japanese grenades are able to be planted into the ground to form make-shift landmines, and knee mortars provide long range ways to launch explosives at the enemy within relative safety. Also katanas. Come on, who doesn't like katanas? Another crucial part of the Japanese kit is the Banzai charge. This makes your character emit a loud war cry, and the more players that join your charge, the less damage you take and the harder it is for the enemy to kill you.
To tell you the truth, if you can become invested into this game you will not be dissapointed. The characters you play as generally drop like flies, but if you can keep one around long enough to score some kills or just get the literal♥♥♥♥♥♥kicked out of them without dying, you begin to feel attached to your character. All sides have a certain bar that if emptied, your vision turns black and white and the screen beings to blur. Any number of things can trigger this, whether it be being shot at, seeing your best pal get the brains blown out the back of his head, or getting shelled by artillery. You begin to feel sorry for your digital character, glad that he is in the virtual trench instead of you. Your character bursts with personality, generally being courageous and strong when shooting at the enemy, and whimpering and praying to something, anything for rescue when being shot at. This game is fantastic. Well worth the price. I bought it, and so should you.

"So, imagine a TCG except you play your cards into a hex-based battlefield and your units must advance onwards to the opponent's shrine (like their nexus in LoL), positioning themselves near fonts along the way to give you bonus mana. Once you kill your opponent's shrine, you win!"
"So, duelyst?"
"Well, yeah, except that the battlefield is WAY BIGGER, fonts (mana spring tiles) can be contested by the enemy if the enemy is nearby them, and they provide a mana bonus as long as you control them. Also, cards have more than just attack and health - they have AP, which they gain every turn depending on their speed. They use this AP to do everything - move, attack, use special abilities"
"Huh."
"Yeah, and there's stuff like terrain on the battlefield too. Also, cards have plenty of abilities, ranging from stuff like Flight and Damage Shield to things like Boon of the Wind (grant bonus to closest friendly flying unit when played) and Escape (gain stealth after damaged at end of turn)"
"Stealth? How would that work?"
"It's really cool - basically your opponent just no longer sees the unit. It stays hidden until it is revealed somehow - say, you attack with it, your opponent moves a unit onto the exact same spot, casts an AoE spell which damages the unit. Some units have detection which reveal stealthed units in a radius around it."
"Sounds really complex"
"And it is. Takes a lot of time to learn. But it's a really good game. There's no RNG in attacks - no accuracy, no criticals, That intro above? Doesn't even say anything about relics or equipment, deckbuilding rules, faction bonuses, range etc."
That said, the game is really good once you sink your teeth into it. It stopped being p2p when it got acquired from SOE (it used to be that you can only acquire new cards with real cash), there's even a training grounds mode where you can only use preset decks to play with, so in that mode you're not losing out due to a low collection. But that said, you will lose lots and lots of games against experienced players because you just don't know how to play well.

Most of all, The Beginner's Guide is the most human experience I've ever had in a game. For that, I am forever grateful.

It is finally finished! This beloved series that just keeps growing on ya! I'm extremely impressed by the way that Dave Gilbert developed this story. By the end of the whole series I felt very connected to Rosa, Joey, and the cast of characters from the entire series. It is also amazing to see the games improve as they progressed, getting rid of elements that detracted from the game and replacing them with elements that helped push the game along. I'm not much of a mystery/clue finding type of gamer, so if a game series is able to get me to enjoy something that I'm not that into then the game is pretty special. For this fifth and final installment here are some of the pro's and con's of the game.
Pro's: The storyline is marvelous in this game, lets just say everything wraps up rather nicely. I absolutely love Rosa and Joeys relationship and think that the actor who plays Joey does an amazing job and yes the hilarious banter is still there. The puzzles were fun, as usual. I was glad that this game had some different puzzles that the other four games had not done before and the continued ability to switch between Rosa/Joey. The length of the game was good, comparable to Convergence and Deception (Unbound and Legacy both seemed a little short).
Con's: One word, the art. Still hate it and always will! I also think it is funny that I love and hate the consistency issues. I think that making the necessary changes from game to game is a good thing to do, but it really makes you feel like they should have done that in the previous games and can be a little jarring when Joey is drawn different, the style of music changes, the mechanics change, or the voice acting is different.
As I've said in many of the other reviews, some of these games by themselves are not the greatest (cough...Blackwell Legacy), but if you can get through the first boring chapter in the book then you will find a pretty amazing series one that will not disappoint.
Blackwell Legacy: 6/10
Blackwell Unbound: 8/10
Blackwell Convergence: 7.6/10
Blackwell Deception: 8.2/10
Blackwell Epiphany: 8.5/10
Blackwell Series: 8.2/10
Check out my other point and click adventure reviews on my page!

London, late 1800s. Bats have stolen the city, taking it to deep and eldritch caverns far below the earth. Socialites rub shoulders with devils, and death is often an inconvenience at worst.
This is the setting for Sunless Sea, a roguelike from Failbetter Games. If you've played Uncharted Waters, it is a lot like that series - you sail from place to place, looking for opportunity for trade and new land. Where this game truly shines, however, is the story and writing. Fallen London, the game that inspired this one, is text-based - and it shows. The writing is witty, atmospheric and clever.
The gameplay is clearly not the main focus of the game, but it feels solid and fun - if slow and, at times, overreliant on opportunities the writing gives you. If you simply want a sailing/economy simulator, you may be better served looking elsewhere. However, those who take to zailing the Zee for stories and atmosphere will not be disappointed.
All in all, I would wholeheartedly recommend Sunless Sea to anyone looking for a little more substance in the writing, as well as anyone who wants to experience a truly unique setting. You're bound to come back with an interesting Zee-Ztory or two.

There are few games out there with as much to explore in story as Sunless Sea. If you're interested in worldbuilding in story, this is your game. The game tells you mostly nothing, save how to play it, which is pretty simple. The real draw here is exploring the various islands throughout the sunless sea.
The game is littered with hints here and there of what this world might be. You'll quickly figure out from context clues that you're actually underground and that there is an above world sea. You're comepelled to figure out more about this world because it is legitimately interesting. The world is populated by various races of sentient and non-sentient creatures, as well as different cultures of humans: from intelligent apes to the decaying mummified elders. And while many might make the lovecraftian parallels, and indeed it is part of the game's tags on steam, the parallels run deeper than "tentacled monsters exist". The atmosphere is dreary, almost nihilistic. It paints a picture of a picture of an uncaring universe marred by insanity and violence. If you've read Lovecraft or Poe, you'll be right at home reading through the various text within Sunless sea. This isn't the pop-culture Lovecraft you might know, this is the actual Lovecraft.
This game is one part reading one part resource management. If you aren't interested in reading, this isn't your game.
The gameplay itself will challenge you to make wise decisions every step of the way. As with life, you'll get no rewards without risking something. Sometimes it's a chance motigated by your attributes, other times it's a decision like "Should I try and visit this island with this much fuel in my tanks?". After some time, you get into the groove of visiting islands to get the local news and then returning to London to cash in. This is your real bread and butter and there's some semblance of a main quest you're trying to accomplish. Each time you die, you play as an heir with potentially new goals. Along the way, you'll also have a miraid of side quests to accomplish, though no quest can really truly be done alone; you must be efficient with your fuel and supplies and this usually means plotting a course to hit as many islands as possible.
If you want to sit back and relax and enjoy a story, this is your game.

I got this game last night, and have already put about seven hours into it. The gameplay is fantastic, and it makes you feel like an action star when you do something ridiculous like taking someone's gun, shooting them, tossing the gun in the air, morphing into another person, catching your gun, and killing someone else.
The game's campaign is about two hours long, and the storyline can be straight-up garbage at times. Apparently the developers underestimated just how great the gameplay is, choosing to interupt you every three or four levels with some stupid plotline. There was even a part where you are forced to quit the game!
After getting through the storyline though, the game really opens up. There are multiple challenge modes that create a twist on the campaign with special restrictions like katana only or only weapons and punching. There are also endless modes, which put you against endless enemies in either a timed setting or a regular setting. All of these modes makes the storyline well worth the annoyance, and I found myself enjoying the game much more with these types of modes.
While the price is a little high, I do recommend this game. The gameplay is fantastic, and I can easily see myself putting another 10-15 hours into it.

I have taken to playing as many RPG Maker games on Steam as possible, and the ones this game caught my attention as it was in a series, had favorable reviews, and just looked fun. The game, once you get into it, is quite fun, actually. No matter the difficulty, the boss fights are always exciting, and the frequent side quests allow me to level up, explore the world, find items, and fight enemies instead of just grinding. The writing is also quite playful, with the characters originally being each introduced in a serious manner, only for the frequent banter causing you to realize this isn't a serious game. The game's tone very much reminded me of the Paper Mario games, with frequent jokes  (just the whole auction house quest) and fourth wall jabs (An entire town full of purposely generic NPCs) being handeled in a way that they don't feel inconsistant with the game's mythology and darker villains. This isn't an inventive groundbreaking RPG Maker game, but it is exactly what I expect of a good standard rpg made with it, a creative story, very nice puzzles, and endearing characters.

Another solid, stand-alone, story driven game from Telltale Games. For those of you who are familiar with Telltale games, the gameplay here is the same as literally all other TTG games post-The Walking Dead. To those of you who arn't, WASD movement with point & click interaction and a heavy emphasis on choices & character development.
Many of the negative reviews are due to glitches and save cloud problems which have largely been patched now. I only experienced one minor graphical glitch during my whole play through where a characters mouth did not move as he spoke. Aside from this, the action scenes are highly entertaining and the voice acting and story are both solid. Probably the only Batman game where you will play as Bruce Wayne more than Batman but don't be fooled, its more fun than it sounds.
To Telltale fans, the controls and gameplay will be very familiar to you.
For Batman fans with no knowledge of Telltale Games, I recommend trying the first free episode to see if you like it as the gameplay here is in no way similar to the Arkham series but is, in my opinion, very good in a very different way.
