Outlast is one of the most harrowing first-person horror experiences to come out in a long time, and that's in an intentional way, not in a "this game is so bad it hurts" kind of way. Outlast will brutalize you by way of your character and his ordeals, while keeping you going just to figure out just what the hell is going on.
The excuse for Miles, the protagonist, hanging around to document the goings-on at Massive Mountain for the sake of journalism or whatever once everything goes to♥♥♥♥♥♥is a bit thin, but frustration with that is quickly cast aside as you start hunting for a way both to escape the now-sealed facility and do so with the scoop you came for in the first place. Strange things are going down at this asylum, and it's more the horrors man's own mind can manifest that you have to deal with than it is any sort of monster.
One thing I particularly enjoyed about Outlast was its variety of traversal methods; you're encouraged to look up, down, and all around for ways out of different situations, or to die trying. Vents, busted-out walls, and other unexpected passages abound through the environments, and most situations require using more than one path to get around the things or people that stand in your way. I also liked, to some extent, the handful of prominent residents populating the asylum. While in some ways, they felt like themed bosses that weren't entirely necessary, their quirks added variety to their respective haunts, and kept things from being a long run of dodging basic inmates. The game also made a very good point of how there's no way you're getting through things unscathed, both mentally and physically. The hiding mechanic was also a delight, especially given it doesn't always work as well as you may hope.
The camera, especially its night vision function, becomes so essential that it risks becoming the Detective Vision (a la the Arkham games) of Outlast, in that you'd likely be better in leaving it on all the time and getting used to a green-tinged world. However, this is balanced fairly well by the need for batteries to run that night vision, forcing you to use it intermittently when supplies are running thin. It was nice to have other gameplay functions involving the camera as well, such as unlocking more information about the story and the events leading up to it by filming certain things and areas as you go along.
Whether the supernatural hokum introduced in the game's late chapters was entirely necessary is debatable, but after dealing with everything the game throws at you up to when that becomes the centerpiece, it feels natural enough. I imagine it'll see more explanation and involvement in the sequel, as the Whistleblower DLC didn't seem to touch upon it quite so much.
This is an absolute must-play for any horror fan, and I highly suggest snagging it and the Whistleblower content as soon as possible. After all, we've only a few more months (as of this posting) before there's a whole new Outlast to explore.

Five Nights at Freddy's is a Psychological Horror game, that had a very...interesting story behind it. Now, why would you play this? Well, some people play it because they love horror, or they want to beat the super hard mode
But....this game isn't really a game meant for the horror to it....it's meant for the knowledge behind the game. I never bought this game, a friend gifted it to me, for me to get super scared, but now, I figured why he's so addicted to the story behind the game. It takes place in a local pizzeria, but there have been several stories about...missing kids...after they were "killed". The game explains nothing further then that. It's up to you to figure out. I really don't like horror games, but a game like this, almost made me want to get the "second" one. I never did get it, and I will, but, I'm only going to get it for the story.
Let me tell you about the core gameplay in this, if that's what you want the game for. You have the night's watch, there are 4
animatronics, that think you are an endoskeleton, out of it's suit. And the Pizzerias rules, you must never be out of your suit, in that case, the animatronics will come after you, and try to stuff you into a suit. Wouldn't be so bad if it wasn't full of wires and such right? The game is very VERY challenging. Well, Bignastycupcake™, what makes you say that? Well, there's power, and you have such a limited amount. Can't stay in your cameras, you will run out of power, you can't keep your doors closed. Oh yea, theres doors, well, they drain power. And you can't just sit in your office, or a animitronic will get you. So you must keep watch. You might want to turn on those ears, you'll need em. You will hear a noise when an animatronic is in your office, and my god, is it the most disturbing noise one could hear. Another reason you need to keep your ears on, one of the animatronics
will make a noise, and it is INVISIBLE, you can't see him when hes at your door....so better be listening....
If you LOVE puzzles/mystery, get this, and uncover the story behind it. The Game Theorists do a well job on figuring out, on the backstory of this game. They always say it's
a theory correct? Well, you can figure it out your self....unlock the true meaning behind this game, and figure out whether you can survive the game enough, to figure out the puzzle, or you can simply just be a loser and not.
Well, what are you waiting for? That 5.00$ isn't gonna spend itself!

Edit: Based on the game many years ago, so some of this changed since then.
PoxNora has a special place in my heart. I played it for hundreds of hours prior to steam when the game was still young and they had just changed the game to remove all random numbers (no "hit chance" or "dice rolls" - pure strategy without random numbers). Back then it was a revelation and since then most other strategy games I play ended up being disappointing when I compare them to PoxNora.
Why did I quit and don't recommend it?
It's a digital trading card game. You needed to invest significant money and trading to get a competitive deck. There were limited edition cards that were being sold for several hundred dollar. Then suddenly previously limited cards were suddenly sold on a "first come" basis without a warning, increasing in price the more frequently they were bought. Powerful legacy cards that rarely saw action got picked up for a dollar or two -- yet the price jumped very high within a day and most people missed out making the matches very unbalanced suddenly.
Then the new expansions kept adding insane epic cards (powercreep...), while completely devaluing other cards. In the end I had to sell my cards because I had spend significant cash on them and the company kept devaluing them with each update.
Moral of the story:
There is a reason classic trading card games are being replaced by living card games (fixed expansions instead of booster packs) because people rightfully think trading card games are robbing their wallet. A game where you buy digital cards for insane costs yet the company only changes a database entry and at any point in time can make your investment worthless? Great idea. Thumbs down.

I'll be short.
The art is great, the writing is fantastic, the universe and atmosphere is spot on.
The actual gameplay and combat is horrendous. Same for the economy.  The UI also takes more than a while to get used to reading properly.
I have about 20 hours in this, uncovered most of the map minus 2-3 locations and got to the end-game point where i was hunting down specific things and chasing down 500 hp monsters.. and it was at that point where i drew a parallel to another game.
Terraria.
You have the same 'this is my map that will become my home' feeling, there's the same long-term item/quest progression and while the universe is more interesting here, it's not too far thrown from Terraria's offering of a 'living'/evolving world. Sadly, this is where i realised how much i disliked moving the ship across the zee, the actual core gameplay of moving and shooting the ship, and how much time that took to get to the good bits, the role-playing events, the storylines and the outcomes. For some reason, some of Terarria's 0.05% drop rate items felt LESS like a grind that getting Echoes here, and that was because the core game was still fun to play. Eventually you'll end up with ships with an Aft weapon and Forward weapon but by the time you get there to enjoy variety, you can kill anything in the game with a Deck gun you purchased 20 minutes in the game and the starting ship. A final note on the gameplay, the game doesn't tell you this, but selling pretty much anything is a mistake. Minus stories which you can sell if they go over say 10 to the University, you should be keeping everything else you stumble upon, even to the risk of overflowing your cargo, since you'll need it for some quest at some time and getting that item back will be a HUGE hassle. Secrets/Skill points also apply for that since you can trade them in for unique items at a certain spot.
Either way, all in all, if you can get Sunless Sea for anything under 10E, pick it up and spend a weekend with it, it's not a bad experience, just don't expect to be kept drawn in too much.
PS: For a game that also has rogue-like passing-down/legacy mechanics, you really lost a ♥♥♥♥ tonne of things upon dying to the point of wondering why it's even really there, one of the most expensive things you can never get back is your ship. Setting yourself up for the next character takes more time and effort that just keeping your current character alive and properly fitted.
PS2: Speaking of rogue-like, for a game with so much unique content and poor core gameplay, i don't know why anyone would play a legacy of multiple characters with this. You'd be doing pretty much the same things, with a slightly-randomised map, nailing down the first three hours to doing the same things anyway until you get your actual sea-legs and can afford trips and events which you have already mostly seen anyway and know in which order to do to be MAX EFFICIENT.

Never before have I been so astonished at a game's ability to pull me in and immerse me in the world so much that theories and questions are constantly coming up in my mind. This game is so artfully made, so eloquent, and with the best unexpected humor, to call it a masterpiece would be a trivial compliment in scale to how fantastic this game truly is. The gameplay is everything I could hope for in a sea (or zee) captaining experience, not to mention with a lore unlike any other, so convoluted and enigmatic, yet more satisfying and wholesome than a chest full of riches. The story and mysterious world surrounding this game are by far the greatest I have ever encountered so far in a game, yet to the initial few playthroughs, hidden. Its one that is initially unseen and unspoken, yet once you find it, its like the Neath itself, unfathomably extensive and mysterious. The only negative aspect I have to say is that the game isnt easy, and I dont mean that as in it's unfair or that I simply cant play well, it's the fact that while youre exploring and learning more and more, you are at a constant struggle to survive. There is no simple farming for money, there are no quick tips to beat difficult enemies, theres not even a constant map over your multiple captains' lifetimes. So if you enjoy a real challenge, a unmatched immersive story, and have a hankering to be a hardened, monster-wrangling, zee-loving gentleman fighting to survive in an industrial revolutionary underground ocean, there is no better game for you than Sunless Sea!

Very simple controls allow the player to get the full idea of movement within minutes, and after that it's only up to the player's perception to figure out how to advance through Limbo. And perceptive you will indeed have to be: the game does not provide any hints for you whatsoever. You're on your own from the start, which is quite refreshing + making each step of progress satisfying.
Some of the puzzles might need to get solved for the first time by trial and error (where error = death), but the game loads right before the puzzle "room" after that, so there's no frustrating punishing you for something you couldn't predict. But, you don't have to worry about a lack of challenge either - puzzles can take some thinking to crack + there's always that
achievement to aim for.
Aesthetics are minimalistic, but despite that (or perhaps thanks to that) pleasing. I personally recommend playing the game at night with the lights off, so the world around becomes fittingly black'n'white just as well.

Tropico 5 is a great development of the series. A common complaint for Tropico 4 was that it was too much like Tropico 3, so this is the answer for those that wanted something different. Luckily they didn't change anything about the game that made the previous ones so great. I recorded this video with no music, because sadly Youtube griefs me anytime I've done that for any Tropico game... so the video is a bit lacking. Just play some Hispanic music in the background and you'll be all set.
The age system is the biggest difference in this iteration of the game, other than perhaps multiplayer, and although it is a valiant effort... it becomes tedious after progressing through it a few times.  It works ok for the story mode, but the best part about the age system is that it can essentially be turned off during sandbox games by setting the starting era to Modern Times.
Multiplayer looks good... but I haven't played enough to really get a feel for it yet.
The best change to Tropico 5 is the Dynasty system. Building your dynasty is fun, and finally gives you a reason to have a fat stack of cash in your slush fund.
So all in all, I'm really happy with the game. I sometimes miss the simplicity of the older games, mainly because of the addition of the age system, but the Tropico series is still my favorite city builder, and I expect to play Tropico 5 for many, many more hours to come.

The final part of the Blackwell series does what you’d hope the final episode of a series would do. Every scrap of story left hanging from earlier parts is brought back and wrapped up here, rewarding you for sticking with it to the end. The production values are better than ever, and when I started it I hoped I would be here saying it was perfect.
It might be because I played them all back to back, but I didn’t like how transparent the story structure felt. The second game established a structure which all the later games followed. This worked for the second and third game. But by the fourth it felt old, and doing it again for the final game made it weaker. I don’t want to overdo this point though, it didn’t by any means ruin the game for me. It’s just one of a few things that made it not as good as it could have been.
Another weak point is the solutions to a few of the puzzles. A common point and click problem: the pixel hunting. In this game there are loads of locations, some with busy visual styles. There’s a couple times where I wanted to rip my hair out because I overlooked a 4 pixel thing on a table right next to a pile of identical stuff I couldn’t interact with.
I also didn’t like how it ended. Parts of the third act were very exciting and made me giddy. But how it ultimately ends made me go “oh ok”, instead of jumping off the walls in excitement as I was hoping. That said, it wasn’t bad! I feel myself warming up to the ending as I’m writing about it. I still very much recommend this series to anyone who is on the fence about playing it. As point and click adventures go, this series, and this final chapter, are easily among the better ones.

Believe the hype. Irrational Games' incredibly acclaimed horror/action first-person shooter is a remarkable showcase of the games industry's potential for intelligent storytelling and important societal and political relevance.
is almost as perfect as a game can get, and it is undoubtedly one of the most fun, engaging, and smart games I have played in a long time.
In
, the player is Jack, a generic, middle-aged every-man type character who - after his plane trip takes a detour into the middle of the Atlantic Ocean - finds himself in the underwater city of Rapture, where he must alter his genetic code with plasmids, gather a unique arsenal of weapons, and collect the genetic enhancing drug ADAM in order to survive and escape a crumbling oceanic dystopia.
The story is presented as simplistic in the beginning, only to give way to a deeply complex narrative who's subtle roots take subconscious hold very early in the game. Partly through player-exploration (in the finding of citizen recorded audio logs) as well as through linear progression, the player uncovers the dark past of his underwater prison as he finds himself caught between the battles of the city's objectivist/utopia-ist greed monger Andrew Ryan, and a rebel named Atlas who helps the player escape during the game's opening moments. The story works both as a basic narrative, as well as a critique of Utopianism, and the Ayn Rand-founded philosophy of Objectivism. In a moral based storyline, the player witnesses impressive narrative twists and moments that don't disrupt flow, in addition to observing a prediction of an Objectivist society come to life - a world where everyone is only in it for themselves. Not only is the story impressive in and of itself, Bioshock works perfectly as a critique of the ideals of Objectivism/Utopianism, making it one of the most politically and philosophically in-tune games ever.
The games accomplishment of deep and rich player immersion is truly remarkable. There's a reason why Rapture has become one of gaming's most recognized locations, and it's resident Big Daddies (and accompanying Little Sisters) some of the industry's most infamous enemies. The games' haunting atmosphere and dark narrative are truly top tier and induct the player with a sense of despair and loneliness, adding to the immersive feel. Surely one of the most captivating experiences I've had with a game.
In terms of gameplay,
hasn't aged a day. Using a unique assortment of weapons (ranging from the famous wrench to more heavy weaponry like the flame-thrower) as well as an array of biological "super power"-type weapons called Plasmids, the player fights their way through armies of Rapture's now-insane citizens called Splicers (driven to their state due to overuse and abuse of the ADAM drug). The gameplay is not only fun and gripping, but also inventive, especially for the time of its release. It's very open-ended, despite the linear design, and the player choice is extremely well-implemented. And the Big Daddy fights are challenging in the best way possible - as well as being equally rewarding. In short, the gameplay in
is not only superb in its field of First person shooters, but it's some of the best in any game, period.
Also worth noting are the graphics. For a game made in 2007 (7 years ago at the time of this review), the game looks great. However, even despite its technical prowess, the art design and level composition is truly incredible. It's one of the many factors that bring Rapture to life, and make it one of the most impressive gaming achievements to date.
is surely one of the best games ever made. Filled with memorable characters, enemies, and locations, as well as providing an engaging storyline and relevant societal critiques, this is what a game should strive to be. A landmark achievement.

The wonderful finale to one of my favorite series of games ever.
The graphics are gorgeous, and the voice-acting and atmosphere are spot-on. You can really tell how far the series has grown and developed since the Blackwell Legacy, as Epiphany presents darker themes, more complex (yet still logical) puzzles, and more advanced graphics. All elements have become perfected in this installment. Of course, since Epiphany is the final installment in a 5-game series, it is best enjoyed only after playing the previous games since by then you'll have a greater understanding of the characters and backstory - and those games are definitely worth playing and come at good prices. All of the previous plot threads are tied together, and a lot of information is revealed in this game that wouldn't make sense without playing the previous games first.
The story comes to a peak in this game in terms of emotion, and manages to tackle more serious themes skillfully. The characters are well-rounded and interesting as always, and the banter between Rosa and Joey is still present and brings great humor to lighten the mood. The final scenes of this game were very-well done and gave the series a proper grand finale that it deserved, but it can be a lot to handle at first after playing the previous games and becoming so attached to the characters. This is truly one of the few games that broke my heart. The entire series has made me greatly admire the skill and effort of Dave Gilbert and his team.
I give this game a 10/10, and I strongly recommend the entire series to anyone who enjoys adventure games.

I bought it for 8 cents just because, and I didn't really expect a particularly engaging game. In fact, it is far from a masterpiece, and I don't think it's worth its full price.
The battle system is somewhat simplistic (but maybe I'd be expecting too much from a RPG Maker game, I don't know), and the setting is not the most breath-taking I've ever seen, but this game does have its strengths.
For starters, I loved the soundtrack, not to mention the light-hearted (for the most part) atmosphere which I didn't expect from a game with such a title and the humour. Holy♥♥♥♥♥♥ the surreal situations and interactions I've witnessed.
SPOILER: This is a game where you see a dude make a bomb out of a wooden stake, a plastic frog and a book about cats (yes, the subject is apparently important), and a bridge out of a rose, a diamond, a bucket of straw and a BOOMERANG. If that doesn't sound awesome, I don't know what does.
I had paid it 8 cents, true, but I'd recommend it anyway if it was discounted by, say, even a mere 50%.
Another nice feature is that you don't have to grind levels in order to advance through the game. I mean, if you do happen to be needing some, the quests are far more rewarding (experience-wise) than battling countless hoardes of monsters. Oh, and no random encounters à la Final Fantasy I-X, which is also good.

I stumbled out of the damn, unfamiliar terrain stretching before me...
...four hours of light left...
...the valley walls grasped at the heavens, the cave swallowed me into its enigmatic depths, then spit me out into yet another desolate forest...but there, before me--a bridge! A hargbinger of sanctuary...a cabin must be close now...
...darkness was upon me...I desparately needed shelter...
I stumbled down the road, finding nothing, until my body temperature was dangerously low. I started a fire, used the last of my firewood, tried to sleep for a few hours...but no, a barking awoke me, there would be no rest for me.
I fought desperately, stabbed blindly, until the wolf was driven wimpering away. I was not unscathed, however...my coat was torn, my arm badly sprained. What's worse, I realized a blizzard had begun, whipped snow around my head, and scattering the dead remains of my fire...
...I fled further into the darkness...
...I could barely feel my limbs, I needed warmth. I sprinted through the storm, grabbing up whatever twigs I could. In the lee of a hill, I began another fire...I ate, watching my food supply dwindle.
The fickle wind changed directions, my fire snuffed out.
...I fled further into the darkness...
...Again, I repeated the process, gathering twigs, gnawing at what I had left, grabbing what rest I could, and again, the wind changed...
...I fled further into the darkness....
...Finally, a couple hours after dawn, the storm lifted. By that point, my condition was so bad the world was hazy...whenever I turned my head, afterimages burned across my field of vision.
I stumbled around the hill I'd sheltered behind, blinking in the sun...and froze.
There, right next to where I'd been stumbling blindly all night, was a town.
I edged towards it, overcome...
...I had survived the night...my salvation was at hand...
...then behind me, I heard a barking...
..I did not even have the energy to put up a fight.
I entered the long dark.
Would die an ironic death at the loveless hand of the bitter north again...11/10

This game has always been one of the strongest battlefield tactics/strategy card games available. That being said it is not a game for eveyone.
History Feel free to TLDR.
This game has suffered a mixed history. It began its life small with not nearly enough content and prices comprable to magic cards, which was silly. As a reslt the origonal creator inevitably sold off his partly successfull game to another group who for some reason thought they could do better by doing nothing different. When they realized they were dumb they sold it on merrit of; a now larger card base, how good a game it was, and how established it was to Sony. Sony who proceeded to host the servers and change nothing. When sony realized they were stupd and finally thought to ask the question hey what is this and hy did we buy it again? They decided they would offload the cash hemoraging game on some poor other fellas. And here we are today.
The newst owners have introduced some systems which make this game legitimatelly possible to play for free. Between the player to player untaxed card trading, and free pack give aways this game is now a game i reccomend.
The game has a depth that no card game or strategy game has ever attained, so far. Your average round will have around 1000 damage smattered across a playing field and the the one who is victorious in a battle of equalls is the one who simply lets 75 of that damage fall to close to home. It's a exciting struggle of wits on a battle field that feels like true magic. With a game as old as this the stock of spells available leaves you guessing the kind of wizard your up against the whole way through, which is exactly as magic should be.
Failings.
*It's largest failing is the games pace is very slow. However the reason for this is the complexety of the tuns and thought behind them. Average game 40 minutes, 20 personal turns, 40 total.
*The second failing is there are very pivitol game mechanics that are not explained anywere.
*A HUGE learning curve, thankfully most of it can be done in single player.

As an Alpha, the Long Dark is a very impressive game crafted by the Unity engine. When played at medium or hard difficulty, the game truly pushes the limits of the player on how to survive in the winter wilderness of northern Canada, and on easy mode is a tranquil experience as the game describes.

Hopefully with future updates the game will become more expansive and immersive (and please god let the story mode be amazing).

The Moorhuhn gallery shooters are a thing of the past, but they are still fun enough to play for nostalgia. And this one, Moorhuhn X, is probably one of the best in the series.
While the franchise branched into several genres, most Moorhuhns games are one-level gallery shooters, where you shoot a great number of chickens with your shotgun. Why? There is no real reason. We just loved shooting video game chickens in Europe near the turn of the century.
The store title is misleading, because this game here is actually a remake of the fifth instalment of the main series, originally called Moorhuhn X. It was sort of a turning point back then, where they introduced a new chicken design and a bonus level (although reaching it is quite tricky).
Moorhuhn X is also considered to be the best of the series by many, thanks to the fun level design full of secrets to explore in the allotted short time limit. Still, by today’s standards, it is still nothing more than a one-off novelty game made for those who want a little nostalgia.

I personally have worked in call center for 7 years. I was the guy who probly called you about Directv, Bank of America, or even sprint. Actually you called me because I was inbound not outbound. So what is actually cool about this game is you can name your Call Center whatever you want design it how you like and ultimatly run a call center. You will start by naming the call center setting up your 1st 3 rooms being inbound outbound and back office. In the call center world this doesnt always happen at the same site. It is ultimatly based on your contract. I have only ever had to do Inbound in most of why I did unless it was to call someone back. Now something that you will notice that is very real is that you will have a high turnover in this game, Why you may ask? Thats the Nature of the Beast in a call center either your worked to hard or not enough and youll defently experince this. Now as far as Gameplay is concerned it can be a bit slow at times and stacked against you do to the point you cant hire who you want when you want. you have to work to unlock all of this. In the call center world you would work from the ground up with HR Supervisors Opperations managers trainers QA teams and Tech. This is where the game loses it for me when you start out you have the option for IB OB and BO and thats it no HR no Supervisors to push no Opps managers no Trainers and for some reason this game doesnt have Quailty associates which is the key to a call center without Quality control that guy that is speaking with you on the phone could call you a dumb ignorant stupid head and there is nothing you could do about it except leave the company if that is your choice. So in Closing the game is good its not excellent or great it is good it delivers on some funny bits but it falls short on authenticty when it comes to the point of where you have to unlock everything. the game should be like here is your money build and thats it. so 3 stars out of 5 because it is fun youll have a good time playing it and there is a challenge the its not 5 stars because again lack of authenticty and the fact they make you unlock stuff that you need early on in the game. Do I recommend this game ? Yes especially if you work , have ever worked or are planning on working in a call center it will give you a bit of a taste or give you a parody of what it is like. Enjoy!

10/10 Best MultiPlayer Shooter Hands Down. As a Battlefield 4 Premium member, I wish I played this first, I wouldve never bought a BF4 Premium membership. I should mention that even thought I own CoD Black Ops II I have yet to play any CoC multiplayer. Who knows, maybe that is better, but I doubt it.
The most important part of a multiplayer shooter is that when you place a bullet somewhere it should go there. This is not the case with BF4. Matter of fact that game is broken and its a shame. If that game had worked well it wouldve easily blown this away.
What I like about this game too is that it has great tactical aspects that actually work. So many shooters try to be tactical-with each title having its own distinct issues-they never seem to actually pull off being a tactical shooter well enough to be recognized as such.
Another thing that it great about this game is that even if you get a bunch of people "running and gunning" if enough people focus on playing the objective your team still has a good chance to win the round. As someone who is still trying to get the hang of the game there are many times that I lose track of whats going on and I resort to "running and gunning" and it doesnt seem to throw the team off too much.
One major "Pro" for this game is very little annoying chatter. Compared to other games like BF4 or Insurgency there are a lot of people taht are just talking to make noise. Or they have a terrible mic and keep yelling into it for no reason. Ive never come across that yet. That alone makes the game awesome and worth buying.
The only thing I dont like about the game is that stupid pop-up screen before a match. I would thin kthat once you agree to the servers' rules you wouldnt have to do that again until you changed servers. For some reason it pops up at every match. Thats annoying but its extremely minor. I can live with that.

Believe the hype. Irrational Games' incredibly acclaimed horror/action first-person shooter is a remarkable showcase of the games industry's potential for intelligent storytelling and important societal and political relevance.
is almost as perfect as a game can get, and it is undoubtedly one of the most fun, engaging, and smart games I have played in a long time.
In
, the player is Jack, a generic, middle-aged every-man type character who - after his plane trip takes a detour into the middle of the Atlantic Ocean - finds himself in the underwater city of Rapture, where he must alter his genetic code with plasmids, gather a unique arsenal of weapons, and collect the genetic enhancing drug ADAM in order to survive and escape a crumbling oceanic dystopia.
The story is presented as simplistic in the beginning, only to give way to a deeply complex narrative who's subtle roots take subconscious hold very early in the game. Partly through player-exploration (in the finding of citizen recorded audio logs) as well as through linear progression, the player uncovers the dark past of his underwater prison as he finds himself caught between the battles of the city's objectivist/utopia-ist greed monger Andrew Ryan, and a rebel named Atlas who helps the player escape during the game's opening moments. The story works both as a basic narrative, as well as a critique of Utopianism, and the Ayn Rand-founded philosophy of Objectivism. In a moral based storyline, the player witnesses impressive narrative twists and moments that don't disrupt flow, in addition to observing a prediction of an Objectivist society come to life - a world where everyone is only in it for themselves. Not only is the story impressive in and of itself, Bioshock works perfectly as a critique of the ideals of Objectivism/Utopianism, making it one of the most politically and philosophically in-tune games ever.
The games accomplishment of deep and rich player immersion is truly remarkable. There's a reason why Rapture has become one of gaming's most recognized locations, and it's resident Big Daddies (and accompanying Little Sisters) some of the industry's most infamous enemies. The games' haunting atmosphere and dark narrative are truly top tier and induct the player with a sense of despair and loneliness, adding to the immersive feel. Surely one of the most captivating experiences I've had with a game.
In terms of gameplay,
hasn't aged a day. Using a unique assortment of weapons (ranging from the famous wrench to more heavy weaponry like the flame-thrower) as well as an array of biological "super power"-type weapons called Plasmids, the player fights their way through armies of Rapture's now-insane citizens called Splicers (driven to their state due to overuse and abuse of the ADAM drug). The gameplay is not only fun and gripping, but also inventive, especially for the time of its release. It's very open-ended, despite the linear design, and the player choice is extremely well-implemented. And the Big Daddy fights are challenging in the best way possible - as well as being equally rewarding. In short, the gameplay in
is not only superb in its field of First person shooters, but it's some of the best in any game, period.
Also worth noting are the graphics. For a game made in 2007 (7 years ago at the time of this review), the game looks great. However, even despite its technical prowess, the art design and level composition is truly incredible. It's one of the many factors that bring Rapture to life, and make it one of the most impressive gaming achievements to date.
is surely one of the best games ever made. Filled with memorable characters, enemies, and locations, as well as providing an engaging storyline and relevant societal critiques, this is what a game should strive to be. A landmark achievement.

Yes, it seems like Tropico 3 and 4 may have been the peaks for this franchise - I too have been playing since the original. The game looks better but you certainly don't feel like you have the freedom to be a true dictator (fewer personality characteristics, PAINFULLY dumbed-down almanac, dumbed-down economic system, dumbed-down faction system, not enough edicts, etc.). It seems like they also brought alot of half-baked concepts into this game (research, trade, constitution,  etc. - all good ideas) whereas maybe they should have focused on just one of those concepts and made it really decent. What happened to our pre-election speeches? (We need MORE of those types of things).
It's almost as if the game is under new mangement and that the management is out of touch with what has made the game such a great hit - we don't care so much about what El Presidente looks like, we want more gameplay freedom.We care about having a wider range of political and economic options so that we can tweak and abuse our little island nation for our purposes! Why can't we specifically control wages or rent prices anymore - what if I want a farmer to make twice as much as a doctor?
As a fan of the franchise, I feel like #5 has simply taken several steps in the wrong direction - we needed a political and economic system that had even greater depth, not much, much less. It seems like the developers are getting carried away with the looks and zaniness of the game rather than the original concept of the game - that in which a control-freak dictator can run his island nation however he likes, with an endless array of customizable methods on how to do just that! Think Tropico 3 and 4 but with an even  greater range of economic and political freedom and abilities - we can't even place trees, fountains or intimidating statues anymore...
Overall, a 4/10 - a beautiful game but not nearly the political and economic game it once was. I do like the addition of tanks, though. Also, the concept of trade deals is a good one but still seems not completely thought-out. I will be sticking with previous versions of the game to satisfy future dictatorial urges...I hope the franchise makes a 180 for the next release. Instead of making a good model even better, they seem to have tried to renovate the franchise, which, to me, is undermining what has made the franchise so good. I recommend it to those who are new to the franchise, but would further recommend previous versions.

Red Orchestra 2 is an incredible game. I bought it since I heard so many good things from it, and I'll tell you that the good things you hear about it are absolutely true. Please note that this game is VERY far from the run-and-gun twitch shooters.
The Goods:
The depth of gameplay is absolutely incredible thanks to realism like the use of cover, the adjustable weapon sights, lack of crosshairs and ammo indicators, bleeding, immersive character audio/sounds and so much more. If you're looking for realism in a shooter, you should definitely buy this game. It features a somewhat slow, but careful and smart gameplay.
It's a perfect game...... is what I'd like to say, but it has some flaws.
The Bads:
The learning curve for beginners is very steep, but I don't consider it much of a flaw; the game's depth obviously means that a new player would have a hard time getting familiar with the game. Overcoming the learning curve may be hard, but the reward outweights the effort by a longshot in my opinion.
Don't take the warning lightly, be prepared to die endlessly without even getting a single kill when beginning.
The second problem of mine is the technical difficulties, first I had this keyboard problem which was fixed, and the ongoing problem is that it keeps crashing and forcing me to force-shutdown my computer.
The third is the lack of servers, I'd really like a local or very near server ( I'm in the Philippines ), so I don't have to play with 160+ ping every time. It could also be a problem of mine since my internet isn't very good, but I don't think that's the whole case.
All in all, the game is absolutely incredible, but the lack of servers and crashing keep me from endlessly playing it.

I can't believe I'm not recommending a Telltale game. Tales from the Borderlands and the Game of Thrones series are two of my all time favorite video games of the last 5 years, but this one just fell super flat story wise. In all the ways that Tell Tale games usually succeed, this one failed miserably. 6/10 rating for me with a few explanations below:
NON-SPOILER REVIEW
Pros:
- Unique fighting elements. The detective mode does get stale at times, but overall, I dig the mechanic
- The characterization of Lady Arkham in the final episode is very good. The voice actor does a wonderful job emoting and making you feel a connection with the character
- You can customize Bats' tech color. It's a small thing, but it's a nice touch.
- Gordon is a gem. A true gem.
- There's a real sense of helplessness throughout the game. Sometimes, this is a huge boon for the story and feels earned in the narrative context.
- I really love how they focus much more on Bruce Wayne than Batman.
- New take on the typical Batman backstory. Love the shake ups with major characters' backgrounds.
- The Falcone story arc is great
- The Joker
Cons:
- Super weak story telling. At every turn, you encounter a cheap characterization or an unearned plot twist.
- Two-Face feels SUPER FORCED and really cheapens the emotional nuance of Harvey's character
- More bugs than previous Tell Tale games. Was disappointed to see stuttering cut scenes and characters sharing dialogue with no moving mouths often
- Sound design and music/dialogue balance is off
- Boring Bruce Wayne voice actor. I would have preferred someone with more depth and more vocal range. Troy Baker is just not the right person for this job
SPOILERS:
The Vicki Vale reveal was probably the worst, most unearned part of the game plot wise. It was so out of left field and so rigid and blunt. I like the fact that they transformed a seemingly 1 dimensional character into something more, but Vicki had been all up in your♥♥♥♥♥♥and just annoying the entire game. The total 180 into jabbing Bruce with a syringe of Bane juice would have felt more earned if Tell Tale had just done a little more work to establish some kind of investment with her character originally.
Selina is an utter afterthought. Her characterization is boring, cliche, two dimensional, and really she just comes off as a sex object and trope of a female character. Some of the moments with Bruce that are quieter are fun, but her appearance in the final episode, especially, leaves much to be desired.
It kind of annoyed me that they revealed all of a sudden that Vicki had been abused by The Vales. Obviously, that seed had been lightly laid on the ground when Bats found the kid in the under the stairs storage place, but come on. Abuse can't be your crutch for every "psycho" villain who wants revenge on someone. It was a very unnecessary way to "explain" the twist on Vicki's character. Don't cheapen the great choice you made just because you feel you owe the audience an explanation. Sometimes, people just want to see the world burn or want someone to pay for other people's crimes. Vicki didn't need to have a trope-ridden abuse backstory. She earned her revenge through Cobblepot's back story. And I guess that's my main issue: Vicki didn't really get a backstory. She got an afterthought that used the rich narrative behind Oswald's backstory as diluted inspiration. It was a very sad way to see Tell Tale treat a female villain.
Side note: I loved how people are like "Well that's OBVIOUSLY a girl" when they first see Lady Arkham. Like, the character model is not gendered at all; they just happen not to be a super buff character model. In fact, I wouldn't be surprised if the character model they chose that isn't gendered is easier to animate (oh wait that's Ubisoft...I digress with my bad joke).
The best part about this entire game? The Joker. It's like the opposite of Suicide Squad. The Joker was in this game as a minimal character and his characterization was 20 times any of the other characters combined with the exception of Gordon, Alfred, and Grogan. I wonder if this was intentional.
Lastly, props to Erin Yvette for her perfomance in the final episode. I really loved the passion and emotiveness of her voice. It changed Lady Arkham from a cheap parlor trick into a flesh and blood human which is, unfortunately, what Tell Tale's writers couldn't accomplish in the previous 4 episodes.
Like I said, very sad to be not recommending both A) a Tell Tale game and B) A Batman game - two of my favorite things. After Tales from the Borderlands, I think Tell Tale really had a high bar to hurdle and this game just didn't make it for me.

Telltale brings their talent at crafting expertly written stories of mystery, intrigue, wrought full of emotion, to the Batman canon. Telltales take on the Dark Knight is one of maturity; rarely has Batman or his stories unfolded around such adult depictions of the criminal underworld. The interpretation of such is tantilizing, if only to see this imagination unfold in R fashion.
While purists of the Batman canon may not like the liberal changes Telltale has taken with Batman's canon and origins, others will find the reimagaination to be refreshing and fun. As the story unfolds, much of the gang is here: Two Face, Pinguin, Joker, Szasz, Vicki Vale, and so on, but their stories are changed just enough to keep it interesting, as you decide how their fates will unfold.
If you are a fan of Batman, or have enjoyed ANY of Telltales other efforts, buy this.

Sadly this is another series that loses its idea as it gets diluted down to bland and simplified. Earlier incarnations of tropico were a lot less politically correct, and thus gave much more lols and feels in general. This time that downward trend is taking a huge step, and the specialness of idea is really watered down to just another citybuilder.

(Rent selector anyone?) Almanac, your primary source of information is also infinitely worse than its predecessor.
Some design choises like removal of essential buildings (jail?) or lack of missions points really obviously towards truckload of DLC coming up. There are lots of complaints about bugs, and i did experience teamsters jamming and sound glitches.
Seems to be that devs are running out of ides, or more likely the businessmen don't let them be used anymore. I guess it is the sad fate of every succesful game. No risks are allowed, everything potentially offensive is removed and for the sake of larger audience, everything is "simplified". Result is tasteless, bland and just riding on tales of glorious past.
If you get a steam special discount bundle with DLC included, it is worth it. For full price, definitely not. Already tropico 2 was better as game, and part 3 or its full-price expansion 4 is way better as story.

Hi, my name is astrosoup. I am a veteran of the franchise, and I really like Tropico 5.
I just can't wrap my mind around some of the criticisms being levied against this game. I read all the user reviews before booting it up, with phrases such as "gutting the franchise" and "total let-down" setting me up for a huge disappointment. I'm happy to report that this game is 100% Tropico and the rumors of its demise have been highly exaggerated.
To begin, the interface has been incredibly improved. Clear categorization and images of each building help me find what I'm looking for much more easily than any version before it.
Also, the game looks fantastic. To my eyes, its a little heavy on the saturation, but even still, Tropico has never looked better.
Most of this has to do with the details of how buildings fit together so nicely. Tropico has a history of forcing you to put things in awkward places due to obscure rules about terrain leveling, etc. Alot of that is gone, and I find myself actually staring at my cities fondly, proud of what I have designed. Building textures look better than ever, and farms can fit the contours of your roads, buildings, etc. Even the decorative garden options look good! Anyone complaining about beautification options in this version has either a short memory or has never played Tropico before. These games have always been lacking in little things to make your island look nicer, but Tropico 5 does it better than ever. I have been enjoying the art of city-building, which is something Tropico has never delivered to me before.
Also, the new campaign style is far improved over the old system. Like much they have done away with, the ritual of starting from scratch worked for Tropico 1, but never quite made sense in Kalypso's version. I never made it very far in the campaigns, simply because I got tired of constantly starting my island over. In Tropico 5, the campaign takes you through various time periods, with only a couple of islands. With each era, the game challenges you in a new way, keeping it feeling fresh and forcing you to change your play styles, while allowing you to build on your previous work. The hackneyed mission narratives have been tossed out in favor of a richer meta-narrative that spans all of your missions. Watching a third of my populace suffer in shacks while I desperately cling to power by throwing large amounts of money at foreign powers gives me a sense of what it is like to be a true developing world dictator- the artful mark of a good sim.
I like how buildings seem to (so far) maintain their "look" as you move into a new era, as opposed to magically changing skins. It really keeps a sense of continuity and history, allowing me to look back fondly on my colonial roots. Also, assistance from NPCs, such as extending deadlines, or taking bonuses can be forfeited for Swiss bank funds, so that the size of your swiss bank account actually reflects the amount of extra help you did or didn't accept along the way. For the first time, in the 5th generation of the series, the swiss bank account actually means something to me!
Furthermore, alot of the charming hangups that marvelously infuriated me in Tropico 1, and mildly annoyed me in 3 & 4, have finally been ironed out. Ships come on a regular schedule and get loaded immediately. Construction office run more smoothly- no more bursts of activity followed by months of stagnation. I now build about half the amount of construction offices I used to in order to compensate for this. Goods move efficiently. You don't need to build giant parking garages every 10 yards. In general, things just work better. All in all, it has been a major improvement.
This is not to say the game is perfect. As others have mentioned, it would be nice to have a little more data available when making decisions, especially in terms of trade and the economy. I'd like to know the market price of goods before I build a production faciltity, for example. The system for clearing fog of war is expensive and not very well thought out. There are some peculiar design decisions here and there, but none of it is game-breaking.
I should note that I do experience occasional crashes with my GeForce 660 video card. At least I'm assuming its the card, because Tropico 3 & 4 have always had trouble with it. So save often, even though its a bit of the chore. The autosave doesn't unfortunately doesn't happen often enough to have your back. Also, don't buy it quite yet for the multiplayer experience, until they fix the game speed issue (set to fastest) and the no-saves policy.
This game is a fantastic step forward for Kalypso's stewardship of the Tropico franchise. Nothing will ever beat the original, but this one certainly beats 3 & 4. Most of the ire seems to be centered around the removal of peripheral features, such as locking people up in prisons, or setting individual wages, etc. Yet, for every building they removed they added a handful more. This is anything but a DLC 'money-grab' as some allege, as it is brimming with engaging new content, spanning several eras. Honestly, Kalypso took flak for making 4 a carbon copy of 3. I don't really miss anything they removed in the new version, and if I ever do, I have THREE PREVIOUS VERSIONS that I can go re-play. I, for one, am glad that they changed things up a bit for T5. It's still 100% Tropico, but in a spiffy new form.
Also, they added a VERY DIFFICULT mode for both the economic and political game mechanics. Of course, I started the campain out on this, daring to hope that Kalypso has indeed returned a degree of difficulty into the franchise. I haven't lost or anything yet, but I did feel on a couple of occasions that my decisions did matter a tiny bit. So there is another positive change. Also, I am having to deny elections, so we shall see...
Great work Kalypso. Please fix the crashing issue. Thanks for being responsive to the community. And thanks for treating our beloved franchise with respect.

The game shares many, oh so many, things with touhou it's kinda funny at the beginning, but if you can get past that the game is surprisingly enjoyable.
Difficulty wise, it's pretty fair, when starting you might feel a cheap death or two coming your way, but thats part of these games anyway, you need to replay them to get a feeling for different patterns.
You cannot hoard auras (bombs), nor do you recover any after deaths, so it makes for some resource management.
Gaining lives or auras isn't score based, instead it rewards kills and managing to gather the drops, which is imo silly since they have grazing system in the game, which is essentially allowing a bullet to enter your sprite area without it hitting your actual hitbox, effectively giving you no reason to actually do it apart from score attacks if that's your thing.
Boss patterns vary enough to keep each one interesting and the runs entertaining over multiple plays and best of all, everything on the screen is very clean and simple to keep track of even during chaotic looking attacks.
Offers a fairly good challenge for anyone seeking such.
The story is a mess when first starting out, it opens up somewhat after clearing the game with more and more characters... even after that it's still a confusing pile of things to be honest. But it's a shmup so you most likely aren't playing it for the story anyway.
All the characters bring different play styles with them, some are fun, some not so fun. Each one has their own story, which shares acts from others and mainly differs at the finale. They all were fun in their own way, not that memorable, sadly, but varied enough to make me want to play them all. Also the art in this game is kinda cute.
You will need to clear the game once to unlock each normal character to play.
The soundtrack is chiptune(ish) which is interesting and somewhat weird, but it grows on you. Ofcourse you can always mute it, incase it bothers you alot.
TL:DR: Try it. I found it surprisingly entertaining, so you might too. Should please anyone looking for a pretty decent and simple shmup to play, even if just wanting to try the genre.
Fun, varied, colorful and clean patterns and characters, great music and overall a fun challenge. ...Plus it's free.

I'll just list off the pros and cons of this game
Pros:
- Amazing artstyle
- The controls feel great
- Beating bosses feels rewarding
- It's challenging, but not unfair
- Great soundtrack
- Bosses feel refreshing and unique

- The difficulty can feel a bit artificial at times, eventually it feels like you're just dying over and over again to learn the patterns of the bosses

I tried balancing out the pros and cons, but honestly couldn't think of more to complain about.
If you're up for a small challenge, I would definitely recommend this game. If you tend to give up games fast because you die, then this game probably won't be for you. It's not that it's "hard", but rather that you have to learn the bosses skillsets and how to counter them.

This is a game that revolves around you taking a new job at a pizza place with 4 animatronics that are very similar to the ones at a Chuck E. Cheese place. The names of these animatronics are Freddy Fazbear, Bonnie, Chica, and Foxy, although there is also Golden Freddy, which may have been intended as an easter egg. The animatronics go into a free-roam mode at night and will try to stuff you into a Freddy Fazbear suit, which will kill you because of all the animatronic parts and cross-beams that are inside. To combat this, you must monitor their actions and block them from getting in to your office by closing the doors after you check to see if they are right outside with the light switch. Of course, you may think that "Oh hey, I'll be safe if I keep the doors closed at all times," But the doors, lights, and security cameras all take from the limited power that you have, so you need to use your power wisely. As the week progresses, the animatronics become more and more agressive, and will likely attempt to get into your room every few seconds in later nights. Also, ALWAYS remember to keep an eye on Foxy and Freddy, as they will ♥♥♥♥ your game up if you don't watch them.

I don't usually bother to review games, but this game deserves a real mention.
This is a 2 player chess like fantasy game where you summon champions from your deck each turn and send them to destroy your opponents shrine, equiping them with various weapons, casting spells and deploying relics along the way.
Its also a collectable game where you obtain new runes through play gradually building more powerful decks, this is quite addictive in inself as you want to try all the different playstyles but need to invest serious play time in order to get all the runes (or real cash if you prefer, but its NOT Pay To Win!!!).
Firstly you have to look past the some would say 10+ year old graphics, and the annoying little quirks (like you have to go into the rune forge twice to be able to view runes) and the fact that you can't play in full screen mode or resize the screen.
But if you do there lies a game which is strategically ahead of its time, there is soooo much depth and some brilliant design ideas at play.
Some of the real gems amongst the play themes  include:
Stitched: which are evil rag dolls come to life, upon death they turn into a pile of rags which you can then reanimate again,
Worms: where your deploy zone grows each time you deploy one gradually overwhelming your opponent as you deploy behind his lines
Wtiches: where using a certain spell can make them incredibly powerful.
Zombies: a shambling wall of diseased meat spreading disease as they go
Skeletons: boney anahilation
Liches: telepoting undead mages
Spirits: invisble death
Dread: where you use champions which lower your foes damage rendering them near useless
and that's just the 'Forsaken Wastes' faction, there are 7 others with just as much depth and variation to choose from:
Savage Tunda: Think snow people, creatures that like cold, Yetis etc
Forglar swap: Frogmen and other kinds of weird swamp creatures
Ironfist Stronghold: Humans, dwarfs, clerics, babarians etc
Underdepths: All kinds of weird and wacky Demons
Kithir Forest: Elves & forest creatures
Sundered Lands: Dinosaurs, Lizardmen, creatures from a bygone age
Shattered peaks: Hill/mountain creatures such as Cyclops, a flying critter race and various goblin type things
All these can then be sub divided into various races/play style just like the previously described Forsaken Wastes faction.
You are in fact free to combine any champions as you see fit to come up with ingenius combos that wreck face.
There are currently over 2000 runes to choose consisting of champions, relics, spells and equipment from which to design your deck (30 runes) with more added every quarter.
I could go on, but if you have read this far, what are you waiting for its free so give it a try...
I highly recommend this game, its simply genius.

I played this game on Pilgrim mode just to explore the areas and get used to the game mechanics. I was lucky enough to store two houses full of food (fish, venison, sodas, and 8 gallons of H2O) and 19 rounds of rifle ammo. I was ready to shoot some things for extra warmth. Every animal you aim for runs away in this mode, so I was fairly confident....However, I spot a bear and have him within my rifle sights. I pull the trigger and the damn thing charges me!!! The hatchet, knife, and all the other gear I had in my backpack didn't help me in the least! I was left with 6 health so I bandaged myself up before I passed out and stumbled my way back to camp. I eventually died of hypothermia in my sleep. Thus ended my seven-day adventure in the frozen tundra of Canada.
Play this game and find out how long you'd survive in the frozen wastes. Some areas are better for gathering supplies than others. Try to have a cache in each area that you can come back to, because you never know.

It's quite difficult at the beginning to plundge into this game. You will probably find yourself revolving around, trying to figure out wth are you suppose to do, scrounging for fuel and supplies. However, once you've reached a certain point in game, when you actually know what to do, the real game starts. I honestly can't remember when was the last time I've spent 5 hours in a single game session.  I even started making my own notes about where I can buy specific wares, at which port. I do realise tho, that there are easier ways to do this, but where's the fun in that?
Nevertheless, its a cruel world out there. The game expects you to die. I mean literally, it wants you dead, and you know its true when you realise that most of the achievements refers to dying. There are various ways to die in this game, it can be an awfull contingency that can jeopardize the whole game, or some creature that will one-shot you from a distance. If you thought dying in dark souls is the worst thing that can happen, you are clearly a landlubber. In here, you can easily lose hours of gameplay in a single slip up, which forces you to stay sharp the whole time. Of course there are ways to ease your death with heritage system and stuff like that, but you will always suffer some loss.
Overall, I highly recommend this game for everyone who digs that kind of climate, or just seek for a well-written rpg.

PoxNora is an old favorite of mine I can't help but play a bit here and there throughout the day. Steam doesn't like the launcher, so my time is certainly up around 1,000 hours, and while I only have a handful of the legendary rarity runes, that's not what this game is about. Anyone who claims PoxNora is pay to win, or pay to play in its current incarnation, clearly missed a lot of updates.
It is entirely possible to be competetive in PoxNora with all commons. That's not fair to say when you get matched with anyone whom has amassed every rune in the game to date, and knows the metas, but generally speaking, Desert Owl Games makes every attempt to balance runes to reflect a general value, and metagame viability. There are good commons, there are "meh" commons. There are good legendaries, there are "meh" legendaries. If you're clever with your battlegroup composition, no PvE campagin should be an issue for you.
But if you have some sort of morbid obsession with PvP (which I just don't get), nothing's stopping you from utilizing Steam or the forums to find fellow new players and generally anyone willing to "scrub up" and break out their low-tier battlegroups to mentor you a bit. There are seldom a dozen players on these days, but we're overjoyed when we see a new name in the lobby (and we look).
As it stands, barring limited edition runes from past events, PoxNora can be play 100% F2P. There is no non-limited edition rune you cannot get from playing F2P, and ALL runes are tradeable. The only immediate limit is that the newest expansion available will always be for premium currency only, but using the rune trader, or PoxBox— the automated, unofficial "rune pool" —you can trade for any rarity, including limited edition, from any expansion.
So if anyone actually finds this game's listing in the sandpit that is the Steam store, reads this review, and might be interested in the game, let me know. I've been around, I've seen some things. I'm totally willing to do some practice matches, or help you construct your first F2P battlegroup. A lot of the common-only options are actually quite appealing, I find.

Ok, you're still reading, so on to the proper review...
Sunless Sea is set in the Fallen London's setting. You do not need to know that browser game to enjoy the setting (i didn't), but it's refreshing to see a dark world that is its own, original thing, rather than an umpteenth uninspired reuse of the H.P. Lovecraft cannon.
It's the end of the 19th century, you were born underground in Fallen London, and now you're gonna try your luck sailing the Underzee, the dark and foreboding sea under the world, hoping to achieve fame, fortune, or maybe some secret goal of yours...more likely, you will die from the many dangers that awaits you, or maybe you will just go insane from the horrors you will face.
But who knows ? Maybe years later, one of your distant heirs will be smart enough to use your experience and achieve what you couldn't.
You sail across the Zee on your boat, trying to find new ports and thus new opportunities to fulfill your goals. I won't spoil how many there are, but the Zee is vast, and each port is very unique. Along the way, you will meet new characters, find new stories and quests to pursue. Sunless Sea is a deep game (no pun intended) you will still be finding brand new stuff 50h in, when most games have already revealed most of their content.
Even after 90h, i've only reached one ending, and there are many stories threads that i never had the opportunities to finish. There are so many characters, so many unique places that i just love to visit, so many stories that are a pleasure to read. This will often lead to quests where you will have opportunities to change things in the Underzee, for better of for worse, according to what you want your captain wish to achieve, or what you want to personally discover.
There is a lot to read, but you're never forced to read if you're not in the mood like it. Most players I have talked to told me they started the game by rushing things, without reading much, and it's a perfectly fine way to play. You will have many opportunities to read what you've missed before when your current captain inevitably die and his/her heir starts their own journey.
Sunless Sea is very much a slow-paced game. The actual sailing on the water takes a long time, especially with the starting boat, and even upgrading things will just make it more likely for you to take long journeys that takes hours rather than really speed things up. But it's not a boring pace. It just emphasizes the creepiness and loneliness of you and your crew. The game is about strange places and creepy atmosphere, and the slow pace emphazises that perfectly.
However, you will from time to time meet enemies to make for a nice change of pace. The combat is really one of my favorite parts of the game. It's a much needed change of pace, it's challenging enough that you're happy when you beat a tough enemy, but it's easy enough that you can usually escape if things go wrong, which is a good thing because the game is already very unforgiving in its other aspects.
A common misunderstanding about the game is that it's too difficult, that you're gonna be stuck with no fuel in no time. Sure, the game IS difficult. You're gonna die a lot.
But it's not gonna be due to basic survival like "having enough fuel and supplies to go back to London". Though your earlier captains might struggle with that it's just because you do not know enough about the game.
But the game is not about theses things, it's actually quite easy to survive. With each new captain, you will better understand how things work, and the many many opportunities to get ressources on the Underzee.
You will know you're starting to get good at the game when you're not worried about the day-to-day survival, but you're trying to think about how to win the game.
Which brings us to another negative point that is often raised about the game: grinding. Some people think the game is all about grind, because they found one thing that gives them ressources and try to do it over and over again. That's not how you're supposed to do things. Don't worry too much about ressources, try to explore, try to discover new stories and finish new quests, in short, enjoy the game instead of grinding it...and the ressources will pour in quite easily.
However, for end-of-game characters, characters that are trying to reach an ending, there is definitely some grinding to do because most of the endings require a lot of ressources. That's probably the one negative thing i have to say about this game, it takes a while between the moment you think you're gonna be able to win, and the actual winning. But still, there are so many things to do, that you shouldn't worry about that until very late into the game.
It's hard to talk in details about Sunless Sea, because anything could be a spoiler. But on the whole, i will say it's one of my favorite games ever. It has a very unique world, it's bursting with things to do and discover, and it has one of the best soundtracks I've ever listened to (listen for free or buy it at bandcamp:
). Its slow-paced gameplay would, in another game, be a handicap, but it fits the atmosphere of Sunless Sea perfectly. Summing up the game is so hard...Exploration, discoveries, interesting characters, horror, great stories and hard choices to make...it has all of that and much more.

Finishing Blackwell Epiphany, the fifth and final Blackwell game, feels like the end of an era. And it's impossible to talk about this game individually outside the context of the entire series.
The Blackwell games are the kind of games you enjoy while sipping on a smooth whiskey and listening to slow jazz. Luckily, the games' soundtracks provide some amazing jazz, so you only have to worry about the whiskey.
The art is a purposefully pixelated retro style, which works because the gameplay and philosophy behind it is very much in tune with the visually similar point-and-click adventure games of the 90's.
The puzzles can be occasionally obtuse and frustrating, but for the most part once you learn the mechanics you'll know what to do next. And if you don't, the one tried-and-true adventure game formula of exhausting all conversation options and trying to combine every item with everything interactable will inevitably work.
Where the game really shines is the voice acting. Dave Gilbert continually got very talented people to work with him and the games are so much better for it. Both Abe Goldfarb and Rebecca Whittaker deserve to win awards for their multiple performances.
The series just kept getting better and better, making Epiphany easily the best entry of them all. The story really shines when it gets dark and serious, and Epiphany succeeds tremendously there. I'm so glad the writing didn't shy away from some really rough places and concepts. Bravo for taking a risk and going there.
This game is like the icing on the layered cake of the whole series. Its creators should be very proud of it. You won't find better on the indie adventure game scene. I'm beyond excited for what the team at Wadjet Eye games does next.

But while combat and gameplay are two great aspects, the best parts are arguably the setting and plot. Rapture is a really well designed environment that never fails to keep its consistency. It's a bit light on the technical side, but this game is getting old. The story is delivered pretty beautifully and the audio diaries skillfully tell a lot of substories or add details to the main story.
Also, the Little Sisters are ridiculously cute in a special way.
Would easily recommend, a great game that everyone playing FPS should finish at least once.

Blackwell Epiphany is a point-n-click adventure and a grand finale of Blackwell series. Those who expect a story arc which Deception somewhat started at the end will not find it there, instead it bring another, more Blackwell-ish, main story. It's one of the best adventure games recently too.
This game still uses same engine as other ones used, though support widescreen too, it was released only one year ago after all. Shift+Tab will still do a weird thing to the game, while pressing Tab key again would fix it. It also had more glitched and small bug than usual, like Durkin the detective still talking in location which he leaved if you phone or even game crashing when calling partner in some case, happened one time. Do save.
Blackwell Epiphany is a big finale of a series and ends it on a high note. It's the most polished and ambitious game in the series, in pretty much every aspect. It didn't introduce any big new features in the gameplay, but continues what Deception figured for the best. Well, aside from having ability for Rose and Joey, the spirit guide, to explore multi-screen areas serapately, with new button to call your partner to the scene. Helps.
As modern adventure game, you can't die or get into dead end. Blackwell is fairly standart adventure game, somewhat. It uses inventory system much less, instead focusing on talking, getting notes, combining clues and searching Internet in your smartphone, with typing. As well as ability to switch character to Joey, though he still doesn't play as much part as Rose. Still does. Still teamwork.
The setting, whole setting of a game is telling you that the game it's the finale. Where the tale ends. Having a never ending night with snow falling, urban background with green pallette to it, it creates unique and dark, deep atmosphere. Not to mentioning that the pixel-art is the best here, very professional and has a great work put into lighting. No complaints about sprites, animation or background aside from nitpicking, it's just plain amazing!
Music delivers professional quality as well. It's dark and ambient, yet has moments of sadness and jazzyness, with electronica at intense moments. Even has some memoriable pieces.
And plot is probably the biggest, best thing about this part. But immeditly I should warn you that it doesn't really follow what Deception set up to. Instead, Rose and Joey the spirit guide got even bigger problems to handle, as after solving the nice dark intro case they just had the most unlikely and logic shattering thing to happen right in front of their eyes, setting out to solve their final mystery. And well, plot is very emotional, especially to those who already got attached to pair of out heroes, it's just plain awesome and exciting. I wanted to clap at the final parts, especially at part where Joey and Rose had to act serapately, psychological thing. And an ending will not be just "it's OK" either, it will punch you into stomach. Whetever you like it or not, you still will not ignore it.
And yes, the game mostly has a feel of mystery and ugency to it, slowing down in the middle only to deliver the traditional "solve two ghost cases in same time" thing, which is still welcome.
And yes, the game still inclused commentary mode extra. In each area, you get to choose by yourself if you want to hear Voice Bloober, Artist Commentary or Game Designer Commentary. And yes, I feel it's more worth it this time, I got to enjoy hearing more about game design than just voice acting. It's great.
Really, looking back, Blackwell is a great series and I got attached to it already. And it's one awesome finale. Will miss it. And maybe those loose plots will be delivered in another game, not related to Blackwell family itself...
So yes, highly recommended adventure game, but promise to beat the previous parts first. Worth it.
