Do you like gun-toting marines, werewolves, aliens and scantily-clad chics with huge♥♥♥♥♥♥  Well, too bad, because Bioshock doesn't have any of that, bro.  However, if you're a few IQ points above par then you will be happy to know that Bioshock is a great FPS game, and a somewhat intellectually stimulating game to boot.  It has tremendous atmosphere, beautiful graphics, solid gameplay mechanics, a good story with an interesting plot, and philosophical underpinnings based on the selfish, elitist, batshit stupid writings of Ayn Rand.
The game takes place within the city of Rapture, a metropolis built entirely under the ocean.  The period in which the game takes place is the 1950s or 1960s, but it was built decades before and it retains the hallmarks of a bygone era.  Music played from phonographs, architecture in the art deco style popular into the 1940's, colloquialisms often heard in those really old Black & White movies, and an enemy reminiscent of Orson Welles in his magnum opus 'Citizen Cane'.
The game is also dark.  It's bright, beautiful graphics highlight the urban decay, political warfare, literal warfare, and human experimentation that has taken place in Rapture.  It's at times gruesome.  And it is at times relentless in the shear amount of violence that takes place, or has taken place.  Which is interesting when you consider the name of the city and what it means.
Rapture:
1. the state of mind resulting from feelings of high emotion; joyous ecstasy
2. (often plural) an expression of ecstatic joy
3. the act of transporting a person from one sphere of existence to another, esp from earth to heaven (vb)
4. (tr) to entrance; enrapture
The game is an FPS, but it is a high-brow FPS.  It's not merely running and gunning everything that moves, even though it does often feel that way.  It maintains an intellectual hold throughout.  It is the direct descendent of System Shock 2.  System Shock 2, for all intents and purposes, is the father of the Bioshock series of games.  And System Shock 2 is better in almost every way.  I know - sounds crazy, when you consider that System Shock 2 was released in 1999 and Bioshock was released in 2007.  Of course, Bioshock is better looking, graphically, and it has a panache that System Shock 2 can't approach, being of a technologically inferior era.  However, System Shock 2 isn't just an FPS game; it's also a roleplaying game.
I suppose it's cheesey to make so much of System Shock 2 when talking about Bioshock, but it's impossible not to.  And the reason it's impossible not to is because Ken Levine sold Bioshock to the gaming industry and to the gaming public as System Shock 2's "spiritual successor".  It wasn't just another game; it was a System Shock 2-like game!  System Shock 1 & 2 were amazing, immersive, revolutionary, and intelligent games.  System Shock 2 had 3 character classes (career paths) to choose from, you had skills and abilities, you had to research items using software and chemicals, you had to suss out information in emails, audiologs, and do your best to avoid enemies, because weaponry was hard to come by and it degraded over time and then you had to chuck it, or fix it.  There is alot to say about System Shock 2; there is a reason it is a cult classic now.
Bioshock is a step down.  Possibly even a tumble down a flight of stairs.  Bioshock is what System Shock 3 would be if it had fallen out of a tree while playing cops & robbers, hit it's head on a rock, and was just never the same again.  Now he needs to be fed pureed ham with a spoon and can no longer talk in complete sentences.  So sad.  There are no classes, no skills to upgrade, no specializing in certain skills and attributes at the expense of others.  Sure, you get Plasmids and Tonics, but none of that is permanent - you can swap them out if you want.  And you can afford just about everything in the course of the game, which makes it all moot in the end.  Bioshock was originally meant to be System Shock 3.  It was supposed to continue the saga of Shodan, the artificial intelligence that made your life a living hell on Citadel Station in System Shock 1, and on the Von Braun in System Shock 2.  They couldn't make that game, for numerous reasons, so this lump of a game is the best they could do - a stream-lined, dumb-downed shooter meant to appeal to a broader audience.  Of course, it worked.  Good job!  Not System Shock, but still pretty good in relation to other FPS games!  Beats playing something as mindless and repetitive as Halo.
Anyway, Bioshock is a great game, despite it's shortcomings, and despite the ancestry it was sold on.  It is great for at least one play through.  I first played it on the Xbox 360 and enjoyed it.  I have now finished it again on the PC, and not only was it enjoyable, but I think it was more enjoyable on the PC.  That said, certain aspects of it do become tedious - like the constant fighting and frequent hacking, but at the end of the day you are not going to find a more satisfying FPS than Bioshock, and if you can, well....  it's probably because you were dropped on your head as a child, or you were born with a genetic defect that made you think... well... in a special way.  In which case Halo, Call of Duty 3, Battlefield 4, and Serious Sam are out there just for you, Stupid!

This game has so much potential, and it's only just in Alpha, I've played just under two hours and a hand full of different chapters given in the singleplayer, the missions vary from defending fortified beaches, securing Axis batterys and taking cities.
Pros:
-Lots of WW2 era weapons, and is lore friendly to the specific factions you play.
-Very factions on both sides, such as the Canadians, Italians etc.
-Drivable vehicles this includes German and American tanks in specific missions.
-Inventory mechanic, makes the game interesting as you may have to scavange for ammunition or even other weapons and tools.
-Varied missions, though there is more too be added/changed in the future what is currently avaliable is decent.
-A funny tutorial where your first target is a German in his underwear.
-Voice acting, though I would imagine there is much more voice work to be done in future.
Cons:
-The AI can be a little unpredictable at times, they can be brain dead one moment and the next shooting you right between the eyes, though this can make the player act more cautious.
-A fair few of the textures and models clip and disapear at times, but yet again this can be looked over, the gameplay makes up for this.
-The interface for the inventory could be somewhat improved visually, but for an alpha it suits its purpose.
-Finally, this may just be me being a grammar Nazi, fitting for the theme of the game, but there were misspellings here and there, for example on the health bar, but that is very small and minor details.
Now as the game is in alpha, bugs can be expected, I myself encounted a few, and I urge anyone who plays this game report the bugs they experience aswell, I would love to see this game develop more and become a solid, well developed early access game.
I will watch this games and developers career with great interest and will spread word about it, it does deserve more coverage!

Making its way to retail shelves and digital platforms four years after its predecessor, Just Cause 2 is Avalanche Studio's answer to the gaming community's outcries for a lavish, modern day action sandbox. Building on the defining characteristics of the original Just Cause, this sequel aims to refine the unique grapple hook and parachute mechanics, while adding depth to its side missions, characters, and massive world all the while boasting an enormous map that is four times the size of Grand Theft Auto V.
Welcome to the island of Panau, where you are free to travel by land, sea, and air. Once again, you are in control of Agency operative Rico Rodriguez, more commonly referred to in this release as Scorpio/Scorpion due to the emblem on the back of his signature jacket. He has been called back into action to find Tom Sheldon, the man who hired him during his last adventure, as Tom is suspected of going rogue. Just like the debut release, this title is another tale of gangs, drug cartels, and a corrupt government; although it does have less of an emphasis on overall revolution and anarchy. Overall, the story is still just as lackluster as what was featured in the first game, though the title makes up for this with a campaign that is packed with explosions and high speed mayhem.
Your first handful of hours in Panau are going to be superb. You'll absolutely love being able to slingshot your way around the island with your grapple hook and parachute, all the while causing massive amounts of chaos. There's plenty to do and a lot to see if you have the time to put in; over 350 points of interest to discover and complete, more than 1000 resource items to find, hundreds of collectibles to locate, dozens of gang side missions, 9 strongholds to take over, over 100 vehicles to cruise in, 7 main story missions, and more destructibles than you'll know what to do with. Yes, Just Cause 2 is absolutely overflowing with things to do, as a sandbox game should be, but therein also lies all of its major flaws.
Let's start from the top and talk about how this game forces you to grind out chaos points in order to unlock the next story mission. You gain chaos points by, well... causing chaos around the island; blow things up, complete locations, conquer strongholds, finish side missions, you get the idea. This is most likely done for the sole purpose of elongating the game, since the 7 story missions only amount to maybe two hours of playtime at best. All of the aforementioned tasks that you have to complete to earn chaos points get exuberantly repetitive after a few hours, you'll begin to notice that a lot of the points of interest have the same layout, and pretty soon you'll grow tired of hunting down that last collectible or fuel tank in order to complete an area; it's always the same in the end. What's worse is that if you're going for 100% completion, don't even bother as it is literally impossible without a third-party fan made patch... the developer forgot to include 6 items and never corrected it, so the most you'll get is 99.95%.
Another major pain point of Just Cause 2 is the lack of the game remembering anything that you purchase from the Black Market. You can call in a chopper to deliver some sweet weapons and vehicles after you've paid for them with your blood-soaked money, but the vehicles will disappear after you start a mission, when you die, or even when you load your save file back up again. What happened to the garages from the first game? Sure, they were useless there, but they'd be very handy here. This is specifically and inherently irritating when it comes to the dual turbo boosters for your parachute, which you're unable to use with any of the DLC parachutes by the way, since the game considers it a vehicle and not an add-on. Needless to say, all of the cash that you earn from missions and pick-ups is going to be wasted on rebuying these things again and again.
There's also the technical aspect of it all, since this game does not work well on anything newer than Windows 7. I'll go ahead and save you a load of hassle by saying this: set your launch options to include /failsafe. I went through a dozen or so "fixes" to get this title to run properly, and that is the only one that made the game stop constantly crashing. This mode makes the loading screens a little bit longer, but it will save you a lot of time in the long run since every crash will set you back significantly in the realm of grinding chaos points.
On the up side, the island is beautiful and the fact that the weather is almost always bright and sunny with clear blue skies makes this a "feel good" game. There's also a decent mod community that's dedicated to bringing out the best in Just Cause 2, including mods to improve textures and even make the game more like its 2015 follow-up. If you're into multiplayer, there's a free mode with extra achievements included with the base game.
Even though this review dogs on every negative trait of the game, Just Cause 2 isn't necessarily a bad title, it just doesn't have any versatile content. The island of Panau is absolutely amazing for about 5-8 hours, but grinding out to the staggering 20 hour mark just to complete the story is a trial in itself. If you want a game that will last you well beyond 40 hours if you're going for as close to completion as you can get, then you'll love Just Cause 2. However, if you want a sandbox title that masks its repetitious nature better, then you'll need to look further than here; this is one game that has been severely over-hyped.

Ah Five Nights at Freddy's. A good survival management like "horror" game. Why I use quotations on the word horror is because when you get down to it, after a while, the jumpscares are not really scary and you'll know the patterns of the animatronics as you progress through the 5 nights of the game. There is a few more stuff to do after the fifth night but, i'm not gonna spoil it. You just have to play the game to figure that out.                                                                                                                                                                        It's a different type of "horror" game and I like the style of gameplay here as someone who doesn't play a lot of horror games like myself. Closing the doors at the right time to avoid getting killed by the robots, making sure you don't lose power cause everything you do in the game absorbs power, checking the hallways with your light button in the office and checking where the rest of the animatronics are in Freddy Fazbear's Pizza, it's all neat stuff and the atmosphere of the game (IMO) is great. As I said before in the second sentence of this review, the games jumpscares after a while you get used to them almost to the point where the jumpscares are laughable at times. While the jumpscares are not that scary as you move on from nights, the theorys and hidden plot of Five Nights at Freddy's is some of the most interesting and creepist storys i've read in a while. In short, if you can look past the iffy jumpscares, the screen tears, and how short the game is, for 5 bucks, i'd recommend Five Nights at Freddy's. 8/10

Sailing on the wide black zee can be tranquil or terrifying. Though the story aspects of the game are scripted out beyond your control, the comprehensive atmosphere of the world depends entirely on your own perception. Little Pox History:

FREE TO PLAY: This is a huge thing, since the Owls have come, they have made so much more accessible for FREE, with in game gold (earned from doing single player / skirishers / PvP (normal and ranked) you can buy nearly all runes and can buy all avatars and single player campaigns.

I've sunk 215 hours into Dungeon Defenders 2. I've played since pre-release and the game has certainly changed since then. I'll post a TL:DR at the bottom of this if you don't want to read through the fat of the post.
Note that I have also sunk hundreds (~600) of hours into Dungeon Defenders 1, including it's DLC and mods.
Dungeon Defenders 2 is not DD1, not even close. A lot has changed since then.
I'll start with the three biggest changes from DD! to DD2
1. Gamemodes.
-Gamemodes have changed. There are no unlimited waves and there aren't challenges or scenarios as there were in
DD1. In DD2 there are 3 gamemodes. Campaign, Trials and Incursions.
-Campaign is as it sounds. You progress through a campaign and level up while earning rewards and learning to play
your chosen characters. You can play on different difficulty settings of your choice. Campaign can also be replayed
as much as you like.
-Trials Are the biggest and toughest mode in this game. Trials have diffculties crom Chaos (c) 1 to C7 with more
being implemented. Trials have different maps and different enemies depending on the difficulty chosen. They also
have different tiers of rewards. This is the end-game content, and by far, the bulk of the content.
-Incursions are essentially challenge or themed maps. They have specials rewards depending on the map chosen. As
it stands now, you must complete different trials difficulties to unlock different incursions, Incursions have different
challenges or themes. For example, in one incursion (godlin king) you must collect and bring gold to the center of
the map to appease a tyrant all the while still holding off enemies. In another map, you may face constant debuffs,
or enemies immune to status effects.
2. Loot
-Loot has changed since DD1 and since the release of DD2. There are now these things called "shards." A shard is an
equipable and upgradeable stat. They can be placed in armor, weapons or relics (which will be explained later in the
review). Shards come in different colors and types. Some shards afffect weapons and armor which will then directly
affect your heros stats., and other shards will affect towers. There are also class shards which will directly affect your
heros abilities, such as adding new affects or increasing chances for certain things to occur.
-Relics are new equipables. They can upgraded and modified using shards. They directly affect your twoers. You
equip them on your hero in a tower slot and can add shards and upgrades to them, which will then directly affect
the tower associated to the slot the relic occupies.
-loot drops have also changed. There is a lot less loot than DD1 but that's probably for the better. You no longer
convert loot into mana which yo uwould then convert into upgrades. Now you can sell loot for gold, which can then
be used for upgrades or to buy more items. You cna also receieve pet eggs, pet upgrades and pet re-roll items.
-Medals. Medals are a special currency earned from doing quests and completing maps. They are used to buy
upgrades, buy new characters, etc. They are your main currency once you complete the campaign.
3. Gameplay and Characters.
-DD2 is still DD1, but with some features added and some removed. The original 4 characters are still in the game,
with some new characters as well. The original 4 characters have some changed abiltiies and towers, but nothing
too unfamiliar from DD1.
-Characters can now also progress into ascension levels. After reaching level 50, your character will still level up,
giving you points which can be added into a skill tree, upgrading the character or their towers.
-Mana has also changed. There are now 2 types of mana. Ability and tower. Ability mana is used by characters to cast
spells or use abilities. Tower mana is now used to construct, upgrade and repair towers. This changed from DD1. You
no longer have to split mana between character and tower.
-Characters can now also be bought using ingame currency (medals) or special currency (gems/real-world-money).
This is a pro or con depending on where you stand.
For the most part, the game has changed. It is not DD1 but it is still a DD game. There are changes that players may or may not like, but in the course of developing a series, games tend to change between each iteration. Take series like Fable, Fallout, The elder Scrolls or Orcs Must Die for example.
If you enjoyed DD1 you will enjoy DD2 to an extent. If you were a die-hard fan of DD1 and want another game exactly like it, well then DD2 may not be for you.
Personally, I enjoy the game. It is certainly the next step in the DD series. Though, there are changes I personally do not like, they have not ruined the game for me.
Give it a try, at the very least, do the tutorial and level up a few levels. I certainly recommend the game.
TL:DR Good game. Not DD1 but still a DD game.Lots of changes, both bad and good depending on where you stand with them. (Not to mention constant updates).

First off: I did not even touch the multiplayer part, so I am not going to comment on that. From what I have heard, it does not run all too well, so I guess I am not missing out on any possibly redeeming aspect. I am a long-time fan of the Tropico franchise and had a lot of fun with 3 and 4.
Tropico 5 introduces some interesting new mechanics, which sounded cool at first:
For example, there is the ability to fight. Disappointingly, this boils down to building some Barracks, Army Bases and other Military sites, since you cannot really control anything significant during an invasion of your island. Your soldiers move out automatically (following the same annoying pathing that also causes Teamster's Office hickups), the only thing you can specify are priorities (works just as fine as with Construction Offices - for which I would have to be in a super-sarcastic mood to call it good).
Then, there is a tech-tree which you can research subsequently using research points generated by various buildings (Libraries, Colleges, you get the idea). The main flaw in tech-progression probably is the fact that you get your hands on most interesting things rather late in the game (but at that point at an incredibly high rate). Have an airport? Well, that's cool, some minutes later, you will be able to build a luxory version of aforementioned.
You can destine managers to your production facilities in order to boost efficiency or grant other boni to the laborforce and or building's vicinity. As far as I understand, these managers don't level up (even though a star rating is visible for all of them), unless they are one of your heirs (which you can upgrade spending money from your swiss bank account). However, character progression is not as fun as in e.g. Tropico 3, since the traits are kept very basic in Tropico 5.
I have never seen Tropico as a hard-core simulation but rather a feel-good game. Earlier titles did achieve exactly that. Tropico 5, however, does not. Not only because the additions in terms of gameplay mechanics neither feel well thought out nor turn out to be interesting in any way. It is more, because the current iteration offers little to no feedback. Also the prequels did not show all too detailed information on what's wrong or doing well on your island, but this time, the lack of feedback reaches an annoyingly high level: Imagine, you are on a campaign mission, trying to accomplish a specific task when an election comes up. No problem, you think, my supporters greatly outnumber the critics. 1-2 months in the election phase, your ratings suddenly drop from ~60% to 45% - time to act! Opening the score overview, you however notice that all your ratings are well above 50% - too bad, so take a trip into the blue and build a Cathedral, a Hospital and some Entertainment buildings (all that using "quick construct" and taking a money penalty scaling with the building's cost, since Tropicans are still utterly incompetent when it comes to building stuff). "Phew" - you tell yourself, seeing the rating passing the magic 50% threshold again. 1 month before election, Autosave hits. Afterwards you are told that only 49% voted for you.
Would this have happend just once playing the career, I would not bother. But things like that keep happening constantly. Even if your island's economy florishes, you provide food through numerous supermarkets, keep crime rates low using police stations, reduce polution,... Problems only rarely amount from a lack of money (you usually have access to some very lucrative products at any point in time, and at a surplus once you reach cold war ages). They result from poor feedback: If you check a police station, an overlay shows you current crime rates. Waste disposal sites show you polution. Religious buildings _do not_ show saturation, neither do supermarkets or hospitals. Then again, Newsstations show a "Liberty"-overlay - is that what you would call consistency? I wouldn't.
...And then, there is bugs. Your game will crash, your game will freeze. Just now, trying to finish the campaign, the game froze, killing the entire progress of that particular mission. Not, that it happens often, but considering other annoyances, this is the tip of the iceberg.
Bottom line: It plays like 3 or 4. It looks a little better than 3 or 4. The music is still nice. The game provides even less feedback than the predecessors. The gameplay additions are not worth it. The campaign is comparably boring. The early ages evolve incredibly slow. Just too many flaws to keep the constant "holiday"-feeling up.

This game is truly a genre of it's own. I suppose an appropriate label for it would be an FPS RPG, but one can't simply slap that tag on it and begin comparing it to other popular titles that fit that bill, such as Fallout and Deus Ex.
To be more specific about the unique qualities of this game, it's the atmosphere and environment that enable this game to transcend the standards of FPS RPGs. The city of Rapture is a wonder, consuming the player with a sense of despair and insecurity. Surrounded by splicers who have developed a severe addiction to ADAM, a substance that alters one's DNA, and subsequently one's mind as well, they are willing to destroy anything in their path so as to procure this coveted material. But as you struggle to survive, brutalizing splicers as they maniacally babble to themselves, you begin to cultivate the feeling that you're becoming one of them, using similar means to acquire the ever elusive ADAM. As you progress through Rapture while collecting supplies, equipment, and weapons, you are constantly attempting to convince yourself that it's all part of your grand plan to escape, that you will once again experience the light of day. But when the game arrives at it's final moments, you are met with the cruel understanding that you will never depart Rapture, because while your physical self manages to endure the horrors of the mysterious city, you know that your mind will never escape the pure insanity that is Rapture.
The characters are additionally a breed of their own. Andrew Ryan is perhaps one of the most superb villains I have ever encountered in any game. Exquisite voice acting brings this character to life, as he fluently speaks the language of the era, the player is made aware that he has not only been transported to a distinctive city, but he is also existing in a different time. Ryan persaudes you that the grotesque remnants of a city that you are surrounded with were once grandeur and vibrant, and will be again. While I believe the decision to not provide the character you play as, Jack, with a personality may have been a peculiar one, I understand that the emphasis is not on Jack, but rather on those around him and the lasting impressions they establish.
The gameplay has an arcade style to it. It involves an extensive amount of quickly dashing about, looting corpses and procuring a variety of weapons and unique ammunition for said weapons. While this all becomes a bit repetitive, the speed with which you move about easily compensates for whatever monotonous tasks you are forced to perform. There are multiple frightful encounters early on that will sufficiently maintain your spot on the edge of the seat as well, so don't expect to becomed lulled into a rythmic sense of grinding. The constant echoes of deranged voices will remind you that danger is never far away.
9/10 for the bizarre Bioshock, I applaud 2K Games for taking a chance with a game of this nature, seeing as nothing of this sort has been done before. However, after having personally experienced this thriller for myself, I think it's safe to say that their risk has most definitely paid off.

BioShock is a first-person shooter video game developed by Irrational Games (at the time named 2K Boston), and published by 2K Games. The game was released for Microsoft Windows and Xbox 360 platforms; a PlayStation 3 port by Irrational, 2K Marin, 2K Australia and Digital Extremes was released in October 2008, and an OS X port by Feral Interactive in October 2009.
BioShock is set in 1960, in which the player guides the protagonist, Jack, after his airplane crashes in the ocean near the bathysphere terminus that leads to the underwater city of Rapture. Built by the business magnate Andrew Ryan, the city was intended to be an isolated utopia, but the discovery of ADAM, a plasmid which grants superhuman powers, initiated the city's turbulent decline. Jack tries to find a way to escape, fighting through hordes of ADAM-obsessed enemies such as the deadly Big Daddies, while engaging with the few sane humans that remain and eventually learning of Rapture's past. The player, as Jack, is able to defeat foes in a number of ways by using weapons, utilizing plasmids that give unique powers and by turning Rapture's own defenses against them. BioShock includes elements of role-playing games, giving the player different approaches in engaging enemies such as by stealth, as well as moral choices of saving or killing characters.

That said, this game isn't great, its inspirations are obvious and it's inspirations are to the extent that Jigoku is too afraid to take risks and do its own thing. Danmaku Unlimited also has very similar if not the exact same mechanics as Touhou, but Danmaku Unlimited has its own unique theme and style in regards to presentation, which helps it stand out from the crowd. Jigoku Kisetsukan: Sense of the Seasons is a bullet hell shmup game inspired by
. In it you take control of one of the girls
and fight your way through five stages worth of bullets.
The game can be quite obviously described as
: cute girls flying around shooting fairies or other girls in the face with lasers. But it's a bit more than that. The game has a unique, pixel / chiptune art style most reminiscent of the older PC-98
games rather than the modern ones. The graphics are very well-made, with each stage having its own theme, and the music, while kind of repetitive, does set the good mood for every moment of the game and is kind of catchy at times. Besides chiptunes, we are going to hear some metal too, which I personally enjoyed.
As far as gameplay goes, it's pretty much
: you fly around shooting stuff and dodging hundreds upon hundreds of bullets. Most of the core mechanics are the same, with the only major differences being the
lenient timing on the deathbombs and the fact that your bombs (called "Aura" in this game) do not regenerate if you die. In terms of bullet patterns, some of them I swear were lifted straight from certain spellcards in
, but that might be just me having a few years worth of experience playing those games. The game has more-or-less
level of difficulty when it comes to different difficulty levels: Easy, Normal, Hard and Lunat-I mean Hell. It's fun blasting stuff to bits and getting between bullets, which is what matters the most in this type of game.
The character arts, while not as rich in details as for example
ones, are pleasant to the eye and nice to look at. It might resemble dA level of drawing a bit, but that's not a bad thing.
Now, onto the negatives. The game has crappy controller support, accepting only XInput controllers and being unable to even detect DirectInput ones. Considering most of the PC controllers use DirectInput, that hurts a lot, especially considering that the trial version of the fifteenth
game came out literally two days earlier and doesn't have this issue. I personally suggest using JoyToKey to bypass that (and swapping Focus from Shift to a different button, this button's kind of clunky when it comes to JTK).
Overall, the game may not be perfect, but it's worth playing, especially considering it's free. I recommend it to both
enthusiasts and players new to the genre.

This is a very good game. The presentation and design are amazing, I love the artstyle. It's a very innovative game, one for the ages. It's basically this generation's Pong, a game universally loved and adored, a game that spawns countless more. The ability to change the camera view is ground breaking. The weapon variety is astounding. The music fits the incredible, desolate setting very, very well. Without giving too much away, the story is mind-blowing. You are stranded on an intergalatic farm, hurtling through space. Your navigator, "The Farmer," has been severly injured and left to die on the side of a barn. Each day you must hunt down the pigs which threaten your base, and fight to uncover clues about what happened to the Earth you've left behind. I can see this game being very influential in the development of games to come.
Did I mention it has Co-op? The way the story and atmosphere lends itself to multiplayer is astounding. Everything about this game is amazing. It is truly a masterpiece, the likes of which video gaming has never seen. The Mona Lisa, Beethoven's symphonies, none of those works of art hold a candle to this generation-defining magum opus. One does not "play" this game. One experiences it, lives it. The immersive graphics assist the game in drawing the player, defending their last bastion, this floating farm, from these otherworldly invaders. Words cannot describe the sensations this game has made me feel.

I originally reviewed this game back in 2013, but the current state of reviews for it, have irritated me to no end. So, I have decided to update my review.
Project Zomboid, is perhaps the single game that does 'zombie survival' right. It has atmosphere, character and most importantly, a dedicated team behind it.
The survival aspect, your character needs to eat, drink and sleep. Deal with depression, boredom, panic and illness. All of this is on top of the obvious, dealing with the zombies. Whilst nearly everything in this game is customisable, from number of zombies, to their cognition, hearing and sight, to experience rate, custom maps and even how fruitful farming or foraging can be.
The game has several presets, for different levels of gamers. With 'Survival' being the accepted norm. In this mode, zombie mortality rate is at something along the lines of 96% mortality rate from bites, and 25% from scratches. Now, this is only magnified, by the fact you can have literally hundreds, if not thousands of zombies on screen at once, should you have the settings set to do so.
This game forces you to learn how to play and survive. It's not a casual 'I'll run around with a shotgun and take out hundreds of zombies at a time'. This is a survival game, truly.
Without mods, your character starts as an 'average joe'. With no specific skill set, unless a career has been chosen. This game has one of the most well done trait/perk systems I have seen, since the original Fallout games. This gives a rich and rewarding feeling, to have survived long enough to learn how to build and operate machinery, houses and farms. It also gives a much larger sense of profound loss, when you finally succumb to anything in the world. From lack of food, to fever, to the hundreds of zombies that are attracted to sound and sight.
This game is nothing short of a masterpiece, I love it, and 90% of the reviews agree with me. You can't go wrong with this game.
This brings me nicely on to my next point, please don't be put off by the other recent reviews, slating the dev team behind this for 'slow updates'. They have gotten more abuse than I can comprehend, from this angle. They have continued to update and support this game to the best of their ability, for years. The dev team consists of only six people, up from four in previous years.
In this time, they have updated the graphics - twice, adding in 3D models whereas it was a game consisting of sprites (Still an option you can revert to, in the game settings.) and then they quietly worked on double definition models, behind the scenes. They are currently working on an animation system, which has taken a while, granted, but will magnify the gameplay threefold.
This game, is more than worth the price of admission. Do yourself a favour, and buy this amazing game, you really can't go wrong.
TL;DR, This game is amazing. Buy it.

The Long Dark is tremendously atmospheric, stylish, and beautiful.
I've been playing this game on and off over the past several months. It has become my go-to when I felt that I needed a game with a great immersive atmosphere and unrelenting difficulty. The Long Dark is so immersive that I grab blankets and hoodies to warm up with because this game literally makes me feel cold.
The game mechanics are also fairly straight forward and easy to grasp - I've handed the controller (the game plays great with a 360 controller) after a death to a friend watching me and watched them just get straight into it without having to explain much. And of course, the only real objective [in the EA sandbox] is to just keep surviving, which can be difficult with the abundance of fierce beasts and uncooperative weather.
The voice actors are also great. You'd thinking hearing people whining and commenting on things in a game like this would get annoying, but the dialogue stays at an acceptably scarce level and when it does happen, the character's lines are pretty understandable/believable/yeah, you're right, it is damn cold.
All in all, really fun and immersive. If you don't come into a game wanting to survive as long as possible, or if you're the kind of person that gets easily frustrated with watching hours of struggle go wasted due to one unfortunate wolf attack or wrong step, you might get bored or♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥at this game pretty easily.
The best advice I can give - just immerse yourself; be your character, keep fighting, and if you're going to fade into the long dark, don't let it take you easily.

I tried writing a review of this game before, but back then I didn't think I had given this game a fair shake. First off, this game is not a card game, its essentially a strategy board game similar to... well, I don't know of many that are still played in this day and age so I'll just go with classics such as Heroscape and Necromunda. (You don't even know what those are do you)
You play by assembling your battlegroup from runes (cards that essentially work as model figures) and supporting them with spells and equipment. As far as these types of games go, Pox Nora is deep, and has had years to develop its rune catalog. There are eight factions, of which a battlegroup can be composed of at most 2. Runes have rarity and differing efficiency values, but all are useful in some way or another. That being said, discovering this usefulness can be tricky as the game is not straightforward and figuring it all out is essentially trial and error. There is a tutorial, but it's terrible, and the steam interface could use some improvement.
Is the game P2W? No, not anymore. It used to be, which is when I first started writing this review some time ago when the gold income was paltry and winning battles didn't give out free runes (cards. You know what? I'm just going to call them cards) Now, its possible to get really good cards for free without ever having to play another player, which is a good thing because, quite frankly, I find the community could try a little harder to accomadate newer players. It will still take lots of games and lots of times to put together your own battlegroup, but the game has many free battlegroups you can play while collecting your set, and no, they don't suck.
The graphics are a bit dated, but if you don't mind that, then their's no reason to talk about it. If you do mind it, your either going to look past it, or not. Either way, they are what they are.
To sum up, if you like card games and board games, and don't mind dated graphics or figuring things out by yourself, give Pox Nora a shot. The game is improving with time now that its under a new developer, but it still has a long way to go to compete with powerhouses such as MTG or Hearthstone.

I actually read other reviews before playing the game, and they only made me want to play it more. I have a thing for cheesy fundamentalist Christian propaganda, though I’m an atheist, and I knew what this was going in. I would have played it eventually anyway, since I liked the concept even without the Christianity, and I have a sort of bile fascination for amusingly bad but playable games, and I love visual novels. But as soon as I found out it was full of super fundie Christianity, I downloaded it immediately and began to play. Jackpot!
And wow! I certainly got what I was looking for, though I was kinda disappointed that
. The truly despicable thing about this game is that it doesn’t let the player know right away that it’s a Christian game. But then everything she says turns out to be true and the only way to get the “good” end of the game is to
. The description of the game is intended to lure in people interested in the paranormal, occult, and UFOs thinking that they’ll get a decent game about the subject matter with an open mind or at least a funny comedic take, but what the game ends up doing is preaching about how those are all evil and demonic, literally. There is legitimately a bonus section to the game that tells players that UFOs are demons in disguise. What. the. literal. hell.
As for the art and writing, the art was at times passable and at times terrible, while the writing was pretty amateurish and the characters were cardboard stereotypes, sometimes even going for racial and gender stereotypes. The music was bearable, even amusing at times, but the backgrounds were awful, a mixture of shopped images, drawings, and photos.
Despite the mixed art and writing quality, I might have given this a thumbs up for the cheesiness and interesting concept. Maybe. Here are a few items that I enjoyed about
:
Gameplay -
holds a striking comparison to other Indie titles when it comes to the control layout: it is entirely straightforward. As you may or may not have experienced in prior games, this title utilizes the directional keys for basic movement-with down allowing your character to drop down and grab onto a ledge-, the Space Bar to jump, and the Control key to interact with objects and the environment itself; others have stated that this is much more fluid while playing with a plug-in controller. This painless layout aides the player in not forcing them to have to remember too many needless actions; if the controls could be remapped, a player could even be able to play it with one hand. In summary, the controls are of simple design for a simple game. As described previously-without revealing too much in terms of story progression-the player directs the young boy through treacherous territories, which prompts the solving of intricate puzzles. These stages-numbering twenty-four in total-generally require the player to test the mechanics in a ‘truth and error’ approach, unless applied thought is given to the situation for a considerable amount of time prior to action. A decent reaction time is necessary for certain portions since platforming is included into the general mechanics, which can be somewhat frustrating and rewarding due to the intense precision specific stages necessitate.
Atmosphere -
is very black and white in terms of its color palette in that it is literally variants of black and white (if you have read my previous reviews, you know that I am not permitted to make jokes due to the overall lack of comedy involved, hence this current display.) This helps to depict the grim depth of this title’s occurrences, as well as developing tone that is not distracting from the gameplay. Even the game’s playstyle is murky since the protagonist’s death is intended to remind the player what they had done wrong in a specific segment and as an indication of how the level’s mechanics are set. The game shifts seamlessly between transition periods with minimal loading and intractable events.
Throughout, however, you may just become attached to said protagonist as though his struggles become your very own. The protagonist portrays no vocal characteristics, though the background effects add enough ambience to compensate for this.
TL:DR - For those with keen senses in regards to game mechanics, you will find
to be trivial yet enjoyable. This title is a deep, brooding tale with no words and only atmosphere to speak its demented thoughts. It is a relatively short title that can be frustrating at times but is worth its cost as an experience. Though the protagonist does not and cannot outwardly portray his ideals, you will surely fight for him to learn of his sister’s fate. You will learn much as a player and an adventurer, but do not lose hope in
. Thanks for reading.

Before proceeding, let me tell you this, this will be long and I will try to point out why I didn't like Tropico 5 in detail, if you want the resumed version just check it in the end.
To start it off, I didn't enjoy Tropico 5 like I did with Tropico 4, really, it is FAR worst than 4, the humor is way more childish, voice actors changed for your loyal Penultimo that sounds nothing like him and honestly makes him far more boring and, worst of all, the story is just... lame. It felt like it was written in a rush, making it simple with a more than disapointing ending.
BUT the game isn't compleatly bad, the mechanic is far more challenging and the era things aswell as the multiplayer are both good, which makes the game enjoyable. Sadly the game doesn't explain many of its new concepts, making it confusing and really frustrating, you'll have to dedicate a good while just checking each screen the game has to fully understand how everything in it works.
Tropico 5 also adds a limit to your total population, making your growth stop at a rather bad point, max 2000 people, you'll start to feel such effects of a limited population way before too, at around 900. Some structures feel useless too, such as the subway and the garage, both say they'll increase the efficiency of nearby houses, but they don't really change.
Speaking of apparently useless structures, many buildings have an awful tooltip, lacking explanation for how it works. During my first plays I made factory ranches, an upgraded version of ranches and then suddenly it stopped producing. I searched, read the tooltip again and again, checked efficiency, everything seemed normal, only after a lot of frustration I checked the forums to find out it required a supply of corn.
Some new concepts are also interesting, but really badly planned out, such as the manager for buildings and dynasty members. Both should help you improve your buildings and offer some sort of use, but they really feel useless, it is REALLY had to see a change in a building with managers. Your dynasty members are basicly that too, improved managers and frankly nothing else. You could also see your swiss bank account has a new use, improving your dynasty members, which isn't that hard and after a while you just say ♥♥♥♥ it to the swiss bank account.
Speaking of dynasty members, you can customize them and your character, but frankly? Customization is just AWFUL compared to Tropico 4. Meager 4 or 5 suits which you won't EVER see as your characters are really, really small. Remember how you had to use your presidente for all sort of things? Boosting constructions, moving him to make speeches, help improve a building, you actualy cared for the character and tried to keep track of him. In Tropico 5 you make and forget about him, what is the point of following him if he won't do♥♥♥♥♥♥ You can't control him either.
Lastly, upgrades are now boring, really boring. In Tropico 4 you could upgrade something and it would change visually, even if it was a small detail it was a change and it was fun! You could see you had improved that building! In Tropico 5 nothing changes, absolutly nothing, I forgot how many times I ♥♥♥♥ed up because I forgot to upgrade a building because I had NO idea what was and what was not upgraded at that point.
Resuming: Tropico 5 is not Tropico 4, see it as a different, harder and way more rushed version of it, otherwise you won't get to enjoy it and YOU WILL be frustrated.

Since beating The Beginner's Guide, I've read a ton of reviews and interpretations, curious to see how others were affected by the game, and here is where the genius (and hilarious irony) of the narrative hits hardest. I interpreted The Beginner's Guide as a statement about how appreciators of art, games, literature, and any other creative work look upon the creator instead of themselves. Instead of allowing the piece to affect them and perhaps alter their world view, viewers and critics use the piece to deconstruct the psychology of the creator, and then use it to squeeze out (and criticize) what they feel the creator's "message" is, despite not knowing the creator well enough at all to make any kind of assumptions about them.
That is exactly what the majority of editorial reviewers did. They used this game to make assumptions about Davey Wreden, digging into his personal life and tying it to The Beginner's Guide to find "the meaning."
Wreden created a powerful, interactive way to teach that lesson, likely knowing full well that the response would illustrate it further. Everyone interprets art differently, but critics rarely consider the effect their judgements about the creator's psychology or philosophies has on the creator. It's not a creator's job to explain the significance of the three dots. It's not your place to add lampposts. As a writer who also buries much of her work in folders instead of sharing it with others for fear of the same treatment, this game affected me significantly.
Artists will experience this game very differently than critics. I consider The Beginner's Guide one of the most valuable narrative gaming experiences I've had in a very long time, so buy it. Play it. When you review it, remember: "The fact that you think I am frustrated or broken says more about you than it does me."

I do recommend the game, but I am against most of its game design decisions, for more, read this short review.
At first I'll separate this review between the art part of the game and the "game" part of the game, then making my own point about the game as a whole. And btw, the game is overrated.
-Art-
So, for real, the art is incredible, the game is a silhouette masterpiece, strengthening semiotics above everything else, the black and white tone makes us think that we are in fact alone in Limbo and everything is terrifying, you can't trust anything out there, it's even philosophic, you can't trust some silhouettes, and those can lead to your demise.
The animations are pretty good and work pretty well, the protagonist has pretty good animations overall and the art direction was impecable through the whole game, it feels solid differing foreground and background, and the game objects were easy to pick from the pure art assets. The sounds and soundtrack are pretty good, they do their job pretty well.
The lack of narrative in the game was probably intentional to save money, time and programming, but in the end, it was well blended into the overall atmosphere, making up a silent game where every player has a particular reaction to the game experience. Or at least from the art experience, because the gameplay is not as deep as the art.
-Gameplay-
Over my gameplay I didn't find gamebreaking bugs or even major bugs, it was overall an almost bugless experience, I enjoy that. But...
The game design is pretty unorthodox, you are given almost no clues to discover if something is going to kill you until that thing is about half second away from killing you, since you have to rely on silhouettes, the game may create illusions on what you see and kill you purposedly while you think you're safe. Most of my deaths were because I didn't have a clue that I was going to die until death was unavoidable.
Out of the puzzles, they were well thought and utilize pretty well the game mechanics, but they are a bit too old and are not innovative as previous puzzle indies did, such as World of Goo and Braid. I came up to this game seeing the good reviews and everyone around me talking so well about it, that I finally decided to give a try. But what I found out was only old-fashioned puzzles and the so hated timing related  puzzles.
There are too many timing related puzzles in this game that some levels are frustrating, strict timing that comes close to "1 second you're dead" timing is not so cool in a puzzle game. While these mechanics do work in action oriented games,  puzzle games as slow as this one may feel too burdened, and the player feels remorse because the game has such strict timing requirements even after he already knows the answer to the puzzle, he can't get to go ahead because the timing won't let him execute it correctly.
Over to the controls, they don't feel good, and they don't feel tight. I saw myself jumping to death more than a dozen times, grabbing random things or letting them go randomly, mainly jumping was the main issue, the jumping seems a bit off, I'm not asking for Super Meat Boy controls over here, but I just wish I didn't die so much because of the bad controls.
Over to mechanics, most of them were ok, apart from killing you without your knowledge at first, and then, after you died, you could study the puzzle. Only one mechanic was "bad" in my opinion, which is the brain maggot-larva. This mechanic is awkward and annoying, it doesn't transfer a good game design idea and it doesn't feel good to be played with, the game would be better if those larvas were left behind and more attention was given to the gravity-sound relation near the end of the  game.
-My Opinion-
In my honest opinion, this game is pretty overrated, mainly people see everyone talking so good about it that they feel bad and overlook the negative aspects of the game. If this game was stripped of its graphics, atmosphere and sound, with just Unity or whatever placeholders, you can see that the pure gameplay and game design is not  so well executed. While many games around that didn't get as much attention as this one would still be fun to play with even with placeholder crappy graphics.
Most of the people who find this game good may enjoy timing event puzzles or may not come from a particular puzzle gaming past, because I can't really find any joy in disheartening and frustrating puzzles that punish me because I couldn't time them correctly even after i figured out what was the answer. Nevertheless, the art makes up for everything that the game design lacks.
My particular rating would be 7/10 mainly because of the art.
But for the overall public, I think that this game is a 8/10.
Just get over it, it is overrated.

Rosangela Blackwell is a struggling author living in New York, and a medium. Enter Joey Mallone, a ghost and spirit guide tied to the female members of the Blackwell family. When Rosa's aunt, Lauren Blackwell, passes after being in a coma for decades, Joey is 'released' from Lauren and enters Rosa's life. Details are revealed throughout the five installments of the Blackwell series regarding the female members of the Blackwell family, how Joey came to be, what happened to Aunt Lauren to trap her in a comatose state, etc. Together, Rosa and Joey seek out and help tormented ghosts trapped in the physical world cross over to "the other side" throughout the series.
In BLACKWELL EPIPHANY, the fifth and final installment of the game series.
Rosa’s now fully embraced her quest to find trapped spirits in New York and help them to move on.  We finally discover the origins of the two most prominent characters of the series, and learn a little more about a shadowy organization that is the antithesis of everything Rosa and Joey stand for. Many answers to things will be brought to light which have been hanging over the series since it's inception. The Blackwell series has always been focused on human stories, which has made this series so special. It definitely stands strong on its own merits with the incredible writing of Dave Gilbert.
EPIPHANY begins and immediately takes a serious dark turn when people's souls are ripped apart right in front of Rosa and Joey's eyes. And there's the ghost of a little girl which hits Rosa and Joey harder than others -- but, for the most part, not treated as all that different or special than the others along their journey.  Death is unfair. Rosa and Joey know and accept that. It's the race to get the little girl's ghost ‘safe’ before whatever is destroying souls can take her death as easily as it took her life. There are other ghosts to be dealt with, too. From the TV news anchor desperate to leave her past behind, to the brother and sister striving to deal with childhood abuse.
How does one end such a phenomenal series? When you get to the last act, everything kicks into high gear heading for the finish line ... the grand finale. And, wow! What a finale! The very last scene is ... dare I say ... perfect!
Thanks, Dave, for such a wonderful experience over the past decade with the Blackwell series. Kudos!!!
(To enjoy the story at it's best, the games should be played in order of creation. 1st 'LEGACY' -- 2nd 'UNBOUND' which explores the events and time that Lauren Blackwell and Joey were working together in the 1970s (while Unbound turned out, unintentionally, to be a prequel to Legacy, it should be played after Legacy to not only help enlighten the player as to what happened in the first installment, but also gives the player clues as to what is coming in future installments) -- 3rd 'CONVERGENCE' which takes place about six months after the events in Legacy -- 4th 'DECEPTION' which takes place some time after Convergence -- and 5th 'EPIPHANY', which is the final installment in the Blackwell game series.)

I played Touhou, so I thought, why not pick this up? Disregarding the fact that it's free, this is how I feel about it:

When I rate stuff, I rate it on how distracting it is to me. Now let's see how distracting the game is.
The graphics weren't stunning, but they did what they were supposed to do (if their goal was to do some old school graphics thing, they pulled it off). It felt very simple to me, but at least it wasn't distracting. You know, ugly. At least it wasn't ugly-distracting.
The music was okay. Not Touhou-tier okay, but at least it did not make me mute the game. When I played for the first time, the only time I actually took note of the music was when there were no enemies to take down. So nope, not distracting at all, in a good way.
Difficulty-wise, the game felt a bit easy in Normal mode. The thing I noticed about the game is that most of the time there's a rain of bullets coming your way. Sure that's bullet hell for you, but I actually would like a bit more of those laser stuff coming at me (like the ones with the bosses). Give me more lasers please.
One surprising way that this game was made easy as well are the death-bomb mechanics. I don't know how it is in the other modes (if it is any different), but if you can bomb, there's a timer when you get hit. That few seconds is huge. It makes it too easy to death-bomb.
Another thing to note is that once you die, the aura is kept at your current state. I find this kind of annoying. If you were really bad a certain pattern, have no more bombs left and die (u nid 2 gitgud boi), you probably will die again because you can't bomb.
I think the game is a good start for people looking to get into bullet hells. Easy, lets you learn about death-bombing, limits you with your bombing (2gitgud) and it's free!

Five Night at Freddy's starts as a psychological horror game but ends up more of a resource management game. The first four nights were a lot of fun, quite creepy and sometimes scary (although mostly because of jump scares). But by the fifth night the game is all about the resource management to the point where the psychological horror disapears. You are not going to finish it on the first attempt and the chances are by the time you complete this you will be numb and possibly even bored.
Night five is like trying to juggle twelve eggs. The basic idea is pretty simple, but executing it without making a mistake is the problem. It can take a lot of practice and many hair pulling moments. For me night five was not fun, and that is where the problem arises: Night Five is where the game really starts. You will spend more time on night five (and beyond) than the first four days.
It is not a bad game, and if you like juggling eggs whilst avoiding jump scares it will be sheer joy for you. But for me it was four nights of fun and one very very long night of frustration followed by a brief moment of sheer extasy when I finally finished night five .... and then a painful moment when I saw what was next.
In the end I recommend this game because it is an experience I am glad I had, and feel it is one most lovers of horror/jump scare games should try once. But do not expect to enjoy every minute of this game unless you are masochistic in nature. Hair pulling and keyboard violence should be expected.

My Game Play:

This game was not what I expected. By that I mean I was pleasantly surprised. I was expecting a dark, over gritty story, and instead got a charming little adventure. Sure, there are parts that are darker, but the majority of the gameplay is quite pleasant, both in tone and to play. Granted, I picked the “Easy Setting” to get through the game faster (because I’m a lazy person), but there was still some challenge to the game despite that. The official artwork is seriously misleading in what the content of the game is like. But I wouldn’t consider that a bad thing (especially how great they look).
This game is a good example of what you can do with default RPG Maker assets. True, I think there are some custom assets in the game, but a lot of this game works with the default icons and tilesets and…it actually gives it charm. For me, at least. But it may be a deterrent for some other people. (I’m looking at you, SakifX9.)
The writing in the game was, overall, decent. Make no mistake—this game is no literary masterpiece. Not by a longshot. But there were a lot of moments I thought were cute. However, as a writer myself, I remember reading the dialogue and constantly thinking of little tweaks that would improve it. There were some moments that I thought would be just that much better if they reworded slightly. But it’s also worth noting that I found myself skimming through text during the latter half of the game. True, there were probably a lot of good moments I missed, but I always got the gist of things. If you think this invalidates my opinion on the writing in this game, then I can’t blame you.
One major complaint I have about the game, though, is the multitude of puzzles. It’s clear that’s what the developer/s love to do, but I’m not a person that particularly enjoys them. Sure, puzzles are kinda something to expect with the RPG package, but my brain just isn’t built that way. I usually avoid looking up walkthroughs until I get hopelessly stuck. I got hopelessly stuck in two places in this game due to the puzzles. One of them wasn’t mandatory, so I just gave up after a couple hours of frustration, but the second one was mandatory to continuing the plot. That is bull. It should not take me looking up the strategy guide to be able to beat the game.
(Also, to anyone who is interested in buying this game, do not, do not, do NOT do the Treasure Dungeons! Ever! You get the first key in the main quest...DO NOT FOLLOW UP ON IT! Why? I sat through it, all five of them, putting in hours and hours of work, and the reward was super lame. Like, lamer than I could even expect. If you’re doing the quest called Grammy on the Run, then you’ll have to do all five, but DO NOT DO ANYTHING MORE THAN FINDING HER! I’M DEAD SERIOUS! If you’re a person who doesn’t enjoy puzzles, THEN STAY AWAY!)
A second complaint I have is with the quests are in this game. After a while, they started to really get on my nerves for one reason: they’re rarely straightforward. I know it’s kinda standard RPG territory, but this game really went overboard with it. I’ll make up an example to avoid potential spoilers:
You come across a guy who wants a flyswatter he left at his ex-girlfriend’s house. You go to her house, and then she says she sold the flyswatter to a peddler after the two broke up. You find this peddler halfway across the world only to discover that he sold the flyswatter to a witch. You find the witch in a remote location only to be told that the witch DOES have the flyswatter, but she put a curse on it for the lulz, and anyone who touches the flyswatter will instantly die. So you have to explore the nearby swamp to collect the necessary ingredients to create a potion to break the curse. Once you collect all eight ingredients, the witch breaks the curse on the flyswatter, so you can finally take it with you. You then travel back to the first guy and give him his flyswatter. He rewards you for your efforts with a borderline useless item (and you usually get some EXP too).
Like I said, that’s not an actual quest in the game, but over 75% of the quests in the game operate like this. Sometimes the rewards are worth the effort, sometimes they’re not. Again, I shouldn’t complain, since quests like this come with the territory, but this game REALLY went overboard with it. Again, not a deal breaker for me, but it might be for you, dear reader.
After that little tangent, let me just say that the music in the game is awesome and perfectly atmospheric. Granted, I recognized one track from an RPG Maker Music Album, but that doesn’t mean it isn’t a good song.
One halfhearted complaint I have is on the artwork and face graphics themselves. They’re beautiful and realistic. However, they create artistic dissonance between them and the pixel artwork of the rest of the game. Again, not really a complaint, but they just seem really out of place.
Also, this game has commentary in it! About a whole range of topics to: mostly on RPG Maker Game Logic, but there was this long segment that criticized playwriting and acting. I think one of my favourite moments in this game was when the characters were watching a play in a mansion, and the developers actually took the time to show the actors run on and off stage. However, there was some commentary that I found either weak or just didn’t understand. There was this entire town whose dialogue was apparently shallow and weak, but I found it just fine. On the other hand, some commentary was hilariously spot on. All the characters you come across are using RPG Maker XP sprites, but then they come across a city of “dwarves”, which is made up of entirely RPG Maker VX/Ace sprites. THAT made me laugh, even though my game’s characters are made up of these sprites.
Probably one of the biggest disappointments of this game was the character of Viper; at least for me. At first I thought she looked really cool, but she was so inconsistently written that I became turned off of her character. There were several moments where they could have developed her character, but didn’t. Other times they tried to develop her character in ways that contradicted what was already established. Lastly, after she joins the party, she takes up around 70% of the dialogue, leaving 30% for the other characters. The title implies that Lily and Sasha are the main focus, but then why does Viper hog so much screentime? The game kept trying to build her up as someone important and useful, when really, she wasn't. There IS something that happens near the very end, where you were supposed to feel sorry for her, but I was just too annoyed with her, so I actually found it very satisfying.
Also, fair warning for any of you out there thinking of getting this game, the ending is pretty big sequel bait. I didn’t mind this, since I have the sequel as well, but it makes me dread playing it because I know there’s another sequel after that which I don’t have. The ending can work on its own, I guess, but really, this is a game that you play to play the entire series, not just the first entry. Which confuses me…why have three short games when you can combine them into one long game? I dunno. Anyway, just thought I’d warn you all.
Despite all of this, I still recommend this game. Sure, Viper annoyed me a little, and I found the puzzles a bit overkill, but if you, dear reader, play it, maybe these things won’t rub you the wrong way like they did for me. Is it the best game ever? No. Every game has its flaws, and I think the positives outweigh the negatives with this one.

I have re-written my review, as i last wrote it in 2013 having played 20 hours.  I'm now up to 80+ hours and the year is 2015, a lot can change in that space of time...
There is only one real negative to this game and that is the multiplayer, or rather trying to play with your friends.  It's easy enough to just join a server and play online, obviously if all your group join the same server you can play together; however, the problem comes when you want to set up a private game with your own rules.  It is not easy to do (I could just be being a bit of an idiot though, feel free to leave comments if you know of a better way than what I came up with) and in the end my group had to use Hamachi to create an online LAN.
By far and away the biggest positive has to be the developers, they up date this game so much! When I started playing there where only a handful of skills (blade, blunt, lightfooted, sprinting, cooking, carpentry, sneaking) now there are at least double that number.  Same goes for occupations (think character classes), when I began there were only 4 or 5.
The game is really challenging, mistakes are punished; I would compare it to dark souls in its difficulty, in that if you die you can attribute it to a mistake you have made.
Crafting/survival mechanics are great, build a house, trap animals, fish, farm, explore and scavenge.  Stay out in the rain too long, get wet, get cold, get ill and die.  Don't prepare well enough for the power and water to shut off - starve and die of thirst.  Climb through a broken window without removing the glass, maybe you will be fine, maybe you will cut yourself, maybe that cut will get infected because you have no medical kit. Walk into the wrong part of town, get surrounded, get eaten.  Or lose all hope, drink a bottle of bleach and kill yourself!
Combat is very simplistic, which helps create tension when fighting off hordes.  Time attacks well and zombies go down easy.  Mess it up and it is easy to get overwhelmed.
Mods galore, this game is early access but it has more workshop content than most!
One final negative, there is no real story to the game yet, hopefully it is going to arrive relatively soon, so late game can end up getting a bit stale.  The journey to that point is absolutely fantastic though.
Without a doubt, the most value for money I have ever gotten from a computer game... Ever.
Big shout out to the developers for doing such a good job.  Guys like you are why early access was created and it is a pity more developers don't work to your high standards.

The Long Dark (TLD) is, without a doubt, one of my favorite games of all time. The art and environment are beautiful. The audio work is masterfully created and constantly evolving. The game mechanics are refined, but could use further tweaking, which I have full confidence in Hinteland Studios to do.
Although without currently a story mode, TLD sandbox mode provides a self-generated emotional experience that tickles your visceral senses. This is the perfect game for fans of survival-themed TV shows, which would be me, or those who simply appreciate the challenges that natures heaves. Your "enemies" in this game are the choices you make. Yes, there are wolves and bears, but you have the choice to completely avoid them. In TLD sandbox, you create the story and are rewarded or punished accordingly.
Hinterland Studios has done an incredible job of bringing the Canadian wilderness to your desktop (I say this without ever spending a minute in the Canadian wilderness). The immersiveness of the environment is felt immediately. Audio cues, such as the music transitioning in when you come upon a key location or when the skies clear for the sun, is quite moving. This game literally gives me chills and startles me when either a wolf growls unexpectely (or you think one is growling) and chases you while you find shelter indoors. You constantly battle the sense of desperation, cold and fear against hope, warmth and relief; fighting and thinking about the former is key to survival.
The graphics, or more appropriately the artwork, is very good albeit not AAA-esque (and it isn't meant to be). For example, the sheet of ice crystals that form on your screen when walking outside, as if they're forming over your eyes, reminds you how cold it is. I would love to see the graphics be further refined to imbue more realism, but overall, it's fantastic.
Game mechanics are good. Inventory system is easy to navigate, but I wish more items were made stackable. Overall, it's a very simple game that doesn't require twitch reflexes or advanced skill. The most difficult action is to shoot the bow and arrow, but with practice, one can master this pretty quickly.
As with any early access game, we should see a lot of new content coming our way, including the story mode. If sandbox is able to lure me in this much, I have high hopes that story mode will do the same and add some context to the actual gameplay. Highly, highly recommend this game.

I haven't finished the game yet; I'm at about 35% completion, so take that for what it's worth.  So far, the game has been a lot of fun.
Combat mechanics aren't very complicated; each character has
1.  A weak attack, a strong attack, (both of which start generic but can be altered by runes)
2.  A powerful attack, heal or buff unique to that character, and
3.  Team attacks based on the other people placed on the team with them.
In place of a static MP system, characters use Stamina, which regenerates in battle.
The dialogue is pretty entertaining, with characters feeling pretty well fleshed out in personality.  This occasionally gives rise to conflict within the party, which gives the group a degree of believabilty many games lack.
EDIT: I forgot in my first draft to mention the puzzles, which deserve recognition.  While they wren't quite as common or as intense as Lufia/Lufia II, they bring those games to mind.  Specifically, a LOT of the side quests offer tangible rewards for playing through puzzles, so while they aren't "necessary," those of us who enjoy such things get a warm fuzzy feeling AND better gear.
My only complaint (and it's a doozy) is that as of the time of this writing, gear bonuses are not being added properly to your chars.  I haven't done my homework on things like Strength, and Agility, but they seem to be working.  However, Spirit (which adds HP) is NOT being added to the characters' HP totals.  This means characters whose gear focuses on toughness (like Griffin, one of your early chars) suffer, since their gear gives up points in other stats which do seem to be added in.  Hopefully the devs will fix this.
In all, it's been a fun game so far.  Seems a bit brief, but for the price, the length is reasonable.

Rate: 8.5/10
Overview: Isometric Rogue-lite
Similar Games: Faster Than Light
The Good:
+ Art style that reflects Victorian Gothic atmosphere which adds to the mood of the game
+ In sunless sea you navigate a ship to explore distant locations. Every location you visit has its own story where you get to choose how things play out, almost like a choose your own adventure novel. The choices you have are based on the resources you collect and your stats. The stories are excellently written and really play out in different ways depending on the choices you make.
+ You also must manage fuel, supplies and fear. Mismanaging any of these resources to a large degree will result in death. Surviving the sea can be a daunting task, between managing resources, avoiding/attacking enemies or making the wrong choice in a story just adds to the danger you face.
+ Collect money to buy new ships, weapons, engines, resources etc.
+ Certain locations are randomized every game
+ You can select your own victory conditions at the beginning of the game.
+ Soundtrack
Average:
The game is REALLY slow paced and may not be suitable for every gamers tastes. It takes a long time to really gather money and start making progress unless you exploit some of the games mechanics. Ships also travel slowly to build tension but also adds to the tedium of travel.
The Bad:
The game crashed on me a lot and nothing but a hard reset would fix the problem often causing my save file to become corrupt.
Conclusion:
Unlike other Rogue games this game takes a long time to complete a single play through depending on skill level. The sea is harsh, cruel, and dying is common place, but if you can stick through the bad times you may realize the game is a lot of fun.

I've never written a review on steam but after playing this game I felt the need to. I don't know where to start with this game or this review and it'll probably be a lot of just me rambling at you if you decide to read this. This game hit me on every personal level possible, even ones I didn't know could be hit. I'm going through a rough patch of life, roughest patch yet and have been for some three years now. I'd heard about this game and I was stumbling through steam sales when my brain told me "buy The Beginner's Guide." So I did, not thinking anything of it. Then I installed the game and started playing, expecting a slight romp through game design and how we percieve others, only to wind up spending the game looking at myself as I went. I spent a good chunk of my play time just sending quotes to my girlfriend because of how well they applied to my life even when they were said in the context of this game. As I went on I started to relate even more, chosing the options that had less to do with game design and more to do with general failure and self actualization. When I had to shoot the stage, part of me insticually did it, but part of me didn't want to. The walking backwards from the stage part was a fantastic visual representation of what it feels like to have anxiety, even if it was not what Coda wanted. The thing that stood out the most came during the clean house chapter, where Davy talks about not staying in the darkness and having people to tell you things would be OK, that was the part I needed most. As the game spiraled I didn't know what to do and when it ended I wanted more, some sort of proper closure that would bring it back to to the reassurance I was getting at the begginning, but there wasn't more, and I realized just the impact this game had on me.
TLDR: I'm at a bad place in life, this game is the most impactful game I've played in a long time.
