I do recommend the game, but I am against most of its game design decisions, for more, read this short review.
At first I'll separate this review between the art part of the game and the "game" part of the game, then making my own point about the game as a whole. And btw, the game is overrated.
-Art-
So, for real, the art is incredible, the game is a silhouette masterpiece, strengthening semiotics above everything else, the black and white tone makes us think that we are in fact alone in Limbo and everything is terrifying, you can't trust anything out there, it's even philosophic, you can't trust some silhouettes, and those can lead to your demise.
The animations are pretty good and work pretty well, the protagonist has pretty good animations overall and the art direction was impecable through the whole game, it feels solid differing foreground and background, and the game objects were easy to pick from the pure art assets. The sounds and soundtrack are pretty good, they do their job pretty well.
The lack of narrative in the game was probably intentional to save money, time and programming, but in the end, it was well blended into the overall atmosphere, making up a silent game where every player has a particular reaction to the game experience. Or at least from the art experience, because the gameplay is not as deep as the art.
-Gameplay-
Over my gameplay I didn't find gamebreaking bugs or even major bugs, it was overall an almost bugless experience, I enjoy that. But...
The game design is pretty unorthodox, you are given almost no clues to discover if something is going to kill you until that thing is about half second away from killing you, since you have to rely on silhouettes, the game may create illusions on what you see and kill you purposedly while you think you're safe. Most of my deaths were because I didn't have a clue that I was going to die until death was unavoidable.
Out of the puzzles, they were well thought and utilize pretty well the game mechanics, but they are a bit too old and are not innovative as previous puzzle indies did, such as World of Goo and Braid. I came up to this game seeing the good reviews and everyone around me talking so well about it, that I finally decided to give a try. But what I found out was only old-fashioned puzzles and the so hated timing related  puzzles.
There are too many timing related puzzles in this game that some levels are frustrating, strict timing that comes close to "1 second you're dead" timing is not so cool in a puzzle game. While these mechanics do work in action oriented games,  puzzle games as slow as this one may feel too burdened, and the player feels remorse because the game has such strict timing requirements even after he already knows the answer to the puzzle, he can't get to go ahead because the timing won't let him execute it correctly.
Over to the controls, they don't feel good, and they don't feel tight. I saw myself jumping to death more than a dozen times, grabbing random things or letting them go randomly, mainly jumping was the main issue, the jumping seems a bit off, I'm not asking for Super Meat Boy controls over here, but I just wish I didn't die so much because of the bad controls.
Over to mechanics, most of them were ok, apart from killing you without your knowledge at first, and then, after you died, you could study the puzzle. Only one mechanic was "bad" in my opinion, which is the brain maggot-larva. This mechanic is awkward and annoying, it doesn't transfer a good game design idea and it doesn't feel good to be played with, the game would be better if those larvas were left behind and more attention was given to the gravity-sound relation near the end of the  game.
-My Opinion-
In my honest opinion, this game is pretty overrated, mainly people see everyone talking so good about it that they feel bad and overlook the negative aspects of the game. If this game was stripped of its graphics, atmosphere and sound, with just Unity or whatever placeholders, you can see that the pure gameplay and game design is not  so well executed. While many games around that didn't get as much attention as this one would still be fun to play with even with placeholder crappy graphics.
Most of the people who find this game good may enjoy timing event puzzles or may not come from a particular puzzle gaming past, because I can't really find any joy in disheartening and frustrating puzzles that punish me because I couldn't time them correctly even after i figured out what was the answer. Nevertheless, the art makes up for everything that the game design lacks.
My particular rating would be 7/10 mainly because of the art.
But for the overall public, I think that this game is a 8/10.
Just get over it, it is overrated.

Like others I had heard good things about this game. As a long time fan of the Myst series I had no issues diving into a puzzle game, and with the atmosphere LIMBO presented it seemed right up my street.
However, if truth be told, I don't like this game.
Whilst the black and white design with the foreground and background elements are an interesting design choice I often found them cumbersome, impacting on the area which I could interact with making it hard to see at times what I was doing.
My biggest issue with this game is the puzzles. Not because I found them difficult, I found them pretty straight forward. No I disliked the puzzles because they are so damned picky. Often I found that the timing between tiggering a puzzle and getting through it was so fine that if I accidentally jumped it would screw me over.  I know that dying is part of the game, and I have no issue with dying when it's due to my own stupidity, I do find it tiresome dying constantly due to ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t quibbles that the puzzles seem to have and they seem to have a lot of them.
I found this was compounded by the choice in control movements which you can't seem to change. WSAD is pretty much the defacto choice for key layouts, not the arrow keys. Hell I'd have been ok with the arrow keys as an option if the jump button was not the same as the up button.
I also found the lack of sound/music volume control in the settings page equally silly.
All in all I found this to be an exercise in frustration, not an exercise of fun.

After playing another John Wizard Game, Dawn's Light, years ago, I was very pleased to see their games appearing on Steam. Both Dawn's Light and this game are the best RPGMaker games I have played, owing largely to the humor and the creative use of the engine.
You can never predict what you will see next in Lilly and Sasha. Houses, NPCs, quests, and other things are scattered around the fields. You might fight a goat, walk up the path a little bit to start a photography quest, and then ultimately find yourself in a Harvest Moon parody. All in the same field screen. For similar reasons, it is worth talking to everyone you see and doing all the quests. Some of the quests, such as one that involved watching an NPC interrogate people, caused me to burst out into laughter. There are also a couple of little easter eggs for those who have played Dawn's Light.
Puzzles appear throughout the game (generally consisting of pushing objects around with different goals). They are easy early on, but they get progressively harder towards the end of the game. But don't pass on the game just because of some potentially annoying puzzles. I recommend looking at the solutions in the guide (available on the bottom right-hand side of the store page where it says "view the manual") if puzzles like this aren't your thing.
Most experience comes from quests, so you can pretty much fight as much or as little as you want to. You shouldn't feel compelled to grind anything unless, perhaps, you are playing on hard difficulty (I didn't try it).
This is a game that, quality and creativity-wise, should set a standard for other RPGMaker games, and I am very much looking forward to starting the sequel.

Da wäre einmal das man keine Skills außerhalb der Kämpfe benutzen kann. Immerhin sieht man die Gegner auf dem
Bildschirm, es gibt also kaum Zufallskämpfe. Aber trotzdem ist es lästig. Entweder geht man nun den ganzen Weg
bis zum Inn zurück um zu heilen oder man muß Items benutzen. Und da Gegner kaum Loot haben (Items und Geld)

Entscheidung. Zumindest braucht man sich keine Sorge über sein Gepäck machen....auch der Händler hat so gut
wie nichts zu verkaufen.

Allerdings dauert es seeehhhr lange bis sie den nächsten Level erreichen...und so berauschend ist dieser Bonus auch nicht.
Weiter gibt es noch einen Unterschied im Kampf. Jeder der 3 Recken hat 100 Aktionspunkte. Nun kann man zwischen
4 Aktionen wählen. Items benutzen...umsonst. Schnellangriff, kostet kaum Punkte, haut aber auch nicht viel rein.
Großer Angriff/Heilzauber liegt bei 40 Punkten. Und dann noch Gruppenangriff, der bei 60 Punkten liegt...und meiner

mal für 6 Angriffe...danach macht man ein kleines Nickerchen bis wieder genügend Punkte vorhanden sind.

There is only one real negative to this game and that is the multiplayer, or rather trying to play with your friends.  It's easy enough to just join a server and play online, obviously if all your group join the same server you can play together; however, the problem comes when you want to set up a private game with your own rules.  It is not easy to do (I could just be being a bit of an idiot though, feel free to leave comments if you know of a better way than what I came up with) and in the end my group had to use Hamachi to create an online LAN.
By far and away the biggest positive has to be the developers, they up date this game so much! When I started playing there where only a handful of skills (blade, blunt, lightfooted, sprinting, cooking, carpentry, sneaking) now there are at least double that number.  Same goes for occupations (think character classes), when I began there were only 4 or 5.
The game is really challenging, mistakes are punished; I would compare it to dark souls in its difficulty, in that if you die you can attribute it to a mistake you have made.
Crafting/survival mechanics are great, build a house, trap animals, fish, farm, explore and scavenge.  Stay out in the rain too long, get wet, get cold, get ill and die.  Don't prepare well enough for the power and water to shut off - starve and die of thirst.  Climb through a broken window without removing the glass, maybe you will be fine, maybe you will cut yourself, maybe that cut will get infected because you have no medical kit. Walk into the wrong part of town, get surrounded, get eaten.  Or lose all hope, drink a bottle of bleach and kill yourself!
Combat is very simplistic, which helps create tension when fighting off hordes.  Time attacks well and zombies go down easy.  Mess it up and it is easy to get overwhelmed.
Mods galore, this game is early access but it has more workshop content than most!
One final negative, there is no real story to the game yet, hopefully it is going to arrive relatively soon, so late game can end up getting a bit stale.  The journey to that point is absolutely fantastic though.
Without a doubt, the most value for money I have ever gotten from a computer game... Ever.
Big shout out to the developers for doing such a good job.  Guys like you are why early access was created and it is a pity more developers don't work to your high standards.

TL;DR You're better off if you just watch a walkthrough of this game really.
It is the same guy who made The Stanley Parable, how could this game be a disappointment?!
...
Well it actually is a bit disappointing, regardless of its creator.
Now, there's literally almost NOTHING to talk about this game, because, for short, it is just a "walking simulator" as The Stanley Parable, but the main difference between this game and that one, is pretty much that little gameplay present in SP which is totally ABSENT in this game.
The plot is actually pretty nice, but i'm not going to spoil anything because if you already know the plot of this game there's literally no reason for you to buy it in the first place; let's just say that you're a player who plays someone else's games, with a narrator in the background.
...And this is where the game falls off pretty quickly. Unlike SP, where you are given a story which you can shape and remodel as you make several choices, you're left here with a really linear storyline you can't interact at all with.
This game is basically like this:
"Here's the story, walk to the end and remember to solve a few puzzles while you're at it"
This game is so OBSESSED with its unique and only story that you can actually explore a bit the surroundings of some maps, only to be told by the narrator itself that basically "doing X won't take you to Y" several times, as if it had been done just to mock off everyone who was waiting for a game akin to SP (!).
So yeah, this is a BAD game with a GOOD plot, that fails where The Stanley Parable succeeded: creating a game whose main focus was the story while still retaining some bit of entertainment and/or extra stuff and such to make you actually WANT to play the game even with its lack of proper gameplay.
In The Stanley Parable, you get to hear very hilarious humour as you make the story itself yours, familiarize with the only other character in the game and still find the usual morale at the end;
In The Beginner's Guide, all you get is jogging time with an obnoxious narrator that actually laughs at your (pitiful) attempts at finding something to make the game more... gamey.
And just for the record, one could think that comparing this game to The Stanley Parable might not be a good idea, but then again, this game would still be just a walking simulator with a story that either gets to you or bores you to death while you can't find anything else to entertain yourself with in there.

I said earlier that it's nothing like The Stanley Parable. But inevitably, people will compare the two. They both are "games about games" and they both feature walking around listening to narration. And in a way, the two are related. You can't help it - the same person is behind both.
The fiction of The Beginner's Guide (TBG) is that it's a guided tour by the developer, Davey Wreden. "Davey" (I use the quotes to denote the in-game Davey Wreden) narrates directly to us, the players, as he takes us through a compilation of small games made by a friend of his nicknamed "Coda". "Davey" says he compiled and released these games, in the form of TBG, in order to encourage Coda to start making games again after he stopped, and to help him out of a depression.
"Davey" clearly admires Coda's work, pointing out all sorts of ideas, patterns and themes in Coda's games, and wondering at the thoughts and feelings that gave birth to them.
Through the tour, we get to know Coda and "Davey" better.
It's difficult to say much more about TBG without spoiling anything. What I've written above will have to be enough for you to decide if you want it.
Now I'll continue with my opinions on the game with major, complete spoilers.
SPOILERS FOLLOW.

At the moment I'm some 5.5 hours into the game. Turns out it's not really a "simulation" nor a "strategy" game (as implied by the Steam tags) but a "click-and-wait" game. Luckily I got it at a decent discount.
The premise is promising and could make for a very interesting game. Thus it's a real shame it's almost not a game at all. Your business runs on its own and you just have to keep adding new rooms and people when you have the money -- and usually you don't have the money, so most of your time is spent waiting for money to accumulate. There's also not much to stop the money from accumulating, except for the random message dialogs that randomly pop up and require you to click "OK". The game is literally unable to advance a single in-game day without you being present clicking something. Forget about SimCity and the like where you could leave the game to run for an hour and come back. This game runs a minute or two and after that it need you to click a button.
Building a new room into your call center costs $3000 or more. At least in the beginning (for the first couple of hours) you won't make more than a few hundred dollars a day, so you wait. And wait. And wait. Occasionally someone quits and you need to replace him or her, and that of course takes away from the small pile of money you had accumulated.
Upgrading rooms costs $5000 or more, so your money seems much more well spent just adding rooms than upgrading them. Or at least I think so. The game lacks proper statistics so it's difficult to get an overview of your situation. Sure, you can read the thoughts of all of your employees and you can see a list of your clients (up to a whopping number of two (2) within my first 5.5 hours, or two in-game months), and you can click on all of your rooms and get to know some stats about them. But there's no list of rooms, or heat maps of any kind. There is a list of employees, but it appears that you cannot sort it, and the filter system (for choosing which types of employees you want to see) is really clumsy, requiring multiple clicks on a different screen from the actual list! So while you can get the details of a detail, there's no real big picture available.
Talking about your employees, you can hire different kind of people: inbound (IB) agents to receive calls, outbound (OB) agents to make calls, managers, janitors, etc. The different professions are very stereotypical. They might've been true in the 1960s or funny in the 1990s, but seriously, it's 2016 now. When a manager's work description is "putting fear in the agents" and you see him running around and shouting at people, I don't even. Similarly, a "Coach" turned out to be a cheerleader girl waving pom-poms. Seriously??
You can also educate your employees (just a click of a button and ta-dah, they are instantly smarter!). The education levels are very sketchy too, like a manager learning a class "Management By Fear" or another person learning "Lying 101".
Yet another profession is the Project Manager. They unlock new things for you to do. However, you cannot decide what, so most of the time they unlock the possibility of building an even taller building (10 floors, 15 floors, ..., 50 floors, ...) when your building is still less than 5 floors tall and you'd much rather have, say, some better education levels or some new room types. (Not that it'd matter, you wouldn't have the money to buy those things anyway, until after waiting for quite some time.)
All in all this game seems to waste its potential really badly. It's not a game that you play intensively, but a game that you put into the background or on your second screen while facebooking or something, and just check out occasionally to click "OK" on that dialog. I believe I'll still give this game a chance for a couple of more hours to see if the money would start pouring in a little faster and if that would make it funnier, but I have my doubts.

Several scenes have static .jpg quality backgrounds which are just downright horrid. (In their GoT game there were backgrounds of similar manner but they at least look stylized enough to be forgivable)
Choices seem to matter better little to the outcome of the story except for minor details, nothing is really groundbreaking here.
The games holds your hand all the way to it's conclusion. The only instance where it feels like you have some freedom is when inspecting crimes scenes but even then Batman is more than sure to tell you that you are dumb and that you should probably link this evidence to that other one in the corner.
I can recommend this game to anyone who wants a nice story which is told in the matter of 7 hours maybe a little more. But as a long time fan of Telltale games I feel betrayed.
Quality of their work in Batman is low compared to their other works and this decay in quality seems to have started with their GoT series which even with static backgrounds, tons of QTEs and feel, I managed to enjoy a lot.

This would be my third favorite Tellatale game (after Wolf Among Us and Borderlands) if it wasn't for the technical issues and difficulties that the game was riddled with and weren't fixed up until the 4th episode got released. Thankfully, most of those issues are fixed by now, as Telltale released a giant "patch" or rather - the game re-downloaded itself in its entirety and a lot of (specifically two) new performance options were added, making the game a lot more stable and playable even with low(er) end rigs - I have a four core i2500k and an Nvidia 560Ti (both components over 5 year old) and I haven't experienced any fps drops after the patch.
Let's just not talk about the♥♥♥♥♥♥show before they patched it as it is irrelevant to you - most likely a potential buyer - and focus on how the game is now.
It's pretty good.
Now that we cleared that up, let's go into detail.
The recipe is a simple one - everyone likes Batman and (mostly) everyone likes Telltale games (apart from the nay-sayers "OMG CHOICES DONT MATTER HURR DURR"). It works with all their games - people enjoy Walking Dead, Borderlands, Game of Thrones and Wolf among us comics... wait, I don't think that many people have heard of WAU before the game came out. But it's an exception. Point is - making games out of popular franchises is Telltale's recipe for success, and it works.
This is the part where I'd speak about technical stuff. Let's not do that and move onto something more important - is the story good?
Pretty. Good. I have several things I didn't like (that much), so let's pinpoint them.
The main villian - we'll call her "The Lady" (nickname I randomly chose) to avoid spoilers, because I don't wanna get yelled at - I'm not sure if she appears in the comics, since I've never read them (because I can't read words writen on paper... they're slow, don't glow and and I have to move my eyes from side to side... what a pain, right), but I've played all the Batman videogames and seen all the movies, which makes me a very hardcore casual fan and I gotta say - god damn the villian in this game is... boring. Nono, not the right word. She sucks. Yes, that's it. Or at least Telltale failed to make her interesting, the first time we get some actual background on her, is in the very last episode and it goes pretty much like "oh ye she got bullied and wants revenge by killing everyone in the city, hehe" and then it's game over, her character feels very shallow. There were at least four other characters that I'd rather have as the main villian over her, but they are just clowning around and don't do anything interesting.
Hmm, I'm trying hard to squeeze out some words that would♥♥♥♥♥♥on the story, but I actually enjoyed it, so I'll spare you of my poop (haha ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ jokes), let's talk gameplay.
You push buttons and if you fail, something bad happens and if you succeed, something bad happens to the baddies. What else would you expect, it's a Telltale game. Oh wait, almost forgot - there are some sort of detective minigames where you click on one thing and connect it to another and Batman says something smart, which brings the player closer to the imagination of the "world's greatest detective" himself... by connecting two things... together... yeah, it's a waste of time and energy. Telltale tells decent tales, but god dammit do their minigames suck donkey D.
Last thing worth mentioning - the game is roughly 8 hours long, averaging less than 2 hours per episode, making it fairly short, but enjoyable. Just like my♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ Wait, what.
Now that we've gone through all the boring stuff, let's focus on the most important thing - is the game really worth your money? No, what would really be worth your money, would be giving me a job, so I don't end up homeless. However, waiting for a juicy 30-50% sale would make it worth for sure, so just get it then, it's not a bad game at all.
Oh, one last thing - there's a lot of implications, that point to second season, so it's quite likely that we'll get Telltale Batman 2. Obviously depends on sales, but I look towards a continuation. Mainly because I like being disappointed. Mmm, sweet disappointment.
//EDIT: I thought about what I wrote about the main villain's character and realized, that some of the other (side-) characters, or rather the way their stories were told, also felt a little bit shallow. I don't think it's because their personas (created by the comic book authors), it's more the way Telltale presents them. Or maybe it's the game's length being too short. I'm probably just overthinking it, let's just stop here, the game's enjoyable, that's all that matters.

Project Zomboid is Day Z meets Minecraft in a 2D isometric world. Still in alpha, but with plenty of game play to keep players entertained for hours, Project Zomboid drops you in the middle of a suburban landscape as the sole (in the current build at least) survivor of a classic zombie outbreak. You will die, this is inevitable. The question (and objective) the game poses is: how long will you survive?
Surviving isn't as simple as staying indoors and out of sight however. Like a normal person you have needs. Hunger, thirst, sleep, and entertainment are periodic needs that must be fulfilled lest you risk your health and sanity. Satisfying these needs will require venturing outside and scavenging for supplies. At first it all seems so simple: find some food to eat, maybe some magazines to read and you're all set, water's still coming out of the tap after all and as long as the window shades are closed no zombie will come looking for you, that is until one follows you home and starts pounding on the window.
"Maybe he'll just go away" you think, but before you can act the window is broken and the zombie is inside. Run or fight, those are your options. You've spent too long gathering supplies to run and you're too tired to get very far so you're going to have to fight, but with what? Quick! To the counter! The kitchen knife. You grab the knife just in time and violently stab the intruder over and over before finally it succumbs.
Maybe the house isn't as secure as you thought and now the window is broken. Perhaps if you had a hammer, some boards, and nails you could barricade it up. If you're going to head out to find these things however you'll need a better weapon and you'll have to find that too. Maybe surviving isn't going to be so easy afterall.

I'm completely gutted that Tropico 5 is such a terrible game. I've been a fan of the series who followed every release back to the original Tropico, and in the week leading up to the Tropico 5 release (of which I pre-ordered a 4-pack) I replayed Tropico 2 : Pirate's Cove through for about the 30th time. Old graphics, a few annoying design flaws, but even in 2014 still a spectacularly fun game, just like Tropico 1, Tropico 3, and Tropico 4... but not Tropico 5. For the first time in the history of the Tropico series we've got a new Tropico game released that is not only not a fun game, it isn't even a Tropico game. Packed with bad design decisions, content compromises, and maddeningly simplified with console limitations/mainstream stupidity in mind, for the first time in Tropican history we've got a game that can't be fixed with patches because the base game is so incredibly, irreparably broken. Tropico 5 is a corporate "game-by-committee" insult to each and every fan of both Poptop's original Tropico creation and Heinimont's mostly-faithful torch-bearing continuation of the series since then. It's a bad game, badly designed, falsely advertised, and will never become a proper Tropico game without a complete overhaul of every design mechanic of the strategy gameplay.
Let's begin with the interface. Gone is the functional and useful interface we all know and love, with the traditional Tropico feel, intuitive layout, plenty of options, and helpful tooltip popups for every sub-menu or screen. The layout for Tropico 5 is much simpler, missing many important screens, with less information on every screen, and with almost no tooltip popups on any screen. Building upgrades no longer have any graphical representation, and the upgrades aren't located on the primary building screen, so you're forced to tediously check every single upgradeable building on your island with 2 mouse clicks on parts of the screen that are never near each other. This is unforgivably tedious and by itself makes the micromanagement of Tropico 5 unbearable beyond words, especially considering that buildings freshly built or destroyed in disasters revert to the default settings, necessitating constant micromanagement of every single building on the island.
What about the lack of content? Tropico 5 advertises, even to date, "Choose from over 100 buildings from each of the individual eras." This is false advertising. Counting all the buildings up I can only come up with 91 total, and that includes every building from all the eras. Maybe campaign mode has a few unique buildings used only in the campaign, but I never saw any, and even then there's no way to get "over 100 buildings from each of the individual eras." I count 91 buildings in Tropico 5 and 117 in Tropico 4, so this is simply false advertising. No way around it. Furthermore, every Tropico fan who owns Tropico 5 will be quick to tell you why they lied about it: tons and tons of vital and important buildings and even building types are missing from Tropico 5. Take just one example: Prisons. In Tropico 4 you had Jail, Labor Camp, and you could turn the colonial fort into a dungeon for your personal dictatorship needs. Tropico 5 has no prisons or even a concept of jail. You cannot arrest anyone in Tropico 5. Crime is reduced to an overlay and a happiness number, and occasionally you see Crime Lord characters appear in the game that you can have a marginal interaction with. By marginal, I mean Bribe, Banish, Kill, or Discredit, the same 4 actions you have available for you to deal with every single island inhabitant in the game. To quote someone from the forum, "How does El Presidente run a dictatorship without prisons?" To heavily belabor this point, what about salt mines, fire stations, radio stations, wind power, solar power, and condos? "How does El Presidente run an island paradise without condos?" Why is there only one type of restaurant, "Restaurant", when Tropico 4 had "Restaurant", "Gourmet Restaurant", "Ship-O-Rant", and "Cosmic Pin", all of which were better rendered, described, and implemented?
This brings me to the graphics of Tropico 5, the major selling point of the game, yet still underwhelming and poorly implemented. Tropico 5 requires DX11 for reasons that I can only describe as dishonest. It doesn't need DX11 or any of the hardware functions implemented therein, and the official excuse for the requirement, and I directly quote from the official Tropico 5 Steam forum, "The game and engine were redesigned from scratch as was requested by many players", simply does not hold water. Tropico 5 is coming to XBOX360 soon, an old console that is only DX9 slightly extended, and in such context the publisher/developer excuse can be clearly viewed as PR nonsense meant to cover up the fact that Tropico 5 is a functional disaster. The graphics aren't very good, there are only a few high end features added on near the end of the development cycle purely for marketing window dressing, and tessellation, if implemented, has been implemented so poorly that it renders the overall graphic package functionally of a lower quality than Tropico 4. HBAO/SSAO simply can't cover up bad design, and forcing the DX11 requirement on top of the substandard graphics is just insulting.
The biggest success of the Tropico series was always in the gameplay, and the gameplay is where Tropico 5 fails the most spectacularly. To understand the level of failure you have to understand how previous Tropico games were successful. In Tropico 1/3/4 you started with a few people, a palace, a couple farms, maybe a tenement, and a blank slate to design a society. If you wanted a peasant serfdom that you ruled through fear of your military might you had many avenues through which to engineer this society, any the effectiveness of your approach was purely determined by how well you engineered your economy, balanced competing concerns, and reacted to changing circumstances. As one example, you could focus on mining, pay the miners/police/military high wages, and give the finger to everyone else, dominating and controlling their lives through fear, imprisonment, labor camps, many detailed and useful edicts, and even through pathing and placement of buildings (indeed, in Tropico 2 the latter is essential for accomplishing ANYTHING). Now what can you do? The budget tool replaces rent/wages/cost and a lot more, and since it only has 5 positions, you've got no subtlety to your economic engineering. Low means low EVERYTHING: rent, wages, maintenance cost, production output, housing quality, etc, etc, etc. Same for high, which functionally turns the budget 5-way into a Win/Lose slider.
For all intents and purposes, Tropico 5 is not actually a Tropico game at all. Tropico was always a social engineering game, and in Tropico 5 you do not have the necessary tools to engineer your desired society... or ANY society. All you can do in Tropico 5 is build, react to popups, and set the 5-way Budget selector (the Win/Lose slider) to "Win" on every building that you build. It's really that simple, and there's no room to do much else. You could always set the Win/Lose slider to "Lose" I suppose. There's no way to win or lose creatively when there is not an underlying framework governing the simulation. Simcity 5 proved this very clearly, and Tropico 5 insists on following in those same pointless, infuriating footsteps. The fact that someone found 10 DLC confirmed titles listed in the launch config files says it all. Tropico 5 is a greedy, absolutely cynical cashgrab for mainstream/console gaming dollars and it throws away almost every good idea that brought the series this far. Spending 108 dollars to pre-order a 4-pack of this worthless game is a watershed moment in my 34-year-old life as a computer gamer. If you can't trust Tropico, who can you trust?

This game is a survival masterpiece. Most survival games (or probbaby all of them) lack the reality. I mean let's say you are alone on an island. Is it reallistic to craft an axe, cut some trees and build a house in few hours (or few days)? It would take weeks for one human to do so and I'm in doubt that this would be possible at all (imagine you need to transport lumber - how?). Another thing - you are getting hungry what would you do? In most games you just hand kill an animal which by chance came near you. Too easy.
You won't find such things here. The game is as reallistic as possible. You can't build. You have to relay on what was already built. You can craft only some basic stuff like fishing hook, bow and arrows, skin clothes, torches etc. Hunting is really dificult. Unless you find a rifle (you will still be very limited with ammo though) you will either have to craft a bow (using which is very difficult) or try to get some food by chance. Of course you need to gather wood to boil things etc.
Your main evemy is cold. Until you craft some better clothes you can't stay outside for a long time so you need a lot of planning. You will have to explore with a lot of common sense too - never go out too far without a chance of getting back. You will have to account for changing weather. You have no map, no compass and when visibility drops you are lost in a moment.
This game can give you a lot of fun for tenths of hours even though it's just a sandbox. Survival and exploration in the most realistic way. We are still waiting for the story mode. My guess is it won't be as deep as for example Fallout but still combining the most reallistic survival with a thrilling story can be perfect. I hope this game can be modded in the future so there could be more missions on different custom-made maps.
If you are not sure whether to get this game or not, wait for the story mode. It might skyrocket the fun even more. In one sentence - the most reallistic survival game out there.

Blackwell Epiphany is the final game in the Blackwell series of games, and it effectively realizes the entire series' full potential. It takes everything introduced in the previous four and makes it the biggest and best of the bunch. It ends on a bittersweet note, though it gives everything proper closure.
The Blackwell series has never been about the gameplay or the puzzles. At its core, it's truly been about the characters. Rosa Blackwell, Joey Mallone, and the rest felt real and believable. The dialogue reflected this wonderfully, and it was their personalities intertwined with the narrative that made the games a true delight. Though, I personally can't shake the feeling that there could have been more done with these characters, perhaps more focus on their behavior outside of matters concerning the plot. But, with what it is, it's executed masterfully.
The Blackwell series had me entirely engrossed in each and every installment with its genuine characters, interesting narrative, and shining quality and passion. It stands out as a definitive example of a modern point-and-click series definitely done right.

I only just recently picked this up from the Humble 2K Bundle
. For some combination of reasons I completely missed the BioShock heyday, although I did manage to absorb that it quickly became a crowd favorite and got a lot of positive attention. It only took about 30 minutes of playtime for me to see why -- BioShock is something of a steampunk cover of System Shock 2. And that is the highest of compliments.
BioShock is a complex adventure in a richly-detailed world with an FPS combat mechanic. The story is compelling, the visual style is exquisite and the atmosphere is so dark and immersive that it provokes physical reactions from the player to in-game events (ie: certain moments in this game will make you jump).
There seems to be a lot of room for variation in your character's skills, abilities and weapons, the world is full of interactive bits and pieces, and the levels are large and invite exploration.
BioShock is likely to appeal to gamers of all types, and I highly recommend it to anyone.

If you're a fan of old school RPG's I would highly recommend this game to you. RPG Maker games tend to get a bad rap, mostly for their low quality and lack of original resources. But this game suffers from none of these problems.
The sprites and tilesets are reminiscent of the old Final Fantasy games. And the art and monsters, (Though seeming drawn on MS Paint) are really colourful and well made.
The music too is all original and quite catchy.
The game play although at most times is very typical of RPG Maker, there are a few times the game uses it in ways I haven't seen before.
The game suffers a little in the dialogue at times, but overall the story is very enjoyable.
You can tell a lot of heart went into the making of this game, and I love that I get to play something I can tell someone else really loved making. It reminds me of the “game” I always wanted to make when I first got my copy of RPG Maker 2000 back in the day. All in all I really enjoyed this game, and I recommend it to anyone looking for a good old RPG!

Bob walks out the house in the morning. He starts to cross the street, he looks to the left. It is clear so he walks ahead. Bob gets hit by a car from the right.
Bob walks out the house in the morning. He starts to cross the street, first he looks left and then right. It is clear so he walks ahead. Slips on some spilled oil and gets hit by a car.
Bob walks out the house in the morning. He starts to cross the street, he looks left and then right. It is clear so he walks ahead. Steps over some spilled oil and reaches the other side. He gets a call on his phone and doesn't notice a cyclist who knocks him back into the road. Bob gets his by a car.
Welcome to Limbo. Population: Bob.
But first, an English lesson.
Skill (noun) ~ the ability, coming from one's knowledge, practice, aptitude, etc., to do something well. Usage: "The dancers performed with skill."
Recollection (noun) ~ the act or power of recollecting, or recalling to mind; remembrance. Usage: "Bob had perfect recollection of everything he did wrong when crossing the street."
It's too bad that the developers of this game confused these two. There is apparently some underlying artistic expression happening in Limbo related to depression and suicide. So they sat down one day and figured the best way to express that was to just kill the player over and over again by making it impossible to progress without actually having fore-knowledge of what will happen next. Then they remembered that they were actually supposed to be making a game and threw in some puzzles, some of which were very clever but ultimately the result is that Limbo feels like it wants to be doing two very different things and can't make up its mind.
Schizophrenic design and a focus on the theme of depression... somehow they didn't think it was a bad idea on paper. I'll say this though, they certainly captured the essense of suicide. Because they completely killed any hope of this game being entertaining.
As a final note, the game is sickeningly violent. That may seem like an odd thing to say because the game is all greyscale but the fact is that the developers have intentionally gone to great lengths to make the main character's deaths as vivid as possible. The game repeatedly has the main character dismembered, bisected, beheaded, crushed and impaled all with gruesome detail both visually and aurally. You can hear the bones crunch and flesh tear as well as see and hear blood splatter. It isn't pleasent and it may be the singular reason for the high reviews as many see this kind of morbid stuff as highly entertaining. Furthermore if you are a parent looking to buy this for a child, thinking that it is harmless, you need to look elsewhere.

A sane man would turn back, dock back at London and resupply. But no. We zailors will steam on, eastward and onward to uncharted waters until we see land or die. (There is always, of course, the risk that the former will lead to the latter.)
Why?
Fuel and supplies are so expensive that your port reports and trading and repeatable grindable quests just aren't enough. After a while of playing you actually become afraid, not of dying at zee, but returning to harbor without a notable success because you'll

when you finally make it back from your impossibly risky voyage with a cargo hold full of wonders. You feel triumphant, because this time you can actually afford to resupply

A hugely enjoyable finale to the beloved series. It doesn't tie up every loose end, and not every plot development makes quite as much sense as you might like, but as a chance to reconnect with these characters and see them through one last, sweeping adventure, it is not to be missed. The voice acting and pixel-art backgrounds have never been better, and the story itself is longer by far than any of the previous entries, giving you chance to really lose yourself in the spectral mysteries and companionable snark of the Blackwell world.  If you enjoyed the other Blackwell games, it is unthinkable that you will not get a tremendous kick out of this one.
Q. I liked some of the other Blackwell games, but not all. Which features does this use?
A.You can still swap between Rosa and Joey, you can use inventory objects on the outside world, and you can once again combine entries in your notes to make fresh deductions (a feature I deeply missed). The art is SVGA-ish pixel art, as opposed to the cartoony drawings in some versions of earlier games, and as I say, it's probably the best art in the series (though the oddly stiff walk animation from Deception seems to have lingered just a bit).
Q. Do I have to play the other games first?
A. Technically no- most major plot points are recapped or alluded to in the game. You will, at the very least, be able to follow the gist of the story. But why punish yourself that way? The earlier games are funny, clever, and quick to play, and give the events of Epiphany a real impact. To say nothing of the countless grins and gasps you get from recognizing some long-forgotten plot development suddenly blossom on the screen. Unlike the vast majority or videogames, the Blackwell series has a real sense of *history* to it, and it's a treat worth savouring.

TL;DR If this review is too long to read then this game isn't for you.
It is hard to recommend Sunless Sea on the basis of the amount of time it takes to accomplish anything. Personally I don't feel that it's too annoyingly grindy but more so the fact it can take an eternity just to get from port to port. Now this isn't because the port are that widely spread out, (though the further east you go the more distance between stops becomes apparent) it's just the crawl at which you unhappy little steamer goes at. I realize this is most likely the real speed at steamboat would move but it does make for a long uneventful trip.
In the visual department I can't help but feel that the game would have benefited from a much larger budget, but where would one source money for what is essentially a niche title. Double edged sword aside, the art style is functional and still carries the foreboding that the writing lays on thick.
The main event for Sunless Sea is the writing and boy there is a lot of it. Not a complaint by any means just, wow. The head writer certainly missed their calling as a Lonely Planet contributor as many things are described quite intricately. Sights, sounds, touch and sometimes smells are all covered in the expansive reams of text that you are likely to skip through to see the effects bullet points that punctuate the page.
There are many different nagging effects that can be afflicted to you character with the prime one being terror. Terror is a constantly growing annoyance that will result in more catastrophic events the higher it gets and is affected by events at port (e.g. hugging kittens lowers terror while upending its litter tray raises it) but also rises by just boating around, with light less travel being the most effective means of getting the willies.
Surviving in the Zee (not a typo, games name for the underground sea) is more of a task of having enough supplies and fuel to make the trip. Not all ports trade in the goods required to get from a to b with most of them being a pick up or destination for specific types of cargo. So you will spend most time running errands with exploration being a byproduct of these services.
Money is a hard commodity to come by as most tasks don't give a respectable amount of dosh for your efforts. You can partake in trading goods but this is only rewarding if you want to take on shady dealings with some undesirables. This brings me to a story that I had within the game.
I was returning to sunken London with my lucrative first endeavor of smuggling light from the surface when I realized that I hadn't completed the quest for the blind bruiser. Now the blind bruiser is a delightful unforgiving chap who I would buy my shipment of sunlight at a tidy profit but returning to London without completing his errand would only yield his disappointment and a friendly knife to my side.
Realizing this just before making port in London I turn around and head off to pick up whatever he so desperately desired that was willing to dance on my lifeless corpse should I not do it for him. This wasn't that big of an issue I had fuel and supplies to go get it, what I hadn't accounted for was being attacked by a shark.
The sharks in the game aren't that common outside of the area that blind bruiser sent me to. The shark did a fair amount of damage to my hull and devastated my supply of hapless crew. Stupidly I used my supplies to fix my hull to a semi respectable state before taking my journey home and this was the beginning of my downfall. I was double burning my fuel to get home quicker as my limited crew limited my traveling speed, and I needed to get home before my surplices dried up and everyone starved.
As I was heading home my crew had become peckish and started feasting on each other and I was willing to look over this cause the payoff was so close and I could always get more delicious crew back in sunken London. If you've played any of the previous Blackwell games and enjoyed them, you'll enjoy the conclusion too. Epiphany is a few hours longer than previous entries in the series, and while some of the plot points are a bit far fetched, it's absolutely worth seeing how it all plays out.
If you haven't played any of the Blackwell games yet, I still highly recommend them. The pixel art looks great (at least in my opinion), the voicovers are good, though some characters in the earlier entries are a little weaker, and the stories of each game are all strong on their own, and even stronger when taken together as each new game has more events to reference back to.
I found the puzzles in this game were a little stronger than previous entries - what I had to do next made sense, without being overly obtuse. I'll admit I did look up a walkthrough once, but even then what I'd missed did make sense. If you do choose to pick up this game, try not to look things up unless you're really stuck - the feeling of solving a tricky puzzle is worth it.
Overall, I highly recommend this series to any fans of old point and click games, ghost stories, or anyone just any game with a good story in general.

Though the gameplay takes a while to get to grips with, (Massively less time if you've played the previous title Fallen London) Sunless Sea is a Beautiful game with a heavy focus on narrative while still very much being a survival game. Plenty of times I've found myself cruising with little coal left, hoping for a dock with a merciful price on coal before realising that I don't have enough food to go on, and that I may need to lose a crew member for the sakes of my ship.
Now although it isn't triple A graphics they are beautifully done despite this and the general atmosphere of the game constructed without any of the games text already fills you with a sense of foreboding, of being a Very small fish in a much larger pond than you should rationally be in.
The Narrative of the game is wonderfully written, and is a fully immersive experience, placing you as the captain of a Ship in the underwater ocean of the Fallen London universe.
Your motives for taking the ship out, as well as what you plan to do with it once you disembark is entirely your own to decide, and you will make this decision a few times as your first captain will Die. And likely the next few. While it isn't cruel Sunless Sea is difficult, and makes you work hard to keep sailing, and unlike with other similar sailing games (Assassins creed 4 is the first that comes to mind) You cannot possibly sustain yourself at sea, even if you did decide to go full pirate, (No easy feat in this game) and so you're forced to interact with the various ports, engaging you with various plot lines unique to each isle. You often find yourself making the decision to help the other isles, to deal with the larger picture of the games political scene or stick to you and your own, keeping the ship afloat while you persue your own goals.
Whatever you choose you find yourself with a long journey fraught with hardships. And I wholey reccomend anyone with a love of roguelikes, or any fans of H.P Lovecraft's literary works to buy this game.
TL:DR Sold my Daughter, Ate my crew, got killed by a living iceberg.

I didn't find Telltale's Batman to be very fun, entertaining or truly interactive. Telltale has taken whatever success it had with The Walking Dead Season 1 and has tried to mimic it in Batman. Choices do not have appropriately weighted consequences, and drama is thrown in without consideration of the characters' purpose within the Batman universe.
When you get to play as Batman, don't expect a lot - this is an adventure/conversation simulator first and an action game second. The detective sequences are weak: connect the dots between 5-6 obvious clues is as difficult it get. The action sequences don't offer many choices of attack, with that there are a few in the first episode that feel good because of the scale of the room, but nothing is kept to that standard throughout the season.
I found the decision making in this game to be underwhelming. There are some interesting choices made at the beginning of the series that ultimately fall apart at the end, because TTG simply did not take the time to flesh out the choices well enough. Shock value does not make the story any more intriguing.
As a Batman fan, I disliked the story that Telltale put forth. It destroys the mythos surrounding the Wayne family, and makes Alfred out to be a self-loathing individual. I do not believe for a second Wayne Foundation was helped by the Falcones. There are many other side-effects of that relationship that would have cropped up over time, and Alfred certainly would not have kept the secret for that long.

Before we start, I understand this is a free title. I'm judging and recommending it by the amount of time I've put in to the game to essentially complete it to the fullest, not the amount of money (Or lack there of) I've spent.
Jigoku Kisetsukan is a Bullet Hell curtain fire game that is heavily based on the
(I will be making A LOT of comparisons later on between the two) about a girl named Tenshi having a strange feeling and uncovering what's causing it. Could this game become a new predecessor for the Touhou franchise, or a complete dud? Well, here's my opinion:
Gameplay 6/10: You get to play up to seven different characters, each with their own unique shot type or trait along with a unique final boss, which is actually pretty interesting and I don't see that happen often in games. You can also perform a special attack that clears the screen while dealing a little bit of damage to the boss (You can store up to 2 at a time) depending on how much aura you have. My only real issue about the mechanics is that I find it VERY difficult to recover from dying in later stages.

But since it feels a lot like your traditional bullet Hell game, for me to say I hate the gameplay for this game is like me saying I hate the gameplay for the bullet Hell genre (I don't). The new mechanics make me feel that the game is trying to be something else, and I can see that but is it really?
Visuals 7/10: I actually really enjoy them and are probably my favorite aspect of the game. They remind me a lot of Cave Story but in a shmup setting. Although some sprites do look a little off, a majority of them are well done. The artwork for the characters do feel a little uninspired but are still much more appealing to look at compared to early Touhou games.
Difficulty 5/10: No, I don't find the game difficult, I 1cc'd my first run, so my score isn't based on the game being too hard (but that's not saying it's too easy). Once you get the hand of not dying in the first two stages, the next three aren't much harder. The difficulty only ramps up significantly on the Final boss (Let's just say I've managed to die not once, not twice, but five times on the Fear of Past and Future boss). My issue is that because the difficulty doesn't increase enough, the game stays static in a sense and there isn't a challenge outside of actually swapping the difficulty from normal to hard mode or achievement gathering.
Simply put, it's better to have a simplistic Stage 1 and work its way up to a heavily challenging End Stage than a difficult Stage 1 that slightly increases from there.
Sound 6/10: I'm not a fan of chip tune. But I DO like a couple of tracks from this game, most notably the third stage and boss' themes. However, I find most songs I might not really listen to on my own time, being more average than fantastic (Not implying that they're actually bad, just... Y'know, average).
Story 3/10: Out of the respect for the developer, I'll be keeping the spoilers tag for those interested in finding out the whole Story for themselves. If you can't finish the game six (let alone once) times, yet want to still know my opinion, by all means:
Call it a nitpick, but when I see a story like in Touhou, I get something that enlightens me a bit whether it be about Japanese folklore or some good fortune cookie logic (Shikieiki Yamaxanadu from Touhou 9 does very good examples of this). With Jigoku Kisetsukan, I feel the story is there for the sake that there's a story while executing this poorly.
Overall, despite it being heavily based on Touhou, I think that's one of Jigoku Kisetsukan's biggest flaws. It's more known to me as a free Touhou-on-Steam rather than something more independent. Ultimately, the game's very standard with some flaws, and that just doesn't make the game too memorable. For that, along with my time feeling wasted by trying to discover the story in its entirety, I can only recommend it to people who can't obtain a schmup in any other way, or to a schmup fan in desperate need of a new game, and that demographic's too low for me to give this a general recommendation.
Touhou didn't start out good either, it took about 6 installments to gain its popularity. I hope Jigoku Kisetsukan will continue to expand and show its independence away from the Touhou Project while gaining the same attention but in its own special way.

Thirdly is as I mentioned before is that around Day 50(10ish hours of gameplay) things really slow down and everyday you're just repeating the same tasks as the day before.(Just like Real Life!) Most of this review is from the first 30 minutes or so of gameplay, though I have continued and added a little more to it since then.
The short version:
Pros:
Unique art style for battle and some scenes
Devs went out of way to provide a free guide and tables (sadly not in pdf form)
Enemies shown prior to battle so you can avoid them, also hints at what enemy you will face.
Cons:
Art style needs getting used to, and makes one playable character appear almost zombie-like
No noticable notification that you leveled up.
Immature main character.
The long version:
I want to recommend this, but I just can't.  Rather than using the typical sprites you probably see in several other rpg maker games, it uses hand-drawn art for battle, and I do like this... ... however the art looks like it was done with little to no effort.  Heck, to me one of the characters you get as of the second battle looks like a zombie.
Also the hero is at least 17 years of age, and yet I can't help but feel that his lines were made by a 12 year old often tormented by an older brother.  Evidence includes one of the very first thoughts of the morning involve tormenting the little sister, and occasional reference to a "tickle monster".  The other characters I don't mind so much, but hopefully once the party leaves their home town the hero will start acting more mature.
One more thing that now that I realized, what almost feels like it's missing from this game is a little notice that you leveled up.  It's not a big deal, but just something to let me know I leveled up other than showing new skills next time I go to use a skill (I may or may not notice when I go to the menu beforehand)
(Just now realized after paying attention to my "next xp" and mathing when I leveled up, there is a notification, but all that happens is your character's status changes from "[normal]" to "level up" on the battle screen so you almost have to look for it every time)
A redeeming factor that I forgot to mention is that instead of using a random battle system, enemies show up outside battle so you may avoid them.  Also their sprite outside battle hints at what type of battle it may be.
I will give credit to the devs though, as they have provided something of a free guide, though it's hard for some people to read it as some of the guide was made on a spreadsheet rather than putting it in pdf format.  (I'm using open office, but I can't help but wonder if it would look different in microsoft excel)

I'm reviewing the early access version. We are still waiting for the story mode.
This game is a survival masterpiece. Most survival games (or probbaby all of them) lack the reality. I mean let's say you are alone on an island. Is it reallistic to craft an axe, cut some trees and build a house in few hours (or few days)? It would take weeks for one human to do so and I'm in doubt that this would be possible at all (imagine you need to transport lumber - how?). Another thing - you are getting hungry what would you do? In most games you just hand kill an animal which by chance came near you. Too easy.
You won't find such things here. The game is as reallistic as possible. You can't build. You have to relay on what was already built. You can craft only some basic stuff like fishing hook, bow and arrows, skin clothes, torches etc. Hunting is really dificult. Unless you find a rifle (you will still be very limited with ammo though) you will either have to craft a bow (using which is very difficult) or try to get some food by chance. Of course you need to gather wood to boil things etc.
Your main evemy is cold. Until you craft some better clothes you can't stay outside for a long time so you need a lot of planning. You will have to explore with a lot of common sense too - never go out too far without a chance of getting back. You will have to account for changing weather. You have no map, no compass and when visibility drops you are lost in a moment.
This game can give you a lot of fun for tenths of hours even though it's just a sandbox. Survival and exploration in the most realistic way. We are still waiting for the story mode. My guess is it won't be as deep as for example Fallout but still combining the most reallistic survival with a thrilling story can be perfect. I hope this game can be modded in the future so there could be more missions on different custom-made maps.
If you are not sure whether to get this game or not, wait for the story mode. It might skyrocket the fun even more. In one sentence - the most reallistic survival game out there.

I usually do a playthrough of a game before I rate it. Usually, if I don't it's either because I love the game so much it's necessary for me to review it, or I dislike the game. Because unless they're patient (Which I am not) they have completed a playthrough and then put a negative review down. In this case, I chose the former. You've heard of the game. Gotten many nominations for best game of last generation. Obviously, I wouldn't consider it the best game of last gen (Mass Effect 2 and Skyrim. 'Nuff said) but it's quite amazing. I couldn't resist and had to review this now. I already know what happens next anyway. :/
The graphics are impressive for a nearly 7 year old game. They still look beautiful, and when I take screenshots, they look great compared to other games. And because atmosphere is considered part of the "graphics" section of my reviews, I have reasons to add on. Bioshock is partially horror, but more of a story rich shooter. I won't talk about gameplay or story yet. The atmosphere is perfect. The whole time I've been playing, I thought, "Please get me to a nice place, please get me to a nice place..." and then I realize Splicers and Big Daddies are swarming the whole place. The game has an uncomfortable atmosphere, but it's quite amazing.
The game is a first person shooter. The style is similar to Valve's source engine games, get a few weapons, use scroll to get them, and you can't aim down the sights. Since I've played 400 hours on TF2, I'm used to the controls. Even if I didn't play TF2, I would've dealt with the controls. You can switch between weapons and plasmids, which are special powers run with EVE. It's used for puzzles on occasion, but mostly it's used to weaken the enemy significantly so you can go in for the final blow. The game so far is relatively balanced, none of the enemies really are intimidating until you encounter the Big Daddy. They're intimidating and will stop at nothing to kill you if you touch it or the Little Sister it protects. They're terrifying and monsterous. They also in a way decide your ending. They're probably the most difficult enemies in the game, excluding the final boss. You make decisions and decide Little Sisters' fates. You can rescue them for a good ending or harvest their ADAM and become stronger. One problem I have with the game, though is that it feels linear and it ruins the game a little bit, because I'd love to explore Rapture some more. Overall, the gameplay is pretty solid, along with some quick puzzles and decisions that affect the end of the game, it does not disappoint.
The story is absolutely amazing, but there's a huge event towards the end of the game. Would you kindly make sure I don't go out of hand with this next short overview of what happens? Your name is Jack. The year is 1960. Your plane crashed near a mysterious lighthouse. When you enter, you discover a machine. When you go in and pull the switch, you realize that you're in an underwater city ruled by "madman" Andrew Ryan called Rapture. It was corrupted by ADAM, which is a drug that makes people insane. A man named Atlas helps you and started the catchphrase "Would you kindly..." which became one of the biggest quotes in video game history. And let me warn you, once you get to "it" (Bioshock fans know what I mean) then your mind will be blown. Bioshock's story is one of the best, darkest, stories that ever appeared in the gaming world.
The audio is probably the first weak point of the game, unfortunately. The voice actors did an average job with their roles, but th music fits in nicely. I would say Andrew Ryan had the best voice. He sounded terrifying, influential, and takes the role of the villain well. Sometimes, however, the voice actors seemed careless or it had the microphone sound, like the person was farther away. Unfortunately, it's not all that great, despite Bioshock being an amazing game.
The worst part of the game is the replaybility, but it's not really supposed to have strong replayability, seeing how linear Bioshock already is. There's two endings, you could play for both, but usually people just play one time and be done with it. Either way, Bioshock is still an unforgettable game.
In the end, with some pretty serious flaws like it being linear and the average voice acting.  However, based off of what I've seen so far, BIoshock is one amazing game and one you don't want to miss, horror fan or not. I highly recommend the game and can't wait to beat it. Now, would you kindly buy this game?

I bought and played this game before it was released on Steam this year.  Here is a quick review for the game:
Characters--9/10:  In games you play, you always have at least one character that you hate or think is poorly written.  However, in Elements, I liked all the characters and could symphatized with almost all characters and cared about what happened in their past.  In addition, I believe that how the story incorporate each character into the story was well done.
Music--8/10:  The music in Elements is pretty solid.  There are some memorable pieces in the game and I do like the Battle theme and boss music theme.
Graphics--9/10:  I loved the graphics of Elements.  I especially liked the full portraits of the characters during battle.
Story--10/10:  The main highlight of Elements is its story.  While I will not spoil the story, I will say that the story will put you on rollarcoster of emotions.  Since you will most likely get attach to most of the characters in the game (since their characterization is done very well), some scenes in the game will hit you very hard.  Furthermore, the game does an excellent job in building the world and the conflict that surrounds the game.  In addition, the way story is written allows the player to see how each character grows as a person as the game progresses.
Overall, I would give this game a 9/10.  I enjoyed it very much especially the characters and story.  Do not let the fact that it was made in RPG Maker deter you from this game.  It is a very well made game and I would highly recommend it to anyone.

I was so excited when I saw that Pox Nora had switched to a new owner! And then I found out that it was available on Steam! (I don't know if this is a new thing, or if PN has been on here a long time, but for me it was new.) I decided to give it a try, despite bad experiences previously, and I was overjoyed to see that the client had gotten major updates; it looks fantastic and is very easy to navigate. and Desert Owl includes various daily challenges to help people new to the game to catch up. There is also a set of activities that all new players must travel before they can jump into an actual multiplayer competition, each of which also adds to the player's bank and allows them to score new "runes" (cards.) There is a microtransaction mechanic in which a player can buy rune packs (thus the bank of game coins that I mentioned,) but players can also join a "training" match, in which players have balanced starter decks and only player skill counts.
The gameplay was just as fun as I remembered, too. Essentially, each player generates "nora" (mana) automatically each turn, and they can then play runes from their hand onto the board. Some runes are characters, others are equipment that is played directly onto said characters, and some are spells that have instant effects on the boardstate. The board also has nodes, locations that can be captured by characters that move into their sphere of influence. Nodes give extra nora each turn and act as secondary (or sometimes primary) summoning locations for the characters. Ultimately, each player is trying to destroy their opponent's primary summoning point, a shrine, and receive a revamped animation as the building is destroyed by magical explosions or stone spires that stab upward through the ground, or...
But.
As the Curators' recommendation explains, this game "took a trip down the p2w slope under SOE." I was there, and I saw this happen. I played, and I payed. I have a collection of runes from that time, but when I began playing, I quickly found that, 1.) nobody plays the skill-only training matches, and 2.) everybody's decks are still broken at the bottom of the p2w slope. I thought I might just have been a poor strategist until I hung out in the chat forum and read people's posts; nope, I still believe that I am a poor strategist, but this does not account for the entirety of the current metagame. Pox Nora involves runes of various rarities, from common to rare. Wait, no, then there is Exotic. Oh, also legendary. You get the idea. Further, according to the players talking in the forum, two of whom were in the top 5 players in the current iteration of the game, a player must have no fewer than 5 exotics to be competitive.
The curators claim that the game was "reclaimed by the old devs and revamped." I believe this is true, but the p2w slope is slippery, and the game has not recovered. It is still crouched at the bottom of the p2w slope, and if you want to be competitive, you will have to descend to its level to do so.
