tl;dr: 2D top down racer where the cars handle differently and have different raci.ng lines. Some you have to oversteer, some you have to brake early for and accelerate out hard. Tons of tracks and a track editor Dead online multiplayer, awesome local co-op. If you like racing games, you'll dig it. If you want a fun party game, you can have six people at once, two per controller. AI is okay, and if you like chasing fastest laps, you can enjoy the time trials.
More words:
I like racing games. For the most part, I play racing games. That's about it. Sims, arcade, whatever, I like racing games. If you like racing games, this has a ton of appeal. It's a 2D topdown racer with a hadful of cars, all of which handle differently, and a lot of tracks.
The motorcycle cuts wide sweeping lines where if you get your lines right you won't have to lift or brake. The "Sportscar" oversteers constantly, it's always drifting. In contrast to the motorcycle which is cutting tight lines, the sportscar is all about drifting.
Then there's the "Formula" car, a high downforce open cockpit car, in which you actually have you to brake. The fastest lines require you to go on the brakes early, and accelerate out. You actually have to take racing lines. The in-between is the rally car, where you can drift, or take the racing line. A couple comedy cars round out the lineup.
Then there's tracks. There's a lot, they're varied, there's Lagoon Sea, Hungry Ring, Minizuka, Dabu Abi, these are what you think they are, and there's more than that. In addition to familiar tracks, there are dozens of fictional tracks, most of which are fun, few of which are frustrating. If that doesn't do it for you, and you want to make a "Spa Day" track, there's a track editor with a minimal learning curve.
Local co-op! I have people over to play games, and this is ideal. You can share one controller with two people. One trigger is throttle, one bumper is brake, one analogue stick is steering. Super ideal for schmoozing on that guy or girl you're crushing on.
Online multiplayer is a bust, no one plays, but AI is there and can give you a challenge. The AI can really frustrating as you always start last, and end up doing a lot of bumping into other cars. Passing in corners is easy, but on high speed tracks without a lot of braking zones, passing can almost be impossible.
I paid $9 to get a two pack, but if I had paid $12 for the one copy it'd still be worth it. I'll be busting this out at parties for a long time, and for now it's fun to go through and unlock everything, and try to set hot lap times in time trials.
If you like racing games, it's worth it at full price.

Prologue: NO I IN TEAM.
Some of the best moments I've ever had playing video games came during the era of Battlefield 2 + 2142. For me, the introduction of Commanders and Squad Leaders - with points granted for following orders - was something entirely unique. Working in tandem with a bunch of strangers, usually without the use of a mic, with the single goal of victory in mind, generated a greater sense of accomplishment through victory than the pursuit of a positive kill / death ratio. Unfortunately, the playing community on these games has dwindled, while the likes of Call of Duty, with its multi-platinum sales, has dictated the way in which EA has demanded DICE produce further editions of the series. Truly there was a gap in the market, with the only alternative fps that would cater for me being Counter Strike; which in itself was an entirly different animal. There may have been alternatives I didn't know about, namely the first Red Orchesta, but this was a game that never came onto my radar.
Fast forward a few years as the numbers dwindled on the 2142 servers, forcing me to find an alternative. After some minor research, I syumbled upon Red Orchestra 2, and what can I say, it ticked every box including ones I didn't realise existed or even needed ticking. If Battlefield 2 / 2142 encouraged team-play, RO2 demanded it; always will a well disciplined team, of average players, armed with an intelligent Commander reign victorious over a team of brilliant individualists. Of course, the game does give perks for team work, such as extra points for assist kills and defending cap zones etc. but lacking these bonuses, team-work would still be the back-bone of this game as the player-base knowingly understand it is the only way defeat can be avoided, even if it doesn't necessarily guarantee success, as the opposition will more than likely fight fire with fire.
General Pros and Cons:
PROS:
#More mature player-base - having kids flame out on VoIP is an extreme rarity.
#Campaign mode - a more involved an enlongated way to sew map victories together, as each team vies to hold each territory by succesfully attacking and defending on the campaign map.
#Map Design - Sure the player limit is capped at 64 & the maps are usually quite large - Bridges of Druzinha springs to mind - but the fact only one or two objectives are ever in play means the action is condensed into one section of the map. While player respawns act as single waves coming from a relatively sizable distance away. The pace of a packed server is quite remarkable, with each contol point always within 1 good attack from falling.
#Vehicles - Despite a couple of 'tank only' maps (which are avoided like the plague by the community) the maps only ever have one tank per side; one tank for the attacking team - to add some balance - or none at all. This keeps the infantry as the most relevant forces on the map, which should be the case in a FPS; while keeping a wild card in the pot at all times if not dealt with appropriatly.
#Team Balance - Both the Germans and the Russians have their strong and weak points. The Assault class is probably the most varried between the two armies, so I will talk about the differences a little. The PPS SMG for the Russians is unparalleled in close quarters and can take out entire squads with a rapid firing of bullets; however, when engaging anything over 50 meters it quickly becomes far less useful than the German Mp40. While, the Germans have access to the mk42b (arguably the games best all-rounder) for experienced Elite Assault troops. Like I said with pretty much every other class, the difference in guns in negligable. This minor differences means that certain maps are delibaretly avoided or chosen in Campaign mode, as it may bring out the best in a particular weapon - namely the over-powering of the PPS in the level Appartments.
Furthermore, each team can only have certain amounts of each player type, meaning that more than half of the battleground consists of regular rifleman armed with a bolt action non-scoped rifle - amplifyig the importance of knowing how to play your class.
#Fair leveling system - Most the upgrades awarded for leveling up provide major upgrades for extremely situational circumstances; bigger magazines for an smg or a bayonette for a rifle. This means that a lvl1 private entering the game for the first time doesn't have to be out-gunned while he builds up a feel and understanding of the game, while it also provides an incentive for experienced players to level all the available classes.
The only exception really comes with the sniper classes, who can swap out their bolt-action rifles for semi-auto rifles afer leveling up enough - although if it takes you multiple shots as a sniper, you're doing it wrong - or indeed the German Elite Assault class, who can unlock the games only Assault Rifle the MK42b - but on the flip side the Russians will have unlocked the drum magazine for their pps at this stage, which can inflict unimaginable carnage in certain circumstances.
#Steam Workshop - Addons provided by the community for free, what's not to like?
CONS:
#Realistic damage - a positive in my eyes, but I know people have complained about the inability to fire back at an aggressor. Nine times out of ten, spotting the enemy before they spot you means they will be the one filled with bullets. A good knowledge of the map layout aswell as ensuring the team has secured the flanks is of paramount importance.
#No weapon points for leaving a round - Annoyingly, if you leave a game prior to the end of a round, any of the points that you would have gathered for leveling up your weapons will be lost. Not too big of an issue you would think, but maps like Bridges of Druzihna have a one hour time limit, so you could lose 45 mins of good progress because real-life kicks in.
#Steep learning curve - Unlike some games which have beginner only servers, RO2 will not hold your hand at all, meaning that learning the intricacies of the game can be a grind which leaves your character in the grave more times than you would have liked.
The fact each team only has a set number of 'premium' classes also means that if it is clear you do not know how to play one of these roles, you'll be a considerable liability for your team. The only way of getting comfortable with a role is either through the games atrocious single-player campaign, or by spending time on a server populated solely by bots (there are many), just so your learning experience doesn't hinder the fun of others.
#Auto balance - Some matches can be incredibly one sided, due to team-work over VoIP or better use of Commander or Squad Leaders, and while the game does have an auto-balance feature it rarely pans out that it gets the switches correct.
It is a delight to see that Tripwire Interactive didn't cave into the pressure that was created by the rise of the modern console twitch-based shooter, ala Call of Duty. This game is a gem, that may not appeal to everyody, but certainly fills a gaping hole in the market that was brought on by a barrage of sub-par fps games. Indeed since its release there have been a few more gems that cater to a similar audience, none more so than the RO2 add-on Rising Storm, which is based on the Pacific Theater of WW2. It keeps much of the same gameplay mechanics, while injecting it with a completely different pace through level-design and weapon variation; meaning it offers enough of a change to make it worth the investment while keeping enough of the original so you know you'll like it if you liked RO2. Also, check out Insurgency for similar mechanics on a smaller scale.
This is by someway a marked improvement from the games which I had craved, as the team-work aspect is necessary for success; you are more likely to find team driven players on any random server here than during the golden-years of Battlefield.

Race Online:
~~~~~~~~~~
The pressure is as high as it can possibly be. Straps tight, nomex suit and a helmet. Ten drivers are on the edge, their eyes fixed on the starting lights. As soon as the three lights turn green, the season will be on its way! The question is, which position would you be standing in at the end of the season?
Race online is a top down racing game where you take control of a car, a bike or a UFO, and race either against nine other competitors handled by the computer, or challenge nine of your friends on a local multiplayer mode.
The main menu will give you access to what type of modes you’d like to play. You will have the choice to play single player, career mode, a single race, a time trial or a local multiplayer game. The career mode consists of three seasons. In season one, you’ll race on five different tracks with a fairly easy difficulty status. In the second season, the difficulty will increase significantly around ten tracks and the last season will consist of fifteen tracks with a high level of difficulty. The goal is to accumulate as many points as possible to become the champion and earn a large amount of money. If you don’t want to play the career mode, why not try your luck on one of many single tracks, or beat your last lap in the time trial! You will indeed receive money if you win a single race but the amount will be notably lower than the career mode. Otherwise, you can start a local game with your friends.
You can play online by hosting or searching for a game, but I must admit that I’m having difficulty finding online players at this stage.
Another option is available for the creative mind by jumping straight into the editor mode, which is rather fun and gives you plenty of re-playability. Create your own tracks and see if you can reach the highest position on the podium.
Gameplay-wise, it is fun and addictive. It can become quite challenging depending on the track and their obstacles. As you earn money, you will be able to purchase other vehicles available to you. However, they all have their own specification and you will need to adjust your driving style to successfully win a race or a season.
Graphically, Race Online looks good and the controls are responsive whether you use the keyboard or a game pad. I personally prefer to use the gamepad for this game.
Positives:
~~~~~~~

-	Nice graphics
-	Plenty of tracks
-	Track editor
-	Several modes of play
-	Achievements and trading cards
Negatives:
~~~~~~~~
-	Need more vehicles
-	Hard to find an online game
A challenging, addictive, fun and well-presented top down racing game!

The whole series is an enjoyable plate of oldschool adventure gaming goodness and paranormal detective work. But Epiphany is the most mechanically cohesive and intuitive of the series. It's the one you'd want to shove into the hands of someone hesitant to play point-and-click adventures, and then they'd just be lost for want of several episodes of back story.
It's not perfect. Recording quality is always iffy on Wadjet Eye games and it's disappointing that the logic mechanic that lets you combine note entries is pretty much an abandoned afterthought. But Epiphany finishes up a good yarn with some satisfying conclusions. It's a fitting end to a great series.

Sunless Sea is a naval action-roguelike with a bit of a british folklore spin. You play a sea captain tasked with an arbitrary goal (selected at start) and a small boat and crew. Through exploration and challenges, you are expected to grow as a character and gain additional crew, cargo, and special items. There is a great deal of lore to be found to help explain the universe your character lives in as well as his or her backstory and ties to local people and culture that grow as you interact with them.
Sunless Sea takes an interesting approach to handling the whole roguelike mechanic by treating just about everything as an item. Rather than gaining levels, you build secrets from fragments of discovered places and successful challenges, and then spend those secrets on boosting your stats. Additionally, it will be necessary for you to manage the terror stat, which slowly increases whenever you are in dark waters or suffering consequences from failed challenges. Hunger also plays a factor and you will need to keep a healthy amount of supplies handy in order to feed your crew. Lastly you must manage fuel consumption through meticulous navigation and careful use of the oil lamps.
Unfortunately, that’s about where all the good points for this game end. Combat is slow paced and typically the belligerent with the greater firepower or hull strength will win, regardless of piloting skill. The majority of your time will be spent doing tedious errands from point A to point B while desperately trying to conserve fuel, supplies, and mitigating terror. It’s definitely as boring as it sounds and despite all the attempts at creating a humorous or entertaining narrative, the story starts getting repetitive the 3rd or 4th time through.
Simply put, Sunless Sea just wasn’t as fun I thought it was going to be. The premise is interesting: Naval battles in a London-esque setting in a sea “under the sea” fraught with terror and danger. The execution, on the other hand, is incredibly dull and left me wondering what else I could spend my time on. From what I’ve read on forums, the game used to be a lot more fun/playable but a good deal of that has diminished in the light of recent patches. Play at your own risk.

If you grew up in the 80's or early 90's playing videogames, then you will appreciate the overwhelming nostalgia this game tosses at you right from the start.  I may be writing a review for this game, however, it revolves around the entire series as a whole and should be played as such.  From the start, you realize this is just like any point and click adventure from old.  The minimalist approach to the interface is overshadowed by the thought and heart poured into a truely enticing story and wonderful characters.  I do recommend you start with the first entry, and enjoy the ride for the entirety.
Does that sound too good?  Well, realize, this is actually a review, not just gushing compliments of a few aspects of the game.
Once you take the plunge in the first game (the first in the series, not the precursor game which I did not know about till I completed the 5 Blackwell games), you will get a sense that the creators want you to learn, and the tutorial aspect is not necessary.  It takes a bit, but once you get into the swing of things, you will start combining notes, using the few items you collect in the game properly, and later in the series, you will get the hang of swapping between your main character and their  ghostly companion.
The weaknesses of each series seems to be repeated.  I personally felt that some of the 'puzzles' were simply 'do in the right order no matter what information the player has seen', 'luckily you clicked the right notes in the right order' or even 'glad you visited this person now after you did one thing' to progress.  Later entries in the series seemed to try for less linearity, however, it really boils down to perfect order.  Maniac Mansion, this is not.
The story, characters and a large portion of the quests, however, make up for the handful of blunders.  I won't spoil the series ending, but be prepared, it is a doozy.

To be blunt, Batman - The Telltale Series is a game that has a lot of really great ideas that completely fails to stick the landing. It brings back a lot of old comic story lines (like Harvery Dent running for mayor, becoming close friends with Bruce, and then turning into Two Face when it all goes disasterously wrong) and tries to put a spin on existing Batman lore by asking a new question: what if Bruce Wayne's parents were secretly part of the mafia? Most of the ideas that Telltale brings together are actually pretty decent on their own, but the problem is that they try to do too many at once and fail to do any of them justice. More importantly, most of the choices are ultimately cosmetic and the climax is never really built up before hand, so the end experience is just boring and dissatisfying. If Telltale had just committed to just two or three plotlines, this could have been an incredibly strong game, but this game just desperately needed an editor to cut down the excess ideas down to the essentials. Unless this game is on a really good sale (or you're just a huge afficionado of all things Batman), I can't recommend buying this game.

This has the makings of a great survival game - think Winter in "Don't Starve" from a first person perspective, in a real world setting (no carnival music, no magic, no fun-silly items, ect).  The game is frightening: I often have to remind myself that I am the only person left in the area and that deer and rabbits aren't deadly, a crazed half frozen zombie man isn't about to charge me from that small grove of Cedar.  Playing this game makes me want to start a fire next to my computer to stay warm.
One of the many things the devs did justice to was the atmosphere; the creaking and groaning of the buildings during a storm, as well as the whistling of the wind, is both immersive and keeps you awake, panning your view when you're outside.  When moving between camps I am typically looking around, just admiring the landscape and atmosphere of the world.  Then a noise comes from somewhere I'm not looking and I nearly♥♥♥♥♥♥myself.
My first play lasted nearly 15 days, brought to a slow end by a bear attack that left me nearly dead.  When I recovered, dazed as I was, I finished off the bear, and the wolf which appeared before the bear even hit the ground.  Giddy as I was at seeing (and killing) my first bear, I checked the carcass.  Then I realized that I couldn't move my legs anymore.  Or my hands.  Or anything.  I died frozen to the carcass of a freshly killed bear, in many ways it had the last laugh.  My second run is going well, but bullets are getting scarce....
Now for the nit-picky parts!
I've only played on the 'medium' difficulty, and I've heard this is adjusted by difficulty, but every task I do seems to drain me.  It requires about 12 hours of sleep to fill the energy bar, but if you sleep for more than six hours straight, you wake up starving and dehydrated to the point that your condition will begin to deteriorate.  My guy can't even stay on his feet for more than six hours without turning into a wet noodle.  The hunger/calories is neat, but I think they need to be related, not the same stat - it seems kind of absurd that I need to eat three to four kilograms (6-9lbs) of meat a day to keep from starving.  Warmth is the only mechanic which I feel doesn't need to be worked on; at first you lose a lot of warmth being outside, especially in weather, but once you pick up more appropriate articles of clothing weather is more of a nuance, a nuisance, rather than a deadly show stopper.  As other people have suggested, it would be really cool to see your stamina improve as you survive longer, perhaps even have your hunger and thirst requirements reduced (or at least have their drain mitigated).  The problem I can see with that is that it ultimately makes the game easier as you progress and might require greater challenges to be presented to keep the player engaged.
All that said, this game is seriously one of the best lone-survivor games I've played and it's still being developed, definitely worth at least taking a look at (especially if you spent all that time reading the wall of text above)!

This is a game that works for me on nearly every level. I've spent 25+ years working in the outdoors of the Pacific Northwest so this was like playing in my backyard. I am not going to talk about all the aspects of this game that are great but will highlight a few. Played now for over a year - the updates & changes have been awesome! Here's the only negatives (?) imo.
-Some players may not be satisified with the art / graphics. Personally I think they work, are simple and quite beautiful.
-The rifle mechanics are a bit confusing. I have owned and used a .303 extensively so I'm not blowing smoke when I say a wolf shot in the chest at 10 feet is, at the minimum, going to be knocked off it's feet. EDIT: Since writing this review I have one-shot 23 wolves in a row. Curious...
-Black bears normally do not attack when shot. 95% of the time they run away from the direction the pain originated from. In this game they attack 80% of the time. And they move at the speed of light. They cover 25 yards (the distance I typically shoot them) in about a second. ?? I've been charged 6 times in RL and as dangerous as that was I can tell you: bears are fast BUT not that fast.
That's really all I can say that is remotely negative.
I can tell you that the basic stats of keeping your body temperature up, monitoring your fatigue, keeping hydrated and watching your calorie intake is, in RL, critical to your survival outdoors. Reading the wind, clouds, type and intensity of snowfall, wildlife behaviour are also extremely important. The balance that this game has with making these characteristics important but not needlessly difficult to learn is brilliant.
The crafting mechanic is simple and useful. The amount of steep and hazardous ground and easy going terrain is well balanced. The need for light sources is well thought out but not unduly taxing.
After dying on day 1.5 on my first play through I was embarassed (stood too close to a fire and burned to death). My second play through I was mauled to death by a black bear on day 59 hour 22. I was equally embarassed, I KNOW bears extremely well - what the hell was I thinking? Now I am approaching 350 days of survival.
Some advice to new players: Just like in the real outdoors there are the obvious needs of shelter, food and water. But the real key to survival is caution and patience. Don't push that extra two hours into the hills if the weather looks sketchy. Don't take a shot unless you have the near perfect or perfect angle. You can always go exploring the next day when the weather is better and there is always another deer or bear to take tomorrow.
Edit: Fantastic devs, constant improvement and real love for their creation!

Pox Nora is a fascinating and incredibly fun SRPG-TCG headed by a development team with an eye on balance.  This is a easy-to-play slow-to-master turn-based SRPG with TCG elements in that you deploy cards onto a battlefield littered with obstacles and they attempt to protect your base and destroy that of the opponent's, while capturing objectives.  With something like 2000 cards over the last seven years of expansions, there's a huge element of 'gotta catch em all'.   Fortunately, they've recently been taken over by a development team (Desert Owl Entertainment) interested in sustainable growth; which means BALANCE.  A full-blown rebalance of all 2000 cards has recently been completed; so that the core runes essential to a strong strategy are often inexpensive.
In a pleasant change from other F2P games, it's genuinely easy to obtain new cards ('runes'): Play a quick game vs AI?  Here's 100 gold and a free, random rune from the faction you played (Including rares!).  Play a campaign?  Here's 600 gold.  1900 gold buys a weaker 'core set' booster pack, and 3150 buys an 'extended set' booster pack.  They give out around 1000 gold a day through free dailies; and simply playing matches to complete these dailies will net you around 1500-2000 gold a day.  Members on the forums set up 'Rune Pools' where you can trade in a card for a card of equal rarity easily; allowing a new player to set up inexpensive strategies all the time.
As a much older game, this has a level of strategic depth and complexity rarely seen in video games, requiring reading (and reading comprehension!) beyond Hearthstone; which I would consider a successful competitor in the F2P TCG arena.  I would seriously recommend this game; as either the F2P or if you want, as something to sink forty bucks into.

Race Online looks like a very simple game on first glance and is easy to get into. The tracks are all nicely designed with great attention to detail and the gameplay is nice and simple. So simple in fact that the absense of rebinding doesn't matter as it pretty much gives you all the ways to control that you could come up with on both the Keyboard and Controller.
I would go as far as saying that this is one of those games that are easy to learn but hard to master. The 6 vehicles all control very differently and they all have very defined strengths and weaknesses. One would want to master each vehicle and pick accordingly to the upcoming tracks in order to gain the best results. I was very surprised by the depths the choice between 6 vehicles added considering that other racing games have about a hundred cars that all feel more or less the same.
The singleplayer campaign offers a lot of content as it provides 3 increasingly long and difficult cups for each vehicle.
The track editor seems like a great way to increase longevity but I didn't give it a try yet. I will update this review once I've given it a shot.
All in all I really like this game and it's future seems bright as more content is added. While the asking price is a little questionable in its current state I'd definitely recommend buying the game on a sale, especially if you have friends to play with.

They do a great job of emulating the classic overtop arcade racing games but there are a few bugs and downfalls mixed in. There are different cars to unlock and different "series" to complete but it only takes a few hours to unlock everything. There is a huge amount of tracks to race at as well. There are even a few IRL tracks such as Mazda Laguna Seca and SPA that have been transformed down to pixel tracks. This game is perfect if you are looking for quick and fun races for a short amount of time. The problem is that it gets slighly boring and too easy after a while.
The customization is very limited. There is no option to change difficulty, set amount of laps, or even set races for all cars to be in the same class. The only way to set cars in the same class is the career mode. You can change the color of your car but that's about it.
Multiplayer is dead, There is a online mode but there are zero races going on at any time.
There are also a few annoying bugs in the game. I've consitantly run into an issue where AI cars get stuck and cannot correct themelves by simply turning or going in reverse. There has even been a few races where only 1-2 AI cars manage to finsh. Occasionally there is a bug that messes up the running order if you manage to lap a car. For me at least, Track customization is completely broken. The game crashes everytime I try to test a track I made.
Overall it's an good game based on gameplay alone, I'd give it a 7/10.

The interesting thing about this game is its story. The steam synopsis briefly says “Uncertain of his sister's fate, a boy enters LIMBO” but the game itself doesn’t even tell you that. There is no dialogue, and really no explanation for what is going on, or why things are trying to kill you. However, there are several clues throughout the game that sort of give you a feel for what’s going on, and people have also made various interpretations of the game’s meaning. Personally, I think the lack of story helps in this case, as the imaginative, dark world you’re in tells its own tale.

Sort of like if Mario had a
bad trip. In terms of it's basic mechanics, LIMBO's basic premise is that the protagonist (who seems to be a young boy) wakes up in a forest, and it's your job to guide him through the many dangerous in this terrifying world. The game pairs traditional platforming with light puzzle-solving elements through a fairly linear exploration/progression; basically, keep going right, and solve the puzzles so you can keep going in that direction. Though this a short game, in the process of completing it you'll pass through forests, caverns, sewers, and derelict factories and cities.
The atmosphere is utterly enthralling; the entire game is in grainy black-and-white; there is almost no soundtrack, only very dark and minimalistic ambient effects; there is no dialogue at any point in this game, and the only other NPCs you meet all try to kill you in a variety of ways. And this game really is dark; giant spiders impale you on their legs, boulders crush you, worms take control of you and often force you to run off cliffs, and bear-traps crush you in their vice-like grip.  his is an utterly hostile and terrifying world. One section has the player cross a lake by jumping across the floating corpses of people forced to wade into the lakes to their deaths by mind-altering worms. Having crossed the lake, the solution to the next puzzle is to then drag one of the bodies out and to push it over a ledge onto a button, which causes a huge block to fall crushing the body, which would have been you had you activated the button yourself. This is a very, very dark game.
And the puzzle-solving elements do become quite challenging as the game goes on, through it never reaches the difficulty of games such as Braid. The game steadily introduces new mechanics to keep things fresh, with switches that can reverse gravity or active giant magnets, while the feedback for failure is always immediate and brutal. Thankfully the game has no loading screens even upon death so you can be back to have another go in a matter of seconds.
The plot itself is thread-bare. There is no dialogue and no non-hostile characters besides one recurring one, whose finding seems to be the only real objective in this game. That does not mean the plot is not there though, and to me it seems like the team behind this deliberately left the game open to interpretation; the game is called LIMBO, how does that relate to the environments you find yourself in and the things that happen to you on your journey? Who are these other people you encounter from time to time? What happened to these factories and sewers and cities? These questions are never answered straight-forwardly, but it's for you to decide for yourself what this game is about and to me that makes it more powerful.

Just finished the game and I must say that it left me quite an impression. Not your typical cheerful platformer by any stretch of the imagination... This game is grim and brutal. Also be prepared to die a lot. In a gruesome manner. Did I mention you play a small child?
There is no story, no spoken or written dialogue or narration, no music and no indication of why this poor child is going through this. We can only assume the kid died and is going through some kind of hell over and over. The highpoint of the game is the fantastic atmosphere. The b/w graphics set the tone greatly and personally mezmerized me and I just had to keep playing. The graphics may look simple but they are quite detailed and never disorient, despite the lack of colors. Furhermore, the animation is very smooth adding more charm to the already very visually appealing game.
The puzzles are mostly logical and of easy to average difficulty. I wouldn't expect a seasoned puzzler to be seriously challenged and even the casual gamer may not need to consult a walkthrough for the most part. That said, I think the makers did a great job with the puzzle design so that while they occupy the player they do not become so cumbersome that make him quit or get annoyed enough to distract from the overall tone of the game.
My suggestion is to dim the lights, throw some ambient music like Goblin or Zombi or even some atmospheric black metal like Agalloch or Myrkyr or Burzum on your media player and enjoy the ride. It was a truly great gaming experience.

Maybe it's because I was spoiled by its predecessor (which you can't help but compare it to), but I found Tropico 5 very disappointing. The first thing you notice - right off the bat - is it lacks the charm and personality of the Tropico series. While Penultimo returns as hilarious as ever, all your old friends like Reverend Esteban, El Diablo and the Mighty Chinese Dragon (who's hungry for your goods) are conspicuously absent. As such, factions and foreign powers feel like numbers on a page instead of personalities.
The campaign is way too short with way too little variety. You can grind through it (fairly effortlessly) in a few days, during which you'll get to play on four islands. That's right. FOUR islands. Two of which are basically the same. As for the running of Tropico, in pandering to the needs of the crown, the people and the powers that be, you get the feeling of being a thankless civil servant rather than being a power-mad dictator in love with his own reflection, as was the case in Tropico 4.
While the implementation of Dynasties was a great idea - in theory - it was lacking in execution. Instead of three traits, now you only get one per Dynasty member. And a grand total of about four or five costumes. Thinking about sending el Presidente to a construction site to speed things up, or a building to boost service? Think again, as the option to do so is gone.
On the positive side, it *looks* nice. But as it's a Tropico game (and not a super-realistic bro-shooter), it doesn't really need to. If anything, the mandatory DX11 requirements have screwed a lot of people out of playing it in the first place. I'll have to double check, but I could swear the background music (with a couple of exceptions) is the same re-heated soundtrack from Tropico 4. Come on, folks. There's a wealth of Calypso/Carribean/Latin music to choose from. Get a LITTLE creative!
In summary, I REALLY wanted to like this game. I really did. Tropico 4 is still one of my favourite games of all time. It's sad to see what could have been an amazing game not fully realised and ideas not fully explored. Until such time as there's adequate DLC (I have no doubt they'll churn it out piece by piece in $5 increments) to give it a little variety and scope, I can't really recommend it. Go play Tropico 4. It's still a damn good game if you want to indulge your inner megalomaniac.
P.S. As if it weren't bad enough you can't build a giant golden statue of yourself any more, you can't build ANY statues. How the hell are you supposed to feel like a tyrant if you can't remake Tropico in your likeness?

I would recommend this game BUT, and that's a big but!!! The game has a lot of future potential. Meaning the content and overall design of the game is outstanding. However, it is lacking in some key aspects.
One of the biggest issues in Tropico 5 is bugs, this alone would have been fine and I'd still recommend the game even with the bugs. It is the second big issue that is the problem on top of the bugs namely that there are some important design oversights in the game.
It is mostly in little things, here one little thing and there one little thing. All these little things really add up though to cause a great deal of loss to personal enjoyment of the game. Combine these little design oversights with the bugs in the game and you have yourself a recipe for a day of fun gaming - ruined!
For example, if you play on Sandbox mode with all difficulties set to medium and give yourself unlimited money. You’d think with this unlimited money you could make the so-called perfect island, this however is simply not yet possible in Tropico 5 due to a combination of design flaws and game bugs.
Firstly, unlimited money is not really unlimited, meaning there will be many times in the game that certain things will say you do not have enough money for it! Wow, well lot of good unlimited money setting did me!
Then there are the design flaws, as you play in sandbox mode with unlimited money (and same issue exists on normal modes), your city naturally will grow to become quite large and fill the entire island. The game simply has no good management tools to manage such a sheer number of different buildings. This task is made harder by the game’s bugs. For example if you set “all buildings” to the same budget level. This only sets the current buildings of that exact type. Meaning you still have to set it for each different farm that farms a different crop. It also means when you build new buildings they all start at the default budget regardless.
Secondly, you have the design flaws in both the UI and the actual game mechanics hampering your play. Some buildings allow you to upgrade all to the new version. However, not all buildings offer this functionality oddly enough. It is as if the developers were not working in a team and one developer thought, hey! I’ll add this feature. But no one else knew about it on the development team. Thus only the buildings that one developer designed has those functions. Then the small upgrades completely lack them. If you have 20 buildings to upgrade, well you gonna have to click 20 freaking buildings individually! Crazy right!
If this wasn’t bad enough, the game mechanics are pretty messed up. I gave my citizens all the rights in the world, built them all the stuff they wanted. But apparently 20 Cathedrals on a small Island just is not enough to satisfy religious needs... what??? To add more insult to injury, I made everyone on my Island filthy rich, gave them all the best entertainment, luxuries, environment, everything possible within the game and STILL I had rebels by the dozens, I had 100s of citizens leaving my Island. I just don’t get it, I had so many empty jobs and as soon as I’d hire foreign nationals they’d leave in a heartbeat despite having all their needs fulfilled to the maximum and happiness ratings in the 90 range on all elements except religion (due to the above issue).
As a result this really has discouraged me from playing. I love challenging games, but I hate it when a game is challenging not due to design, but due to design flaws and more importantly, game breaking bugs and issues.
And it is a real shame, as there is so much potential for enjoyment to be had in this title. Multiplayer modes (full of issues still though), great single-player content, a wide array of different buildings and technologies. But yet it is all lost due to the game bugs and design flaws.

Ah. Blackwell.
On one hand, this is a fantastic series and ends without wearing out its welcome, but at the same time, this is like two games crammed into one [which is sort of awesome but tedious if going for the "leave under 300 footsteps" achievement]. It has a very Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows feel in that it's really designed for the fans who've played through the first four--while I wouldn't recommend it, it IS possible to play Unbound, Convergence, and Deception without first playing Legacy. Epiphany really needs to be played last to be satisfying.
Spelling this out: DO NOT PLAY THIS IF YOU HAVE NOT PLAYED THE OTHER BLACKWELL GAMES FIRST.
Overall, I basically love everything about Epiphany... except... I've listened to the commentary, and I understand the reason for the ending, but... I really wanted it to end differently. It's such a Deus Ex Machina, besides being the least probable outcome [even being a series about ghosts and mediums], and... I dunno. I do get and like the imagery and respect how that's the only way it could happen--it's just kind of... aww.
The commentary is particularly insightful at the third act twist [where the Epiphany is explained], and I highly recommend listening to it if you have the chance. Wonderful writing, though maybe I would've changed the one thing, definitely a good sign-off to the series.

Note: This review will be written with respect to the four prior Blackwell games. I've also decided to leave my Obligatory Header in those reviews as well. If you've been reading these in order, you already know my scoring philosophy and standards.
Story: I don't normally do this first. The normal structure of these reviews is Gameplay, Story, Graphics, Audio. For this game, though... I've gotta bring the story top and center. Deception left me with a feeling of disappointment on the story front, especially after Convergence and its utter excellency. This game does have a few not so compelling spots, but I like to think that's for pacing's sake. The high points are well worth any wait, and they most definitely make up for any minor blemishes this game has. It does jump the shark a little bit at the end, but for drama's sake, it's top notch. I'd be lying if I said I didn't get a little choked up at the end. What that one reviewer said was right, though. This really is an incredibly satisfying ending to a series which has always been about pretty great writing. 10/10.
Gameplay: We've also gone back to the quality of puzzles in Convergence. They all make sense, don't require any incredible leaps of logic (despite a few instances where my solution would've worked just as well as the game's), and are often quite clever. 8/10.
Graphics: The art in this game is quite frankly amazing. All the characters and backgrounds have a great amount of detail to them, the art is very clean yet stylized, and it all just looks great. 5/5.
Sound: Voice acting: perfect. Music: Perfect. Fits the mood impeccably. 5/5.
Overall scores are: 10/8/5/5; cumulative score of 9.3/10. I will definitely be looking forward to more of Dave Gilbert's works.

If you like Darkest Dungeon's hopeless feel and dark themes this game is a good fit. The writing is very good  and long voyages that youa ren't certain you are ready for can be tense and fun. Still much like Darkest Dungeon this game suffers from feeling like you are not actually progressing. Most of your income goes back into refueling, resupplying, and repairing. There is no real way to permanently game over, but each death nearly resets your game since you can only carry a little bit over, however unlike a rogue like where that is just fine, each run of this game takes hours, going back and fourth through the sea.
Part of the system of what you can carry over to your next run allows you to pass your map along. This seems nice for the convenience of knowing where everything is since the map randomizes things a bit each new run. However you should never EVER pick this option because one of the key ways to gain experience in this game is by discovering new locations, and if they are already on the map you cannot get experience for them.
Personally I found the first run through the game to be MOSTLY a lot of fun. THe sense of discovery was strongly in place and each event was new and interesting filled with unknown risk.
Everything in it becomes repetitive though. Same locations to discover, same events with the same flags and requirements. Sure you can try new things on another run, but you are going to have to repeat a lot of things to get some of your things back.
Furthermore the game isn't fun if you turn your back on events and don't go exploring. However diving headlong into some events without actually having a reason to be there can absolutely ruin a run with little to no gain. The frost castle for one should only be entered if you know what you need from it, but if you haven't seen the start of the quest you need to enter for, how could you know there even is a specific thing you should be entering for rather than just a new and dangerous adventure to be had for possibly great rewards?

Play at your own risk.

Positives:

+Great atmosphere

Early Access Review
---------------------
Even in it's current state, this is still a lot of fun to play. At the moment it lacks the story based mode, though this will be added at some point in the future.
The sandbox mode is very playable and I have not encountered any serious bugs.
A couple of times I sprained an ankle or wrist for no obvious reason, and another time my freshly snared rabbit was trapped too far inside a tree trunk to harvest. But that's it.
There is no villain in this game to defeat. The goal is simply to survive as long as you can, but that is still a big challenge.
How long will you last?
At times it is a desperate struggle when you are running low on food or trapped in a blizzard with almost no visibility and your firewood has run out. Mistakes or bad luck can sometimes be fatal, even when you think you were doing well.
Likewise, you should never give up until death is certain.
One time I was starving and had no weapon. I was desperate to find the rifle so I could hunt deer and fend off the wolves. On my way to a possible location I was attacked twice by wolves. I was freezing, exhausted and down to 7% health now. As I got closer to my destination, I heard the familiar snarl of another wolf ahead. I backed off slowly and circled round it.. it followed me but did not charge... eventually I made a run for it towards the bridge and thankfully there was the file. I picked it up, loaded, spun round and shot the wolf between the eyes just it was about to finish me. The cooked wolf meat fended off starvation and I made a full recovery. That was day 21. It is now day 102 on that same game and I still alive.
I have played numerous times before this game, usually ending in hypothermia, starvation or wolf attack. Most of the enjoyment I have gotten out it so far is learning from what I did wrong, finding out which strategies that work and exploring the different maps.
After day 102 (and after 80 hours play) its starting to get a bit samey so I am starting to get bored of the sandbox mode and feel I need to play the story mode now to get more enjoyment out of it.
There are still things for me to do in my current game - I have only explored about 2/3 of the coastal highway map and I have yet to venture to desolation point. Or I could start again at the highest difficulty level (I played on moderate).
However, I can say that I have got definitely got my money's worth out of the game so far.

Banished is a deceptively simple sim game that hides a good deal of complexity.
Spend some time with a recently banished group of settlers building up a sprawling village filled with tiny villagers who (if you play your cards right) live long enough for you to grow attached to them. Though the game's pace is slow, the choices you make still make a great deal of difference as to the survival of your town (and you can speed up the rate of play simply and easily if the pace bothers you).
Much thought was placed into the creation of Banished and it shows. Definitely pick it up if you enjoy city building and simulation games. An active mod community doesn't hurt either! For a real change of pace try installing the mod that makes your villagers age appropriately to the years passing. It's a whole nother game entirely!

Cuphead Review
TLDR: It's good, play it.
Cuphead is quite a gem. The visuals are incredible and draw everyone in. The controls are simple and feel good and the game is super simple. The game focuses on boss fights with only having a handful of side scrolling levels. The game feels very difficult at first, but the game does a great job of teaching you how the fights work and you progress over time. I feel like the difficulty was pretty perfect, not too easy but not too hard where it makes you want to break your controller. I was able to beat the entire game 100% without looking at a guide or videos or any form of advice.
Some more specific insight after completing the game:
Try different weapon combinations. After the first world, I got stuck at a boss and then I remembered that you can unlock other weapons. Many of these weapons will do very well in certain fights. I honestly didn’t use the small 3 way spray once until the very final boss. I spent most of my time using the bullets that went back and forth. Really helped to clear the random trash mobs that fly in. The auto aiming weapon is actually pretty great do despite its lower damage. You have to look away from your target often to dodge things; being able to just hit your target regardless of which direction your facing really adds up over time.
I didn’t get a lot of mileage with the other supers. I just used the first one. I also used the immune dash power up for awhile, but switched it for the extra life later on. Again, I felt like the benefit of having another life was better than doing more damage.
Summary:
All in all, I mainly love the solid design of this game. Both in visual and gameplay. Most AAA titles nowadays are boring and full of complex menus and just feel like a drag. Games like super meat boy, thumper, transistor and Cuphead (and more) really make me enjoy playing games. If you are a fan of classic action games, play this.

I haven't played into this game much yet -- but I've still played enough of it to give it a "recommended" review IMO.  Why?  Because the game is FREE and fun.  That's good enough, right?  Obviously a game being free alone does not warrant its download -- but if it's a fun game that achieves its gameplay goals, *that* does.
Anyway, as has been said before, "Jigoku Kisetsugan" draws HEAVILY from the "Touhou" series.  It's not IDENTICAL, mind you, but the similarities definitely shine through.  It IS close enough that, were it not free, (and, were it not standard procedure to mimic / rip-off / pay homage to Touhou) it could approach reprehensible.  But... that is not the alternate reality we live in.  As it stands, this is a very fun little shooter by a new(-ish?) developer, with a LOT of promise for the future.
My only major gripe with the game, so far, is the fact that you seem to get 1 starting "bomb" per CREDIT, not per life -- at least on Normal difficulty.  IMO this is absurd, not because the game is especially difficult, but because it's standard procedure in the genre and combat feels a bit bland without it.  Then again, I am still "learning" the game.
Anyway, it's fun, it's free, and it's *almost* Steam Touhou.  Check it out!

When I was younger I had an Amiga 1000 instead of an IBM.  (They weren't called PC's back when pterodactyls were delivering our E-Mails.)  Classic Load Runner was an IBM game not an Amiga game.  So I sort of missed out on this classic game.  So, for me it’s really awesome to see this remake with the "classic" levels.  (As far as I am able to discern they are the same layout if not entirely identical to the originals.  However, I could be off given I have to search the internet for info on the original.)
Based on this alone I wanted the new Lode Runner and been happy.  The game is simple but allows for a wide variety of levels with just the basic components.  And you get over a hundred of those levels.  But you also get an adventure mode with a bunch of new levels and new enemies.

AND you get a level builder with access to a community levels server that gives, well, LOTS of levels.  Probably there will be millions in the not too distant future.  A simple rule that you must be able to beat the level in the editors play test mode before publishing it somewhat makes certain that there are no ‘unwinnable’ levels.  Though I found one frustrating one where you have to die multiple times in the correct order to win the level so it’s not perfect.  But these seem to be pretty rare.

You also get some funky camera stuff.  3D and first-person views and close up stuff.  But that all turns out to be way less cool than it seemed like it would be when I first heard of it.  (Sort of like FPV Pac-Man turned out to be.  Seemed like it would be cool.  Wasn't.)
Sorry.  I can find things to nitpick in any game.
So.   Short version.  There's a lot to like here.  Most of it permutations on a very solid simple formula.  But it's a good formula and there’s a LOT of it here.  This game gets the Selva seal of approval and a rare dew claw up.  Yes, I recommend this game.  You MAY need a little nostalgia to get full value out of it.  But given the deluge of modern military shooters and... stopping myself before I get started... Given the 3xA space these days a solid Donkey Kong-esque platformer is refreshing.  And this is a good one.

I don't recommend this.
I'll start with the technical issues. For a voxel based game that really isn't trying to do very much, this runs like crap. My computer isn't at all state of the art, but I expect more than 20 fps at minimum settings. Which leads me to another technical issue: there are no real options to work with. You can turn off backgrounds, pick between two resolutions, and make it full screen. That's roughly it. I can't even disable V-sync. It astounds me that a somewhat official game being released to steam in 2017 doesn't have these basic settings. The whole thing smells vividly like a hacked together pc port for consoles. I haven't checked this, but the menus also can't be controlled with the mouse, and the menu prompts come up as controller inputs. You do the math.
On to the graphics. This game isn't much to look at. The blocky voxel aesthetic looks a little cheap when it's done right. Meanwhile, this game doesn't know how to do it right. The blocks are huge so enemies come out looking blocky and goofy. The platforms just look as low poly as they actually are. The one saving grace here is that you can create your own character in a relatively well designed editor. This is where the voxel based graphics really tend to shine, and it's likely the gimmick that inspired this ill conceived aesthetic. You can also edit your pickups. The thing that bothers me more than anything else is that they didn't even get the classic mode right. They literally just had to rip the textures from the original game to make me happy. If they wanted to go above and beyond, then they could have crafted a modernized version of those graphics. Instead this game will continue to force feed you the same drab platforms that they've thrown at you in the other modes. It just looks lazy.
They've also got this really weird first person mode where you can't see anything and have to look at a normal screen overlay just to play. I have no idea what they were thinking with that gimmick.
Finally, the gameplay. I wont say much about this. You probably already know how loderunner plays if you're interested in this revival. Some of the mechanics are still very fun. I love messing up and getting trapped in my own hole. This game doesn't add any new wrinkles to the formula though. In fact, basics like bombs are nowhere to be seen.
My final verdict: You'd be better off just downloading the original loderunner. It's more charming graphically, and it plays better as well. This game runs much more poorly than it should, it looks terrible, and it does the bare minimum that it can get away with. The single thing of value that came out of this is the neat little character editor, and even that isn't an original idea.
Not my favorite game, but the story line is compelling and touches on compelling philosophical positions and takes them to an extreme. Suffers a bit from consolitis.
I'll just leave the words lamp post here, and highly recommend the game to anyone who is willing to try something different out.

LIMBO is a puzzle platformer indie title released in mid 2010. It was originally released as an Xbox Live Arcade exclusive, before eventually moving to the PlayStation and PC in 2011, it latter got  another port to PlayStation Vita and iOS, and yet another one onto the Xbox One and PlayStation 4, this goes to show just how popular this game is and how well received of a title it was.
This is a 2D side scroller platformer which uses the Box2D physics engine, which you may of heard of because it is also used in Angry Birds, and plenty of online Flash Games.  You play as a young boy, and travel through the world filled with dangers and traps as you search for your lost sister.  The puzzles in this game have a very trial and error theme to them. You probably will die a few times on the puzzles before you figure out the correct way of doing it. Each death comes with a horrific image of the poor boys rag dolled body plummet, get chopped up, speared, drowned, pretty much any sort of tragic death, this poor lad will go through it all.
The graphics are very simple, but very elegantly produced. Its a 2D side scroller so don't expect to see mind blowing realistic graphics; what LIMBO offers is beautifully crafted black and white tones. it is amazing how much atmosphere is generated just from the colour tones alone. The use of light and grain effects really create a spooky atmoshphere which alot of games try to produce but fail to capture as well as LIMBO.  This game is often used as an example that videos games should be classed as a form of art.
LIMBO has a very open ended story; the main plot is you are trying to find your lost little sister; and that's about as much information as you get. I don't want to spoil the ending too much, but I was a LITTLE bit disappointed with it and I really hope that there might be a sequel eventually to this game to find out more.
There is next to no audio in the game, and no music. All of the sound effects are very minimalist, this fits in well with the spooky atmosphere which is being created, and probably makes it feel all that more eerie
A couple of puzzles in LIMBO had me scratching my head quite a bit before I was finally able to figure out what to do. I would warn you - there is a lot of jumping style puzzles and platforming events to get through. In my opinion, jumping puzzles are the worst, but they obviously have to be in platforming games so I just had to battle on through. The game does offer a very good respawn/checkpoint system though. If you die, you won't end up miles and miles behind where you just were, you'll normally spawn right before you messed up to let you try again - this made the trial and error mechanic work so much better as you don't have to replay content you have just got past.
This game's world is so well made, yet it doesn't have anything to interact with other than the puzzles, the minimalist theme keeps you on track the whole time, and you have little chance to explore off the track, simply because there is nothing to explore, it's a one track minded game, essentially you need to get from A to B, and you cannot come off the track. That's not necessarily a bad thing; games these days are often too "open world" style, and often overwhelm the player with too much to see. I liked how LIMBO kept me focused on the task at hand, which was the puzzles and progressing through the dark world I was in.
To play LIMBO from start to finish, it took me just under eight hours. That felt like the perfect length for the game, I would of liked to see a little more of the plot unfold, but it does leave it open ended for a possible sequel in the future. I see little reason to play it through more than once. It's 100% linear, and you will always end up with the same outcome and even the puzzles don't have more than one way to complete them, so unless you want to go achievement hunting, there is no reason to replay LIMBO.
LIMBO is certainly a highly popular game, and is so for good reason. The game does very little wrong in any of the criteria, and it showcases just how an indie game should be developed and published. The game has gone from strength to strength since being released on Xbox Live, and it still alive and kicking on the current gen consoles. For the price of £6,99, you are getting a simply amazing game.

Race Online is a nice looking retro racer from top down perspective and is somewhat fun to play but if you're looking similar gameplay than in legendary Slicks 'n' Slide or Turbosliders you will be disappointed. The car handling is quite different and isn't what you would expect for a car as they move and handle like solid blocks, get stuck easily and you can't reverse you way out. There's not much difference between how cars (sports car, formula, tractor, etc.) handle and move. Also seems that track obstacle's or car's collision model isn't quite what the graphics show.
Overall the game feels ready and I didn't experience any bugs although the game crashed couple of times. The tracks are a mixed bunch, some are nice to race but often tracks are a bit annoying (due AI & collision model) and track profile isn't "professional" style. Some tracks look unfinished. The career mode is quite easy as the only difficulty is to get pass the AI cars after start and not to get stuck to them or pushed. Even on harder difficulty levels the difficulty comes from getting stuck to obstacles as the track is narrow and you can't pass or you crash to AI cars which are stuck. Also the grinding part of getting new cars and upgrading their parts feels artificial. The game ran quite nicely on my Macbook Pro (late 2013).
As the game is still in early access I hope the developers will enhance car physics and model before the release. They could take some example from e.g. Turbosliders which is fun to play but still competitive. Or maybe developers have played Turbosliders as the graphics and some of the tracks look similar.
Will be interesting to see how the multiplayer works when it's released.
In this development state I can't recommend this game. I hope the game gets better but I doubt it as the car physics are a big issue for games like these to change later on.

Did you play Lode Runner back in the 1980s?  Did you like it?  If so, you can stop reading now and just go ahead and buy the game now.  The entire classic set of 150 levels are included and this is pretty much a perfect update to those levels.  The graphics are significantly improved while retaining a retro/pixel-art feel.  In addition, all the timing on the levels is retained, too.
In addition to that, there are plenty of new modes with different graphics and options that are also nice updates.  And there's a 1st person perspective that you can play, too.  The graphics on the new modes are super-nice, too.  And, a staple of all Lode Runner games, a great level editor.  Mix in leaderboards, community levels you can download, and you're looking at a loaded update that is truly an example of how to "remake" a retro game and do it right.
The game isn't perfect - the controls in the menus are a little wonky - but the gameplay is perfect and the game is a tremendous value.  I give this my highest recommendation.

This game is incredible. I haven't enjoyed playing a game this much in a long time.
You can play as a Commander class which can call in recon planes, mortor bombardment, arty etc. You can be a squad leader which allows your squad to spawn on you and you can mark areas of the map for the commander to call in a bombardment. Or you can be a soldier, choose your "class", rifleman, assault, sniper, machine gunner etc. There are a good amount of weapons, the maps are large but easy to learn and they are open enough to using flanking tactics.
Rising Storm as amazing. Here is just one tiny part on one map during one match that took place:
I was playing as the Allies and we were fighting fiercly to take an enemy position that was heavily fortified. As we approached our Squad Leader marked the position and told the Team Leader over comms it was marked. The Team Leader confirmed, calling in a recon plane and dropped arty. Everyone took cover as we watched explosions landing just ahead. Round after round hit, dirt flying up in the air.
Our next wave of reinforcements had arrived and were crossing the river to meet us on the far bank closest to the enemy. All of a sudden we hear "Arty has been cancelled, push forward" and with that everyone got off their bellies and charged into the trenches, bayonets ready, itchy triggy fingers awaiting the huge onslaught, expecting heavy losses.. and.. and... nothing. There were no enemies. None. Where were they? We quickly moved throughout the fortified position, taking positions facing outwards for any glimpse of our opponent. After taking a nice spot behind some sandbags that were stacked up with a good view hole to see into the jungle, I took a knee thinking what they could be planning.
I hear movement in the jungle, then I hear screaming.. "Booonzaiiiii" I take aim and start firing. There are so many, rifles pointed our way, bayonets fixed and they are charging right at us screaming. I pop off a few rounds and take down two of them when I see an officer with a sword leading the charge. I Line up my rifle to take him out, and I die. They had surrounded us and a few of them broke through on my right flank, rushing through the trenches swords swinging and bayonets stabbing everything in their way.
I respawned and the battle continued. With moments like this happening all the time, I don't know how this game isn't more widely talked about. Incredible experience that everyone should try.

Limbo has a catchy art design and an interesting, depressing atmosphere. Sadly those are the only real selling points of this otherwise quite generic puzzle platformer.
Limbo is all about style: a noir-like, minimalist, but nonetheless unique art style. If you wouldn’t mind staring at what you see in the preview screenshots for 2-4 hours, then Limbo will definitely be your game. And it knows how important first expressions are, because the initial atmosphere is superb, the eerie forest sets a very memorable tone.
Still, it is mostly just a façade. A façade that hides a fairly generic puzzle platformer set in the most overused and tired settings for such games, a boring factory. A façade that tries to hide the fact that the game has no story: all you do is walk right and try to get past various obstacles that prevent you from walking right.
As for puzzle mechanics, there are a few clever ones, like a parasite that makes you unable to stop moving in one direction (usually towards a pit), or some gravity manipulation. They are too rare though in the endless sea of uninspired box and switch puzzles. And they aren’t even difficult puzzles; the difficulty comes from trying to implement the easy solutions with incredibly tight timing and jumps. You’re gonna die. A lot. (©LordKat)
If puzzle platformers are your thing, by all means, get it. Despite my musings, it is one of the better ones to come out in these years. Just don’t have too high expectations for it.

TL;DR: It's a
, improved version of Dungeon Defenders that does the campaign much better, has some balance problems, its premium currency is too expensive but ultimately unnecessary, and while it has many technical issues, it still delivers an excellent experience.
It goes to show that the developers knew what they were doing and that the first game's success was not a result of mere blind luck. Surprisingly, this game has been given a refreshing new coat of paint while also retaining much of the feel of the first, a feeling powerful enough to keep many players interested in the game for thousands of hours.
-
Upon writing this review, games can be frustrating to actually get into. Not only do you need to wait for around 30 seconds for it to connect to a server(
) each time you try to go anywhere - be it the online town hub, your private tavern, a public or private game, not even counting the (albeit short) loading screen, quite often the game will simply stop in an
loading screen until you restart the game, upon which you can immediately be faced with said infinite loading screen again.
+
Once in-game, the combat just feels right, it's feels meatier and flashier than the first- a facet of the game that actually feels rather polished. Being able to use multiple heroes greatly varies your choice of different approaches to combat while improved loot diversity amplifies this effect further. Cheating stats is thus far impossible in the game, which means higher difficulties will continue to remain relevant if you decide to go down the path of online matchmaking. No more ballistas firing at the rate of a minigun.
+-
However, while more diverse, your loot needs to be funneled quite narrowly to progress at a decent rate. If you want to be effective, forget using your full set of heroes for active combat or anywhere near your full set of towers at all until you reach the final stage of the loot grind.
The good side to this is that you can acquire one single good item relatively early on, upgrade it and immediately be useful to your team with that one tower, instead of always relying on one high-level player for everything and having the others confined to upgrading, repairing and flailing at the enemy.
+-
Once you have reached the final stage of the loot grind, instead of a lack of decent loot
, you're limited by imbalances inherent to the towers themselves. Certain towers are much better than others and will dominate high ranked play. The towers' different strengths and weakness could actually be really fun, knowing which different towers to put where in a map, to weave an intricate, impassable defense has always been satisfying, but the balance and gear system make this very hard to justify for the results you'll get for your effort.
However that effect that is lessened by the fact that you can use up to 4 different heroes in any one game and swap between them at will, a major improvement to the single player experience of the first game, in which you had to rely on others to compensate for your chosen hero's weaknesses or vastly outgear the level to do it by yourself, something that would likely take immense amounts of time on your own for the very same reason you're grinding for.
,
-
The tutorial teaches you just enough to be an effective nuisance to future teammates. People, especially at lower levels, tend not to understand the abovementioned systems or tower placement strategy, which means you often see people building unupgraded towers that do next to nothing other than waste valuable build space, effectively working against the team's victory by their presence. You see people placing towers that would be useless even with the best gear in game, such as anti-air in an area that flying enemies will never reach, but is close to being overrun by ground. The third and final type of "teammate" is one that connects to your game as you are building, instantly presses ready and stares into the abyss as the countdown ticks down to your inevitable demise as you desperately try to place down enough defenses, knowing they will fall in but a moment as said teammate kills a whopping two orcs before your core falls.
-
The premium currency is way too expensive. I've seen costumes costing up to around 48€ while seperate heroes cost 15€ in gems each, which means getting one means weighing that one hero or costume against potentially multiple fantastic standalone games you'll probably have more fun with.
-
The amount of content available is similar to but better than the original's base game, but seeing as this one has been out for far less time, the amount of content you can access if you are willing to pay for dlc will be far greater there than if you spend that money here.
That being said, if you do not want to buy DLC (and don't have a friend to taxi you to the DLC levels) then this game will likely be a better option, even when discounting any future content they may patch in. There are also no cheaters here. At least not yet.
It's a fun, albeit flawed game that has much potential, and despite being F2P delivers very satisfying gameplay that will surely please tower defense/action rpg fans. Over time, this game will likely overtake the original as it gains new content, fixes its problems and builds a community. For now, it's up for debate.

At this point, I think that the game is rather dull and uninspiring in its current state.
You know when you have this great idea you love, but people end up hating it? The ingame UI dressed in a cell phone is just that. Tedious, clumsy, unresponsive, no feedback, inaccurate, annoying eventually. Everything is mouse driven, not even F1, F2, F3, F4 to set the game speed, which also resets every time your phone rings. More hotkeys for keyboard driven control would be nice.
That's all you do during the day, customers most commonly call to ask if something is in stock, or to complain; to which you either aplogise or give them free stuff. All in-game related data is displayed on virtual sheets of paper, that you can't drag around, to have the more important ones side by side.
"[...] the most comprehensive and accurate retail store simulator ever created [...]" has shallow mechanics, a small static table of items to stock up on and sell, with no real market research at hand, and full of fantasy quantities of money / prices.
Employee salary seems to range from $400 to $700 daily, that's $12,000 to $21,000 a month, or $144,000 to $252,000 annually. Yet, your employees are so unhappy, they quit every couple of days. Meeting with your employee to ask how they feel, does cost you $500... wait, what for? A little stress relief for $500?
And I can't get over the hiring process, especially when you find people through word of mouth and like none of them; the game repeatedly reminds you with an extra message box, that you'll lose the roster and the money you spend on job ads. Sigh.
There's fantasy prices for marketing, too - $100 cold calling, $250 newspaper ad (one expensive newspaper), $500 for some sign flipper, $1000 for a radio ad, $1500 for a networking seminar (don't as me how that's advertisement), $2000 for a TV ad.
But of course you're not allowed to spend ANY money on marketing unless you end up with $2,000 or more at the end of the day, because you're "too close to the red". How does that make sense? Who owns this business, the developer, or the player? Who is he to tell you how and when to spend your money?
You can have at most 2 employees working in the store, although you can hire up to 4. Using the 2 spare ones gives your 2 main ones a stress relief, so they're less likely to quit their $144,000+ anual salary job. Break room upgrades are not yet implemented. You will not be able to serve customers yourself when things get busy. You'll sit at your desk all day long, answering your annyoing cell phone.
I can't see how this game would live up to its promise of being the most comprehensive and accurate any time soon. I've played Tycoon games 20+ years old with deeper mechanics.

I grew up on adventure games dating all the way back to the original King's Quest. I love the genre - faults and all. Some of my favourite games are adventure games.
The Blackwell series completely surprised me. It had incredibly engaging characters, an intuitive investigation system, and puzzles that are challenging, but not impossible.
All of this comes to a head in this fifth and final entry in the series. Its gameplay time is roughly twice or three times longer than previous games, with a lot room for character, mystery, and puzzle development. The series has improved with each game, whether it was in puzzle design or its interface. Ending the series on such a high note leaves you wishing there was more, but also feeling satisfied by its tear-jerking finale.
Honestly, if you're reading this and thinking of getting it or the series as a whole, I say yes. Absolutely. I say this especially as a fan of adventure games. The Blackwell games are a gem in the sea of adventure games and you're doing yourself a disservice by not playing them.

I first began playing Tropico 4 last year and was impressed with the extensive campaign and dlc missions.  As many other reviewers have already mentioned, Tropico 4 was also full of humurous subplots and crazy characters.  Compared to its predecessor, Tropico 5 does not overwhelm you with tons of buildings, nor does it force you to repeatedly rebuild your island kingdom every mission.  On the other hand, the humor seems more subdued in this version, while the soundtrack (although a little more varied than Tropico 4) is still a little too repetitive for my taste.
Overall, there is much to commend about Tropico 5.  The graphics are quite beautiful, the era progression system adds variety to the game, and there is enough crazy story in the missions to get you laughing (and keep playing).  Veteran dictators may find issues with certain details of Tropico 5 (e.g. the awkward AI combat system and the generic voice acting), but players looking for a fun and addictive city building game will be quite pleased with Tropico 5.

Of the Telltale games I've played (Walking Dead Season 1&2, The Wolf Among Us) this is the least interactive.  Huge sections of this "game" amount to either walking from cutscene to cutscene, pressing 'e' to continue, or going through insipid and tedious quicktime events.
Dialogue is actually quite rare and where it does occur the conversation choices feel completely meaningless.
There are some fun ideas, but they are executed in the most threadbare and lazy way possible.  For example, you are (very) occassionally offered some choice in how fights will go.  In practice, this amounts to Batman smashing an enemy into, say, a bar rather than a pool table.  This didn't matter in previous titles because fighting was a minor part of the story.  Here, it's everywhere.
Performance-wise, the game is a joke.  Frame rate frequently drops into the gutter for no reason, sound ends up out of synch with what's happening on-screen.  It's a godawful mess and screams of a rushed product.
