Can't say enough about this game. Simply amazing. It's probably the best zombie sim you will play. I bought this game over a year ago on Desura and have enjoyed it since (with and with out bugs). There is a lot to deal with. Unlike Day Z you don't have to worry about other players. This is great because it puts the focus on survival and zombies. The game will have co op and multiplayer later from what I understand. The game itself is open world so you get dropped in and have to scavange and fend for yourself. One of the first things you will probably want to do is establish some sort of safe house. From there what you do is entirely up to you. You can choose to loot nearby buildings, kill zombies, look for other NPC's, build a farm,  etc.
The game has a fairly deep building system. it works kind of like Dead Rising except not as crazy. You can grab a bat and put it together with nails to form a nailed bat or you can combine liqour with a rag for molotov cocktails. The building system also extends to safe houses. You can barricade doors, windows, etc. This is vital in case your house gets hit by a zombie horde. Most safe houses don't stay safe for long. There are a lot of factors that can put your home in danger. Looter NPC's making too much noise and attracting zombies are just a few of the dangers.
You can't just stay in your safe house however, eventually hunger and other factors set in. Your character is susceptible to things ranging from boredom to sleep deprivation. Some of these things can be curbed a bit because the game offers a nice character creation system. You can invest in things like courage to make yuor character less likely to freak out during a zombie fight. You can also choos to make him a better runner, etc. This seems generic but there is a neat little twist. For every "good" trait you choose you must balance it out with a "bad" trait. This prevents you from making a super powerful character. Some traits have a higher cost than others and this really creates a balanced and unique character creation system.
One of the things I really enjoyed about this game is the fact that you can adjust the zombies. You can make them Romero style (slow) or 28 Days Later (runners). You can also adjust minute things like infection spreading. This is simply fantastic since it gives you the ability to play with different zombie types. This isn't the only thing you can change however. This game has a great modding community and the developers seem to support modding for this game heavily. There are already a bunch of great mods out for this game and I would highly suggest you try some out.
One of the things I didn't like about the game is the inventory system. You need to carry bags to lighten your carry weight. The more you have on your body the slower you move. Makes sense and a great system used in other games.  Different bags have different carry capacity. The problem I had with this is that while you are out and about you really want to carry a minimum set of things (weapons, food, etc). While out scavenging you may have to find some where to sleep for the night or may need some supplies. Carrying items in different bags seems a bit cumbersome. I understand the need for the bags but I feel like it could be done a little better.
Over all this game has a lot going for it and I was very excited when it was green lit on Steam. If you want a nice variety in zombie simulation you should give this game a try. It has a lot going for it and you can definitely see the developers have a lot of love for the community and zombie fans in general.

I have truly enjoyed this game. I'm not entirely sure I "get it," but I have had tons of fun dying at sea and seeing how far I can push my luck.
Sunless Sea looks like a seafaring action game. It is not.
It has some elements of a trader-type game. It's not that either.
At its core, Sunless Sea is a vast collection of choose-your-own-adventure stories. An assortment of little, text-based adventures where your stats determine the likelihood of your outcome. Many of the island stories have interesting and varied outcomes that can affect the future of the island to the point of killing its entire population, leaving behind a deserted waste. Some of the stories made me sad. A few made me laugh, but the overall feel of the stories - and all of Sunless Sea - is one of desparation.
This is a survival trader game. But the currency of trade is often nothing more than "zee stories," "current news" or intangibles like that.
The islands mix up for each playthrough, and some of the stories have random elements, but the game is definitely (fortunately) not procedurally generated. No offense to roguelikes, but I feel that a well- constructed, scripted game usually has a much deeper and interesting plot than one which is random. However, it is hard to say that Sunless Sea has any great overarching meaning or ultimate story. It is more or less an open-world concept in which you can sail about and experience beautifully-written adventures.
That said, combat is plentiful if you choose to partake. Enemies range from squiddy sea creatures to pirates. Killing them can yield goodies.
You can also upgrade your ship. New engines, new guns and other items will make you all but untouchable out on the zee.
I have loved this game very much. Replay value is alright. The graphics are simple, appropriate and very moody. Some of the islands are really good looking and fun to discover. The musical score is a bit limited, but the songs are haunting and appropriate. I sometimes get them stuck in my head, even though they are not exactly catchy.
Without being a blatant ripoff or homage, this game is less Lovecraftian than Lovecraft-inspired. I have seen no Lovecraftian homages or Easter eggs of any kind. But the hoplesss sea-fear and archaic writing all contribute to a fantastic, subterrenean world that Lovecraft would instantly appreciate.

It's a decent Touhou-type bullet hell game. If you have some experience in the genre, go ahead and give it a try. It's free, eats almost no space on your HDD and an old 10+ years old toaster, like mine can run it.
However, if you are totally new to the genre, I'd recommend Crimson Clover instead. Reason: Jigoku Kisetsukan is HARD. Just look at the trailer video. Those aren't extraordinary fights, no, that's pretty much the difficulty level across the board. Your screen is going to be filled with projectiles pretty much all the time, not just during bossfights. Add to the fact, that you have 3 lives, and two continues (if you've used up all of your lives) and that's it. If you run out, you have to reset the entire progress, not just the level. So if you run out of continues on the last level, you have start the entire game all over again. So if you're new to this, chances are that you won't even make it to the end of the second level on your first try. On easy. On hard, you probably won't live long enough to even see the first boss. So only try this if you have some experience with the genre, or you have the patience of a saint.

After seeing Nilesy play this (and not do particularly well, if I'm honest), I thought I could do better. When it was cheap in a sale, I grabbed it.
As a business sim, it's rather lacking. The economy is very predictable and very easily exploited to make money a waiting game rather than a commodity. If you make sure you have a few thousand to pay your employees at the start of each day, you never need worry again. Set up a situation where you're earning more than you're spending and leave it running for a few ingame days to let the income pool.
Or at least you could do that, if the game didn't pause every few minutes to tell you that one of your hundreds of employees isn't feeling well. Thanks, but that's what the HR Report's for. Between pauses for sickness, deal changes and end of day reports, the flow of the game jitters too much to easily farm money. Granted most if not all of these pauses auto-continue on their own, but for those 30 seconds or however long, your entire business is paused. When 5 people go sick in one day, that's a lot of wasted time.
Then there's the worst aspect of the game; theft.
There's a chance that one or more of your employees - especially in the late game - can start stealing from you. One or more times an ingame day, you'll get a pop up saying that x amount of money has been stolen and that you should find the thief. This x can be as low as $100, but I've seen it as high as $5000. Of course by that point I earned five times that a day, but the pop ups were annoying.
The way you find the thief is to read the thoughts of your employees (that's a mechanic, Rollercoaster Tycoon-style) to find the one who thinks "they won't notice it missing". This can be any one of your hundreds and there's no way to sort by thought (unlike RT). You have to go one by one or wait until their theft obviously impacts their lifetime earnings.
I eventually worked out quicker ways, but it's a drag. You catch one and there are two new ones the next day.
Menu-heavy games usually allow the keyboard to move and select. In this one, however, you have to click everything. Sick employee, click the OK. New day, click the OK. Another bloody thief, click the OK. It's bloated, unwieldy and quickly becomes a drag. I only have so many hours in it because I had it on in the background when I was doing other things. And even that's just so I could satisfy my 100% achievement compulsion.
Now that I have, I immediately uninstalled it and will probably never go back to it.
Kinda funny in places (company names and some descriptions can be a good laugh the first time), but the mechanics need fine-tuning, the economy balancing and the menus un-terribling. Nilesy made it look kinda fun, though.

First debuting in 1983, Lode Runner was one of the first platformers to challenge what gamers thought a platformer was through its puzzle-driven style. The game has also historically been interested in creating more features for the player as they were one of the first to include level creation in their games.
Now after 34 years, Lode Runner Legacy by Tozai Games promises to bring back not only the classic Lode Runner, but also introduce a new adventure mode featuring a modernized Runner with a whole new set of levels. The well loved level creator is still included and levels can now be uploaded and shared with Lode Runner enthusiasts around the world. In addition, there is now an item and character creator. A puzzle mode has also been implemented for those who really love a challenge.
The gameplay is pretty simple with only the joystick and B to shoot. The difficulty and fun comes from trying to solve the puzzles and avoid various enemies. The level creator has a surprising amount of customizability. The item and character creator, however, require a little more skill and pixel knowhow.
The only problem I had with this game was the inconsistency when toggling through menus and other on screen options. Sometimes the controller could be used and sometimes only the mouse and keyboard would work. This made switching game modes or even the blaster’s side of attack a little clunky feeling. This thankfully does not at all get in the way of actual gameplay, which is quite smooth once you accept the fact that you cannot jump. Another feature of the game I did not feel was that successful was the FPS camera as I felt that it was super awkward to control and I just ended up looking at the minimap to maneuver the level. I will also say that the AI did seem a little silly at times and seemed to get caught on the ladders as they all tried to climb at once.

Lode Runner Legacy is a modern adaptation of the classic Lode Runner. As such, it doesn't contain any of the additional items or gimmicks that were introduced in Presage Software's Lode Runner: The Legend Returns/Mad Monk's Revenge. What it does contain is the traditional Lode Runner gameplay with 3D voxel graphics, similar to what you would find in a game like 3D Dot Game Heroes or Voxatron.
The game contains an Adventure mode consisting of 50 levels, a Puzzle mode consisting of another 50 levels, and Classic mode which contains the original 150 levels with different 3D voxel graphics designed to simulate the look of the original game. As is always standard with Lode Runner games, it features a robust level editor with options for customizing the level size (Small, Medium, Large, X-Large), player sprite, enemy type, enemy sprite, item sprite, music, etc. There are also editors that allow you to create your own player, enemy and gold item models. All of these characters, items, and levels can be shared with the community through Steam Workshop integration, and you can also compete for high scores on all the various levels with the Leaderboards.
The major downside of this game is that the mouse hasn't been implemented very well and doesn't work properly with the menus, so until that's fixed you will find using the keyboard or a controller to be the easiest way to navigate around. Also, because the game is still new, there isn't a ton of content in the Workshop yet, but new stuff gets added every day and as more people get the game and create content for it, that will only improve.
Overall, if you're a Lode Runner fan, particularly of the classic style games, then this is the perfect game for you. The amount of content and customisation options alone make the $15.99 price definitely worth it.

Back in the early '90s when I was a kid and playing my dad's old Atari/Commadore 64 games from the '80s, "Lode Runner" was one of my favorites. The classic mode gameplay is pretty faithful to the original game. They've inserted some unnessecary 3D graphics effects to appeal to the youngsters, but other than that, the level design and gameplay is satisfying.
You control your "runner" solve puzles, outsmart your persuers, and collect all the tresure on the map to advance to the next level. Just like you remember.
Gameplay is fast paced, the puzzles are simple, yet some can be challanging, and the controls and mechanics are easy to pick up.
Overall I would reccomend this game to all of you who remember playing it as a kid. While they've added unnessasary graphics effects, the core gameplay, and level design is exactly what you remember. As far as the non-classic remake mode goes, well... I'll leave that for the youngsters to review. I'm perfectly happy with the game as it was 30 years ago.

This game is incredible. I haven't enjoyed playing a game this much in a long time.
You can play as a Commander class which can call in recon planes, mortor bombardment, arty etc. You can be a squad leader which allows your squad to spawn on you and you can mark areas of the map for the commander to call in a bombardment. Or you can be a soldier, choose your "class", rifleman, assault, sniper, machine gunner etc. There are a good amount of weapons, the maps are large but easy to learn and they are open enough to using flanking tactics.
Rising Storm as amazing. Here is just one tiny part on one map during one match that took place:
I was playing as the Allies and we were fighting fiercly to take an enemy position that was heavily fortified. As we approached our Squad Leader marked the position and told the Team Leader over comms it was marked. The Team Leader confirmed, calling in a recon plane and dropped arty. Everyone took cover as we watched explosions landing just ahead. Round after round hit, dirt flying up in the air.
Our next wave of reinforcements had arrived and were crossing the river to meet us on the far bank closest to the enemy. All of a sudden we hear "Arty has been cancelled, push forward" and with that everyone got off their bellies and charged into the trenches, bayonets ready, itchy triggy fingers awaiting the huge onslaught, expecting heavy losses.. and.. and... nothing. There were no enemies. None. Where were they? We quickly moved throughout the fortified position, taking positions facing outwards for any glimpse of our opponent. After taking a nice spot behind some sandbags that were stacked up with a good view hole to see into the jungle, I took a knee thinking what they could be planning.
I hear movement in the jungle, then I hear screaming.. "Booonzaiiiii" I take aim and start firing. There are so many, rifles pointed our way, bayonets fixed and they are charging right at us screaming. I pop off a few rounds and take down two of them when I see an officer with a sword leading the charge. I Line up my rifle to take him out, and I die. They had surrounded us and a few of them broke through on my right flank, rushing through the trenches swords swinging and bayonets stabbing everything in their way.
I respawned and the battle continued. With moments like this happening all the time, I don't know how this game isn't more widely talked about. Incredible experience that everyone should try.

I admit, I was excited about this for a while, did the whole EA buy-in to do alpha and beta.  I had alot of fun with the development of the game early on watching the game develop...that was until they opted to adopt a heavy MT(micro transaction/in-game shop) option.  While this buisiness model will net more income for them, over the old DLC system, it creates a lack of achievement players from the original loved.
Previously DLC gated hostable content and achievements that unlocked various cosmetic items, costumes, special drops etc.  Players did not need DLC if they knew someone who had the DLC they wanted to play, they would just join their game.  The only Notable Exception is the Eternia Shards DLC, as they were designed more as an Expansion over add-on DLC, extending the original story.
The cuurent DD2 systems make all playable content available with the base game, however costumes, pets, certain items, sotrage space, etc.  While DD2 base is F2P over DD buy in once and mostly non-mandatory DLC addons, like most F2P games its 'playable' without spending anything on the game, however the QoL suffers greatly making purchases feel extremely forced.
The main complainst are around the system change from DD to DD2, the gameplay itself is smooth, you just get to those points where you find an item that can be so much better if you spend money to upgrade it over the free way.  That said DD2 does have 'alternative' ways to get paid items, the catch is its limited to daily and event special quests...
--While thats fine and well, they made it so EGGS, which pets hatch from expire after 24hours...pets are those items that paying money can make them incredibly better over the free system, while collecting the daily currency to get the same effect will take much longer.  Example: Find a really nice EGG that with a few upgrades can be incredible, however what is needed will take a week worth of dailies to achieve, but by then you egg would have been expired for 6-days by the tiem you have what you need.  -- Here lies that 'forced' feeling to spend additional money for sake of making the most of a 'lucky' drop.

"Limbo", a game from Denmark, takes you - a small boy - through a dark, nearly liveless world where you need your wits and logic to survive.
Surely this is one of those games that can call themselves art. And it's unlike most of the games: It contains no colours (outside of black, white and grey), no dialogues, hardly any music and you are also not told what's the actual story you're going through (even the game's marketing has little to say about it). It's a game ruled by pure atmosphere. At first it does seem to be at least a peaceful world but the game will take you deeper and deeper into grim and violent dimensions as you need to solve puzzles around problems in order not only to go further but also to survive. And you'll need all your wits since the main character has not the greatest jumping skills or any tools or weapons. And the game can be tricky as hell to you, especially near the end.
Last but not least: The gameplay. It's pretty easy to control. You need nothing more than the arrow keys and one key for operating stuff like pushing/pulling levers or grabbing crates to pull.
If you're into solving puzzles then this is your game. If you love games full of beauty and atmosphere then this is your game, too.

Pox Nora struggled through a long and arduous phase of being owned and subsequently undervalued by Sony Online Entertainment. A menagerie of bugs and balancing changes would go unresolved for months, it was extremely difficult to break into the game as a new player, and the the game had a distinct pay-to-win model unless a player was savvy enough to take advantage of third party resources like PoxBox and the like.
And then it all changed.
No, the fire nation didn't attack, Desert Owl Games came to be, and took over PoxNora for the better (far, far better). With the advent of DOG's game revamp, the entire collection of more than 1,300 cards were redesigned and retuned, the maps were uppdated, mechanics and the engine were retuned, the player rewards system was completely reinvented, and the free-to-play model was resdesigned to eliminate the necessity to spend money.
Now, it is extremely easy for new accounts to break into the game, receiving dramatically more gold per day from new challenges in addition to the daily skirmish, a new, highly expanded and more rewarding tutorial system has been implemented, a new skirmish mode has been implemented that dishes out free runes, and now all runes are available for purchase with gold rather than cash with the exception of the most recently released expansion pack.
The revamp is still in swing and changes still need to be made, but Desert Owl Games are really putting effort into making PoxNora a good game again, and are very public and open with the changes they make. They have implemented a new player council to aid them in development and provide an officiated voice for the players, and are just generally cool dudes.
Whether you're brand new or you long abandoned the game, this shiny new construction is definitely worth giving Pox a chance.

Performance-wise, the game is a joke.  Frame rate frequently drops into the gutter for no reason, sound ends up out of synch with what's happening on-screen.  It's a godawful mess and screams of a rushed product.

Tropico 5 is a strange experience. In many ways it is better than its predecessors but yet in other respects worst - especially without the DLC of the previous games. One of the key issues with the game is that it doesn't feel as though the game has really changed the formula all that much... Yes they've added some "eras" but frankly they add little to the game - all that changes from era to era is the ability to access a few new buildings and appease a new set of world powers.
It just feels as though Tropico 5 is being sold on the basis of being "revolutionary" and "game-changing" when all it is in my opinion is a prettified version of Tropico 4 with a few nifty features thrown in (arguably this is not a bad thing...but let me explain) - such features are the trade, research and constitution. While these features are good I feel as though didn't get implemented or used to their full potential. For example the constituion in my opinion needs more options; there also needs to be a greater variety of tech and research options (at the momment its just a load of icons that have to be pressed in more or less a set order to progress) and lastly the trade feature I believe would be better if it gave you the freedom to import as much as you like (assuming you had the necessary funds, rather than having to use up your export ships).
Additionally another area I would really like to see improved is the variety of buildings - both in terms of style and new buildings, undoubtedly these will be added as part of DLC but it would have been nice to have more from the initial release. For example a greater range of housing options, restaurants, government buildings and public services would help make towns feel less duplicated as it doesn't take long to exhaust all of the construction options.
Despite these gripes Tropico 5 does have several great features, namely the graphics and overall design do really make the enviroment look like a real "Tropico"-al Island and the models are all very well detailed too. Plus the economy and government approval system also feel more realistic and fluid. Quests are also varied and interesting which ensures a steady stream of tasks and rewards - these actually make you feel more engaged with the outside world.
Another feature of the game that is core to Tropico 5 is the multiplayer aspect but as I haven't really played it enough I have decided to not comment on this feature.
Generally speaking Tropico 5 is a great game and for any fan of the series it is certainly a must buy, but that being said I do feel as though it's not as "revolutionary" as they appear to make out - it is simply the great Tropico series you have known and loved but back and better than ever...

As far as horror games go this is easily one of the more enjoyable in my opinion. There clearly was time well spent developing the story and gameplay and anyone who enjoys being startled, scared, or flatout frightened sometimes should give Outlast a go.
The good
-The storyline kinda grabs hold of you right away in more ways than one. (The history of the building, why everyone lost, and why the character you are playing as chose to cover this story in the first place
- The graphics arent horrible. On the games highest settings I thought that the game looked quite nice. It is a rather dark game so the textures might not look as good in rooms with a lot of lighting but the developers had to prioritize where they wanted to put their efforts and I was impressed overall.
- The nightvision aspect when using your camera (the only item you can wield) looks the way it does in real life. I was very impressed with this portion of the game.
-The suspense... Oh the suspense. And stress and the peace you will be making with whatever god you align with because sometimes you dont know if you will make it out alive even though the whole time you know IT IS JUST A GAME...
-The controls. It is really a very simple game when it comes to controls which puts a higher importance on this portion of the game because there is much less you can get wrong which makes any mistake much more noticable and I think they nailed the controls.
The not so good
-The chases can get somewhat repetitive at times. I know that you cant really do tons with a game that relies solely on running whenever an antagonist is spotted but its a little too much sometimes. Just running A LOT!
-There are gaps in the game when you dont get a lot of story. It is again just running with no real emphasis on what I believe is this games biggest selling point and that is the story.
-Some of your enemis in this game have almost zero detail put into their textures. While in an excellently crafted room your eyes are distracted by a fairly ugly individual and I am directly mentioning the coding here.
-Sometimes the interactive furniture and objects around you are very inconvenient. Imagine trying to run and as you cut a corner the game forces you underneath a bed which you had no idea existed until you are being forced to crawl into "hiding" while being chased and in clear view of your hunter. Now I know this could just be poor game mechanics on my part however not everyone is going to be a god at this game so they might have similar issues and this issue could have been addressed in development.
After all things considered I REALLY enjoy Outlast. I would recommend it again and again to anyone who likes playing games within this genre.

Yes, it's finally out, and it is glorious.
PROS:
+Probably the most beautiful handdrawn animation I've seen in games since Skullgirls.
+Widely varied bosses with a multitude of phases and attacks, leading to fullscreen chaos.
+Incredible jazzy soundtrack; buy it with the game.
+That Soulsborne-esque rush of finally triumphing over a particular challenge.
+I'm not a fan of control schemes where movement and aiming are bound to the same stick, with a button that holds you in place so you can precision aim; but I feel Cuphead pulls it off with a smaller screen, since it's easier to see things coming and know when it's time to move.
CONS:
-This is more of a warning than a dislike on my part, but this game is HARD. REALLY HARD. The early bosses alone could take several attempts, even on Simple difficulty - and you'll need to beat them on Regular difficulty to proceed through the game.
-Parry-Slapping feels a little bit finicky. I might be messing it up, but there will be times I'm mashing Jump when about to hit a pink object, but still take damage for some reason. The Automatic-Parry Charm became practically mandatory for me.
-The Run-and-Gun levels aren't all that fun, but you need to do them to get most of the game's coins so you can buy new powers.
-The Chaser bullets tend to home in on less-than-ideal targets; one boss shoots projectiles that shoot MORE projectiles when shot, so of course my Chasers would repeatedly home in on those instead of the boss.
-I wish the boss's health pool was on screen rather than only visible in a game over screen, so I can get a better idea of my progress than just getting different phases. On the other hand, seeing the boss at a sliver of health may cause you to throw caution to the wind and end up dying, leading to more frustration.
-Use a controller. (Also, if you're using a PS4 Controller, turn off DS4Windows; in my experience, it made my whole computer freeze up for about 30 seconds when I started or closed the game, or open the Steam Dashboard. The game has native PS4 Controller support anyway.)
BOTTOM LINE: Get ready for a beautiful, charming, fun, BRUTAL adventure. And bring a friend, because misery loves company.

As a fan of golden era animation in all of its surreal, (and generally unfortunate) politically incorrect glory, discovering
was a bit of a revelation; the game I never knew I wanted.
And it's a masterpiece, or damn close to being one.
Aesthetically,
is on point, the culminating artistry of pie-eyed cel animation, watercolor backdrops, technicolor saturation, natural film filter and swinging jazz soundtrack an honest work of love. Bad puns and surrealist slapstick seal the deal.
Controls... perfect. Cuphead -- our titular protagonist -- is weighted just right, every button press instant; effortless, something countless modern platformers fail to ever get right. That said, parrying certain objects or enemies can be unusually frustrating in comparison (i.e. the rolling ladybugs on "Treetop Trouble").
is boss-centric at its core. While some games fail to provide enough variety in that format, this one does not; from visual design to shuffling phases, every boss fight feels fresh, and platforming stages scattered between further prevent any potential burnout. The same cannot be said for the horizontal shoot 'em stages; their rarity leaves them feeling out place, and the plane itself is honestly too sluggish for the amount of projectile avoidance required. Doable? Yes, but I dread them every time, pretty like the rest of the game as they may be.
Despite this, the challenge level throughout is wonderfully consistent; a hard game, but for the right reasons. Every stage pushes you to a new degree of twitch skill multitasking, but never do they feel impossible, even past the halfway mark where I currently sit.
There's a scoring system present, but as with most games that try to rate player performance over a simple, number-based tally, it's incredibly arbitrary; a stage I feel I did well on nets me a C, but one where I made an♥♥♥♥♥of myself? B+ or higher. Frankly with a game like
, the only accomplishment that matters to me is making it to the end while having fun along the way.
Local co-op only is also a letdown, especially in 2017. Not everyone is fortunate enough to have their friends close by. This includes myself.
But when your game is near-exemplary, a few missteps hardly detract from the overall picture, and that's where
stands: a work of interactive art worthy of praise despite imperfection.

I found a trapper's cabin that could provide shelter, and allow me to rest and not freeze.  I rested, repaired what gear I could, and stayed as long as I could.  Food was becoming scarce though. I needed to forage, so I had to leave.  This would be a good home base though; as long as I could find food, I think I could survive.
I left my cabin, and plunged into the cold.  I scavenged sticks as I could, as I knew I would need the warmth.  I found very little food.  I started to freeze, but I pushed on looking.  Without food I would die.  I was down to my last MRE.
Much to my bad luck, a storm came on.  The world was white out and I lost my bearings.  I stumbled through the storm hopnig to find some respite somewhere.  I was starting to freeze, and hypothermia was kicking in.  I saw a large rock outcropping up ahead, and found a spot in the lee protected from the wind, that allowed me a spot to start a fire.  I could rest here, and warm up and press on later when the storm broke.  I lit my fire, and sat down to warm up.  I was starting to starve.  I had to eat my MRE, but it was much needed calories.  My stomach full, and finally warm, I got comfomtable.
Until the wind changed direction and blew my fire out.  Damn!
Out into the storm I stumbled, and pushed into the wind.  I was out of tinder, so another fire was out of the question.  Pushing on, there was nothing I could do but begin to freeze.
On I pushed into the whiteout, hoping that I could find someplace to offer shelter.  And lo, ahead I spied a famliar rock formation.  Coming around the corner, I could see the trapper's cabin!  I stumbled forward, hypothermia almost taking me.  I mangaged to make it to the cabin, get inside and stumble into bed to sleep and try to get warm.  I died from hunger in my sleep.
I would die from hunger again in my sleep.  10/10

I bought this game about a year ago during the peak of the (unfortunate) zombie/crafting survival horror genre. It looked like it had a lot of the elements I found interesting in those games without the ridiculous premise and overbearing concept of zombies, so naturally I was intrigued. I played it for an hour and thought it was mediocre. A week or so ago I had seen that they had made some updates so I figured I would give it another shot and see what had changed. This game has improved by leaps and bounds. I'm very impressed and eager to see how good it will be when it launches.
Remember when Fallout: New Vegas added Hardcore Mode where you had to eat and drink regularly or succumb to the desert environment? It was a cool idea, but was very poorly executed and went from a sideshow feature to a completely ignored nuisance you had to handle every few hours as the game progressed. The focus was never on the survival, at the end of the day it was still Fallout. This game uses that same concept but absolutely nails it. It's the best take on survival I've played.
The enemies of the game are just animals with slightly more aggressive tendencies than their real-life counterparts, yet they still tend to be more threatening and scary than any zombies I've seen in games in the past 10 years. And the real threats of the game, starvation and the cold, easily outdo the wildlife. They keep you on your feet and provide just the right amount of persistent danger at all stages of the game where they are always something you have to keep in mind without going so far as to make you feel powerless against them. The atmosphere does a great job of reminding you that your death may be lurking right around the corner, while simultaneously making you feel genuinely proud of small accomplishments that make you slightly more safe and secure.
This is where the game really shines. It balances narrowly at just the right difficulty to make it challenging and rewarding, and there is a ton of depth beneath the surface that you can learn as you go along. I hesistate to use the word realism, but most of these less obvious mechanics are reasonable, such as wind direction affecting the range wolves detect you, where to position your emergency fire in a blizzard to ensure it doesn't get blown out, and smart locations to camp outside when you are forced to.
The replayability is surprisingly good. There are a lot of possible starting locations and the equipment you start with and find is different in every game, even if it's the same map location. There are a lot of roads you can take and the beginning of the game feels almost entirely different each time for the first few tries.
Story mode is promised in the future and it has a really solid foundation to work from. I expect it to be very good after what I've seen here and will definitely play it as soon as it's available.
- The graphics really aren't that great.
The models are low poly, the textures that aren't hand-drawn (which are ok) leave something to be desired, the animations for the animals are clunky, and there are virtually no effects apart from the weather (which actually looks fantastic), such as lighting and shadows. While they're also not awful, and the problems rarely really impact the gameplay,  they seem more fitting to a game made a decade ago and don't meet much of today's standards. Not a particularly strong point to the game, which is unfortunate, because the environment is so important. Some screenshots to highlight:
- There's not much to do.
As of right now there's only sandbox so it's expected to some degree. Still, the amount of upgrades and development you can go through are fairly limited later on, despite the early game being well-varied. Some achievements are clever and put an interesting spin on things, but it's still a very sandboxy sandbox and you're going to feel sooner or later like the only thing you're doing is surviving to survive, not progressing towards a goal.
- Be ready to walk.
No, not run. And basically everywhere you go, unless you're escaping a blizzard or rabid wildlife. Personally I consider this one of the game's strengths. It pulls off very well the idea of managing energy, calories, and what you should carry with you to maximize your probability of living until tomorrow. That said, it requires a lot of patience and being able to enjoy the "journey" and not just the destination. It's not tedious to me, but whether it would be for you is something to ask yourself before you buy.
It's original, fresh, and challenging. I'm having a lot of fun playing it. If it's your kind of game, it's excellent. If it's not your kind of game, there's a possibility it might be a little boring. It is fairly priced though, so if you're on the fence, I definitely recommend it.

I still prefer Sierra's 1994 game Lode Runner: The Legend Returns. It had bombs and other tools, and teleporters. It made the levels more interesting and puzzle more elaborate than simply figuring out which blocks to zap in what order. Also had different worlds with different aesthetics.
I would recommend this game if you want a voxel-based iteration of basic Lode Runner. It will likely give you short spurts of fun. I don't think this game can be played for long periods of time and remain fun.
There is a 50 level adventure mode, 50 level puzzle mode (with leaderboards), and you can play player-made levels. The player made levels will probably be the source of most fun. I am disappointed with the lack of bombs, such as were in the Sierra version of the game, and how deaths look in general. Dying is almost like in Super Mario where he has a "ouch" frame before the screen cuts out, but that "ouch" frame is the only thing you get, nothing else. The death animation in this game feels like they took the lazy route.
For pricing, I would not have gotten the game at the current price of $15.99 if I knew bombs weren't in the game. With the perceived level of content I see, I would pay between $5 to $8.
If you can get the 1994 Sierra Lode Runner: The Legend Returns, I would personally stick with that one, as I feel there is more to enjoy there. If you want leaderboards and simple gameplay with a little puzzling challenge (but not as much as it could have been) then feel free to pick this up.

I'm a newbie for this game having purchased it some time ago and leaving it in my pile of unplayed games.
I'm glad I did dust it off though!
The game is a challenge to play. As you have to manage the effects of cold, thirst, hunger and fatigue.
A few times I've had to hole up in a cabin and wait to get over hypothermia.
The longest I have managed to survive is 8 1/2 days and it was a shame I died I went fishing and set myself up for 5 hours of fishing. During this time I caught Hypothermia and faded into the Long Dark. I didn't see a way to cancel the fishing as I could have aborted the fishing and returned back to camp but perhaps I missed something somewhere. This is a niggle that I hope either I simply missed or will be added in an update.
The graphics are great they are well drawn hand help to really convey the sense of loneliness and the cold. The sound is excellent too and I seem to get a good frame rate on my old laptop. Although there are strange sounds that sound like they are emanating from my body as I walk around. Often I think it's wildlife and have a good look around.
There are some nice touches in the interaction between the wildlife such as I noticed on my final day where I observed a wolf patrolling the lake and then saw it take off chasing after a deer in the middle of the lake the deer ran off and tried to evade the wolf but was eventually taken down. Touches like this give the game a real sense of atmosphere.
Overall it's a great game with no hand-holding so it's tough at first to learn the ropes. I had to use one of the great guides in the steam community to learn some real basic stuff that I completely missed how to do. It makes a refreshing change as there are no zombies! Just you the cold and the wolves. I find that although the first map is small there is plenty to do and it is comforting after you've died for the umpteenth time where things are.
Thumbs up to Hinterland for making an engrossing game.  I'm hoping to make it to 10 days on my next go!

Call me late to the party, by about seven years, but Bioshock is a perfect example of all that is good in gaming and stands tall as one of the greatest games of human history.
Coming into the game with the mindset of someone who played and loved Bioshock Infinite, I set my mind back to 2007 when the game was released: Measuring it up to the standards back then, the result? I was completely blown away.
Bioshock was ahead of it's time with amazing graphics, fluid gameplay, immersive environments and a story that left me on the edge of my seat in anticipation.
Taking the role of Jack, a silent protagonist you venture deeper and deeper into the eery and unsettling depths of the underwater city of Rapture, radio contact directs you to your goals and you can find audiographs to learn more about the history of such an incredible city. The environments feel isolated, making the player feel trapped and uncomfortable and sets up for a terrifying setting where you square down with the mutated and insane denizens still roaming the submerged streets.  The balance between environment and story are so perfectly intuned that it is easy to lose yourself in the setting and be completely immersed in the story, sinking hours at a time into unlocking the secrets this modern Atlantis leaves to find, building up to one of the most shocking twists you will ever experience. The story, lore and setting of the entire game is incredible, and when you finish playing through the game I highly recommend going online and reading up more, because the history of Rapture is so well written that I can spend days scratching around to find every little tidbit of information.
To defend yourself you are given a large arsenal of firearms and Plasmids (genetic modification tonics that alter your very DNA and give you powerful abilities) that you can use in many ways: Set up traps and take advantage of the environment to maximize the damage potential of plasmids, or you can use your guns to plow through your foes in a very satisfying way, as each and every firearm has a good feel to it and carries a wonderful punch. As you progress in the game, enemies get tougher and tougher, requiring more firepower to take them out. Throughout the game you can collect and combine upgrades to your weapons giving them more damage output as well as numerous other bonuses such as recoil reduction or firing rate (at the same time giving your weapon a visible upgrade, making them look absurdly bad♥♥♥♥♥, as well as gene tonics that you use to give yourself powerful buffs to your combat and hacking expertise.
The level design is flawless, being understandable but far from straightforward; offering plenty of opportunites to explore and loot, finding every little scrap of ammo and utilities to give yourself as much of an advantage as possible.
Now I have to apologize, but there is one part about Bioshock that wasn't perfect and if I can say so safely: was bad. I'M SORRY I'M SORRY I DON'T WANT TO SAY IT BUT I FEEL I NEED TO POINT THIS OUT.
So be advised, mild spoiler alert: Skip this paragraph over if you do not wish to have spoilers.
In the later stages of the game you partake in (ugh) an escort mission. One of the types of missions that gamers almost universally despise on a molecular level. The objective is to guide a little girl through a splicer infested area and protect the little rat because she's the only one who can open the doors for you. Now the flaws with this is that throughout the game up to this point you set the pace yourself, you moved, fought and explored as you saw fit, because this was your experience and you experienced it as you wanted: Then this little bedwetter waddles in and sets the pace for you, robbing you of your control  as she struts thoughtlessly into automated turrets and other dangers. But the worst part is that the nosepicker is just about one of the most annoying characters I've ever seen: She repeats the same small handful of dialogue over and over without end, and practically NEVER SHUTS UP. I honestly wanted to shoot her myself, but I seemingly needed her to open the doors for me, to which I wanted to physically pick her up and use her as a battering ram.
This portion, although short-lived, felt so far out of place and was a blemish on an otherwise perfect game.
Finally, Bioshock was built on an outdated engine, which results in some game-breaking issues as a result of incompatabilites with modern technology, such as inconsistent mouse sensitivity and flat-out broken audio. To which I refer you to these guides on Steam that have both solved these issues:
Mouse sensitivity -
Audio fix -
With thanks to the creators for their help, without them I would have never been able to experience this beautiful game.
So in conclusion: Bioshock is a great experience that has triumphed over the test of time, with an atmosphere, gameplay and story that has earned it critical praise. I do not only recommend Bioshock, I worship Bioshock as a shining beacon to all that is good in gaming.

The Steam version of this software was a buggy and unplayable pile of crap, though I did end up downloading the game off of the Desert Owl website. That works. Let's talk about the game itself.
PoxNora is a deliciously complex game that has been made more accessible by the ability to pick up cards from the core sets just for playing. It's easily the crunchiest game I've ever played, and I typically find my turns running out because I'm READING the six or seven abilities each character has.
This is a GOOD thing.
Currently, however, the game is critically flawed from bad rules language and hard counter design. Here are some examples.
1 - There is a race of squid people (think mind flayers) who fling passive psychic damage across the map. Though this psychic damage is ranged, abilities that reduce damage from creatures of a small size do not reduce, abilities that counterattack when an ally is shot at range are not triggered, yet abilities that amplify psychic damage function properly. I spent an hour fighting these "damage every turn" pings, ended up beating them, but still understood nothing about them beyond "they have a range of 6 and do damage to me". It was frustrating and the 50-60 words about them on the tooltip was nowhere near enough.
2 - Block and dodge state one range, but show another. This is seen all over the place.
3 - Some maps hard counter certain decks, and map selection is totally random. Do you not have a fast flyer and the other guy does? Awesome, you have a disadvantage on round 0. There are two maps that will utterly crush you in this manner, and it's simply not fun to have to design decks around them because they, like certain OP cards, MIGHT show up. In a game with as little RNG as PoxNora, the fact that the game can be decided before the first card play by the MAP selection is a slap in the face.
4 - Hard counters. If something is OP, they're more likely to make an OP response than nerf it. (Summons and summons-killing) This reduces variety and player interaction considerably.
5 - Inconsistent rules. Let's say you magic up an enemy to be unable to attack for a turn. If it's an archer with rain of arrows, that works. If it's a pirate tortoise who can call in an AoE artillery barrage, it doesn't. What makes cannonballs so different from arrows? I'm not sure, but the rules certainly treat gunpowder as "not an attack".
If you can get around these sorts of issues, and the resulting barrier to entry, the game's quite fun. I won two newbie tournaments in a row, and felt I was doing quite well. That being said, the bad design kept coming back to smack me on the head once, maybe twice a day, and it seems every time I ended up losing, it was because the game did something contrary to what the cards said they were going to do, like the aforementioned turtle pirate artillery barrage. As I design games for a living, this really, really upset me, and leads me to believe that there's really not somebody proofreading their work.
And, honestly, who wants to support somebody who builds something that complex, then ignores proper documentation?

Like, I would assume, most people who bought this game, I picked this up as kind of a joke purchase. I thought it'd be something I maybe fired up for ten minutes and then dropped; something I could mention off-hand to the guys at work who think it's hilarious that I have played more than 50 hours of Euro Truck Simulator. However, it was surprisingly engaging - my first 40 minute session felt like a third of that and I only stopped as I was interrupted, and to my surprise I've since returned to the game.
It's a fairly straightforward management game, but so far seems well-balanced, introducing mechanics over time and neither too challenging to feel like good results are attainable, nor so easy that you feel like you're just coasting.
The basic mechanic is building up your building to build up your business (a la Unholy Heights), combined with a very rough sort of worker management - you can hire and fire staff, assign rooms full of them to accounts, educate them and essentially add modifiers to their mood/productivity etc. by hiring other staff. There are a variety of roles covered, so balancing the ratios is the part of the game you'll have to think about the most.
Full disclosure, you will spend a fair bit of time just waiting - I presume that will be reduced as the game progresses and you start earning more money, but I've reached a slightly uneventful plateau where I just have to wait a couple of days to add a new building, and that's a little tiresome even on the highest speed.
I like the art style - it's nothing novel, but it's well executed, and you should be able to see at a glance whether the visuals are for you.
The music is a little cheesy, but I guess that's to be expected from a game about a call centre.
Overall, I'd recommend this as a cheap purchase (I got it in a bundle), but this price seems pretty fair anyway. Don't buy it expecting an immersive cinematic experience, but for the money, it's pretty good.

Limbo is a beautiful, atmospheric puzzle platformer with a hard edge. What story it has is largely implicit—the game contains no dialogue. You simply wake in a dark wood, apparently a child, and set off to explore the dingy place in which you find yourself. But the genre of the game is certainly horror, though without most of the usual tropes. You are fragile—easily hurt, unable to swim, essentially defenseless—in a hostile and trap-ridden place. You will die many times. And the game does not divert your gaze from your death but rather renders each different mode of your demise in somewhat disturbing detail.
The artistic style of the game simultaneously keeps this from being too macabre and contributes greatly to the eerie atmosphere. The game's graphics are entirely silhouettes in shades of grey. Yet the landscapes and objects feel very detailed. Beautifully done lighting effects give the impression of a layered world mostly in shadow. All this makes for a beautiful noir environment well worth admiration in its own right. This game is more immersive with black and white outlines than much I’ve played that had expensive 3D-graphics.
A subtler strength of the game is the way its physics feel naturalistic—you are acutely aware of the weight of objects and the force of gravity.  I doubt that the game’s engine is particularly remarkable in this regard, it’s an aesthetic effect. Great attention has been paid to the visual details of motion. But I think it also comes from player movement: in many games you play as a character with outsized physical capabilities. Even in shooters and platformers where such isn’t part of the story your movements are subtly superhuman (think of the lateral jumping featured in most platformers). Not here. Here you have a painfully tiny lateral jump and a rather slow top speed. Here objects don’t just slide easily into place but are dragged only with great effort.
The largest complaint I had with LIMBO was that it was too short. Though the puzzles were good, and admirably varied, not too many were very difficult. If one is adept at this sort of thing one could easily complete the game in just a few hours. They are an excellent few hours though. The puzzles are crisp, things to be grasped, not just fiddled with. For a little while LIMBO takes you to an unsettling, engrossing otherworld. And I’d very much like to visit again.

Now for the actual review.
Regardless of any technical issues, this game is a truly underrated multiplayer experience. It is a beautiful perspective that can put you first person inside of a tank when an explosion hits, and you look around to find your commander missing. You later discover that your commanding officer's leg is now sitting in your lap, and realize the task that you must now complete while down a man. You may be traveling through the trenches only to have your buddy get his head ripped apart by a sniper round, while the lower body of your team's sniper flies right past you. Sure there are some glitches and bugs, but this game is truly different from any other fps in that you feel as if you're actually in the action, losing your friends to snipers and grenades.
"When your squad falls around you, it's up to you to hold that position until reinforcements arrive. It doesn't matter how many times you've been hit, what percentage of your friend's body is intact, or how many men are trying to kill you. It's when you see dwindling numbers on your team's resupply that you realize how many men have died for you, and so you better do them proud. But when the count reaches zero, it's time to make your final stand."
-Lt. Woofel, Squad Leader One, Red Army

For anyone who wants to read a story about a valient battle and sacrifice, keep going. I'm just going to rant on about how much fun I've had with this game.
Our Russian army had decided to take the Bridges of Druzhnia (I think thats spelled right) against an overwhelmeng German force. The initial assault on A and B lasted nearly fourteen minutes and cost us nearly 150 reinforcements. Further attacks up past D and E cost us an additional hundred. Fueled by our losses, my Squad headed the assault on G, when the roar of The Buzzsaw was heard from the upstairs window. Rushing forward, we made it to the wall but at the cost of six good men. I sent my men on a dual flank before tossing a grenade through the upstairs window, watching as the LMG fell from the window followed by a grey-sleeved arm. Our Commander linked up with our group and commended us for our actions, before pushing us onward. The success of our assault with minimal casualties earned us a feared reputation and a simple, yet accurate nickname: Alpha Squad.
At this time, we quickly rushed our assault forward and knocked out the next positions with ease, until we came to the final bridge, section N. Fifteen minutes remained on the clock, and only a hundred of our reinforcements were still alive. We recieved an order from our commanding officer to halt, and recieved the most motivational speech of all time, as we prepared to fight against all odds. Once all of our teams were strategically placed, we recieved the final order to charge the position from three sides.
The following events took place over approximately ninety seconds:
Our original plan failed catastrophically. Our initial force was obliterated within seconds by the enemy artillery and machine guns. Two unnamed members of Alpha Squad plus myself and our MG moved underneath the bridge to hit with a surprise attack so that our engineer could take out the tank traps. The enemy fire was too intense however, so our engineer only had time to deploy the charges before a Buzzsaw across the river cut him down. During this time, our sniper and commander were to be located on our side of the bridge, laying down cover fire, but they were no match for the German beast and were forced to get into cover. The other four members of my squad were not so lucky, as they had just seen the flash before it ripped them to pieces.
While the suppressing group was pinned and taking heavy fire, the Germans brought their Antitank rifles out to take down our T34. However, my smoke grenade had impaired their ability to properly aim, and so fortunatley most of the shots missed the tank. However, the sniper was hit by one of these stray rounds - his body was only partially recovered. I felt tremendous guilt over the loss of a friend, but continued to push onward.
Our CO got right up in the action, using the tank as moving cover while he laid down fire with his PPSH. When that was empty, he simply tossed it to the side and pulled out his revolver. After being hit and bandaged three times; a shot to the right arm, one in the leg and another in the stomach; he was on the verge of dying. In his love for the mother country, he pulled out a grenade and rushed forward, taking two more Germans with him.
Our MG gunner used the distraction to set his position and took out seven Germans, including their Commanding Officer before a grenade landed just behind him. The explosion took off both of his legs and killed him outright, along with the other two soldiers that were coming up behind us. The blast also crippled my left arm, and in a fit of rage over my dying comrades, I didn't bother to bandage it. Being the final surviving member of the most elite fighters on the Eastern Front, I rushed forward with my PPSH, fully loaded with 71 rounds. It was my job to make sure that the tank made it to the final position, regardless of the cost. While firing at the exposed Germans, a sniper caught me in the chest with a single shot, which I immediatly knew would be fatal. The screen slowly faded to black, but my final breaths would not go silently. I died with my finger still squeezing the trigger, finishing off two more jackboots that tried to stop our desperate assault. Our sacrifice was minimal compared to the 800 Russians that were lost in the assault, but it had allowed enough time for our final remaining men to capture the position and win the game.

is not quite as good of a Tropico game as it's predecessors, however, it is a better city-builder. Tropico still maintains much of it's comedy and charm but, unfortunately, something feels like it is missing since Tropico 4.
The new interface leaves much to be desired as much of the information that El Presidente's are used to is now either buried or missing. Want to know which buildings are profitable and full? Too bad. Want to know where the oil is? Use a magnifying glass! The lack of a Tropico 4 style interface leaves much to be desired and makes it difficult to get the information you need.
It also seems that with the addition of the new interface we've also lost the fun faction interaction that we've come to expect. They do still exist but they've essentially taken a back seat to everything and are much harder to find with much fewer missions.
The addition of the new dynasty system is pretty cool. Your new family members offer you some nice bonuses, more benefits, and you can use them as new 'managers' which help you run buildings better. You can even send them on fun little missions and storyline quests for more bonuses. However, with the addition of these new folks you also lose direct control of El Presidente himself. You can no longer tell him where to go, who to visit, and what store to promote. I used to LOVE that feature from Tropico 4 and it helped pass the time and improve production. Now all El Presidente does is wonder around like an NPC. Furthermore, you also have a lot less options in character creation when it comes to El Presidente and can no longer pick from a vast number of backgrounds, histories, bonuses, and penalties; now you pick ONE bonus and that's it.
As I said, Tropico 5 is likely the best city builder of the series. The addition of the new grid or city layout system makes placing and organizing structures MUCH easier. Due to the new era system you also have building that grow and change as time passes. Farms, for example, get nice upgrades and then can be transformed into Hydroponic Farms which are much smaller and more efficient.
Overall, I have been enjoying Tropico as a good city builder but I often miss the micromanagement, humor, and the style of Tropico 4. Everyone expects at least a dozen DLCs (ten confirmed so far) and I hope that future patches improve Tropico 5 back up to Tropico 4's level.

I've been a fan of the series since Tropico 3. Tropico 3 and 4 are roughly similar, with Tropico 4 adding more content. They're wonderful games, and I hightly recommend them. On the other hand, tropico 5 has had a serious overhall. There are some similarities, but the whole feel of the game is very different for me (other reviewers disagree). Here's a quick overview of the differences between Tropico 4 and Tropico 5:
-First and foremost, this game is HARD! The previous Tropico's were a piece of cake. You could easily win an election 85% for you 15% against (on average, without trying). In Tropico 5, if the people love you, you're usually riding around 65% for 35% against if they love you. Usually it's more 50%/50%, to a lot less. Electrion fraud is often a necessity, and even then it won't guarentee a victory. With rebel attacks, uprisings, and invasions... there's no "you get one to two chances before you lose" deal. If you can't repel them, they'll burn down your palace, and you'll lose the game.
-Tropico 5's timeline is more well developed than Tropico 4. Tropico 5 no longer keeps track of the actual year (AD) but rather the Dynasty's time in office. You begin in Colonial times, and progress through WW2, the Cold War, and Modern times. Just like in Tropico 4's expansion "Modern Times", buildings and edits become unlocked as you progress through the eras. However, you don't progress through the eras just by letting the time pass. Certain objectives need to be met.
-The Blueprints from Tropico 4 are non-existant. Instead it's been replaced by a research system. You need to build a library, hire researchers, etc. You get to choose which research (edits, upgrades, buildings).
-The international relations has been completely redone. Other nations/pirates/etc can invade. In tropico 4, an invasion by a world super power means you lose the game. In Tropico 5, your army is pitted against the invader's army. You're also able to establish trade roots between you, and other nations/pirates. This will either increase or decrease your relations with certain parties, as well as offer more or less favorable prices for specific goods.
-Building managers are included, which can provide a specific benifit to the building.
-Instead of being able to control wages, you invest money into a specific building. This increases wages, job quality, etc.
-You have to pay to send out explorers to your island. Without this, you cannot discover new resources, or build beyond your prediscovered area. This is annoying, and I've read many complaints on this. But it's more realistic than Tropico 4.
-Building placement has been improved. Farms and ranches work within defined perameters, rather than having patches spring up near the farm wherever is best. Also, it's a lot easier to fit buildings closer together and make the most of your land.
-The graphics have been "updated". In my opinion, it's a bit of an eyesore compared to Tropico 4. With this graphic update, I've heard of people having issues with the graphics running at all on their machines. My computer is only two years old, and had the latest, top of the line graphics card when I bought it. Never even had a so much as a stutter playing any AAA title, and yet I had to turn down the graphics for this game to run smoothly.
There's also one major con I want to point out to those who are not familiar with Kalypso media. There will be between 5 to a dozen DLC ranging between $4-$6 that add minimal content and brush up the game. This is true for almost every game they've published since steam, and they're usually "patch update" quality. It's one of the things I dislike most about the company, and it is certainly this way with Tropico 5. You're not paying for the complete game. For that, I'd expect to chip out another $40 over the next few years.

As far as horror games go this is easily one of the more enjoyable in my opinion. There clearly was time well spent developing the story and gameplay and anyone who enjoys being startled, scared, or flatout frightened sometimes should give Outlast a go.
The good
-The storyline kinda grabs hold of you right away in more ways than one. (The history of the building, why everyone lost, and why the character you are playing as chose to cover this story in the first place
- The graphics arent horrible. On the games highest settings I thought that the game looked quite nice. It is a rather dark game so the textures might not look as good in rooms with a lot of lighting but the developers had to prioritize where they wanted to put their efforts and I was impressed overall.
- The nightvision aspect when using your camera (the only item you can wield) looks the way it does in real life. I was very impressed with this portion of the game.
-The suspense... Oh the suspense. And stress and the peace you will be making with whatever god you align with because sometimes you dont know if you will make it out alive even though the whole time you know IT IS JUST A GAME...
-The controls. It is really a very simple game when it comes to controls which puts a higher importance on this portion of the game because there is much less you can get wrong which makes any mistake much more noticable and I think they nailed the controls.
The not so good
-The chases can get somewhat repetitive at times. I know that you cant really do tons with a game that relies solely on running whenever an antagonist is spotted but its a little too much sometimes. Just running A LOT!
-There are gaps in the game when you dont get a lot of story. It is again just running with no real emphasis on what I believe is this games biggest selling point and that is the story.
-Some of your enemis in this game have almost zero detail put into their textures. While in an excellently crafted room your eyes are distracted by a fairly ugly individual and I am directly mentioning the coding here.
-Sometimes the interactive furniture and objects around you are very inconvenient. Imagine trying to run and as you cut a corner the game forces you underneath a bed which you had no idea existed until you are being forced to crawl into "hiding" while being chased and in clear view of your hunter. Now I know this could just be poor game mechanics on my part however not everyone is going to be a god at this game so they might have similar issues and this issue could have been addressed in development.
After all things considered I REALLY enjoy Outlast. I would recommend it again and again to anyone who likes playing games within this genre.

Blackwell Epiphany is a generally excellent final chapter for the Blackwell series. It runs longer than its predecessors, and features all the staple mechanics of the series: you have your Joey and your Rosa, you solve mysteries and save ghosts, and you engage in lots of conversations with a colourful cast of New Yorkers. What is noteworthy, however, is what the game *doesn't* contain; specifically, it doesn't really address the major cliffhanger set up at the end of Blackwell Deception, opting instead for an entirely different (and rather more cosmic) climax. There are also a few moments where the game just seems to "forget" about a character or a plot point, and a somewhat annoying "cheat" right at the game's final puzzle, where all of a sudden a staple mechanic from the series works a different way from how it always has. Those are minor annoyances, though, and overall the gameplay is smooth and engaging, and the dialogue is brilliant. The voicework by Rebecca Whittaker and Abe Goldfarb has come a *very* long way since Legacy, and is now quite good. Plotwise, there is one major twist that is far too obvious, but several surprises, and an ending that is probably not at all what you're expecting.
Overall, I'd give Blackwell Epiphany 4/5. It's quite a good game, but it seems to be perhaps a bit too ambitious; it's like there was too much stuff trying to cram its way in. Also, the setting gets rather high fantasy by the end, and I prefer the more down-to-earth setting of the first three games.

The world created by Bioshock is awesome and disturbing in equal measure. It is evident in the attention to detail that a lot of love has been lavished upon the creation of Rapture.
Despite the borderline cartoony graphics there were more than a few nappy filling moments and I found the splicers genuinely terrifying. This seems a common problem with FPS's though and I should acknowledge that this is a very old game at the time of review.

The fifth and final entry of the Blackwell series is both thought-provoking, intense and emotionally devastating.
Since this is the last part of the series, it's by far the longest - and it took me roughly ten hours to beat; which is about the length of two Blackwell games. I definitely recommend that fans who play this should do so with small breaks since there's a lot to take in. Literally all of the unanswered questions that have been bothering me - on top of Epiphany's plot, in addition - was crammed in and some bits may have flown over my head in the process.
Thankfully, the mysteries surrounding Joey and the Blackwell family are finally revealed and I was happy to get that closure.
Epiphany pulls out all the stops when it comes to drama, and I found myself feeling weary of what would happen to the majority of the characters - not just Joey and Rosa - which is great because that shows that the other characters are relatable and likable.
The story itself does a complete turnaround and you won't be expecting the culprit behind it all and the resulting ending!
I really enjoyed Epiphany, not quite as much as the others because of the depressing undertones and some of the events that unfold, but it's still a Blackwell game and it holds up to its predecessors.
The only complaint I have is that the events could have been spaced out a bit more so that it wasn't just one thing immediately after another - it felt overwhelming at times. Also, the ending wasn't favorable in my opinion but I suppose it fits.
Be sure to bring lots of tissues...

This game brings without a doubt the essence of the old bullet hell genre.

With 4 levels of difficulty you can go easy or normal to get ye ol' reflexes back in action, and/or go straight into the chaotic abyss that will soon be your colourful jellybean dodging, wrath indulging, existence at Hard or Hell difficulty, for that is where this jewel really shines.
"But my friends call me "Hawk eye quick scope McGee" in Cod, so It should be easy."
.......Oh boy you are in for a treat.
Undoubtedly the game is very unforgiving, and you will release a few screams in anger and a few keys from your keyboard will visit new and exotic places of your room via Angry-Fists airlines, but...after a few reassembly's you'll start to notice your sight getting sharper, less distracted on the shiny colours, and most important you'll improve that hand eye coordination that made anyone who threw you a ball burst into laughter at your bleeding nose.
Graphics are kept retro, as what Japanese games concern.
Story and dialogue are scarce at best but I think no one ever came for the bullets and stayed for the story, although the few dialogues will surely get a smile out of you.

Controls are as simple as one, two, three...no, really there are two buttons and movement.
And last but not least, it's FREE!
No hidden scams, just plain free!
I left that point for last for I don't like forgivingness on a game because it's free.
A game is a piece of art, and as such it must transmit the feeling of perfection on it's own terms.

-Variety of characters with different attack styles to fit everyone like a glove.
-Variety of difficulties from peaceful to "mouse to the wall!"
-Unforgiving.
-High replayability.
-Joystick compatible.
-FREE!
Final Score:
9/10 would destroy Joystick again.

It really feels like a Private Eye story at the end of the day. Conversation with the ghost is witty, and is part of the hint system. However, I have not used the hint system often, as it was clear what I had to do. The only point I was really stuck was when I have to pick up a key card I did not know it was there in all the filth.
Dialogues are good, and voice acting was up to that quality too. However, I would have prefered to have a voice with accent for the asian man you meet. Rosangela's actions are believable, as she is still a human.
