I've been a fan of the series since Tropico 3. Tropico 3 and 4 are roughly similar, with Tropico 4 adding more content. They're wonderful games, and I hightly recommend them. On the other hand, tropico 5 has had a serious overhall. There are some similarities, but the whole feel of the game is very different for me (other reviewers disagree). Here's a quick overview of the differences between Tropico 4 and Tropico 5:
-First and foremost, this game is HARD! The previous Tropico's were a piece of cake. You could easily win an election 85% for you 15% against (on average, without trying). In Tropico 5, if the people love you, you're usually riding around 65% for 35% against if they love you. Usually it's more 50%/50%, to a lot less. Electrion fraud is often a necessity, and even then it won't guarentee a victory. With rebel attacks, uprisings, and invasions... there's no "you get one to two chances before you lose" deal. If you can't repel them, they'll burn down your palace, and you'll lose the game.
-Tropico 5's timeline is more well developed than Tropico 4. Tropico 5 no longer keeps track of the actual year (AD) but rather the Dynasty's time in office. You begin in Colonial times, and progress through WW2, the Cold War, and Modern times. Just like in Tropico 4's expansion "Modern Times", buildings and edits become unlocked as you progress through the eras. However, you don't progress through the eras just by letting the time pass. Certain objectives need to be met.
-The Blueprints from Tropico 4 are non-existant. Instead it's been replaced by a research system. You need to build a library, hire researchers, etc. You get to choose which research (edits, upgrades, buildings).
-The international relations has been completely redone. Other nations/pirates/etc can invade. In tropico 4, an invasion by a world super power means you lose the game. In Tropico 5, your army is pitted against the invader's army. You're also able to establish trade roots between you, and other nations/pirates. This will either increase or decrease your relations with certain parties, as well as offer more or less favorable prices for specific goods.
-Building managers are included, which can provide a specific benifit to the building.
-Instead of being able to control wages, you invest money into a specific building. This increases wages, job quality, etc.
-You have to pay to send out explorers to your island. Without this, you cannot discover new resources, or build beyond your prediscovered area. This is annoying, and I've read many complaints on this. But it's more realistic than Tropico 4.
-Building placement has been improved. Farms and ranches work within defined perameters, rather than having patches spring up near the farm wherever is best. Also, it's a lot easier to fit buildings closer together and make the most of your land.
-The graphics have been "updated". In my opinion, it's a bit of an eyesore compared to Tropico 4. With this graphic update, I've heard of people having issues with the graphics running at all on their machines. My computer is only two years old, and had the latest, top of the line graphics card when I bought it. Never even had a so much as a stutter playing any AAA title, and yet I had to turn down the graphics for this game to run smoothly.
There's also one major con I want to point out to those who are not familiar with Kalypso media. There will be between 5 to a dozen DLC ranging between $4-$6 that add minimal content and brush up the game. This is true for almost every game they've published since steam, and they're usually "patch update" quality. It's one of the things I dislike most about the company, and it is certainly this way with Tropico 5. You're not paying for the complete game. For that, I'd expect to chip out another $40 over the next few years.

I found this game very enjoyable and exciting. Along with the constant fear of death looming over my shoulder(Which is realistically scary and easy), I've had some of the most intense survival scenerios fighting off endless waves of soldiers, in one desperate attmept to stay alive. Also this game has got to be one of the most realistic First Person World War II games to date; from the actual dates of historic battles, to even the fact of not having access to certain weapons during a time when they weren't yet in service.  Although you will occasionally find an NPC doing a number on a wall, and some simply standing at the deployment with no idea what to do, the NPCs can actually fight for a change, instead of the norm of having the players be the only ones to get any kills. As far as the visuals go, the team behind the game did an excellent job at depicting the weapons from the war. For example; In the Rising Storm version, the United States soldiers have access to the Colt M1911A1, which in very detailed texturing shows the realistic patents and inscription on the slide of the handgun. Overall I'd give this game an 8.5/10, seeing as my few complaints have to do with the PvP aspect of the game.
Conclusion; If you enjoy a good FPS game with lots of gunfire and guys running towards you with a katana, buy this game!

Outlast isn't really a game of skill, and as it turns out, that makes sense. You're not a cop or a soldier or a genetically enhanced superhero. You're just a reporter. And as a reporter, you don't possess many skills with which you can fend off the hulking brutes, knife-wielding stalkers, and other homicidal maniacs who lurk in the halls of the dilapidated Mount Massive Asylum. You can't shoot them, or punch them, or rip pipes from the walls to clobber them with. You can only run and hide. You're always in danger, and when that danger is nipping at your heels and all you can do is flee, desperately hoping to shake off your pursuer, Outlast is a terrifying roller-coaster ride. Unfortunately, the pacing stumbles in a few instances when Outlast stops coasting forward on its own momentum and requires you to go hunting for the track yourself, but these are small setbacks in what is usually a deeply unsettling experience.

SUPERHOT is a short, extremely immersive bullet-time shooter. Filled with innovative concepts, game mechanics, strategy and story features, SUPERHOT deserves to be a contender for 2016's indie game of the year.
Sitting in front of a DOS prompt, the player controls a fictional version of themselves and gets a message from a friend, offering to play a newly cracked virtual reality game called superhot.exe. After playing for a bit and claiming that there is "No plot, no reason for anything, just killing red guys," the player ends up getting caught; this is when the game begins to take control, and perspectives change.
The campaign is broken into several playable segments, separated by command prompt chat between the player and their friend/SUPERHOT console. Although SUPERHOT can be beat in one sitting (~2 hours), restarting the game will provide some interesting launch screen/interface changes.
The core gameplay of SUPERHOT focuses on forcing the player to run around and kill red guys; however, the unique difference between SUPERHOT and other traditional shooters is its “time moves when the player moves” mechanic. Success is attained in this game with careful planning and skillful use of the player’s time manipulation abilities.
When the player is fully stopped, time is slowed down almost to a standstill, but not quite. This adds a sense of pressure and forces the player to think and utilize strategy before making a move, all in a timely manner. Performing an action, such as shooting or throwing, will cause time to progress forward for a short moment. Moving the camera around does not incur a time boost.
The player can jump, shoot, throw, melee, disarm enemies, and pickup objects. An unlockable mechanic earned in the middle of the campaign adds another crucial aspect for survival (
). SUPERHOT utilizes various weapons, including: pistols, shotguns, machine guns, bats and katanas. There is limited ammo (with no conveniently placed ammo refills), so it is very important to count bullets, as firing with an empty magazine will incur a time boost. Any single type of injury will mean death to the player (punch, bullet, swing, etc.). There is no health bar or any form of health recovery. The same goes for the red guys, with the exception that it will require multiple punches to down an enemy.
As the story proceeds, the difficulty will progressively increase. There will be situations where the game will forcefully put the player in an extremely undesirable, surrounded, dangerous scenario. At times, it may be helpful to alter strategies: change targets, reposition the character, use a different weapon, weave through pillars vs. edge shooting, etc. Many enemies will be moving while they shoot, or run to reach a better vantage point. It’s imperative to learn how to lead the bullets, or allow the enemy to stop running, in order to progress through the game without too much difficulty. It is also possible to lure enemies into firing upon each other.
Although all red guys are the same (there are no tanks or bosses or enemies with unique abilities), gameplay is kept fresh with the change in weapon types that each enemy uses, or with a variance in position and environment. For instance, the player may be faced with a hallway full of continuously spawning shotgunners, or a stairwell of katana wielding vanguards and machine gun toting snipers.
SUPERHOT’s artwork is very minimalistic in essence. Throughout the campaign, an immersive, computerized virtual reality is created with the help of screen warping and command prompt interfaces. The game emphasizes white, red and black color palettes to detail the prioritized objects of interest. Although it might seem too basic at first, a lone red shape in the distance will soon seem terrifying. Gunshot animations are also provided, including a muzzle flash. The shatter mechanics, with regards to the animation and sound, are also beautifully satisfying - the shards will glow and fade into oblivion.
Launched near the end of February, SUPERHOT has achieved critical acclaim and garnered a relatively huge fan base. Multilingual support was added in April, and the Discussions board is still very active. With the SUPERHOT Team’s focus shifting towards developing SUPERHOT VR, the base game may begin to lose a bit of developer interest, however, the player count continues to rise.
Unfortunately, SUPERHOT does not seem to support VR gear. Instead of adding VR support to SUPERHOT, the developers are creating an entirely new game from the ground up with VR support – SUPERHOT VR. This decision seems to be mostly due to the fact that the team would have to rebuild SUPERHOT, and that simply adding VR is just not as feasible as they originally thought. The new SUPERHOT VR is designed to make the player physically live through SUPERHOT's action choreographies instead of merely creating them. Currently focused on an Oculus Rift premiere, there is possible support for other gear in the future (source: SUPERHOT Team's Tomasz Kaczmarczyk to Polygon). A newly revealed gameplay trailer for SUPERHOT VR was released at E3 a few days ago, shown below.
Even though SUPERHOT spreads itself through many different genres, it transcends expectation and earns a recommendation for any gamer willing to immerse themselves in a great story. Although it is rather short, the innovative gameplay and unlockable features provide enough content for an enjoyable experience. SUPERHOT IS THE MOST INNOVATIVE SHOOTER I'VE PLAYED IN YEARS!

Sunless Sea is a beautiful game with beautiful writing.  But make no mistake--it's *hard*.
When you get started, it's hard to make enough money to break even while you start to reveal the map. (Quickstart guides exist and are worth reading.)
Despite the game's insistence to the contrary, it's hard to recover from a character dying.   And I think the marketing isn't doing new players any favors by pushing the idea that you play for the Invictus achievement (completing the game without manually saving).  New players should manually save in every port.  Death is too common and (at leat until well into the game) too big a setback (which is odd in a game set in the Fallen London universe, where Death isn't quite such a big deal as it is on the surface.)
What makes the game really fun is the stories (which are a lot like quests in more traditional RPGs) and the dark tone.  You and your crew slowly suffer mental damage ("Terror") from spending time on the unterzee, far from light or hope, or when something dreadful happens.  Fans of resource allocation games will find a lot to like, too, especially in the early- and mid-game, where ever voyage seems to end with a desperate race for port before running out of food, fuel, or sanity.
As noted elsewhere, combat is simplistic and repetitive....but this isn't really a fighting game.  The economic system doesn't make much sense...but it's not a trading game, either.  It's about exploration and horror and, once you're a bit into the game, the politics of the great powers.  The stories are so good that I have passed up a chance to declare victory because I ended up with a story option that was just too good to pass up.  (In my current game, I'm almost to that point again, and seriously considering repeating that choice so that I can see what happens with other choices instead.)  That seems like a pretty strong sign for a game.

From my personal gaming experiences, this game mostly relates to The Settlers. You build a village while managing resources and population. The major difference being that Banished does not contain any warmaking and it is in fact faster-paced. And as you probably already noticed from other people's reviews, the game is quite a challenge at first.
The learning curve is steep. Really steep. The tutorials don't really teach you how to play the game, but merely how to use the UI. You learn the game mechanics through playing the game... and failing at it.
My first clear learning moment was when my 20-something population village suddenly started to die off due to old age. I quickly learnt the importance of houses, which you need to build to control population growth. Too many houses can cause your village to grow too fast and lead to severe famine due to too little workers and too many children. With too few houses on the other hand, the aging of population may catch up.
The second learning moment was when I struggled with food production. My food reserves started dropping and nothing managed to get it up again. I was even having 18 workers gathering food out of a total population of just above 20. This taught me a lesson on building locations. Food gatherers need old trees to gather food, and multiple hunting locations is important as well.
After your first couple of village failures, you get the hang of it. Your villages become more successful and robust against anything the game can throw at you. If your village is finally self-sustainable, there is really nothing more to it than to expand. Increase population, expand food production, repeat. Although the learning curve is steep, it is really not that high.
There are only a limited number of buildings. And it gets a bit dull over time. When you need to expand food production, you can decide to build another hunter... or farmer... or a fisherman perhaps? The choices really are limited. Yes, there are a dozin different types of fruit and vegetables you can farm, but why do these even make a difference? The crop fields or orchards basically all look the same. I am missing more and diverse buildings.
Eventually the game misses a purpose. When your village is striving, nothing really gives you any goals to expand it even further. There are some achievements to be earned, but that may never be a substitute for a lack of gameplay. Unfortunately this is a disease of modern-day games, achievements do not equal gameplay!

The main one being the "bullets" on the screen, and the paterns to each spread with each enemy you run across in the game. Seems like the genre advanced even further since I last played it, and happy that it did. They have come a long way.
Sure there are plenty of other games out there, possibly even better ones by some of the more dedicated followers of the genre. However for someone like myself it is just another simple game to focus on in short bursts that can last anywhere from 15 minutes to an hour.
Granted I have not, as of this review, gotten very far in the game; at least i see my own progress as I get sometimes further with each try. This is on easy. If you don't have experience in this genre, and don't have much eye hand coordination with a limited amount of memory; then don't let the name fool you, as it may not be as easy the name implies.

This  game is pretty good, it has everything that tropico 4 has and more even! The era system really gives players a fresh new feeling everytime they move through from an era to another. If you're not here for the laugh, then the in game city building system will sure to attract you if you're a kind of person that likes to build a buzzling metropolis from an island. This game is for you, every person that lives in your country will have an impact to your rule, because that individual can be a crime lord that will promote crime, a rebel, or a very educated person that work on buildings that normal people arn't qualified for!
The new biggest difference that this game is from tropico 4 is that it has a new military system, it now has tanks and aircraft carriers. And soldiers now fight in squads, which makes it a little more realistic than it's predecessor. Although combat will feel very limiting as you are not commanding the squad like how an rts should be, instead it's pretty much a auto fight where squads will only defend one single building and you can't move them anywhere else but only "retreat" to another building and defend another spot. The team which the most soldier's or more superior men are more likely to win.
And last but not least, the new multiplayer system! With the combat system, you can fight other players, like attacking infrastracture, military buildings,etc. But that's all really, you can't personally command them to move to a specific location or even target a building of your will. And that's a downpart, but really, this is quite innovative for a city building game. You must race against your rivals for techonogies, money and military, you can form an alliance with one of your rivals, or war with another. This is all good but there is another major flaw that the game has, server issues, and oooooh, it takes quite a long time to find a proper game before you can begin. They must fix this! I waited for 20 minute for the autosearch match and i got nothing! searching for custom game is also a dread. But from what i know, they are still fixing the problem, i have faith in them!
In conclusion, i'll give this game a 7.5/10, It offers a brand new experience for both new and old players of tropico. There are many new buildings, edicts and factions that players will have to look out for. Multiplayer is fun! When is works, and the new military system on the multiplayer will help keep players active on military achivements. I will recommend this to my friends and city building adicts. If you're not a fan of city building games, don't get this, but if you are, join us in tropico 5!

Would I recommend this game?  I want to.  But I can't, not right now...
For one, the game requires a videocard that supports DirectX 11, (updating your drivers won't make a difference) which was not a problem for me since my desktop is fairly beefed up, however, running the game on my laptop or an older desktop is absolutely out of the question.  What's more, I didn't notice anything indicating the game would not run without DX11, and numerous people have apparently bought the game only to find out that it's unplayable.
With that out of the way, a few other issues...
The game has a seemingly steep learning curve- you'll have the basics figured out without much effort, and then BAM!  You find yourself in one no-win scenario after another.  After restarting campaigns a few times and even playing around in Sandbox mode, I realized the gameplay is actually just wonky sometimes.
The game also reduces all the micromanagement I loved about Tropico 4.  You can't see who's visiting your buildings or other minutia that used to aid in figuring out how to resolve issues with your island.  Everything is sort of streamlined (or tries to be) which actually to me seemed a little too dumbed down.
The dynasty system is a novel idea but nothing to get excited about.
The variety of buildings comes drastically short.  I want to believe that that the reason for this is because, I don't know, the game was rushed.  However, I have this odd feeling it was intentional and a few months down the road we'll be seeing DLC with more buildings.  And then more DLC.  And so on and so forth.
To be blunt, everything about the character customization sucks, and the rendering of the characters themselves is absolutely butt ugly.
Drop down the price, fix some gameplay issues, add content, and I would definitely recommend.  Right now I feel like the game is an unfinished product.

A singleplayer game worth your money.
Tropico 5 is a fair game for a fair price, an enjoyable Dictator simulator that while borrows many visual assets from previous games, has gameplay rebuilt from ground up. As a player who never touched campaign mode, the focus on a deep and richer sandbox mode is exactly what I wanted. Here are some ups and downs from my experience.
-DON'T BUY FOR MULTIPLAYER
Anyone buying Tropico 5 for multiplayer should definitely wait a long time, its a half-baked feature that may very well need an entire expansion (or two) to get right.
-ALMANAC
The new Almanac technically has most of the information you could get from 4, but its not very intuitive.  It takes a long itme to figure out where the important info is scurried away. Sometimes you need to scroll down, sometimes its behind an inconspicious word button. You have to explore every nook and cranny to find what you need.
+DYNASTY
The Dynasty mechanic was kind of a letdown. Its an upgrade from T4, where each skill doesn't go into a massive pool, but is tied to a specific character (who can potentially die in certain circumstances.)
+ERAS AND MISSION STRUCTURE
The Era system is the real game changer. If you've seen TotalBuscuit's T5 preview, you'll know the game has a very rigid, formulaic mission structure at the start, the Colonial Era. This is the most defining and brilliant of changes made to the Tropico series.
These Colonial missions are guide you to very specific objectives, ignoring these usually  results in a premature ending. This is done to prevent you from falling into a routine which in prior games, would kill the fun of these games after awhile. These mission chains will seem binding, that you HAVE to do exactly what these missions tell you or fail. However, as your understanding of the game mechanics come together, you can figure out how much breathing space you have to fulfill the missions while building the Tropico you have in mind.
+-COMBAT
Combat is all about expectations. Its no RTS. Its a little hands off, but for me personally its hard to react to changing circumstances. Your firepower comes only from three sources: guard towers, soldiers and tanks. If all of these sources of attack power are gone, you're effectively done.
The most depth I've found with the system is grouping Guard Towers, so that the tankiness of the towers are complemented by consistent firepower which can kill enemy units and actually turn battles around. There should be ways to react to a bad situation, by cutting deals or accepting demands.

Whilst many other zombie games have you blasting them away with shotguns and rifles, this game offers a different experience that will have you jumping out of your skin every time you discover a zombie hidden in a bathroom.
This is not a game about getting a high body count, it's a survival game.  Initially, you must find or make a safe (ish) house - then scavenge for supplies.  If you survive long enough you'll find that the water and power go out and so you need to find alternate sources.  All the time, avoiding or, if you're lucky, killing the zombies - without getting bitten or scratched and succoming to the zombie plague yourself.  If you do die - you can create another character in the same world map, retaining any strongholds that your earlier self managed to create.
It has a "sandbox" mode where you can tweak the world settings, "last stand" mode to attempt to withstand repeated attacks by a horde, lua scripting for player-made mods, and an enormous world map.
Still in beta, it has a few bugs and is not yet feature-complete, but is still very playable and has an active community supporting it due to the fact that the community has funded the development from the early stages.

Remember this is telltale, not Xcom or Fallout. This has not improved. It sometimes does not matter your choices.
•	C: Could be a con like most films once you see it once, you may need time to go over it again.

From my personal gaming experiences, this game mostly relates to The Settlers. You build a village while managing resources and population. The major difference being that Banished does not contain any warmaking and it is in fact faster-paced. And as you probably already noticed from other people's reviews, the game is quite a challenge at first.
The learning curve is steep. Really steep. The tutorials don't really teach you how to play the game, but merely how to use the UI. You learn the game mechanics through playing the game... and failing at it.
My first clear learning moment was when my 20-something population village suddenly started to die off due to old age. I quickly learnt the importance of houses, which you need to build to control population growth. Too many houses can cause your village to grow too fast and lead to severe famine due to too little workers and too many children. With too few houses on the other hand, the aging of population may catch up.
The second learning moment was when I struggled with food production. My food reserves started dropping and nothing managed to get it up again. I was even having 18 workers gathering food out of a total population of just above 20. This taught me a lesson on building locations. Food gatherers need old trees to gather food, and multiple hunting locations is important as well.
After your first couple of village failures, you get the hang of it. Your villages become more successful and robust against anything the game can throw at you. If your village is finally self-sustainable, there is really nothing more to it than to expand. Increase population, expand food production, repeat. Although the learning curve is steep, it is really not that high.
There are only a limited number of buildings. And it gets a bit dull over time. When you need to expand food production, you can decide to build another hunter... or farmer... or a fisherman perhaps? The choices really are limited. Yes, there are a dozin different types of fruit and vegetables you can farm, but why do these even make a difference? The crop fields or orchards basically all look the same. I am missing more and diverse buildings.
Eventually the game misses a purpose. When your village is striving, nothing really gives you any goals to expand it even further. There are some achievements to be earned, but that may never be a substitute for a lack of gameplay. Unfortunately this is a disease of modern-day games, achievements do not equal gameplay!
It is really amazing that his game was created by a single developer. The game concept is great and it is executed well. The game in its current state is fun and enjoyable, but I still see a lot of room for expansion and improvement. Long term game objectives, buildings and features can still be added and I would strongly recommend the developer to do so. This game will keep me busy for many more rainy weekend hours to come!

This game is pretty terrific. The movement system is really satisfying - the character moves quickly and jumps high, so you get a great range of motion within the level. The combat is solid - each enemy has their own gimmick and their own amount of health, and none of them feel overpowered or repetitive. The weapon choice is (mostly) interesting - it varies from crowbars to rocket launchers, with two low-power but infinite ammo selections (the ankh and the energy gloves) that feel like they have a niche rather than just being either overpowered or worthless. My favorite thing about the game is the scroll mechanic, because almost every scroll has a caveat that will make you change your play style, and their conditions are really creative.
That said, I'm not so fond of how repetitive this game can get. As with every roguelike, power gain is incremental and you have to run it over and over, which is fine and a part of this style of game. For some reason, though, it feels more repetitive than, for instance, Rogue Legacy. I think a part of that might be the fact that this game has no backstory at all. We don't know who the redneck is, we don't know why he's in Egypt, we don't know why he's immortal, and we don't know why he feels the need to repeatedly enter temples and kill everyone in them. Rogue Legacy is a lot clearer on who the character is (the son of a thief blah blah bad family name) and why he's doing what he's doing (blah blah vengeance) so you can at least understand why his struggle is important enough to devote dozens of generations of his family to attack the monsters in the castle. Immortal Redneck doesn't have that, which is fine, but doesn't trip my trigger the same way Rogue Legacy did.
So all in all, YES, I recommend this game. It's a lot of fun and definitely worth a playthrough. Just make sure to leave your love of story at home.

All of the worst qualities of a "roguelike" but none of the benefits.
I don't know about you but one of my favorite things about roguelikes, regardless of what form they take, is that your run, for better or worse, can make for some really interesting scenarios. in a lot of roguelike games it takes your quick wits, your cunning, your foresight to make real progress, to leap over previously difficult challenges. After a lot of trial and error, and figuring things out, eventually you can defeat a good roguelike.
This game doesn't boast itself as being a good roguelike, but it does rob a fair number of mechanics, and so one might get the idea that you could defeat this game in the same way. This is totally wrong, and makes the game feel frustratingly punishing, unfair, and RNG based.
let me give you an example:
in most roguelike games, you come accross powerups, which can potentially give you an advantage. a lot of roguelikes also make available powerups which are only good circumstantially, or worse, aren't useful at all and in fact, can negatively impact your game. A good game will communicate to you which powerups are which, even in an abstract way and it is up your knowlege and memory as well as decision making to figure out if it is worth taking.
In Redneck Rampage, you find powerups, but there is no indication of whether it's a good powerup or a game ending one. in one instance, i was given a powerup which removed my crosshair, which basically made progressing an exercise in frustration.
you DO find weapons, rarely, which serve this purpose better, you can pick and choose which one you take with you, which can be interesting, as you only have three weapon slots, however the RNG of the powerups are pretty frustrating, and although one could decide not to take any, that hardly seems like a good solution. If a mechanic is so bad that it forces the player to make motions to avoid it completely, i'd say that's a good sign it needs rebalancing.
secondly, and this is probably just personal opinion, but I find a long term, stat-based progression in this kind of game to be kind of intolerable. questions come to mind when I have the ability to just straight up upgrade my base attack power, questions like "is it actually possible to beat this game on my first try?", "am I wasting my time be trying on each run or am I just grinding points to get more upgrades", and finally "how long will I be grinding lost cause games before I can ACTUALLY play the game, the way it should be played, where I have the base stats required to get to the end?
I WOULD say that the stat upgrades are just a way for the game to lower it's difficulty, allowing the player a better chance of getting to the end, rather than providing an arbitrary hurdle, EXCEPT that alternate "characters" are also tied to the stat upgrade tree, meaning if you want to have alternate playstyles available to you, you NEED to upgrade your stats. I just feel like stat upgrades are conceptually a bad idea in a roguelike, even a game PRETENDING to be a roguelike. I didn't like it in rogue legacy, I don't like it here, and I will continue not to like it.
but, hey, the good:
the combat is pretty fun, there is some good level designs here and good variety in the enemies. The variety in the weapons as well as special abilities are also really good, and the overall look and feel of the game is solid. nice art style, good graphics, pretty good if not forgettable music, and I do dig the bad-mouthed protagonist.
if there was a cheat code I could enter which just added "true roguelike mode" which removed the stat tree and gave the base stats you needed, and all of the playstyle characters, I think my tune would change. I would even be willing to pack for a small dlc pack which added this option. food for thought.

Outlast isn't really a game of skill, and as it turns out, that makes sense. You're not a cop or a soldier or a genetically enhanced superhero. You're just a reporter. And as a reporter, you don't possess many skills with which you can fend off the hulking brutes, knife-wielding stalkers, and other homicidal maniacs who lurk in the halls of the dilapidated Mount Massive Asylum. You can't shoot them, or punch them, or rip pipes from the walls to clobber them with. You can only run and hide. You're always in danger, and when that danger is nipping at your heels and all you can do is flee, desperately hoping to shake off your pursuer, Outlast is a terrifying roller-coaster ride. Unfortunately, the pacing stumbles in a few instances when Outlast stops coasting forward on its own momentum and requires you to go hunting for the track yourself, but these are small setbacks in what is usually a deeply unsettling experience.

Well, they certainly saved the best for last.  I just finished Epiphany and absolutely loved it.  The Blackwell series has been an exceptionally memorable experience.  I'm sitting here trying to think of another game's story that I would put above this but I'm coming up blank.  Of all of the adventure games that I have played this one, (well, the whole series) comes as highly reccomended as I can express.  Each game in the series weaves in all of the different plot threads and mysteries and the finale actually manages to answer all of the questions and bring a clean and definite closure to this incredibly well-crafted and heartfelt story.  A satisfying and definite ending is a rare thing, but they have managed it here.  Epiphany's story takes some very dark turns, even moreso than previous entries, but is underpinned by the uplifting relationship between Rosangela and Joey.  The development of the main characters, and their friendship with eachother is done very well and you really care about them individually and as a team by the end.  The soundtrack is great.  The voice acting is great.  Puzzles are great.  Pixel art is great.  If you are or ever were a fan of classic adventure style games, or a fan of a great story, play this series from start to finish. I've got mixed feelings about Sunless Sea. It's atmospheric and intriguing in the beginning, great music, interesting islands to visit, but most of the time you just spend cruising around doing nothing. This is still fun for the first ten hours or so, until it starts getting tedious.
The game urges you to explore, yet in practice it just penalizes you for curiosity. You're exploring a new region and you want to go visit this island, then that island and then the next one. You try to make sure you have enough fuel and supplies to get back to London, the home port, and usually it works out. However, sometimes you just don't find islands to sell you more fuel, or you run out of money to buy them. And then you die. Although you can inherit something useful from the previous captain, starting again as a new character in practice means all of the progress you made is lost. That's the name of the game in rogue-lites, I know, but in Sunless Sea the Core Gameplay Loop is that you just sail the empty sea, which is extremely boring until the novelty wears off. I just want a fast forward button in this game.
Dying and having to start again in Sunless Sea does not mean that get to try another type of playstyle, although there are a few different "classes", but the differences are very minor. No matter what kind of character you have, you always do the same things. Nor does dying present a new challenge to overcome, it just means you have to do more sailing. The core gameplay is very easy, the difficulty in the game comes solely from the fact that sailing back and forth between London and other islands is boring. You want to explore and take risks, which will only cause difficulties. I guess this is a profound statement on the nature of man or something, but it just doesn't make for fun gameplay.
The best way to play would be to plan the route you're gonna take from London and back in advance, and do not deviate from it. It probably assures you will be safe, but this is boring. Exploring is fun, but if you want to complete the game you should avoid long expeditions. So either you have fun and you die, or you're bored to death by playing it smart. But I have a third option, find some other game in my Steam collection to play.
It would be nice to be able to record what items are sold at a certain port as well. I don't feel like using actual pen and paper to do it. And resorting to using a wiki is sort of lame.
The combat system is very simple and not fun either, but I think it's only a minor flaw, since the best bits of Sunless Sea are exploration and the atmosphere. The combat doesn't matter that much.
Bonus points for Lipiäinen Point though.

The biggest and best game of the Blackwell series. If you've played other games in the series you'll know what you're getting into, but to put it simply this is Wadjet Eye's finest work to date - a point and click game that I can easily recommend alongside classics in the genre.
Once again, players take on the roles of both Rosa Blackwell and Joey Mallone, their job is, as always to help lost souls move on, and as before there are a large number of ghosts that need saving, each with a different story to tell. Unlike previous games, all the ghosts in this game tie directly into the primary overarching narrative, adding considerable gravitas to proceedings and helping to shake things up. There is some assumption of prior knowledge of the series, the game doesn't waste time retreading how Rosa and Joey do their jobs but instead dives right into the main course. In terms of gameplay. The dual characters mechanic returns once again and players must make use of both Rosa's and Joey's different abilities to solve puzzles and overcome dialogue based obstacles throughout the game. Puzzles are for the most part fairly simple, there's no hair tearing moments and bizarre solutions to impede your progress - for the most part everything is pretty logical. The clue system from previous games returns, requiring players to combine topics/clues from their in game notes page to determine links and hypothesise potential solutions to problems. This works well for the most part, with Joey again serving as an in-game hints system that the player can utilise as much or as little as they desire. The focus here is very much on the story, there are also plenty of references to previous games for fans yet the game is also strong enough to stand on its own.
In terms of game length, the game feels longer than previous entries, I think Wadjet has finally hit upon the optimal length for its games with Epiphany after previous entries were criticised for their short length. The narrative and writing quality are consistent throughout, Wadjet Eye have been going from strength to strength with this series and Epiphany is no exception. I did notice a new mechanic in play early in the game, where the two leads would spontaneously begin short, unprompted banters discussing their current location, etc, not unlike the party banter systems employed in several rpgs. Sadly this fizzled out quite quickly and is only seen in the first third of the game.
The artwork in Epiphany is fantastic throughout, it's building on a similar aesthetic to Blackwell Deception but everything is more detailed and beautifully rendered in pixel art. They've found a really great style to use (and artist to bring it to life) and they neatly sidestep the animation issues that many other modern point and clicks exhibit because of it. Hoping to see future games maintain the same style and level of quality.
The music is nice and fits well with the tone of the game for the most part, it did seem to be a little on the quiet side this time around and is very much in the background for most of game. In terms of other audio - Wadjet's voice acting on the technical side of things has come a long way now, there's none of the issues the plagued earlier entries to be found here which is great. All series regulars reprise their roles in Epiphany and they all give solid performances.
In terms of story, this being the final game in the series, Epiphany wraps up the Blackwell series and answers most of the questions you might have had. I won't lie though, I wish we'd have seen some more entries to the series before the finale.
Sadly there is one significant dropped plot arc which occurs (or rather should have occurred) between Deception and Epiphany that I felt hurt the continuity between those two games somewhat. Based on the ending of Deception and where Epiphany picks up it felt that we'd skipped a step in the story of Rosa and Joey and just leapt from there to the series finale, which is an unusual and unfortunate misstep. Aside from this one issue the series as a whole flows nicely from one game to the next. I won't talk about the ending here as I think that's something best experienced and I don't want to colour anyone's view on it, suffice it to say I felt it was a fitting ending but it's not the one I would have gone with.
There's always been a certain sense of familiarity with the Blackwell series and the protagonists thankless task of helping the dead move on all the while the hustle and bustle of New York. There's something that's quite grounded in reality about the series that makes it quite endearing and relaxing to play, this is underlined through Dave Gilbert's commentaries that are embedded within each game you really get a sense that you're experiencing these locations through his memories and the series as a whole just really has a sort of personal touch that's difficult to describe and I don't often see/feel in most games. That, married with the real world setting really heightened the experience for me across the Blackwell series.
Ultimately, Blackwell Epiphany is highly recommended, as a fan of the series this was a deeply satisfying game to play. If you've never played the Blackwell series before, or if it's sat in your Steam backlog, start with Legacy and work forwards from there - if you're a fan of the genre, you won't regret it.

To begin, this game is fairly incredible. This series is even more so. After seeing Bioshock 1 and 2 on a steam sale, and hearing a lot of good rep about the series, i decided to try the demo. The demo was good, not groundbreaking but good, it seemed like a game that i might actually enjoy to a degree. Admittedly I had already played Bioshock Infinite and absolutely adored it (Review for another day :P), and even so i had heard that the original games were very different from Infinite. Another rumor about these games were that both 1 and 2 were very horror focused.
Genre/Themes
Upon playing the game i was extremely surprised, first things first if you are thinking about passing up this game because of the horror, please do not. While this game is "scary" it isnt like other games in the genre (incidently i hate the horror genre XD) instead of having tacky jumpscares and monsters that will haunt your dreams for a number of weeks, the first two games focus a lot on a creepy atmosphere and an incredibly haunting setting (In which i will get to later). In this game i just found myself so immersed into the Bioshock universe so much, that these scary parts just felt like another part of the story that made it so much more amazing. This is horror done in an extremely unique way and unlike any other game i have seen in the past. I cant do games that are scary just for the point of being scary, games like slender, this isn't one of those games.
Setting
Okay so my absolute favorite part of this series, is the setting. This game has quite easily the greatest setting for any game I have ever played. It's this kind of, stereotypical "utopia gone bad" kind of setting, but just done so incredibly well in a very unorthodox way. In addition there is so much backstory to the universe that it had probably more than a hundred audio tapes in each game that tell you about the story and the characters, from a different point to view, and even a book that gives a small insight into Rapture. And honestly, who doesnt want a game set in an underwater metropolis with superpowers? This kind of scale of a setting just hasnt quite been done before, and 2K have done a brilliant job in making it feel dead and haunted, but strangely alive....
Story
So this is the point in which there is a big divide between Bioshock 1 and 2. Many of the fans of the series believe that Bioshock 1 had the better story over it's sequel. In my opinion they are both amazing, but Bioshock 2 had a better story with better characters. In saying that, Bioshock 1 just has one of those moments where your jaw just kind of drops off of your face, only to return about a week later. The ending just had me sitting there staring into space going 'What the hell did i just see..." Its difficult to describe in text the incrdible story in these games.
Gameplay
Another big divide between 1 and 2 i feel the gameplay was a lot more polished in 2 than in 1. Anyway, this game features a very interesting system of combat, you have both your weapons and your superpowers, or plasmids. There's around 11 different plasmids in Bioshock 1, ranging from firing electricity out of your hands to stun an enemy or electrify a pool of water that will in urn kill all the enemies nearby, to releasing a swarm of bees from your hands that will attack and distract the enemies while you deal with the stronger enemies. As well, the game really tries to encourage you to combine plasmids and weapons to deal with enemies, or even at times combining two plasmids together to create dangerous traps. Even the enemy types in this game are brilliant, known as splicers, the plasmid crazed humans attack you in search of Adam, the currency that fuels the power of plasmids. Theres splicers that use explosives, others that attack with mind powers, some that slimb on walls, and some that will rush at you and try to get in your face and cause as much damage as possible. And finally the centrepoint of the Bioshock franchise is the big daddies, the "hulking palukas" are one of the hardest enemies that you'll face. Diving suited, armored giants that are the engineers and protectors of Rapture, will guard little sisters, the Adam factories. LIttle sisters are little girls transformed by use of a sea slug, that converts adam into more adam, without Adam in Rapture, you will not last long. It's up to you whether you choose to rescue the little sisters, saving them from the seaslug and enslavement, only giving you a small amount of Adam, or harvesting them, killing the girl in the process but giving you the motherload of all Adam....
Some of the bad points
While this is indeed an amazing game, and by extension quite an  incredible series, Bioshock 1 does have a number of issues that you'll find irritating as you play through the game. The first of which i feel is the weapon/plasmid system. While theoretically, the combination of superpowers and explosives are a match made in heaven, in this game using the actual implemented system is quite hard to master. Say you have three enemies, the first of which you want to set on fire, the second you want to headshot with a crossbow, and the third you want to electrocute with a bolt of lightning. Now, plasmids and weapons work on a kind of mode system. This means to switch between plasmids and weapons you need to switch modes, done with the right mouse button. Moving back to the example. To first set the enemy on fire, if youre using a weapon you need to right click to switch to plasmid mode. Then you need to aim at the enemy and left click to fire your Incinerate! blast. Moving to the second person you then need to switch to the weapon mode, which takes around a second to do, select the right weapon via scrolling, weapon wheel, or number selection, aim, and then fire. Spinning towards the last enemy you then need to switch back to plasmid mode, select Electro Bolt using the same tactics as above, and fire it into the pool of water at the last splicers feet. While this may work all good and well when the enemies are still, when the splicers are sprinting towards you ferociously, the combat gets extremely difficult to take control of. Each animation of switching mode, switching weapon, as well as the time it takes to register that an enemy is attacking you, combined with the time it takes you to aim. It is most likely that youre nearly dead by the time youve figured out how you want to deal with the splicer. This system really slows down the combat, in certain cases this can be good, but when the splicers are so fast paced and agile, having to take 10 seconds to even be ready to fire is an extrememly frustrating endeavor.
Warnings
Small warning for horror here. As i mentioned before this game isnt really jumscare heavy, at all really. In saying that though, there are a few moments which may freak you out because something unexpected just happened. This is a quick example.
*SPOILER WARNING*
There is a small section near the beginning of the game, around a third of the way through. This is the area where you first find the shotgun. Now as you walk into the room, you see the room is filled with complete dakness except for a spotlight in the middle, shining directly onto your new shotty. As you go to grab it, the lights cut. Inevitably you will freak out to some degree. The spotlight then turns back on, and you get suddenly attacked with 3 or 4 splicers all at once appearing out of the darkness trying to kill you. Very well done scripted section, but absolutely terrifying.
*SPOLIER OVER*

This review stands as a full review of the entire Blackwell series. I was introduced to this series a meager four days ago. I was intrigued by the old-school point and click "talkies" I had grown up with on old CD-ROMs from Fate of Atlantis through the Monkey Island series all the way to the newer Telltale Games products. I hardly knew what I was getting myself into.
The Blackwell series stars the Blackwell family, mainly Rosa and introducing her Aunt, Lauren, in Unbound. At some point in the past, their Grandmother suddenly became saddled with a ghost, Joey, who was her spirit guide. Unable to take the pressure (limiting plot spoilers), she died and Joey passed onto the aunt. It turned out he is a spirit guide, destined to guide Mediums like the series protaganist Rose to lead lost spirits to the final destination.
This is where the puzzle element comes into play. Like most adventure games, you interact with the environment through investigation, item manipulation and conversing with other characters. The first game in the series, Legacy, is fairly light on puzzles and is easily completed, but the series quickly grows into a satisfying old-school adventure title as the series progresses. Epiphany is the masterstroke of the series in this regard, with multi-threaded and complex puzzle threads that still fit well within the realm of logic.
However, where the series truly shines is in the storytelling. The writing, character development and accompanying voice acting is near perfection. The series easily hooks you into the characters and makes you care about them. The slow reveal of the history, feelings, pain and emotion of each character over each of the five games easily drew me into the Blackwell world. With Epiphany, the entire series wrapped up in a way few games, movies or even television shows could ever hope - satisfying, even if bittersweet.
There are a couple of hiccups in the game, primarily in code bugs in Unbound that cause voice tracks to trigger improperly, one being an ugly spoiler mid-way through that gave away part of a conversation from the game's finale, but otherwise is solidly coded and well designed. The graphics may also be a bit of a put-off to more modern gamers since it is intentionally created in a low resolution, non-widescreen format to mimic the old CRT monitors some of us older gamers were stuck with nearly two decades ago. But the artwork presented in close-ups, photos, desktop backrounts, and other areas is fantastic and feels alive.
I whole heartedly recommend the entire five game series. Go back to the Blackwell Legacy and pick it up from there and don't stop until you finish up Epiphany. The game is a well build emotional ride with solid puzzle mechanics fit for a good old school adventure game. From someone used to adventure games being the high-energy comedy like Day of the Tentacle, The Blackwell series was a huge surprise. Though the surprise was pleasant and I believe it will be so for everyone else who gives this a try.

Game is a great idea, tower defense + RPG elements, awesome.
However the loot system just murders the game.
I am a strategic player, and probably spent more time reading about the game than actually playing.
From what I have gathered, the loot system is constantly changing, and for the worst.
If you don't follow a specific method to gearing up, your gear progression will likely stagnate, whereas, if you do, you can reach Chaos Trail 7 gear in a very short amount of time.
When the game spawns new gear for you to loot, it looks at your current best gear's MAIN stat, and completely ignores the secondary stats, and the slots, and the rarity. Due to this pathetic mechanic, wearing slightly older legendary gear can actually slow your gear progression versus wearing common gear with a higher main stat, but horrible secondary stats and no slots.
This is 100% counter-intuitive and illogical. To make up for this stupidity, we need to set up a "mule", to wear the most recently aquired gear with the highest main stat or cash value. If this is not done, going up loot tiers takes forever.
This is practically an intended exploit, or cheat. Why must we jump through hoops to progress at a quicker rate? It is not fair to players who do not care to read up on all this garbage that they need to do to get better gear. It is just stupid.
I won't even talk about the hilariously unbalanced towers lol.
All in all, cool game, good idea, horrible execution.
Do not recommend touching it with a ten foot pole unless you like wasting your time mucking around with item management instead of actually playing, or until they fix the damn loot system and tower balancing.
TL;DR, Loot system breaks the game. Dont play.

Pox Nora is a great game if you are interested in complex strategic, turn based game play paired with trading card game mechanics; allowing tremendous freedom both while building your battlegroup (pulling from thousands of unique units) and while playing.
Building your collection can be slow but is not too difficult, as playing against the AI rewards you with runes (cards) and gold to buy packs which provide a wider variety of runes. In addition, starter bgs (decks) are available either for free or for very small amounts of gold, and give you access to pre-built bgs  with a pretty decent power level that you can use in any mode. Artwork on the cards is excellent, on par with great tcgs like mtg.
Once you hit the competitive ranked play, there is a serious spike in difficulty, as many players have been playing the game for years and will play at a very high level. However, if you enjoy the challenge, it provides the best and most interesting matches, and matches you up against an enormous amount of different strategies. Balance is functional although not perfect, and in a constant state of flux, as relatively regular patches rebalance units and modify the meta.
Finally, though not a pay to win game, the wider access to runes players can get by spending cash can sometimes make it feel like it is, especially if you aren't running a strong bg (deck). However, many, if not most, of the strongest runes are in the lower rarities, so if you're willing to test around you will be able to put together something quite powerful.
All in all, Pox Nora is a game for a specific kind of gamer, lacking impressive graphics or simplified gameplay, but more than making up for it in strategic depth, great gameplay, style and uniqueness. Try it out, and see what you think.

I've been playing Poxnora on and off since 2008/09. You can immagine - that's a long time. And I saw it's good and bad sides. There are a lot of good sides in this game and only a few ( now ) of downsides. Back in 08/09 this game was full "pay to win" type of a game. You could only get basic, pathetic, starter decks, that couldn't level up at all and you couldn't buy any packs with virtual money ( gold ) that you get from playing. Basically, gold was non-existent back then.
Then SOE ( Sony Online ) took over. They made it "free to play" finaly with implementing gold which you could spend on buying individual high value runes. Then, you could trade those high value runes for a bunch of smaller value ones that you need for your decks. And the more you played the game, the more you got "rich" and could build a better, more competitive deck.
Then DOG ( Desert Owl ) took back the game again. They nerfed 95 % of the runes ( by the way completely destroying all of my high value runes by doing that ), but I think it made the game more balanced now. A lot more balanced actualy. There ARE still some overpowered high value runes ( mostly legendaries ), which are hard to kill on the "battlefield", but a lot less of them, than before, when SOE was running the game. You can't buy individual runes anymore with gold, but now you can buy packs and boxes with it. Which I think is even better ( lot better ). Since in those boxes and packs, you have 10% for an exo and 5% for each exo to become a legendary. So, if you are lucky, you can get on a roll and get rich a LOT faster than we used to, when we had to grind gold like madmen, to get the rune which was worth 150 000 gold. ( there were 500 000 gold runes later as well ).
This game is unique in so many ways. Strong deck is not the only thing you need. You need to closely put together your deck considering a lot of things ( stealth detection, destroying equipment, anty-spell, anty-heal, boost-heal etc ) all depending on your deck synergy. And then, you also have to play the perfect game once the match starts, with perfect strategy, since every bad move might mean turnover and you losing the game, no matter how good your deck is. I remember beating 10-15 games in a row in ranked matches with only common / uncommon / rare runes, but in a deck which had amazing synergy and me focused on the game 100%.
So if you are looking for a CONSTANT challenge, never the same battles, literally MILLIONS of possible deck builds, this IS THE GAME! Elves, Dwarves, Barbarians, Demons, Liches, Undead, Zombies, Witches, Paladins, Warriors, Voils, Dragons, Lizards, Swamp creatures, Frogs, Snakes, Beasts, Fairies, Treefolk, Wizards, Titans, Constructs - they are ALL in this game spread out into 8 unique factions! Don't even look for anything else, there just isn't anything like it out there. This game is amazing!

Play Length: About halfway through the game, from what I can tell.  As I didn't complete the game, please take this review with a grain of salt.
Positives: The look of this game is very distinct and interesting.  The artstyle alone does a pretty good job of creating atmosphere.  The game's sound is also helps with that.  This game is all about charging forth through a bleak landscape, soaking up the atmosphere, solving puzzles, and moving forward.
The puzzles are decent.  They require some thought, without being too devious.  They require you to pay attention to everything and to think.  That's always a good thing for a puzzle game.
Negative: I kind of wish that this game had more exploration, and wasn't just a linear left to right affair.  A bit more creativity and thought behind the game world's structure would have been nice.  I also feel like this game would have benefitted from some light combat elements.  That's not always necessary for puzzle games, but I feel like it would have fit the mood and tone of this game.
One thing that kind of dulled my enjoyment of the game was the death-heavy nature of the puzzles.  I don't mind dying a lot in games, but games where you die a lot tend to have a certain silly feel to them.  I'm not talking about Dark Souls where you might die once every 15 minutes or so, I'm talking about rapid fire deaths along the lines of Meat Boy.  This fits Meat Boy, with it's irreverant tone, but doesn't really fit a game that is trying to have a forboding atmosphere like Limbo.  Unfortunately, I think the game's designers made this choice because it's a popular structure for current indie games, but to me it just doesn't fit with the game's atmosphere.
As far as the soundtrack goes, it could definitely have been better.  There's a temptation with games like this to go for ambient, quiet, non-intrusive music, but I think that's a mistake.  It's possible to have music that is both atmospheric and memorable.  Some ambient music is okay, but there should be some memorable music to balance it out.
Overall: I didn't enjoy the game quite enough to finish it.  But I didn't dislike it either.  Overall, I would give it a mild recommendation.
About my rating system: I have two things I rate on.  Overall score, and soundtrack.  Personally, I feel like game soundtracks are tremendously undervalued; to me, it's a vital factor in getting me into the game.  For the score, I grade on a scale of 1-10, and I try to grade in such a way that each number has a meaning and equal importance.  The meaning of each number are as follows:
0: Garbage, 1: Awful, 2: Poor, 3: Underwhelming, 4: Mediocre, 5: Decent, 6: Good, 7: Great, 8: Excellent, 9: Phenomenal, 10: Masterpiece
Limbo's score:
Game Rating: 5 (Decent)
Soundtrack Rating: 4 (Mediocre)

I know my time playing the game as of writing this review is short, but I can safely say that it's my kind of game. It's very much in the Geometry Wars family... perhaps a bit too much, but with skill trees and lasting ship upgrades thrown into the mix, it's got enough going on to make it its own game.
It's fun to play, with good twin-stick controls and lots of variety in enemy type, complete with "boss battles" and differing objectives (I started one level only to be told my weapons weren't working, so I had to stay alive and dodge rather than fight). Secondary objectives add to the mix in each system, and environmental hazards are factored in as well.
Controller support is outstanding with my Xbox 360 controller. Colored icons that look like buttons make things easy to navigate (always a nice touch). Everything is smooth and responsive. The only gripe I have control wise is that bombs and "super weapons" use a control scheme that's completely inpractical in a twin-stick shooter - you use your targeting controller to place them, while continuing to move about with your main controller, and then once releaced, you have to go back to shooting RIGHT EFFIN' NOW or you're dead.
There's a difficulty curve here, but death penalties are minimal, and it's pretty easy to pick up and play. The visuals are flat but functional - nothing special, but perfectly servicable. The game's main downfall is the sound - unimpressive effects and a flat-out boring soundtrack. If the dev could address THIS particular problem especially, I think this would be a pretty awesome game.
At only $4.99 US regular price, the game is well worth it. I got it for 40% off, and I can only say LUCKY! If you're into twin stick shooters and persistant upgrades, then it's worth a play... but turn off the music and play your own.

Banished is a great village building game. The few options for creating a new map create a wide variety of situations, ranging from deceptively easy to deviously difficult. I myself have yet to manage to build a successful village starting from the more difficult starting options.
The game as it is provides three different embark options that determine how many resources your settlers start with, and thus how difficult it will be to get established. Then you have two choices of terrain generation to choose from, plains or mountains. Mountains, of course, are more difficult to survive in. And finally, you have the option to provide a seed number or randomly generate one, so you can easily play the same map as someone else, or share your map with a friend to see who can create the more successful village.
Once in the game, you will have a small number of villagers, a reserve of resources, and perhaps a building or two depending on the difficulty you chose. For example, on the easiest difficulty, you'll have enough houses for everyone, a storage barn for your finished goods, and a stockpile for raw resources. Again, depending on the difficulty, these resources may last you a while, but you'll need to be smart about getting resource production started quickly, otherwise you'll never see the end of your second winter.
Once you're settled and have a stable supply of resources, your job is to expand. Build houses to encourage families to grow, build a town hall to attract migrants, build hospitals to heal diseases quickly. resource management is the name of the game, and people are a resource as well. Lack of housing can kill just as effectively as lack of food. Nothing is worse than realizing that the citizens who were able to bear children were all stuck living with their parents until they died, at which point they were too old to have children themselves, and all you can do is watch everyone slowly die of old age.
Along with the base game, there is also a built-in mod manager, where you can easily enable and disable mods without even having to exit your current game. Mods are easily found and installed from the Steam Workshop, or you can install them manually if you so desire. The variety of mods available is what makes this game go from great to amazing. There are mods that do everything from removing a bit of micromanagement, or making your villagers need to eat less food or live longer, to adding new content, and even expanding the game to the point of making the base game seem incomplete by comparison (see Colonial Charter or Banished Mega Mod).
If you're on the fence about this game, get it. it's simple, but addicting, and difficult. Soon you'll be on your way to trying to trade for that last seed you don't have, or wildly scrambling to assign more villagers to food production before half the population starves.

This is a game for people who have time to spend on a fairly low-key, non-social experience.  If that's a deal-breaker, this isn't for you.  The trailer is *badly* misleading and halfway spoils one of the best parts.  This is not an exciting game with challenging combat and awesome Lovecraft-inspired boss monsters.
With that said, this game is a box full of fascinating experiences which gives you the sense of having lived another life.  The atmosphere is perfect.  The writing is sublime.  The art and music are beautiful.
It's a grim, painful world you struggle to survive in, and not in a fun way.  The fun is in exploring the world, not overcoming its challenges.  The challenges are trying to ruin your fun, and sometimes, they succeed.  They take your time up, take options away, make you do time-consuming chores.  The fear of such losses, which can be measured in hours, meshes perfectly with the atmosphere of oppressive terror.
The best way to enjoy this game may be to take permadeath even more seriously than the game does: once you've had a good run and come to the end of a life that didn't end early because of your lack of understanding of some basic thing, which let you see all or most of the map, walk away.  Maybe come back in a year or two, maybe never.
This isn't a game with any real goal.  You're not out to slay Cthulhu and return London to the surface.  It's a world.  You have your life in it, without seeing nearly all there is, and then you're gone from it without unravelling all of its mysteries.  Leaving it behind with unfulfilled desires suits it.

Here's a review from a Touhou fan who really appreciates a good bullet hell shooter.
And this is a good bullet hell shooter.
Graphics - The character portraits are cute and lively, while the gameplay graphics have a more retro pixellated feel. It all feels very charming and indie. The bullet shapes and colors are almost exactly like Touhou's, which makes for some very pretty patterns.
Sound - Chiptune soundtrack with some names that might be familiar if you're into the chiptune scene (I personally recognize Zabutom). The tracks are energetic and distinctive, though it sometimes feels like something is missing. Also, the sound effects are well done, with clear cues for everything necessary in a bullet hell shooter. There are no harsh sounds, like Touhou's infamous chimes and bells.
Gameplay - Stages are well-paced, though the enemies may come through a bit faster than you're used to. The bosses present a variety of challenges to overcome, and there are even some attacks inspired by Touhou spell cards. The normal difficulty feels easy enough for those curious about the bullet hell genre, while Hard and Hell modes are sure to provide a great challenge for veterans. Plus, there's six different playable characters with their own shot type, dialogue, and unique final boss.
Overall, there's a whole lot to be enjoyed in this FREE game, and it definitely ranks well among the other bullet hells on Steam, such as Danmaku Unlimited and ExCeed. There's no catch, no microtransactions. If you're even a little curious about bullet hell shmups, DOWNLOAD THIS RIGHT NOW.

Its basically an unforgivable RTS, with absolutely no violence it will keep you tense and busy for hours, it might also kill time very easily if you let it play its magic.
While the repeatibility is I believe a bit low, one playthrough will definitely keep you entertained, you have to manage a population of townfolks which is constantly, exponantially growing, with absolutely no means to slow it down.
You'll need to cope with your citizen needs, and be constantly on top of things, even one step ahead. The pace is quite slow at first, then it starts to get a bit intense (remember the "exponantial" bit), but you need to be patient if you want to play it right, you can't rush things. If you do, you'll lose.
, it is not your typical RTS, and its mechanics resemble more of a
: you can't control your people, you control their environment, decide the layout of the city so it provides for the needs of each of your citizens.
Tools given in-game allow you to micro/macro-manage your city, and you'll learn fast that nothing can be left unchecked. The pace will also grow exponantially as your population increases and your town expands. No really, this game is quite cool because it has solid mechanics.

To begin, this game has totally captured me.
First impressions of this game were bleak for me. When I was shown this game, I wasn't excited. It didnt stound out to me right away. The Long Dark made me want to just walk away from it and start playing something else. The graphics were the first thing I noticed, I wasnt a big fan. When I realized that this was how the game was designed, it changed my outlook on it. I started seeing all the amazingly simple landscapes that were absolutely breathtaking.
The mechanics are great. When people say "survival games", I think of survival horror games like RE and The Last Of Us, where the game focuses on altercations and on keeping the characters safe.
Where TLD(shorted for The Long Dark) makes this an actual survival, is in the upkeep. Yes, there are fights with wildlife. That isn't your biggest concern. The thing that you must keep an eye on is your character.
Are they rested?
Are they warm?
Are they hydrated?
Are they full?
Are they injured?
All that can change.
Wolf attacks and you need to perform first aid, you rest for 10 hours and realize you need food, but arent able to find any, how long can you make it looking for other food sources? Can you make it to another building? Are you able to keep yourself warm on the way there? Will you find yourself at the mercy of the wilderness and become the prey for a winter storm?
Only time will tell on your journey away from The Long Dark...

As others have said, this is a difficult game to review. I played this on my laptop while laid up from surgery, with literally nothing else to do. I didn't use the wiki or try to get outside help, and I'd say it was about 45 hours before I really had a good idea how to play the game for a while without dying. The fact that I sunk this much time into the game shows how addictive and compelling it is. You definitely get that "one more quest" thing going.
Similar to roguelikes like FTL, some of the "advancement" in the game involves completing some task that unlocks benefits for your next game. The difference is that a game of FTL takes a couple of hours at most, whereas a reasonable game of Sunless Sea clocks in around 10 hours. The game is not forgiving at all; you must carefully plan out your trips and avoid detours and unnecessary risks, or you stand an extremely good chance or dying. Lots of things that seem harmless can cripple or kill you without much warning.
If you put any value on your time, just turn off perma-death (make a manual save) after you die the first couple of times, and save every once in a while. That way, you can have the fun of exploring without the risk of having to repeat 10 hours of gameplay. Otherwise, you would need to consult the wiki on every trip and decision, which takes a lot of the fun out of it.

I've gotta say, I was hoping to enjoy this. The premise sounded awesome, time moves only when you move. But that's not entirely accurate. Time does move when you are standing still, just a little, so you can't take all the time you want. I wonder why the developers decided on that as opposed to going all the way and making time completely stop until you move?
Second, yes it is fun to blaze through a level being the bullet dodging, katana throwing ninja that you are. However, for me it degraded into memorization. Because bullets still move even when you are just turning the camera, most of my deaths came from behind. To succeed you have to memorize which enemy will come from where, and when, and how long you have to turn from opponent A to opponent B before his shotgun makes quick work of you. And that is not skill, that is memorization.
Lastly, after you complete a level, you are given access to a stunning replay of your victory in real time. Awesome, right? To see what all your death defying twists and turns would look like to a bystander? Except... the name of the game flashes in the middle of the screen the entire time, blocking most of your view. Why in the world was this deemed a good idea?
All in all, I think this is a very interesting concept that will probably do very well, but I do not find it to be a solid game nor an enjoyable game, but rather a frustrating exercise in memorization.
