Eugh.  I played Runespell and I tried to like it, I really did.  It's based around Poker/Solitaire mechanics, where you select cards from Solitaire-like stacks and then stack them on to other cards, and if you complete a Poker hand you get to deal damage.  But this game has a fairly punishing difficulty for a game which revolves a lot around random chance, but even worse, the differences between e.g. a straight and a flush and three of a kind are fairly minimal, whereas the Straight Flush and Royal Straight Flush are absolutely crushing if you get them.  This can result in a fight being repeated over and over, trying to get the SF/RSF.  This means it doesn't feel like you "won" even when you do.
Nevermind that the Runespell mechanics depend on dealing or receiving damage to charge up your Rage... and then you have to not be hit with Fear, which takes away your hard-won Rage.  And it takes precious actions to use Runespells, actions that could be spent sorting cards into hands and attacking, when the Runespells often cost a lot and are not all that advantageous.
If you are wondering if it has a story... uh.  It doesn't, really.  You're yet another boring "mysterious wanderer" who remembers nothing and has no characterization except being Generic Reluctant Hero #8894691, and some special powers because you are also the Chosen One.  The other characters are relatively flat and enjoy very little characterization, and what they do get is fairly ham-handed... most characters only have about a dozen lines at best, going up to two or three dozen if they're a major villain or an early ally.  And no, it's not a huge cast, either.
If you do play it, buy the Glory I runespell (only costs 10 Rage) at the first opportunity and use it before attacking, every time, preferably with multiple hands built up to attack from.  It's one of the very few Runespells worth your time.  Don't waste too much time on "guard" runespells, as the AI is intelligent enough to avoid attacking while those are up.
Or, better, don't waste your money?

Sunless Sea a superbly put together game, with atmospheric music, beautifully illustrated maps and images, and lots of well-written prose. It's by the same folks—and set in the same world—as Fallen London.
And it is the world, more than anything, which makes the game so captivating. With a distinctly Lovecraftian feel, London has fallen underground, and lies on the edge of a dark subterranean sea. You are a ship's captain, and while you can trade in physical goods like coffee and wine, it becomes rapidly apparently that what's most widely valued on the shores of the unterzee are *stories*.
Memories of distant lands, the heart-thumping excitement of a sea-monster rearing from the depths, the memories of having tea with a most civilised devil, a vision of the surface where the sun is said to still shine... all of these can be traded. And while it's never explicitly mentioned in the game, it's clear that they are traded *permanently*.
A secret in the unterzee has a real value, because in sharing that secret with another, you lose the memory of it yourself. It's said there are far-off islands with marketplaces for memories and forgotten tales. And as a captain of a ship upon a dark and terrifying sea, one can fetch a high price for some of the memories of what you have seen...
I cannot stop playing this game, late at night, with the lights dimmed, and a leather bound journal and fountain pen close at hand.

First and foremost, don't let my time played on Steam fool you, since I got the game on here only recently. I've been playing the non-Steam Version on and off since its release however. Also, if you prefer the short version of this review, feel free to skip down to my summary. With that out of the way, let's talk the game.
Banished is a classical city builder sprinkled with survival elements. You build up your town, meet the needs of your citizens - mainly for food, firewood and health through food variety and herbs - and mine for classic resources like stone and iron.
While this may sound simple at first glance, like many things in Banished, it is only in theory and much can go wrong. Grow your town too fast and you will run out of workers, but build too many houses at once to get new workers and you won't be able to feed them all, leading to starvation and yes, in Banished, that means the actualy death of your population and maybe your entire town.
In the same vein natural disasters add another form of challenge. Entirely optional - as you can opt to disable them at game start - catastrophes such a spreading fire or a Tornado suddenly whirling through a carefully build up district can easily bring down a vital part of your economy, dooming your poor little town. And while you can arm yourself against some things, building a well in every district for example might be expensive but it also allows your citizens to put out fires before they can spread, you can only wait out others, like the Tornado and hope for the best.
While this may sound like a flaw to some, it is to me one of Banished greatest strength, as it is this mechanic that allows your towns to never feel "quite the same". Different things happen to them. Maybe you won't expirience a Tornado. Maybe it will be there in your second year, when there's not much to be destroyed- or in Year 50 when you've just gotten to a good place. You might opt not to spend all this stone for wells on your next run and maybe your city can survive "the great fire".. Maybe all of these happen and produce a food crisis to boot. But which ever way, it will be part of your towns history, making every one feel unique and memorable.
Banished is a solo project, developed by Luke Hodorowicz, with nothing but its soundtrack produced by another person. For that it is a fantastic achievement. It also comes with a few quirks, which I notice are a big part of the more negative reviews on here - and partly unwarrented - which is why I'm going to touch on them quickly.
As mentioned, Banished is a one person project, its content in its Vanilla form is therefor limited and you won't find the building variety or production chain complexity you see in triple A titles. There is no two ways about that. What people tend to forget, however, is that Banished was actually developed
of the modding community providing additional content. And they have. From total conversion to dozens of buildings that perfectly tie into the Vanilla "feeling" of Banished. There is, as a matter of fact, more quality content on the workshop and the Banished forums than you could ever run in a single game.
In short, from my personal feeling, the AI is not half as bad as it's made out to be. Especially in comparison to similiar games, even those coming from big publishers. There are some minor flukes such as laborers tending to dilly-dally around while you're waiting for them to finish a project, but then, there's been a fix on the workshop for that as well since 2014. This issue might also come from the fact that, behold, Banished actually did what Sim City promised and couldn't pull off: actual, uniquely calculated AI. Every single one of your citizens has his or her own life. Their schedule, their family, their habits, their priorities. They are their own person. This becomes especially apparent if you enter "follow" mode and just observe a day in the life of one of your people. You will notice that what they actually do does make sense for them and that maybe the builder you're desperatly waiting on for your new project is busy collecting firewood and food from the Market to care for his/her family and that's why they're not showing up.
Banished might not be a perfect game in its Vanilla form, but what it does set out to do, it does amazingly well. Wether it actually warrants its price tag or you'd rather wait for a sale is for you to decide, but keep in mind that there is a heap of free, high quality content to be had on the Workshop and if you're willing to utilize that, this game can provide you with hundreds of hours of fun, long after that first "vanilla achievement run".
It is also a memorable expirience. I tend to play this genre a lot and for me Banished is easily one of my favorite games within there. In large part due to the fact that - through its survival elements and disaster mechanic - it does not suffer from the classical city builder problem of "once you know what to do, it's always the same". Every town is unique, every town has its own struggles to deal with and eventually its own history.

The "rogue-lite" genre kind of exploded there for a short while and then quickly died down. It's a shame because I feel like it is a genre that hasn't quite reached it's potential. Every genre has that one game or so that dominates it and although are a few strong canidates, there's nothing really that takes the cake. Regardless, here is another entry and a pretty good one at that.
If anyone has ever played Paranautical Activity then you kind of know what to expect here with only a few additional things. So I have mixed feelings about this game because, on the one hand, it draws you right in and is incredibly fun. On the other hand, though, this game has a horrid learning curve and your population will starve to death  multiple times. That's the issue with it.
Pros:
Beautiful af. Music is immersive. Weather is realistic. AI intelligence.
Cons:
Your population will starve to death. A lot. Many years into the game. Or they'll freeze. And I played it over and over and over trying many different approaches but it always ended the same. It's aggravating and wastes lots of time trying to figure out a way around it. Also, there's not any actual "goal," per se, so... it gets boring after a while. That's not unique to this game, though, so it's expected enough and not a huge deal.
Maybe I'm just a sucky player, but I ended up having to watch some Youtube videos of others who figured out how to get past the starving/freezing to death thing.
All in all, I recommend the game, but I say to watch some videos first, otherwise you'll have this population built up and you'll be going along thinking things are going great and then, BAM! your population will quite suddenly surpass your food surplus and they'll all die. -_- Still worth playing, but I'd catch it during a sale.

If you've played Rogue Legacy, this game is like that except a first-person shooter and much less thought put into it and quality.
As I said, this game is a first-person shooter. You enter a pyramid and fight through a series of randomly generated rooms, collecting loot to upgrade your character with when you die. And you will - while regular levels are a tough but fun challenge, some of the bosses are just ridiculous. This is made far worse by the fact that it takes so long to even get to them, and sucks most of the fun from the game.
The in-run upgrade system is definitely no good either - you power up temporarily by picking scrolls up. You don't see what a scroll does until you've picked it up. There are probably two bonuses for every penalty, but some of the penalties are so huge that picking up scrolls can just about end your run if you get one of the worse ones.
Overall, not worth the price or your time. Good idea, but some of the design decisions make you wonder what the devs were thinking.

The first time I sat down to this game on a Saturday morning, I ended up playing it for over 14 hours straight. This has not happened to me in a long while now. Imagine Lovecraft's eldritch, cosmic, non-anthropocentric horror combined with the cheery absurdity of Pratchett, and all this in an environment of Victorian steampunk. The Fallen London setting is marvelous, imaginative and compelling. The same should be said of the actual writing itself, although as a direct side effect of this, one requires a really good command of the English language to fully appreciate the subtleties utilised within. The vocabulary is often baroque and antiquated, but it feels only right.
This is mostly a choose-your-adventure novel with significant RPG elements and a side of trading/exploration (sadly, the trading is not profitable enough to be worthwhile). Be aware that there's not that much combat, when it does happen it's fairly basic and you'll spend a lot of time trying to avoid it anyway. Struggling against hunger, fear and empty fuel tanks all at the same time seems like a hopeless effort at first. But as you probe and learn the game mechanics and memorise opportunities connected to particular locations, it soon becomes manageable.
I feel forced to rag on the pacing, which is probably the game's biggest flaw. It is glacial. And it threatens to scuttle most new players' opinion of the game as if it were the Lifeberg in front of the Titanic. The back and forth travel between ports feels like filler of the worst kind after a while. Consumables are sort of expensive and don't last long. Money is very hard to come by, even with the most advanced strategies. I ended up running the Curator's Quest on several throwaway captains and retiring with 2x50% cash legacies just so I could have enough Echos for ONE. PROPER. GAME. Anyone who knows what that means will also know how long that took. That is very bad design at no fault of my own. So there you are, pinching every penny and Fragment for the exploration Ambition. And then some horrible, unavoidable randomness decides to come along, for example the Curse of Salt. And you are forced to throw away 7 Secrets lest the curse run its unacceptable course and threaten your double legacy, thus your cash nest egg. Nope. This is not my first roguelite, but the game's slow pace makes any and all such setbacks particularly aggravating.

"recommend" is such a weird word - especially in a format where whether or not I recommend this game directly has a an implication about whether or not I like this game. Because I do - I really liked this game. It's one of the powerful things I've encountered in a while. But recommend? It'll have to come with some qualifiers: It made me sad - I cried and now I sort of ache from the experience. The game in uncomfortable and intrusive but it's powerful and beautiful. So I do recommend it but you have to know that I would never say this game is a pleasant experience.
I think anybody who is any kind of creator should play this - at least to understand something about yourself and your own work if not your creative peers. I played this game all in one sitting, and I think that's how it should be played. The headspace it brings you to is an all at once type of experience.
Even if the story is fabricated, which is something I'm still debating, it is powerful. There's an honesty to it - about the lonliness and sadness that come with creation, with art. It leaves you feeling hollowed out and almost horrified but somehow I also feel renewed - energized about my work. I simeltaneously need the longest nap ever to recooperate but I also want to draw until my hands fall off.
At its essential core the game is telling you this - be honest to your art work. The creation has to be FOR you - the minute it becomes not for you, for pleasing other people, is the second you've lost yourself. I'm thankful for this game, despite my tears.

The minute-to-minute play is just so boring, most of your time is spent going in between islands not doing anything. In a story-driven game it is just unbearable to have to grind money to be able to actually progress in items and ships. In twenty hours of gameplay (in merciful mode after dieing twice) I have only upgraded my ship to the Corvette and gotten a few upgrades. The combat is terrible, the rogue-like aspects are poorly thoughtout. I feel like this game should have 2 completely seperate modes. A Story Mode, where the rogue-like elements are cut out and it's much easier to progress in ship and upgrades and you can just relax and enjoy the stories as you go. And then a Rogue-like mode, where they add all of the randomization of islands, cut out the story completely except for random events, and add more enemies to fight with perhaps some form of strategy to the combats instead of just trading hits until someone dies.
In spite of the tremendous writing, I just can't recommend this game. I think the gameplay is just too boring, and worse, it takes too long to grind any kind of money so the boring gameplay is even more obvious because you have to do too much of it to get the awesome writing. Makes me really sad because I wanted to love this game. Revamp the combat system entirely please and tone down on the grind and this game could be expanded on like forever...

BioShock is Irrational's finest offering to date, as well as the swan song for the Irrational brand in a way, since they recently relinquished their longstanding and well-established studio name for the more corporate, faceless tag of 2K Boston and 2K Australia. BioShock is a first-person shooter set in the fantastically unsettling city of Rapture, a metropolis built under the sea by the megalomaniacal Andrew Ryan. Throughout your lengthy stay, you'll find options for combat as intricate and enjoyable as the story and characters are to interpretation, something that only a handful of games can ever claim to offer.
But to call this game simply a first-person shooter, a game that successfully fuses gameplay and narrative, is really doing it a disservice. This game is a beacon. It's one of those monumental experiences you'll never forget, and the benchmark against which games for years to come will, and indeed must, be measured. This isn't merely an evolution of System Shock 2, but a wake-up call to the industry at large. Play this, and you'll see why you should demand something more from publishers and developers, more than all those derivative sequels forced down our throats year after year with only minor tweaks in their formulas. It's a shining example of how it's possible to bring together all elements of game design and succeed to the wildest degree.
Customizing the arsenal.
Things kick off with your plane smacking into the ocean and your character having to take refuge in Rapture to survive. Irrational plays on the conventions of the first-person perspective by thrusting you through experiences that toy with and vastly strengthen that fragile, intangible bond between in-game protagonist and yourself. At times, it forces upon you moments of reflection, which is so important and rare in games, where you contemplate the nature of blindly accepted game conventions, which we can't get into for fear of spoiling things. It lays a relatively straight narrative path for you, but it never feels linear, a result of the gameplay as much as the narrative.
The target in BioShock, Andrew Ryan, is anything but a prototypical villain. He's a man of bottomless ambition who built a city under the sea, obsessed with the idea of what makes a man, what differentiates a man from a slave. He's the Randian hero, a man who holds his own creative vision above all else, and he's Rodion Raskolnikov's exceptional person, someone who can be excused for committing crimes to achieve a goal--and he knows it. His vision, Rapture, is clearly a colossal failure. The driving force behind the game is your quest to discover why this man's alluring vision of an artistic utopia failed so completely and why you've stumbled upon it. Even though Ryan spits out what seems to resemble totalitarian propaganda, you can't help but sympathize with him. He has alluring ideas, speaks them with conviction, and comes off as a sympathetic visionary despite his severe eccentricities.
As you continue through Rapture, you'll discover it speaks to the nature of what a single-player game is--why do we choose to play a game that isn't online, where you can't interact with others? Like reading a novel, it's to form your own impressions, to see the same events, hear the same words, and come away with a unique viewpoint. The thematic blending and twining of BioShock's personalities is so powerful, it acts like any good book or movie, assaulting you with its ideas, popping into your thoughts when you least expect it, and broadening your understanding of what a game can achieve. Instead of painting Good and Evil across the foreheads of Rapture's denizens with a neon brush, Irrational gave everyone murky motives, much like the shadowed, soaking environments you're constantly plodding through, or the blurred vision you get after walking under one of Rapture's ubiquitous waterfalls.
Hey guy, might want to check your pants!
It's the little ideas that pop up from time to time that make this world so believable: the piano plinks that resonate as you browse menu options; the guitars you can actually play randomly scattered around Rapture; the way every room is realistically constructed reflects both the heights to which Rapture managed to climb as well as the decadence and sense of voracious, selfish entitlement that brought it smashing down. You'll hear some of the voice-overs muse, "Why do they wear the masks? Maybe there's a part of them that remembers how they used to be, how they used to look, and they're ashamed." Little bits like that get tossed at you, and you don't necessarily have to absorb them--they're not essential to plot or anything, but they're instrumental in making BioShock as immersive as it is.
The game is broken up into large sections, each separated by load times. Don't worry; these aren't load times like in Half-Life 2 where the game pauses unexpectedly. Instead, the load times are logically placed and never jarringly interrupt the experience or mar the immersion. Each section comes with its own cast of NPCs who aren't mere stage bosses--oftentimes you don't even engage them in combat. Instead, you are battling their ideals and their insecurities, grappling with their motivations as much as the splicer minions who so frequently assail you.

My feelings on Limbo are conflicted. On the one hand, I feel that the game overall is quite good. The puzzles are well done and the game is fairly entertaining throughout, but I also feel there are a few issues that hold the game back.
My first major gripe with the game is its minimalist story. The game is supposed to be about a boy trying to find his sister, but the game just begins with you waking up in a field and then progressing along a 2D plane. There is no introduction as to who you are or why you are here. One could argue that this leaves the player to create his or her own story, and normally that would be ok, but the game gives you absolutely nothing to base your thoughts on. The only reason I knew the game was supposed to be about finding the boy’s sister is because the description on Steam says so. If you want to leave interpretation up to the player, that is fine, but at least give them something to go off of. I have no context as to why I’m going through these trials or why there are people/creatures trying to kill me. It feels frustrating to me as a player because I want some context. The setting for this game is fantastic and I would love to know more about it, but the game offers no explanation.
On a somewhat related note, the game offers nothing in the way of instruction, either. Not even at the very beginning of the game. To find out the controls, you have to open the pause menu and check them out yourself. There is a growing complaint that video games hold the player’s hand too much, but this game does the exact opposite. You basically have to find out everything yourself as you go. For me, this lead to some frustrating moments where the solution to a puzzle was pretty simple, but I missed it for so long because I didn’t know I could move that object etc. The protagonist does move his arm a bit when he is in range of something he can touch, but that does not show up when running. As a result, you may run past the solution to a puzzle a few times before finally getting it.
My final gripe with the game is its use of trial and error. On your first playthrough of this game, you will find yourself dying… a lot. The game uses trial and error as the primary means of solving puzzles. You’ll often find yourself dying to things that you didn’t know could kill you. The player is forced to run through things and die several times before he can fully understand how things work. This can get pretty frustrating after a short amount of time. These deaths feel cheap and unfair. Deaths should serve to punish the player when he makes a mistake. Instead, there is a sense that there is no way to get through the game without dying unless you know exactly what is going to happen and where it will happen.
All that being said, the game is still deserving of praise. First and foremost, the art style in this game is fantastic. The usage of black and white is incredibly well done and creates an interesting world that is fairly grim. It fits the game world which is hostile and brimming with evil. Using a limited color palette, the developers create a world that is surprisingly engrossing. It is easy to get lost in the game as you walk around and wonder what these places are and who (or what) lives there.
Additionally, the puzzles are pretty solid as well. I’m not exactly a puzzle game buff by any means, but I found the difficulty to be reasonable (barring one or two exceptions). They are complex enough to require some thought, but not too complex for the average player. I was able to solve most of them after some critical thinking. This area does suffer a bit from the game’s minimalistic approach though. The exceptions I refer to are frustrating because it usually involved doing something that I had no idea I could. The lack of any indication left me scratching my head until I got so frustrated I had to consult a guide.
Finally, the art style is awesome. The world is portrayed as fairly negative and hostile, and a simple black and white color scheme really helps convey that. It’s another factor that helps immerse the player in the world of the game. The contrast between light and dark has some interesting elements, and are even used in puzzle solving a bit.
Overall, I’d say that, despite the problems I found in the game, it was a quite enjoyable experience. I dwell so much on those negative aspects, but I feel that they hold the game back from truly being a masterpiece. It has so much potential, and I just wish the developers would have done things just a bit differently. That would have taken the game from “great” to “fantastic.”

I've been taking the time to think about BioShock. On one hand, there is the "Cult of Shock 2" that retain a savage disdain for BioShock because of it's extremely obvious narrative and gameplay similarities to System Shock 2. On the other hand, there are gamers that reasonably acknowledge that BioShock's elements are derivitive of System Shock 2 and claim that the elements were streamlined for a newer generation. I know BioShock fans that have given copious amounts of evidence and suggestions to back this up, and I don't necessarily agree or disagree with that. That is a matter of prefrence.
When someone takes the time to deconstruct and analyze System Shock 2, you'll find that it is a deeply and intracately woven role-playing experience where the player needed to become familliar with varying amounts of important elements to create their characters, specialize in specific statistics, and
as an introduction to it all and
to experience the game properly. Many critics praised these very aspects that made System Shock 2 one of the greatest games ever created and the sales were
.
When someone takes the time to deconstruct and analyze BioShock, you'll find a game that has that overall feeling of intracacy laced within the narrative with more understandable gameplay elements that were designed, in principle, to appeal to a large audience. There are elements that can be considered RPG elements and the game had the basis of it's core gameplay display itself as a suspense game in a few areas and a balls-to-the-wall action FPS in most others. The gaming community—especially the parts of it that sided with the "Cult of Shock 2"—was split and BioShock became 2K Games' most profitable franchise at that time.
When you take a look at the bigger picture, System Shock 2 and BioShock are two completely different games in principle and two very similar games in execution. When you get down to it, the "dumbing down" of System Shock 2's qualities was enforced, not by a corporate publisher or a greedy fat man in a black suit, but by the developers' own desire to make their baby, System Shock 2, more understandable. If you take the time to search up some interviews and stuff for System Shock 2 featuring Ken Levine and Looking Glass Studios (which is now 2K Games), you can tell that System Shock 2 was their pride and joy, and it must have been devastating when it became ignored by the central PC community.
To that extent, I can understand more reasonably (and even
) a few of my previous issues with this title. I used to have a
hatred for this game based on System Shock 2, and my previous review that I wrote for this game was an over-glorified comparison to System Shock 2. I'm not going to make the same mistake here in this rewrite, as I've come to the conclusion that to judge BioShock by System Shock 2 would be very unfair, as I think any fan of System Shock 2 would probably agree when I say that System Shock 2 is the better of the two titles.
BioShock, on its own, is an
game. I don't think it's the
that the gaming industry seems to think it is, but I don't think that it's the
that the "Cult of Shock 2" thinks it is. It does a few things right and it does a lot of things wrong, and in the very end it's up to the fans of System Shock 2 to decide whether or not they want to take BioShock as its own experience. As one of the
fans of SS2 out there, I'm reviewing this game from that perspective.
The gameplay elements found in BioShock all consist of unorthodox forms of first-person shooting and RPG elements
. This game borrows implicitly from SS2's horror elements by including a few scenes that really do peak the player's intrest, but the attempts at horror are completely futile. The game can't be called a survival game because it isn't one, and resource management is way too easy, even on difficulty settings over Normal. These sections are far and few between as most of the game plays as a balls-to-the-wall action shooter. However, these sections are mediated by fluent pace changes every so often. Whereas other games from 2007 would often have you just shooting at everything coming by, this game takes a slower, more methodical approach to let you appreciate the vibe of what you're doing and really take in the enviorment as well as the NPCs populating it. The NPCs are hopeless drug addicts; you're a killer, and you feel like one...except when you deal with Big Daddies and Little Sisters.
Despite everything else wrong with the game,
, and anyone who tells you otherwise hasn't played this game. The Little Sisters, on the other hand, are the *lowest* rung on the morality ladder. Essentailly, the Little Sisters are little girls that you can either choose to save or harvest for Adam. You get more Adam for harvesting them and less for saving them. If you save all of them, you get the good ending, and if you harvest just ONE of them, you get the bad ending. Without spoiling anything, they both mean absolutely nothing and you can just watch them on YouTube. Without any character development, killing or saving the Little Girls becomes based on the reward. Would you rather have less Adam or more Adam? Exactly.
The gunplay is very unsatisfying. I'm going to be a hypocrite for a few characters and say that SS2
had unsatisfying gunplay, but you almost never used your gun because ammo was low and most of the gunplay was backed up by the horror elements of the game. Here, the weak sounding weapons and overexaggerated reactions result in gunplay that feels like a chore to sort through. There are moments when it's satisfying to take down a Big Daddy, but that's satisfaction from the
and not the actual gunplay.
Besides shooting, BioShock includes two performance enhancing bodily modifications called "Plasmids" and "Gene Tonics". Plasmids are essentially powers you recieve from completing missions (and you can always buy them at the vending machine). Gene Tonics are the RPG Elements
numbers I was writing about earlier. They are pretty much character enhancements that set up your character to adopt certain play styles. For example, you can put together an invisibility tonic and a melee damage tonic to take on the role of a stealth assassin. For the game's other shortcomings, that's pretty cool.
The game also features hacking mini-games in the form of circuit-based puzzles. You connect a set of pipes so water can successfully travel from one end of the circuit to another. While doing this, the game pauses and you always will have the right pieces at the right time, killing tension. If they really wanted to include some much needed tension, then they could have accelerated the current of the water whenever a piece was misplaced, or they could have provided a certain amount of each directional pipe, causing some inevitable ambiguation as to where to construct a direct path. They also could have made it so there was a tangible loss with each failure. There is no tangible loss when dying. There are Vita Chambers, which are essentially respawn points that make the game much easier than it already is, and then there's just going
.
Like I said, I don't hate BioShock, nor do I carry the attitude I once had towards it like the "Cult of Shock 2". I don't think it's a revolutionary work of art either. I think it's okay. Not terrible, but not great. It's great in some areas and abhorrent in others, and what's there good is great and what's bad is horrible.

In it's current release state, I'm hard pressed to recommend this to anyone in regards to fans of the series or as a general interest to city and econ simulation et al. Without delving into past Tropicos too much, these title pretty much abolished everything decent that was good about the past games and while I wanted to strive to figure out the best way to win and be efficient in Tropico 3 and 4, I find myself logging off in frustration a lot with the fifth installment.
Don't get me wrong, there is a lot of good and a ton of potential for future DLC's (hate to think that maybe this was a focal point, but it's quickly becoming industry standard). Unfortunately, the bad and the outright annoying is so prevalent that the whole experience gets ruined pretty quickly.
Rebels often seem to rebel without any reason. Protests are totally arbitrary and "negotiating" with protestors oftentimes has you build or create something to contend with one of the few problems you're probably not having. Construction costs are astronomical. Power plants are very confusing and either buildings need a ton of electricity to run and maintain optimum efficiency, or the power plant itself is severly inefficient given the amount of cost to build and maintain them.
Healthcare, schools, and entertainment are a beast of their own. While a single newspaper or television seems more than enough to land me at sufficient levels for happiness, I'm finding that multiple buildings that should have the same effect as a liberty increasing building in a different capacity don't actually do anything, or the difference is so minute that I couldn't even tell.
These things all strike me as bugs, but with the lack of feedback from the developer it's hard to maintain that allusion forever. Essentially, I'm trying to save you money. Even if you're dying to play this, or something has piqued your interest, just wait it out. Eventually I think most of the issues will be fleshed out, but, for all intents and purposes, buying this is equivalent to something that only works some of the time.

An unfortunate case of style over substance in my opinion. The game mechanics themselves, specifically movement and platforming, are utilitarian and functional yet none of them are particularly well done, and there is never a significant incentive to provide a consistent drive for the player to proceed. I never really felt engaged or made to care about the character himself or various yet short lived scenarios presented by the game.
To its credit the game does have a rather unnerving atmosphere from time to time, and the art style is unique and aesthetically pleasing, but for me personally visuals alone are not enough to carry the game as a piece of interactive entertainment in terms of a recommendation. I even surprised myself by only playing in extremely short bursts due to sheer boredom, something I would not expect of myself and that is magnified further due to the prevalence of the game's short length.
When considering LIMBO and its (optimistically speaking and from a completionist standpoint) 5 hour experience, this alone should speak volumes with respect the lack of interesting and engaging content from a gameplay and narrative perspective. It may be an arguably artistically driven catalyst for indie games in the eyes of mass media and at first impressions, but in terms of player involvement and value proposition it is unfortunately lacking, indeed in terms of both quantity and quality.

This is the second instalment in the Assassin's Creed Chronicles series, and it's a decent follow-up to the first part, China. Like the other games, it's essentially Ubisoft's take on Mark of the Ninja, but not nearly as freeform or as good as that game.
This instalment is more colourful than the previous one, with an interesting setting and protagonist. The story is still as naff as usual (it's an Assassin's Creed game, after all), but the plot is just an excuse to make things happen, after all. For the most part, the game is challenging in the right way, more of a puzzle at times than an actual stealth game, but some of the unfortunate tendencies from the third instalment (Russia) are rearing their ugly heads in this one.
Russia is an absolute exercise in frustration, and India, especially in the second half, veers into this territory, like the objective where you have two-and-a-half minutes or so to clear a large area of 10 guards, or some of the chase sequences. Yes, chase sequences. Again. Fortunately, unlike Russia, the chase sequences tend to be mercifully short, with a checkpoint right at the beginning (usually *after* the brief cinematic), so that restarting them isn't nearly as head-bangingly annoying as in the third (and so far final) instalment in this series. There are still a few that will make you pull your hair out, though, and the sequence with the wall of light chasing you is almost as annoying as some of the most frustrating parts of Russia.
I tentatively recommend India, but encourage you to check out China first, if you haven't played it already. If you have played China, this should be a no-brainer, but be aware that there's some parts that are quite frustrating and annoying. Skip the third instalment, Russia, since it's frustrating rubbish (despite the excellent presentation). If you only want to pick one game in this series, go with China.
Or better yet, play Mark of the Ninja if you haven't, since that game was obviously the source of inspiration for the Assassin's Creed Chronicles games and it's superior to them in virtually every way. Seriously, Mark of the Ninja is excellent.

Amazing game, really underrated.
Most earlier critisism of the gun-play and lack of immersion have been addressed, leaving the game in a very good place.
Pros;
-Plenty of weapons to cycle through during runs, with some good ones to strive to get
-Great selection of scrolls (which function as randomly generated buffs/debuffs) which make every run unique
-Decent enemy variety, letting each weapon have it's place in a fight
-Amazing room variety, so there's plenty to explore, with hidden chests in almost every room if you keep an eye out
-Really nice soundtrack
Cons;
-Poor balancing of weapons is a major issue right now, nothing game breaking but there's lots of weapons you won't even glance at if you are playing to win
-Odd hit registration for the player, leading to some confusing deaths or extremetly frustraitng moments
-Repetitve, though obviously so because it's a Rouge-like. Still, if you want thousands of hours due to constant content, don't expect this game to be that for you.
-Did I mention the balancing issues? Right now the real meta is to not unlock any of the favors (active abilities) in the skill tree because they all have their own weapons and once you buy them, the weapons are added into the random drops in-game. This is bad because a lot of the really good weapons are not attributted to the favors (understandably so, because then they'd be a must pick) and if you simply refuse to buy the favors, you massively increase your chances of something like an SFG9000 or a Rocket launcher dropping.
Overall, the game is still insanely fun to play, and the new infinite mode really allows you to have fun with a good run.
tl;dr 9/10, Cons aren't large and the game itself is very fun.

"recommend" is such a weird word - especially in a format where whether or not I recommend this game directly has a an implication about whether or not I like this game. Because I do - I really liked this game. It's one of the powerful things I've encountered in a while. But recommend? It'll have to come with some qualifiers: It made me sad - I cried and now I sort of ache from the experience. The game in uncomfortable and intrusive but it's powerful and beautiful. So I do recommend it but you have to know that I would never say this game is a pleasant experience.
I think anybody who is any kind of creator should play this - at least to understand something about yourself and your own work if not your creative peers. I played this game all in one sitting, and I think that's how it should be played. The headspace it brings you to is an all at once type of experience.
Even if the story is fabricated, which is something I'm still debating, it is powerful. There's an honesty to it - about the lonliness and sadness that come with creation, with art. It leaves you feeling hollowed out and almost horrified but somehow I also feel renewed - energized about my work. I simeltaneously need the longest nap ever to recooperate but I also want to draw until my hands fall off.
At its essential core the game is telling you this - be honest to your art work. The creation has to be FOR you - the minute it becomes not for you, for pleasing other people, is the second you've lost yourself. I'm thankful for this game, despite my tears.

I'll open the review by stating plainly: I quite enjoyed my time with this game (though got bored with it after about 17 hours, YMMV). I am giving the game a "not recommended" rating specifically because the developer has chosen to make the VR version of the game Oculus exclusive. Hardware exclusivity of the sort console gamers have long since accepted as "normal" is NOT ok. It does NOT belong on PC. And I will NOT be supporting this game, any offshoots of it, or the developer unless they change their policy. It's extremely disappointing to see a promising and yes, quite innovative, indie developer take such a consumer-unfriendly route.
That said, I should try to give at least a passing review of the game. SUPERHOT is the most innovative shooter I've played in years (truly). The "story" or "campaign" is odd, and quite short - the real meat of the game lies in the challenge modes. As you probably know if you're reading this review, the central conceit of this game is that time only moves when you move. That's mostly true - time moves at a crawl when you're not moving. As a gameplay gimmick it works quite well. Using the slomo mechanic, you can chain together improbably amazing feats such as throwing a cup at a dude to disarm him, punching a gun out of another dude's hand, grabbing that gun out of midair to shoot the first guy, then dodging three shotgun blasts from another guy so you can grab the katana from the wall (where you threw it a earlier) to cut him in half. Gameplay is really solid and a lot of fun, is what I'm saying.
Aesthetically, the game knows what its trying to do and achieves it. The art style is more about making information easily visible and creating a cool-looking world than maximizing visual fidelity, but it works. Look at the screenshots or gameplay video if you want to know more about the art style. I dig it, personally.
Performance-wise, I'm somewhat mixed. I run a GTX 760, which is a bit old but should still have zero problems maintaining 60 fps on a game with graphics such as these. Most of the time, that is the case - unless I'm using more than one monitor. For some reason, even though only one of my monitors (the one I'm running the game on) is even plugged into the graphics card, I get very low FPS and stutter whenever I try to play the game with secondary monitors enabled. This doesn't happen often, but I have noticed it in other games such as Enter the Gungeon. In any case, just know that you could run into that problem. Game seems to run fine (for me at least) if I stay in single monitor configuration.
All that said - I'd encourage you to look elsewhere for your purchasing decisions as this developer has shown themselves to be more concerned with making a quick buck than doing what is right for consumers. Hardware exclusivity does not belong on the PC platform. Period. I won't lie, it's a good game - but I'd encourage you to not support these kinds of practices. I'll edit this part out if the dev changes their policy on exclusivity, of course.

In this review I will be discussing the indie puzzle adventure game Pocket Kingdom which was released December 8th of 2016. Pocket Kingdom is developed by 08 Games and published by Plug In Digital, and WhisperGames.
In Pocket Kingdom you play as the pilot on a hot air balloon. While flying through the air searching for the floating islands, you stumble upon a hidden city amongst the clouds—where you crash land. After crashing you meet with locals who leave hints as to the location of your crashed zeppelin and give you clues about the divine secrets and mysteries of the “Pocket Kingdom” along with other useful bits of information. From here the game takes off and it’s up to the player to solve puzzles, explore the many different side scrolling levels and find the keys and other items to open doors and progress further. Another thing to note is that talking to most (if not all) of the NPCs is highly helpful as many of them have something to say about either the storyline, where to go, your crash location and even tips on how to traverse puzzles. The only thing that was a bit off-putting about this type of talk to everyone, explore everything playstyle was that at times I felt a bit lost, or unsure of where I was to go or who was who and what was where. This isn’t so much the case when it comes to the mechanics of the game itself. There are sign posts throughout the game’s levels which offer bits of helpful information and help the player understand how to use tools and other items. However, I would note that as a player, if you feel lost at the beginning of the game, that’s quite normal given the amount of lore the game throws at you right off the bat. If that’s the case, I would suggest that you continue playing and pay attention to the NPCs dialogue as it can be very helpful in understanding where you are and where you need to go next.

It is art (just not very good art). Whether its story is true or fiction, following an artist's arc with a medium has to be more interesting.  Staring at parts of projects and doodles isn't fun when the story is more meta than substance. It was impossible to relate to the characters or lack thereof and that struggle was crystalized when we come to the conclusion that "oh... the premise is that these non-games, 'interactive' scenes aren't really for us..."  Its biggest sin story-wise is that it didn't have the balls to even attempt to get to the 'why' - I understand the creative process is the hero and villian here, the elixor, bomb and princess - but give us something to sink our teeth into. So then I blink, it's over, I try to think about it a bit more and conclude by comparing the experience to the finished products of artists who want my attention and money, or refuse to pretend like they don't, and realize I just wasted mine.
With an art projectic, you have no right to complain about bugs - bugs are part of it, of course. But this lack of artist ownership is a new low.  What's worse, it plays on the 'found art' idea meaning no one is responsible, certainly not the publisher of this. And who am I to judge - this whole thing isn't even for me according to the storyline.  All this helps me not care, which is the opposite of what I want in a linear story-only, non-puzzle, puzzle walker-thingy.  The more I think about this even being real or a real re-creation, the less I like that they are charging so much for it, quite frankly.  Then, if it's entirely fiction, it's just a con job of an art project to justify shotty production and the disturbing sucking sound of the complete vaccuum of idea or narrative whatsoever.
"From the creator of 'The Standley Parable'"(which I love btw - and why I bought TBG to... begin with). So lemme think... Is TBG awkward and weird? Sure.  But it's so much more depressing than exciting and pales in comparison to the relationship established with an aware narrator instead of the oppose.  I know if you put 'prison simulator' on the description that's a bit of a spoiler, but that's perhaps better than 'The Standley Parable... without choices.'  If it's a prequel to TSP, then it should have said so, maybe that would have helped?

I just get sick of non-sense rather easily.  In fact, I'm not even slightly interested in clicking on 'Community' to investigate if Coda is real or not... I just don't care.

On the one hand, I have to reccomend this game. It's free, a decent bullet hell SHMUP, and kinda fun. The music is fine, the pixel-art aesthetic is cute, individual character designs seems interesting by themselves (especially the final bosses), and the lives system specifically is something I find fairly interesting from a developer standpoint. Also, the scoring system is decent, which helps.
BUT BOY IS THIS A FLAWED GAME. The biggest problem here is the bombs/aura system. On the one hand, dying in this game is fairly forgiving; in general, the patterns are easier than a lot of other games, and it gives you a short period of time to bomb once getting hit, like in Touhou, so you don't lose a life. The problem is that once you die, your aura doesn't reset, meaning that once you start dying and have no bombs left, chances are you will keep dying until you have to use a continue. Combined with the fact that your power level will decrease every time one dies, and I found myself having to slog for almost a minute through a single pattern until the timer FINALLY ran out. At that point, that just overly punishes dying, and leaves barely any room for player mistakes. The player is basically required to learn how to play perfectly.
That being said, one can practice every single stage on any difficulty using the "Training" mode, without having to unlock them first, so players can actually learn how to play perfectly.
BUT, that just leads into the other problems I have with this game. While the dev seems to understand how to make good, challenging, patterns, they are SUPER generic, especially if you've played other bullet hell games. I found myself saying "Oh, this is Cirno, just modified a little" or "Huh, that looks an awful lot like Mokou". They feel slapped together and inconsistent, without any definable traits that can be given to the characters or their patterns. Speaking of characters, the game barely has any definable ones. The characters just seem thrown together from a grab-bag of different stories, and they have barely any defining characteristics, including their bullet patterns or their music. I admire that the game seems to try something a little different, adding a surrealist bent to it's story (SPOILERS: The overarching theme of facing/dodging one's greatest fear), but I don't beleive that that was intentional. There's just too much inconsistency in the aesthetics and the story for that to be true.
In short, as a "Touhou-lite" game that you can play just for fun, this comes with a tentative reccomendation, especially as it is a free game. Just be aware that the flaws are rather first-gamey, and that it's not as engaging or coheisive as a main-line Touhou or any other bullet hell.

The tutorial misses a LOT, and you quickly find yourself wondering what to do next, what to focus on, and how the mechanics of the game work. Many problems are found in the first 30 minutes of playing (e.g. "hire X person to enable upgrade feature". Hire that person, game still says "hire this person to enable this feature"). Controls are frustrating (Can't easily move people between desks, have to do 1 at a time, which becomes increasingly lengthy when your offices are jam packed. This includes other micro-managing such as schedules, very cumbersome and frustrating design), the reports are semi-pointless and unhelpful, many offer no useful information and they also don't link to in-game objects (can see a report of employee happiness, but cant click to view employee, you must remember their name and scourer through your offices trying to find them). This game lacks a lot, and while it could be an excellent sim with a great and fun concept, it is poorly designed and bites off more than it can chew. Spend your money elsewhere, there are many other office sims which perform far better.

Once one of your characters die you can pick up on the same exact world with a new one.  So you can work from life to life finding equipment your previous person had dropped or gathered.

I got the first episode free on the Windows store yesterday. I am on Windows 10 and play with a plugged in Xbox One Controller.  I enjoyed the first episode so much I purchased the game on steam that has all the episodes. First, the game ran great on the version from the Windows store. The Steam game I actually paid for had some issues. I play at 1440p and the Steam game graphics looked terrible and I could not read the text well. A little searching and I found a solution for my graphics issue. Go in Steam apps, common, batman the Telltale Series and right click on Batman_win7 and select Properties. Click on Compatability tab. Click the box to "Run this program in compatabilty mode" and select Windows 8. Also in the same tab click the box "Disable display scaling on high DPS settings". I was enjoying this game. The music's good, the graphics look great, the new trade system is nice... But then I hit a wall: The game will not load past the loading screen on a campaign mission. I go to the forums, and other people are having the same issue. There's a workaround, but it's not working for everyone. And there's no official response from the developers on when or if they intend on fixing it. Other heavily advertised features of the game, such as Multiplayer, are locking up on players frequently. Oh, and it doesn't have a save functioon, so even if they do happen to make it some ways into the game, they gotta start from scratch if they have to leave. Still others complain that the game won't even start. Again, there are workarounds, but it should not be incumbent upon the consumer to find fixes for a "finished" game that was just so recently released.
New games have bugs, I get it. I can understand the traffic glitch that forces your teamsters to get stuck, unable to transport  commodities to the docks for export and causing your economy to plunge. That's annoying, but it's an easy fix in game once you recognize it. I cna understand how trade ships might just magically disappear from your inventory, preventing you from utilizing them. Annoying, but you still at least have trade ships, and the computer freighters still come to export, so that's more of a minor inconvenience. I can even forgive them for forcing you to accept new immigrants at a steady speed even when you've indicated in your Constitution that the borders will be closed.
But I can not understand how the developers decided it a releaseable product when players are unable to complete Sandbox missions because the game doesn't register that they've accomplished the primary objective on the mission. Or how they determined a final release should have a game breaking bug, the likes of which I haven't seen in a game of this budget since Big Rigs. I guess a 30% success rate on multiplayer matches making it through era changes was high enough by Kalypso's standards. And maybe that's why they didn't figure the mode needed saves; because no one makes it far enough.
I want to recommend this game. It's got good potential; even though they reduced the total amount of buildings, and therefore functionality, from previous Tropicos; or put a heavier emphasis on the military's role without expanding on the mechanics behind the military units, forcing you to watch the horribly programmed AI duke it out and hope that your side wins.
But at its current stage, I can not and will not recommend this unfinished garbage to anyone.

This is pretty much a multiplayer only game, reviewing it as such is crucial.  If you're looking for a single player experience, look elsewhere.  That being said, this game is amazing.  RO2 is a modern looking, realistic WW2 FPS.  Though it started out with more than a few bugs, it has been updated and polished quite nicely over the years.  Before I get into details, I'll also include that you will get to experience both the Eastern front as well as the island battles of the Pacific Theatre, easily one of the most unique features about this game.
Gameplay is quite fluid.  Moving around the map, crouching, sprinting, all feel quite good and realistic.  Sounds, weapons, chatter, maps, and skins all create an immersive atmosphere.  The horrors of war will be on full display the minute you step into a populated server and you're going to love every second of it.
Though the learning curve of RO2 is moderate to high for most, which I personally love, this is ultimately a game of realism.    You will most certainly die from one well placed shot, but you can also do alot of damage with one placed shot yourself.  Though, one man can do quite a bit of damage to the enemy if he knows what he's doing, this game stresses teamwork tactics and sticking close to your squad mates.  Getting into cap zones, and picking guys off from there is the name of the game.  Working with your teammates and coordination is key.  You won't find much in regards to Rambo'ing around the map as it simply won't work unless your an experienced veteran.
Easily one of the more realistic WW2 shooters out currently.  I've played this game since launch, and over the last few years, the game has made great strides towards being very, very good.  With the most recent update, which included the release of the MG42, battles on the Eastern front feel about ten times more intense.  Worth every penny, would buy again.

Whilst officially a sequal to the Tropico franchise, the game iteslf feels at times more like a reboot with the amount of changes made. Nonetheless, all changes made feel for the better and while the game istself is not without bugs as of launch, it seems to run fine overall.
The dynasty system is well implemented and gives an incentive for multiple playthroughs . The fact that your fully upgraded dynasty can be used in multiplayer matches helps add an interesting, even competetive dynamic to things. Though multiplayer itself could use a bit of polish (but, as it is the first time it has been implemented in the franchise, it gets a pass).
Military units and buildings have been changed significantly, as have the way battles work. Your military units are no longer simply all the soldiers on your island, but a select number of "squads" whose numbers and types are based on the functioning military building on the island. There is also the added feature of changing targets in battle, leading rebels, uprisings, mutinous soldiers, and even invasion forces (which may now be fought off, albiet only with a strong military) to choose muliple, and differing target during an engagement, eventually leading up to an attack on your palace. However, the introduction of tanks and a Tropican air force allow new methods of handling those who are not staisfied with your benevolent rule.
The singleplayer game is much more challenging and dynamic than in the past, as well as much longer. The eras not only extend the length of the average sandbox game, but also make it so that at no point can you get too comfortable with dealing with economic and political situations (a problem that made prior games quickly become dull). Each era has its own issues to address, but also new ways to address them (and previous problems). For instance, the colonial period is more or less a race against the clock to declare independence before your gubernatorial mandate expires, while the Cold War will see you plunged into a tug-of-war between the US and USSR, with Tropico serving as the rope.
Gone, however, are the humorous election speeches and dozen or so characters that made the humor of the old games stand out. That is not to say that the humor is absent, but don't expect it to not be as omnipresent as in previous titles, as more focus seems to have been put into new mechanics and gameplay, and less on hiring VA's for voicework.
Another issue is the lack of customization options as of launch. The new customization screen for your dynasty allows you to alter the outfits and appearance of your up to seven dynasty members, allowing for greater variety and reflection of whatever imposed personalities you dictate (no pun intended), this even includes cusstomizing the color of said outfits, a completely new customization option from previous games. However, as of launch, there appears to be barely (if even) seven outfit choices for male and female characters. This is gratly disappointing compared to previous titles in the series, which allowed for a variety of possibilites in the look and feel of characters.
Also of note is that while the graphical style of the game has been altered somewhat from Tropico 3 and 4, do not expect too much improvement. Buildings look to be rendered at about the same quality as before, as do the enviornments and characters. This may be because of the scheduled Xbox 360 launch (they had to keep it within the limits of the console most likely). Though one notable improvement graphically is the inclusion of a grid overlay, which makes city planning much easier and more efficident.
All in all, Tropico 5 (or simply "Tropico," according to the title screen) is a new direction for the series, with several new feartures added and refined. Yet all these many changes seem to be for the better overall, alowing for a more dynamic and challenging experience whilst still maintaining the overall humor and atmosphere of previous titles. A bit of polish and refinement is needed, but it will most likely be covered in coming patches. It is disappointing that many options for buildings and customization shall likely be held back for DLC purposes, but thus is the way of our times.
I give them game four out of five stars, for its number of (good) changes, but leaving one for the necessity of minor AI fixes and lack of certain promised features (like encountering tribes) and for a significant lack of building types compared to prior titles like Tropico 4 ( a disappointing things for a "city-builder"). I highly recommend this title for any fans of the Tropico series, and also as a good starting point for those who have yet to play but show interest in the franchise. Overall, a strong entry into this classic series that serves as a breadth of fresh air.

Playing through this so far I've found several good and bad things about Tropico 5, let's get the non-game affecting stuff out first.

First the music compared to 3 and 4 is boring, instead of the super upbeat music that kept me up before, now seems to put me to sleep.

Second The customization is lacking compared to let's just say 4, outfits are lacking along with some other things that really need to be better.

Third the new interface is nice, apart from the build menu, which is way too big while having a lot of empty space in it.

Fourth is the island condition overlays, this grid is nowhere near as easy and use as from older games, making planning harder than it should be.

My biggest part, the voice acting sucks, I'll be 100% blunt, I don't know if they were going for a much more realistic feel or what, but most of the jokes and writing for it, is really boring and flat out lame. Plus your new advisors are bland to me. Apart from the new communist advisor whom is muuuuch better.

Now the game play and all that.

My biggest complaint is the lack of the customization for your Character, yes the dynasty thing is a good idea, since having one guy live through colonial times all the way to modern is kinda unrealistic. However they should of taken this a step further, your first guy/girl should have skills more related to the period, and be able to fully customize the names and the other non-game effecting settings. Same for the new members, they get more skills based on the era. If you played the older Tropicos you know how much your character could affect things, in Tropico 5 you might as well forget it, since it's not a part anymore really, Dynasty members are really just free mangers and used for events.

The gameplay is solid though, anyone who ever touched Tropico 3-4 will understand how this game will work right off the bat. The gameplay is smooth and fluid, the era system is a very nice change of pace from always being in the cold war era. Researching new buildings and the like is also a interesting feature, but they should of maybe branched it so you can effect your island in the long run.

Now will this game turn out better with DLC? I hope so, since this game has a lot going for it, and if it's in a sale pick it up, it's a good time killer if you want something new to play. As for me, I'll wait until the first few DLCs come out before I'll give it a full yes or no. Since it seems they still got some bugs to work out.

But yes pick it up when it hits a sale, it'll be worth it in the end, as you'll suck many many hours into this game, even though I may not care for it as much as the older ones, I'm still happy I got it.

Finally a meaningful update to the series which isn't in forms of additional buildings or edicts. The 'era system' feel like a nice change, and gives the game a political upgrade for each era. Start as a governer, then deal with the Allies & Axis during World Wars, etc.
The research system is a nice addition which breathes life into the series. Perhaps it feels a bit light, but it's a change that most people who like the series will surely embrace. Hopefully we'll get more of it down the road.
The new Constitution system completements the Edict system quite nicely. Although I've experienced some strange effects from the constitutional options, it does give you power to shape your regime to your linking.
The new Trade system allows you to set up contracts with the existing world powers and supplement your income. I was a bit taken aback how people are more keen on exporting than importing, but I still managed to score some really good contracts which greatly increased the value of the trade goods.
Although the era system is a nice addition, I was a bit sad to see that if you finished your era faster than intended. The next era warps you to a set start date. So there are gaps in your timeline which would have been nice to simply allow you to progress through eras at your own pace without messing with the date.
The family system is interesting, but takes away of the more expansive good/bad trait system of previous games. I was also a bit sad to see that rulers didn't really seem to age, and for some extremely odd reason my first daughter/son's avatar had super wrinkly faces as if they were in their 80's. Made me laugh more than it was annoying.
To my fellow micromanagers out there, there is some form of streamlining to parts of the game. You no longer control wages and instead set the budget of a building which will in turn chage the level of income of it's employees. (poor, rich, etc.) I was a bit disapointed in that, since you could have interesting income discrepencies and use it to keep people loyal. Now that bulding effiency is also tied into the budget, you might end up wanting to put everything at max budget just to get the efficiency increase.
The new Almenac generally does a good job at giving decent oversight of your island and it's various statistcal information. Wealth, politcal factions, etc. They took a step away from having little people icons and went for a name/value based list. This allows for greater insight with less clicks, but it's a bit less cute. I'll take the better oversight instead.
I've never really played scenarios so I can't really comment on that, but the sandbox is quite fun to play with. And the new constitution system can lead to perhaps a greater replay value to try and use the various options which aren't all politically correct. :)

The very first thing I do after installing any Assassin's Creed game is to change the key bindings. Binding Sprint/High Profile to Right Mouse and Left Hand to Shift has got to be the weirdest thing any game has ever done. Sprint is Shift, Left Mouse is attacks (because you use your stronger index finger) and Blocking/Left Hand is Right Mouse (because you use your middle finger which is weaker). This is the way things have always been. Fighting is done entirely with the mouse. The mouse is your weapon, the extension of your hand through which you control your character's hands.
Not only is holding down Right Mouse with your middle finger all the time is awkward and painful, but it makes the parkour puzzles a lot weirder as well. Space and Shift go hand in hand, they are close so holding them down both at the same time is easy, and releasing one while holding the other just comes naturally. Your right hand controls the character's arms, your left hand controls the character's feet. Combining Space and Right Mouse is just awkward, it's like playing the piano with a hand and a foot. On top of it, Interact is sometimes E and sometimes Shift.
With this in mind, it wasn't a surprise to me at all that the platform games should have their own set of weird controls. I'm the sort of fan who would buy a tetris game if it had the Assassin's Creed logo on it, so I weirdly enjoyed playing them. However, that doesn't mean I have to like everything about them.
What bothered me most were the controls, specifically of the ranged weapons. The different weapons are bound to 1 2 3 and 4. Your weapon selection gets reset to 1, which means that at the beginning of each checkpoint you have to check if you have the right one chosen.
You use the weapon with F which, okay, I guess all the good bindings were taken. You aim it with the mouse, which is sensible after all. And then you have to fire it with G, while you have F held down the whole time. That just doesn't make  sense. If I have F held down anyways, why can't I fire the thing with my mouse since I'm already aiming with it? That requires you to perform a combination of 4 unrelated keys in a very tight situation. It takes a while to get used to.
What I would have done is have your primary weapon bound to 1, the ranged ones bound to 2 3 4 and 5. When I have to switch, I switch, I hold down the Left Mouse and aim, then fire the thing by releasing Left Mouse. If I want to cancel, I hit Right Mouse. This is also common sense.
Heavy attacks are bound to H which is the weirdest thing ever because it had me checking, during very difficult combat, where H even was. By the time I was done I'd be dead. The Use key is bound to W which had me hitting E instead several times.
After playing 2.5 of the 3 Chronicles games and having had to put up with their insane controls, I felt compelled to write this long essay about how proper key bindings should be. Pretty sure I have carpal tunnel by now. I don't think anyone's going to read this but if there is any chance that someone does and we have proper controls in the next Assassin's Creed game I consider this time well spent.

I hate to admit this to myself, but the gunplay in this game is really dissatisfying and I haven't picked the game up in weeks even though I'm very interested in seeing more of the game's content. No location damage is lazy and frankly inexcusable. Your coy "don't bother aiming for headshots, mummies don't have brains" load screen tip is not funny and feels like a halfassed excuse for you to just not do the critical work of coding location damage. The reloading in this game is INSANE, most weapons take a ridiculously long time to reload for a guy that can sprint and jump at 30mph. The gun sound effects are generally weak, only a few feel very 'heavy' or real.
@Devs: You need to do a study of the gunplay in Overwatch or Warframe and release a major update, although I guess this game is already dead and I'm too late to the party. You need location damage (doesn't always have to be the head, get creative), you need good hitreg sounds and UI effects, you need to retune reloading, and you need to make all your guns sound and 'feel' heavier than peashooters and paintball guns. There's a bow in this game, which got me very excited as I love the bows in Overwatch and Warframe, but the bow in Immortal Redneck feels more like a kid's plastic trash bow, it's awful. Seriously more than anything this game needs location damage.
Incidentally, I strongly dislike the "Roguelite" concept, it creates a weird difficulty curve. A good roguelike should technically be completable on your very first playthrough. This game actually requires you to die repeatedly to build up the skill tree. The marketing for this game presents it as having "nine classes with skill tree" but it's really just different weapon loadouts and the tree is nothing like an RPG tree, it's more like Rogue Legacy.
As it stands now, I'm massively disappointed. So close to the mark--an FPS with infinite replayability and variation--but so far from it, because it feels more like an RPG that's been forced into first person mode than an FPS with RPG elements.

Immortal Redneck is one of my favourite games of the year.
It shows up like another roguelite FPS but as soon as you start to play it uncovers as a funny, challenger and addictive game.

There is also a skill tree ( literally a tree) which gives the players the possibility of enhance its stats, modify items benefits an also unlock a lot of God's Favours ( Classes / characters ). Each favour modifies the game experience and has its own play syle, but all of them were  quite usefull when mastered. (NOT SEKHMET -.-)
IR has a  lot of different chambers, monsters, perks, weapons and classes. There's also a Twitch mode which brings your Twitch followers the ability to manage your luck.
Finally, in one of the lastest updates, they added the "Infinity Tower" mode. This update allows the player to enter into a mode where there is no floors limit and the difficult escalates a lot
I've found a really nice game that I totally recommend.

Banished is a Sandbox game.
Depending on the difficulty you play on, you have X amount af villagers and houses to start with.
You have to build a fully functional Village/City by building houses, Fishing docks, farms and more.
You can also assign people to be builders, farmer, hunters, ect.
There are few building resources like Wood, Stone and Iron.
You can gain the resources by building Forester lodge, Mine and Quarry.
Your Villagers also needs warm clothes and firewood when the winter hits. You can gain firewood with a Wood Cutter and Wool by sheep you can have in a Pasture. You'll need a Tailor to make the clothes and you can also get a blacksmith for tools.
You have random of what you can start with in Pastures and Crop farms.
To gain other Crops and animals you can trade via a Trading Post.
You can also build schools to educate kids, chapels to gain religious people and cemetery to bury dead people.
There is Hospitals to heal and cure people and with a Gatherers hut you can get herbs and a Herbalist to make medicine out of the herbs.
You can also build tunnels though mountains and bridges across water.
Stockpiles for yeah, putting your resources on and Storage barn for storage of food and resources like tools, wool, leather, etc.
There are many thing to do and thanks to the modding community there can be a lot more to do.
