I like to play bullet hell game. And since this was free, why not give it a try?
Overall I would recommend it since it is free and it is pretty interesting to see how different spellcards of Touhou got combined together (Seriously, I was laughing non-stop through the game. The bosses' attacks are.... fun in a sense.). It has almost the same mechanics as Touhou so if you know the basics you're good to go.
I have only completed the first character upon this review (Tenshi, 1cc Normal first try) so it will be mostly based on this one experience.
The normal difficulty for first 2 stages are harder than most other bullet hell games. Mostly due to unexpected patterns when you think it is safe to go to auto-collection point.
And the more I play, the more it become a 'Try-to-guess-the-original' game. I was thinking of "Ah, hi Satori, your lasers look good today. Oh? Suddenly Byakuren graced this occasion. How gracious. Mokou, please do not sudden leapt at me like that!"
That happened in just a spellcard for a boss.
The monsters pattern are also strikingly similar to QB shooting and exCeed (Touhou is already a given). Stage 3, it is almost the same as QB Shooting's 5th stage, barring rockets flying alongside you.
The music is almost the same for all stages (at least that was the impression I had while playing). It feels like the music is there for the sake of it, and does not fit the characters / their danmaku style. Not a single sound track has a lasting impression on me.
And Tenshi is just Reimu in disguise.
====================================
Update after finishing Easy/Normal with all characters and losing Hard at last spell card :
There... isn't any story.Yes, you do know a little more about the characters, but there is no story to be seen. You could look at the bios for more backstory but...
The difficulty range, to be honest, is pretty narrow. For the stage battles,  I do not feel much difference between easy and normal (except for more bullets) and between normal and hard (much more bullets but still easy enough to dodge). Spellcard battles on the other hand have nice difficulty increase.
The playable characters (excluding the hidden characters) have attacks all exactly the same as Touhou's characters. Youmu's short range attack, Marisa's laser, Aya's spread attack, Reimu's homing, Yukari's hold position. Personally I prefer to use homing / laser. The laser girl has movement speed that is ridiculously slow (which is actually good in spellcard battle) and limited range of attack (straight above her), but her damage output is way beyond what others can dish out (other than perhaps the hidden hidden character, or the hidden character if you placed your position correctly)
Even after repeated playthroughs, the music still does not leave much of an impression on me, except perhaps some of the different last stage bosses.
And I am not sure if I am glad that there is no lasers in this game, or am agonized that a straight chain of bullets are replacement for lasers. Either way, curving lasers are sin. (Wait, there are lasers.... and I hate Shou's (of Touhou) laser spellcards. Alien girl is my achillies heel.)

SUPERHOT is a first person time manipulation game, releasing in February 2016, developed and published by SUPERHOT Team.
The game play is what makes SUPERHOT, what it is. You play from a first person perspective as you navigate and complete challenges and levels through the single player modes. How you progress will be dictated on how well you are able to manipulate time to your advantage. Time only progresses when you move your character, whether it be simply moving your camera angel, or by taking a step forward, time will go on. As soon as you stop, time will freeze, allowing you to plot your next move accordingly. Throughout the game you will gain access to different weapons in the form of shotguns, machine guns and samurai swords. These all play key parts in the levels you find them and are often the key to completion.  Whilst most levels are actually pretty short in terms of the content available, playing them out in the slowed down time frame can mean you are sometimes acting out the scene for up to five minutes. Once you complete the level by eliminating all of the enemies, you will get to watch back the scene in full speed, allowing you to marvel at the spectacle you have just created; most of the time, it is something of pure beauty to watch as your character glides through the level chopping off heads, getting headshots, and perfectly catching enemies off guard.
Graphically, SUPERHOT is very clean, almost medical like art style. The whites, blacks and reds all contrast well against each other. The game runs on the Unity engine so the fidelity of the animations, and character models are all really high quality, with very high production values found right the way through the audio side of the game with top notch narration and sound effects.
This game is hard, but you soon get to grips with the game play and you can often conquer most levels after a handful of attempts of just correcting your own mistakes. I personally really enjoyed the trial and error aspect of this game, as the reset time for each failure was quick and snappy, allowing you to get straight back into the action after messing up. On top of the game’ s story mode, SUPERHOT, also includes an endless mode – this is where you have literally an endless amount of enemies come at you. We also have a challenge mode that will basically replay the single player missions but give you additional certain rules and hurdles to overcome at the same time too.
I managed to finish the single player story mode to SUPERHOT in just under two hours, which was a little short for my liking, but where you will get the most mileage and replay value out of SUPERHOT, is the challenge mode and endless mode; you will be able to get countless hours of entertainment out of both of these game modes if you enjoy the gameplay enough. I would have liked to see a longer story mode, but we can’t have everything I guess.
SUPERHOT is definitely one of the surprises to come out of 2016. It may be priced a little on the high end given the short story mode, but it can be almost made up by the two extra modes. I’d personally recommend the game even at the regular price of £17.99. The game also has VR support which will just be amazing to see how it plays out on that format.

This game had been sitting in my library for well over two years without being played. In hindsight, I'm not entirly sure why I didn't play this game sooner. This game is absoultely amazing in almost every possible way: the gameplay is excellent, the story is rich with twists and turns and the influences of art deco makes the immersion that much better.
In BioShock, you take on take on the role Jack who finds himself in an underwater city named Rapture after his plane crashes in the sea. You venture through the city, introducing yourself to plasmids which alter your genetics and give you special abilities. Throughout the city, there are numerous types of enemies which vary in terms of difficulty and appearance. There are also many different types of weapons such as the revolver which have a wide array of upgrades that you can find throughout the course of the game.
The story itself could sell the game on its own without the need for all of the excellent gameplay. I won't give away any spoilers, but this is the sort of story that is like a roller coaster; what you thought was true at the beginning of the game is completely false by the end and is reformed by a completely different reality of the story itself. In summary, this game is absolutely excellent and I highly recommend it.
Final score: 8.5 out of 10.

This is pretty much a multiplayer only game, reviewing it as such is crucial.  If you're looking for a single player experience, look elsewhere.  That being said, this game is amazing.  RO2 is a modern looking, realistic WW2 FPS.  Though it started out with more than a few bugs, it has been updated and polished quite nicely over the years.  Before I get into details, I'll also include that you will get to experience both the Eastern front as well as the island battles of the Pacific Theatre, easily one of the most unique features about this game.
Gameplay is quite fluid.  Moving around the map, crouching, sprinting, all feel quite good and realistic.  Sounds, weapons, chatter, maps, and skins all create an immersive atmosphere.  The horrors of war will be on full display the minute you step into a populated server and you're going to love every second of it.
Though the learning curve of RO2 is moderate to high for most, which I personally love, this is ultimately a game of realism.    You will most certainly die from one well placed shot, but you can also do alot of damage with one placed shot yourself.  Though, one man can do quite a bit of damage to the enemy if he knows what he's doing, this game stresses teamwork tactics and sticking close to your squad mates.  Getting into cap zones, and picking guys off from there is the name of the game.  Working with your teammates and coordination is key.  You won't find much in regards to Rambo'ing around the map as it simply won't work unless your an experienced veteran.
Easily one of the more realistic WW2 shooters out currently.  I've played this game since launch, and over the last few years, the game has made great strides towards being very, very good.  With the most recent update, which included the release of the MG42, battles on the Eastern front feel about ten times more intense.  Worth every penny, would buy again.

Tropico 5 a good game, don't get me wrong.  However, if you try to play the game in sandbox mode you quickly learn that the game is designed to be mission based, like Omerta was, rather than a true sandbox like the previous tropicos.
You have 4 stages, the colonial era, the world wars era, the cold war era, and the modern era.  You progress to the next era by fulfilling objectives, even in sandbox mode.  In sandbox mode the game does not even tell you what the objective are, but once  they are fulfilled your "reward" is to advance to the next era until you win.
If you played the previous Tropicos for the campaigns this game if probably for you, however if you want a true sandbox city builder, Tropcio 4 is a better option.  This Tropico seems to care more about the campaign than the sandbox mode.
It's a nice minimalistic 2D Assassin's Creed that can give you the same experience as if you're playing any other game from this series.

It's like Rogue Legacy crossed with Ziggurat.  It gets rid of the stupid multi ammo system and trades level ups for purely found upgrades.
While it feels and plays really nice, the gameplay loop is just lacking.  It doesn't have any major progressive unlock system of Rogue Legacy, or equipment selection.  You get something similar in a single-selectable-glyph, but in the early parts of the game they're minor to inconsequential.
The different "classes" via gods commonly feel more like punishments than fun alternative options, as many of their abilities are inconsequential to detriment, with starting weapons and stat alterations that don't offset this.
The bosses are also largely pains to fight, as it shifts rapidly away from fun gameplay to dealing with waiting through loops until you get to damage cycles and ammo shortage.
I really think that the game would drastically benefit from having Tower of Gun's linear level layout, as exploring is as annoying an assinine as it is in  Ziggurat, making playing either a choice of being the same thign every time or exploring for upgrades and loot and having to deal with tons of meaningless backtracking.  There's never anything to gain by going back to any room that you were in previously.
This game isn't a hard not-recommended, but I think a lot of people are going to find that continued play will become more of a chore than a sense of play and progress, more just doing floors for the "privelege" of attempting a boss and that experiencing just being one of time consumption than involved gameplay.

An utterly unremarkable rogue-lite FPS game. But. But in the subgenre of remarkably bad games, the utterly unremarkable one is king. But there weren't even ten good or at least above mediocre games in this year so far. But there were no any singleplayer FPS games in about last ten years — only abysmal garbage or walking simulators about MARINES or spunkgurgleweewee about MARINES or MARINES vs nazis or MARINES in hell.
Considering total lack of hitscan enemies, the core gameplay falls somewhere in post-quake1 (sub)subgenre of the FPS games — movement is the only way to survive. And at first, movement, while inoffensive, feels really floaty and unengaging, but when you unlock second jump everything clicks. Now, on top of running at great speed, you can jump across the whole room and above melee enemies. You can even make a build with quintuple jumps and play attack bomber pouring bullets on enemies from above.
Speaking of which, there are a fair number of pleasant, unusual and effective guns to use. Some of which, to be fair, are outright ripped from other games. But on the other hand, outside of real guns there never were an all-stars FPS with best guns from different games.
Levels consist of randomly connected pre-made rooms with some minor changes. Rooms themself are fine, some even with secrets. And considering the limited amount of rooms with relatively regular placements of enemies, it against plays toward the FPS games of that era, when memorizing enemies placements was encouraged and resulted in great speedruns with unbreaking flow.
Rogue-lite part took note from rogue legacy, but improved it for grown up people, who don't have time to waste on virtual gambling. First, you can unlock the choice of several builds, and take one fitting for you, by guns or by skills. Then there is an upgrade to have a random gun at the start of the pyramid, so you have a chance to get rid of least useful one you had by default. Next, the upgrade tree is balanced rather good, so it's not often that you can't purchase anything. So with persistence you can, in time, overlevel the enemies (it took me twenty five hours to finish it). Also there is a shop, where you can buy random skill or medallion to skip first boss of the pyramid (or use some other medallions). Scrolls with skills can be bad or good, but most importantly, there are several scrolls which radically change the resource management, for the current floor or for the whole pyramid.
In the game there are three pyramids (+ infinite basement) with one boss on the third floor and separate final boss on the seventh. And the first pyramid is the most peculiar (also most inspired by Serious Sam), not only it has less archers, and most of its rooms later just reskinned and mixed in into other pyramids, but both bosses of the first pyramid are more of puzzle-like type. First boss of the second pyramid is generic sponge, second reminds more of the sonic boss. First boss of the third pyramid is like an ogre — it just has layers. And annoying spamming generic ranged enemies. And final boss of the game is just a rather easy bullet sponge with high damage.
Graphically, game is buried under a ton of console cinematic soap, but almost all of it can be turned off. And while FOV goes quite high, the virtual lens is so wrong, that you can't go above one hundred fifteen, without it being detracting to the gameplay. (while Halo 1 and Half-Life 1 were pretty good at one hundred fifty)
Storyline and writing are garbage, and are quite embarrassing at that, even while being imaginative mash-up (maybe?). I remember only Accused Farms requesting such theme. Narrative, on the other hand, is quite fitting for chosen story.
But in the end (it doesn't even matter) it's kinda one of the best games of the year, because there were no games in this year.

Could be a good game, and is to a degree, but the negative scrolls and poor balancing make this nothing more than a lesson in futility.
The game quite often (like every time without fail) removes all your good weapons that took you hours to find without recourse, and hits you with unfair negative stats. Because of this, the only character capable of beating a pyramid is the weakest one, which is Sekhmet the healing class, because of the higher defense and healing ability. No other class can compensate for bad scrolls, and this ruins the fun of the game.
Some of the more fun characters that start with better weapons also have ridiculously low defensive stats, and the tank guy has reduced speed and jumping capability, making him completely useless in harder pyramids.
Beating a pyramid also resets your character, so you have to beat the next one from scratch.
Because of the horrendously poor game balancing, and constant bad scroll pickups, you will die and restart constantly, and eventually become too frustrated to play the game anymore. I've maxed out most of my upgrades, and cannot get past the 3rd pyramid. Mostly because of the bad scroll drops, which instantly ruin your run.
Recommendation: Buy Strafe instead, as Strafe allows you to reset bad upgrades, buy ammo and health, buy useful upgrades, and has better level design. Immortal Redneck has fancier graphics, but that's all it has. The game is nothing but unbalanced and frustrating, and I don't think the IR devs care to fix it, unlike the Strafe devs. Total Biscuit was right to give this game a negative review, because even though the devs addressed some of the problems, the negative scrolls remain in the game, and it ruins the experience.

For years I've been looking for a way to express to family and friends why video games are a valid form of art. Nearly always the response is that video games have little biots of art but are mopstly just for fun and being violent. There are some games which look and sound immacualtely beautiful (my personal go-to in the discussion of video games as art is The Last of Us), but what this game does is show that video games can be an expression of oneself. It shows that video games aren't all about high scores and gameplay, they're about showing the player a piece of another person, a chance for the player to live inside someone else's head for a few hours.
I consider video games a very valid art form which is why I'm quite disappointed to see a lot of reviews criticising a game like this solely on the merit that it "doesn't qualify as a video game", largely due to the lack of immersive gameplay. But some video games are meant to be expeierneced, and through them something more meaningful can be achieved.
I highly recommend playing this game, espeically if you've not seen any footage so far.

Before playing the game I did have knowledge that it was mostly a walking narrative, that people found it emotionally moving, and it would take about 1.5 hours to experience. I purchased the game exactly for this experience. Unfortunately, I did not have the experience I expected.
* CONTAINS SPOILERS *
As I was progressing through the story, I thought of several ways I thought the direction might go. All of which seemed more interesting to me than the actual ending. Which made it all the more disappointing.
1) Maybe Coda has a dark secret that we'll uncover through his games and find his final games as a way to heal and ask for forgiveness (Inception-ish)
2) Maybe Coda is meant to be (me) the player and by answering questions in a personal way, I will uncover a truth about myself and experience some sort of insight.
3) Maybe Coda took their own life and the narrator is sharing a message they found while playing his/her games as a sort of tribute to this deceased person.
The second direction/thought fell flat pretty quickly as a I realized how limited the options were and how they didn’t matter. It clearly became about the narrator and his experience with Coda and not about me the player. Which made it all the more distant when I was expected to believe that the game I purchased and was playing was the narrator sharing Coda's work because he thought Coda needed help.
The first and third directions/thoughts seemed more entertaining to me if this game wasn’t going to be insightful. I would have liked something deep and meaningful... but at the very least it should be entertaining.
The actual ending left me wondering who this game was for. I read a few positive and negative reviews on steam afterwards and what I gathered was that the people that understood this experience were creative types (possibly game programmers) who suffer from social anxiety disorder and depression. That doesn't paint a very good picture but I can understand how some of the events in the game would affect these types of people more.
There are two strong points that I took away from the experience:
1) Being creative is a personal outlet that has its ups and downs
2) Sharing a personal experience with others via a game can lead to judgement/misinterpretations by the player (which can cause anxiety/depression)
I consider myself a creative introvert and I'm also a professional game developer but I don’t suffer from depression or SAD. I think about games as art in my own work but I would never make a game like The Beginners Guide. It takes time and effort to make a game. Heck, it took 10 people at Everything Unlimited to make this short one. So why make a game about the difficulties of making/sharing games when it’s obviously not a firsthand issue with the developers? I think this would have been a lot better if they made a documentary video of the real Coda and his struggles and sold that for $10. (For R.)

There's not much to this game, it's short, there's almost no interaction, it's just a very basic walk-through with a rather irritating narrative over the top.
While I like walking simulator first person games, I prefer polish and depth. What we have here is not polished, and is somewhat pretentious. There's nothing memorable here. Some of the levels were probably made in under an hour including textures and everything.
The whole "making a game" narrative has promise at first,  but then you catch on to the hoax.  It doesn't go anywhere, it doesn't get better. As you progress, you encounter what he calls "games", but they are not games.
Even by "edgy hipster minimalism" art school standards, the "games" you encounter are nothing more than test levels; demo mechanics which developers make to learn the engine.  Making an actual game from a bunch of test levels, is lazy and fake.
There's missed opportunity to do something great with the premise. The basic test levels could have progressed and become a huge complicated level with interaction at the end, but we never see this conclusion.  The whole game is a series of basic test levels which the irritating narration insists has deeper meaning. But of  course there is no deeper meaning, it's fake art.
But it seems he has pulled off the hoax, making a few dollars with this game and receiving praise. Well, my review isn't praising the game, but is a warning to those thinking of buying. What we have here is the result of creative block, lack of a game idea becoming the game literally. All his  cutting room floor test levels and game engine testing, is what this game is made of. This is curious and unique  for about 10 minutes,  after which you are left wanting more... but never receive.
Disappointing.

Cuphead, a side-scrolling shooter with a focus on challenging boss encounters, is a beautiful, hand-written love letter to old-timey cartoons.  Inspired by the ragtime and jazz fever-dream of early 20th century animation, the game is a feast for the eyes and a whetstone for the senses.  A difficult shooter fest that dares you to keep up with the ever-increasing odds of its demanding duels and the sensory overload of its lavish presentation, Cuphead is instantly addicting, blindingly beautiful, and deeply rewarding.
The game starts out as any good natured oldie would, as brothers Cuphead and Mugman hit a hot streak at the dice table in the Devil's own casino.  They're so lucky in fact, that the Devil himself joins their game and dares them to ante up their souls for a big payoff if they win.  Cuphead agrees beside his more reluctant brother, and throws the Devil's dice, losing the game by landing on snake-eyes.  When the Devil tries to collect, the brothers beg for another way to pay, and thus their journey begins as the Devil tasks them with collecting the souls of all his other debtors in exchange for getting to keep theirs.  It's charming, rife with toonish absurdity, and true to the old "moral of the story" style that many old cartoons were structured with.
The game proper sees Cuphead (and Mugman if there is a second player) navigating an overworld map filled with kooky characters and animated props indicating a boss fight against one of the Devil's debtors.  When you stop at one of these props and start a fight, you're instantly assaulted with jazzy tunes and a larger than life cartoon boss, all in pitch-perfect style of old toons like Popeye and Betty Boop.  Each boss fight has multiple stages and can change up their rhythm in satisfying and surprising ways as well.  In true oldies fashion, many of the boss characters pull huge bombs out of pants pockets, transform into fighter planes, and move in crazy and creative ways as the battle ensues.  It keeps the player on their toes and deftly translates the trademark insanity of old cartoons into harrowing battles against unpredictable foes.
Utilizing finger guns that shoot actual bullets, Cuphead can shoot in eight degrees, dash to avoid enemies, and perform a parry ability against pink-colored projectiles by pressing the jump button while in midair.  Parrying these pink objects (or simply hitting enemies with bullets) fills a super meter which can be used to unleash more powerful attacks and special abilities.  Being successful in the course of the game also nets you gold coins which can be spent on the overworld shop for equippable charms that give passive bonuses or new types of bullets such as homing bullets or a spread shot.  It never arms you to the teeth due to only being able to equip so many abilities at once, but it does give you new ways to tackle a tough boss in case the standard bullet type or charm isn't working as well as it did on the last one.
In so many ways, Cuphead is like what would happen if a time machine melded together with an arcade machine.  It's a twitchy and hard as nails side-scroller with an astonishingly crafted tone of emotive, old-timey drawings brought to life.  Nothing looks like this anymore, and bringing this aesthetic to life after so many decades of being lost is only a single reason why Cuphead is so special.  Even if you didn't grow up with the oldies, it's impossible to resist the meticulously stylish and refined game that is Cuphead.  It's a brisk trot through a wonderland of arcade dreams and irresistible cartoon energy, and it earns every moment of it.

As someone who has played this game for so long (level 99 with 2:1 KDR) while expecting change, balance and bug fixes... I can positively say that this game is sub-par in every category. The art, the level design, the UI, the balancing in general are at completely unacceptable levels even when the game was released. There are a number of bugs and exploits that will frustrate even the most apathetic player. Balance is completely absent with a strong bias towards the German team (given the weapons and maps) with even more imbalance with specific maps that may favor an attacker/defender too strongly.
These things are easily detectable with metrics, which, so far, Tripwire has managed to completely ignore over the last several years. I'm sorry, but when you see the Russian team winning only 10% of the time on a particular map based on a sample of 1000+ games, that means you need to fix or remove that map immediately. The same issue occurs with a weapon like the "MKB" with its obscene KDR metrics compared to every other weapon in the game. While there are boundaries, it is stupid and amateur for developers to ignore such metrics. This is why a lot of players grow frustrated and leave.

This game is easily one of the most addicting I've ever played. Despite some of the major, teeth-grinding glitches, it is very fun.  The game description is essentially what it says; it's a zombie apocalypse simulator. If you loot a house, it's gonna stay empty. If you die with loads of loot at your safehouse, it's going to stay there until your new guy can find it again.
The game also adds a great challenge to its survival aspect. It's not like traditional zombie games like Dead Rising where you can kill 500 zombies within five minutes. I get nervous when I'm up against more than two. You know how in the movies when a character is bitten, and then they turn? That's exactly what happens in Project Zomboid. One bite is all it takes for you to lose the character you've spent the last couple of hours leveling up.
Despite the many, many bugs in this game, it's a great idea and it provides endless hours of fun, scavenging and zombie-slaying!

I've been playing this game for 5 years. It's everything I've wanted in a turn-based strategy game. It combines CCG and miniatures elements in a fantasy setting with a close-knit player community, and I can't see myself quitting until the game itself has shut down.
If you decide to play it, it's technically Free to Play, although you should know that if you want to be a competititve top-ranked player you definitely will need to make some purchases. If you want to just relax and have fun though, you can get MANY of the game pieces via in-game currency and many players have made "F2P" accounts and maintained top ranks with them.
There's an expansion with 70-80 new game pieces every 3 months or so, along with a "midterm" expansion every month and a half with 8 new "Legendary" game pieces, so PoxNora is continually expanding the thousands of pieces it features. I recommend this game to anyone who's into M:tG or turn-based strategy, for sure.

This style of gameplay is not really my cup of tea, but that's why I didn't particularly like this game.  It's because it didn't quite live up to my expectations with regards to the "puzzle" and "music" parts of the game.  I found the controls and menu layout to be a little wonky; I was slightly lost.  The "puzzle" portion, due to the loose mechanics of the game, feels more like a game of trial and error and tweaking rather than something enjoyable.  This is made a tad worse by the wonky controls.  The most "musical" it gets is...mixing instruments together, except that you
to mix
of the instruments together each time — there's no choice.  If you really want something musical, go play a game like Circuits instead.
Edit: I just realized I should be a bit more positive about this game after getting a bit further in it.  The music is indeed spectacular: mostly piano and strings, but a nice orchestral feel.
Edit 2: OK I just dug into the game's samples and found out why the loops aren't perfect (thus ruining the immersion factor somewhat): they use MP3 format, which is terrible for looping because it adds silences on the edges of the sound sample.  Even if the MP3s are well-calibrated sample-for-sample, the silences still don't make the loops as smooth as they should be.  The devs probably should've used OGG or WAV format instead.  (As an aside, you can find parts for three unused songs in the game's files.)
Just goes to show that you don't have to have amazing graphics or animations to make a fun original game

Tropico 4 was one of my favorite games. Tropico 5 keeps enough of the core gameplay from 4 while adding enough features (like trade, exploration and research) to make the game more complex and justify the purchase. I would recommend it to anyone who is a fan of the Tropico series, or simulation builders in general.
UPDATE: I've played through a lot more of the game now, and I stand by my original recommendation. On its surface, the game appears to be lacking in features compared to Tropico 4, but I think that's just because certain things are more hidden inside the Almanac now. Although they are more hidden, things are more connected in the menu, so it's easier to find out, say, who lives in a shack, where they work and how much they make. I would recommend this to anyone who has played Tropico before or not, especially with the sale price.

Don't let the release date fool you - Auditorium is a older game than its Steam incarnation. The original game was released in 2009 as a web app, and the Steam version does show its age in that regard. The graphics are underpowered by modern standards, and the audio doesn't loop cleanly.
But, to this day, Auditorium remains one of the most creative and enjoyable games I've ever played. The mechanics are intuive but incredibly challenging as you continue playing. In the last 7 years, I've played through this game multiple times over, and my solutions to each puzzle are always different than the last time. Even though it's aged poorly, it's still fun to come back to every once in a while.
Unfortunately, Auditorium doesn't get a happy ending. Its sequel, funded via Kickstarter in 2012, is one of the most notorious bits of vaporware to ever come out of the Kickstarter platform. It's a shame, too, because a sequel to this game would have been wonderful. Instead, it and Cipher Prime are posterchildren for unfulfilled Kickstarter campaigns.
If you have an unplayed copy of this game, you should definitely play it. If you don't... well, after 4 years of nothing but broken promises, it's hard to recommend giving Cipher Prime your money.

Take one part Faerie Solitaire and two parts Puzzle Quest and mix in a little Poker or Yahtzee for good measure and you will get something like Runespell: Overture.
You're a changeling of some sort and you fight monsters and take quests in exchange for coin and buffs (which come in the form of power-up cards). There's a story but it's not the strongest element in the game. Like the Puzzle Quest games, your battles are determined by playing a mini-game. Instead of match-3 though, the game is a card game similar to poker in which making certain combinations of cards (pairs, 5 of a kind, full house, flush, straight) will do a certain amount of damage to your opponent, who is trying to do the same to you.  The ability to steal some cards from your opponent, plus the limited number of moves you get per turn to move cards or play power-ups adds just enough strategy to the game to keep it interesting.
Admittedly, the game can get a bit repetitive after a while and I found the dialogue options to be a bit tedious but fortunately the game allows you to skip them if you want. It's an easy game to learn, and it's an entertaining casual game to play. It seems to be pretty short and the achievements don't seem too difficult to collect if that's your thing.

Tropico 5 adds a lot to the series including a tech tree, improved (though still lacking) combat, a new starting date, new economic system, a family tree, and whole wack of new edicts and buildings.
Now to start my review I must state that I am running on an Intel HD 3000, which is below the minimum requirments. Even so I was able to get graphics up to a lowish-medium. Though the opening menu tanked to an awful 1 or 2 frames per minute. So navigating it was next to impossible. But once in a game I was getting the 30 that made gameplay bearable.
The Tech Tree and New Starting Date fit in well allowing for a game to start as early as the age of enlightenment and go on till 2014+. Each era involves new challenges such as pleasing a monarch or stopping your Island from becoming the next victim of Nazi Agression. The tech tree is simplistic. You need 'X' amount of tech points to get a piece of technology. You get these points from building various buildings or from a specific type of manager. While tech does not advance the era it does help you gain the requirments to do so. For example during the first era you have to make the people become loyal to you. To do this you need to make more people want independance.  A building that helps with this is the Newspaper which you unlock near the end of the Colonial Era Tree.
The combat has been revamped to include a more diverse list of units. Including Infantry, Tanks, Naval Units, and an Air Force. Though in the classic Tropico fashion none of these you can actually control in a real combat situation. Speaking of combat situations you'll be seeing a lot more of these during the course of the game. From pirates, to a full blown invasion from the US.
The economy has been changing in three major ways. First off building can now have managers which give the building a small passive bonus (Example: 5% increased production). Second you no longer set an individual dollar amount for the building. (Ex. In Tropico 4 you'd set a building to pay 20 bucks a month) Now you set them to pay the workers a very low, low, medium, high, or very high wage. Though not a feature I enjoy it does make it simplier. Lastly you can now build a trade fleet which can do trade mission. These usually involve you buying or selling a single resource to a single faction at a better price. (Ex. Generally Cooca will get you 800 bucks per 1000 units. But with a trade deal to the US you can get 900 bucks per 1000 units.) Though this does have a political consequence.
The family tree allows your president to have family members. Who can replace them as president or act as a better version of the manager. Outfits and characters models have been severally limited from previous titles. This reaks of possible cheap five dollar DLCs in the future.
In general there are more builds and edicts. Each era having there own list of 10 or so. Each era also has a bunch of era approprite unlocks for buildings. Plantations in the Colonial Period, Steel Mills during the World Wars, and so on, and so forth.
Three last changes worth mentioning, you now have to explore your island with the majority of it spawning with a thick cloud of war. Second immigration is now much higher with ships now coming in loaded with immigrants. Also your country now has a constitution which gives you a series of passive bonuses.
One last thing, election are now much harder to win, be warned.

The recommendation is pretty weak because I didn't actually like the game.  I think it has the potential to be enjoyable and it is fairly unique, so that alone might be worth it to you.
This game is essentially puzzle quest but with a solitaire combat system instead of matching gems.  It's not fast by any means.  Essentially you build poker hands to charge attacks, then launch the attacks at your opponent.  Essentially you spend the entire game moving stacks of cards on top of each other to make a combo of five, and the higher the combo on the damage scale, the more the attack will do.  You can also 'steal' cards from your enemies so long as they aren't stacked.
The combat is cool once or twice, but after that it becomes so repetitive.  Nearly every fight is identical, save for the select few where you need to charge and use special attacks to win.
Beyond the gameplay, the music, sound effects, story and graphics are all ok.  They're mediocre, they're fine, they're acceptable.  Without a doubt they are not great and won't sell the game, but they sustain it without detracting.
All around, that describes the experience: alright, ok, passable.  It's not thrilling or revolutionary, but it is unique and if that's what you're looking for in a game then you'll find it here.

It's another story-driven walking simulator, a genre I enjoy, but I understand not everyone does.
Like Stanley Parable, it has a very simple setting, graphical style, and a narrator. It has some of the same themes about what is a video game, choice, and creativity. Unlike Stanley Parable, you can't ignore the narrator - in fact, in this game you are stuck on rails, with very few real choices. You are watching a story unfold. Beginner's Guide is not nearly as funny, and probably less approachable than Stanley Parable.
But Beginner's Guide has some interesting exploration of mental illness, friendship, and solitude, and I found the ending to be very satisfying.

To quote of a single SUPERHOT developer who is speculating (which someone gave me in the comments of this review), "We'll circle back to other platforms shortly after the initial release. It's likely not even going to be a very long wait." It's probably okay to wait a few weeks between headset-compatible versions being released, but the potential problem with that (which, honestly, doesn't seem to affect multi-console games that are released for individual consoles between intervals) is that there would be incentives to seriously delay other headset-compatible versions to make things effectively exclusive. If you gave it a month of exclusivity at the most, then I think it would be fine to have that temporary exclusivity.
There are two sides to the argument. On the one hand, having exclusives licensed by VR hardware designers funds the production of games made for VR. On the other hand, you fragment the player base and are a chode. If you are going to have errors no matter what, error on the side of freedom. Shortly delayed freedom, however, is about the best that you could get trying to compromise both sides, I would think.
There's actually something that could really shut down this whole "need" for exclusivity. Instead of funding developers to get them through making an entire new game, how about you fund people who work on making the hundreds or thousands of current games compatible with VR?
Now, sadly, I'm not Ross Scott, but here are some of his gripes with VR as it is. He doesn't touch on exclusivity in this context, but he does talk about some things that are connected with it around 9:30.
The point still remains that being a chode is being a chode. If SUPERHOT is guaranteed to come to all VR headsets, consider this review obsolete in the context of SUPERHOT. In fact, consider this review a positive one saying, again, "I enjoyed this game made by devs who are not chodes." But as it stands right now, things aren't perfect, so I'm going to be mad, sleepy, and less coherent than I normally am.

I find Sunless Sea a difficult game to review as it is so unusual.  I don't think I've ever played a game quite like it.  The art is fairly simple yet perfectly evocative.  The writing is exceptional.  To try to categorize it I think it would best be described as strategic story telling.  You attempt to guide your character through the life of a Zee Captain, earning enough money and knowledge to uncover the game's secrets and work out the details of its story.  You make choices regarding what resources to stock up on, how to outfit your ship, where to travel, and the actions you take when you get there.  Through these actions the story reveals itself to you.  Make the right choices and you progress.  Make poor choices or encounter a bit of bad luck and you will likely find yourself meeting a colorfully terrifying end.
If you don't mind doing a little reading as you play and perhaps keeping good notes on what you find this is a very enjoyable game with the potential for significant depth (no pun intended) of story.  The game may be a little slow paced for some.  Advances in wealth and ability are not easily earned.  I often find myself precariously balanced between poverty, insanity, and starvation, hoping desperately that my fuel does not run out before I can make it back to port.
Ultimately I find the game to be enjoyable and rewarding.

2K Games blows my mind with a phenomenal first person shooter that goes above and beyond to provide an incredibly experience. BioShock does something magical, beyond gameplay it the complete and total mind-♥♥♥♥.
A plane crashes in the middle of the ocean and you are the sole survivor. As you are swimming from the wreckage you notice a small tower standing. What does the tower offer, but the amazing city of Rapture. The underwater city is completely in ruins and everyone is completely mad, but why and how will you ever escape. As you maintain communications with one other sane person it is up to you to make sure you both can make it out alive.
The campaign occurs across a variety of different areas as you take pods to go between. Each area even has multiple zones within it which can either be cross very quickly or can take a long time. The difficulty scales brilliantly in this game, and you can go from Easy to Hard depending on the experience you want from the game. With multiple endings, depending on if you save all the little sisters or kill more than one. The campaign puts you to the test with an amazing story, secrets through the game, and multiple puzzles/challenges. The campaign is long and has fourteen levels, which vary in length and even include epic boss fights that put you to your wits.
BioShock plays like a typical First Person Shooter in many ways, but mixes in elements of RPGs to give variety. You gain these abilities called plasmids which you can buy with Adam (a type of in game currency) that can give you spells or tonics which give you buffs. There are many different weapons which throughout the game you can upgrade to make the weapons more efficient. There are seven weapons (wrench, pistol, machine gun, shotgun, grenade launcher, chemical thrower, and crossbow) and a camera. Unlike in Dead Rising the camera in this game actually serves a purpose, making you stronger/more effective against enemies as you take more pictures.  I personally played this game on hard and used the wrench almost the entire time without plasmids, so you can really choose the way you want to play with BioShock; either running through guns blazing, or taking your time sneaking around.
BioShock is an amazing game that offers a brilliant campaign, beautiful story, and amazing gameplay. This game mixes RPG, Puzzles, and FPS all gift wrapped into one fantastic game. You can have an epic struggle playing the game on hard or just enjoy the story playing on easy. There are loads of secret recordings spread throughout the game that develop the story and keep offering you more. BioShock is completely worth every penny even at full price. If you are frugal like me, then just wait till it’s on sale as it totally will.
Pros:
+Brilliant story that provides incredible replay value.
+Amazing combat system that allows you to choose how you play. (Either melee, guns blazing, or shooting magic everywhere)
+Loads of guns that allow you to mix your strategy, each with three different ammo types.
+A camera that allows you to increase your character strengths.
+A solid campaign with fifteen different levels.
+Secret recordings that give you more elements to the story and create a deeper experience
+Loads of different tonics which allow you to buff yourself and enhance your gameplay experience
+Loads of different plasmids that allow you to shoot electricity, fire, ice, and even bees.
Cons:
-The volume for the recordings cannot be adjusted, they use the same levels as the gameplay volume. (In order to hear the recordings I had to crank up my speakers and hide in a corner)

Pocket Kingdom is a rich and wonderful puzzle game that is an amazing example of progression in game design. What attracted me to this title were two things; one believe it or not, was the Steam suggestion tab. In a rare lightning in a bottle moment the suggestion system actually worked. Secondly was the wonderful art from the screenshots. I knew I had to get my hands on this game and I am glad to say that I didn't regret it.
The setting for Pocket Kingdom is of the steampunk variety with a big dollop of magic. You are a down on his luck adventurer who takes on a job to find a mystical floating island and take a picture of the slumbering god that inhabits it. Needless to say, easier said than done. You get shot down by pirates, thus begins the adventure. While the themes are very familiar in Pocket Kingdom the entire lore is original and at times a bit odd. The reason for that is that Pocket Kingdom does not hold your hand much in this game.
From a lore standpoint the game acts like its lore is all common knowledge, there are names thrown around and you feel like you are always trying to catch up to what is going on. It's not a gripe necessarily, but I do feel that to fully grasp every single detail of the story, that it might benefit from playing the game twice.
Now there are signs to tell you what buttons do what and occasionally a use this tool here type of thing, but you do feel very much bewildered when the game starts. I didn't mind this to be honest and I felt like I was on an adventure in a strange world.
Upon heading up the cliffs after your "landing" you soon discover that you are not the first and surely won't be the last to land on this island. There are several districts all brimming with their own people, factions, and lore to digest.
The inhabitants tell you the basic rules of what they have learned to call, "Pocket Kingdom." Doors and ladders are the only means of traversing from area to area, as physics is warped and walking left might just leave you all the way on the right.
Additionally, the god of the island is a trickster and puzzles are springing up all over the island.
Lastly, escape is nigh on impossible and you're out of luck!
Those rules are very important as you begin taking on the various puzzles the island has to offer. The game is played from a classic side-view and the basic goal is to explore, find useful gear, and get off the bloody island. Also, if at all possible, snag a picture of this supposed God.
How you go about this is completely on you, this is a game you will beat at your own pace. I absolutely loved the progression in Pocket Kingdom, the puzzles get harder and harder but never did I once feel overwhelmed.
The puzzles involve boxes, levers, and lasers. Things get tricky though when you begin throwing in grappling hooks, rocket launchers, and gravity pads begin to appear. Remember I said physics is warped? Yeah you can fall and land on top of the screen. It definitely takes some time to wrap your head around and makes puzzles dynamic as hell. I applaud the puzzle design as I couldn't imagine how the developer came up with such clever ways of using a simple concept.
When it comes to difficulty, there is going to be plenty of trial and error, no puzzle will stop you but some will take longer for you to figure out. Experimentation is key here but it never got tiresome for me. Also there is plenty of that "AHA" feeling when you get things working the way you want. It's very satisfying.
There is an over-world map that you can traverse that is riddled with secrets, passages, treasure, and easter-eggs. Progression is handled beautifully here as well, as you gain access to different parts of the island bit by bit. Going about finding all the rooms on the island is quite a task. Attention to detail is important and exploration is usually rewarded.
As a reviewer, my tip to you would be generally if you are looking to get somewhere that chances are there is a passage nearby.
Along the way you will collect gear that will help you navigate the island and make getting around less of a grind.
The aesthetics are strange but in good ways. The area that I felt was the weakest was the Sprite design, as you run into many characters that all look the same. However, the areas themselves are magically archaic, feeling old but brimming with an unseen life. Certain areas have a great amount of detail to them and look wonderfully rustic. Each area has generally its own theme and all of them are well done. My favorite is easily the Abandoned Temple, with the Pirates coming in a close second.
Overall I was very impressed with the game itself, it's designed very well. There are some gripes here though, the UI is particularly wonky, at one point getting locked on the reset progress screen, much to my terror.
Using the Steam overlay caused a few graphical errors where my character was in a place he actually wasn't. Nothing restarting the game didn't fix but enough to note.
The music/sound in the game was on par, but did get a bit grating on the ears sometimes. The music tends to repeat itself.  Not a huge complaint and honestly this will vary depending on personal taste. The game does feature Steam Cards/Achievements, and happily does have full controller support.
From a replay aspect, that is up to how much you care to fully understand the world of Pocket Kingdom. You could just get all the secrets and discover all the rooms and call it a day. That took me about six hours in total. I imagine a second play through would take significantly less.
Pocket Kingdom is a satisfying game in all regards. I am honestly very happy I discovered this game and greatly recommend it. You have seen games like this before so while not on high on the charts for innovation, if you loved games like Escape Goat or Blackhole then you should check out this game. It's fun, relaxing, and I loved the great puzzle design.
At the ridiculously low price of $6.99/£4.99 this is guaranteed to pay for itself in enjoyment.
Oh, and a nod for the people who have played it; Room 74 is impossible to find.

Limbo is the bully of puzzle platformers.
Unlike Super Meat Boy and Shovel Knight where every death feels deserved, only one in twenty deaths will you be like "yeah, I messed up there."  It's going to pick on you like you refused to give it your lunch money the day after its dad got drunk and wailed on it.
"Do you want me to punch you?"
"Hmm, well, there's this obvious thing right there I should probably avoid, I'll just not step on that button-like thing."
*SMASH*
"Okay, so that button-like thing is a platform, I'll use it next time."
"Let's try this again, do you want me to punch you?"
"Okay, now to step on that platform-like... *SMASH* button... ow."
The game doesn't reward you for learning from puzzle to puzzle.
Some of the puzzles are brilliant, some of them are just downright ridiculous.  (Not ridiculously hard to figure out, more like here're 3 things.  Notice how these three things interact with one another, now push this all the way to one side, start this thing swinging, clime a ladder, flip a switch, jump down, jump on that, grab that, count to three, run right, run left, faster!, run back right, push the jump button 3 times to climb this stack of boxes then jump again to grab that ledge before you're dead for the 50th time.)
The number of puzzles you're going to figure out, but spend 8 attempts redoing because once you get them down pat they require near pixel/frame perfect jumps is just depressing.
Speaking of depressing, the amount of times this game makes you just wait for your death is painful.
"Well, I know this boulder's going to be chasing me, guess I'd better run to the right in the pitch black to get a head st... and I fell down, oh, there was a ladder there in the darkness I couldn't see and I've now fallen into a pit to just wait for the boulder to come crush me... yup, that seems about par for the course by this point."
It's obvious that this game was just meant to punish you.  There're so few places where the penalty for failing a puzzle on the first try is that you just have to try again, and so many where it's you have to watch a death animation and then wait for it to reload the checkpoint.  The only thing that 30 years of gaming gives you on this game is knowing that you can push crates, and knowing to run to the very edge of a cliff before jumping, and that's it.
Some things will be intuitive, while some will just be boulder-out-of-nowhere,-pixel-perfect-jump-over-it-to-a-place-where-there-are-spikes-but-the-boulder's-going-to-smash-them-away-and-make-a-perfectly-smooth-landing-platform-but-you-don't-know-that-until-it's-bashed-you-against-a-wall-and-you-have-to-go-back-to-the-checkpoint-first insane.
If you like dying, and wondering how far that set you back (The one saving grace that will get me to the end of this game is that the checkpoints are never more than 2 puzzles behind you.  Even I'M not stubborn enough to beat this game if the checkpoints were few and far between.), then get the demo so you can say you've played it, and pick this game up when it's 90% off.  Everyone else should just watch a video on youtube of someone playing this game and call it a day.

Manage a vaguely Caribbean island, starting with cash crops, mining, and shacks, and build your way up to lucrative manufactured goods, tourism, and skyscraper apartment buildings. Along the way, try to satisfy the needs of your people to keep them happy enough that they won't overthrow you. If you fail at that, or anger a major country too much, there's always your military!
Though fun to play, Tropico 5 has a lot of problems. It refuses to load the second campaign scenario for me, and victory conditions in sandbox mode just outright don't fire. These issues, along with other technical and game design problems, detract from the overall experience enough that I would recommend holding off until the developers release a major patch.
While the writing maintains the same quirky Cold War/dystopian flavor as previous entries in the series, it lacks the same punch as Tropico 4 had. The cast of characters, one of Tropico 4's strongest points, has been gutted. The new characters just don't have the same cartoony faction personalities, and don't offer anything new or different to make up for it.
All that aside, you still get to build and manage resource/manufacturing enterprises, distribute wealth as you see fit, enact edicts and constitutional amendments to define the nature of your dictatorship, and set up tourist traps to rake in the tourism cash. Those parts are a lot of fun, and give you a lot of freedom to develop your island however you want to, whether that means a nation of happy, healthy citizens who gratefully vote to renew your mandate, or oppressed factory workers who endure squalor, surveillance,  and sub-par wages in order to maximize your Swiss bank account.
Speaking of the Swiss bank account, the dynasty system is an interesting new take on player avatars. The perks from leveling and deploying dynasty members are nice, but I'm mostly grateful that they give the Swiss bank account a purpose other than "because that's the kind of thing El Presidente does."
Still, it would be so very nice if I didn't have to fight the UI to find exactly the right corner pixel to click in order to close a building info pop-up.

Auditorium is a puzzle indie game made by Cipher Prime Studios (Splice, Fractal, Intake). As it's Cipher Prime's standard, they tried to make an unique game, which ended up successfully.
Gameplay revolves around using direction changers of sound wavelength that you have to direct into a speaker. You might experience a similar feel to a puzzle games built around gravity, as you'll have to set the reach radius of direction changers. But there are actually not just objects to change directions, there are also speed modifiers or attractors.
What's really worth praising is the fact that levels doesn't have a specific solution - it's up to your experiments that leads to your own way of activating the relaxing music (beating the level). In combination with great soundtrack and gorgeous flow of differently coloured wavelengths, Auditorium is worth even to those who aren't much into puzzle games, but want just to relax for a while at a casual game.
To name the biggest flaw of the game, is the fact that it's made in really low resolution for today's standards. There isn't a HD remake expected, so you'll have to put up with small window mode or blurry fullscreen. But to those who don't mind that, Auditorium is worth recommending.

Thumbs up because it's a nice enough game (the stealth parts are good fun, it has nice art, alright music and the voice acting isn't too bad although not too remarkable either) and to counter the probably numerous reviewers who tend to bash Ubisoft titles only because of Uplay.
Still it probably could've been better. It feels a little short, the ending came rather abruptly, and maybe half of the levels - sometimes in direct succession - are timed-based with you having little freedom in your approaches but encouraging to kill guards to get through them quickly as possible, as they are only rated by your speed and not by how many sightings, alerts or kills you've had (or not) as is the case with the stealthy levels. This is rather a downside because if people have ever asked for stealth elements that feel rewarding and fun it's the Chronicles games that of any AC titles have them (Chronicles: China had such time-based levels too, but they didn't feel like taking up as much space as they do in Chronicles: India). Oddly enough there are even parts where you are mostly forced (!) to snipe enemies down with a rifle, sometimes semi-silently, but still in a rather easy and cheaply feeling manner.
The timed-based parts aren't too bad, but can feel forced (Has there ever been a Precursor temple in AC that hasn't collapsed after you went through it? They apparently haven't been the greatest of architects...) and they have their somewhat unnecessarily difficult parts particularily when being in the need of tailing a person. I got slight moments of frustration when having to deal with some unprecise moments in controlling Arbazz during those time-based sections but those were luckily rather few and the checkpoints in this game are placed rather nicely. That aside the controls never felt too bad. Arbazz didn't always do what I wanted, or in the speed I had expected, but once you have your route through a section of guards mapped out and know how to do it it's usually doable in a fair manner.
After you've completed the game you unlock two modes which may give incentive to play the game again to grab all the collectibles (often coming with little lore snipplets), complete secondary objectives, unlock all the character/gear buffs or to play with increased difficulty. You also unlock a couple challenge rooms in Animus VR environment style which actually look pretty nice and fun to play, but I wonder why they didn't create another one or two main game levels if they had time to do these challenge rooms.
The story isn't much worth mentioning. There is a some background lore, which can feel a bit messy, but maybe only to the various names tossed in and out. It's your old Assassins-vs-Templars-arms/power-race thing. There were some nice artifact/Precursor ideas which I don't want to bring up because sort-of-spoilers but they remain vague and never translate into something you can grasp too well, before long you've finished the game and can only hope some of it is used in future titles (some of it is in Syndicate, but I wish there was more).

It's not perfect though - as others have said, it's a bit pixellated, audio tracks sometimes stop, and there are noticeable gaps in the looping, particularly in the early levels. It's also very fiddly at times, which is perhaps inevitable for a game about directing a stream of particles around using area-of-effect forces: it's hard to be precise, and sometimes a level needs you to be. After playing through the first half in a single sitting, the last few stages I played in short sessions as otherwise it would be too frustrating.
I picked it up in a sale, and don't regret that. It can be very relaxing, and there are no other games like it.

Runespell: Overture is a single-player turn-based RPG that uses poker rules and the game takes between 8-10 hours to complete.
Combat involves setting up poker combinations (flushes, full houses etc.) with different combinations dealing different amounts of damage. You can use your own cards or even steal individual visible cards from your opponents.
Dealing and receiving damage builds 'rage points' (essentially mana) that can be consumed to use spells (damage spells, defense spells, etc).
I would recommend this game for someone who wants a throwaway game to occupy a bit of time.
Pros:
- Easy-to-grasp gameplay concept
- Novelty poker rules are interesting in the RPG genre
Cons:
- Forgettable 'plot' - weak story
- Can be frustrating at times due to the RNG nature of cards
Short preface: I absolutely love the game concept and bought the flash version years ago on cypherprime's web page. This review is about the technological aspect of the steam version,

Like many other works of narrative fiction, TBG tells what people often refer to as a
. The story is centred around two game developpers: Coda, who created the levels that make up TBG without ever intending to publish them, and Davey, who has concocted the levels together to make TBG, and who narates the entire game by commenting on each level and detailing his interactions with Coda during the time period each level represents (the levels collectively span 3 years of history). The tale of the interactions between Coda and Davey is both TBG's strongest point and its most common criticism. Reading the negative reviews of TBG has shed light on something that I have never given much thought: drama is subjective. I have known people who think that Coda; I have known people who think like Davey. There is no suspension of disbelief required required on my behalf for their personae, because I have no disbelief in them to begin with. I cannot write the characters off as “Bah! They're just angsty/immature/irrational/etc” because I've interacted with individuals who genuinely think like they do. Were the production value in the narrative guidance not so high, and were this not a paid game, I might have even believed that this was a piece of non-fiction. To me, the story of TBG felt very real and quaintly human. It hit me very close to home, and playing through its narrative was an amazing experience.
A lot of people also seem to think that TBG is a window into the process of game development, and I feel that this is a terribly gross inaccuracy. This is a tale not about game development, but about the creative mind, and the game dev considerations only hold true for games driven by the creative mind of an individual – games that are not driven by the market, or even targeted at specific audiences. And if this creative process is personified as Coda in TBG, then Davey is the personification of retrospection, a facet of human nature that I (unfortunately) seldom ever see explored in fiction. From the very beginning of TBG, you are made aware that what you are shown is a chronicle of sorts composed by Davey that documents his interactions with Coda. Unlike most narratives presented in the first person, however, Davey's narration presents more than a mere transmission of information – through his narration, Davey presents a thought-inducing reflection on his past that is clouded in dreadful irony (of which he is only barely aware). This reflection by itself becomes something to scrutinise and to think about – gone is the narrator whose sole purpose is to tell you what is happening.
In summer of 2015 aired the second season of Oregairu. By the end of the second season, I felt betrayed by the series, and I felt I could no longer trust the reviews given by other people, for while the vast majority seemed to think that the second season, if anything, was even better than the first, I thought it was a disastrous train wreck that completely ruined what made the first season great. I give season 2 of Oregairu a
of flack because I consider it to be a story about angsty and immature teenagers who have trouble communicating, a story that I found to be incredibly tedious because it felt completely removed from the world I live in, and because never in my life have I dealt with situations even remotely similar to theirs. With TBG, I find myself in a very similarly polarised crowd, but I am suddenly on the other side of the recommendation schism. Many reviewers feel that the story is incredulous, or that it fails to achieve the emotional connect that it seeks, and my experience does not match theirs at all. I find TBG is a refreshing perspective on human nature that I do not often see in fiction. There were times where a single sentence made me pause the game because I became embroiled in my reaction to it. TBG has amplified difficult questions I've had to deal with in my own life and has given a new perspective on decisions I have taken in the past. Although it come at a steep price/hour ratio, I believe the experience to be well worthwhile.
Your mileage may vary.

If I would have to describe Sunless Sea in one word I would have to say: distances. True, I could have said seafaring, terror or loneliness. However most striking about this game are the distances you have to travel to explore the Underzee in all its horrifying beauty and to assure you, you will have to travel a lot.
The exploration takes a lot of time in the beginning, but once you have located all the islands the process of exploring shifts from traveling the zee to the encounters on the islands. There you will find the stories of terror the developers want to tell. Each story might take a different turn if you fail to succeed in a skill challenge. Don't worry if you fail, your next captain (Did I forget to mention this game is roguelike? Oops! Well, it is.) might succeed. But even if you succeed, the story might go south as your choice of action was the wrong one (I still grieve for my magician. But I had to eat him. He asked for it. Sort of.)
Which brings me to the story itself. Although you might choose a background for your captain (you don't have to) and therefore give him a reason, why he sails the Underzee, there is not a real story, but a lot of small stories, which merge into the story of your captain (I promise, next time I will save you Bob [the magician; I called him Bob]). Every location and every officer has its own story you can experience, for example the tireless mechanic aka Mike (yes, I called him Mike) has stolen something and is now plagued by nightmares and you can help him, if you want to (you don't have to). Each of these stories circle around fear, horror and nightmares. It is fascinating to experience the terrors the developers came up with. As long as its sailor's yarn you can bet its in this game, but in Sunless Sea it's real. Blood-sucking bats, gigantic moths and living icebergs. Only the kraken is missing. (And freak waves. They are missing too.)
The combat system is rather simple and repetitive. There is no damage control like in FTL and as the ships are steam-powered (or is it oil?) there is no need to take the wind into consideration (like in Pirates), so either keeping your distance or getting in close behind the enemy is the choice until your gunners have a firing solution (yeah, you don't have to do that). Then it's hitting the button for the weapon and repeat until either your enemy or you are on the bottom of the Underzee. Fighting multiple enemies might happen but its also rather rare and with a bit of intelligent navigation avoidable (which you should do).
Besides the monsters you can encounter neutral or hostile ships such as pirates on the zee. However you still might to experience the feeling of loneliness because the frequency of encounters is rather low due to the fact these encounters are mostly bound to spawning points near certain locations. This might be a deal-breaker to some, but I promise you in these moments of loneliness you will start to worry if your fuel and supplies (2 of 3 main resources, the other is money) will suffice or your terror-level will not rise too high before you reach the next port. (If it gets too high, you might experience nightmares or even worse succumb to madness, which equals death). All this is supported by a wonderful soundtrack which creates a dense and dark atmosphere.
However don't expect any voice-over. Except for the soundtrack and some sound effects this game is silent. No “Sail Ho”s, no “Arr”s will accompany you on your voyage. The voice of the narrator will be your inner voice. To some this might be another deal-breaker, but what do you expect, this is a 20€-game after all.
Furthermore after a certain point, depending on your playstyle, it might occur that you will just travel back and forth between two locations to advance one particular storyline and there is nothing much you can do in between, because you already have the biggest ship and finished the storylines of the ports on the way. This happened to me after round about 70 hours (!!!) in one iteration (maybe I'm playing it wrong). The distances then become a menace. I wished that the game becomes more difficult the longer your captain survives, but it doesn't. But this is high level nagging.
After all it's a good game, definitely worth a try.

I don't really want to give Sunless Sea a negative review, but I feel that it has more negative aspects than positive ones.
Pros:
+Excellent writing. Every story I read draws me into their world and I feel like I'm there with the captain.
+Risk/reward gambling. You can go farther out into the Unterzee for more profits/adventure, but the risk of something going wrong and dying horribly also increases with your distance from London.
+Everything has lore, and lots of it. If you're not a fan of reading a lot, this game isn't for you.
+Randomization of events keeps the game interesting as you make your rounds collecting port reports.
Cons:
-Permadeath. With a game this lore heavy, permadeath should not be a thing. You can avoid permadeath by making manual saves, but you'll still lose lots of time every time you die and read/skip the same things over again.
-The game actively punishes you for going faster. You'll have worse fuel efficiency with stronger engines and you can only do an event once per day (roughly a minute at zee), so quickly hopping from island to island is kind of pointless.
-The combat is super basic. For ships, stay behind them and shoot them. For monsters, back away and shoot them. That's it.
Overall, I'd give it a 6/10. I loved exploring the world, but once it was explored I had to mine for more stories, killing tons of time in the process. Initial impressions are excellent, but the late game suffers from slow gameplay and the same stories you've heard before. Get this game on sale if you can, since it's worth about 10 hours of great storytelling.

This is a very interesting game with a very profound and well-written (Gothic/Elder Gods/Horror) story. There is incredible potential in both the game itself and the game universe.
There is one, major, glaring flaw, however:
THE GRIND
From very early on in the game, you discover that you need fuel and supplies to continue playing. How do you get fuel and supplies? By Grindng. How often do you Grind? You always Grind. Why? Because if you don't Grind, you don't live.
Imagine WoW if your level 90 Paladin could potentially starve to death every few minutes, and needed a constant stream of Lesser Wolf Meat in order to keep playing. Want to go on a raid? Uh, sorry, I can't ....I have to go grind for 30 minutes so my dude doesn't starve to death. That is, in a nutshell, the gameplay of Sunless Sea.
It's understandable why they did this. The game requies some kind of economy to keep things interesting and to keep you questing. There is a threshold, however, beyond which the GRIND stops being fun and starts to be a chore. Exploring a vast underground gothic hell-planet is fun. Making constant supply runs from port to port just so you can, maybe, one day, buy a level 3 spotlight so that you can possibly, somehow, defeat the Death Crab (or whatever) in between supply runs is.....
Well, it feels more like *work* than an actual game. It feels like real life. Keep working so that you can live.
But I don't play games to feel like I'm at work. Therein lies the problem.
Devs: please fix your crazy GrindFest so I can give you a good rating. Sunless Sea has limitless potential, but playing currently feels more like a job than my actual job.

Limbo is the bully of puzzle platformers.
Unlike Super Meat Boy and Shovel Knight where every death feels deserved, only one in twenty deaths will you be like "yeah, I messed up there."  It's going to pick on you like you refused to give it your lunch money the day after its dad got drunk and wailed on it.
"Do you want me to punch you?"
"Hmm, well, there's this obvious thing right there I should probably avoid, I'll just not step on that button-like thing."
*SMASH*
"Okay, so that button-like thing is a platform, I'll use it next time."
"Let's try this again, do you want me to punch you?"
"Okay, now to step on that platform-like... *SMASH* button... ow."
The game doesn't reward you for learning from puzzle to puzzle.
Some of the puzzles are brilliant, some of them are just downright ridiculous.  (Not ridiculously hard to figure out, more like here're 3 things.  Notice how these three things interact with one another, now push this all the way to one side, start this thing swinging, clime a ladder, flip a switch, jump down, jump on that, grab that, count to three, run right, run left, faster!, run back right, push the jump button 3 times to climb this stack of boxes then jump again to grab that ledge before you're dead for the 50th time.)
The number of puzzles you're going to figure out, but spend 8 attempts redoing because once you get them down pat they require near pixel/frame perfect jumps is just depressing.
Speaking of depressing, the amount of times this game makes you just wait for your death is painful.
"Well, I know this boulder's going to be chasing me, guess I'd better run to the right in the pitch black to get a head st... and I fell down, oh, there was a ladder there in the darkness I couldn't see and I've now fallen into a pit to just wait for the boulder to come crush me... yup, that seems about par for the course by this point."
It's obvious that this game was just meant to punish you.  There're so few places where the penalty for failing a puzzle on the first try is that you just have to try again, and so many where it's you have to watch a death animation and then wait for it to reload the checkpoint.  The only thing that 30 years of gaming gives you on this game is knowing that you can push crates, and knowing to run to the very edge of a cliff before jumping, and that's it.
Some things will be intuitive, while some will just be boulder-out-of-nowhere,-pixel-perfect-jump-over-it-to-a-place-where-there-are-spikes-but-the-boulder's-going-to-smash-them-away-and-make-a-perfectly-smooth-landing-platform-but-you-don't-know-that-until-it's-bashed-you-against-a-wall-and-you-have-to-go-back-to-the-checkpoint-first insane.
If you like dying, and wondering how far that set you back (The one saving grace that will get me to the end of this game is that the checkpoints are never more than 2 puzzles behind you.  Even I'M not stubborn enough to beat this game if the checkpoints were few and far between.), then get the demo so you can say you've played it, and pick this game up when it's 90% off.  Everyone else should just watch a video on youtube of someone playing this game and call it a day.
