The amazing part of this game is that while there are still a lot of bugs to be worked out, and despite the fact that many of the features are not available, I still get emotionally drawn in to each and every one of my characters as they struggle for survival. I hope that each time I play, if my character can just hold out for one more day, help will arrive and they will make it. But they never do make it, which is what makes their struggle that much more powerful.
I feel like I want to write a story about how each of them lived and died in the zombie apocalypse. Their stories will always be etched into my mind -- every time they had to kill their first zombie; every time they set off a house security system and had to run like hell before the mindless hordes arrived; every time they had to scrounge through dozens of houses to find even a drop of water after the utilities have been shut off.
Every time new features are added to this game, there is more and more complexity added to the story of these characters. Give this game a chance if you are looking for a look into what would really entail a zombie apocalypse. People like to tell themselves and each other that they would hole up in a sporting goods store and would fend off the zombies until the cavalry showed up. Would they really? Would they be able to take the strain of smashing in the skulls of other human beings, regardless of their current undead status? Would they be able to do this to their friends and family? Would they be able to hide by themselves in a boarded-up house for days, months, years on end without going insane? I honestly do not know if I could do these things.
This game allows a peek into the gloomy sense of inevitable death which would be inherent in any apocalyptic scene. Give it your time, and you won't regret it.

If you look at the market for Rogue-like/lite FPS games there isn’t really a lot going on. There are classics like Ziggurat, Tower of Guns, Heavy Bullets and more recent attempts like Strafe. Overall this genre feels pretty niche though and that’s really a shame, because it can be so good if done right. And this is where Immortal Redneck comes in. It takes a lot of ideas of other games in the genre and manages to improve on them.
After an incident, our protagonist from Kansas finds himself in the ancient Egypt. Luckily, he brought some guns with him to fight the enemies that wait there. At the beginning of a run you start at the bottom of a pyramid and fight your way through 7 floors until you reach the top. There are bosses, chest rooms, challenge rooms, everything you would expect a Rogue-like to have. In total there are 3 pyramids, each with their own unique design, rooms and enemies. They can also be seen as some sort of difficulty selection, since the pyramids get progressively harder. I love how each pyramid got its own unique feel. There was clearly a lot of work put into the interior design of each pyramid and they all look fantastic.
A good Rogue-like also needs variety, would get boring if every run feels the same, right? To provide that, there are 9 characters to choose from, each with different abilities and stats, aswell as numerous weapons and scrolls you can find in the pyramid. The scrolls are the only pickup, next to weapons, that alter your gameplay. They can improve movement, change up your weapon stats or take your weapons away. It’s sort of a risk reward system. Should I take the scroll and maybe get an advantage? It could also be one that makes the run a lot more difficult.
Now to another point why I love this game so much. The movement. Its fast paced (and by fast I mean really fast), tight and exactly how it should be. The fast movement speed combined with the ability to jump multiple times gives you a freedom of movement I only remember from older FPS games. For some reason jumping around rooms in sonic speed with some funky music in the background is insanely fun to me and that’s probably what makes this game so good.
So, what do you get with Immortal Redneck after all? A polished game, with fantastic movement, beautiful artstyle and a bunch of replayability. At this time it’s by far my favorite contender in the genre and I would recommend it to anyone that likes some good, fast-paced FPS action.

Runespell Overture (Card/Poker/RPG/Strategy Hybrid)
For options we have Graphics Quality (Fastest, Fast, Simple, Good, Beautiful, and Fantastic), Windowed or Fullscreen, Drag and Drop or Click and Click (when moving cards around), and Sounds (Music and SFX).  You can also choose a screen resolution anywhere from 640x480 to 1920x1080.
The tutorial is very well-done, teaching you the ropes without being annoying.
So what kind of game is this?  It looks like an RPG that you play with cards, but that's not it at all.  The primary thrust is actually a solitaire game...  It's battle-solitaire-poker with RPG elements! *evil grin*  Whee~!
How does that work?  Looking at the screenshots will help a bit.  As you can see, we and our opponent are each dealt a set of cards, solitaire-style.  Ours is on top, theirs is on the bottom.  We need to create poker hands by grouping cards in sets of five.  If you don't know the poker hands, no worries -- the game will show you what groupings are "legal" to play.  Each "hand" will deliver a certain amount of damage, depending on the cards you've chosen.  For instance, a pair of cards (the other three cards in the group would be non-related) will deliver less damage than a flush.
In each round, you have three moves, and then your opponent gets three moves.
But wait, there's more!
You can steal your opponent's cards, and vice versa!  If you grab a card from his area (or the other way around,) the card underneath does NOT flip over until it becomes his turn, but whenever you clear a pile on your side, you can immediately have access to whatever card is next in the pile (assuming that it's still your turn.)  You CAN'T grab more than a single card from each others' piles -- if something is stacked on the other side (grouped,) it's off-limits to you.  You can of course move multiple, grouped cards around on your own side.
Here's an example of how it might work:
You already have three Kings grouped, and take a fourth King to add to the pile, then grab a King from your enemy's cards to make five-of-a-kind (yes, unlike real poker, you can have five of the same card.)  You use your third turn to select the five kings and deal damage.
This is where the strategy comes in.  Now that it's too late and you've used all of your turns, you see your adversary grab that Jack of Hearts from your cards to complete a Royal Flush!  EEEK~!!
Here's what you could have done to prevent it and still get your five Kings:
Forget about your three Kings for right now, grab his king, and place it on your single King, making a pair.  Grab the Jack of Hearts and put it on top of another card -- ANY other card!  It's better if you can do something with it, of course, but the point is to keep that card AWAY from your opponent.  Now you can do one of two things:  Do something beneficial (like moving a card to help yourself and/or hurt his progress) or you can move the pair of Kings on top of the three-of-a-kind, and make your attack in an upcoming round.
But wait, there's more!
Along the way we earn (via battles) and find special-use cards that can do anything from give you extra moves before your turn is over to poisoning to shielding yourself, to adding to your hit points, and more! You can only have a certain number of cards with you at the time of each battle, and (most of) the cards have finite-uses.  When they run out uses, you can use the money you earn to recharge the cards.
Be sure to SAVE before each battle!  You can abandon your progress if you wish -- it's an option to exit or go back to the main menu without saving.
There a bit more to it than that, including a storyline, but I'll let you discover that for yourself. ;)

What killed this game for me, however, is the relatively large number of timed missions (which I hate, no matter what game it is) and the number of missions that judge you based on how quickly you play through the level, so they - more or less - are also timed missions. In some cases there were multiple timed or time-judged missions in a row! This is not what Assassin's Creed is all about. I don't care if the developers attempt to excuse this under the guise of a "platformer". The regular, non-timed missions are wonderful to play. But once you take away the ability to strategize how to approach an enemy in your own way, you take away the fundamental reasons that define why we love Assassin's Creed. The timed missions are thrown in there like those pathetic tower defense missions in "Revelations", except the timed missions here aren't optional.
I don't remember if there were this many timed missions in "Chronicles: China", but the large number and frequency of them in "Chronices: India" killed my desire to continue playing or play in Plus mode after I finished it. If the levels in "Chronicles: Japan" are like this, I definitely will not buy it and will instead go back and play "Black Flag" for a fourth time. If I want to deal with timed platform levels, there are plenty of other games to scratch that itch, but that's not why I want to play anything related to "Assassin's Creed".

Runespell: Overture is poker on steroids.  I find myself blowing five hours in one sitting playing this game.  The game is based on poker, but spiced with a dash of magic the gathering like elements.  You play a nameless stranger whom others refer to as a "changeling," and the very first battle is a seamless tutorial on playing this game.  Basically, your goal is to reach a castle called "skullgrim" and discover the truth about yourself. Along the way, you will encounter allies and enemies, and pick up cards ("runespells") that you will need to get through the battles.
The first thing that struck me when I launched the software is the beautiful graphics and animation for the game.  The illustrations for people and characters are excellent, and the animations are fluid.  The game mechanics are easy to pick up, but the mental challenge rises noticeably as you move on to battle increasingly difficult enemies.
The game is based on poker, and requires five card combinations in order to deal damage.  The games are 1 on 1 between your Changeling and the opponent, and the object of the game is to reduce the opponent's health to zero.  However, Runespell offers two twists to this classic game.  First you are permitted to take cards from your opponent's side of the table during your turn, when you have three action points or make three moves.  And the opponent can do likewise during his turn.  The cards are all laid out on the table, and thus the game incorporates a metagame element, where you have to be aware of your opponent's hand at all times.  The card stealing could be utilized to strengthen your own hand, or block your opponent from making a combination.
The second twist in Runespell is the use of Runespell cards, which could deal direct damage to your opponent, and add a protection to your character.  The game allows the use of these cards through accumulation of "Rage" points, which you receive when you either deal damage or receive it.  The rage points are also utilized to call allies for assistance.  However, the game limits the abuse of runespells by adding restrictions.  First, you need to unlock them either by obtaining them from defeated enemies, chests, or purchasing from a merchant.  Second, the quantity is limited; in other words you have a limited supply of them for the ENTIRE GAME.  The quantity restriction does not apply to non-player character allies, though.  Early in the game, your opponents will have little in the way of runespells.  But as the game progresses, the opponents will be formidible precisely because of these abilities.  So it becomes crucial for you to prepare counters to these attacks before you engage these enemies.  However, there is no penalty for dying in this game, and you could even flee at any time if the battle goes poorly.
For players who are not familiar with poker, the game has an icon for "poker help" on the lower right corner of the screen.  This pulls up a helpful guide on the combinations available, plus the amount of damage that each combination metes out.  This guide is helpful even for experienced poker players, as you decide which combo to aim for or just attack to clear out the table for new cards.
Runespell: Overture may be repetitive, but the game is challenging and poker fans will definitely find this game delightful and fun to play.

Sunless Sea was a big surprise to me. I had been eyeing it for a while, finding the idea of navigating through a wide, unknown ocean with roguelite mechanics and lovecraftian atmosphere highly enticing, however it took me a while to get around to playing it. A friend of mine finally convinced me to buy it when it was on sale, and I began playing. I expected to at least somewhat enjoy it... I did not expect to spend so many hours on it though. The game really sucked me in way more than I bargained for, and now that I finally completed my captain's ambition - writing their "Zong of the Zee", a compilation of an entire life full of adventure, dread and the dark abyss below - I feel I can line out some of the pros and cons of the game.
Pros:
- The great writing. Just so you know, if you do not enjoy reading, this game won't be for you. About 75% of the charm comes from the both highly amusing and deeply unsettling little stories that await you in the varying harbors you travel to. I won't give anything away since it works best when you get surprised by what you find, but if you like lovecraftian horror and a good chuckle, then I can almost guarantee that you will enjoy it.
- The exploration. Yes, this game is a roguelike, so there is no set map of the islands you can encounter. Well, okay, a few of them are set in place, but most get shuffled around with every new captain you set out to zee with. Finding and exploring the stories of these islands is pretty much what this entire game is based around, and it is a real adventure every time you run into a new place. Sadly, once you know the islands, finding them again in later playthroughs isn't nearly as great as it was the first time round.
- You can choose between roguelite mode and normal mode. I preferred being able to save my game at any point, it was a much more relaxing experience than having to dread every move you make. In roguelite mode, when you die your captain stays dead, and you can set out again with a new captain from London, though all the islands in the Unterzee will have moved again, meaning that your charted maps from before are worthless. You can set some treasures aside for your potential heirs while you're still alive, meaning that your next fresh start will be a bit easier. It's a pretty neat mechanic.
Cons:
- The combat is functional, but kind of boring. It's a very basic battle of who has the higher HP, with very little strategy involved. It is not so bad that it ruins the game, but it doesn't add anything substantial to it either. The monsters of the zee just are a lot scarier when you can't shoot guns at them.
- It can get a little repetitive when you're grinding towards specific objectives. Sometimes, you basically turn into a trading vessel driving a set route from island to island, transporting goods (or smuggling sunglight) while trying to get enough money for your next goal, or things along those lines. It is something you can just disregard and keep adventuring, but I found it to be a very profitable, yet also quite boring tactic.
Overall, Sunless Sea is a game I would recommend to any lovers of Lovecraft and exploration. There is also a big expansion in the works that will add submarines to the game, which I'm quite looking forward to. But until then, my work as a captain is done now that my life's work has been composed. I will set out to zee again once I get the opportunity to pole that big eye with a torpedo.

I have to disagree with other reviewers here, and vote it down. However, keep in mind that it says 'played 0.5 hours' for a reason. This is NOT a solid review, and at best a first impression (though I've attempted it four or five times now).
To its credit, the game is elegant and simple. There's this stream that goes in one direction and you have to place 'circles' to break that flow. Some send the flow in a certain direction, others make it loop, and...I haven't gotten around to even explore them all. In any case, these circles come with an adjustable intensity that increase or decrease its effect.
And the point of the game? Set the circle so the stream goes through all the ...erm...volume squares (whatever they're called. just look at the pics or video, okay?). That the music only starts playing when the stream passes these squares is pretty original...
...unfortunately, this is the sort of game I just don't get. I get that it's supposed to be meditating or calming, or something, but on my end, it achieves exactly the opposite. I blame controls mostly (or rather: my inability to grasp them...feel free to blame me). Those streams don't "break" easily, resulting in many attempts at just getting me nowhere except in a "COME ON...go THERE, you...!!!" kind of growling voice. The proper placement is far from where I intuitively want to place them, which makes combinations a matter of blind luck. Again: to me. I can understand that if you understand the game, it'll be much more fun. But there is also some delay if you change things. And that makes juggling the stream even harder. More than once, I thought I had it...then it turned out that the act of me moving the circle temporarily had it touch all the needed squares, yet in the final form didn't hit one or even either one.
It's not for me. I usually tend to like minimalistic, abstract and (especially) original games, but that doesn't mean it gets a free pass. I'm not sure why it's tagged as "music" either. Yes, it has music, but it's in no way part of the gameplay (yes, it plays a larger role than the average game, but not by much. Or at all, if you take a strict definition of a music game).

Banished has a lot of potential but it really fails to live up to this, as a result of poor AI and obsure mechanics. I have fond memories of playing it when it first came out for many hours, but always the same frustrations arise.
The game is challenging, but for the wrong reasons. Not because it is designed well, but because it is designed poorly. You are often forced to deal with chain reactions as a result of a 'bottleneck of stupidity,' usually a villager hording a material for no reason or not building a vital construction despite it being prioritised. Eventually, the town will become large enough so that any challenge (read: AI stupidity) is made irrelevant so you just keep expanding and expanding with the same buildings again and again.
I have a number of questions concerning the game.
Why do villagers keep idling for no apparent reason?
Why does health gradually decline despite all needs to stabilise it being met?
Why does one household decide to horde the entire harvest of a particular crop, plunging the village into starvation?
Is there an answer to these? Probably. But no answer is surrendered by the game; very rarely do I have the feeling that I am fully aware of what is going on.
I greatly admire the ability of one man to create this game, but really, it is more like an alpha after being released for over two years.
I really *don't* want to give this game a negative review because really, it can be enjoyable. But I don't feel that I can give it a positive one.

I recommend this game for every Shmup fan on steam because it's free.
BUT :
This is a Danmaku made by a guy (Italian I think), and we can clearly see that he's a fan of Touhou. Everything looks like Touhou, the enemy Health bar, the first character, and the spellcards are pretty similar. That's not a bad point.
BUT (So many Buts, pun intended), it fails at creating a real atmosphere. You just have a background (like fog, space etc), and you're shooting enemies familiar to the elements (example : Aliens or Robots in space). Of course, the main goal on a game like this is to score a maximum of points, but it looks generic.
Gameplay is pretty much the same as Touhou or eXceed, you can graze (you have to if you wanna score anyway), you can bullet cancel with bomb, you also can cancel your death with bombs. You have a focus button to slow down and make your hitpoint visible.
The problem with the game, is the optimization. Sometimes it's full of colorful effects and the game runs at 60 fps. Sometimes, just because of the moving background, the game runs at 45/50 fps, creating a feeling of playing into the Matrix. Looks really weird.
Music-wise, it's good, not great. It's good because I heard some Dubmood in it, but like I said, it fails at delivering an atmosphere. Think of Touhou (very traditional music) or eXceed (more action = more agressive music). Jigoku offers good music, but that kinda feels off for this type of game. Musics don't fit that well to stages/bosses.
FINAL : It's free, so why not give it a try ? I still recommend it, but if you wanna play something more serious, go for Touhou, eXceed, Ikaruga or even Alltynex Second.

So aliright. As a seasoned tropico series player and a fan of the city builder genre, here is my slightly biased but informative review. :P
Tropico 5, the highly anticipated island dictatorship simulator sequel to its other relatively sucessful dictatorship simulating brothers (I'm looking at you numbers 3 & 4) is quite well "fun"
Seriously if you like games for their humor, this one won't sell you short on that. Looks neither. I like the visuals, they're welcome and refreshing for the series. However, if I have any complaints, its these new charachters and the changes to the old ones. Why does our wonderfully idiotic but always faithful Penultimulo now have a burly voice? What happened to our crazy environmentalist radio dj? Why am I not singing "Estabon no santos, le lavisidas navidad"? Though, I guess I just have to accept that these little changes come with that little uptick of a number change.
And while I'm not really a big fan to character changes like this, I can say that I do welcome a ton of the mechanical and core gameplay changes. Being able to side with Nazi's and Soviet's alike has been quite fun. And adventuring through (spoiler) with (spoiler) has been humorus and debilitating to my lungs. However, the little things have also done a ton for me. Country houses that also make food, orderly plantations, teamster offices a that function when you go beyond 1k in population, and ship traffic mechanics that at least attempt to wait for ships to pass (they still collide sometimes), shows that the devs took a good chunk of time to fix some of the core issues that layed within this iterations predacessors.
Overall, I'd say if your aquantied with the series, its good enough to grab and play again. If you really like haiemont/kalypso, pick it up at full price even. And if your new and don't know if you want to pay full to dip in, don't worry, give it a month or two and it will hit sale. And trust me, soon as you do you'll be glad you did.
However, be warned, 200 + hours of your life may dissappear when you do. :P

After a few days of drooling over this game I finally picked it up. Being a tropico fan and play every single title, I was expecting change in the new title judging from the screenshots but how different did this game compare to tropico 4? Tropico 5 does it's best at trying to make a safe move forward in the series while having some negative effects from this change. When tropico 4 came out, us players noticed new features which weren't too new. Tropico 4 was basically an upgraded rework of tropico 3+ abosulte power, taking certain buildings out and adding buildings from AP into the base game of tropico 5. Tropico 5 in the same case took some featues us fans enjoyed and brought them to a new level while reworking different systems in the game. If you continue reading this review, please note I play tropico for the sandbox aspect god mode and no god mode so I can sit back and create my perfect island.
Buildings - When I play tropico, I play it to build a unique island with loads of features and areas to create the perfect island. The let down I see in every base tropico game is there is a lack of buildings. Many of these buildings have been reworked in tropico 5 but non the less there is a lack of contact in this case. As I built my island I wanted to make it huge and filled with loads of locations for my citizens to enjoy and this was possible. Plenty of buildings were redone like the police station and the mansion but there was some feeling of content missing. In tropico 4 we received modern times which allowed for modern buildings to be added over time to replace older buildings. This feature was not my favorite due to the loss of buildings and forcing me late game to build only modern high rises which I found boring. In tropico 5 this was fixed and you can continue to build what you want at the cost of happiness(housing quality) The problem I found was tropico 5 tries to take modern times to a whole new level by adding different periods. This was cool and allowed my setllment to properly expand but this cost some content. Where are my condominiums to create an old town? Where are all the different theatres and such. Just like tropico 4 did to tropico 3, tropico 5 takes certain content from tropico 4 and modern times and tries to jam pack it into a full game.  Another problem I found with the new ways buildings works it the upgrade system. The menu's were redone and now each building has multiple tabs. This became a problem when I built my little carribean suburb consisting of 100 houses. When I hit a period of electricity I found that to enable electricity in every house was a hassle and was necessary to bring up housing quality. It would of been smart just like farm upgrades to allow a electrify all upgrade, uprading all homes to electricity. Another negative I found was the lack of carribean in some of the buildings. We used to have the option to build farms that looked like 20th century third world farms. That added a carribean feel in the game which I enjoyed. Tropico 5 instead brought the idea of plantations which seems fitting due to the colonization period of the game. Plantations existed in tropico 4 as dlc but were never a full feature as the main farm. I could continue to rant about my urge to have a million different buildings but I won't bore you with that, I'm just going to say some buildings should return: Immigration office(I like it more than a constitution which takes some time to update), City park(Necessary for a good metropolis), Condominiums(More valuable than apartments), Crude tenemants(Allowed for some low income areas.) Some buildings in tropico 5 were gould though, I enjoyed the added embassy system which allowed for more diplomatic relations and the abillity to build little gardens to put filler land. The redesign of the teammaster and construction offices were also a nice touch to the game. The game also lacked more skins for buildings like what the apartments used to have.
Mechanics- If there was one area of tropico 5 that grinded my gears the most, it would be the new mechanics. There were some great features in tropico 4 that gave me full control of the game. In tropico 4 I was able to set wages for each education level or building type. In tropico 5 the education version was erased and the building type was created into trash. Every time a building is built it is built as the default income level. This was annoying because I would have to set my wages for the buildings over and over again. On top of that for house rent and for building salaries their was no slider! You basically have 5 levels of wealth to pick from and it was annoying. I miss being able to make some homes free, now I can't do that. Kalypso should of kept that system instead of reworking it. Another feature I disliked even though it was realistic, was the research system. It was a waste of effort and a blatant civilization knock off. I understand why this is in the game(the different time period progresssion) but it was just not needed. Kalypso could of kept the buying building permits instead and put some effort into other aspects of the game. The last mechanic I want to touch upon is the trading system. Again kalypso proved itself to put a more realistic touch to tropico. No more import, export system like we had in the older tropico games. To run trade you now needed ships! ship ships ships ships ships. To progress anywhere in my island I needed alot of ships so I can export my large industry. Unlike old games where the dock would just import and export now you would need a trade agreement for a certain good and it would cost you a ship. This feature would be ok if you can send multiple resources on one ship but no, you need a ship per good which ended me up wiht a giant port area with 10+ docks. Another problem I found was that in tropico 4 importing was a great feature. No more focusing on raw resources if I didn't want to, I could import and still make a large profit. Now in tropico 5 I need to import each good individual ship by ship which became an annoying hassle. And for some reason my 20 team master offices couldnt get the goods to any of my factories...
Other dissapointments- The game lost it's touch. I felt a lack of good music, the other tropico games had tons of jams and had some nice radio anchors. Tropico 5 if anything should get the award for most annoying news anchor, even more cringe worthy than betty boom.
I would continue to rant but I would rather you guys not suffer from my terrible grammar and such.
Pros
-New Graphics
-New Feel
-Good Political System(Is actually hard)
-Reworked army system
-Multiplayer(Still yet to try)
-Reworked Building art
Cons
-Terrible import/export mechanics
-Lack of enough buildings(Probably will cost $20 to get 8 more buildings, sigh)
-Dynasty(Fun but get's annoying when family members cause revolutions)
-Rebellions(Stop attacking my guard towers every 5 minutes)
-Terrible music playlist and radio host
-Muh Condos
Final Verdict
The game finally feels different and I will enjoy it. If you own tropico 4 expect something different and I myself will be jumping between both games due to their differences. In the end I will reccomend this game and hope for future content fixes, releases etc. Also hope kalypso will make more than one big dlc for once.

If there was a neutral option I'd choose it - it's exactly the game for a neutral review. That even got me thinking that Valve does it on purpose because if that option existed the rating of all games would've been MUCH lower and the games with "overwhelmingly positive" rating would've been just "positive" which doesn't help to sell a lot of games. I even wanted to choose negative option in the spirit of defiance (I really don't like to me manipulated like that even in such small things) but then I decided that it'd be unfair to post a negative review for a game which delivers on its promise to scare the s*it out of you even if it has some major drawbacks. Again - I'd give it a neutral review but since the negative option is for absolutely terrible games which are no fun whatsoever or fraught with bugs let's give Outlast a positive review.
So let's start with pros - it's REALLY scary. In fact, it's THE ONLY game I've played which managed to scare me (and I've played five Silent Hill games and some other pathetic attempts I can't remember the names of) and it wasn't just cheap jump scares like FNaF but real blood chilling, visceral fear. I'll tell you more - it's IMPOSSIBLE not to be scared when you play this game because you have no means of defending against monsters except for running and hiding and (let's just put it this way) the game exploits our biology. So if you like scary stuff - just get the game and a pack of diapers maybe and if you're not scared take it with a neurologist because there's something wrong you (unless you played it with your butt cheeks clenched and repeating "I'm not scared, I'm not scared, I'm not scared" to prove what a tough guy you are). Also it runs well on Mac OS - I got the same frame rate as on Windows although usually it's significantly lower.
Now let's look at the cons and there's quite a few:
- the story is very, VERY poor - it's better not to think about how cliched and plain the plot is when you play the game (and the last part of the story is the worst, I absolutely hated it),
- the game is awfully short, I finished it in 8 hours but I was playing it safe and read every single document or note with a great deal of attention (and I really regret about this now), also I got confused a couple of times so it can be easily done in 6 hours - even less if you're a hardcore gamer, I think it can be done in 3 hours if you're not hiding from anyone and not looking for documents (or reading them, God forbid),
- poor optimization, I'd expect the game that looks like THIS run at 60 FPS all the time; I believe they could've done better job,
- too few enemies - they recycle like 5 of monsters (not TYPES - the SAME ones - you can't kill anybody there, remember?) throughout the game - it's just lazy,
- notes and documents: I'd have to spend a lot of words to explain my grief with this feature so let me put it this way - it's the ultimate filler to prolong the game up to twice as much it would be without them and they really DON'T matter.
In the end, I think the game's ok, I guess (except for the last act - just suppress that c*ap out of your memory and it'll be ok). I'd recommend it to someone who likes the horror genre - just buy it at a sale otherwise you might be disappointed).

Now for this review:
*Game Budget* The price as of this review is about $40. Normally new games are $50, so this game being $40 is a nice change.
*Graphics* The graphics are a slight improvement over Tropico 4, and the character graphics are horriable. Granit, I have to play it in low settings or risk the game lagging out, but Tropico 4 character graphics were not that bad.

In conclusion to my review, I shockingly do recommend Tropico 5, but only on this biest: I am a fan of the Tropico games and plan on owning them all again some day. I do hope the game devolopers improve the game and read the player reviews for I found them to be very helpful.

It's disappointing to see that almost a year after launching "China", Climax and Ubisoft didn't learn their lesson. This 2.5D game is pretty and has some good moments, but most of them are overshadowed by general mediocrity and some really poor aspects.
The controls are the biggest problem with this game, as they never feel very responsible. Some movements are particularly frustrating, such as trying to climb from the ceiling to the platform above. Add some awful timed sections (quite a lot of them!) and horrible combat controls, and you will have an idea of how often you will be frustrated in this game. It's abysmal for a game that focuses on stealth and platforming. Unfortunately, combat still feels like an afterthought and punishment for getting spotted. You never feel like a particularly skilled assassin - your usual silent kills trigger quite a big noise, which can easily alarm nearby enemies. Climax has decided to add some new character types that are even more frustrating and cannot be killed unless you stun them with a smoke bomb, which makes little sense in an Assassin's Creed game. There's also more helix powers this time around, which allow you to quickly kill enemies with one hit or suddenly become invisible. Unfortunately, certain levels force you to use these powers, which isn't great.
On top of that, the story itself isn't particularly original or engaging. There's some awful dialog and dull voice acting, The repeating lines such as "faster Arbaaz, faster" are quite annoying.  It also feels like the ending comes way too quick - I was surprised to see I finished the game when "the end" achievement popped up on the screen. Once you're done with the story, you can spend more time with the game by starting "new game plus" or play some challenge rooms (there's only six of them).
The visual side is colourful and pleasant to the eye, but unfortunately there's not a lot of graphic options available and the lack of good anti-aliasing settings is a big eyesore.
This is a title that can be recommended for the fans of the series who are interested in the lore. Otherwise, there's a lot of better stealth games out there - for example Mark of the Ninja.

I see a lot of negative reviews so I think I'll address those first:
1.) This game is part of a trilogy that started with AC Chronicles: China and there will be a third game later this year. They didn't release it all of a sudden as a money grab or as a second thought.
2.) No this isn't a full AC game like Syndicate or Unity; it's a 2.5D platformer.
3.) If you understand 2, then you should also know the controls are best with a gampad. I would never recommend using a Mouse & Keyboard for a 2D platformer. Just grap a gamepad off your Xbox or Playstation and use that.
Now for my thoughts:
I really like these games. There's a lot of stuff people have been asking for in an AC game or speculation as to when and where the next game would take place. The truth is, there's so much stuff that Ubi could keep pumping them out for years and years and people would get sick of them or say they're just milking the franchise. Either way, it ends up a no-win situation for Ubi. I like these games because they explore new areas and possibilities without having to do another long 20 hour game they'd charge $60 for. Maybe people will like one enough they'll explore that setting more with a larger game later.
The graphics aren't bad. It's a 2.5D game so it doesn't need the most fancy realistic looking stuff. The controls aren't bad either with a game pad. I haven't tried with a M&K but I guess some people struggle with it. I do love the artwork used in the cutscenes and the voice acting.
As for content you will get a decent 5 or 6 hours in the first play-through. Once you beat it you can do New Game+ where you start with all your unlocked upgrades from the first time through. All in all, I have to say I definitely recommend this game.

Banished is very unique in its play-style. I'm a huge fan of city-builder and strategy games, and so to find a game that really breaks the mold was very refreshing. No tech trees or restrictions is a nice touch, and the idea of being a challenging survival game blended with the usual city builder element is really great. I want to love this game. I want to say its the best city builder game to come out since Sim City 4, but there's a few crucial issues I have with the game.
The most significant issue in Banished is that I find myself staring at numbers and messages more than anything else. It's a constant game of moving around my profession numbers. What's worse is that for being such an interface-heavy game design, the UI itself is actually not very well-designed or thought out. The micromanagement in the game suffers from a serious lack of depth. Once you've planned out your city, which is a matter of ensuring your people don't have to walk too far to drop off supplies or get to their homes, you begin your journey of tediously shuffling around professions endlessly while staring at the event log, professions and resource tabs. You're watching a number (Like food or fuel) slowly go down while you frantically try keep that number up by doing anything you can  but a lot of the time I feel like there's nothing I can do. If my people start dying from starvation, it's nearly impossible to fix it without losing a huge chunk of my population, because when people die the replacements take a long time to get settled into their new home and begin work.

All and all. If you like delicate city building simulations. This game is for you.

Auditorium is a puzzle / music / art game. In it, the player must direct beams of light to pass over audio boxes and to hear music. I'd say that most of the puzzles are fairly easy (there are a couple that are difficult though.) But I believe that the game is visually and audibly stunning.
The gameplay is simple. Light streams out from fixed locations. The player manipulates several different types of lenses to direct the rays of light to audio boxes. The lenses can be resized and can be moved around the screen. Obstacles may appear, and may be useful or a hindrance depending on the circumstances.
Audio boxes play music when hit with the correct colored light. Each box will play one instrument of a piece of music. Different music pieces are separated into "acts." The music is filled out more as the player progresses through each act. The final level of each act automatically plays the completed music. All levels (including the special level) can be played once unlocked.
I was impressed by the designers make creative use of the game's mechanics. I found myself using lenses in unexpected ways. So, a something like a "light gravity well" can scatter light just as easily as it can clump it together, and an arrow lens can bend light just as easily as it can bounce light.
I find the game itself is artistically stunning. It fills me with a sense of wonder when I play it. Each packet of light leaves a feint afterglow in it's wake. Multiple packets of light cause entire areas of the screen to glow. It felt like I was drawing with light as I was moving the lenses around. There were times when I'd rather play around than complete the level. The game encourages this by removing all lenses and obstacles, and showing only the light once each level is completed.
The level design often coveys a feeling related to the music. For example, I found one level of the act of daydream requires almost no effort to complete (I consider it like daydreaming in that regard,) and the way the light moves in Atlantic looks like streams of water moving around.
The music is also good, although each piece is fairly short. By far, my favorite piece is Luminal, followed by Daydream. But, I enjoyed all the pieces of music. The whole thing, from opening scene to end credits, feels professionally done.
The game has flaws. One problem is that the music is short. Most musical pieces last between 10 to 20 seconds. On particularly difficult puzzles, you could hear the same music dozens, possibly hundreds of times before moving on. This can grow tedious after a while.
The game also has minor issues with the controls, At first, I had a bit of trouble figuring out that you could resize the lenses. (A little experimentation and it became intuitive though.) Sometimes when I resize lenses placed next to each other, I accidentally resize the wrong thing. (This often has the effect of scattering light everywhere, which can be fun.) Although, The problem is understandable because you have multiple layers of objects on top of each other, and the game does a good job of handling it.
Overall, I really enjoyed Auditorium and I think it is very well done. If you love puzzles, love that sense of wonder that comes from an hearing amazing performance, love exploring new ideas, and/or love color, light, and music, then you'll probably enjoy this game.
If you just want to hear music, then consider that most of the music is between 10 to 20 seconds long. If you're looking for a challenging puzzle, then know that the game is fairly short and most of the puzzles are easy. Even so, I really enjoyed it.

Banished is what Banished is: A sandbox city-building Sim.
I wholely enjoyed this game. When I first picked it up, I didn't quite understand it. Amonst thinking I was doing things right, then takes me eyes off the tools for a moment and suddenly everyone is starving to death because they can't procure food fast enough due to the lack of tools. For awhile, I stopped playing thinking it was too hard and somewhat unfair (the land generation can be pretty cruel though).
After coming back to it again, learning a few tricks for myself, I saw the game a bit better. I managed to get a population of 1000+ people and getting about 70% of the achievements in 1 town. It was a really fun endeavor to reach that milestone for me.
The game has a few flaws of course. Workers living and working on opposite ends of the map, the tiniest hills are a pain in the butt, old people taking up living spaces from young couples who I need to make me more children but can't because the old people just don't die..., and then there is the lag. I have a pretty decent (not high end but more like medium end) rig but as the town gets bigger you WILL notice the lag, espically if you run at 10X speed. My 1000+ town caused so much lag at 10X speed that 5X speed ended up being faster... and even that was laggy. (8-11 fps VS 18-22 fps).
A few other issues pop up every now and then but in the long haul, the game is enjoyable with a good touch of challenge. It feels pretty rewarding to see the town grow. After that though the game loses replayability unless you are going for 100% achievements. (have fun btw.... 200 years is like 72 hours of running gameplay, twice as so considering the 10-20 fps you get with large towns).
I recommend the game, but only if it is on sale, honestly. It'll consume a good chunk of time until you've played it through like me.

Auditorium is a very neat little...meditation tool? I hesitate to call it a puzzle game because the whole way through a level in Auditorium is nothing but zen and relaxation. When I think puzzle game I think mental stress; this is the exact opposite.
Each chapter is a song which is further broken down into levels of parts for that song. For example, the first level may be the bass line while the second and third levels establish the intertwining melodies. To complete a level all you have to do is direct the flowing particles to a certain destination. While there are some serious shenanigans that must be pulled to complete later levels, the atmosphere and music combined with the peacefully flowing particles creates this meditative trance that entirely drains away all of your stress.
On a side note, this game runs ABYSMALLY. On my overclocked GTX 680 I can only average 20-30 fps. Take one look at a screenshot and you will be baffled as well at such a terrible framerate. That being said, due to the minimalist design, a poor framerate doesn’t destroy the incredible feeling from playing.
Auditorium is a really cool experience, there’s not a ton of content but for a quick relaxing session it really is worth every penny.

TL;DR This game has some great ideas, but the implementation is very flawed. Do yourself a favor and play in merciful mode unless you want to die because of bad game and UI design, losing days of progress. This is made even worse by this being a heavily text based game with a rigid quest system, so dying means just having to read the same text again and redo everything you already did.
Here's a detailed example of what I mean by bad design. You die if you get three wounds. That's pretty fast considering how easy it can be to get wounded and how other things that can kill you will only do so at much higher levels. But the main UI doesn't show you your "wounds" number. Instead you are expected to go to the management menu, called the "gazetter", then go to the "journal" tab, then find the "menaces" section so you can find out how wounded you are. Thats bad enough in that you'll neglect to do all that and do something that kills you. But there are times when you have the option of doing something that can wound you, and the game doesn't let you go to the "journal" tab. So expect to die a few times because of that.
Also there was the time I went to the surface to get a shipment of supplies for cheap prices, and the game made me buy each unit of supplies individualy. This may not sound like much but I bought 70 units and each supply bought required scrolling to the "buy" storylet, clicking the button, then clicking ok, then scrolling again etc.

A nice change from the typical cod/battlefield mechanics. This game almost makes me think it's a fps equivalent to dark souls, the gameplay is straight forward yet hard to master and with almost everyone using iron sights you know you have to earn your kills. I play on realism mode and most of the time a single bullet kills at least from a rifle, this makes gameplay very tense and because friendly fire is on (and there is only an ally indicator at short range) it really makes you and your team think about what they are doing and where they are shooting. The teamplay on this game is great, many people use VOIP and a decent commander can really turn the tide of the battle by orchestrating the battle, and unlike a lot of other games I play everyone seems to actually listen to what the commander/squad leaders are saying and follows orders. The most common class is rifleman and when being the japanese team it's a single shot reload type weapon like a sniper which almost makes it feel like a musket, I actually find this great because it makes combat situations really tense and you see players scrapping around desperately trying to fight off the enemy in the trenches etc.
My best moment so far has been when I flanked the enemy in the trenches on my own with the assault class that comes with an SMG. Because all of the enemy were distracted shooting my team I shot down their firing line and killed about 9 of them with headshots in a few seconds. The commander found out/saw the opening I made and ordered a huge attack up that side so everyone charged into the gap in their defence and we went on to win the match. This games great because it makes you feel like your actions really matter.
The graphics could be better and the UI isn't the best either but it's still a great game to play.

Runespell: Overture melds together classic RPG components with Windows Live's player-vs-player solitaire with poker.  I obtained Runespell for free in a pile of coal during the Steam Holiday Sale 2011 event.  Receiving the game for free, I simply assumed that Runespell was merely a terrible, no-name title that was not worth playing.  It was not until the Summer 2013 that I truly realized what I had come across.
Runespell sports a great soundtrack with honestly a decent storyline.  Often times, card games that try to incorporate RPG elements (or just a storyline) end up drowning out the added components with the basic mechanics the card game - Runespell does not do this.  If you are a cards-only enthusiast, this may stray a little too far from those roots; if you are an RPG-only enthusaist, this may feel more like a card game.  However, if you are willing try a game that can have both, Runespell: Overture is for you.
Verdict: While Runespell: Overture is far from a lump of coal turned into a diamond, but it is definitely a gem.  Simply put, Runespell is a fun, player-vs-computer, RPG, solitaire, poker game - and it is done very well.  The game is so enjoyable that I honestly look forward to a remake or sequel that would incorporated online cooperative and competitive gameplay features.  While it is definitely not worth $10, the current sale of $2 at the time of this review is definitely worth looking into.  Here you will find a game that successfully feels like an RPG, while feeling like a card game.

Let's get the bad out of the way, first: The game's in the running for the absolute ugliest I've ever seen. It's blatantly unfinished, with two out of three game modes to be added later. There's a few nasty glitches, though no longer anything game breaking.
I still have to recommend this as one of the best horror games I've played. Beyond just having some legitimately creepy monster designs, it just has an incredibly effective central mechanic that ratchets up the tension. You're in an abandoned building, filled with monsters. The good news is that you have a 100% effective weapon against them. The bad news is that it's your blood -- every time you try to kill an enemy, you inflict a bleeding wound on yourself and need bandages or you'll eventually bleed out and die. The game becomes an exercise in avoiding combat where possible, and where forced to, it frequently becomes a tense race for the next medkit before you become too far gone and either collapse or get easily picked off by one of the monsters. I've rarely played a game that left me with as much dread and fear as this one did.

Runespell: Overture is a decent and enjoyable game. The story plays out as a fantasy adventure, your character being oblivious to his past and must do battles with numerous foes to advance, making allies and doing quests along the way.
The game play is somewhat unique, using a combination of battle and magic cards to attack your foe. One earns points by creating sets of 5 traditional cards (ace-king: hearts, spades, diamonds, clubs), using rules akin to poker, ie (pairs, 3 or 4 of a kind, straights, flushes, full house etc.). Better hands are worth more attack points (eg. full house > 2 pair). Cards are laid out in columns of which the top card can be taken to make a set, including your opponent's. Meaning strategy is important in order to create the best possible hands while trying to prevent the opponent from doing the same.
The game is simple to play once you know the rules, and can be a good way to spend half an hour or so. Battles can be hard at times but with perseverance the game is not too difficult to beat, I finished it with about 9 hours of game play. I would enjoy a sequel to continue the story as it did seem unfinished at the conclusion. At a discount price the game is worth a shot, if you like card and/or poker-like games. 6.5/10

Banished is very unique in its play-style. I'm a huge fan of city-builder and strategy games, and so to find a game that really breaks the mold was very refreshing. No tech trees or restrictions is a nice touch, and the idea of being a challenging survival game blended with the usual city builder element is really great. I want to love this game. I want to say its the best city builder game to come out since Sim City 4, but there's a few crucial issues I have with the game.
The most significant issue in Banished is that I find myself staring at numbers and messages more than anything else. It's a constant game of moving around my profession numbers. What's worse is that for being such an interface-heavy game design, the UI itself is actually not very well-designed or thought out. The micromanagement in the game suffers from a serious lack of depth. Once you've planned out your city, which is a matter of ensuring your people don't have to walk too far to drop off supplies or get to their homes, you begin your journey of tediously shuffling around professions endlessly while staring at the event log, professions and resource tabs. You're watching a number (Like food or fuel) slowly go down while you frantically try keep that number up by doing anything you can  but a lot of the time I feel like there's nothing I can do. If my people start dying from starvation, it's nearly impossible to fix it without losing a huge chunk of my population, because when people die the replacements take a long time to get settled into their new home and begin work.

• City Skylines
• Stronghold
All and all. If you like delicate city building simulations. This game is for you.

Banished is what Banished is: A sandbox city-building Sim.
I wholely enjoyed this game. When I first picked it up, I didn't quite understand it. Amonst thinking I was doing things right, then takes me eyes off the tools for a moment and suddenly everyone is starving to death because they can't procure food fast enough due to the lack of tools. For awhile, I stopped playing thinking it was too hard and somewhat unfair (the land generation can be pretty cruel though).
After coming back to it again, learning a few tricks for myself, I saw the game a bit better. I managed to get a population of 1000+ people and getting about 70% of the achievements in 1 town. It was a really fun endeavor to reach that milestone for me.
The game has a few flaws of course. Workers living and working on opposite ends of the map, the tiniest hills are a pain in the butt, old people taking up living spaces from young couples who I need to make me more children but can't because the old people just don't die..., and then there is the lag. I have a pretty decent (not high end but more like medium end) rig but as the town gets bigger you WILL notice the lag, espically if you run at 10X speed. My 1000+ town caused so much lag at 10X speed that 5X speed ended up being faster... and even that was laggy. (8-11 fps VS 18-22 fps).
A few other issues pop up every now and then but in the long haul, the game is enjoyable with a good touch of challenge. It feels pretty rewarding to see the town grow. After that though the game loses replayability unless you are going for 100% achievements. (have fun btw.... 200 years is like 72 hours of running gameplay, twice as so considering the 10-20 fps you get with large towns).
I recommend the game, but only if it is on sale, honestly. It'll consume a good chunk of time until you've played it through like me.

Early Access Watcher Reviews Spellgear
Update Version: 0.9.0441
Disclosure: This game copy was bought by the reviewer.
Gameplay Footage:
It is tough to properly judge a multiplayer centric title on the core content without the proper online population to back it. I spent hours of my time waiting for arenas to pop and never ran into a single player once I reached Storm Island. It is harder still when you are dealing with Early Access and the potential fluctuation of content release. This is usually why I try to catch the initial burst of activity during the first week so I have a better understanding of the difference before the re-review six months later. I have spent roughly twelve hours exploring the world of Astarma and believe I have enough to get a general idea of the environment.
Three classes are currently available with each one representing a specific magic type. Tamer (Mage) utilizes fire, Rangers use storm and the Paladin is regulated to frost type skills. Every action performed by the player requires mana including sprinting and jumping. The default attacks used by each class don't use mana, but the Ranger's default requires purchasable arrows. Mana and health are replenished by standing still or using potions, which can be bought or traded for using wild mushrooms scattered around the islands. Equipment can also be found at a few venders in exchange for ingots gained through Crusades or tokens you acquire from Arenas (auction house is not live, most of the vender NPCs are still not functioning).
Combat is tied to the non-target system introduced during the tutorial. All actions are performed using skills and require the player to manually aim toward the intended target to successfully inflict damage. Dodge allows you to cartwheel out of the way of an attack while damage mitigation skills will reduce incoming damage. It is much easier to just strafe around the enemy and ends up making the NPC combat incredibly boring. Every monster type does one or two attacks with varying speeds and depending on the circumstances (fireballs and knife throws) you will not be able to avoid damage. Hit-box sizes also seem to be a problem with certain player skills being too slow to keep up with enemy models, resulting in combat becoming extremely cumbersome.
Quests are the standard kill X amount of Y, collect number of Z and go speak with this individual found in every other game. Unlike most games, however, the quests have you roaming across major lengths of the island map to complete a simple objective. The usual demands of the local peasantry slowly dissipates in favor of teaching the player about the historic properties of the conflict between the Foundation and the followers of Migurat. By the time you decide who to swear allegiance too, the quests will be dried up and Crusades/PvP will be the only real activities to pass the time. Open-world PvP relies on a territory system centered on specific orbs located along the shoreline of the major island. I have yet to see what the territory percentage provides even after I spent two hours destroying every orb to hit the 100% threshold. I have yet to find a group for the Crusades (dungeons with special objectives), but I have been in a couple of PvP Arena matches to understand the general concepts.
The basic rules for capture the flag apply with teams requiring both flags to score a point. Killing enemy players, damaging said players and scoring points provide experience pooled together to unlock upgrade points. Each point can unlock a single improvement that ranges from useable abilities, increased stats and additional potions. The skills are divided into three branches with a powerful ability on offer once all three branches are completely purchased. Once the timer runs out (12 minutes), the match is over and points are applied to your overall rank. The 1v1 map does not have the unlock system, instead relying on the skills each player has to overcome their opponent. This format is nothing particularly special, but the matches can be relatively fast-paced depending on the team compositions.
Inconsistencies are apparent in the environment and are painfully obvious with fall distance. I managed to fall five floors with a net lose of 97 health while falling two floors in other areas to the net lose of 480. I also became wedged into a railing in a few areas that placed me in a falling animation. Some other problems were present, mostly in the form of quest markers not properly displaying and random pop-ins. Regardless, the game managed to maintain a 30 FPS (locked at 30?) the entire time I was playing the game.
Visually the game has some splendid texture detail and lighting, though it could use some better smoothing for enemy models and buildings. Fire effects are a bit weak, but colors are vibrant in most cases. The real treat comes in the form of the night sky, which is absolutely stunning. Ambient sound is pretty good and helps overcome the limited, but fitting music selection. The aesthetic is higher quality than some of the MMOs I have run into recently, it just doesn't stick out much.

This was one of the hardest games for me to review in months and I believe the reason for it was boredom. The combat system is tedious due to limited mana usage and a lack of skill diversity to keep things interesting. Quests are sparse and rely too much on downtime (travel time) to lengthen them. PvP is hindered due to a very limited player base and player interaction is rarely possible for the same reason. Without enough enjoyable content to help offset the wait times for PvP matches, the experience becomes hard to tolerate. Until the content amount increases or the player base increases, I cannot recommend Spellgear. Hopefully when I return in six months the situation will be more lively.

Cons

I'm a few years late to this one. While waiting for Civ VI to inevitably take over my life at the end of this month, I needed some game to tide me over. I went into my backlog and chose this quaint little medieval city-builder.
Banished is a game that offers unforgiving tough love. I feel like this game is the "Oregon Trail" of city-builders, and it's enjoyable as a challenging game of resource management. Unfortunately, it isn't exactly the best at explaining itself, and so it requires a lot of trial and error in order to get going. There's a lot of cycles of cascading success or failure, so you'll likely be restarting your games multiple times before you get anything remotely close to a sizable village. I would also advise that you try to keep multiple save states for your early cities so that if you make a small mistake that starts to spiral into catastrophe, you can reload and fix it without having to restart the entire game.
It lacks a little bit of polish in some areas (owing to it being an indie title), and the extreme failure that you're likely to experience in the first few runs could leave a damaging first impression. But if you stick with it through a few village restarts, you'll find a deep and exceptionally-solid little city-builder.
Core gameplay cycle is simple, straightforward, and elegant. The bulk of the game consists of managing your small work force as the year progresses across the seasons. You gather resources, harvest food, create manufactures goods necessary to your own survival, and construct new infrastructure. There's no division of social classes, so you won't be creating a city in which some small minority of elites live in palatial mansions while the rest of the laborers are huddled in freezing shacks. So the economics of the game remain relatively simple compared to other city-builders, and this game does lack a little bit of the customization and expressiveness that other city-builders enjoy.
The game is also very good at using time and map space as resources. As your city grows, you have to balance your need for growth with the threat of stripping the map clean of resources. Every action that you perform feels like it involves significant trade-offs, and this is where much of the challenge comes from. You have to budget your limited resources and limited time (before the onset of winter) to get everything done so that your people don't freeze or starve to death.
If you like survival games, and you like city-builders, then Banished is right up your alley.

On the surface this seems like a great game, but that's as far as it goes. Beneath the veneer of the visually appealing graphics and simplistic design you think you can see a city builder with a survivalist inspired challenge. In reality, the games poor AI design and unrealistically frustrating features inspire the entirety of the challenge. Good game to paddle with for a few hours, and explore the buildings; but once the honeymoon wears off you'll find you will close it angrily and never open.
If you can't see where I am comming from with the AI, here's a few things that I found myself annoyed at:
- Villagers dying of starvation whilst holding food
- Villagers ignoring buildings that are not connected by land mass but only by bridge.
- Animals walking through the rivers and wandering through mountains (Not really that annoying, just rings of poor code)
- Villagers constantly using coal when there is a huge coal shortage and tool shortage.
- Villagers spend most of their times walking around on unrelated tasks to their purpose. (Is not solved by better building placement beacause they seem to prefer certain buildings over proximity)

Okay, this one's a bit tricky. I'm giving Spellgear a tentative thumbs-up, but really my opinion could go either way.
So far, it has been a relatively enjoyable experience. The combat is fairly fun, though nothing special. They advertise it as a highspeed action non-targeted fun time party, and it's not really all that exciting. You can do some flips to avoid attacks, but when facing PvE monsters it seems to be better to just sidestep a punch manually. The flips (and sprinting and jumping, yes, jumping) take energy from the same resource pool that is used to cast abilities. Side note: in my first PvP match, I accidentally side-flipped off the map. Acrobatics can be dangerous, kids.
I joined a capture the flag match and it was actually pretty fun! The map design was unfathomably tedious, but the skirmishes that took place were pretty sweet. Both teams sort of clashed at the middle, and the one melee class had a hard time joining the fight without exploding, but with proper timing and tactics, it was possible. Once we started working as a team, we could stand our ground pretty effectively. You can queue for these matches as soon as you leave the tutorial.
Regarding the PvE experience, the first 10-15 quests are essentially:
"Go talk to John."
"Hi John.
"Go talk to Sean."
"Hi Sean."
"I can't talk right now. Pretty busy. See if John needs anything."
I haven't played for very long yet, and I've already been tasked with killing some stuff, so hopefully the quests will become a bit more interesting/dynamic.
It's not a very pretty game, and the menu navigation could use some improvement. But as an Early Access title, you gotta be patient and try to help facilitate proper patching.
Like I said, my opinion is sort of good and sort of bad. I genuinely think the game will improve over time, and I'm excited to see how it changes for the better. If you are looking for a polished game, then stop browsing Early Access titles and play Neopets (actually, the Neopets in-game economy exploded a while back. It's fallen into chaos.).
Anyway, I don't really know who this game is for. I don't think I would recommend it to someone who just likes MMORPG's, because so far the questing and PvE stuff is really bland. But the PvP is neat, and could end up being a strong reason to play the game. It wasn't a negative experience, which is why this review isn't a thumbs-down. Maybe you should wait a bit to try it out, or maybe you'd like to be part of the community that's already giving feedback. It's up to you. I'm going to keep playing it for now and see what happens.

Auditorium is a game based around some very simple mechanics that affect how various colored particles move and change color. The game consists of 15 levels of 4-5 stages each. Each stage requires the player to direct particles of specific colors toward each "container" or sensor. Each sensor is associated with one color (or more, in later levels), and the player must find a way to fill the bars of all sensors on the stage at the same time.
Despite the straightforward mechanics of the game, the difficulty of the puzzles lies in the ways the different mechanics interact; it's easy enough to get one stream of particles to go towards one sensor, but when you're dealing with 2 streams, 5 sensors (several of which are multi-color), and a black hole, and you only have a few items to work with, things can get a little tricky. These complex interactions can be a little unpredictable, so later levels may involve a lot of trial and error - even if you look up a solution online, being a few pixels off can throw a wrench into the works.
Despite ostensibly being a game heavily involving music, the soundtrack is not that great. All the stages consist of short repeating loops of music; each sensor, when filled, causes one element or instrument of the music for that level to play. When the stage is completed, the screen changes to indicate this as the music continues to play. Because the music consists of short loops, however, even the best music gets old quickly.
This game is probably best played in short bursts. I decided to sit down and beat most of the game today (I'd probably finished the first two levels years ago), and just finished it. Overall, Auditorium is more of a webtoy than a proper game, but it's still quite enjoyable and challenging for what it is. There's probably not much replay value once you beat it; though theoretically you could mess around and find alternate solutions for each stage, there's no real motivation to do so. I would probably not have paid full-price for the game, but I would recommend checking it out if it's on sale. Plus, you can always check out the demo online first if you're unsure about buying.

If you like keyboard-smashing frustration, go ahead and play this game. And I say this as an Assassin's Creed fan who has played every game available on PC.
Okay, that was harsh, I typed that not long after smashing my keyboard and my hands were still hurt. Now that I've calmed down, let me edit and clarify why I don't like this game:
On the one hand, it has beautiful visual (as all AC games do), and I've found Arbaaz Mir to be an interesting character from the comic. I really wanted to like it. But the game disappoints. After the first sequence, I was greeted with Arbaaz and Pyara Kaur's cringeworthy dialogue. (It's not creepy or anything. It's just that I can really imagine Henry Green facepalming at his dad's jokes.) But that's okay. Maybe I no longer found the character charismatic, but the game could still have something else to offer. So I continued.
I desynched more in this game than I have in any other AC game. It crossed from 'challenging' to 'frustrating' in a few sequences. Every tiny second of mistake or deviation will make you desynch. There's little room for different play styles. I'm a Brawler in these games, but this one no longer has that category, unfortunately. (It's replaced by Silencer, where you take out guards in a non-lethal way, which is a lot like Assassin style but more time-consuming.) This results in lower points and fewer abilities rewarded, which makes the game even more frustrating.
Unlike China, which offers solid backstory (in the database) to a little-known character, India offers little for the character of Arbaaz. I was at sequence 7 and collected database entries, yet I didn't feel like I know much more about him. So there really wasn't much for me to continue.
I'm aware that my review is highly subjective, and that there are people who enjoy it, people with more patient and less desire to deviate than me. Still, I cannot give a thumb up for this one, due to how frustrated I feel with it. This is the first AC game I can't bring myself to finish, and I've played most of them.

SUPERHOT
First-person Shooter
SUPERHOT Team
SUPERHOT Team
is a first-person shooter developed and published by SUPERHOT team. This is the indie darling of the year, and it deserves most of the praise that it is getting.
The plot follows the same gist of many
: you are playing as someone playing SUPERHOT, and someone starts writing weird messages to you. If you are familiar with other games such as
, the game has some decent tricks up its sleave, but, unfortunately, it feels very derivative and not as smart as the aformentioned product.
The game has an interesting art-style: white environments with red enemies and black/blu-ish objects. It all looks very polished, but it got kinda old after a while. Thankfully, some Challenges change the color scheme, giving some much needed variety.
The game is a first-person shooter where time moves only when you do, and later on you also unlock the ability to swap your body with an enemy's. This is done extremely well, and you can't but be amazed at how perfectly it was achieved by the developers.
The only issue I have with the gameplay are the weapons: there are only a pistol, a double-barreled shotgun, a rifle and multiple melee weapons. But still, watching a real-time replay of what you just accomplished is very satisfying.
Dying with one hit makes the game very hard and quite frustrating in certain levels, but having more than one life would've trivialized the entire game. The AI is very smart and usually predicts where you are going to go, so that it can hit you always. After you got the hang on the controls, you can easily outsmart it, especially when knowing where enemies will spawn. The Challenges are also very fun to play, with different modifiers like Katana Only, Fists Only, Throws Kill and many more.
The soundtrack is your typical techno-pop music, and the sound effects are top notch, with sound warping when you move. The words said at the end of each level (SUPER HOT) are quite amusing at first, but they do get annoying after a while
The main game is very short: it took me under two hours to complete it. However, there are plenty more things to do that will keep you coming back more and more: Challenge mode, Endless mode, secret computers hidden in every level... A game musn't be criticised only for the lenght of the main story, but on the rest of the content as well. And here, there's plenty of fun to be had.
Overall, SUPERHOT is a very innovative and polished game that will appeal to most gamers. If you are here for the story, however, you will be disappointed by its short lenght and its expensive price. A must-buy when at 15$.

Auditorium is an audio based puzzle game where you manipulate light streams sending them into audio channels to make music play. To accomplish that you must use a variety of modifying symbols and take into account the field structure of the level. As you light up more and more audio channels, the game rewards you by playing more portions of the music. The game starts you off nice and easy but ramps up to where completing a stage needs a little thinking. Sometimes when you are very close to getting a solution you have to rethink your entire solution because of a symbol being a center piece but it helps you to get creative and try different things.
The visuals are simple but rather pretty to look at and the music is satisfying especially when you get the full song to play on stage completion. If you like puzzle or music based games and were maybe looking for something different than the standard Music Rythmn / Timing game (ex. Dance Dance Revolution, Osu!) then I'd recommend giving this a shot.
