Most of the time you will just be sailing form place to place with nothing to do but stare at the screen inbetween.
While Sunless Sea is a very interesting game, and has a good story, it is far too boring for me to continue playing.
My first and largest gripe would be that most "early" ships have a pitiful cargo hold. While this seems like a trivial problem at first, it really hurts you as you try to progress. Small cargo holds mean less fuel and supplies, which means less time that you can spend exploring before having to return to London for supplies. Yes, you can buy fuel and supplies elsewhere, but they are typically more expensive (a problem especially early game) everywhere else. The first ship with a cargo upgrade is ludicrously expensive regardless if you are grinding or playing the game the "right" way as some people have described. This limitation, combined with the "terror" system, a passive timer that counts down before bad things start happening, means you will have to go back to home unless you want to spend a lot of echo (currency) to stay at zee. You also end up aquiring a lot of trinkets and things that will have to be sold or delievered to make space for fuel and supplies.
This monotony is simply not fun. Simply trading is equally dull, evident from these other reviews.
Yes, you can re-visit ports to gain interesting story developments (which is arguably the whole point of this game), but I was always dissapointed as to what those developments were. They give you just a taste before you have to bring them more items or whatever, which, as mentioned, is typically a journey back to London or across the map. Everything just has to be so damn mysterious. You learn more about the world as you play, but even in my hours so many seemingly crucial things were just left unexplained. I never touched the supplementary reading, but then again I really shouldn't have to if this is truely a story based game as it is advertized as.
Finally, let's talk about the legacy system, a sort of new game plus when you die, except not at all. When you die, you start from the ground up in terms of story progression and officer quests. This is bad, as you will essentially be doing the same things over and over again, just slightly quicker, every time you die or decide to start over. Also, your heir doesn't get to keep your ship and loses most of the upgrades. Why. Why is this when you are psuedo-encouraged to die or retire by the developers? The Long Dark is an early access game by Hinterland set in northern Canada. Although it's a survival game, death is inevitable and, in my opinion, inspires the game's title. There is a story mode planned for release by the end of this year, but for anyone who buys the game right now the sole experience will be the sandbox mode.
Players find themselves randomly thrown into the wilderness with nothing but the clothes they wear, a few matches, a sleeping bag, and maybe a flare or accelerant if they're lucky. The time of day, location and weather conditions are random so it is even possible to start in the middle of the night during a blizzard. However, even starting in the middle of a sunny afternoon, it will still be cold and bleak, and the player will soon need to contend with freezing, starvation, dehydration and fatigue. All of this is represented in an intuitive status screen that players will refer to often. In order to manage these needs, players must seek shelter and find what remains of civilization, which has been devestated by a mysterious geomagnetic event. This event has also disturbed some of the natural wildlife, and wolves that roam the wilderness are unusually hostile and will attack if the player wanders too close.
Even if the player does find shelter and supplies, almost everything found will degrade over time. This includes food, clothing, a hatchet everytime it is used to chop wood or butcher meat, a rifle whenever it is fired, or even a toolkit whenever it is used to try to maintain the hatchet and rifle. This degradation mechanic causes the player to value every decision and plan carefully to maximize resources while continuing the struggle to survive. Although the game is early access, this degradation mechanic has been in the game from the beginning and is considered a core mechanic, so this feature will almost certainly remain in the game all the way until its official launch.
Above all, the reason why I love this game is its atmosphere. Because everything degrades, I always feel a sense of urgency. Even if I kill a deer, harvest and cook the meat, and have a whole locker full of venison steaks in my base, I know that it won't be long before I need more. On top of that, if I use a knife or hatchet to help with harvesting the deer, or a rifle or bow and arrows to kill it, I also know that eventually those tools will wear out, so I also must be vigilent in my search to find replacements. Ultimately, the player will run out of tools and materials to keep those tools in good repair. Although a player may struggle on beyond this point, the odds of survival will decrease further and further until, eventually, the player must face death. Although to some this may sound frustrating, on the contrary that challenge of pushing the boundaries is a large part of the appeal. Because tools are limited, the player is encouraged to think of creative solutions on how to minimize the drain of resources.
Adding to the atmosphere are also the sound and graphic style. Especially since some of the recent updates, the Long Dark really is beatiful -- that is, when it isn't errie or terrifying. Because the time of day and weather both change, there are lots of different possible settings. It could be a bright and clear afternoon, or it might be midnight with a blizzard that has reduced visibility to three feet. It could be a beautiful sunrise looking out across the landscape from a lookout tower or it might be evening, a thick fog, and the errie sound of wolves howling somewhere beyond.
Now, I will end this review with a few points of criticism. Although another wonderful aspect of this game is the sense of exploration and discovery, that does diminish over time. The regions generally have very little that is randomized in terms of the locations themselves. The result of this is that the player eventually learns all of the locations, has very little chance of becoming lost, and no longer sees anything new when traveling the map to gather supplies. I would love it if the game's world could be procedurally generated in the future, but that may be too much to ask because ultimately The Long Dark is being developed with a story mode in mind. Despite this criticism, the world is detailed and fun to re-explore.
The other criticism concerns the wolves which, along with the weather, currently represent the primary antagonist to the player. To beginners, the wolves may seem insurmountable because the wolves roam the world in large numbers and are always hostile to the player except on the game's easiest difficulty setting (in which case they are never hostile and always run away). On the other hand, to experienced players wolves become easy to handle and a convenient source of food. I will address my own criticism by emphasizing that the game is still in early access and, unlike other early access titles, gets monthly, substantive updates. In sum, the wolves are generally a fun antagonist but still a work in progress that will continue to be improved.
Bottomline: If you like survival games, you should pick this up. I understand some people have doubts about early access. If that describes yourself, you might also consider checking out a let's play to get a better sense of what the game is like. But if you do, be sure to find one that isn't more than a month old (although watch one that's a year old if you want to see how far the game has come in that time). Also, avoid watching too much footage so that you can enjoy that sense of discovery I discussed earlier as much as possible. Lastly, watch the movie The Grey, which bears some striking similiaries to The Long Dark in both its setting and theme.

Have you ever played a browser game where you have limited actions that regenerate every couple of minutes? This is basically what Sunless Sea gameplay looks like. In theory it's about sailing a boat over titular sea filled with dangerous monsters, wondrous islands and terrors beyond comprehension, discovering gorgeous new places and desperately trying to stay alive in face of adversity. In practice... it's about waiting until you reach destination where you can read a page or two and make one choice before waiting again.
boring in default state, but can be modded into a very good game.
Writing and World.
Writing is excellent and world has very rich lore. Creators had a lot of incredible ideas, and with help of vast vocabulary, executed them very well. Being non-native speaker, despite my demonstrably good grasp of English I had to reach for help of dictionaries very often (this is NOT a complaint, it's a testament to writer's knowledge of English and it's less often used vocabulary). Graphics are great, illustrations presented along encounters are nice if a bit arbitrary, nonetheless they go well with descriptions which range from vividly gruesome to laconically terrifying and sea (referred to as zee) itself is as good as 2D sprites can get. How good 2D sprites can get depends a bit on your mileage, for me lack of 3rd dimension doesn't detract at all.
From worldbuilding and artistic standpoint, it's definitely a 10/10.
Unfortunately as far as advantages go, that's it.
Combat.
Combat is terribly executed - it's either impossible to win because you don't have right gear/stats to beat this enemy, or you have right gear and just do the same thing over and over to blast enemy without risk (hint: kiting).
Travel.
Travel is slow. Mind-numbingly slow, and as you progress to more powerful engines, it gets only marginally better. Authors claim it's for atmosphere of terror. Except that despite being slow as snail, even the most basic engine can eventually outrun every enemy, so there's literally no danger in combat. Only danger in travel comes from depleting resources (fuel, food and sanity) and random events that occur close to never. Sure, reaching London on last half of a barrel of fuel was a great relief, but that single moment came after trip that took hour or so of transit alone out of which only last minute held any tension at all. Definitely not worth it. It's as if Jagged Alliance 2 devs decided to make everything turn-based instead of engaging TB only in combat and letting players explore locations in real time otherwise (when there are enemies in location, JA2 is RT until you stumble upon them, or until they stumble upon you, then it goes into TB until 2 turns go without any combat or all enemies are killed), JA2 would be pretty much unplayable. Similarly, SS should have had *2 or *3, perhaps even *4 time settings that would automatically disengage as soon as enemy appears on screen or your resources run below certain threshold. Watching boat zail (in-game term) the zee for hours is not fun and heavily discourages exploration.
Ugh, I don't know. It doesn't crash inexplicably, controls are responsive, collision detection is fine. 3/10?
Currency and economic balance.
Your ship needs fuel, your zailors need supplies, if you run out of either, it's game over. If you spend too long in the zee and run out of sanity, it's game over. If you run out of cash to buy supplies it's effectively game over. There's nothing inherently wrong in above, "imbalance", now that's what IS wrong. Fuel/Supplies consumption is high and starting boat has very small cargo hold, this means that trade is extremely hard hard or often impossible. Round trip to other edge of map with basic boat, engine and skeleton crew takes full hold worth of supplies, unless you get lucky with map generation, you are not going anywhere in early game. Trade routes available near your (fixed)starting location/(forced)base of operations don't even net enough to cover expenses (with basic cargo hold size). So what are you supposed to do? Explore because admiralty pays echos (cash) and fuel for reports from other ports. Problem is, they pay so little it doesn't even cover expenses. Trying to combine trade with admiralty payouts may net you double digit profit. You need 7000 for boat with bigger cargo hold.
Literally your only option to progress in game is to risk everything, fill your your cargo hold with enough food and fuel for a one way trip to edge of map and venture forth, not even thinking about turning back until you reach 2/3 of map, at which point your starting supplies aren't enough to get back. Unless you got lucky and found some supplies, cash, valuable cargo AND place with cheap fuel along the way, you are screwed. That doesn't actually sound bad, does it? Well, what DOES sound bad is the following: if you lucked out and came back, your loot and admiralty payouts may net you as much as 500 echoes after expenses. After an hour or longer trip out of which 55 minutes were spent watching zee go by, and only 5 reading about thrilling encounters. Oh, and by the way, you don't start with enough cash/resources for trip like that, you need to figure something out, sorry.
Now you need to do that 20 more times to upgrade and equip your ship. If you die, you start over. If you pick wrong choice in event, you start over. If you misjudge your supplies, you start over. If you lose RGN roll, you start over. If you start over, map is re-generated slightly, but contains all the same locations so unless you progress further than in previous life, you won't see anything new. A bit of your stats or cash carry over from prior life to next one, and there are ways to set up your next Capitan with tiny bit of starting budget, but we are talking about doing exact same thing for 10 hours just to die so you can do exact same thing for 10 hours in next life until, perhaps, after hundreds of hours you eventually get to endgame content. If you play like that you are going to see one, maybe 2 new things in each new in-game life!
All in all, tagline of this game is:
Lose your mind. Eat your crew. Die.
It should be:
Lose your mind. Of boredom. Eat your crew. Of boredom. Die. Of boredom.
1/10 for balance.
That doesn't mean that game is NOT salvageable.
Editing either saves or game files to diminish time wasting parts turns Sunless Sea into very interesting experience, and a game definitely worth playing. Exact changes depend on preference, most fair way is to change game constants so that everything runs faster (ships and combat but also fuel/food/sanity depletion) and occasionally edit save to double/triple profit from last trip.
Luckily, saves and relevant game files are (mostly) human readable and don't use even simplest measures (like checksums) to detect meddling so pretty much anyone can quickly tweak them, hence title of my review. I, however, refuse to give thumb up to game that needs to have it's internals meddled with to be playable,
Just no.

Rarely have I had the experience of painting (or perhaps I should say 'sculpting'?) with music. In fact, unless I'm forgetting something, I've only had it once to date: When playing Auditorium just now. Yes, I've played it once, for perhaps 20 minutes, and it's already got me itching to send this recommendation out into the world.
I won't say that this game is deep, per se. But for me (and perhaps for other music+game lovers?) it is highly satisfying.
If you're curious about mechanics, you basically use gravity wells to shoot particles of raw music potential, attempting to intersect them with regions of space representing instruments. Some instruments require tuned particles, so you must first direct them through color-tuning fields before slingshotting back to instrument areas. Basically, you create galaxies of swirling colorful particles, that, when lined up just so, create a glorious symphony of sounds to reward you.
The effect is marvelous and transporting. On almost every level I've played so far (perhaps the first 15 or so), I've gotten lost in the beauty of my own musical universe of swirling lights. I find myself staring into each beautiful solution, until the desire to make NEW music finally overwhelms the desire to languish.
Duly recommended.

For it to still be in Alpha phase (Period)* and to impress me this much. Literally one of the funnest games I've played in a long time, with the survival aspect challenging you to constantly be on the move and have a sharp eye for the items you need to cover your way through the next few days and worst case scenarios of the zombie apocolypse. Innovating the diablo style point of view, but incorporating an elder scrolls style of detail of items, item creation and it even has a dash of the minecraft sandbox building ability/freedom.
This game really flows and has hours, days and weeks worth of gameplay.
-With game changing aspects including perspective of your character(you can only see what your character would see, then the rest is a fog of war style), which I found was so emersive and really kept me on my toes everywhere, it makes going around corners, going into houses, bathrooms and forests a real edge of your seat experience, my heart still gets pumping everytime I enter a new house.
-Having to take care of your character is one of the most important things to worry about in the zombie apocolypse, he/she can get thirsty, hungry, scared, injured, bored, cold, wet, sick, etc. All of these have negative effects if you don't tend to them, be it less perceptive; so it's harder to hear or see the zombies approach you, your character could get to cold or wet whilst outside from the different seasons or rainy weather; ending up getting sick and begin to sneeze and cough, which in turn would attract more zombies.
-Through a rough and tumble with some zombies, you may require medical attention, luckly enough; you can make bandages out of clothes and sheets you may find. Also.. it never hurts to hit the medicine cabinet in the bathroom to see if they have any painkillers or vitamins they didn't need/get to use. There is also a medical centre.. some where.
-Once you have gathered enough supplies to get you by you may look at fortifying your stronghold; with water collecting barrels, fences, window barracades, sheet rope so you can make a quick exit if a horde of zombies have just busted in to see the new digs. But I guess if you spawn in the right location you could start fortifying straight away, but prioritize in the first few days-weeks on food and water..
-You can set up a farm, once you get the few neccesary components  you can begin to set up your own sustainable lifestyle in which you would never have to go out for supplies and just live off your own land.. but be careful, because the hordes do wander. You may think hey, i'll have my fridge and sink... i'll be fine. No, no you won't. The power and water gets cut off after a few weeks(maybe months if you're lucky), just to get you settled in.
-Meta game has been so much fun for me through this game, sometimes you'll hear a gun go off a few houses down, an army chopper goes over doing a few laps attracting zombies to the area, and they're even going to impliment NPC's within the coming months to make it a more thrilling and unexpected experience.
-All the little things really get me smiling with this game. There is so many things you can do, for eg;
You can use, anything from bottles, cups, mugs, cooking pots and others so you can store water for later, you can do great things once you find the specific tools required for that job, like cutting trees with an axe, then using a saw to cut planks, hammer and nails for your building needs. Using sheets to break line of sight for when you are trundling around your safe house, some houses have alarm systems which can be a god send, or a death sentence..
I am only scraping the surface of this game and it really has blown me away as to how intricate and detailed the develpoers have crafted this game, I am still learning more and more everytime I play it and it will only get better from here, with so much more to come, might as well hop on now..

Just Cause 2 is one of those games that has an average storyline, it's cheesey but fun. But because of its open world, gameplay, patriotic music, themes of revolutionary regime change, and overall hectic chaos, it ends up being a stellar game that everyone can enjoy. There's so much to do in Panau but I'm sure everyone will just get through the Agency missions, a number of the stronghold takeovers and faction missions, as those are enough to get enough chaos to get through the game.
If you didn't play the first one, then you should know that you play as Rico Rodriguez. After the events of the first game, Rico formally retired from the Agency but is thrust back into action when his friend and mentor, Tom Sheldon, goes missing and is believed to have gone rogue on the island of Panau. Panau is also in turmoil as three paramilitary factions are rising after the President, Baby Panay, goes into hiding. Basically, the island nation is kind of like what I imagine N. Korea might be like, with propaganda and altered news playing everywhere. It's just a weird place.
You get to work for each of the three factions and get to know their leaders quite well as you get to do several missions for them. I mean, there are more faction missions than anything else in the game. Just to put it in perspective, I only did 23 faction missions and there were still plenty left on the map by the time I finished the main story. You won't be disappointed by them though. They might seem repetitive, but each faction mission has a different aspect or goal.
The open world is definitely the highlight, alongside the grappling hook / parachute gear Rico has. You could probably travel around the whole just parachuting and using the grappling hook against the ground to keep pusing you forward. Basically, exploring is a lot of fun. There are all kinds of terrain in the game, from forests, to desert, to snowy mountaintops. The highlight in the open world might've been the "Lost" island, where if you fly a plane or helicopter to it, it'll crash from electrical damage and you might even be able to find the smoke monster.
This game is just a lot of fun really. It has a few bugs and the textures aren't the prettiest, but if you're not having fun playing it, you're playing it wrong.

Awesome game! The story is VERY well done, as expected of Telltale Games! Some scenes really feel intense, and there's a lot of emotion behind quite a bit of the story. This game takes place in an alternate DC universe and deviates from Batman's original story in profound ways, but it doesn't matter because the execution is incredible. You will find plenty of references, characters, and elements from the original stories all twisted in a very good way. Overall, very nice storytelling!
My gripes mainly fall to the gameplay, but this is indicative of all Telltale games. I'm not a fan of Quick-Time Events (chains of button prompts), and the action sequences, while a bit interactive and cool, felt very detached, especially after having played the Batman: Arkham series where I actually get to fight myself. Also, there is a lot of "fake choice," where the game tricks you into thinking your actions hold more weight than they actually do. There are about 5 major plot points in each episode which do impact the story, but since the story isn't over yet, we'll have to wait and see how they turn out.
Like with other Telltale games, there is a bar limiting the amount of time you have to decide on a choice. This is very good in prodding the player to think quickly (and sometimes brashly!) like a normal human having a normal conversation would.
The biggest turn-off would be... performance issues! Now, I have a pretty beefy rig so this game was mostly fine, but even with a GTX 980 Ti, there was constant stuttering throughout every episode, and it was incredibly annoying! The graphics aren't even that bombastic, so there's no reason for it to be performing so poorly.
Overall, I like this game very much! Give it a go if you're a Batman fan, you won't be disappointed! Just understand that you're in for a visual novel with not much actual "playing," and there are existing performance issues!

I wasn't sure if I should've recommended this game or warned people away. Personally, I hated the game.
Let's be clear here, I was very conflicted while playing this. In the first few sections, it was creepy and intruiging. The art style, while a bit dull and at times inhibitive to the gameplay, is rarely seen in visual media. The deaths were shocking and gruesome, and game paid little attention to them. My favorite moment was the giant spider chase; I never thought I'd be so terrified in a platformer. It's creative and morbid, two game concepts that often work well together. Once I got to the factory, however, it seemed like everything changed.
Gone were the organic horrors and the inviting atmosphere. The absence of a soundtrack was refreshing at first, yet quickly became boring in that there wasn't another source of tension. There was of course the constant threat of death, yet it was almost encouraged in order to solve the puzzles. The only source of anxiety came from the puzzles themselves, which felt more like a spot-the-difference than a mental excercise. I found myself constantly checking walkthroughs, simply because I couldn't discern which objects I could interact with. This made for an increasingly infuriating experience. And since the puzzles were the only source of stress, every section that wasn't a puzzle was just boring. There were very few chapters in which I felt a sense of achievement after completing them.
The ending is it's own seperate conclusion. [SPOILERS AHEAD]
I've read many reviews that say the game's story is deep and meaningful. And that may be true, but it won't feel like that when you finish it. If I hadn't read the single-line description before playing it, I would've guessed that it was a cut-and-paste love story, where a boy goes through the death-ridden landscape of Limbo to get the girl (it's actually his sister :/ ). Except... she doesn't look to be in any danger. In fact, she looks almost oblivious to the hellish obstacle course right next to her. So what does that mean for you? Were your efforts for nothing? Were those trials even real? Was it a metaphor for the mental obstacles in your own mind? The traditional happy ending raises more questions than answers.
[SPOLIERS END]
Throughout my whole playthrough, I was consantly reminded of Cormac McCarthy's "The Road". It has the same sense of silence, the same dreary atmosphere; the monochrome landscape would feel right at home. "The Road" also has deep themes and meaning, although its a little easier to infer and understand since its primarily in first person. With Limbo, we don't have that same sense of immersion or insight. The ending is the only real bit of story, and it doesn't really explain anything. I tried to find a theme that wasn't along the lines of "effort is meaningless" or "death is to be accepted", but couldn't find anything outside of an emo's diary. I fully admit that the fault may be mine, and that most people might be able to see what I can't. It's the nature of artistic indie games.
Bottom line: would I recommend it? I left it feeling wholly unsatisfied. It was maddening to play, and the ending was severely underwhelming.
As a game? Hell no, at least not at full price. The game only lasts about 2 hours and there's very little replayability. I got it for $2.50, so wait for a sale and you might find it more fulfilling than I did.
As an artistic venture however, go for it. It's very difficult to take a piece of art and merge it with entertaining gameplay. It doesn't deter from the experience much, but it might not be what you expect a game to be (if you've ever played a TellTale game you'll see what I'm trying to get at).
All in all, it's not worth $10, but its not worthless either.

This was one of the games I was most excited for this year. I have been a fan of tropico for a while and have played 114 hours of tropico 4. I pre ordered this and was very happy when it was released a few hours early!
However, I was a bit disappointed by the game; it wasn't exactly what I expected.
What I didn't like:
When I first started I noticed I didn't quite like the HUD. First, the building menu isn't really what I like; You should only be able to see buildings you can build in your era. I also liked the tropico 4 building menu better (where it starts with you picking what category of building you want). Building HUD isn't really greaet either. There are tabs that are a bit confusing, and you don't really see what you want to see.
In tropico 4, you could zoom ALL the way in and see each citizen, piece of trash, or crop, whereas in 5 you can barely zoom in at all. I like to see my little peoples and cars zooming around, but you can't do that as well in 5.
What I also liked about 4 was the fact that you feel so CONNECTED with your citizens: you actually click seperate citizens walking around (i know you can in 5 but I dont feel compelled to) and look at their job, education, age, whatever and look at what they need. I want to actually look through my people and feel like they are real not just look in the happiness section at what they need. And the happiness section is another issue..
I really don't like the happiness section. You are CONSTANTLY having to build new buildings, even though you have NO workers to work them. I am at 887 population, with only 47 happiness because I have no more workers to increase the entertainment or food quality or anything. My happiness went from 82% to 47% in only 1 year even though I didn't destroy any happiness increasing buildings or introduce anything that could have decreased it. Still not even sure why it went down, my population didn't increase all too much.
I've also had a few graphics glitches. Whenever I load a game, my camera is facing down like a top-down game. trying to reangle it makes it zoom, and it doesn't fix until I spaz the mouse around and maybe press a few buttons. Then, while playing today, my minimap randomly had a square of inverted colors right where my city was. I have no idea what caused that one and it didn't go away since I played. Checking out of screenshots will show the glitches
I do not like how you can't customize rent, pay, or fee in this one. Rent and pay are both confusing in how they work.
What I like:
I like how the voting system is actually difficult. In tropico 4, all you had to do was not have happiness at like 0%, otherwise you always win by like 90%. In this game, you have to work hard in the beginning to win the elections (unless you cheat!).
I like how there are lots of buildings!
Combat, combat, combat. tropico 4 combat was simple and lacking. THIS combat is epic! No other word. Axis tanks and infantry storming your beach while your own tanks are firing at them is about the coolest thing you can imagine in a tropico game. You no longer automatically lose when you are invaded, you have a fighting chase.
So in all and all I thought it was 4/10. If they were to update it, I will of course change my review! I will also continue playing and see if I change my mind at all.

Solitaire mixed with Poker. Instead of building suits, you're building poker hands and using these hands to beat enemy AI to death. A better hand does more damage, and the more damage you deal (or take), the more spells you can cast with your building rage.
This system has some nice subtleties, but the rest of the game lets it down. The AI refuses to use any high power hands at all, and instead resorts to using easily buildable hands and spamming abilities to win. This results in a final boss which has a use 5 rage -> do 30 or so dmg loop which it is not bright enough to use.
As for the story dragging you through the adventure, it is lacklustre at best, and is not helped by being left on a cliffhanger at the end to allow for sequels and the "Overture" in the title.
The art style is quite good though.

For fans of the series I think it's a logical chocie to get Tropico 5. I think it's quite decent step forward over Tropico 4, I found it to be more long term fun (as well as harder) then the previous one; the era system and other improvments such as the constitution suit well for Tropico 5.
However on the downside in some areas Tropico 5 was stripped down, much less customization for your members; some options are also gone MIA, for example "work modes" are gone for the most part, many buildings were removed while often for the the better, experts will miss buildings like the Immigration Office or Prisons for more fine grained political control.
Political backgrouds are also removed in favor of the new dynasty system, though this is actually a decent change.
At the time of release, the multiplayer also has some issues such as hangs/crashes, no adjustable speed and no options to create a save game, but hopefully those will be amended in the the future.
But it is also a new and fun experience to play Tropico 5 in multiplayer, though at this point it is still rather problematic to play and the dipomacy options are limited, but since it's a first for tropico, one can hope for fixes and adjustments by the developers.
Despite all those flaws, Tropico 5 still provides a nice boost to fun and difficulty, it provides much of a challange to create a working island state, rebels, military revolts and uprisings are an actual threat now, and pleasing all factions can be diffcult. The eras require you to adjust your economy as well as profitable goods will change thoughout the eras.

Okay - this game creeped me out. It took me forever to get over my fear and play through this gem of a game. Some scenes were so disturbing that I wanted to vomit. Lots of jump scares. The only thing that got me through was I slowly got over my fear when I faced off the same enemy over and over and over again because he kep killing me. Most people complained about that. I actually found it helpful because I got mad and got over it. Slowly the "fear" of the game slipped out of some of the scenes and I could manage enough courage to move forward in the game a bit. The levels are really well done, and the story isn't mind blowing, but decent enough that you move along. Read the notes, read the documents. Slowly it will all come together. I would recommend this game to someone who likes survival horror, I stand with the overall score of above average and give it an 85 out of 100.
